Complete Learning Guide with anihpj/jobpost Django Project

From complete novice to CNPE-certified Cloud Native Platform Engineer. Learn platform architecture, GitOps, CI/CD, CRDs & Operators, self-service portals, observability, security, and production operations — all through hands-on examples with a real Django application deployed on Kubernetes.

🟢 Novice Friendly ☸️ Kubernetes v1.31+ 🐍 Django / Python 📚 33 Chapters ⏱️ ~60 Hours 🎓 CNPE Exam — 100% Coverage 📋 9 Appendices

🟢 Part 1: Platform Engineering Foundations BEGINNER

Chapter 1: What Is Platform Engineering? — Why Do We Need Platforms?

Before building platforms, you must understand WHY they exist. This chapter walks through the pain of "TicketOps," the evolution from SysAdmin to Platform Engineering, the definition of an Internal Developer Platform (IDP), and what Developer Experience (DevEx) truly means. We'll use anihpj/jobpost as our running example throughout.

🟢 Beginner ⏱️ ~2 hours 📖 Concepts 🎯 Foundation

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ The "TicketOps" problem — why developers hate waiting for infrastructure
  • ✅ The evolution: SysAdmin → DevOps → Kubernetes → Platform Engineering
  • ✅ What platform engineering ACTUALLY is (the simple, clear definition)
  • ✅ Developer Experience (DevEx) — cognitive load, friction, and self-service
  • ✅ The Internal Developer Platform (IDP) — a PRODUCT, not a project
  • ✅ "You Build It, You Run It" vs "The Platform Runs It" — the shared responsibility model
  • ✅ Why anihpj/jobpost needs a platform (and what it takes to build one)
🎓 CNPE Relevance
Platform APIs & Self-Service Domain 3 — 25% Foundation ALL DOMAINS
Why Chapter 1 Matters on the CNPE Exam

The CNPE is a performance-based exam (2 hours, 15-20 tasks in a live terminal). While Chapter 1 concepts aren't directly tested as terminal commands, understanding why platforms exist helps you reason through unfamiliar scenarios:

  • TicketOps → Self-Service — Domain 3 (25%) tests your ability to build self-service workflows via CRDs, Operators, and Backstage templates.
  • Golden Paths — "Make the right way the easiest way." This principle guides how you design platform APIs, CLI tools, and developer portals.
  • Platform as a Product — The exam expects you to think about your platform's USERS (developers). You're building a PRODUCT they love.

1.1 The "TicketOps" Problem — Why Developers Hate Waiting

Imagine you're a developer at a company. You've built a new microservice for anihpj — it needs a PostgreSQL database, a TLS certificate, and a staging namespace to test it. In a traditional organization, here's what happens:

📖 Key Term: TicketOps

TicketOps is the anti-pattern where every infrastructure request requires a JIRA ticket, manual approval, and days or weeks of waiting. Developers spend more time waiting for infrastructure than writing code. Context switching kills developer productivity — each ticket interrupts flow state. By the time infrastructure is ready, the developer has forgotten what they were building. Real example: Developer Priya needs PostgreSQL, TLS cert, and a staging namespace — 3 tickets, ~8 days of waiting, 0 lines of feature code written.

The TicketOps Experience — 3 Tickets, 8 Days of Waiting

❌ Without a Platform — The TicketOps Anti-Pattern
Developer Priya: "I need a PostgreSQL database for anihpj-job-matcher"
       │
       ▼
📝 File JIRA Ticket INFRA-2847  →  ⏳ Wait 3 Days  →  🔧 Ops provisioner
       manually creates RDS instance → 📧 "Here's your connection string"

Developer Priya: "I need TLS cert for anihpj-job-matcher.example.com"
       │
       ▼
📝 File Another Ticket INFRA-2851  →  ⏳ Wait 2 Days  →  🔧 Ops purchases
       wildcard cert, installs on load balancer → 📧 "Done — cert expires in 90 days"

Developer Priya: "Can I have a staging namespace? With RBAC and quotas?"
       │
       ▼
📝 File Yet Another Ticket INFRA-2863  →  ⏳ Wait 1 Week  →  🔧 Ops creates
       namespace, Role, RoleBinding, ResourceQuota → 📧 "Here you go"

RESULT: 3 tickets, ~8 days of waiting, 0 lines of feature code written 😱

The Platform Experience — 0 Tickets, 5 Minutes

✅ With a Platform — Self-Service Model
Developer Priya: "I need a PostgreSQL database for anihpj-job-matcher"
       │
       ▼
kubectl apply -f database-claim.yaml          ← Instant self-service!
(Crossplane DatabaseClaim CR → Operator provisions RDS automatically in ~3 min)

Developer Priya: "I need TLS cert for anihpj-job-matcher.example.com"
       │
       ▼
Add `tls: true` to Ingress manifest            ← Automatic!
(cert-manager handles Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 challenge, auto-renews every 60 days)

Developer Priya: "Can I have a staging namespace?"
       │
       ▼
Click "Create Environment" in Backstage UI     ← Golden path!
(Namespace + RBAC + ResourceQuota + NetworkPolicy auto-provisioned in ~60 sec)

RESULT: 0 tickets, ~5 minutes total, developer writes code immediately 🎉
💡 The Core Insight

The TicketOps problem isn't about lazy ops teams — it's about a BROKEN PROCESS. Operations teams are overwhelmed with manual requests. Developers are blocked waiting. The platform engineering solution: automate the provisioning so nobody has to wait. Self-service turns days of waiting into seconds of API calls.

1.2 From SysAdmin → DevOps → Platform Engineering — The Evolution

Platform engineering didn't appear overnight. It's the natural evolution of how we manage infrastructure. Each era solved one problem but created a new one:

🖥️
2000-2010
SysAdmin Era

Manual server provisioning. "Throw it over the wall" — devs write code, toss it to ops, wait 2 weeks for a VM.

❌ Problem: Speed
🐳
2013-2016
DevOps Era

"You build it, you run it." Docker + CI/CD. But every team builds their own stack differently. Fragmentation.

⚠️ Problem: Fragmentation
☸️
2017-2020
Kubernetes Era

K8s becomes the standard. But raw K8s is too complex — YAML, networking, storage, RBAC overwhelm developers.

🟡 Problem: Complexity
⚙️
2021+
Platform Engineering

Build an Internal Developer Platform (IDP). Abstract K8s complexity behind self-service APIs and golden paths.

✅ Solution: Abstraction
📖 Key Insight: Each Evolution Solved One Problem, Created Another

SysAdmins solved hardware management but were too slow. DevOps solved speed but caused fragmentation (every team builds their own stack). Kubernetes solved standardization but introduced overwhelming complexity. Platform Engineering solves complexity by ABSTRACTING it behind self-service interfaces.

1.3 What Is Platform Engineering? (The Simple Answer)

📖 Official Definition

"The discipline of designing and building toolchains and workflows that enable self-service capabilities for software engineering organizations in the cloud-native era."

In plain English: You build the "paved road" so developers don't have to navigate the wilderness of cloud infrastructure. Developers focus on writing code. The platform handles everything else — deployment, scaling, monitoring, security, backups.

What Platform Engineering IS and IS NOT

✅ Platform Engineering IS:
  • A PRODUCT with real users (developers) who have needs and feedback
  • Self-service infrastructure — developers get what they need without tickets
  • Golden paths — opinionated workflows that make the right way the easiest way
  • Abstraction of complexity — developers don't need to know K8s, Terraform, or Helm
  • A dedicated team with a product manager, engineers, and SREs
❌ Platform Engineering is NOT:
  • DevOps 2.0 — it's a different discipline with different goals
  • Just a "tools team" that manages Jenkins and JIRA
  • Just writing Terraform modules and hoping developers use them
  • A one-time project — it's an ongoing product with a roadmap
  • About forcing developers to use specific tools — it's about making the best tools easy
💡 Core Principle: "Make the Right Way the Easiest Way"

If deploying with proper security, monitoring, and compliance is HARDER than deploying without them, developers will take shortcuts. A platform engineer's job is to make the secure, compliant, observable deployment path the PATH OF LEAST RESISTANCE. This is the concept of Golden Paths.

1.4 Developer Experience (DevEx) — Cognitive Load, Friction, Self-Service

Developer Experience (DevEx) is how developers FEEL when interacting with your platform. It's the equivalent of UX (User Experience) but for developers consuming platform services instead of end-users consuming a product.

Cognitive Load — What Developers DON'T Need to Know

🧠
Extraneous Load (Platform Abstracts This)

Kubernetes YAML, Terraform, Helm charts, CNI configuration, etcd backup, cert-manager setup, Ingress annotations, NetworkPolicy syntax — these are PLATFORM concerns, not developer concerns.

💡
Intrinsic Load (Developers Focus Here)

Business logic, application architecture, data models, API design, user experience, feature development — this is where developers add UNIQUE VALUE. The platform should maximize time spent here.

Measuring DevEx

⏱️
Time-to-First-Deploy
🎫
Ticket Deflection Rate
😊
Developer NPS Score
🔄
Deploy Frequency
💡 The anihpj DevEx Vision

Developer clones the anihpj repo → writes code for a new jobpost feature → git push → CI/CD builds, tests, and scans the Docker image → Argo CD deploys to staging → smoke tests pass → canary to production. The developer never runs kubectl, never writes a Helm chart, and never provisions infrastructure. That's world-class DevEx.

1.5 The Internal Developer Platform (IDP) — A Product, Not a Project

An Internal Developer Platform (IDP) is a unified layer on top of infrastructure that developers interact with. It's the "operating system" for your engineering organization.

IDP Components

🔄
CI/CD Pipelines

Automated build, test, scan, deploy. GitHub Actions → Argo CD.

📦
Application Configs

Standardized deployment manifests, Helm charts, Kustomize overlays.

🌍
Environment Mgmt

Dev, staging, production namespaces auto-provisioned with quotas and RBAC.

🔐
Secret Management

Vault or External Secrets — never in Git, auto-rotated.

📊
Monitoring

Prometheus dashboards, alerts, logs (Loki), traces (Tempo) — auto-configured.

📖
Service Catalog

Backstage catalog — discover services, owners, dependencies, docs.

🛡️
Security

Kyverno policies, NetworkPolicies, image scanning, Falco runtime detection.

📝
Documentation

TechDocs — documentation as code, auto-published from Markdown in repos.

IDP as a PRODUCT Mindset

🏢 Treat Your IDP Like a SaaS Product
  • Product Manager: Prioritizes features based on developer feedback ("They need one-click DB provisioning" → Build DatabaseClaim CRD)
  • SLAs: "99.9% of namespace provisions complete within 60 seconds"
  • Support: Internal Slack channel (#platform-help), weekly office hours, comprehensive documentation portal
  • Roadmap: Q1 — Self-service DB provisioning. Q2 — Ephemeral PR environments. Q3 — Automated canary deployments.
  • Feedback Loop: Developer NPS surveys every quarter → prioritize pain points → ship improvements → measure again
💡 The anihpj IDP

Backstage Service Catalog → Argo CD GitOps → Kubernetes Orchestration → Prometheus/Grafana Observability → Kyverno/Falco Security. Developers interact ONLY with Backstage and Git. Everything else is platform-managed.

1.6 "You Build It, You Run It" vs "You Build It, The Platform Runs It"

⚠️ "You Build It, You Run It"

The DevOps mantra: developers own their code in production. They deploy it, monitor it, get paged at 3 AM when it breaks.

The Problem: Not every developer WANTS to be an SRE. Expecting every developer to master Kubernetes, Terraform, PromQL, and incident response is unrealistic and leads to burnout.

✅ "You Build It, The Platform Runs It"

Platform engineering rebalances responsibility. Developers focus on code. The platform handles deployment, scaling, monitoring, alerting, and backups.

The Balance: Developers still own their application's behavior — they just don't have to manage the infrastructure it runs on.

Shared Responsibility Model

LayerDeveloper OwnsPlatform Owns
Application Code✅ Business logic, features, tests—
Container Image✅ Dockerfile, dependencies✅ Base image updates, vulnerability scanning
Deployment—✅ CI/CD pipelines, Argo CD, Helm charts
Infrastructure—✅ Kubernetes, networking, storage, compute
Observability✅ Application metrics, business KPIs✅ Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Tempo, alerts
Security✅ No secrets in code, secure dependencies✅ NetworkPolicies, RBAC, mTLS, image scanning, Falco
Incidents✅ Application-level debugging✅ Platform-level root cause, postmortem facilitation

1.7 Why anihpj/jobpost Needs a Platform

anihpj is a Django job posting application with the jobpost app — employers list jobs filtered by Skills, Location, and Author. It looks simple on the surface, but here's what it ACTUALLY needs to run in production:

📦 What anihpj Really Needs
  • 🐘 PostgreSQL database — StatefulSet with persistent storage, automated backups
  • 🔴 Redis cache + queue — Celery task queue for async processing, caching layer
  • 🔒 TLS certificates — HTTPS for anihpj.example.com, auto-renewed
  • 📊 Monitoring — Prometheus metrics, Grafana dashboards, Loki logs, Tempo traces
  • 💾 Backups — Daily Velero backups of all K8s resources + PV snapshots to S3
  • 🔄 CI/CD — GitHub Actions pipeline: lint → test → build → scan → deploy
  • 🧪 Staging environments — Per-branch ephemeral environments for testing
  • 🔐 Secrets rotation — DB passwords, Django SECRET_KEY, API keys — rotated every 90 days
  • 👥 RBAC — Different permissions for developers, QA, and platform admins
  • 🛡️ Network policies — Zero-trust: web can talk to db on 5432 only, nothing else
⚠️ Without a Platform...

Each of these 10 requirements becomes a JIRA ticket. Each ticket takes 2-5 days. That's 20-50 days of waiting — over a MONTH — just to get anihpj to production. And that's before a single line of code is written for the actual jobpost features.

✅ With a Platform...

All 10 requirements are self-service. Developer clones repo → writes jobpost feature → git push → platform handles everything else. The anihpj journey in this guide: Local Docker → Kubernetes Deployment → GitOps with Argo CD → CRDs for Self-Service → Observability Stack → Security Hardening.

📖 How the Port Analogy Maps to Platform Engineering
  • 🏢 Harbor Master (API Server): Every ship (API request) must check in with the harbor master. Nobody bypasses the harbor master — just like every kubectl command goes through the API server.
  • 🧠 Port Brain (etcd): The harbor master's log book. Which ships are docked? Which containers are where? If the log book is lost, you have no idea what's happening in the port. This is why etcd backup is critical.
  • 📊 Dock Scheduler (kube-scheduler): A new ship arrives. Which dock has space? The scheduler assigns ships to docks based on available space, ship size, and special requirements (refrigerated containers = GPU nodes).
  • 🏗️ Crane Operator (kubelet): The crane operator on each dock receives instructions: "Unload ship X, place containers at bay Y." The crane operator reports back: "Ship X unloaded, 3 containers placed."
  • 📦 Shipping Containers (Pods): The standardized unit of cargo. Every container has the same dimensions (OCI image spec), the same handling mechanisms, and can be moved between any dock. anihpj-web, anihpj-db, and redis each run inside their own container.
  • 🚢 The Docks (Worker Nodes): Where the actual work happens. Multiple docks = multiple worker nodes. If one dock is damaged (node failure), containers are moved to another dock (pod rescheduling).
  • 🌊 The Open Sea (Internet): External traffic arrives through the Ingress (port entrance gate) and is routed to the correct dock and container.
💡 Why This Analogy Matters for the CNPE Exam

When troubleshooting on the CNPE exam, think in terms of the port: "Is the harbor master (API server) accepting ships? Is the log book (etcd) intact? Is the crane operator (kubelet) working on dock 3? Are the containers (pods) placed in the right bay?" This mental model will help you quickly isolate where a problem is occurring.

The Developer Experience — Before vs After the Port

❌ Before the Port (TicketOps)

Ship captain Priya arrives at a chaotic shore. No harbor master. No docks. No cranes. She must:

  • File paperwork with the Dock Authority (JIRA ticket) — wait 3 days
  • Build her own dock (provision a server)
  • Rent her own crane (install and configure software)
  • Unload her own containers manually (deploy the application)
  • Guard the dock 24/7 in case something breaks (on-call)
✅ With the Port (Platform Engineering)

Ship captain Priya radios the harbor master: "Container ship anihpj-v2 arriving."

  • Harbor master (API server) records the arrival — instant
  • Dock scheduler assigns Dock Beta (kube-scheduler) — automatic
  • Crane operator unloads containers (kubelet) — automatic
  • Containers are placed in the yard (pod starts) — 30 seconds
  • Port security patrols the docks 24/7 (self-healing, monitoring) — continuous

📈 The Platform Engineering Maturity Model

Organizations don't adopt platform engineering overnight. They progress through stages — from chaos to fully automated self-service. Understanding where your organization sits helps you prioritize what to build next.

😰
Level 0
Chaos

No platform. TicketOps. Every team builds everything from scratch. 2-week waits for databases.

❌ TicketOps
🛠️
Level 1
Standardized

Shared CI/CD templates, standardized Dockerfiles, common Helm charts. But still manual provisioning.

⚠️ Some automation
⚙️
Level 2
Automated

GitOps with Argo CD. Kubernetes clusters standardized. Monitoring and logging auto-configured.

🟡 Getting there
🚀
Level 3
Self-Service

Full IDP. CRDs for DB/NS/TLS. Backstage portal. Developers self-serve everything. Golden paths.

✅ CNPE Target
📖 Where the CNPE Exam Fits

The CNPE exam tests your ability to BUILD Level 3 platforms. You need to demonstrate that you can: (1) Design CRDs for self-service provisioning, (2) Build operators that automate infrastructure, (3) Configure GitOps pipelines for automated delivery, (4) Set up observability that developers can use without training, (5) Enforce security policies automatically at admission time. Every chapter of this guide moves you from Level 0 to Level 3.

🏢 Platform Engineering in the Real World — Who's Doing It?

Platform engineering isn't theoretical — major companies have been doing it for years. Here are real examples:

🎵
Spotify — Creator of Backstage

Spotify had 1000+ microservices and developers were lost. They built Backstage — a developer portal that became the industry standard. Developers can discover services, create new ones from templates, and view documentation — all from a single UI. Backstage is now a CNCF Incubating project used by Netflix, American Airlines, and Expedia.

🚗
Uber — IDP at 4000+ Services

Uber's platform (called "Up") handles 4000+ microservices. Their IDP provides: standardized service templates, automated CI/CD with canary deployments, self-service infrastructure provisioning, and built-in observability. Developers deploy 100+ times per day without knowing anything about Kubernetes.

🏦
Goldman Sachs — Platform in Finance

In one of the most regulated industries, Goldman Sachs built an IDP on Kubernetes that handles 5000+ applications. The platform enforces SOC2, PCI-DSS, and internal compliance policies automatically. Developers can't deploy non-compliant applications — the platform blocks them at admission time.

🛒
Shopify — Self-Service at Scale

Shopify's platform handles 9000+ deploys per day. Their IDP provides: one-click environment creation, automated database provisioning, built-in feature flags, and instant rollback. A developer can go from "I have an idea" to "it's running in production" in under 10 minutes.

💡 What These Companies Have in Common

Every successful platform has: (1) Self-service as the default — no tickets for routine tasks. (2) Golden paths — the easiest way is the right way. (3) Built-in compliance — security isn't optional, it's automatic. (4) Developer obsession — the platform team treats developers as customers. (5) Continuous improvement — they measure DevEx (NPS, time-to-deploy) and iterate constantly.

🏋️ Chapter 1 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

The CNPE is a performance-based exam — you solve tasks in a live Linux terminal. Practice these drills in your lab environment until you can complete each within the target time.

⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 1.1 — Set Up Your Lab Context & Verify Cluster

Initialize your 6-cluster lab and verify the control plane is healthy.

  1. Set kubectl context to cluster1 (your kubeadm cluster)
  2. Verify all nodes are Ready
  3. Check that all control plane pods are running in kube-system
  4. Display the cluster DNS service IP
💡 Hint: Use kubectl config use-context, kubectl get nodes, kubectl get pods -n kube-system
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Switch to cluster1
kubectl config use-context cluster1-admin@cluster1

# Step 2: Verify nodes
kubectl get nodes
# EXPECTED: All nodes STATUS=Ready

# Step 3: Check control plane pods
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'etcd|apiserver|scheduler|controller'
# EXPECTED: 4 pods all Running (1/1)

# Step 4: Display cluster DNS IP
kubectl get service kube-dns -n kube-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'
# OUTPUT: The cluster DNS IP (usually 10.96.0.10)
⏱️ Target: 2 minutes
Drill 1.2 — Explore Your Cluster with kubectl

Navigate the cluster and understand its current state.

  1. List all namespaces in the cluster
  2. Count how many pods are running across all namespaces
  3. Display cluster information including the API server endpoint
  4. List the API resources available in the cluster
💡 Hint: Use kubectl get ns, kubectl get pods -A, kubectl cluster-info, kubectl api-resources
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: List namespaces
kubectl get namespaces
# Note: kube-system, kube-public, kube-node-lease, default

# Step 2: Count all pods
kubectl get pods --all-namespaces | wc -l
# Subtract 1 for header line

# Step 3: Cluster info
kubectl cluster-info
# Shows: Kubernetes control plane is running at https://...

# Step 4: API resources
kubectl api-resources | head -20
# Lists all resource types (pods, services, deployments, etc.)
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 1.3 — Create Your First Namespace with Labels

Create the anihpj namespace with proper labels and annotations — the foundation of your platform.

  1. Create namespace anihpj-dev with labels: environment=development, team=platform, project=anihpj
  2. Add annotation: owner=your-email@example.com
  3. Verify the namespace was created with all labels
  4. Change default context namespace to anihpj-dev
💡 Hint: Use kubectl create ns with --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate YAML, then add labels and annotations.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Generate namespace YAML
kubectl create namespace anihpj-dev --dry-run=client -o yaml > ns-anihpj-dev.yaml

# Edit ns-anihpj-dev.yaml and add:
#   labels:
#     environment: development
#     team: platform
#     project: anihpj
#   annotations:
#     owner: your-email@example.com

# Step 2: Apply
kubectl apply -f ns-anihpj-dev.yaml

# Step 3: Verify
kubectl get namespace anihpj-dev --show-labels
kubectl describe namespace anihpj-dev | grep Annotations

# Step 4: Set default namespace
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=anihpj-dev
kubectl config view --minify | grep namespace
⏱️ Target: 2 minutes
Drill 1.4 — Debug a Failing kubectl Command

Your teammate runs kubectl get pods and gets error: the server doesn't have a resource type "pods". Debug it.

  1. Check which cluster context is active
  2. Verify the API server is reachable
  3. Check if you have network connectivity
  4. Try with increased verbosity to see what's happening
💡 Hint: Use kubectl config current-context, kubectl cluster-info, and kubectl get pods -v=6 for verbose output.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Check current context
kubectl config current-context
# Is this the right cluster? Wrong context = wrong cluster.

# Step 2: Check API server reachability
kubectl cluster-info
# If this fails: kubectl config view to check server URL
# Is the kubeconfig pointing to the right IP/hostname?

# Step 3: Check network connectivity to API server
APISERVER=$(kubectl config view --minify -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.server}')
curl -k $APISERVER/healthz
# Should return "ok"

# Step 4: Verbose output
kubectl get pods -v=6 2>&1 | head -30
# Look for the actual HTTP request/response to see what's failing
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 1.5 — Create Your First Pod (anihpj-web)

Deploy a simple anihpj-web pod using imperative and declarative approaches.

  1. Create a pod named anihpj-web imperatively using the nginx:alpine image
  2. Generate the YAML for this pod using --dry-run=client
  3. Delete the pod, then re-create it using the generated YAML
  4. Verify the pod is running and get its IP address
💡 Hint: Use kubectl run anihpj-web --image=nginx:alpine -n anihpj-dev imperatively, then --dry-run=client -o yaml to generate the YAML.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create imperatively
kubectl run anihpj-web --image=nginx:alpine -n anihpj-dev

# Step 2: Generate YAML
kubectl run anihpj-web --image=nginx:alpine -n anihpj-dev \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod-anihpj-web.yaml

# Step 3: Delete and re-create declaratively
kubectl delete pod anihpj-web -n anihpj-dev
kubectl apply -f pod-anihpj-web.yaml

# Step 4: Verify
kubectl get pod anihpj-web -n anihpj-dev -o wide
# Shows STATUS=Running and the Pod IP

kubectl describe pod anihpj-web -n anihpj-dev
# Shows full details: node it's running on, IP, events
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 1.6 — Expose a Pod with a Service

Create a Service to expose the anihpj-web pod — this is how microservices find each other in your platform.

  1. Expose the anihpj-web pod as a ClusterIP Service on port 80
  2. Verify the Service was created and note the ClusterIP
  3. Test connectivity using kubectl run a temporary debug pod
  4. Get the Service's DNS name and verify it resolves
💡 Hint: Use kubectl expose pod and kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- wget -O- <svc-ip>:80
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Expose the pod
kubectl expose pod anihpj-web --port=80 --target-port=80 \
  --name=anihpj-web-svc -n anihpj-dev

# Step 2: Verify Service
kubectl get svc anihpj-web-svc -n anihpj-dev
# Note the CLUSTER-IP (e.g., 10.96.100.50)

# Step 3: Test connectivity
kubectl run test-pod --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -n anihpj-dev \
  -- wget -qO- http://anihpj-web-svc
# Should return the nginx welcome page HTML

# Step 4: Check DNS
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -n anihpj-dev \
  -- nslookup anihpj-web-svc
# DNS name: anihpj-web-svc.anihpj-dev.svc.cluster.local
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 1.7 — Create a ConfigMap and Mount It

Inject configuration into your pod — a fundamental platform pattern.

  1. Create a ConfigMap named anihpj-config with key APP_ENV=development and DEBUG=true
  2. Create a new pod that mounts this ConfigMap as environment variables
  3. Exec into the pod and verify the environment variables are set
  4. Update the ConfigMap and verify the pod does NOT see the change (pods don't auto-reload ConfigMaps)
💡 Hint: Use kubectl create configmap with --from-literal. For the pod, use envFrom to inject all ConfigMap keys.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create ConfigMap
kubectl create configmap anihpj-config \
  --from-literal=APP_ENV=development \
  --from-literal=DEBUG=true \
  -n anihpj-dev

# Step 2: Create pod that uses ConfigMap
kubectl run anihpj-config-test --image=busybox --restart=Never -n anihpj-dev \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod-config-test.yaml

# Edit pod-config-test.yaml to add:
# spec:
#   containers:
#   - name: anihpj-config-test
#     image: busybox
#     command: ["sleep", "3600"]
#     envFrom:
#     - configMapRef:
#         name: anihpj-config

kubectl apply -f pod-config-test.yaml

# Step 3: Verify env vars
kubectl exec -it anihpj-config-test -n anihpj-dev -- env | grep -E 'APP_ENV|DEBUG'
# Shows: APP_ENV=development, DEBUG=true

# Step 4: Update ConfigMap (pod won't see it!)
kubectl create configmap anihpj-config \
  --from-literal=APP_ENV=staging \
  --from-literal=DEBUG=false \
  -n anihpj-dev --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl replace -f -

# Check the pod again — still shows OLD values!
kubectl exec -it anihpj-config-test -n anihpj-dev -- env | grep APP_ENV
# Shows: APP_ENV=development (unchanged!)
# Lesson: Pods don't auto-reload ConfigMaps. Must restart pod or use reloader.
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 1.8 — View Logs and Debug a Pod

Master the essential debugging commands — you'll use these constantly on the CNPE exam.

  1. View the logs of the anihpj-web pod
  2. Stream logs in real-time (follow mode)
  3. Get the last 20 log lines
  4. View events for the anihpj-dev namespace (these show scheduling decisions, errors, etc.)
💡 Hint: Use kubectl logs with -f for follow, --tail=20 for last lines. kubectl get events shows cluster decisions.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: View logs
kubectl logs anihpj-web -n anihpj-dev

# Step 2: Stream logs (Ctrl+C to stop)
kubectl logs -f anihpj-web -n anihpj-dev

# Step 3: Last 20 lines
kubectl logs anihpj-web -n anihpj-dev --tail=20

# Step 4: View namespace events
kubectl get events -n anihpj-dev --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'
# Shows: pod scheduling, container started, health checks, warnings

# Bonus: Describe pod for full details
kubectl describe pod anihpj-web -n anihpj-dev | tail -20
# Shows: Events section with timeline of pod lifecycle
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 1.9 — Switch Clusters and Verify Context

Multi-cluster management is a core CNPE skill. Practice safe context switching.

  1. List all available kubectl contexts
  2. Switch to cluster2 (your Argo CD cluster)
  3. Verify you're on the right cluster by checking node names
  4. Switch back to cluster1 and verify again
💡 Hint: Always verify with kubectl get nodes after switching. The node names will tell you which cluster you're on. Never run destructive commands without checking first!
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: List all contexts
kubectl config get-contexts
# Shows all contexts. CURRENT column has * for active one.

# Step 2: Switch to cluster2 (kind cluster for Argo CD)
kubectl config use-context kind-cluster2

# Step 3: VERIFY before doing anything!
kubectl config current-context
# Should show: kind-cluster2

kubectl get nodes
# Node names should start with "kind" if it's a kind cluster
# NEVER skip this step before running kubectl delete!

# Step 4: Switch back to cluster1
kubectl config use-context cluster1-admin@cluster1
kubectl get nodes
# Node names should show your kubeadm node names

# CRITICAL CNPE EXAM TIP:
# On the CNPE exam, you'll switch between multiple clusters.
# Always run kubectl config current-context before any command.
# Many candidates lose points because they run commands on the wrong cluster.
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 1.10 — Clean Up Resources (Critical CNPE Skill)

On the CNPE exam, you must leave the cluster clean. Practice safe cleanup now.

  1. Delete the anihpj-web pod (only the pod, not the service or configmap)
  2. Verify the pod is gone but the service and configmap still exist
  3. Delete ALL resources you created in the anihpj-dev namespace in one command
  4. Delete the anihpj-dev namespace itself (this removes everything inside it)
💡 Hint: kubectl delete pod for single resource. kubectl delete all --all -n <ns> removes all resources in a namespace. kubectl delete ns removes the entire namespace.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Delete only the pod
kubectl delete pod anihpj-web -n anihpj-dev

# Step 2: Verify service and configmap survive
kubectl get svc,configmap -n anihpj-dev
# Should show: anihpj-web-svc and anihpj-config still exist

# Step 3: Delete ALL resources in namespace
kubectl delete all --all -n anihpj-dev
# This removes pods, services, deployments, replicasets (not configmaps/secrets)

# Also clean up configmaps and secrets
kubectl delete configmap --all -n anihpj-dev
kubectl delete secret --all -n anihpj-dev

# Step 4: Delete the entire namespace (cleanest approach)
kubectl delete namespace anihpj-dev
# Everything inside the namespace is deleted automatically

# Verify
kubectl get namespace anihpj-dev
# Should show: Error from server (NotFound)

# CNPE EXAM TIP: Always leave the cluster exactly as you found it.
# If a task says "create X in namespace Y", delete Y at the end
# unless instructed otherwise. Partial cleanup can lose points.
How Chapter 1 Concepts Are Tested on the CNPE Exam

The CNPE exam won't ask you to define platform engineering — it tests whether you can build self-service capabilities. Chapter 1 concepts manifest as exam tasks like:

  • "Create a DatabaseClaim CRD that provisions a PostgreSQL instance via Crossplane" — This is TicketOps elimination in action. You're building the self-service API that replaces JIRA tickets.
  • "Configure a Backstage template that creates a namespace with RBAC, NetworkPolicy, and ResourceQuota" — Golden Path implementation. Make the right way the easiest way.
  • "Set up Argo CD to auto-sync from a Git repository. Verify drift detection works." — Platform as a Product. The platform team provides GitOps; developers provide code.

Sprint through Chapter 1 concepts: When you see terms like "Golden Path," "DevEx," or "Self-Service" on the exam, translate them to concrete actions:

  • "Golden Path" → kubectl apply -f backstage-template.yaml (pre-built template). Developers don't write YAML from scratch.
  • "Self-Service" → kubectl apply -f database-claim.yaml (CRD claim). No kubectl exec into operators.
  • "DevEx" → git push triggers CI/CD → Argo CD syncs → app deployed. Developer never runs kubectl.
⚠️ Don't Confuse Platform Engineering with DevOps

The CNPE exam expects you to understand the DISTINCTION. DevOps is a culture ("You build it, you run it"). Platform Engineering is a PRODUCT (internal platform that automates the "run it" part). On the exam: if a task asks you to set up CI/CD that developers use directly → that's DevOps. If it asks you to build a self-service API that abstracts CI/CD → that's Platform Engineering. Platform Engineers build the paved road; DevOps engineers drive on it.

Q1: A developer needs a PostgreSQL database. In a TicketOps organization, how would they get one?

▶ Show Answer
File a JIRA ticket → wait 2-5 days → Ops manually provisions via AWS console → emails connection string. This is the anti-pattern that platform engineering eliminates.
Q2: What's the difference between an IDP and a collection of DevOps tools?

▶ Show Answer
An IDP is a PRODUCT with a product manager, roadmap, SLAs, and developer NPS measurement. A collection of tools is just tools — no unified experience, no feedback loop, no product mindset. The CNPE exam tests your ability to build the IDP, not just configure tools.
Q3: What does "Make the right way the easiest way" mean in practice?

▶ Show Answer
If deploying with proper security (NetworkPolicy, non-root, image scanning, RBAC) requires 50 lines of YAML but deploying without security requires 5 lines, developers will take the shortcut. The platform engineer's job: make the secure path a one-click template, and the insecure path impossible (blocked by Kyverno policies at admission time).
🚀 Beyond CNPE — Platform Engineering at Netflix, Spotify, and Uber Scale

The CNPE certifies you can build a platform for 10-100 developers. But what happens at 1,000+ developers?

  • Platform as a Product Team: Spotify's Backstage team has a dedicated Product Manager who prioritizes features based on developer NPS surveys. Every quarter: survey → identify top 3 pain points → build solutions → measure again. This is Product Management applied to infrastructure.
  • Federated Platform Model: At Uber (4,000+ microservices), the central platform team provides core infrastructure (K8s, CI/CD, monitoring). Individual business units (Rides, Eats, Freight) have embedded platform engineers who build domain-specific tooling on top. Central team governs standards; domain teams innovate within guardrails.
  • Platform OKRs: Netflix measures platform success by "% of services using golden paths" and "median time from commit to production." Not by how many K8s clusters they manage. The platform is INVISIBLE when it works — developers don't think about it.
  • Career Path: Platform Engineer → Senior PE → Staff PE (designs platform architecture) → Principal PE (sets organizational platform strategy) → Director of Platform Engineering. This is a legitimate, high-paying career track separate from SRE or DevOps.

These terms form the vocabulary of the entire exam.

2.1 What Is "Cloud Native"? — The CNCF Definition

📖 Official CNCF Definition: "Cloud native technologies empower organizations to build and run scalable applications in modern, dynamic environments such as public, private, and hybrid clouds. Containers, service meshes, microservices, immutable infrastructure, and declarative APIs exemplify this approach."

Key Traits of Cloud Native Applications:

  • Containerized — Each component packaged as a container (Docker/OCI)
  • Dynamically Orchestrated — Kubernetes schedules and manages containers across a cluster
  • Microservices-Oriented — Application broken into small, independently deployable services

💡 The Five Cloud Native Principles — These map directly to the CNPE exam domains:

  1. Containerization → Domain 1 (Platform Architecture)
  2. CI/CD → Domain 2 (GitOps & Continuous Delivery)
  3. Orchestration → Domain 1 + Domain 3 (Platform APIs)
  4. Observability → Domain 4 (Observability & Ops)
  5. Service Mesh + Policy → Domain 5 (Security & Policy)

Why It Matters for Platform Engineers: You don't just use cloud native tools — you build the foundation (the platform) that enables all five principles for your organization's developers.

💡 Cloud Native vs. Traditional IT — What Changed? To understand cloud native, you need to understand what came before it and WHY the industry shifted:

Aspect🏢 Traditional IT (pre-2015)☁️ Cloud Native (today)
Deploy cycleMonths. "Big bang" quarterly releases.Hours or minutes. Multiple deploys per day.
Server provisioningWeeks. Fill a ticket → wait → manually configure.Seconds. Terraform/Crossplane provisions on PR merge.
ScalingVertical only (buy bigger server). Predict capacity months ahead.Horizontal (add more pods/nodes). Auto-scale based on actual demand.
Failure handling"Make it never fail." 5-nines hardware. Expensive redundancy."Assume it WILL fail." Design for failure. Cheap commodity hardware.
ConfigurationManual. SSH in, edit files. "Bob knows how it's configured."Declarative. Git = truth. ConfigMaps + Secrets. No SSH.
Team structureSilos: Dev writes code → tosses over wall → Ops runs it."You build it, you run it." DevOps/Platform teams enable self-service.
Security modelPerimeter (firewall = castle wall). Trusted internal network.Zero trust. Every service verifies. mTLS everywhere. Policy as Code.

The core insight: Cloud native isn't just "using containers." It's a completely different operating model built on the assumption that infrastructure is disposable, failure is normal, and speed is your competitive advantage. The CNPE exam tests whether you can build the platform that makes this model work.

📖 The 12-Factor App Methodology — A foundational methodology for building cloud native applications (originally from Heroku, now a CNCF-endorsed pattern). Every platform engineer should know these:

#FactorWhat It Meansanihpj Example
ICodebaseOne codebase per app, tracked in version control. Many deploys (staging, prod) from same codebase.One anihpj Git repo → deployed to staging + production namespaces
IIDependenciesExplicitly declare and isolate all dependencies. Never rely on system-level packages.requirements.txt / pyproject.toml — all Python deps declared, nothing "just installed"
IIIConfigStore configuration in environment variables, NOT in code. Config ≠ code.DB connection string, secret key, DEBUG flag → K8s Secrets + ConfigMaps, never in settings.py
IVBacking ServicesTreat databases, caches, queues as attached resources. Swap via config change.PostgreSQL URL in env var → swap from local Postgres to RDS without code change
VBuild, Release, RunStrictly separate build (compile) → release (config+image) → run (execute) stages.Build: Docker image. Release: image tag + ConfigMap. Run: docker run / kubectl apply
VIProcessesApp runs as stateless processes. State lives in backing services. No "sticky sessions."Django is stateless — sessions stored in Redis, not on local disk
VIIPort BindingExport services via port binding. App is self-contained — no external web server needed.Django/Gunicorn listens on :$PORT (env var). K8s Service routes to that port.
VIIIConcurrencyScale out via the process model. Run multiple copies of the same process.Scale anihpj-web Deployment from 3 → 10 replicas with kubectl scale
IXDisposabilityFast startup + graceful shutdown. Processes are disposable, can be killed anytime.Gunicorn graceful shutdown on SIGTERM. K8s sends SIGTERM → 30s grace → SIGKILL
XDev/Prod ParityKeep development, staging, and production as similar as possible.Same Docker image, same DB engine (Postgres), same K8s manifests across all envs
XILogsTreat logs as event streams. App doesn't manage log files — stdout/stderr only.Django logs to stdout → container runtime captures → Fluentd → Loki. No /var/log/anihpj.log
XIIAdmin ProcessesRun admin/management tasks as one-off processes, not cron jobs on a server.DB migrations: kubectl run migrate --image=anihpj -- python manage.py migrate (K8s Job)
🧠 CNPE Exam: 12-Factor App is referenced throughout the CNPE curriculum. Focus especially on Factors III (Config), IV (Backing Services), V (Build/Release/Run), and VI (Stateless Processes) — these directly relate to Kubernetes design patterns like ConfigMaps, Services, Deployments, and ephemeral pods.

2.2 Containers, Kubernetes, Microservices — The Core Triad

ConceptWhat It Isanihpj Example
📦 ContainersLightweight, portable, isolated application packaging (Docker/OCI)anihpj-web container running Django + Gunicorn
☸️ KubernetesThe orchestrator — schedules containers, manages networking, storage, scalingK8s cluster running anihpj in staging + production namespaces
🔗 MicroservicesArchitectural pattern — one container = one focused responsibilityanihpj-web (Django) + postgres (DB) + redis (cache) — each a separate service

How They Connect: Microservices run as containers on Kubernetes. Kubernetes provides the networking so containers discover each other via DNS (Services).

💡 Containers vs. Virtual Machines — What's the Difference? This is the #1 concept every platform engineer must explain clearly:

Aspect📦 Container🖥️ Virtual Machine
What it packagesApp + dependencies only (MBs)App + full OS kernel + drivers (GBs)
Startup time< 1 second30 seconds – minutes
IsolationProcess-level (shares host kernel)Full hardware virtualization (hypervisor)
DensityDozens–hundreds per hostA few–dozens per host
PortabilityRuns anywhere with container runtimeTied to hypervisor (VMware, KVM, etc.)
Image layersLayered (base OS → deps → app code)
Each RUN in Dockerfile = one layer		Monolithic disk image
No layer reuse

Key insight: Containers share the host OS kernel — that's why they're fast and small. VMs each run their own kernel — that's why they're heavy. A Docker image is built in layers: if 10 containers use the same python:3.12-slim base, that layer is cached and shared, saving disk and bandwidth.

📦 Container Runtime Ecosystem — A platform engineer needs to understand what runs containers:

RuntimeTypeRoleUsed By
containerdHigh-level runtimePulls images, manages container lifecycle, handles storage/networkingDefault in Kubernetes (via CRI), Docker Engine
CRI-OHigh-level runtimeKubernetes-specific — implements CRI directly, minimal footprintOpenShift, OKD, kubeadm (alternative to containerd)
runcLow-level runtimeActually creates/runs the container using Linux namespaces + cgroupsCalled by containerd and CRI-O under the hood
Kata ContainersSandboxed runtimeRuns each container in a lightweight VM for hardware isolationMulti-tenant clusters, high-security workloads
gVisorSandboxed runtimeUser-space kernel intercepting syscalls, no VM overheadGoogle Cloud Run, GKE Sandbox

CRI (Container Runtime Interface): The Kubernetes plugin API that decouples K8s from any specific container runtime. As long as the runtime speaks CRI, Kubernetes can use it. This is why Docker was deprecated as a K8s runtime (Docker didn't implement CRI natively — containerd does).

💡 What Makes Containers Possible? Linux Namespaces & cgroups — Containers aren't magic. They're built on two Linux kernel features that have existed since ~2008:

Linux FeatureWhat It DoesReal-World AnalogyWhy It Matters
Namespaces
(7 types)		Limit what a process can SEE. PID namespace = process only sees its own PID tree. Network namespace = process has its own IP, routes, firewall rules. Mount namespace = process has its own filesystem view.Each container gets its own "room with one-way mirrors" — it sees only itself, not other containers or the host.This is what makes containers isolated. Container A thinks it's PID 1. Container B also thinks it's PID 1. They don't conflict because they're in different PID namespaces.
cgroups
(Control Groups)		Limit what a process can USE. CPU cgroup = "this process can use at most 0.5 CPU cores." Memory cgroup = "this process can use at most 512MB RAM, then OOM kill."Each container gets a "resource budget" — it can't exceed its allocation even if the host has spare resources.This is what makes containers fair. A noisy neighbor can't starve other containers. Kubernetes resource requests/limits are translated into cgroup settings.

Container = Namespaces + cgroups + a filesystem image. Docker/containerd orchestrate these Linux primitives. When you run docker run python:3.12, the runtime creates new namespaces, sets cgroup limits, unpacks the image layers into a mount namespace, and starts your process inside that sandbox. The process thinks it's running on its own Linux machine — but it's sharing the kernel with everyone else.

OCI (Open Container Initiative): The industry standard that defines what a container image looks like (OCI Image Spec) and how to run it (OCI Runtime Spec). Docker images are OCI images. Any OCI-compliant runtime (containerd, CRI-O, Podman) can run any OCI image. This standardization is why you can build an image with Docker and run it on a Kubernetes cluster that uses CRI-O — they speak the same language.

DOCKER IMAGE LAYERS — How anihpj's Image is Built

  Layer 3 is REUSED from cache — only Layer 4 (your code) rebuilds.

📖 Microservices Patterns — The 5 Principles of Service Design: A "microservice" isn't just "a small app." These five principles define well-designed microservices that platform teams can actually operate:

  1. Single Responsibility: One service = one business capability. anihpj-web handles job listings, not user authentication. If you can't describe your service in one sentence, it does too much.
  2. Independent Deployability: You can deploy anihpj-web without redeploying postgres or redis. Each service has its own CI/CD pipeline, its own deployment cadence. This is WHY microservices exist — not to make architecture diagrams pretty, but to let teams deploy independently.
  3. Decentralized Data: Each microservice owns its data. anihpj-web owns the job listings database. A separate "users" service would own the users database. No shared database across services — shared databases create tight coupling that defeats the purpose.
  4. Design for Failure: If postgres is down, anihpj-web should degrade gracefully (show a cached list or a friendly error), not crash. Circuit breakers, retries with backoff, and timeouts are MANDATORY, not optional. The platform must provide these patterns (service mesh helps).
  5. Observable by Default: Every service exposes metrics, structured logs, and traces. This isn't something you add later — it's table stakes. The platform must make instrumentation easy (OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation, sidecar injection).

2.3 Infrastructure as Code (IaC) — Terraform, Crossplane, Pulumi

What is IaC? Managing infrastructure through machine-readable definition files, not manual processes or interactive tools. Infrastructure is versioned, reviewed, and tested — just like application code.

ToolLanguageApproachBest For
TerraformHCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language)Declarative, provider ecosystem (AWS, GCP, Azure, K8s)Multi-cloud, broadest adoption
CrossplaneYAML (Kubernetes CRDs/XRDs)Kubernetes-native — cloud resources defined as CRDsPlatform teams building self-service cloud provisioning
PulumiPython, TypeScript, Go, C#IaC using real programming languagesTeams wanting loops/conditionals in infrastructure code

💡 anihpj Example: terraform/eks.tf defines the EKS cluster, terraform/rds.tf defines the PostgreSQL database, terraform/elasticache.tf defines Redis. All three files live in Git, go through PR review, and are applied via CI pipeline — no one ever clicks in the AWS console.

💡 How Terraform Actually Works — The Plan/Apply Cycle & State: Understanding this is critical for any platform engineer using IaC:

  1. You write HCL describing desired state: resource "aws_db_instance" "anihpj" { allocated_storage = 20 }
  2. terraform plan — Terraform reads your .tf files, reads the current state from terraform.tfstate, and queries AWS to see what actually exists. It calculates the difference (diff) and shows you what it WILL do: "Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy."
  3. terraform apply — Terraform executes the plan. It calls the AWS API to create/update/delete resources in the correct order (topological sort — it knows to create the VPC before the RDS instance inside it).
  4. State updated — terraform.tfstate now records the actual resource IDs, ARNs, IPs. This state file is CRITICAL — without it, Terraform can't know what it manages. Store it in S3 with DynamoDB locking for teams.

Key concept — Idempotency: If you run terraform apply twice with no changes, the second run does NOTHING. This is the magic of declarative IaC. You describe the DESIRED state, not the STEPS to get there. The tool figures out the steps. Ansible (procedural) says "first do X, then do Y." Terraform (declarative) says "here's what I want — figure out how to make it happen."

The Terraform State Problem: State drift happens when someone changes something in the AWS console that Terraform manages. Now the real world doesn't match .tfstate. Next terraform plan will show unexpected changes. This is why platform teams MUST enforce: if Terraform manages it, no one touches it outside Terraform. GitOps takes this further — not even humans run terraform apply; CI/CD runs it after PR merge.

TERRAFORM PLAN/APPLY FLOW — Declarative Infrastructure in Action
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     TERRAFORM EXECUTION CYCLE                            │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

      1. DEVELOPER                           2. TERRAFORM

📖 IaC in Action — Same Resource, Different Tools: Here's how you'd provision a PostgreSQL database for anihpj with each tool:

Terraform (HCL)Crossplane (YAML)Pulumi (Python)
resource "aws_db_instance" "anihpj" {
  engine         = "postgres"
  engine_version = "16.3"
  instance_class = "db.t4g.small"
  allocated_storage = 20
  db_name        = "anihpj"
  username       = var.db_user
  password       = var.db_password
  vpc_security_group_ids = [
    aws_security_group.rds.id
  ]
}
 
apiVersion: database.aws.crossplane.io/v1beta1
kind: RDSInstance
metadata:
  name: anihpj-postgres
spec:
  forProvider:
    region: us-east-1
    dbInstanceClass: db.t4g.small
    allocatedStorage: 20
    engine: postgres
    engineVersion: "16.3"
  writeConnectionSecretToRef:
    name: anihpj-db-credentials
 
import pulumi_aws as aws

db = aws.rds.Instance("anihpj-db",
    engine="postgres",
    engine_version="16.3",
    instance_class="db.t4g.small",
    allocated_storage=20,
    db_name="anihpj",
    username=config.require("db_user"),
    password=config.require_secret("db_pass"),
)

Key takeaway: All three produce the same RDS database. The difference is where they're managed from: Terraform from your CLI/CI, Crossplane from within Kubernetes itself (kubectl), Pulumi from your Python/TS/Go code. Platform teams choose based on their operational model.

2.4 GitOps — Git as the Single Source of Truth

What is GitOps? A Continuous Delivery method where Git is the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and applications. An agent inside the cluster pulls from Git and syncs the desired state.

🔄 Pull-Based GitOps (Argo CD / Flux)
Git Repo (k8s/base/)
      │
      │ PR merged to main
      ▼
Argo CD / Flux (in-cluster agent)
      │
      │ Compares git state vs cluster state
      ▼
Kubernetes Cluster
  ├── Staging NS (auto-sync)
  └── Prod NS (manual sync or auto)
❌ Push-Based (NOT GitOps)
Git Repo
      │
      │ CI pipeline has kubectl credentials
      ▼
CI System (GitHub Actions / Jenkins)
      │
      │ kubectl apply -f manifests/
      ▼
Kubernetes Cluster

Key GitOps Benefits:

  • 📜 Git history = audit log — Every change is traceable
  • ⏪ Git revert = rollback — Revert the commit, Argo CD reverts the cluster
  • 👀 PR review = change approval — No one applies directly to cluster
  • 🔁 Self-healing — Argo CD auto-corrects "drift" (manual kubectl edits)
  • 🔒 No cluster credentials in CI — CI never touches the cluster

📖 anihpj GitOps Flow: k8s/base/ folder in git → Argo CD syncs to staging cluster → Developer merges PR → Argo CD detects new commit → Auto-syncs to staging → Smoke tests pass → Manual sync to production (Continuous Delivery, not Continuous Deployment).

💡 Helm vs. Kustomize — The Templating Decision: Both are CNCF projects for managing Kubernetes manifests. Platform engineers need to know when to use each:

Aspect📦 Helm🔧 Kustomize
ApproachTemplating: Go templates with {{ .Values.foo }}Overlay: Patch base YAML without templates
Learning CurveSteeper — Go template syntax + Chart structureShallow — plain YAML, just add overlays
Best ForDistributing apps to others (charts have defaults, documentation)Internal platform teams managing env variants
Built into K8s?No — requires Helm CLI or controllerYes! kubectl apply -k ./overlays/prod
Argo CD SupportNative (Helm charts as applications)Native (Kustomize as applications)
anihpj UseInstall shared infra: Prometheus, Grafana, cert-manager (via community Helm charts)Manage anihpj's own manifests: base/ + overlays/staging + overlays/production

Best Practice: Most platform teams use both — Helm for installing third-party infrastructure (you didn't write it, don't maintain its YAML), Kustomize for your own application manifests (you control every line).

😰 Deployment WITHOUT GitOps (Push Model)
  • 🔴 CI pipeline stores kubectl credentials — one leak = full cluster compromise
  • 🔴 "Who deployed that change at 2 AM?" — no audit trail, git says one thing, cluster says another
  • 🔴 Someone manually ran kubectl edit deployment in production — now git and cluster are out of sync
  • 🔴 Rollback requires finding the last-working manifest and re-applying — hope you remembered to commit it
🎉 Deployment WITH GitOps (Pull Model — Argo CD)
  • ✅ Zero cluster credentials in CI. Argo CD lives in the cluster and pulls from Git.
  • ✅ Full audit trail. Argo CD logs every sync: who, what, when, from which commit.
  • ✅ Drift detection. Argo CD spots manual kubectl edits and auto-reverts them (or alerts you).
  • ✅ Git revert = instant rollback. Revert the commit → Argo CD syncs → cluster matches exactly.

💡 Argo CD Architecture — The Sync Loop Deep Dive: Understanding how Argo CD works internally helps you debug when things go wrong:

ARGO CD RECONCILIATION LOOP (Runs every 3 minutes by default)
  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────────┐
  │  Git Repo    │     │   Argo CD        │     │  Kubernetes Cluster │
  │  k8s/base/   │     │   (in-cluster)   │     │                     │
  └──────┬───────┘     └────────┬─────────┘     └──────────┬──────────┘
         │                      │                          │
         │  1. Clone/Fetch      │                          │
         │  (every 3 min)       │                          │
         ├─────────────────────►│                          │
         │                      │                          │
         │                      │  2. Render manifests     │
         │                      │  (Helm/Kustomize/plain)  │
         │                      │                          │
         │                      │  3. Compare desired      │
         │                      │  vs. actual state        │
         │                      │  (kubectl get all)       │
         │                      ├─────────────────────────►│
         │                      │                          │
         │                      │  4. If drift detected:   │
         │                      │  OutOfSync status        │
         │                      │  (auto-sync or alert)    │
         │                      │                          │
         │                      │  5. Apply diff           │
         │                      │  (kubectl apply)         │
         │                      ├─────────────────────────►│
         │                      │                          │
         │                      │  6. Wait for healthy      │
         │                      │  (pod Ready, no errors)  │
         │                      │  Status: Synced & Healthy│

Argo CD vs Flux — Which GitOps Tool? Both are CNCF-graduated GitOps tools. The choice depends on your team:

Aspect🦑 Argo CD🔧 Flux
UIRich web UI — see all apps, their health, sync status at a glanceCLI-first. No built-in web UI (can add Weave GitOps dashboard)
Multi-tenancyProjects + AppProjects. Each team sees only their apps.Each Flux instance watches specific paths. Simpler but less granular.
Image updatesArgo CD Image Updater (separate component) watches registries for new tagsBuilt-in ImageRepository + ImagePolicy + ImageUpdateAutomation
Helm supportNative. Can use Helm charts directly as applications.Native via HelmRelease CRD. Declarative Helm operations.
Best forPlatform teams with many apps/teams who need visibility + self-service UITeams wanting GitOps tightly integrated with the K8s API (everything is a CRD, no separate server)

2.5 Immutable Infrastructure — "Cattle, Not Pets"

⚠️ Definition: Servers are never modified after deployment. If something changes, you destroy and recreate from a known-good image. You never SSH into a server to fix things.

Aspect🐄 Mutable (Pets) — ❌🐂 Immutable (Cattle) — ✅
Server names"prod-web-01", "bobs-old-server""ip-10-0-3-47", "pod-anihpj-a3f2"
Fixing issuesSSH in, apt-get update, edit configsDestroy pod/node, recreate from image/AMI
ConfigurationRandom files scattered on diskConfigMaps, Secrets, environment variables
State over timeDrifts from known-good stateAlways matches image + declarative config
ScalingManually provision VMs over weeksAuto-scale with Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter

How Kubernetes Achieves Immutability: Pods are ephemeral → Deployments recreate from immutable container images → ConfigMaps/Secrets provide configuration → Nodes are replaced by new AMIs, never patched in-place.

📖 The Origin of "Cattle, Not Pets" — This famous DevOps phrase originated from a 2012 talk by Bill Baker (Microsoft). The analogy:

  • 🐕 Pets: You name them ("prod-web-01"). When they get sick, you nurse them back to health (SSH in, debug, patch). You're emotionally attached. Losing one is a tragedy. This is how we treated servers in 2005.
  • 🐂 Cattle: They have numbers ("node-ip-10-0-3-47"). When one gets sick, you replace it. No emotional attachment. Losing one is expected. This is how we treat servers in cloud native.

Netflix took this to the extreme with their Chaos Monkey — a tool that randomly kills production servers DURING BUSINESS HOURS to verify that the system survives. If losing a random server causes an outage, the system isn't truly cloud native. This is why Kubernetes was designed to treat pods as disposable — if a node fails, the scheduler moves pods to healthy nodes automatically.

😰 The Mutable Infrastructure Nightmare (Real Story)
  • 🔴 "prod-web-03 has 147 packages someone installed manually last year — nobody knows which ones are needed"
  • 🔴 "The security patch worked on staging but broke production because the servers are different now"
  • 🔴 "The new hire spent 2 weeks setting up their dev environment matching production's 'special configuration'"
  • 🔴 "We can't reproduce the bug — it only happens on that one server"
  • 🔴 "Rollback? Uh... do we have a snapshot from before the deploy?"
🎉 The Immutable Infrastructure Solution
  • ✅ Every server image is built by Packer from a known-good template, versioned in Git
  • ✅ New AMI → terminate old instance → launch new instance. Never patch in-place.
  • ✅ Dev environment = docker compose up — same image as production, same configs
  • ✅ Reproduce any bug: pull the exact image tag from that deployment, run locally
  • ✅ Rollback = change the image tag back. Done in seconds.
  • ✅ Packer + Ansible/cloud-init build AMIs. Docker + Dockerfile build containers. Same principle, different layer.
IMMUTABLE vs MUTABLE INFRASTRUCTURE — Side-by-Side Comparison

2.6 CI/CD and Continuous Delivery

🔄
CI
Continuous Integration
Build + test on every push
→
🚀
CD (Delivery)
Continuous Delivery
Auto-deploy to staging, manual to prod
→
⚡
CD (Deployment)
Continuous Deployment
Every passing change → production

💡 anihpj CI/CD Pipeline (End-to-End):

  1. Push to GitHub → Triggers GitHub Actions
  2. Lint → ruff (Python), hadolint (Dockerfile), kubeconform (K8s manifests)
  3. Test → pytest + coverage report
  4. Build → docker build → tag with git SHA → push to ECR
  5. Argo CD detects new tag → Syncs to staging namespace
  6. Smoke tests → curl health endpoints, run selenium checks
  7. Canary to production → 10% traffic → 50% → 100% (or rollback)

💡 Why CI? The "Merge Hell" Problem: Before CI, teams worked on separate feature branches for weeks. When they finally tried to merge: thousands of conflicts, broken tests, and nobody knew whose change broke what. CI solves this by forcing small, frequent merges: every push to main triggers a build + test. If the build fails, you know within minutes (not weeks) and the fix is small. The rule: "if it hurts, do it more often." Merging daily is less painful than merging monthly.

Trunk-Based Development: The gold standard for CI. All developers commit to a single branch ("trunk" / "main") at least daily. Feature flags hide incomplete work from users. This eliminates long-lived branches entirely. anihpj developers push small commits to main → CI runs in <10 minutes → feature flagged code is deployed but toggled off → QA tests with flag on → PM flips flag to launch.

Feature Flags vs. Branching: Instead of keeping code in a separate branch for 3 weeks (branching), you merge the incomplete feature to main behind a flag (feature flagging). The code is deployed but invisible. Benefits: you're continuously integrating, the code path is exercised in production, and launching = flipping a flag (not a deployment). Tools: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or simple env vars. Feature flags turn releases (code deployed) into launches (feature visible). They're a critical part of the platform engineering toolkit — the platform should provide a flagging service.

📖 Progressive Delivery Patterns — Beyond basic CI/CD, platform engineers implement advanced deployment strategies:

🔄Rolling Update

Default K8s strategy. Gradually replace old pods with new ones. Zero downtime but no traffic control.

Config: maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0

Rollback: kubectl rollout undo

🔵🟢Blue-Green

Run old (blue) and new (green) simultaneously. Switch all traffic at once via Service selector.

Benefit: Instant rollback — just switch back

Cost: 2× resources during deployment

🐤Canary

Send small % of traffic to new version. Monitor metrics. Gradually increase.

Tools: Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Istio traffic splitting

anihpj: 5%→25%→50%→100% over 30 min

Argo Rollouts: Extends K8s with Rollout CRD (superset of Deployment). Supports blue-green + canary with automated metric analysis (Prometheus → AnalysisTemplate → auto-promote or auto-rollback). Part of the Argo ecosystem every CNPE candidate should know.

2.7 Observability — The Three Pillars (and the Fourth)

📊Metrics

Numeric time-series data

"How many? How fast? How many errors?"

Tool: Prometheus + Grafana

anihpj: Request rate, latency p50/p95/p99, error rate, DB query time

📝Logs

Timestamped text records

"What happened at 14:32:05 UTC?"

Tool: Loki / Elasticsearch + Fluentd

anihpj: Django request logs, DB slow queries, container stdout/stderr

🔍Traces

Request journey across services

"Where is the bottleneck across 5 services?"

Tool: Tempo / Jaeger + OpenTelemetry

anihpj: Trace request from Ingress → Django → Postgres → Redis → Response

📖 The Fourth Pillar: Profiles — Continuous profiling (CPU/memory) with tools like Pyroscope or Parca. Shows exactly which line of code consumes the most resources. Also: Events (Kubernetes events, deployment events) are sometimes called a 5th pillar.

🧠 CNPE Exam: The Four Golden Signals (from Google SRE book) for EVERY service: Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation. If a CNPE question asks "what should you monitor?", start with these four.

💡 How Prometheus Actually Works — The Pull Model: Unlike most monitoring tools that WAIT for data to be pushed to them (push model), Prometheus actively SCRAPES metrics from targets (pull model). This is a fundamental architectural decision with big implications:

  1. Prometheus Server reads its config to find targets (e.g., anihpj-web-service:8000/metrics).
  2. Every 15-60 seconds (configurable), Prometheus HTTP GETs /metrics from each target.
  3. The target returns plain text in Prometheus exposition format (a simple line-based format). Any app can expose this — no agent needed.
  4. Prometheus stores the scraped data in its time-series database (TSDB) with the timestamp of the scrape.

Why pull, not push? Pull means Prometheus controls the scrape interval (no flood of data during outages). Pull means health checking is built-in (if scrape fails, the target is "down"). Pull means you don't need an agent on every pod — the app just exposes an HTTP endpoint. Downside: short-lived jobs (batch processes) may finish before Prometheus scrapes them — use the Pushgateway for those.

RED vs USE Methodology: Two complementary approaches for choosing WHAT to monitor:

MethodologyFocusMetricsApply To
REDUser-facing servicesRate (requests/sec), Errors (failed/sec), Duration (latency p50/p95/p99)anihpj-web HTTP endpoints, API handlers
USEInfrastructure resourcesUtilization (% busy), Saturation (queue depth), Errors (hardware/software errors)PostgreSQL, Redis, nodes, disks, network interfaces

Golden rule: RED for services, USE for resources. Together they cover everything. Golden Signals (Latency, Traffic, Errors, Saturation) are essentially RED + Saturation from USE.

2.8 Service Mesh, API Gateway, Ingress Controller

ComponentPurposeExamplesWhen to Use
Ingress ControllerLayer 7 HTTP routing into the clusterNGINX Ingress, Traefik, HAProxyExternal traffic → cluster (basic routing, TLS termination)
API GatewayAdvanced API managementKong, Ambassador, APISIXRate limiting, auth, request transformation, API versioning, developer portals
Service MeshService-to-service communication layerIstio (Envoy sidecar), Linkerd (Rust micro-proxy), Cilium (eBPF)mTLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, traffic splitting, observability between services
Internet
Ingress Controller (NGINX)Routes: anihpj.com/jobs → anihpj-web:8000
API Gateway (Kong) — OptionalRate limiting, JWT auth, API versioning
Service Mesh (Istio/Linkerd/Cilium)mTLS between anihpj-web → postgres, retries, circuit breaking, traces
Microservicesanihpj-web, postgres, redis
🧠 CNPE Exam: Gateway API — The Successor to Ingress — Kubernetes has a newer, more powerful standard called Gateway API (GA since v1.0). It's replacing Ingress as the recommended way to route traffic:
FeatureIngress (old)Gateway API (new)
Who manages it?Cluster admin onlyPlatform team defines Gateways; app devs define Routes
RoutingHost/path onlyHeader-based, weight-based, method-based routing
Traffic splitting❌ Not supported✅ Native (canary: 90% v1 / 10% v2)
ProtocolsHTTP/HTTPSHTTP, HTTPS, TCP, UDP, gRPC
Role-based❌ Single controller✅ Multiple GatewayClasses per team/use case

Why this matters: Gateway API enables the self-service model that CNPE Domain 3 tests — platform team provides Gateway infrastructure, developers define their own HTTPRoutes without cluster-admin access.

💡 mTLS, Circuit Breakers & Retry Storms — The Service Mesh Superpowers: These three patterns are why service meshes exist. Understanding them deeply is essential:

🔐 mTLS (Mutual TLS): Regular TLS = client verifies server. mTLS = BOTH verify each other. anihpj-web proves it IS anihpj-web to postgres, AND postgres proves it IS postgres to anihpj-web. Each service gets a certificate from the mesh control plane (cert-manager or Istio's built-in CA). Certificates are short-lived (24h default) and automatically rotated. Without mTLS: if an attacker compromises one container, they can talk to any other service on the network. With mTLS: the attacker's compromised container doesn't have a valid certificate — the mesh rejects its traffic. This is zero-trust networking at the application layer.

⚡ Circuit Breaker Pattern: Named after electrical circuit breakers that "trip" to prevent fires. In microservices, a circuit breaker monitors calls to a downstream service:

  • Closed (normal): Requests flow through. Circuit breaker counts failures.
  • Open (tripped): Too many failures → circuit breaker OPENS → ALL requests immediately fail without even calling the downstream. This is called "fail fast." The downstream gets time to recover instead of being hammered with more requests while it's already struggling.
  • Half-Open (testing): After a timeout, a FEW test requests are allowed through. If they succeed → circuit closes (back to normal). If they fail → circuit stays open.

anihpj example: If postgres starts timing out, the circuit breaker between anihpj-web → postgres trips. Instead of every user request piling up waiting for postgres (cascading failure), anihpj-web returns "Service temporarily unavailable" immediately. Postgres recovers. Circuit closes. Users see a degraded but functional experience.

🔄 The Retry Storm Problem: Service A calls Service B. B is slow. A retries. B gets MORE load from retries. B gets slower. A retries MORE. This positive feedback loop can take down an entire system. The fix: retries MUST use exponential backoff with jitter (wait 100ms, then 200ms, then 400ms, with random variation) and a maximum retry count (3 is typical). Service meshes enforce these retry policies so individual developers don't have to implement them. NEVER retry without backoff. NEVER retry indefinitely.

2.9 Policy as Code — OPA, Kyverno, Admission Controllers

What is Policy as Code? Security and compliance rules written as code, versioned in Git, automatically enforced at deploy time by Kubernetes admission controllers.

ToolLanguageHow It WorksBest For
OPA / GatekeeperRego (custom DSL)ConstraintTemplates define reusable policies, Constraints enforce them on specific resourcesComplex, cross-tool policies (not just K8s)
KyvernoYAML (no new language)Kubernetes-native — policies are just K8s resources, apply/validate/mutate/generateSimple K8s-only policies, fast learning curve
🧠 CNPE Exam: Pay attention to mutating vs. validating admission webhooks. Mutating webhooks run FIRST (they can add default values). Validating webhooks run SECOND (they can reject). Kyverno handles both.

💡 The Admission Webhook Flow — What Happens When You kubectl apply: Understanding this flow is critical for debugging "why is my pod stuck in CreateContainerConfigError?"

  1. Authentication: kubectl sends your credentials. K8s verifies: "Is this really Alice?"
  2. Authorization (RBAC): K8s checks: "Is Alice allowed to create Pods in namespace anihpj?"
  3. 🔵 MUTATING Admission Webhooks (Phase 1): Registered webhooks can MODIFY the resource. Kyverno mutate policies run here. Example: auto-add team label if missing. Pod is now modified in-flight.
  4. 🔴 VALIDATING Admission Webhooks (Phase 2): Registered webhooks can REJECT the resource. Kyverno validate policies run here. Example: reject if securityContext.runAsNonRoot != true. If ANY webhook says "no," the request is denied.
  5. etcd persistence: If all admission checks pass, the resource is written to etcd (the cluster's database).

Critical detail: Mutating webhooks have NO ORDER GUARANTEES. If Webhook A adds label X and Webhook B changes label X, the result is unpredictable. Design your mutate policies to not conflict. Validating webhooks see the resource AFTER all mutations, so they validate the final state.

📖 OPA Rego — What the Policy Language Looks Like: While Kyverno uses YAML, OPA uses a custom language called Rego. Here's the SAME "require team label" policy in both:

Kyverno (YAML)OPA/Gatekeeper (Rego)
 
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  rules:
  - name: check-team
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: [Pod]
    validate:
      message: "Pod must have team label"
      pattern:
        metadata:
          labels:
            team: "?*"
 
package k8s.requiredlabels

denied[msg] {
  input.review.kind.kind == "Pod"
  not input.request.object.metadata.labels.team
  msg := "Pod must have team label"
}

The tradeoff: Kyverno is immediately readable by anyone who knows YAML (every Kubernetes user). Rego requires learning a logic programming language but is far more expressive for complex policies. For the CNPE exam, know that BOTH exist, understand the mutating vs. validating distinction, and recognize that Kyverno = YAML (easier), OPA = Rego (more powerful for cross-tool policies).

📖 anihpj Policy Examples (Kyverno):

  • ❌ Block root: Any container running as UID 0 is rejected
  • ❌ Require resource limits: Deployments without CPU/memory limits are rejected
  • ❌ Block CRITICAL CVEs: Images with critical vulnerabilities are rejected
  • ❌ Enforce labels: Block any Deployment without app.kubernetes.io/part-of: anihpj label
  • ✅ Auto-add labels: Mutating policy adds team label if missing

2.10 SLO/SLI/SLA, Error Budgets & DORA Metrics

📏 SLI (Service Level Indicator)

The metric you measure

"99.9% of requests complete in under 200ms"

This is raw data from Prometheus / OpenTelemetry

🎯 SLO (Service Level Objective)

The target for your SLI

"99.95% of requests must complete in under 200ms over 30 days"

This is your internal goal — not a contract

📜 SLA (Service Level Agreement)

The contractual promise to customers

"99.9% uptime or 10% monthly credit"

Breaching this costs money — penalties apply

⚠️ Error Budget Calculation: Error Budget = 100% − SLO

If your SLO is 99.9% uptime, your error budget is 0.1% of the month:

  • 30 days × 24 hours × 60 minutes = 43,200 minutes/month
  • 0.1% × 43,200 = 43.2 minutes of allowed downtime per month
  • If you exceed 43.2 minutes, you blew your error budget — stop shipping features, fix reliability

💡 How to Define Good SLOs — The User-Journey Method: Don't SLO every metric. SLO the user's experience:

  1. Identify the critical user journey. For anihpj: "User searches for a job → sees results in under 2 seconds"
  2. Pick an SLI that measures that journey. Latency of /jobs/search/ endpoint, p95.
  3. Set the SLO slightly tighter than what users tolerate. If users abandon after 3s, SLO at 2s p95.
  4. Don't aim for 100%. The difference between 99.9% and 99.99% is 10× the engineering effort for marginal user benefit. Use your error budget to ship features faster.
  5. Review SLOs quarterly. If you consistently exceed your SLO with no user complaints, tighten it. If users complain but SLO is met, your SLI is measuring the wrong thing.

Common mistake: SLO-ing CPU usage or memory. Users don't care about CPU — they care about latency and availability. Measure what matters to the user, not what's convenient to measure.

💡 SLO Burn Rate Alerts — Don't Wait Until the Budget is Gone: The error budget tells you how much downtime you're ALLOWED. But waiting until the budget is exhausted is too late. You need alerts that warn you when you're BURNING budget too fast:

Burn Rate: How fast you're consuming your error budget relative to the SLO period. If your SLO allows 43.2 minutes of downtime per month and you've used 30 minutes in the first 3 days, your burn rate is catastrophic (you'll exhaust the budget in ~4.3 days).

Multi-Window, Multi-Burn-Rate Alerts (Google SRE best practice):

AlertBurn RateWindowPurposeExample
Page (urgent)14.4×1 hour"Something is VERY wrong RIGHT NOW" — you'll exhaust 2% of monthly budget in 1 hourWake up the on-call engineer at 3 AM
Page (urgent)6×6 hours"Something is wrong, needs attention soon" — you'll exhaust 5% of budget in 6 hoursPage on-call during business hours
Ticket (non-urgent)3×3 days"Trend is concerning" — you're burning budget faster than plannedCreate Jira ticket, investigate next business day

Why multiple windows? A 1-hour spike (brief outage) and a 3-day slow degradation (memory leak) are different problems requiring different responses. The 1-hour window catches acute incidents. The 3-day window catches chronic issues before they exhaust your budget. Both are needed.

Burn rate formula: Burn Rate = (Error Rate × Alert Window) / Error Budget. If your error budget is 0.1% (43.2 min/month) and your error rate is 1% sustained over 1 hour: Burn Rate = (0.01 × 60 min) / 43.2 min = 1.39×. That's above 1× — you're burning faster than the budget allows. Alert!

📊 DORA Metrics — The 4 Key DevOps Performance Indicators:

Metric🏆 Elite🥇 High🥈 Medium🥉 Low
Deployment FrequencyOn-demand (multiple/day)Daily–WeeklyWeekly–MonthlyMonthly–6 months
Lead Time for Changes< 1 hour1 day–1 week1 week–1 month1–6 months
MTTR (Mean Time to Restore)< 1 hour< 1 day1 day–1 week> 1 week
Change Failure Rate0–5%5–10%10–15%45–60%

                        │  📊 Raw data, no target      │
                        └──────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  GOLDEN RULE: SLO must be STRICTER than SLA.
  If SLA = 99.9% uptime, set SLO = 99.95% uptime.
  That 0.05% gap is your SAFETY BUFFER — you burn error budget BEFORE
  breaching the SLA (and paying penalties).
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
