💡 What Each Domain Actually Tests — Task Type Breakdown

Knowing the weight percentages is helpful. Knowing what KINDS of tasks you'll face is actionable. Here's what each domain's exam tasks look like:

DomainWeightTypical Task TypesExample Task
Domain 1: Architecture15%Upgrade a cluster, configure etcd backup, troubleshoot control plane, set up multi-tenancy with namespaces and resource quotas"Configure RBAC so Team A can only deploy to namespace 'team-a' with max 4 CPUs and 8GB RAM."
Domain 2: GitOps & CD25%Create Argo CD Application, configure sync policies, set up Helm chart deployment, write a CI/CD pipeline, configure progressive delivery"Create an Argo CD Application that deploys the anihpj Helm chart from the 'main' branch with automated sync and pruning enabled."
Domain 3: Platform APIs25%Create a CRD, write an Operator, configure Backstage component, design a self-service workflow, expose a service via Gateway API"Create a CRD 'Database' with fields for engine, version, and size. Deploy an Operator that provisions an RDS instance when a Database CR is created."
Domain 4: Observability20%Configure ServiceMonitor, write PromQL queries, set up Grafana dashboard, configure Loki log pipeline, define SLO alerts"Create a Prometheus alert that fires when the anihpj-web error rate exceeds 5% over a 5-minute window. The alert must route to the 'platform-oncall' Slack channel."
Domain 5: Security15%Write Kyverno/OPA policy, configure NetworkPolicy, set up mTLS, scan images with Trivy, configure Falco rules, implement RBAC"Create a Kyverno ClusterPolicy that blocks any Pod using the 'latest' image tag and mutates deployments to add 'app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: platform' label."

Key insight: Notice that the highest-weighted domains (2 and 3) are the most automation-heavy — they test whether you can build systems that work without you. The exam isn't testing your ability to MANUALLY operate a cluster (that's CKA). It's testing your ability to BUILD PLATFORMS that make manual operation unnecessary.

💡 CNPE Exam Time Management — 2 Hours, ~25-30 Tasks

The CNPE is a 2-hour performance-based exam in a live terminal. Here's how to manage your time:

PhaseTimeWhat to Do
Setup (first 5 min)0:00–0:05Read ALL task descriptions first (don't solve yet). Flag easy tasks (ones you know immediately). Flag hard tasks (come back later). Set kubectl context. Verify cluster access.
Easy Tasks (next 30 min)0:05–0:35Solve all ~10 easy tasks first. These are typically: create a namespace, expose a service, label a resource, check logs. Build momentum and confidence. You should finish each in <3 min.
Medium Tasks (next 45 min)0:35–1:20Solve ~10-12 medium tasks: configure Argo CD sync, write a Kyverno policy, create a ServiceMonitor, set up an Ingress with TLS. These take 4-7 min each. If stuck for >5 min, flag and move on.
Hard Tasks (next 25 min)1:20–1:45Solve 3-5 hard tasks: create a CRD with validation schema, write an Operator reconciliation loop, configure multi-cluster GitOps. These test deep understanding. Use kubectl explain and --dry-run=client to verify YAML before applying.
Review (last 15 min)1:45–2:00Re-check ALL tasks: did you save output to the correct file? Did you use the right namespace? Did you apply (not just create) resources? The CNPE grades EXACT output — spelling and namespaces matter.

Critical exam tips:

  • 🔑 Use context switching carefully: Every task specifies a kubectl context. The WRONG context = WRONG cluster = ZERO points even if your commands are correct. Always run kubectl config current-context before starting a task.
  • 📝 Read output requirements: Some tasks say "save the output to /tmp/answer.txt." If you solve the task but don't save the output → ZERO points. Read the LAST LINE of each task first.
  • ⚡ Use imperative commands with --dry-run: kubectl create deployment my-app --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml generates correct YAML in seconds. Don't hand-write YAML unless required.
  • 📚 kubectl explain is your friend: Can't remember a CRD field? kubectl explain deployment.spec.template.spec.containers.resources shows the full schema. The exam terminal has this available.
  • ⏱️ Don't fixate: If you spend 7+ minutes on one task, you're losing time for 2-3 easier tasks. Flag it, move on, come back if time permits. Partial credit is rare — incomplete answers usually score 0.

🏋️ Chapter 3 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

The CNPE is a performance-based exam — you solve tasks in a live Linux terminal. Practice these drills in your lab environment until you can complete each within the target time.

⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 3.1 — Classify CNCF Projects by Maturity

Create a sorted list of CNCF projects and classify them by maturity level.

  1. Run kubectl get pods -n argocd to see Argo CD components — this is a Graduated project
  2. Check if Kyverno is installed: kubectl get pods -n kyverno — an Incubating project
  3. Write a shell script that categorizes 5 CNCF projects into Graduated/Incubating/Sandbox and prints a summary table
💡 Hint: Use echo and printf to create a formatted table. Reference: K8s=Graduated, Prometheus=Graduated, OpenTelemetry=Incubating, Kyverno=Incubating, Backstage=Incubating.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Check Argo CD (Graduated)
kubectl get pods -n argocd 2>/dev/null || echo "Argo CD not installed (install with: kubectl create namespace argocd && kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml)"

# Step 2: Check Kyverno (Incubating)
kubectl get pods -n kyverno 2>/dev/null || echo "Kyverno not installed"

# Step 3: Maturity classification script
cat > classify-cncf.sh << 'SCRIPT'
#!/bin/bash
echo "PROJECT          MATURITY"
echo "──────────────────────────"
echo "Kubernetes       🎓 Graduated"
echo "Prometheus       🎓 Graduated"
echo "Argo CD          🎓 Graduated"
echo "Helm             🎓 Graduated"
echo "Envoy            🎓 Graduated"
echo "Falco            🎓 Graduated"
echo "OpenTelemetry    🥚 Incubating"
echo "Kyverno          🥚 Incubating"
echo "Backstage        🥚 Incubating"
echo "Crossplane       🥚 Incubating"
echo "cert-manager     🥚 Incubating"
SCRIPT
chmod +x classify-cncf.sh
./classify-cncf.sh
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 3.2 — Install Argo CD (Graduated GitOps Tool)

Install Argo CD in your cluster — the most important CNCF Graduated GitOps tool.

  1. Create the argocd namespace
  2. Install Argo CD from the official manifest
  3. Wait for all pods to be Running
  4. Get the initial admin password
  5. Port-forward the Argo CD server and access the UI at https://localhost:8080
💡 Hint: Argo CD install manifest is at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml. The admin password is stored in a Secret named argocd-initial-admin-secret.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create namespace
kubectl create namespace argocd

# Step 2: Install Argo CD
kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml

# Step 3: Wait for pods
kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n argocd --timeout=300s
kubectl get pods -n argocd
# EXPECTED: argocd-server, argocd-repo-server, argocd-application-controller, argocd-redis

# Step 4: Get admin password
kubectl -n argocd get secret argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath="{.data.password}" | base64 -d
echo  # newline

# Step 5: Port-forward and access
kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:443 &
# Open: https://localhost:8080
# Username: admin
# Password: (from step 4)
⏱️ Target: 6 minutes
Drill 3.3 — Install Prometheus Stack (Graduated Monitoring)

Install the kube-prometheus-stack using Helm — the CNCF Graduated monitoring standard.

  1. Add the Prometheus Community Helm repo
  2. Install kube-prometheus-stack in the monitoring namespace
  3. Verify Prometheus, Grafana, and AlertManager pods are running
  4. Port-forward Grafana and log in (default: admin / prom-operator)
  5. Navigate to the Kubernetes/Compute Resources/Pods dashboard
💡 Hint: helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts, then helm install prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack -n monitoring --create-namespace
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Add Helm repo
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update

# Step 2: Install kube-prometheus-stack
helm install prometheus prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  -n monitoring --create-namespace

# Step 3: Verify pods
kubectl get pods -n monitoring
# EXPECTED: prometheus-prometheus-0, alertmanager-prometheus-0,
#           prometheus-grafana-*, prometheus-kube-state-metrics-*,
#           prometheus-prometheus-node-exporter-*

# Step 4: Access Grafana
kubectl port-forward svc/prometheus-grafana -n monitoring 3000:80 &
# Open: http://localhost:3000
# Username: admin
# Password: prom-operator

# Step 5: Explore dashboards
# In Grafana: Dashboards → Browse → Kubernetes / Compute Resources / Pod
# This shows CPU and memory usage for all pods — a CNPE exam skill
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 3.4 — Map anihpj Components to Platform Layers

Given hypothetical anihpj components, determine which Platform Stack layer each belongs to.

  1. Create a file layer-mapping.txt with columns: Component | Layer | Domain
  2. Classify: Argo CD Application for anihpj-web
  3. Classify: Prometheus ServiceMonitor for anihpj-web
  4. Classify: Kyverno ClusterPolicy blocking root containers
  5. Classify: Backstage Component representing anihpj-web in the developer portal
  6. Classify: Kubernetes Deployment for anihpj-web (with resource requests/limits)
💡 Hint: Use the Platform Stack table from 3.5. Each component maps to exactly one layer.
📝 View Solution 
# Create mapping file
cat > layer-mapping.txt << 'EOF'
COMPONENT                         | PLATFORM LAYER       | CNPE DOMAIN
──────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────┼──────────────────────
Argo CD Application (anihpj-web) | 🚀 Delivery           | Domain 2: GitOps & CD
Prometheus ServiceMonitor         | 📊 Observability      | Domain 4: Obs & Ops
Kyverno ClusterPolicy (no-root)  | 🔒 Security           | Domain 5: Security
Backstage Component (anihpj-web) | 👨‍💻 Self-Service       | Domain 3: Platform APIs
K8s Deployment (anihpj-web)      | ⚙️ Orchestration      | Domain 1: Architecture
EOF
cat layer-mapping.txt

# KEY RULE:
# If a developer interacts with it directly → Self-Service (Domain 3)
# If it handles deployment/syncing → Delivery (Domain 2)
# If it's about running containers → Orchestration (Domain 1)
# If it monitors/measures → Observability (Domain 4)
# If it enforces rules/policies → Security (Domain 5)
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 3.5 — Install and Configure cert-manager (Incubating)

cert-manager automates TLS certificate management — an essential Incubating CNCF project.

  1. Install cert-manager using the static manifest
  2. Verify the cert-manager pods are running in cert-manager namespace
  3. Create a self-signed ClusterIssuer named selfsigned-issuer (for lab use)
  4. Create a Certificate resource for anihpj.local
  5. Verify the certificate was issued and the Secret exists
💡 Hint: kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/latest/download/cert-manager.yaml. For ClusterIssuer, use kind: ClusterIssuer with selfSigned: {}.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Install cert-manager
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.14.5/cert-manager.yaml

# Step 2: Verify pods
kubectl get pods -n cert-manager
# EXPECTED: cert-manager-*, cert-manager-cainjector-*, cert-manager-webhook-*

# Step 3: Create self-signed ClusterIssuer
cat > selfsigned-issuer.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: selfsigned-issuer
spec:
  selfSigned: {}
EOF
kubectl apply -f selfsigned-issuer.yaml

# Step 4: Create Certificate
cat > anihpj-cert.yaml << 'EOF'
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: anihpj-local-tls
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  secretName: anihpj-local-tls
  issuerRef:
    name: selfsigned-issuer
    kind: ClusterIssuer
  dnsNames:
  - anihpj.local
EOF
kubectl apply -f anihpj-cert.yaml

# Step 5: Verify
kubectl get certificate -n anihpj
# anihpj-local-tls   True    anihpj-local-tls
kubectl get secret anihpj-local-tls -n anihpj
# Contains: tls.crt, tls.key
# This is automated TLS — a core platform engineering pattern
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 3.6 — Verify CNCF Project Status with kubectl

Check which CNCF projects are installed in your cluster and verify their components.

  1. List ALL namespaces in your cluster that contain CNCF project components
  2. For each CNCF project namespace, count how many pods are running
  3. Identify which Platform Stack layer each installed project belongs to
  4. Print a summary table: Project | Namespace | Pod Count | CNCF Maturity | Platform Layer
💡 Hint: kubectl get ns to find namespaces. Check for: argocd, monitoring, cert-manager, kyverno, istio-system. Count pods with kubectl get pods -n <ns> --no-headers | wc -l
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1-2: Find CNCF namespaces and count pods
for ns in argocd monitoring cert-manager kyverno istio-system falco; do
  if kubectl get ns $ns &>/dev/null; then
    COUNT=$(kubectl get pods -n $ns --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
    echo "$ns: $COUNT pods"
  else
    echo "$ns: NOT INSTALLED"
  fi
done

# Step 3-4: Summary table
cat > cncf-summary.txt << 'EOF'
PROJECT        NAMESPACE       PODS   MATURITY     PLATFORM LAYER
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Argo CD        argocd          4      🎓 Graduated  🚀 Delivery
Prometheus     monitoring      5      🎓 Graduated  📊 Observability
Grafana        monitoring      1      🎓 Graduated  📊 Observability
cert-manager   cert-manager    3      🥚 Incubating 🔒 Security
EOF
cat cncf-summary.txt
# This is EXACTLY the kind of analysis the CNPE exam expects
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 3.7 — Implement the Trail Map: Containerize → CI → Orchestrate

Follow the Cloud Native Trail Map by deploying anihpj-web through steps 1-3.

  1. Step 1 (Containerize): Build a Docker image for anihpj-web with tag trail-map:v1
  2. Step 2 (CI/CD): Push the image to a registry and update the Deployment with the new tag
  3. Step 3 (Orchestrate): Deploy to Kubernetes and verify the pod is running with the correct image
💡 Hint: Use docker build -t anihpj-web:trail-map-v1 ., kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-web django=anihpj-web:trail-map-v1
📝 View Solution 
# STEP 1: Containerize (Developer responsibility)
cd /path/to/anihpj
docker build -t anihpj-web:trail-map-v1 .
# This is the ONLY step developers do

# STEP 2: CI/CD (Platform provides pipeline)
# In production: GitHub Actions builds and pushes
# For this drill, simulate CI:
docker tag anihpj-web:trail-map-v1 localhost:5000/anihpj-web:trail-map-v1
docker push localhost:5000/anihpj-web:trail-map-v1
kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-web django=localhost:5000/anihpj-web:trail-map-v1 -n anihpj

# STEP 3: Orchestrate (Platform provides K8s)
kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.containers[*].image}'
# Should show: localhost:5000/anihpj-web:trail-map-v1

# THE INSIGHT:
# Developer does Step 1 (docker build)
# Platform provides Steps 2-3 (registry + CI pipeline + K8s cluster)
# This is the Platform Engineering contract
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 3.8 — Compare Two CNCF Tools for the Same Problem

The CNCF often has multiple tools for the same use case. Compare Argo CD vs Flux for GitOps.

  1. List the key features of Argo CD (Graduated)
  2. List the key features of Flux (Incubating)
  3. Create a comparison table: Feature | Argo CD | Flux | Winner
  4. Write a recommendation for which to use in the anihpj platform with reasoning
💡 Hint: Argo CD has a rich Web UI. Flux has built-in image update automation. Both support Helm and Kustomize.
📝 View Solution 
# Create comparison file
cat > argo-vs-flux.txt << 'EOF'
FEATURE               ARGO CD (Graduated)     FLUX (Incubating)      WINNER
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Web UI                ✅ Rich dashboard       ❌ CLI-first            Argo CD
Multi-tenancy         ✅ Projects/AppProjects  ⚠️ Instance per team    Argo CD
Image auto-update     ⚠️ Separate component   ✅ Built-in CRDs         Flux
Helm support          ✅ Native               ✅ Native (HelmRelease)  Tie
Kustomize support     ✅ Native               ✅ Native                Tie
Sync frequency        Every 3 min (default)   Every 1-10 min          Flux (faster)
CNCF Status           🎓 Graduated            🥚 Incubating           Argo CD
Learning curve        Medium (Web UI helps)   Medium (CRDs only)      Argo CD
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
RECOMMENDATION FOR ANIHpj:
Use ARGO CD — Graduated status means production-proven, the Web UI
is essential for a multi-team platform (each team sees only their apps),
and Argo CD's App of Apps pattern simplifies managing many applications.
Use Flux IF: you prefer everything-as-CRDs and need built-in image updates.
EOF
cat argo-vs-flux.txt
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 3.9 — Explain CNCF Maturity to a Non-Technical Stakeholder

A product manager asks: "Why does it matter if a tool is 'Graduated' or 'Incubating'?" Write a 3-sentence explanation.

  1. Write an analogy comparing CNCF maturity to something non-technical (e.g., building codes, medical trials, academic degrees)
  2. List 3 risks of using a Sandbox project in production
  3. State the anihpj platform's default policy for project maturity adoption
💡 Hint: "Graduated = FDA-approved medicine. Incubating = Phase 3 clinical trial. Sandbox = Lab experiment."
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: The Analogy
cat > maturity-analogy.txt << 'EOF'
CNCF MATURITY = BUILDING CODES FOR YOUR PLATFORM

🎓 Graduated = International Building Code (IBC)
   "Every skyscraper uses this. Proven. Inspected. Insured."

🥚 Incubating = Proposed code amendment
   "Many builders use it. Under review. Probably safe."

🧪 Sandbox = A student's architecture thesis
   "Interesting idea. Might work. No guarantees."

You wouldn't build a hospital using a student's thesis.
Don't build your production platform on Sandbox projects.
EOF
cat maturity-analogy.txt

# Step 2: 3 Risks of Sandbox in Production
# 1. NO SECURITY AUDIT — Sandbox projects haven't been audited.
#    You don't know if there are critical vulnerabilities.
# 2. ABANDONMENT RISK — Sandbox projects may lose maintainers.
#    Your platform now depends on unmaintained software.
# 3. BREAKING CHANGES — No stability guarantees.
#    An update could break your platform with no migration path.

# Step 3: anihpj Adoption Policy
# DEFAULT: Use Graduated projects for all production workloads.
# EVALUATE: Incubating projects on a case-by-case basis
#           (OpenTelemetry = yes, it's de facto standard).
# AVOID: Sandbox projects in production unless no alternative exists.
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 3.10 — Build a Platform Stack Diagram with kubectl

Use kubectl to inspect your cluster and map running components to the 5-layer Platform Stack.

  1. List all Deployments across all namespaces — these belong to the Orchestration Layer
  2. Find all Ingresses — these belong to the Delivery Layer (routing traffic)
  3. Find all ServiceMonitors (if Prometheus is installed) — these belong to Observability
  4. Find all NetworkPolicies — these belong to the Security Layer
  5. Generate a report showing how many resources exist in each Platform Stack layer
💡 Hint: kubectl get deploy -A, kubectl get ingress -A, kubectl get servicemonitor -A, kubectl get netpol -A
📝 View Solution 
# Generate Platform Stack Report
cat > platform-stack-report.sh << 'SCRIPT'
#!/bin/bash
echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════"
echo "  ANIHpj PLATFORM STACK INVENTORY"
echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════"
echo ""

# Self-Service Layer (CRDs — platform APIs)
CRDS=$(kubectl get crd --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
echo "👨‍💻 SELF-SERVICE LAYER (Domain 3)"
echo "   CRDs installed: $CRDS"
echo ""

# Delivery Layer
DEPLOYS=$(kubectl get deploy -A --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
INGRESSES=$(kubectl get ingress -A --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
echo "🚀 DELIVERY LAYER (Domain 2)"
echo "   Deployments: $DEPLOYS"
echo "   Ingresses: $INGRESSES"
echo ""

# Orchestration Layer
SERVICES=$(kubectl get svc -A --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
echo "⚙️ ORCHESTRATION LAYER (Domain 1)"
echo "   Services: $SERVICES"
echo ""

# Observability Layer
MONITORS=$(kubectl get servicemonitor -A --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
echo "📊 OBSERVABILITY LAYER (Domain 4)"
echo "   ServiceMonitors: $MONITORS"
echo ""

# Security Layer
POLICIES=$(kubectl get networkpolicy -A --no-headers 2>/dev/null | wc -l)
echo "🔒 SECURITY LAYER (Domain 5)"
echo "   NetworkPolicies: $POLICIES"
echo ""
echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════"
SCRIPT
chmod +x platform-stack-report.sh
./platform-stack-report.sh

🌊 The Platform Stack as a Maritime Port — Where Every CNCF Tool Docks

Think of your platform as a modern shipping port. Each layer of the platform stack is a different zone in the port — and each CNCF tool is a piece of equipment operating in that zone. This mental model helps you instantly understand where any tool fits and why layers depend on each other.

🏗️ THE PLATFORM PORT — 5 Zones = 5 CNPE Domains
Every CNCF tool operates in one of these five port zones
ZONE 1 · SELF-SERVICE TERMINAL (CNPE Domain 3 — 25%)
🏢 DEVELOPER PORTAL
Backstage (Incubating)
kubectl apply -f template.yaml

Like the port's customer service desk — developers come here to request resources, discover services, and create new applications from templates. One-click environment provisioning.

📋 SELF-SERVICE APIS
Crossplane CRDs (Incubating)
kubectl apply -f database-claim.yaml

Like automated ordering kiosks — developers request a database via a simple YAML claim, and the platform provisions it automatically. No ticket, no wait.

⬇ ⬇ ⬇
ZONE 2 · DELIVERY PIPELINE (CNPE Domain 2 — 25%)
🔄 GITOPS CONTROLLER
Argo CD (Graduated)
argocd app sync anihpj

Like the port's automated crane system — watches Git for changes, automatically syncs desired state to the cluster. If something drifts, it self-heals. Git is truth.

📦 PACKAGE MANAGER
Helm (Graduated)
helm install anihpj ./chart

Like standardized shipping containers — packages Kubernetes manifests with templating and versioning. Install Prometheus, Grafana, or your own apps via charts.

⬇ ⬇ ⬇
ZONE 3 · ORCHESTRATION ENGINE (CNPE Domain 1 — 15%)
☸️ CONTAINER ORCHESTRATOR
Kubernetes (Graduated)
kubectl get pods -n anihpj

The port itself — schedules containers onto nodes, manages networking, storage, and scaling. Everything runs on K8s. The foundation of the entire platform.

💾 CLUSTER DATABASE
etcd (Graduated)
etcdctl snapshot save backup.db

The port's logbook — stores ALL cluster state. If the logbook is lost, the port has amnesia. Back it up religiously.

⬇ ⬇ ⬇
ZONE 4 · OBSERVABILITY TOWER (CNPE Domain 4 — 20%)
📊 METRICS
Prometheus (Graduated)
rate(http_requests_total[5m])

Like the port's traffic monitoring system — scrapes metrics from every service, stores time-series data, fires alerts. The universal monitoring standard.

🔍 TRACING
OpenTelemetry (Incubating)
trace_id: 4bf92f3577b34da6

Like GPS trackers on every shipment — follows a request as it travels through every microservice. Pinpoints exactly where latency lives.

⬇ ⬇ ⬇
ZONE 5 · SECURITY PERIMETER (CNPE Domain 5 — 15%)
🛡️ POLICY ENGINE
Kyverno (Incubating)
kubectl apply -f policy.yaml

Like the port's security checkpoint — every container entering the cluster must pass policy validation. No root containers. No latest tags. No exceptions.

🔍 RUNTIME DETECTION
Falco (Graduated)
falco — watch syscalls

Like security cameras monitoring every dock — detects anomalous behavior at runtime using eBPF. Alerts on unexpected process spawns, file access, network connections.

💡 The Port Dependency Chain — Why Layers Are Sequential

Zone 3 (Kubernetes) must exist before Zone 2 (Argo CD) can deploy to it. Zone 2 must exist before Zone 1 (Backstage) can trigger deployments. Zone 4 (Prometheus) can only monitor what Zone 3 is running. Zone 5 (Kyverno) protects everything in Zones 1-4. This is why the Cloud Native Trail Map is sequential — each step depends on the previous one.

🎓Graduated Projects20+ battle-tested CNCF projects. Default choice for production.
🥚Incubating Projects~30 projects maturing fast. Evaluate against Graduated alternatives.
🗺️Trail Map Steps 2-6Platform engineer owns CI/CD, Orchestration, Observability, Mesh, Security.
🏗️5 Platform LayersEach maps to a CNPE domain. Every tool fits into one layer.
☸️K8s is CentralThe orchestrator everything runs on. All other tools extend it.
🔒Security is Layer 5Not an afterthought — built into every layer from admission to runtime.
How Chapter 3 Maps to CNPE Exam Tasks

The CNPE exam won't ask "What is a CNCF Graduated project?" Instead, it tests whether you can SELECT the right tool for a task:

  • "Set up GitOps continuous delivery" → Argo CD (Graduated) or Flux (Graduated). Both are correct; Argo CD has a UI, Flux is CLI-first.
  • "Configure monitoring and alerting" → Prometheus (Graduated) + Grafana. Prometheus for metrics, Grafana for dashboards.
  • "Implement policy enforcement" → Kyverno (Incubating) for YAML-based policies, OPA/Gatekeeper (Graduated) for Rego-based policies.
  • "Set up service mesh" → Istio (Graduated) for feature-rich Envoy-based mesh, Linkerd (Graduated) for lightweight Rust-based mesh, Cilium (Graduated) for eBPF-based.
⚠️ Tool Selection Traps on the CNPE Exam

Common ways candidates lose points on tool selection:

  • Using a Sandbox project for a production-critical task — Use a Graduated project instead. Sandbox projects can disappear or change APIs.
  • Using two tools that solve the same problem — Pick ONE per layer. Don't run Argo CD AND Flux. Don't run Kyverno AND OPA (unless you have a specific reason).
  • Forgetting that K8s is the orchestrator — Everything runs ON Kubernetes. The platform stack layers are built ON TOP of K8s, not alongside it.
Q1: Which CNCF project would you use for GitOps continuous delivery, and what maturity level is it?

▶ Show Answer
Argo CD (Graduated) or Flux (Graduated). Both are pull-based GitOps tools. Argo CD has a rich web UI and multi-tenancy via Projects. Flux is CLI-first with built-in image update automation. Both are CNCF Graduated and equally valid for the exam.
Q2: What steps of the Cloud Native Trail Map does a platform engineer own?

▶ Show Answer
Steps 2-6: CI/CD, Orchestration, Observability, Service Mesh, Security & Policy. The developer only owns Step 1 (Containerization). The platform engineer builds and operates everything else as a service.
Q3: Why is the Platform Stack model (5 layers) more useful than the CNCF Landscape map (200+ projects)?

▶ Show Answer
The Platform Stack organizes tools by FUNCTION (Self-Service, Delivery, Orchestration, Observability, Security). The CNCF Landscape organizes by maturity (Graduated/Incubating/Sandbox). The Platform Stack tells you WHERE a tool fits in your architecture. The Landscape tells you HOW MATURE it is. You need both mental models, but the Platform Stack is more actionable for building platforms.
🚀 Beyond CNPE — The CNCF Ecosystem in 2026 and Beyond

The CNCF landscape evolves rapidly. Here's what's emerging that every platform engineer should watch:

  • Cilium + eBPF is eating the world: Cilium (Graduated 2023) uses eBPF to replace kube-proxy, implement NetworkPolicies, provide service mesh, and enable observability — all without sidecars. This is the future of K8s networking. Projects like Hubble (Cilium's observability layer) and Tetragon (runtime security) extend eBPF further.
  • Dapr (Incubating): Distributed Application Runtime. Provides building blocks for microservices: service invocation, state management, pub/sub, secret management. Abstracts cloud-specific SDKs. Think of it as "a service mesh for application developers."
  • Platform Engineering Maturity Model: The CNCF is developing a formal maturity model for platform engineering (similar to CMMI for software). Levels: Provisional → Operationalized → Scalable → Optimizing. The CNPE certifies you at the Operationalized level.
  • Green Cloud Native: Kepler (Sandbox) measures energy consumption per pod. Keda (Incubating) scales to zero when idle. Sustainability is becoming a first-class concern — expect CNPE exam content on this within 2 years.

📖 Chapter 3 Summary: The CNCF Landscape can be overwhelming, but the Platform Stack model simplifies it: every tool fits into one of 5 layers (Self-Service, Delivery, Orchestration, Observability, Security). As a platform engineer, you don't need to master all 200+ projects — you need to know which Graduated and Incubating projects solve specific problems for each layer. The Cloud Native Trail Map shows the adoption order: Containerize → CI/CD → Orchestrate → Observe → Service Mesh → Security. Platform engineers own steps 2-6. The anihpj platform uses: K8s (orchestration), Argo CD (delivery), Backstage + CRDs (self-service), Prometheus + Grafana + Loki + Tempo (observability), and Kyverno + Falco (security).

💡 Why This Architecture Matters for the CNPE Exam

This 3-tier architecture is the canonical cloud native application pattern. The CNPE exam expects you to understand:

  • Separation of concerns: Each tier has ONE responsibility. Web serves users. API serves data. Database stores state. Cache accelerates reads. This is microservices thinking — even within a single application.
  • Independent scalability: If your job listing page gets 10,000 hits/second, you scale the Web tier (more Django replicas). You don't touch the database. This is horizontal scaling.
  • State management: PostgreSQL is STATEFUL (needs persistent storage, StatefulSet). Django + Redis + Nginx are STATELESS (can be killed and recreated anytime, Deployment). Knowing which is which is critical for K8s design.

4.2 The Web Tier — Django Templates + Nginx + Gunicorn

The web tier handles all user-facing HTTP requests. It's a three-layer pipeline: Nginx receives the request → Gunicorn runs the Django application → Django processes the business logic.

📖 The Django `jobpost` App — Core Domain Model

The jobpost app is the heart of anihpj. It models the core entities of a job board:

  • Employer: Companies that post jobs. Has name, description, website.
  • Job: A job listing. Belongs to an Employer. Has title, description, requirements. Filterable by skill, location, and author.
  • Skill: Skills required for a job (Python, Kubernetes, Docker). Many-to-many with Job.
  • Location: Where the job is (Remote, New York, London). Each Job has one Location.
  • Author: The user who created the job listing. Each Job has one Author.

Filtering flow: User visits /jobs/?skill=Python&location=Remote → Django ORM queries: Job.objects.filter(skills__name="Python", location__name="Remote") → Returns HTML page with matching job listings.

ComponentWhat It DoesWhy Not The Alternative
NginxReverse proxy: receives HTTP requests, serves static files directly (CSS, JS, images), proxies dynamic requests to Gunicorn on port 8000. Handles TLS termination.Django's built-in server (manage.py runserver) is SINGLE-THREADED and serves static files slowly. In production, use Nginx.
GunicornProduction WSGI server. Spawns 4 worker processes (configurable). Each worker runs a copy of the Django app. Handles concurrent requests.runserver handles ONE request at a time. Gunicorn handles N requests in parallel (one per worker).
DjangoPython web framework. Handles routing (URL → view), ORM (Python → SQL), templates (HTML rendering), admin interface, authentication.Flask/FastAPI are lighter but lack Django's built-in admin, ORM, and authentication. For a job board with structured data, Django's batteries-included approach is ideal.
💡 Nginx Configuration — The Reverse Proxy in Action

Here's the Nginx configuration that routes traffic inside the anihpj-web container. Understanding this helps you debug "why is the static file returning 404?" or "why is the API returning HTML instead of JSON?":

# /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf — inside the container
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name anihpj.local;

    # Static files: Nginx serves these directly (FAST, no Python)
    location /static/ {
        alias /app/staticfiles/;
        expires 30d;
        add_header Cache-Control "public, immutable";
    }

    # Django Admin and regular pages → proxy to Gunicorn
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_connect_timeout 10s;
        proxy_read_timeout 30s;
    }

    # Health check (used by K8s liveness/readiness probes)
    location /healthz {
        access_log off;
        return 200 "healthy\n";
        add_header Content-Type text/plain;
    }
}

Key insights: (1) Static files bypass Django entirely — Nginx serves them directly from disk, ~100x faster than Python. (2) The X-Forwarded-* headers tell Django the real client IP. Without these, all requests appear to come from 127.0.0.1. (3) /healthz is critical — Kubernetes uses it for liveness/readiness probes. If this endpoint fails, K8s restarts the pod.

📖 Django ORM Deep Dive — How Python Becomes SQL

The Django ORM (Object-Relational Mapper) is the bridge between Python code and PostgreSQL. Understanding this helps you debug slow queries and optimize database performance — skills directly tested on the CNPE exam when troubleshooting platform performance issues:

# WHAT YOU WRITE (Python — Django ORM)
jobs = Job.objects.filter(
    skills__name="Python",
    location__name="Remote"
).select_related('employer', 'author').order_by('-posted_date')[:20]

# WHAT DJANGO GENERATES (SQL — sent to PostgreSQL)
SELECT
    "jobpost_job"."id",
    "jobpost_job"."title",
    "jobpost_job"."description",
    "jobpost_job"."employer_id",
    "jobpost_job"."location_id",
    "jobpost_job"."author_id",
    "jobpost_job"."posted_date",
    "jobpost_employer"."id",
    "jobpost_employer"."name",
    "auth_user"."id",
    "auth_user"."username"
FROM "jobpost_job"
INNER JOIN "jobpost_employer" ON ("jobpost_job"."employer_id" = "jobpost_employer"."id")
INNER JOIN "auth_user" ON ("jobpost_job"."author_id" = "auth_user"."id")
INNER JOIN "jobpost_job_skills" ON ("jobpost_job"."id" = "jobpost_job_skills"."job_id")
INNER JOIN "jobpost_skill" ON ("jobpost_job_skills"."skill_id" = "jobpost_skill"."id")
INNER JOIN "jobpost_location" ON ("jobpost_job"."location_id" = "jobpost_location"."id")
WHERE ("jobpost_skill"."name" = 'Python' AND "jobpost_location"."name" = 'Remote')
ORDER BY "jobpost_job"."posted_date" DESC
LIMIT 20;

Key ORM patterns every platform engineer should know:

  • select_related() = SQL JOIN: Follows foreign keys in ONE query. Without it, Django makes N+1 queries (1 for the jobs list, then 1 query PER JOB for employer and author). With select_related('employer', 'author'), it's all 1 query. This is the #1 cause of slow Django pages.
  • prefetch_related() = separate query + Python join: For many-to-many relationships (Job ↔ Skill). Does 2 queries: one for jobs, one for skills, then joins in Python. More efficient than N+1 for M2M fields.
  • Query logging in production: Set DEBUG=False but log slow queries (>200ms) via Django's logging config. Feed those logs to Loki. If you see repeated identical slow queries, add an index or use caching.
📖 Django settings.py — Environment-Aware Configuration

The bridge between Django and Kubernetes is environment variables. Django reads config from env vars, and K8s injects them via ConfigMaps and Secrets. This is 12-Factor App Factor III (Config) in action:

# anihpj/settings.py — Environment-aware configuration
import os

# SECURITY: NEVER hardcode secrets. Read from environment.
SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get('DJANGO_SECRET_KEY')
if not SECRET_KEY:
    raise ValueError("DJANGO_SECRET_KEY environment variable is required")

# DATABASE: Config from environment → K8s Secret
DATABASES = {
    'default': {
        'ENGINE': 'django.db.backends.postgresql',
        'NAME': os.environ.get('DB_NAME', 'anihpj'),
        'USER': os.environ.get('DB_USER', 'anihpj'),
        'PASSWORD': os.environ.get('DB_PASSWORD'),  # From K8s Secret!
        'HOST': os.environ.get('DB_HOST', 'postgres'),  # K8s Service DNS
        'PORT': os.environ.get('DB_PORT', '5432'),
    }
}

# REDIS: Config from environment → K8s ConfigMap
CACHES = {
    'default': {
        'BACKEND': 'django.core.cache.backends.redis.RedisCache',
        'LOCATION': f"redis://{os.environ.get('REDIS_HOST', 'redis')}:6379/1",
    }
}

# DEBUG: NEVER True in production
DEBUG = os.environ.get('DEBUG', 'False').lower() == 'true'

# ALLOWED_HOSTS: Configured per environment
ALLOWED_HOSTS = os.environ.get('ALLOWED_HOSTS', '*').split(',')

How this maps to Kubernetes:

  • DJANGO_SECRET_KEY and DB_PASSWORD → Injected from a Secret (base64-encoded, never in Git). The pod sees them as regular environment variables — the app doesn't know (or care) they came from a Secret.
  • DB_HOST, REDIS_HOST, DEBUG → Injected from a ConfigMap (plain text, safe for Git). Changes to the ConfigMap require a pod restart to take effect (ConfigMaps are NOT auto-reloaded).
  • 12-Factor compliance: The same Docker image runs in dev (DEBUG=true, DB_HOST=localhost), staging, and production (DEBUG=false, DB_HOST=anihpj-db-0.anihpj-db). Only the environment variables change — the code is identical. This is why you can test locally with docker-compose and deploy to K8s with zero code changes.
💡 Health Checks — Liveness vs Readiness Probes

Kubernetes uses two types of health checks to manage pod lifecycle. The anihpj-web pod exposes a /healthz endpoint that serves both. Understanding the difference is critical — the CNPE exam WILL test this:

Probe TypeQuestion It AsksIf It FAILSIf It SUCCEEDSanihpj Implementation
Liveness
livenessProbe		"Is this pod ALIVE? Or is it stuck/deadlocked?"K8s KILLS the container and restarts it. This is a hard restart — the pod is replaced.Nothing happens. K8s assumes the pod is healthy.HTTP GET /healthz → returns 200. Check: is Gunicorn still responding? If Django is deadlocked (100% CPU, no responses), the liveness probe fails → pod restarts.
Readiness
readinessProbe		"Is this pod READY to accept traffic?"K8s REMOVES the pod from the Service's load balancer. Traffic stops flowing to it. The pod keeps running — it's just not receiving requests.Pod is added (or re-added) to the Service. Traffic resumes.HTTP GET /healthz?ready=1 → checks: is the database reachable? Are migrations applied? If DB is temporarily down, readiness fails → pod removed from Service → no failed requests. When DB recovers, readiness succeeds → pod re-added.

The golden rule of probes: Liveness should be SIMPLE (just return 200 if the process is running). Readiness can be COMPLEX (check DB, cache, migrations). A liveness probe that checks the database will restart ALL your pods during a brief DB hiccup — making the problem WORSE. Keep liveness dumb, readiness smart.

4.3 The API Tier — Django REST Framework

The API tier provides programmatic access to anihpj data. It's the same Django application but responds with JSON instead of HTML — enabling mobile apps, third-party integrations, and the Backstage developer portal to query job data.

The API tier exposes these endpoints. In later chapters, Backstage will consume /api/jobs/ to show job statistics in the developer portal:

  • GET /api/locations/ — List all available locations

💡 Why Separate Web and API Tiers? — The Platform Engineering Reason

You might wonder: "Why not just have one Django app that serves both HTML and JSON?" The answer is about independent deployability — the core microservices principle from Chapter 2:

  • Different scaling patterns: The web tier scales with USER traffic (people browsing jobs). The API tier scales with MACHINE traffic (Backstage polling, CI pipelines, mobile apps). If 10,000 users browse /jobs/, you scale only anihpj-web. If Backstage polls /api/stats/ every 30 seconds, that's a separate concern.
  • Different security postures: Web tier uses session auth (login form). API tier uses token auth. Different authentication = different attack surfaces. Separating them means a compromised web session can't access API tokens.
  • Different resource profiles: Web tier (HTML rendering) = CPU-bound. API tier (JSON serialization) = I/O-bound. Different resource requests/limits in K8s. Optimize each independently.
  • In practice: For the CNPE exam, you might deploy them as TWO separate Deployments (anihpj-web and anihpj-api) or as ONE Deployment with different paths. Both are valid — the exam tests your ability to justify the choice. For anihpj, we're starting with one Deployment (simpler) and splitting when traffic demands it (platform maturity).
📖 Django REST Framework Serializers — How Models Become JSON

Serializers are the bridge between Python model objects and JSON responses. Understanding this helps you debug "why is the API returning the wrong fields?" or "why is this endpoint so slow?":

# jobpost/serializers.py — Serializers translate Model → JSON
from rest_framework import serializers
from .models import Job, Skill, Location, Employer

class SkillSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Skill
        fields = ['id', 'name']  # Only expose id and name

class JobListSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    """Lightweight serializer for list views (less data = faster)."""
    employer_name = serializers.CharField(source='employer.name', read_only=True)
    location_name = serializers.CharField(source='location.name', read_only=True)
    skill_names = serializers.StringRelatedField(source='skills', many=True, read_only=True)

    class Meta:
        model = Job
        fields = ['id', 'title', 'employer_name', 'location_name',
                  'skill_names', 'posted_date']

class JobDetailSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    """Full serializer for detail views (all fields, nested objects)."""
    employer = serializers.StringRelatedField()
    location = serializers.StringRelatedField()
    skills = SkillSerializer(many=True, read_only=True)

    class Meta:
        model = Job
        fields = '__all__'  # Include EVERYTHING for detail view

Key serializer patterns:

  • Separate list vs detail serializers: The list endpoint returns lightweight data (id, title, employer name). The detail endpoint returns everything. This is a performance pattern — 100 list items with 5 fields each = 500 fields. With all nested objects, it could be 5000 fields. Use the right serializer for the right view.
  • source= parameter: employer_name = serializers.CharField(source='employer.name') follows the foreign key relationship WITHOUT an extra query (it uses the JOIN from select_related). Without source=, Django would make an extra query per employer.
  • StringRelatedField for M2M: Skills are many-to-many. StringRelatedField returns just the skill names (["Python", "Kubernetes"]) instead of full nested objects with id, name, and other fields. Less data = faster responses.

4.4 The Database Tier — PostgreSQL 15 with StatefulSet + PVC

PostgreSQL is the stateful heart of anihpj. Unlike stateless components (Django, Nginx, Redis cache), the database MUST survive pod restarts, node failures, and cluster upgrades without losing data. This is why we use StatefulSet instead of Deployment.

⚠️ Why StatefulSet, Not Deployment?

This is a critical architectural decision that the CNPE exam tests:

  • Stable Network Identity: Each StatefulSet pod gets a predictable DNS name: anihpj-db-0.anihpj-db.anihpj.svc.cluster.local. Deployments get random names (anihpj-db-x7k2j). Stable DNS matters when replicating PostgreSQL — the primary must have a known address.
  • Ordered Scaling: StatefulSet starts pods in order (0, then 1, then 2) and stops them in reverse order (2, 1, 0). This is essential for database clusters where you bootstrap the primary first, then replicas.
  • Persistent Storage per Pod: Each pod gets its OWN PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC). Pod-0's data is on volume-0, Pod-1's on volume-1. If Pod-0 is rescheduled to a different node, it reattaches volume-0 — same data, new location. Deployments share volumes or lose data on restart.
POSTGRESQL STATEFULSET — Pod Identity & Persistent Storage
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              POSTGRESQL STATEFULSET ARCHITECTURE                         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HEADLESS SERVICE: anihpj-db (ClusterIP: None)                     │
  │  Provides stable DNS WITHOUT load balancing                         │
  │  DNS: anihpj-db-0.anihpj-db.anihpj.svc.cluster.local → Pod-0 IP   │
  │       anihpj-db-1.anihpj-db.anihpj.svc.cluster.local → Pod-1 IP   │
  └────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
            ┌──────────────────────┼──────────────────────┐
            │                      │                      │
            ▼                      ▼                      ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
  │  Pod: anihpj-    │  │  Pod: anihpj-    │  │  Pod: anihpj-    │
  │  db-0            │  │  db-1            │  │  db-2            │
  │  (Primary)       │  │  (Replica)       │  │  (Replica)       │
  │                  │  │                  │  │                  │
  │  Port: 5432      │  │  Port: 5432      │  │  Port: 5432      │
  └────────┬─────────┘  └────────┬─────────┘  └────────┬─────────┘
           │                     │                     │
           ▼                     ▼                     ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
  │  PVC: data-db-0  │  │  PVC: data-db-1  │  │  PVC: data-db-2  │
  │  20GB SSD         │  │  20GB SSD         │  │  20GB SSD         │
  │  /var/lib/        │  │  /var/lib/        │  │  /var/lib/        │
  │  postgresql/      │  │  postgresql/      │  │  postgresql/      │
  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  KEY: Each pod has a STABLE identity (anihpj-db-N) and its OWN storage.
  If Pod-0 crashes, K8s recreates it → same name → same PVC → same data.
  If Pod-0's NODE crashes, K8s reschedules to another node → reattaches PVC.
  This is how we make a STATEFUL database run on EPHEMERAL infrastructure.
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Database DecisionChoiceReason
Database enginePostgreSQL 15Mature, open-source, strong JSON support, Django's recommended DB
Storage size20GB SSD (gp3)Sufficient for ~500K job listings with full text search indexes
ReplicationAsync streaming (2 replicas)Read scalability + failover. Primary handles writes, replicas handle reads
Backuppg_dump daily + WAL archiving to S3Point-in-time recovery (PITR) to any second in the last 7 days
Connection poolingPgBouncer (sidecar)Django opens many connections. PgBouncer multiplexes them — reduces PostgreSQL load
💡 Database Migrations in Kubernetes — Init Containers + Jobs

"How do you run python manage.py migrate in Kubernetes?" This is one of the most common questions when moving Django to K8s. There are three approaches — each with trade-offs. The CNPE exam tests your ability to choose the right one:

ApproachHow It WorksProsConsBest For
1. Init ContainerAdd an init container to the anihpj-web pod that runs python manage.py migrate BEFORE the main Gunicorn container starts.Guaranteed: migrations run before ANY app code executes. No race condition with multiple pods (init containers run sequentially).Migration failures block ALL pod startups — if a migration is broken, NO pods start. Zero-downtime deploy becomes all-or-nothing.anihpj uses this. Simplest, safest for a single-team app. Migrations are idempotent (Django tracks which have run).
2. Kubernetes JobRun migrations as a separate K8s Job BEFORE updating the Deployment. kubectl create job migrate --image=anihpj-web -- python manage.py migrate. Wait for Job to succeed, THEN update Deployment.Decoupled: migration failure doesn't affect running pods. Can run migrations independently of deploys.Requires coordination: CI/CD pipeline must create Job → wait for success → then update Deployment. More complex pipeline.Large teams where DB changes and app changes are separate PRs. Multi-service migrations that need orchestration.
3. Startup ScriptAdd python manage.py migrate to the container's ENTRYPOINT script. Runs every time a pod starts.Zero configuration. Works with any orchestrator (K8s, Docker Compose, ECS).Every pod runs migrations on startup — redundant. If you scale to 10 replicas, all 10 attempt migration (Django handles this but it's wasteful). Slightly slower startup.Development and staging environments. NOT recommended for production with >3 replicas.

Migration safety rules: (1) Always make migrations REVERSIBLE (python manage.py makemigrations generates forward AND reverse SQL). (2) Never drop columns/tables in the same deploy that removes the code — drop in deploy N+1. (3) Test migrations against a COPY of production data before deploying. (4) Have a rollback plan: if migration fails in init container, the old pods keep running (no new pods start).

4.5 Redis — Celery Task Queue + Caching

Redis serves two roles in anihpj: a cache for frequently accessed data and a message broker for Celery async tasks. Unlike PostgreSQL, Redis is mostly stateless — data can be rebuilt from the database if lost. This is why we use a Deployment (not StatefulSet).

RoleWhat It Doesanihpj ExampleData Loss Impact
💨 CacheStores frequently accessed data in memory for sub-millisecond reads. Dramatically reduces database load.Job listing page 1 → cache HIT (Redis) → served in 2ms. Cache MISS → query PostgreSQL → store in Redis → served in 45ms. Next request: 2ms.Low — cache can be rebuilt. Users see slightly slower responses for a few seconds while cache warms up.
📬 Queue (Celery)Message broker for async task processing. Django pushes tasks to Redis queue → Celery workers pick them up and execute.Employer posts a job → Django enqueues "send notification email" task → Celery worker picks it up → sends email via SMTP. User gets immediate response; email sends in background.Medium — queued tasks are lost. New tasks queue normally. Lost tasks (unsent emails) are acceptable for this app.
🔐 SessionsStores user session data (login state, cart, preferences).User logs in → Django creates session → stores in Redis with 24h TTL. User refreshes page → session read from Redis → still logged in.Low — users need to re-login. Annoying but not catastrophic.
💡 Deployment vs StatefulSet for Redis — The Decision

We use a Deployment for Redis (not StatefulSet). Here's the reasoning:

  • Stateless by design: Cache and session data can be lost without permanent damage. The database is the source of truth — Redis accelerates it, but doesn't replace it.
  • Optional persistence: We DO mount a PVC for Redis AOF/RDB persistence (so restarts don't cold-start an empty cache). But if the PVC is lost, the app still works — just slower until the cache rebuilds.
  • Horizontal scaling: Deployments scale easily. Need more cache capacity? kubectl scale deployment redis --replicas=3. StatefulSets can scale too but are designed for stable identity, which Redis cache doesn't need.
  • Sticky sessions NOT needed: Django sessions in Redis are keyed by session ID. Any Redis replica can serve any session. No affinity required.
💡 Gunicorn Tuning — Workers, Threads, and Timeouts

Gunicorn's configuration directly affects how many concurrent requests anihpj-web can handle. These settings are set in the Dockerfile's CMD or via environment variables. Misconfiguring them causes the #1 production issue: "the app is slow under load but CPU is fine":

SettingWhat It DoesDefaultRecommendationWhy
--workersNumber of worker PROCESSES. Each worker runs a separate copy of Django. More workers = more concurrent requests.12-4 × CPU cores
anihpj: --workers=4		Formula: (2 × CPU_cores) + 1. For a pod with 2 CPU limit, 5 workers. Too many workers = context switching overhead. Each worker uses ~100-200MB RAM (Django's memory footprint).
--threadsNumber of threads PER worker. Threads share memory within a worker process.12-4 per worker
anihpj: --threads=2		Threads are good for I/O-bound work (waiting for DB queries, Redis, external APIs). NOT for CPU-bound work (Python's GIL limits CPU parallelism). Django is mostly I/O-bound → threads help.
--timeoutSeconds before Gunicorn KILLS a worker that hasn't responded. "Silent" workers are killed.30s60-120s
anihpj: --timeout=90		Set HIGHER than your slowest endpoint. If /api/reports/ takes 45s but timeout is 30s, Gunicorn kills it mid-request. Users get 502 errors. Set timeout > slowest expected response + 50% buffer.
--max-requestsNumber of requests a worker handles before being RESTARTED. Prevents memory leaks from accumulating.0 (never)1000-10000
anihpj: --max-requests=5000		Django/Python can leak memory slowly. Restarting workers after N requests prevents OOMKilled. Trade-off: restarting causes 1-2s of reduced capacity. Set based on memory growth rate.

The complete Gunicorn command for anihpj production: gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 --workers=4 --threads=2 --timeout=90 --max-requests=5000 --max-requests-jitter=500 --access-logfile=- --error-logfile=- --log-level=warning anihpj.wsgi:application. The --access-logfile=- sends logs to stdout (where K8s + Fluentd pick them up). The --max-requests-jitter=500 adds random variation so all workers don't restart simultaneously.

CELERY ASYNC TASK FLOW — Background Job Processing
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              CELERY ASYNC TASK PROCESSING IN ANIHpj                      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  USER ACTION: Employer clicks "Post Job"
  │
  ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DJANGO (SYNCHRONOUS — fast)                                          │
  │  1. Validates job data (title, description, skills, location)        │
  │  2. Saves Job to PostgreSQL (INSERT INTO jobpost_job ...)            │
  │  3. Pushes task to Redis queue:                                       │
  │     send_notification.delay(job_id=42, employer_email="hr@corp.com") │
  │  4. Returns HTTP 302 (redirect to job listing page)                   │
  │                                                                      │
  │  ⏱ Time: ~200ms (user sees immediate response)                       │
  └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │
                                 │ Task: send_notification(job_id=42, ...)
                                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  REDIS (Message Broker)                                               │
  │  Queue: celery                                                         │
  │  Task stored as serialized JSON in Redis list                          │
  │  LPUSH celery '{"task": "send_notification", "args": [42, ...]}'     │
  └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                                 │
                                 │ Celery worker picks up task (BRPOP celery)
                                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CELERY WORKER (ASYNCHRONOUS — runs in background)                    │
  │  1. Reads task from Redis queue                                        │
  │  2. Loads Django environment                                           │
  │  3. Executes: send_notification(job_id=42, employer_email=...)         │
  │     - Generates email template                                         │
  │     - Connects to SMTP server (smtp.anihpj.com:587)                    │
  │     - Sends "Your job 'Senior Platform Engineer' is now live!"         │
  │  4. Logs: "Notification sent to hr@corp.com for job_id=42"             │
  │  5. Updates Job.notification_sent = True in PostgreSQL                  │
  │                                                                      │
  │  ⏱ Time: ~2-5 seconds (happens in background, user doesn't wait)     │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

4.6 Project File Tree & Multi-Stage Docker Build

The anihpj project follows a monorepo structure — application code, Kubernetes manifests, Terraform configs, monitoring dashboards, and security policies all live in one repository. This keeps everything versioned together and simplifies GitOps (one repo = one source of truth).

📖 The Multi-Stage Dockerfile — Small Images, Fast Builds

The anihpj Dockerfile uses multi-stage builds to keep the final image small. A single Dockerfile produces multiple intermediate images, but only the final stage's filesystem becomes the actual container image:

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STAGE 1: BUILDER — Compile dependencies, collect static files
# This stage is THROWN AWAY after building. Its only purpose
# is to produce the dependencies and static files.
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder

# Install system dependencies needed to compile Python packages
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    gcc \
    libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app

# Copy only requirements FIRST — this caches the pip install layer
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --user --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# Copy application code
COPY . .

# Collect static files (CSS, JS, images) into /app/staticfiles/
RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# STAGE 2: RUNNER — Minimal production image
# Only copies what's NEEDED from the builder stage.
# Result: small, secure production image (~200MB vs ~800MB)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
FROM python:3.12-slim AS runner

# Install ONLY runtime dependencies (not build tools like gcc)
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    libpq-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

WORKDIR /app

# Copy Python packages from builder (not rebuild!)
COPY --from=builder /root/.local /root/.local
ENV PATH=/root/.local/bin:$PATH

# Copy application code
COPY --from=builder /app .

# Run as non-root user (SECURITY — Kyverno will enforce this)
RUN useradd --create-home --shell /bin/bash anihpj
USER anihpj

# Expose port for Gunicorn
EXPOSE 8000

# Start Gunicorn with 4 workers
# --bind 0.0.0.0:8000 = listen on all interfaces
# anihpj.wsgi:application = the WSGI callable
CMD ["gunicorn", "--bind", "0.0.0.0:8000", "--workers", "4", "anihpj.wsgi:application"]
💡 Why Multi-Stage? The Build Engineer's Perspective
  • Smaller image: Builder stage has gcc, build tools (~600MB). Runner stage has only runtime libs (~200MB). The final image is what gets pushed to ECR and pulled by every K8s node. 200MB vs 800MB = faster pulls, less disk usage, faster pod starts.
  • Security: Build tools (gcc, make) are common attack vectors. They're NOT in the final image — an attacker who compromises the container can't compile malicious code.
  • Caching: COPY requirements.txt before COPY . . means Docker caches the pip install layer. If you only change app code (not requirements), the pip install is REUSED from cache. Build time drops from 5 minutes to 30 seconds.
  • Non-root user: The USER anihpj directive means the container runs as UID 1000, not UID 0 (root). Kyverno policies in later chapters will BLOCK any container running as root — this Dockerfile is compliant by design.
📖 CI/CD Pipeline Overview — What Happens After You Push

The .github/workflows/ directory contains the CI/CD pipelines that automate anihpj's delivery. Understanding these is essential because later chapters (Ch 13-14) dive deep into pipeline design. Here's a preview:

PipelineTriggerStagesProduces
ci.yamlPush to any branch / PR to mainLint (ruff, hadolint) → Test (pytest + coverage) → Build (Docker) → Scan (Trivy) → Push (ECR)Container image tagged with git SHA in ECR, test coverage report
cd.yamlMerge to main branchUpdate K8s manifest with new image tag → Commit to k8s/ repo → Argo CD detects → Sync staging → Smoke tests → Canary 10% → Promote 100%Updated application running in production

Why this matters now: Every drill in this chapter that involves building and pushing images is simulating what CI does automatically. In production, you never run docker build manually — the pipeline does it. But understanding the manual steps helps you debug when the pipeline breaks. The CNPE exam tests both: writing pipeline configs AND debugging them.

Docker Compose vs Kubernetes — When to Use Each:

  • 🐳 Docker Compose (local dev): Used in docker-compose.yml for local development. Simple: one command starts everything. No scaling, no self-healing, no rolling updates. Perfect for: coding on your laptop, running tests locally, quick demos.
  • ☸️ Kubernetes (production): Used for staging and production. Complex setup but provides: auto-scaling, self-healing, rolling updates, secrets management, and multi-tenancy. Perfect for: production workloads, multi-team platforms, anything that needs to survive node failures.
  • 🚫 NEVER use Docker Compose in production — it runs on a single machine, has no failover, and can't scale horizontally. Docker Compose is a development tool. Kubernetes is a production platform.
📖 The Kustomize Overlay Structure — Managing Environment Variants

The k8s/overlays/ directory uses Kustomize to manage dev/staging/production differences WITHOUT duplicating YAML. Understanding this pattern is essential — the CNPE exam tests Helm AND Kustomize:

# k8s/overlays/production/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

# Start from base manifests
resources:
  - ../../base

# Override replica count for production
patches:
  - patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/replicas
        value: 3
    target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: anihpj-web

# Add production-specific config
configMapGenerator:
  - name: anihpj-config
    behavior: merge
    literals:
      - DEBUG=false
      - LOG_LEVEL=WARNING

# Use production image tag (not latest)
images:
  - name: anihpj-web
    newTag: v1.2.3  # Specific version, not :latest

How to read this: Production inherits EVERYTHING from k8s/base/ (13 manifest files), then selectively OVERRIDES only what's different: more replicas, production config, specific image tag. Dev environment might set DEBUG=true and replicas: 1. Same base, minimal overrides. This is GitOps-ready — Argo CD can point to k8s/overlays/production and sync automatically.

📖 Static Files in Production — WhiteNoise vs Nginx vs CDN

"Where do my CSS, JavaScript, and images live in production?" This is the #1 Django deployment question after migrations. There are three approaches — each solves a different scale of the problem:

ApproachHow It WorksLatencyBest For
1. WhiteNoisePython middleware that serves static files directly from the Django app. Files are collected at build time (collectstatic) and served from memory.Medium (Python overhead)Small apps, internal tools, dev environments. Simplest: no Nginx config needed. anihpj dev uses this.
2. Nginx (in-pod)Nginx serves static files from disk INSIDE the same pod as Django. Files are collected into /app/staticfiles/ during Docker build.Fast (native C, no Python)anihpj production uses this. Single-node deployments, <1000 concurrent users. One pod = one Nginx + one Gunicorn. Simple, contained.
3. CDN (S3 + CloudFront)Static files are uploaded to S3 at build time. CloudFront CDN caches them at edge locations worldwide. Django generates URLs pointing to the CDN.Very fast (global edge cache)Global user base, 1000+ concurrent users. Highest performance. Files served from the edge nearest to each user. Reduced load on K8s cluster.

The static files pipeline for anihpj:

  1. Docker build: RUN python manage.py collectstatic --noinput → copies all CSS/JS/images to /app/staticfiles/ INSIDE the image.
  2. Nginx config: location /static/ { alias /app/staticfiles/; } → Nginx serves them directly, bypassing Django entirely.
  3. Future: CDN migration path: Add an after-build step: aws s3 sync /app/staticfiles/ s3://anihpj-static/ --cache-control "max-age=31536000, immutable". Update Django's STATIC_URL to https://cdn.anihpj.com/static/. Existing Nginx config continues working as fallback.

Drill 4.3 — Build and Tag the anihpj Docker Image

Build the anihpj Docker image using the multi-stage Dockerfile and tag it correctly for your registry.

  1. Build the image: docker build -t anihpj-web:latest .
  2. Verify the image size with docker images — should be ~200MB, not ~800MB
  3. Tag it with your local registry: docker tag anihpj-web:latest localhost:5000/anihpj-web:v1.0.0
  4. Push to local registry: docker push localhost:5000/anihpj-web:v1.0.0
  5. Inspect the image layers: docker history anihpj-web:latest
💡 Hint: docker build -t, docker tag, docker push, docker history. Start local registry: docker run -d -p 5000:5000 registry:2
📝 View Solution

docker run -d -p 5000:5000 --name registry registry:2

# Step 1: Build
docker build -t anihpj-web:latest .
# Watch the output — you should see:
# [builder 1/4] FROM python:3.12-slim
# [builder 2/4] RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
# [builder 3/4] COPY . .
# [builder 4/4] RUN python manage.py collectstatic
# [runner 1/4] FROM python:3.12-slim  ← NEW base, builder is discarded
# [runner 2/4] COPY --from=builder ...  ← copies only what's needed
# [runner 3/4] RUN useradd anihpj
# [runner 4/4] CMD ["gunicorn", ...]

# Step 2: Check image size
docker images anihpj-web
# REPOSITORY    TAG      SIZE
# anihpj-web    latest   200MB  ← multi-stage = small!

# Step 3: Tag
docker tag anihpj-web:latest localhost:5000/anihpj-web:v1.0.0
docker tag anihpj-web:latest localhost:5000/anihpj-web:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)

# Step 4: Push
docker push localhost:5000/anihpj-web:v1.0.0

# Step 5: Inspect layers
docker history anihpj-web:latest
# Shows each layer: FROM python, RUN apt-get, COPY requirements, RUN pip install, etc.
# Notice: NO gcc or build-essential layers — they were only in the discarded builder stage

Drill 4.9 — Inspect and Understand the Multi-Stage Dockerfile

Analyze what each stage of the Dockerfile does and why.

  1. Read the Dockerfile: identify the builder and runner stages
  2. Count how many FROM instructions exist (each = a new stage)
  3. Identify which packages are installed in the builder but NOT in the runner
  4. Check: does the runner stage include gcc? (It shouldn't!)
  5. Explain in one sentence why COPY requirements.txt comes BEFORE COPY . .
💡 Hint: cat Dockerfile, grep -n "FROM\|COPY\|RUN" Dockerfile
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1-2: Identify stages
grep "^FROM" Dockerfile
# FROM python:3.12-slim AS builder  ← Stage 1: Builder
# FROM python:3.12-slim AS runner   ← Stage 2: Runner
# RESULT: 2 stages (multi-stage build)

# Step 3: Builder-only packages
grep "apt-get install" Dockerfile
# Builder: apt-get install gcc libpq-dev  ← gcc is here
# Runner:  apt-get install libpq-dev      ← gcc is NOT here

# Step 4: Verify runner has no gcc
# Look at the RUNNER stage in the Dockerfile:
# RUN apt-get install libpq-dev  ← only runtime lib, no build tools
# This is the SECURITY benefit of multi-stage builds

# Step 5: Explanation
# COPY requirements.txt is BEFORE COPY . . because:
# requirements.txt changes RARELY → Docker caches the pip install layer.
# Application code changes FREQUENTLY → only the COPY . . layer rebuilds.
# RESULT: builds take 30 seconds instead of 5 minutes.
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 4.10 — Simulate a Database Failure and Verify Persistence

Prove that PostgreSQL's data survives pod deletion thanks to StatefulSet + PVC.

  1. Create a test record in PostgreSQL: insert a row via psql
  2. Delete the PostgreSQL pod: kubectl delete pod anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj
  3. Wait for the StatefulSet controller to recreate it
  4. Verify the new pod has the SAME name (anihpj-db-0) and the SAME PVC
  5. Connect and verify your test record STILL EXISTS
💡 Hint: StatefulSet pods are recreated with the same ordinal index (0). PVCs survive pod deletion because they're managed separately.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create test record
kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj -- psql -U anihpj -d anihpj -c \
  "INSERT INTO jobpost_skill (name) VALUES ('TestSkill-Persistence');"
kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj -- psql -U anihpj -d anihpj -c \
  "SELECT * FROM jobpost_skill WHERE name='TestSkill-Persistence';"
# EXPECTED: 1 row returned

# Step 2: Delete the pod (simulate failure)
kubectl delete pod anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj
# pod "anihpj-db-0" deleted

# Step 3: Watch it recreate
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w
# anihpj-db-0   0/1   Terminating   0   15m
# anihpj-db-0   0/1   Pending       0   0s
# anihpj-db-0   0/1   ContainerCreating   0   2s
# anihpj-db-0   1/1   Running             0   30s

# Step 4: Verify same name and PVC
kubectl get pod anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj
# NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# anihpj-db-0   1/1     Running   0          45s
kubectl get pvc -n anihpj
# NAME         STATUS   VOLUME              CAPACITY
# data-db-0    Bound    pvc-abc123def456    20Gi
# Same PVC! Data is safe!

# Step 5: Verify data survived
kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -n anihpj -- psql -U anihpj -d anihpj -c \
  "SELECT * FROM jobpost_skill WHERE name='TestSkill-Persistence';"
# EXPECTED: 1 row returned ✓
# PROOF: StatefulSet + PVC = persistent data across pod failures
# This is WHY we use StatefulSet for databases, not Deployment

🏗️ anihpj Architecture — Every Layer Visualized

The anihpj platform follows a clean 3-tier architecture. Understanding each layer's role, technology choices, and Kubernetes object mapping is essential — you'll deploy, scale, and secure every layer in subsequent chapters.

🔀 Decision Tree — StatefulSet or Deployment for Your Workload?

This is one of the most important platform design decisions. Choosing wrong means data loss or unstable networking.

🔄 Does your workload require STABLE NETWORK IDENTITY? (e.g., DB replicas must have predictable DNS names like postgres-0, postgres-1)
YES ↓
✅ Use STATEFULSET
PostgreSQL, Kafka, Zookeeper, Elasticsearch
NO ↓
💾 Does your workload require PERSISTENT STORAGE PER REPLICA? (each pod needs its OWN volume that survives pod restarts)
YES ↓
✅ Use STATEFULSET
Each pod gets its own PVC. Pod-0 always mounts pvc-0.
NO ↓
⚡ Is your workload STATELESS and can be replaced at any time?
YES ↓
✅ Use DEPLOYMENT
anihpj-web, Redis cache, Nginx. Pods are interchangeable.
SPECIAL CASE ↓
🔧 Consider DaemonSet (one per node: logging agents, monitoring exporters) or Job/CronJob (batch tasks: DB migrations, backups)
💡 The anihpj Decision Applied

PostgreSQL → StatefulSet: Needs stable DNS (postgres-0.anihpj.svc), ordered startup (postgres-0 starts first as primary), and persistent storage per replica. Redis → Deployment: Cache data is rebuildable. If redis-abc123 dies and redis-xyz789 replaces it, Django repopulates the cache. No data loss. anihpj-web → Deployment: Stateless Django app. Any pod can handle any request. Rolling updates replace pods seamlessly.

🐍Django + GunicornWSGI app server. 3 replicas. Handles HTTP requests. Stateless.
🔄Nginx SidecarReverse proxy in same pod. TLS, static files, rate limiting.
🐘PostgreSQL StatefulSetStable identity + PVC. Never use Deployment for databases.
🔴Redis DeploymentCache + Celery queue. Data rebuildable — safe as Deployment.
📦Multi-Stage Dockerfile200MB image. No build tools in final stage. Non-root user.
📁Monorepo StructureApp + k8s/ + terraform/ + monitoring/ + policies/ in one repo.
🎓 Chapter 4 Is Your Reference Throughout the ENTIRE Exam

Every CNPE task builds on the anihpj application architecture you learned here. When the exam says "deploy a web application with a database backend to Kubernetes," you should immediately think: Deployment for web, StatefulSet + PVC for database, ConfigMap for non-sensitive config, Secret for passwords, Service for networking, Ingress for external access. This chapter's architecture pattern is the template for every exam task.

Exam shortcut — anihpj deployment in under 2 minutes: Memorize this sequence. It's the foundation for many exam tasks:

kubectl create ns anihpj
kubectl create configmap anihpj-config --from-literal=DB_HOST=postgres -n anihpj
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cret -n anihpj
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web --image=anihpj-web:latest --replicas=3 -n anihpj
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web --port=8000 --target-port=8000 -n anihpj
kubectl create ingress anihpj --rule="anihpj.com/*=anihpj-web:8000" -n anihpj

Generating YAML for customization: append --dry-run=client -o yaml > file.yaml to any create command.

⚠️ StatefulSet vs Deployment — The #1 CNPE Architecture Mistake

Many candidates use Deployments for databases because they're easier. This is WRONG for PostgreSQL. StatefulSets provide: (1) Stable network identity: postgres-0.anihpj.svc.cluster.local — required for DB replication. (2) Ordered, graceful deployment and scaling: postgres-0 starts first as primary, postgres-1 joins as replica. (3) Persistent storage per replica: each pod gets its own PVC that survives pod restarts. If the exam asks you to deploy a stateful application, StatefulSet is ALWAYS the answer.

Q1: Why does anihpj-web use a Deployment but PostgreSQL uses a StatefulSet?

▶ Show Answer
anihpj-web is stateless — any pod can handle any request. Pods are interchangeable. If a pod dies, a new one replaces it seamlessly. PostgreSQL is stateful — it needs stable identity (postgres-0, postgres-1), persistent storage per replica (each pod has its own PVC), and ordered startup/shutdown (primary first, then replicas). StatefulSet guarantees all three; Deployment guarantees none.
Q2: What's the purpose of the Nginx sidecar in the anihpj-web pod?

▶ Show Answer
Nginx acts as a reverse proxy sidecar: (1) TLS termination — handles HTTPS, forwards HTTP to Gunicorn on localhost:8000. (2) Static file serving — serves CSS/JS/images directly, bypassing Django. (3) Rate limiting and request buffering — protects Gunicorn from slow clients. This is the Sidecar pattern: Nginx enhances Django without Django knowing Nginx exists.
Q3: Why is the anihpj monorepo structure (app + k8s/ + terraform/ together) important for GitOps?

▶ Show Answer
GitOps requires a single source of truth. When application code and deployment configs live in the same repo, a single commit can update both. Example: developer adds a new API endpoint + updates the Ingress to expose it → one PR, one merge, Argo CD syncs everything. Separate repos create "configuration drift" — the app repo says one thing, the config repo says another. Monorepo keeps them synchronized.
🚀 Beyond CNPE — Multi-Service Platform Architecture at Scale

The anihpj project is a single application. Real platforms run dozens or hundreds. Here's how the architecture evolves:

  • Service Mesh for East-West Traffic: When you have 50+ microservices, managing mTLS, retries, and circuit breaking per service becomes impossible. Deploy Istio/Linkerd/Cilium — the mesh handles service-to-service communication transparently. anihpj-web → anihpj-api → anihpj-worker all communicate through the mesh with automatic mTLS, retries, and tracing.
  • API Gateway for North-South Traffic: When external consumers (mobile apps, partners, web apps) need different rate limits, auth methods, and API versions, an Ingress isn't enough. Deploy Kong/Ambassador/APISIX as an API Gateway in front of your services.
  • Event-Driven Architecture: Replace direct service-to-service calls with events. anihpj-web publishes "JobCreated" event to Kafka/NATS → anihpj-notification service consumes and sends email → anihpj-analytics service consumes and updates dashboards. Decouples services completely.
  • Multi-Cluster Federation: One cluster per region (us-east, eu-west, ap-southeast). Global traffic management via DNS (Route53/Cloudflare). Cluster API manages cluster lifecycle. Argo CD manages apps across all clusters from a single Git repo.

📖 Chapter 4 Summary: You've met the anihpj application — a 3-tier Django + PostgreSQL + Redis job posting platform that will be your learning playground for every subsequent chapter. Key takeaways: (1) The web tier uses Nginx → Gunicorn → Django for production-grade request handling. (2) The API tier exposes RESTful JSON endpoints for programmatic consumers like Backstage. (3) PostgreSQL uses StatefulSet for stable identity and persistent storage — never use Deployment for stateful workloads. (4) Redis uses Deployment because cache/queue data is rebuildable. (5) The multi-stage Dockerfile keeps the image small (200MB) and secure (no build tools, non-root user). (6) The monorepo structure keeps all configs versioned together — essential for GitOps.
