6.5 Cluster Networking Model — Pod-to-Pod, Pod-to-Service, External

Kubernetes mandates a flat networking model: every pod gets its own IP address. All pods can communicate with all other pods without NAT. CNI plugins implement this.

CommunicationHow It WorksExample
Pod-to-Pod (same node)Direct via local bridge/veth pair. No network hop.Pod A (10.0.1.5) → Pod B (10.0.1.6) on same worker. <0.1ms latency.
Pod-to-Pod (different nodes)CNI plugin encapsulates packet (VXLAN/Geneve) or routes directly (BGP). Cross-node hop.Pod A (10.0.1.5) on worker-1 → Pod C (10.0.2.8) on worker-2. ~0.5ms latency.
Pod-to-ServiceDNS resolves Service name → ClusterIP. kube-proxy iptables/IPVS rules route to a random backend pod IP.anihpj-web connects to postgres.anihpj.svc → ClusterIP 10.96.0.5 → iptables → backend pod 10.0.1.10:5432.
External-to-PodNodePort (30000-32767), LoadBalancer (cloud LB), or Ingress (L7 routing). Traffic enters the cluster through these.User visits anihpj.com → Cloud LB → NodePort 30080 → kube-proxy → pod 10.0.1.5:8000.
CNI PLUGIN COMPARISON — Calico, Cilium, Flannel, Weave
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                        CNI PLUGIN LANDSCAPE                              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  FLANNEL (Simplest)                                                  │
  │  How: Overlay network (VXLAN/host-gw). Every pod gets IP from        │
  │  node's subnet. Packets encapsulated in VXLAN between nodes.         │
  │  Pros: Dead simple setup. Cons: No NetworkPolicy support (without    │
  │  additional plugins). Extra overhead from encapsulation.             │
  │  VS Code:
  │  Best For: Learning K8s, small clusters, simple networking needs.    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CALICO (Most Popular, Enterprise-Grade)                             │
  │  How: Can use BGP (no overlay!) or VXLAN/IPIP. Direct routing with   │
  │  BGP means NO encapsulation overhead — near-native performance.      │
  │  Pros: NetworkPolicies (iptables OR eBPF), BGP for performance.      │
  │  Cons: BGP requires router support or full mesh. More config.        │
  │  VS Code:
  │  Best For: Production clusters needing policies + performance.       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  CILIUM (eBPF-Powered, Next-Gen)                                     │
  │  How: Replaces kube-proxy AND CNI. Uses eBPF to program kernel       │
  │  directly — bypasses iptables entirely. Hubble for observability.    │
  │  Pros: Fastest (eBPF), built-in observability, L7 policies,          │
  │  service mesh replacement. Cons: Requires newer kernel (≥ 4.19).     │
  │  VS Code:                                                            │
  │  Best For: High-performance, security-focused, K8s-native platforms. │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  DECISION MATRIX:
  Just learning?          → Flannel
  Production with policies? → Calico (iptables mode)
  Production + performance? → Calico (BGP mode) or Cilium
  Security + observability? → Cilium (eBPF + Hubble)
  Multi-cluster mesh?       → Cilium Cluster Mesh
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
🎉 Real-World CNI Decision — anihpj Platform (3 Clusters)
  • ✅ Dev cluster: Flannel — simple, no policies needed, fast setup for developers.
  • ✅ Staging cluster: Calico (VXLAN mode) — NetworkPolicies to simulate production security. Moderate performance acceptable.
  • ✅ Production cluster: Cilium (eBPF mode) — maximum performance, Hubble observability, L7 NetworkPolicies for PCI compliance (blocking SQL injection at kernel level!).
  • ✅ Platform engineer's job: Not just picking one CNI — managing DIFFERENT CNIs per cluster based on requirements. The CNPE exam expects you to justify these choices.

6.6 etcd — The Cluster Database

⚠️ etcd is the MOST CRITICAL component. If you lose etcd data, you lose the ENTIRE cluster.

Every Kubernetes object — pods, services, deployments, secrets, RBAC rules — is stored in etcd. The API server is the ONLY component that reads/writes etcd. Back up etcd REGULARLY.

Raft Consensus: etcd uses Raft for consistency. A write succeeds only if a MAJORITY (quorum) of etcd members agree. 3-node cluster: quorum = 2, tolerates 1 failure. 5-node: quorum = 3, tolerates 2 failures. Always use ODD numbers.

RAFT CONSENSUS — How etcd Keeps 3 Nodes in Sync
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    3-NODE ETCD CLUSTER — RAFT CONSENSUS                  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────┐
  │  ETCD NODE A          │   │  ETCD NODE B          │   │  ETCD NODE C          │
  │  ROLE: LEADER 👑      │   │  ROLE: FOLLOWER       │   │  ROLE: FOLLOWER       │
  │                       │   │                       │   │                       │
  │  ① Receives write     │   │  Receives heartbeat   │   │  Receives heartbeat   │
  │     from API server   │   │  from Leader every    │   │  from Leader every    │
  │                       │   │  100ms                │   │  100ms                │
  │  ② Appends to its     │   │                       │   │                       │
  │     own log           │   │  ③ Leader sends       │   │  ③ Leader sends       │
  │                       │   │     AppendEntries     │   │     AppendEntries     │
  │  ④ Waits for majority │◄──│  ④ B writes to log   │◄──│  ④ C writes to log   │
  │     (A + B = 2/3)     │──►│     (ACK)             │──►│     (ACK)             │
  │                       │   │                       │   │                       │
  │  ⑤ Commits write      │   │  ⑤ Commits write      │   │  ⑤ Commits write      │
  │     Returns success    │   │                       │   │                       │
  │     to API server      │   │                       │   │                       │
  └───────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────┘

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  WHAT IF LEADER (A) FAILS?                                               │
  │                                                                         │
  │  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐                         │
  │  │ A: CRASH │     │ B: FOLLOWER    │ C: FOLLOWER                        │
  │  │ 💀       │     │                │                                     │
  │  └──────────┘     └─────┬──────────┘     └─────┬──────────┘             │
  │                         │ election timeout    │ election timeout         │
  │                         │ (150-300ms no       │ (150-300ms no            │
  │                         │  heartbeat)         │  heartbeat)              │
  │                         ▼                     ▼                          │
  │                   ┌──────────┐          ┌──────────┐                     │
  │                   │ CANDIDATE│          │ CANDIDATE│                     │
  │                   │ votes for│◄────────►│ votes for│                     │
  │                   │ self     │  race!    │ self     │                     │
  │                   └────┬─────┘          └────┬─────┘                     │
  │                        │ B wins (2/3 votes)  │ C loses                   │
  │                        ▼                     ▼                           │
  │                   ┌──────────┐          ┌──────────┐                     │
  │                   │ B: LEADER│          │ FOLLOWER │                     │
  │                   │ 👑       │          │          │                     │
  │                   └──────────┘          └──────────┘                     │
  │  Election takes ~1 second. During election: writes UNAVAILABLE.           │
  │  Reads still work.                                                       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  QUORUM MATH:  3 nodes → quorum=2 → tolerate 1 failure
                5 nodes → quorum=3 → tolerate 2 failures (BUT more overhead)
                2 nodes → quorum=2 → tolerate 0 failures (NEVER use 2 nodes!)
  Why odd? 3-node and 4-node BOTH tolerate only 1 failure, but 4-node costs
  more. Always use odd numbers. For production: 3 or 5 nodes.
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Raft Leader Election — The Heartbeat That Keeps etcd Alive: In a 3-node etcd cluster, one node is the LEADER (handles all writes), and two are FOLLOWERS. The leader sends heartbeats every 100ms. If followers don't hear a heartbeat for 150-300ms (election timeout), they become CANDIDATES and start an election. The first candidate to get votes from a majority becomes the new leader. During an election (~1-2 seconds), etcd is UNAVAILABLE for writes (but reads still work). This is why you need ODD numbers — a 2-node cluster can NEVER reach majority (quorum = 2, but with 1 failure, only 1 node remains → no quorum). Always 3, 5, or 7 nodes.

Critical commands:

  • ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-snapshot.db — saves entire cluster state
  • ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-snapshot.db — recovers from backup
  • ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member list — see all etcd members and their status
🧠 CNPE Exam: Expect a task to backup and restore etcd. Know the exact flags: --endpoints, --cacert, --cert, --key. These are in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/. The restore command creates a NEW data directory — you must update the etcd manifest to point to it.
📖 etcd Internals — MVCC, Compaction, and Why etcd Grows Forever

etcd stores data using MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control). Every key has a revision number — a monotonically increasing counter across the entire cluster. When you update a key, the OLD version is NOT deleted. It's retained with its old revision. This is how watches work: a controller can say "give me all changes since revision 15432" and etcd replays them.

The problem: Old revisions accumulate FOREVER. Every Deployment update, every Pod status change, every heartbeat — all stored permanently. An etcd database starting at 100MB can grow to 8GB+. This is database bloat.

The fix — Compaction + Defrag: Compaction discards old revisions. Defrag reclaims disk space (the DB file actually shrinks).

# Check current etcd size
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=table
# DB SIZE: 2.1 GB  → problem!

# Compact (delete old revisions)
REV=$(ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint status --write-out=json | jq '.[0].Status.header.revision')
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl compact $REV

# Defragment (reclaim disk)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl defrag

# Check again → DB SIZE: 350 MB (down from 2.1 GB!)

Platform responsibility: Schedule automatic compaction (API server does it hourly) + defrag (manual, run weekly). Monitor etcd_mvcc_db_total_size_in_bytes via Prometheus. A bloated etcd causes: slow API responses, snapshot timeouts, and crashes at 8GB quota.

📖 etcd Backup Automation — CronJob for Daily Snapshots

Never manually run backups. Schedule them with a K8s CronJob that mounts the etcd certs from the host and writes snapshots to a persistent location. Restore drill for the exam: (1) Move kube-apiserver.yaml out of manifests/. (2) etcdctl snapshot restore snapshot.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restore. (3) Edit etcd.yaml to point --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restore. (4) Kubelet restarts etcd. (5) Return kube-apiserver.yaml. (6) Verify with kubectl get pods -A.

6.7 Static Pods and Control Plane Management

Static Pods are pods managed directly by kubelet, NOT by the API server. Kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ — any YAML file there becomes a static pod. The control plane components (api-server, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) run as static pods in kubeadm clusters.

Key facts: (1) If you edit a manifest file, kubelet restarts the pod automatically. No kubectl apply needed. (2) If you DELETE a manifest file, kubelet stops the pod. (3) Static pods appear in kubectl get pods -n kube-system with a mirror pod on the API server — but the API server CANNOT delete them. Only kubelet can.

💡 Static Pod Lifecycle — How kubeadm Bootstraps the Control Plane

kubeadm writes 4 YAML files to /etc/kubernetes/manifests/. kubelet detects them and starts each as a static pod. Each creates a mirror pod visible in kube-system. If you kubectl delete pod a control plane component, kubelet RESTARTS it — mirror pods are reflections, control is at the kubelet level. To PERMANENTLY stop a component: MOVE its manifest out of the directory. Move it back → pod restarts. This is how you "pause" a control plane component for maintenance.

📖 Scheduler Scoring — How K8s Picks the Best Node

The scheduler uses 2 phases: Filtering (eliminate nodes that can't run the pod — insufficient resources, taint mismatch, port conflicts) and Scoring (rank survivors by preference). Key scoring plugins: NodeResourcesFit (prefers less-loaded nodes), ImageLocality (prefers nodes that already have the image cached), PodTopologySpread (spreads pods across zones for HA). Highest total score wins. Tie → random pick.

SCHEDULER SCORING — How a Node Wins the Pod
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SCHEDULER DECISION: Where should anihpj-web-xyz run?                    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  AVAILABLE NODES (3 workers):
  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
  │ Worker-1     │  │ Worker-2     │  │ Worker-3     │
  │ CPU: 2/4     │  │ CPU: 3.5/4   │  │ CPU: 1/4     │
  │ Mem: 3/8Gi   │  │ Mem: 7/8Gi   │  │ Mem: 2/8Gi   │
  │ Disk: 50%    │  │ Disk: 85%    │  │ Disk: 20%    │
  │              │  │              │  │              │
  │ taint: none  │  │ taint: none  │  │ taint:        │
  │              │  │              │  │ critical=true │
  │ zone: us-    │  │ zone: us-    │  │ zone: us-     │
  │ east-1a      │  │ east-1b      │  │ east-1c       │
  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  PHASE 1: FILTERING (eliminate impossible)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Worker-3: ❌ ELIMINATED — has taint critical=true, pod has no          │
  │ toleration.                                                           │
  │ Worker-1: ✅ PASSES — enough CPU (needs 250m), memory (needs 256Mi)    │
  │ Worker-2: ✅ PASSES — enough resources                                 │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PHASE 2: SCORING (rank the survivors)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Plugin              │ Worker-1 Score │ Worker-2 Score │ Weight        │
  ├──────────────────────┼────────────────┼────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ NodeResourcesFit     │ 8 (more free)  │ 3 (nearly full)│ 1 (default)   │
  │ ImageLocality        │ 10 (cached!)   │ 0 (needs pull) │ 1             │
  │ PodTopologySpread    │ 5 (1a has pod) │ 8 (1b, fewer)  │ 2             │
  │ NodeAffinity         │ 10 (matched)   │ 10 (matched)   │ 1             │
  ├──────────────────────┼────────────────┼────────────────┼───────────────┤
  │ TOTAL WEIGHTED SCORE │ 8+10+10+10=38  │ 3+0+16+10=29   │               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  🏆 WINNER: Worker-1 (score 38 vs 29)
  Scheduler updates Pod.spec.nodeName = "worker-1" → kubelet takes over
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
💡 kubeadm Bootstrap Walkthrough — How the Control Plane Comes Alive

When you run kubeadm init, here's exactly what happens step-by-step:

# 1. Preflight checks — are we ready?
kubeadm init phase preflight
# [preflight] Running pre-flight checks
# [preflight] Pulling images required for setting up a Kubernetes cluster

# 2. Generate self-signed CA certificate (valid 10 years)
kubeadm init phase certs all
# [certs] Generated ca certificate and key
# [certs] Generated apiserver certificate and key
# [certs] apiserver serving cert is signed for DNS names [kubernetes, ...]
# [certs] Generated etcd/ca certificate and key

# 3. Write kubeconfig files for controller-manager, scheduler, kubelet, admin
kubeadm init phase kubeconfig all
# [kubeconfig] Wrote "admin.conf" — THIS IS YOUR ~/.kube/config

# 4. Generate static pod manifests (written to /etc/kubernetes/manifests/)
kubeadm init phase control-plane all
# [control-plane] Wrote static Pod manifest for kube-apiserver
# [control-plane] Wrote static Pod manifest for kube-controller-manager
# [control-plane] Wrote static Pod manifest for kube-scheduler

# 5. Start local etcd (static pod)
kubeadm init phase etcd local
# [etcd] Wrote static Pod manifest for local etcd

# 6. Wait for control plane to be healthy
# kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ → starts all 4 pods
# After ~30 seconds: kubectl get pods -n kube-system shows control plane

# 7. Upload kubeadm/kubelet config to cluster as ConfigMaps
kubeadm init phase upload-config all

# 8. Mark the node as control-plane + add taints
kubeadm init phase mark-control-plane

# 9. Generate bootstrap token for joining workers
kubeadm init phase bootstrap-token

# 10. Install CoreDNS and kube-proxy as addons
kubeadm init phase addon all

After init: kubelet runs as a systemd service. Control plane runs as static pods. You join workers with kubeadm join <IP>:6443 --token <token> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>. Understanding this flow means you can troubleshoot ANY kubeadm cluster issue — from certificate expiration to manifest corruption.

😰 Control Plane Upgrade Gone Wrong — A Real Platform Engineer Story
  • 🔴 Scenario: You run kubeadm upgrade apply v1.29.0. The new kube-apiserver won't start. kubectl is dead. What now?
  • 🔴 Diagnosis: SSH to the control plane node. Check crictl ps | grep kube-apiserver — no container. Check journalctl -u kubelet -f — kubelet says "manifest parsing error: unknown field 'encryptionAlgorithm'." The new API server manifest has a field the old kubelet doesn't understand.
  • 🔴 Fix: Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml, remove the unknown field. Kubelet detects the change, restarts the API server. Within 30 seconds, kubectl works again. This is why you ALWAYS have SSH access to control plane nodes.
  • 🟡 Lesson: kubectl relies on the API server. When the API server is down, you need node-level access. Always maintain both paths: API access (kubectl) AND node access (SSH/journalctl/crictl).

🏋️ Chapter 6 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

The CNPE is a performance-based exam — you solve tasks in a live Linux terminal. Practice these drills in your lab environment until you can complete each within the target time.

⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 6.1 — Inspect Control Plane Components

Identify and verify all control plane components are healthy.

  1. List all pods in kube-system: kubectl get pods -n kube-system
  2. Filter for control plane: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'etcd|apiserver|scheduler|controller'
  3. Check component statuses: kubectl get componentstatuses
  4. Describe the API server pod: kubectl describe pod -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver
💡 Hint: Control plane pods run as static pods. Their names include the node name. Use kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'etcd|apiserver|scheduler|controller'
kubectl get componentstatuses
kubectl describe pod -n kube-system -l component=kube-apiserver
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 6.2 — Backup and Restore etcd

Take an etcd snapshot and verify it.

  1. SSH into the control plane node
  2. Run: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key snapshot save /tmp/etcd-backup.db
  3. Verify: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/etcd-backup.db
💡 Hint: Cert paths are standard for kubeadm. snapshot status shows hash, revision, total keys.
📝 View Solution 
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  snapshot save /tmp/etcd-backup.db
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /tmp/etcd-backup.db
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 6.3 — Trace a Failed Pod Scheduling

Create a pod with impossible resource requests and debug it.

  1. Create a pod requesting 100 CPUs (impossible): kubectl run greedy --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml → edit resources
  2. Check status: kubectl get pods — it should show Pending
  3. Describe: kubectl describe pod greedy — find the Events section
  4. Check scheduler logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-scheduler --tail=20
💡 Hint: The Events section tells you WHY scheduling failed. Scheduler logs show the filtering/scoring process.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl run greedy --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > greedy.yaml
# Edit: resources.requests.cpu: "100"
kubectl apply -f greedy.yaml
kubectl get pods  # STATUS: Pending
kubectl describe pod greedy | grep -A10 Events
# Events: 0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient cpu.
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 6.4 — Locate and Inspect Static Pod Manifests

Find the static pod manifests that define the control plane.

  1. SSH to a control plane node
  2. List manifests: ls -la /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
  3. Read one: cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml
  4. Count how many static pods are running: check kube-system
💡 Hint: 4 manifests: etcd.yaml, kube-apiserver.yaml, kube-controller-manager.yaml, kube-scheduler.yaml.
📝 View Solution 
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests/
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml | head -30
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -o wide | grep $(hostname)
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 6.5 — Check etcd Cluster Health

Verify your etcd cluster is healthy and has quorum.

  1. SSH to control plane node
  2. Check member list: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl member list
  3. Check endpoint health: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl endpoint health
  4. Explain: what happens if 2 out of 3 etcd members go down?
💡 Hint: endpoint health shows each member's status. Quorum = (total/2) + 1. 3 members → quorum=2.
📝 View Solution 
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  member list --write-out=table
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key \
  endpoint health
# 2/3 down → no quorum → cluster READ-ONLY
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 6.6 — View Controller Manager and Scheduler Logs

The control plane logs tell you what's happening behind the scenes.

  1. View scheduler logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-scheduler --tail=30
  2. View controller-manager logs: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-controller-manager --tail=30
  3. Watch logs in real-time as you create a Deployment: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-controller-manager -f (in one terminal) while running kubectl create deployment test --image=nginx (in another)
💡 Hint: Controller-manager logs show the reconciliation loop in action.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-scheduler --tail=30
kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-controller-manager --tail=30
# In terminal 1: kubectl logs -n kube-system -l component=kube-controller-manager -f
# In terminal 2: kubectl create deployment test --image=nginx
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 6.7 — Verify CNI and Node Networking

Check the CNI plugin and pod network configuration.

  1. List CNI pods: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|flannel|weave'
  2. Check node pod CIDRs: kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.podCIDR}'
  3. Get a pod IP and verify you can ping it from another pod
💡 Hint: Each node gets a /24 CIDR range for pod IPs. All pods on a node get IPs from that range.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|flannel|weave'
kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].spec.podCIDR}'
POD_IP=$(kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.podIP}')
kubectl run pingtest --rm -it --image=busybox --restart=Never -- ping -c2 $POD_IP
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 6.8 — Identify Which Node a Pod is Running On

Trace pod placement and understand how the scheduler made its decision.

  1. Create 3 pods: kubectl create deployment spread --image=nginx --replicas=3
  2. Check which node each pod is on: kubectl get pods -o wide
  3. Describe one pod to see scheduler events: kubectl describe pod <name> | grep -A5 Events
  4. Explain: why did the scheduler choose those specific nodes?
💡 Hint: -o wide shows NODE column. Scheduler spreads pods across nodes by default (anti-affinity scoring).
📝 View Solution 
kubectl create deployment spread --image=nginx --replicas=3
kubectl get pods -o wide
POD=$(kubectl get pods -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl describe pod $POD | grep -A5 Events
# Events: Successfully assigned default/spread-xxx to worker-1
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 6.9 — Simulate a Node Failure

Cordon and drain a node, then watch pods reschedule.

  1. Cordon a worker node: kubectl cordon <node>
  2. Watch pods: kubectl get pods -o wide -w (in a separate terminal)
  3. Drain the node: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
  4. Uncordon: kubectl uncordon <node>
💡 Hint: cordon = no new pods. drain = evict existing pods. uncordon = allow pods again.
📝 View Solution 
NODE=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[1].metadata.name}')
kubectl cordon $NODE
kubectl drain $NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
kubectl get pods -o wide
kubectl uncordon $NODE
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 6.10 — Draw the Cluster Architecture from Memory

Recreate the architecture diagram without looking at references.

  1. Draw the control plane (4 components) and their connections
  2. Draw worker nodes (3 components) and their connections
  3. Label each arrow with the protocol/port
  4. Identify which component is the single point of failure in each plane
💡 Hint: API server:6443, etcd:2379, kubelet:10250. API server is stateless (HA possible). etcd is the critical SPOF.
📝 View Solution 
# Draw on paper or whiteboard:
# Control Plane:
#   kube-apiserver (port 6443) ← ALL components talk here
#   etcd (port 2379) ← ONLY apiserver talks to etcd
#   scheduler (port 10251) ← watches apiserver for unbound pods
#   controller-manager (port 10252) ← watches apiserver
#
# Worker Nodes:
#   kubelet (port 10250) ← registers with apiserver
#   kube-proxy ← watches apiserver for Service/Endpoint changes
#   Container Runtime ← controlled by kubelet via CRI
#
# SPOF: etcd — if etcd loses quorum, cluster is read-only

🌊 The Kubernetes Cluster as a Maritime Port — Every Component Visualized

The most intuitive way to understand Kubernetes architecture is through the maritime port analogy. Every K8s component has a direct parallel in a modern shipping port. This mental model helps you diagnose problems: "Is the harbor master accepting ships? Is the logbook intact? Is the crane operator working?"

🏗️ KUBERNETES CLUSTER = A MODERN MARITIME PORT
Understanding K8s architecture through the shipping port analogy
🧠 CONTROL PLANE — The Port Authority (manages everything)
🏢HARBOR MASTER
kube-apiserver
:6443 — The ONLY entry point

Every ship (API request) must check in with the harbor master. Nobody bypasses him. Stateless — can run multiple behind a load balancer.

📖PORT LOGBOOK
etcd
:2379 — Distributed key-value store

The harbor master's logbook. ALL cluster state recorded here. Raft consensus. If lost, the port has amnesia. BACK IT UP.

📊DOCK SCHEDULER
kube-scheduler
Watches for unbound pods

A new ship arrives. Which dock has space? Checks capacity, special equipment (GPU), restrictions (taints). Assigns best dock.

🔄PORT CONTROLLER
controller-manager
Reconciliation loops

Constantly checks: "Are there exactly 3 anihpj-web containers?" If one fell overboard → orders replacement. Self-healing brain.

⬇ ⬇ ⬇ API Server Watches ⬇ ⬇ ⬇
💪 WORKER NODES — The Docks (do the actual work)
🏗️CRANE OPERATOR
kubelet
:10250 — Node agent

Receives instructions: "Unload ship X." Reports back: "3 containers healthy." If kubelet stops reporting → node marked NotReady.

🌐TRAFFIC DIRECTOR
kube-proxy
iptables / IPVS rules

Routes traffic to correct container bays. Maintains routing tables updated in real-time. Service IP → Pod IP mapping.

📦CONTAINER YARD
Container Runtime
CRI gRPC API

The actual container yard. Unpacks images, creates namespaces, starts processes. Controlled by kubelet via CRI.

🔧 Under the Hood — etcd Raft Consensus: Why 3, 5, or 7 Nodes?
Raft Consensus — The Algorithm That Keeps Your Cluster Consistent

etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm to ensure all etcd nodes agree on cluster state. Understanding Raft explains why you need odd numbers of etcd nodes and what "losing quorum" actually means.

Raft Node States:        Leader Election:           Write Flow:
┌──────────┐             ┌─────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────┐
│ LEADER   │◄── writes   │ 1. No heartbeat  │        │ 1. Leader receives  │
│ (1 only) │    go here  │    from leader    │        │    write request    │
└────┬─────┘             │ 2. Follower →     │        │ 2. Leader appends   │
     │                   │    Candidate      │        │    to its log       │
     │ replicates        │ 3. Candidate      │        │ 3. Leader sends     │
     ▼                   │    requests votes │        │    to followers     │
┌──────────┬──────────┐  │ 4. Majority wins  │        │ 4. Majority ACKs    │
│FOLLOWER  │ FOLLOWER │  │    → New Leader   │        │ 5. Leader commits   │
│  (N-1)   │  (N-1)   │  └─────────────────┘        │ 6. Leader responds   │
└──────────┴──────────┘                               └─────────────────────┘

QUORUM = (N/2) + 1  →  3 nodes: quorum=2 (tolerates 1 failure)
                        5 nodes: quorum=3 (tolerates 2 failures)
                        7 nodes: quorum=4 (tolerates 3 failures)

LOSE QUORUM: Cluster is READ-ONLY. API server returns 503 on writes.
No new pods, deployments, or config changes. Existing pods KEEP RUNNING.
⚠️ Platform Engineer's etcd Rules: (1) ALWAYS odd numbers (3, 5, 7). 4 nodes = same fault tolerance as 3. (2) 3 nodes for most production. 5 for critical infra. (3) BACKUP before any etcd operation. (4) Monitor disk latency — Raft is sensitive to slow disks. Use SSDs. (5) NEVER run etcd on same disk as workloads — I/O contention breaks Raft.
📡API Server:6443. Only talks to etcd. Stateless, horizontally scalable. AAA pipeline.
💾etcdRaft consensus. Odd nodes. BACKUP RELIGIOUSLY. Use SSDs only.
📋SchedulerWatches unbound pods. Filters + scores per node. Down = pods Pending.
🤖kubeletNode agent. CRI control. Reports pod/node status. Self-healing trigger.
🌐kube-proxyiptables/IPVS rules. Service IP → Pod IP. Per-node routing.
📦CRI Runtimecontainerd/CRI-O. gVisor/Kata for sandboxed. OCI standard.
🎓 CNPE Exam — etcd Backup & Restore Is a Guaranteed Task

Every CNPE exam includes at least one etcd task. You MUST know this from memory:

# BACKUP (exam provides cert paths)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%Y%m%d).db \
  --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 \
  --cacert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/ca.crt \
  --cert=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.crt \
  --key=/etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/server.key

# VERIFY the backup
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot status /backup/etcd-20260101.db

# RESTORE (use DIFFERENT data directory!)
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot restore /backup/etcd-20260101.db \
  --data-dir=/var/lib/etcd-restored \
  --name=master-1 \
  --initial-cluster=master-1=https://127.0.0.1:2380 \
  --initial-advertise-peer-urls=https://127.0.0.1:2380
# Then edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml → change data-dir → kubelet restarts etcd

K8s architecture debugging speed run:

# Control plane health
kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'etcd|apiserver|scheduler|controller'
kubectl cluster-info

# Node health
kubectl get nodes && kubectl describe node worker-1 | grep -A5 Conditions

# Kubelet debugging (on the node)
systemctl status kubelet && journalctl -u kubelet -f

# Container runtime
crictl ps && crictl images
⚠️ Control Plane Failure Scenarios — What the Exam Tests
  • Scheduler down: New pods stuck Pending. Fix: check /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml — kubelet auto-restarts static pods.
  • Controller Manager down: Deployments stop reconciling. Fix: same as scheduler — check static pod manifest.
  • etcd quorum lost: kubectl hangs or returns 503. Fix: restart etcd on failed node, or restore from backup if multiple nodes lost.
  • API Server down: kubectl returns connection refused. Fix: check crictl ps | grep apiserver, inspect manifest at /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver.yaml.
Q1: If etcd loses quorum (2 of 3 nodes down), what can the cluster still do?

▶ Show Answer
READ operations still work (kubectl get, describe, logs). WRITE operations FAIL (create, apply, delete). Existing pods keep running. Cluster is effectively frozen. Restore from backup if quorum cannot be reestablished.
Q2: What ports must be open between control plane and worker nodes?

▶ Show Answer
CP→Worker: kubelet :10250 (HTTPS). Worker→CP: API server :6443. etcd peers: :2380. etcd clients: :2379. NodePort range: 30000-32767 on ALL nodes.
🚀 Beyond CNPE — Multi-Master HA, etcd at Scale, and Cluster API
  • Stacked vs External etcd: Stacked runs on control plane nodes; external uses dedicated etcd cluster. For production with >50 nodes: external etcd on dedicated SSDs with 10Gbps networking.
  • etcd Defragmentation: etcdctl defrag monthly on each etcd member. Fragmented etcd = higher latency. Schedule during maintenance windows.
  • Cluster API (CAPI): Declarative cluster lifecycle. Instead of kubeadm, create Cluster CRDs. "K8s managing K8s." Used by enterprises managing hundreds of clusters.
  • Karpenter: AWS next-gen node autoscaler. Provisions optimal instance type/zone based on pending pod requirements. 1000+ nodes in minutes.

📖 Chapter 6 Summary: The Kubernetes control plane (API server + etcd + scheduler + controller manager) is the brain. Worker nodes (kubelet + kube-proxy + container runtime) are the muscle. etcd is the most critical component — lose etcd, lose the cluster. As a platform engineer, you design, deploy, and maintain the control plane itself. The CNPE exam tests cluster architecture decisions, etcd backup/restore, and troubleshooting control plane failures.

Pods, ReplicaSets, Deployments, Services, Namespaces, ConfigMaps, Secrets, and Labels/Selectors. The building blocks every platform engineer uses daily.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~2 hours📦 Objects

📖 Chapter Overview: Every Kubernetes platform is built from the same set of core objects. Pods are the smallest unit, ReplicaSets maintain count, Deployments manage lifecycle, Services provide stable networking, Namespaces partition resources, ConfigMaps and Secrets inject configuration, and Labels connect everything. Master these — they're the building blocks for everything that follows.

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • Create and manage Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, and Secrets

📋 CNPE Domain Mapping: All 5 CNPE domains build on these core objects. Domain 1 (Architecture) uses Namespaces for multi-tenancy. Domain 2 (GitOps) deploys Deployments via Argo CD. Domain 3 (Platform APIs) extends these with CRDs. Domain 4 (Observability) monitors them. Domain 5 (Security) protects them with NetworkPolicies and admission control.

7.1 Pods — The Smallest Deployable Unit

A Pod is a group of one or more containers that share network namespace, IPC namespace, and volumes. Every pod gets its own IP. Containers inside a pod communicate via localhost. Pods are EPHEMERAL — they can be killed and replaced at any time.

📖 Pod Lifecycle — Pending → Running → Succeeded/Failed

Pending: Pod accepted, scheduler finding node, pulling images. Running: At least one container started. Succeeded: All containers exited with code 0 (Jobs/CronJobs). Failed: Container exited with error. Unknown: Node unreachable — kubelet stopped reporting. Check with: kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.status.phase}'.

💡 QoS Classes — Who Gets OOM-Killed First

K8s assigns OOM scores: BestEffort (no requests/limits, score 1000) killed FIRST. Burstable (requests set, limits higher, score based on ratio) killed SECOND. Guaranteed (requests == limits, score -998) killed LAST. This is why Kyverno policies should block BestEffort in production — a BestEffort pod is the first victim when memory runs low.

anihpj-web Pod: Contains 2 containers — Nginx (reverse proxy, port 80) + Gunicorn/Django (app, port 8000). They share the pod IP and can communicate via localhost. Nginx proxies to http://127.0.0.1:8000.

📖 Multi-Container Pod Design Patterns — Sidecar, Ambassador, Adapter

When should you put multiple containers in ONE pod vs separate pods? The rule: same pod = same lifecycle. Containers in a pod are scheduled together, scaled together, and die together. They share network (localhost), IPC, and volumes.

PatternWhat It Doesanihpj ExampleOther Examples
SIDECAREnhances the main container without changing it. Runs alongside, shares resources.Nginx sidecar: Reverse proxies to Gunicorn. Handles TLS termination, static files, rate limiting. Gunicorn doesn't know Nginx exists — it just listens on localhost:8000.Istio Envoy proxy, logging sidecar (Fluentd), Cloud SQL Auth proxy
AMBASSADORProxies external connections. Main container talks to localhost, ambassador handles external complexity.Redis Ambassador: If Redis was external (AWS ElastiCache), an ambassador container handles TLS + auth. Django talks to localhost:6379 — ambassador proxies to external Redis.Twemproxy for sharded Redis, any external DB proxy
ADAPTERTransforms output. Main container emits in one format, adapter converts to standard format.Metrics adapter: Django emits custom metrics on :9090. Adapter container scrapes them, converts to Prometheus format on :9091. Prometheus scrapes :9091.Prometheus exporters (Redis, Postgres), log format normalizers

When NOT to use multi-container pods: If containers have independent lifecycles (different scaling needs, different update cadences), use separate Deployments + Services. Only group containers that MUST share fate.

💡 Init Containers — Run Setup Before Your Main App Starts

Init containers run BEFORE app containers and must complete successfully before the app starts. They're perfect for: waiting for a database to be ready, running migrations, setting up permissions. Unlike app containers, init containers run SEQUENTIALLY (A finishes → B starts → C starts → then app containers). If an init container fails, the pod restarts (depending on restartPolicy). anihpj example: an init container runs python manage.py migrate before Gunicorn starts — ensuring the database schema is up to date before any requests arrive.

📖 Probes Deep Dive — Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes

Probes are K8s' health-check system. They determine whether your container is alive, ready for traffic, or still starting up. Misconfigured probes are the #1 cause of unnecessary pod restarts in production.

ProbeWhat It ChecksOn FailureOn SuccessUse Case
livenessProbe"Is the app alive or deadlocked?"Container is KILLED and restarted (crash loop).Nothing — container keeps running.Detect deadlocks, infinite loops, memory corruption. DO NOT check external dependencies here!
readinessProbe"Can this pod serve traffic RIGHT NOW?"Pod removed from Service endpoints. No traffic sent.Pod added to Service endpoints.Wait for DB connection, cache warmup, or heavy computation. Route traffic only when ready.
startupProbe"Has the application finished starting?"Container is KILLED (same as liveness).Liveness and readiness probes take over.Slow-starting apps (JVM, ML models). Disables liveness/readiness until startup completes.

Probe types — how K8s performs the check:

  • HTTP GET: Kubelet sends GET to container on specified port/path. 200-399 = success. Anything else = failure. GET /healthz → 200 OK.
  • TCP Socket: Kubelet tries to open TCP connection. Connection established = success. Refused/timeout = failure. Good for databases (PostgreSQL on :5432).
  • Exec: Kubelet runs a command INSIDE the container. Exit code 0 = success. Non-zero = failure. cat /tmp/healthy — if file exists, healthy.
  • gRPC: (K8s 1.24+) Kubelet makes a gRPC health check call. Requires the app to implement gRPC health protocol.

anihpj probe configuration — with explanation:

livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz          # Django health endpoint
    port: 8000
  initialDelaySeconds: 30   # Wait 30s after start before first check
  periodSeconds: 10         # Check every 10 seconds
  timeoutSeconds: 3         # Timeout after 3s → count as failure
  failureThreshold: 3       # Fail 3 times in a row → KILL container
  # Total: 30 + (10+3)*3 = 69 seconds before restart

readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz?ready=1  # Separate endpoint that checks DB connectivity
    port: 8000
  initialDelaySeconds: 5    # Check almost immediately
  periodSeconds: 5           # Check frequently (traffic routing is critical)
  failureThreshold: 1        # One failure = remove from Service immediately

startupProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz
    port: 8000
  failureThreshold: 30       # Allow 30 failures (30 × 10s = 5 min startup time)
  periodSeconds: 10
  # Gives Django migrations 5 minutes to complete before livenessProbe activates

Common probe mistakes platform engineers must block:

  • 🔴 Liveness probe checks the database: DB is slow → liveness fails → K8s restarts pod → new pod also can't reach DB → restart loop. Liveness should ONLY check if the app process is alive, not its dependencies.
  • 🔴 No startup probe for slow apps: Django migrations take 2 minutes. Liveness probe fires after 30s → K8s kills the pod mid-migration → corrupted database. Add a startup probe with high failureThreshold.
  • 🔴 Readiness probe too aggressive: failureThreshold: 1, periodSeconds: 1 — a single hiccup removes pod from Service. Use at least failureThreshold: 3 to tolerate transient errors.

7.2 ReplicaSets — Maintaining Pod Count

A ReplicaSet ensures a specified number of identical pod replicas are running. If a pod crashes or is deleted, the ReplicaSet creates a replacement. It uses label selectors to identify its pods. You rarely create ReplicaSets directly — Deployments manage them for you.

HOW A REPLICASET WORKS — The Label Selector Pattern
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  REPLICASET: anihpj-web-7f3a2b  (desired: 3)                            │
  │  selector: matchLabels { app: anihpj-web, tier: frontend }              │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                    │
            ┌───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐
            ▼                       ▼                       ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐    ┌─────────────────┐
  │ POD abcde       │    │ POD fghij       │    │ POD klmno       │
  │ labels:         │    │ labels:         │    │ labels:         │
  │ app: anihpj-web │    │ app: anihpj-web │    │ app: anihpj-web │
  │ tier: frontend  │    │ tier: frontend  │    │ tier: frontend  │
  │ IP: 10.0.1.5    │    │ IP: 10.0.1.6    │    │ IP: 10.0.1.7    │
  │ STATUS: Running  │    │ STATUS: Running  │    │ STATUS: Running  │
  └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘    └─────────────────┘
           ▲                      ▲                      ▲
           └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┘
           ALL match the selector → ReplicaSet "owns" them
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  If Pod fghij crashes → ReplicaSet counts: 2 Running, desired=3 → CREATE pod
  If someone creates a pod WITH matching labels → ReplicaSet owns it AND
  deletes it (because count would be 4, exceeding desired: 3)
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

How ReplicaSet watches its Pods: Every second, the Replicaset controller queries the API server: "Give me all pods with labels app=anihpj-web, tier=frontend." If the count ≠ desired replicas, it creates/deletes pods. This is the same reconciliation loop every K8s controller uses. The label selector is the OWNERSHIP LINK — pods with matching labels belong to this ReplicaSet.

😰 ReplicaSet Anti-Pattern — Two ReplicaSets Fighting Over Pods
  • 🔴 ReplicaSet-A: desired=3, selector: app=web. ReplicaSet-B: desired=2, selector: app=web.
  • 🔴 Each ReplicaSet sees 5 pods with app=web. A thinks "too many! delete 2." B thinks "too many! delete 3." They FIGHT — pods are created and deleted in an infinite loop.
  • 🔴 Solution: Unique selectors (app=web, component=api vs app=web, component=worker) or let Deployments handle ReplicaSets (they add pod-template-hash automatically).
💡 ReplicaSet YAML — The Key Fields
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: ReplicaSet
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  labels:
    app: anihpj-web
spec:
  replicas: 3                     # How many pods I want
  selector:
    matchLabels:                  # WHICH pods are mine
      app: anihpj-web
  template:                       # Blueprint for new pods
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-web           # MUST match selector!
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: anihpj-web:latest

Critical rule: template.metadata.labels MUST include ALL labels in selector.matchLabels. If they don't match, the API server rejects the ReplicaSet with "selector does not match template labels".

7.3 Deployments — Managing Application Lifecycle

A Deployment provides declarative updates for Pods and ReplicaSets. It manages rolling updates (gradually replace old pods), rollbacks (kubectl rollout undo), scaling, and pausing. The anihpj-web Deployment: 3 replicas, rolling update with maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0.

💡 Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod Chain

Deployment creates ReplicaSet, ReplicaSet creates Pods. When you update a Deployment (new image), it creates a NEW ReplicaSet and scales down the old one. kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj-web shows all revisions — each is a ReplicaSet.

📖 The Controller Reconciliation Loop — Observe → Diff → Act

Every K8s controller runs an infinite loop: Observe current state (via API server watch), Diff against desired state (from spec), Act to reconcile. The Deployment controller watches Deployments, ReplicaSets, and Pods. Every second: "Does reality match spec.replicas: 3?" If 2 pods exist → create one. If 4 exist → delete one. You never tell K8s to "create a pod" — you declare "I want 3" and the controller figures it out. This same pattern powers Argo CD, Crossplane, and every Operator you'll build.

ROLLING UPDATE — How Deployments Replace Pods With Zero Downtime
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  DEPLOYMENT: anihpj-web  (replicas: 3, update: RollingUpdate)           │
  │  maxSurge: 1 (allow +1 extra pod during update)                         │
  │  maxUnavailable: 1 (allow at most 1 pod to be down)                     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  BEFORE UPDATE — All pods running v1.0.0
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReplicaSet 1 (v1.0.0):  3/3 Ready                                    │
  │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐                                        │
  │  │ P1   │  │ P2   │  │ P3   │    All 3 serving traffic               │
  │  │ v1.0 │  │ v1.0 │  │ v1.0 │                                        │
  │  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────┘                                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  STEP 1 — Create new ReplicaSet, scale UP by maxSurge (1)
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReplicaSet 1 (v1.0.0):  3/3 Ready    ReplicaSet 2 (v2.0.0):  1/1    │
  │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐         ┌──────┐                       │
  │  │ P1   │  │ P2   │  │ P3   │         │ P4   │  ← NEW pod v2.0       │
  │  │ v1.0 │  │ v1.0 │  │ v1.0 │         │ v2.0 │                       │
  │  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────┘         └──────┘                       │
  │  4 total pods (3 v1 + 1 v2) — maxSurge=1 allows 4                      │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  STEP 2 — Scale DOWN old by 1, scale UP new by 1
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReplicaSet 1 (v1.0.0):  2/2 Ready    ReplicaSet 2 (v2.0.0):  2/2    │
  │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐                   ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐              │
  │  │ P1   │  │ P2   │                   │ P4   │  │ P5   │              │
  │  │ v1.0 │  │ v1.0 │                   │ v2.0 │  │ v2.0 │              │
  │  └──────┘  └──────┘                   └──────┘  └──────┘              │
  │  P3 terminated gracefully (SIGTERM → 30s → SIGKILL)                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  STEP 3 — Continue until old ReplicaSet = 0, new ReplicaSet = 3
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReplicaSet 1 (v1.0.0):  0/0 (kept for rollback!)                    │
  │  ReplicaSet 2 (v2.0.0):  3/3 Ready                                    │
  │  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐  ┌──────┐                                        │
  │  │ P4   │  │ P5   │  │ P6   │    All 3 now v2.0                      │
  │  │ v2.0 │  │ v2.0 │  │ v2.0 │    Zero downtime!                      │
  │  └──────┘  └──────┘  └──────┘                                        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  IF v2.0 crashes → kubectl rollout undo → ReplicaSet 1 scales back to 3
  OLD ReplicaSets are NEVER deleted automatically → kubectl rollout history
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
⚠️ Rolling Update Strategy — maxSurge and maxUnavailable

maxSurge: Maximum number of EXTRA pods allowed during update (over desired count). Default: 25% (1 extra per 4 desired). maxUnavailable: Maximum number of pods that can be UNAVAILABLE during update. Default: 25%.

Production values for anihpj (3 replicas): maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 — creates 1 new pod before killing old one, never loses capacity. Development: maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1 — kills old pod first (saves resources, tolerates brief downtime).

📖 Deployment Strategies — Recreate vs RollingUpdate vs Blue/Green vs Canary

Kubernetes Deployments natively support two strategies. For advanced strategies (Blue/Green, Canary), you need additional tools like Argo Rollouts or service meshes. Here's the full comparison:

StrategyHow It WorksDowntimeResourcesRollbackBest For
RecreateKill ALL old pods → create ALL new pods. Simple, brutal.⚠️ YES — full downtime during pod replacementMinimal (no overlap)Instant (just old version)Batch jobs, dev environments, stateful apps that can't have 2 instances
RollingUpdateReplace pods one-by-one. Old + new coexist during update.✅ ZERO (if configured right)+1 extra pod during update (maxSurge)kubectl rollout undoMost production workloads. Default K8s strategy.
Blue/GreenDeploy entire new stack (green) alongside old (blue). Switch traffic via Service selector change.✅ ZERO2× full capacity (both stacks running)Instant (switch selector back)Critical workloads needing instant rollback. Requires Argo Rollouts or manual Service update.
CanaryRoute small % of traffic to new version. Gradually increase. Monitor for errors.✅ ZERO+X% extra (canary pods)Instant (shift traffic back)High-risk changes. Requires Argo Rollouts, Flagger, or service mesh (Istio/Linkerd).

anihpj strategy: RollingUpdate for web (stateless, 3 replicas, no downtime). Blue/Green for database schema changes (migrate → verify → switch). Canary for major Django version upgrades (route 5% traffic → check error rate → ramp to 100%). The CNPE exam asks you to CHOOSE the right strategy — not just implement it.

7.4 Services — Stable Network Endpoints

Pod IPs change when pods are replaced. A Service provides a STABLE IP (ClusterIP) and DNS name that doesn't change. It load-balances traffic to healthy pods matching its label selector.

TypeAccessUse Case
ClusterIPInternal onlyanihpj-web → postgres via postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
NodePortExternal via <NodeIP>:30000-32767Quick testing. NOT for production (bypasses load balancer)
LoadBalancerExternal via cloud LBProduction. Provisions AWS NLB/ALB automatically
😰 Without Services — The Hardcoded IP Nightmare
  • 🔴 anihpj-web pod gets IP 10.0.1.5. You hardcode it in Django settings. Pod crashes → replacement gets IP 10.0.1.9. Django still tries 10.0.1.5 → connection refused.
  • 🔴 You update the Deployment. Old pods terminate, new pods start with NEW random IPs. Every hardcoded IP connection breaks.
  • 🔴 Scale from 3→5 pods. How do you add 2 new IPs to nginx config? Every scale event becomes a manual ops task.
🎉 With Services — Stable DNS and Auto-Discovery
  • ✅ Django connects to postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local — this DNS name NEVER changes, regardless of pod recreation.
  • ✅ Service selector app: anihpj-web auto-discovers new pods. Scale 3→5 → Service immediately includes all 5. Zero config.
  • ✅ kube-proxy updates iptables rules within seconds. Failed pods auto-removed from backend. Healthy pods auto-added.
SERVICE TRAFFIC FLOW — DNS → ClusterIP → kube-proxy → Backend Pod
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HOW A SERVICE ROUTES TRAFFIC — End-to-End Flow                          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────┐
  │  anihpj-web  │  Pod wants to reach postgres
  │  Pod         │  DNS query: "postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local"
  │  IP:10.0.1.5 │
  └──────┬───────┘
         │ ① DNS Lookup
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │  CoreDNS     │  Returns: postgres.anihpj.svc = 10.96.0.5 (ClusterIP)
  │  (kube-dns)  │  This ClusterIP NEVER changes!
  └──────┬───────┘
         │ ② Returns 10.96.0.5
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │  kube-proxy  │  Looks up Service "postgres" → 2 healthy endpoints:
  │  (iptables)  │  10.0.1.10:5432 (READY) and 10.0.1.11:5432 (READY)
  │              │  Randomly picks one → rewrites packet destination
  └──────┬───────┘
         │ ③ Packet routed to chosen backend
         ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  BACKEND PODS (selected by label app=postgres)                       │
  │  ┌─────────────────┐         ┌─────────────────┐                     │
  │  │ Postgres Pod 1  │         │ Postgres Pod 2  │                     │
  │  │ IP: 10.0.1.10   │         │ IP: 10.0.1.11   │                     │
  │  │ STATUS: Ready ✓  │         │ STATUS: Ready ✓  │                     │
  │  └─────────────────┘         └─────────────────┘                     │
  │  kube-proxy picks one → rewrites 10.96.0.5:5432 → 10.0.1.10:5432    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  KEY: DNS resolves Service NAME → ClusterIP (virtual, no interface).
  kube-proxy translates ClusterIP → real Pod IP. This is a 2-step process.
  If the chosen pod goes down → kube-proxy removes it from the iptables rules
  within ~5 seconds (endpoint controller sync period).
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

7.5 Namespaces — Virtual Clusters for Multi-Tenancy

Namespaces partition a physical cluster into virtual clusters. Each team gets their own namespace with resource quotas, RBAC, and NetworkPolicies. Platform engineering pattern: Namespace-as-a-Service — developers request a namespace via a self-service portal and get it pre-configured.

NAMESPACE-AS-A-SERVICE — Platform Engineering Pattern
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    PHYSICAL KUBERNETES CLUSTER                           │
  │                                                                         │
  │  ┌───────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────┐  ┌───────────────────┐   │
  │  │ NAMESPACE: team-a │  │ NAMESPACE: team-b │  │ NAMESPACE: team-c │   │
  │  │                   │  │                   │  │                   │   │
  │  │ Quota: 10 pods    │  │ Quota: 20 pods    │  │ Quota: 5 pods     │   │
  │  │ CPU: 4 cores      │  │ CPU: 8 cores      │  │ CPU: 2 cores      │   │
  │  │ Mem: 8Gi          │  │ Mem: 16Gi         │  │ Mem: 4Gi          │   │
  │  │                   │  │                   │  │                   │   │
  │  │ RBAC: team-a-edit │  │ RBAC: team-b-edit │  │ RBAC: team-c-view │   │
  │  │ NetPol: allow     │  │ NetPol: allow     │  │ NetPol: deny-all  │   │
  │  │   from team-b     │  │   from team-a     │  │                   │   │
  │  │                   │  │                   │  │                   │   │
  │  │ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ │  │ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ ┌───┐ │  │ ┌───┐             │   │
  │  │ │ P │ │ P │ │ P │ │  │ │ P │ │ P │ │ P │ │  │ │ P │             │   │
  │  │ └───┘ └───┘ └───┘ │  │ └───┘ └───┘ └───┘ │  │ └───┘             │   │
  │  └───────────────────┘  └───────────────────┘  └───────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                         │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ SYSTEM NAMESPACES (never touch unless you know what you're doing)│   │
  │  │ kube-system  │  kube-public  │  kube-node-lease  │  default      │   │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
  Each namespace = isolated boundary with its OWN: ResourceQuota, RBAC,
  NetworkPolicy, LimitRange. Teams can't see/access each other's resources.
  But they SHARE: physical nodes, CNI network, cluster DNS (CoreDNS).
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

ResourceQuota: A namespace-wide limit on total resources. Prevents one team from monopolizing the cluster. LimitRange: Sets default requests/limits for pods that don't specify them. Together they enforce fair sharing and prevent untracked resource consumption.

💡 ResourceQuota + LimitRange — The Platform Engineer's Guardrails
# ResourceQuota: Hard limits for the namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: team-a-quota
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "10"            # Max 10 pods
    requests.cpu: "4"     # Total CPU requested ≤ 4 cores
    requests.memory: "8Gi"
    limits.cpu: "8"       # Total CPU limits ≤ 8 cores
    limits.memory: "16Gi"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "5"
---
# LimitRange: Default values for pods without explicit requests
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: team-a-limits
  namespace: team-a
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:              # If no limits set
      cpu: "500m"
      memory: "512Mi"
    defaultRequest:       # If no requests set
      cpu: "250m"
      memory: "256Mi"
    max:                  # Hard upper bound
      cpu: "2"
      memory: "2Gi"

Why this matters: A pod without requests/limits can consume ALL CPU on a node. LimitRange ensures every pod gets sensible defaults. ResourceQuota prevents namespace explosion. Together they're the platform engineer's multi-tenancy guardrails.

🎉 Namespace-as-a-Service — Self-Service Platform Pattern
  • ✅ Developer opens Backstage portal → clicks "Create Namespace" → enters team name, requested CPU/memory → submits.
  • ✅ Backstage triggers a pipeline that creates: Namespace + ResourceQuota + LimitRange + RBAC (RoleBinding to team's AD group) + NetworkPolicy (default-deny) + ServiceAccount.
  • ✅ Developer gets a fully provisioned namespace with all guardrails in ~30 seconds. No platform engineer involved.
  • ✅ This is the "Golden Path" — self-service with baked-in security. The CNPE exam tests your ability to DESIGN this, not just configure it.
📖 Namespace Naming Convention — The Platform Engineer's Standard

Good naming prevents chaos across hundreds of namespaces:

  • <team>-<environment>: team-a-dev, team-b-prod
  • <app>-<stage>: anihpj-staging, anihpj-production
  • Avoid: test1, johns-namespace, temp123. These tell you nothing.
  • Label namespaces: kubectl label ns team-a-dev environment=dev team=team-a cost-center=1234 — labels enable queries like "show me all production namespaces."

7.6 Labels, Selectors, and Annotations

Labels are key-value pairs that organize objects. Selectors query objects by labels. Services use selectors to find their backend pods. Annotations store non-identifying metadata (git commit, build timestamp). Labels are the GLUE of Kubernetes. Example: app: anihpj-web, tier: frontend, environment: production.

FeatureLabelsAnnotations
PurposeIdentify and select objectsStore non-identifying metadata
QueryableYes — kubectl get pods -l app=webNo — not queryable by selector
Used byServices, Deployments, ReplicaSets (selectors)Tools: kubectl, monitoring, GitOps
Size limit63 chars for key, 63 chars for valueNo size limit (but etcd has 1.5MB total per object)
Examplesapp: anihpj-web
tier: frontend		git-commit: a1b2c3d
deployed-at: 2024-01-15
💡 Kubernetes Recommended Labels — The app.kubernetes.io Standard

Every resource SHOULD have these 6 labels. Argo CD, Helm, and kubectl all understand them:

LabelExampleMeaning
app.kubernetes.io/nameanihpjThe application name
app.kubernetes.io/instanceanihpj-prodUnique instance of the app
app.kubernetes.io/version1.2.0The current version
app.kubernetes.io/componentwebThe component within the architecture
app.kubernetes.io/part-ofanihpjThe higher-level application this belongs to
app.kubernetes.io/managed-byhelmThe tool managing this resource

Why this matters: Argo CD uses these labels to group resources in the UI. Helm adds app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm automatically. If you use these labels consistently, every tool in the ecosystem understands your deployments.

📖 Selector Types — Equality vs Set-Based

Equality-based: environment = production, tier != frontend. Used by Services and ReplicaSets (matchLabels). Simple: matches or doesn't.

Set-based: environment in (production, staging), tier notin (frontend), app (exists), !critical (does not exist). Used by Deployments (matchExpressions), RBAC, and NetworkPolicy. More expressive.

Production example — anihpj staging Service that matches ALL frontend AND backend:

selector:
  matchLabels:
    app: anihpj-web
  matchExpressions:
    - {key: environment, operator: In, values: [staging]}
    - {key: tier, operator: NotIn, values: [batch]}  # exclude batch jobs
🎉 Label Strategy — The Platform Engineer's Auto-Discovery Pattern
  • ✅ Every anihpj resource gets: app.kubernetes.io/part-of: anihpj, app.kubernetes.io/environment: production
  • ✅ Services auto-discover pods by label (app: anihpj-web) — no hardcoded pod IPs.
  • ✅ Prometheus auto-discovers scrape targets by label (prometheus.io/scrape: "true").
  • ✅ NetworkPolicies allow traffic by label (from: podSelector: tier: frontend).
  • ✅ Argo CD groups resources by app.kubernetes.io/part-of in its tree view.
  • ✅ A well-designed label strategy means you NEVER lookup pod IPs — you query by label instead.

7.7 ConfigMaps and Secrets

ConfigMap stores non-sensitive config. Secret stores sensitive data (base64 encoded, NOT encrypted by default). Both can be mounted as environment variables or files. anihpj ConfigMap: DEBUG, ALLOWED_HOSTS, DB_HOST. anihpj Secret: DB_PASSWORD, SECRET_KEY.

🧠 CNPE Exam: Secrets are base64 ENCODED, not encrypted. Anyone with kubectl get secret -o yaml can decode them. Use Sealed Secrets, External Secrets Operator, or Vault for production.
📖 Secret Management Tools — From Basic to Enterprise

Base64-encoded Secrets in etcd are NOT production-ready. Here's the evolution of Secret management — and what platform engineers should deploy at each maturity level:

ToolHow It WorksEncrypted in Git?Auto-Rotate?ComplexityBest For
Encryption at RestAPI server encrypts Secrets before writing to etcd. Built-in. Configure with EncryptionConfiguration.N/A (etcd only)❌ No⭐ LowFirst step. Every production cluster MUST enable this. Prevents etcd compromise = secret exposure.
Sealed SecretsEncrypt Secret with cluster's public key. Only that cluster can decrypt. Encrypted YAML is safe in Git.✅ Yes❌ No (manual)⭐⭐ MediumGitOps workflows. Devs commit encrypted secrets. Controller decrypts in cluster. Simple, effective.
External Secrets OperatorSyncs secrets from external store (AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault) INTO K8s Secrets.✅ Yes (in external store)✅ Yes (if external store supports it)⭐⭐⭐ MediumCloud-native. One ExternalSecret CRD → auto-syncs → K8s Secret stays updated. anihpj uses this for DB_PASSWORD from AWS Secrets Manager.
HashiCorp Vault + Vault CSISecrets NEVER touch etcd. Vault CSI provider mounts secrets directly into pod filesystem. App reads from file.✅ Yes (in Vault)✅ Yes (Vault dynamic secrets)⭐⭐⭐⭐ HighEnterprise. Dynamic DB credentials (new user per pod!), audit logging, multi-cloud. Most secure — secret never exists as K8s object.

anihpj secret flow (Production): Developer creates ExternalSecret CRD → ESO fetches DB_PASSWORD from AWS Secrets Manager → creates K8s Secret → Deployment mounts it via env var → Django reads os.environ['DB_PASSWORD']. Rotating the secret: update AWS Secrets Manager → ESO auto-syncs to K8s → trigger rollout restart.

📖 Encryption at Rest — Making Secrets Actually Secret

By default, Secrets in etcd are plain base64 (easily decoded). Enable EncryptionConfiguration on the API server to encrypt them with AES-CBC before writing to etcd. Add --encryption-provider-config=/etc/kubernetes/encryption-config.yaml to the kube-apiserver static pod manifest. Existing Secrets won't be auto-encrypted — rewrite them with kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -. This is a Domain 5 (Security) tested skill.

💡 ConfigMap Updates — 3 Ways to Reload Without Manual Restarts

ConfigMaps injected as env vars require pod restart. ConfigMaps mounted as files update on disk within ~60s (kubelet sync) but apps may cache old values. Three solutions: (1) Reloader — watches ConfigMap changes, auto-restarts Deployments. (2) Mount + inotify — app watches mounted file for changes. (3) Versioned ConfigMaps — name includes hash (anihpj-config-a1b2c3), update Deployment to reference new name → rolling update naturally.

KUBERNETES OBJECT RELATIONSHIP MAP

🏋️ Chapter 7 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

The CNPE is a performance-based exam — you solve tasks in a live Linux terminal. Practice these drills in your lab environment until you can complete each within the target time.

⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 7.1 — Create a Deployment with Resource Limits

Create a Deployment for anihpj-web with 3 replicas, resource requests/limits, and health probes.

  1. Write a Deployment YAML for anihpj-web: 3 replicas, image anihpj-web:latest, container port 8000
  2. Add resources: requests (256Mi, 250m), limits (512Mi, 500m)
  3. Add liveness probe: HTTP GET /healthz every 10s, timeout 3s
  4. Add readiness probe: HTTP GET /healthz?ready=1 every 5s
  5. Apply and verify: kubectl get deploy,pods -n anihpj
💡 Hint: kubectl create deployment --dry-run=client -o yaml for a starting template.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl create deployment anihpj-web --image=anihpj-web:latest --replicas=3 \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml -n anihpj > deploy.yaml
# Edit: add resources, livenessProbe, readinessProbe
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl get deploy,pods -n anihpj
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.2 — Expose a Deployment with a Service and Test DNS

Create a ClusterIP Service and verify DNS resolution.

  1. Expose the Deployment: kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web --port=8000 --target-port=8000 -n anihpj
  2. Check the Service: kubectl get svc -n anihpj
  3. Test DNS from a debug pod: kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox -n anihpj -- nslookup anihpj-web
💡 Hint: Full DNS name: anihpj-web.anihpj.svc.cluster.local
📝 View Solution 
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web --port=8000 --target-port=8000 -n anihpj
kubectl run dns-test --rm -it --image=busybox -n anihpj -- nslookup anihpj-web
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.3 — Perform a Rolling Update and Rollback

Update the anihpj-web image and verify the rolling update, then rollback.

  1. Update image: kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-web anihpj-web=anihpj-web:v2.0.0 -n anihpj
  2. Watch: kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
  3. Check history: kubectl rollout history deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
  4. Rollback: kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
💡 Hint: rollout undo reverts to the previous revision. --to-revision=1 goes to a specific one.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl set image deployment/anihpj-web anihpj-web=anihpj-web:v2.0.0 -n anihpj
kubectl rollout status deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
kubectl rollout undo deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 7.4 — Create ConfigMap and Secret, Mount in Pod

Inject configuration into pods the proper way.

  1. Create ConfigMap: kubectl create configmap anihpj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=false --from-literal=DB_HOST=postgres -n anihpj
  2. Create Secret: kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cret123 -n anihpj
  3. Update Deployment to mount both as env vars using envFrom
  4. Verify: kubectl exec <pod> -n anihpj -- env | grep -E 'DEBUG|DB_'
💡 Hint: Use envFrom.configMapRef and envFrom.secretRef in the Deployment spec.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl create configmap anihpj-config --from-literal=DEBUG=false -n anihpj
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cret123 -n anihpj
# Edit deployment: add envFrom to container spec
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl exec $POD -n anihpj -- env | grep -E 'DEBUG|DB_'
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.5 — Create Namespace with Resource Quota

Set up multi-tenancy with ResourceQuota.

  1. Create namespace: kubectl create ns team-blue
  2. Apply ResourceQuota: max 10 pods, max 4 CPUs, max 8Gi memory
  3. Try creating 11 pods — the 11th should be rejected
💡 Hint: kubectl create quota or write a ResourceQuota YAML.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl create ns team-blue
kubectl create quota team-blue-quota --hard=pods=10,cpu=4,memory=8Gi -n team-blue
# Create 11 pods — the 11th fails with "exceeded quota"
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 7.6 — Query Objects with Label Selectors

Use labels to filter and find specific resources.

  1. List pods with label app=anihpj-web
  2. List pods across ALL namespaces with tier=frontend
  3. Show labels on all deployments: kubectl get deploy -n anihpj --show-labels
💡 Hint: kubectl get pods -l app=anihpj-web, kubectl get pods -A -l tier=frontend
📝 View Solution 
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web
kubectl get pods -A -l tier=frontend
kubectl get deploy -n anihpj --show-labels
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.7 — Scale a Deployment Manually and with Autoscaling

Scale up and down, then set up HPA.

  1. Scale up: kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=5 -n anihpj
  2. Verify 5 pods are running
  3. Scale down to 2 and verify
  4. Set up HPA: kubectl autoscale deployment anihpj-web --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=80 -n anihpj
💡 Hint: kubectl scale for manual. kubectl autoscale for HPA.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=5 -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web
kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=2 -n anihpj
kubectl autoscale deployment anihpj-web --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=80 -n anihpj
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.8 — Debug a CrashLoopBackOff Pod

A pod keeps crashing. Debug and fix it.

  1. Create a pod with a bad command: kubectl run crash --image=nginx --command -- /bin/false -n anihpj
  2. Check status: should show CrashLoopBackOff
  3. Describe: kubectl describe pod crash -n anihpj — note exit code
  4. Check logs of previous instance: kubectl logs crash -n anihpj --previous
💡 Hint: --previous shows logs from the LAST crashed container.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl run crash --image=nginx --command -- /bin/false -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj  # STATUS: CrashLoopBackOff
kubectl describe pod crash -n anihpj | grep -E 'State|Exit Code'
kubectl logs crash -n anihpj --previous
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.9 — Create a NodePort Service and Access It Externally

Expose anihpj-web externally via NodePort.

  1. Create NodePort service: kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web --type=NodePort --port=8000 -n anihpj
  2. Get the assigned port: kubectl get svc -n anihpj
  3. Access externally: curl http://<NODE_IP>:<NODEPORT>/healthz
💡 Hint: NodePort range is 30000-32767. Get node IP: kubectl get nodes -o wide.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl expose deployment anihpj-web --type=NodePort --port=8000 -n anihpj
kubectl get svc -n anihpj
NODE_IP=$(kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.addresses[0].address}')
NODEPORT=$(kubectl get svc anihpj-web -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.spec.ports[0].nodePort}')
curl http://$NODE_IP:$NODEPORT/healthz
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 7.10 — Design a Complete Label Strategy

Apply a comprehensive label strategy to all anihpj resources.

  1. Define labels: app.kubernetes.io/name, app.kubernetes.io/part-of, app.kubernetes.io/environment
  2. Label the namespace: kubectl label ns anihpj environment=staging team=platform
  3. Verify all pods inherit the right labels via their Deployment template
💡 Hint: app.kubernetes.io/* labels are the Kubernetes recommended standard.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl label ns anihpj app.kubernetes.io/part-of=anihpj app.kubernetes.io/environment=staging
kubectl get pods -n anihpj --show-labels

🗺️ Kubernetes Object Relationship Map — How Everything Connects

Understanding how Kubernetes objects relate to each other is the key to platform engineering. This visual map shows the ownership chain from external traffic down to running containers, and how configuration flows through ConfigMaps, Secrets, and ServiceAccounts.

🔗 K8s Object Ownership & Data Flow Hierarchy

From Ingress → Service → Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pod → Container — and how ConfigMaps, Secrets, PVCs, and ServiceAccounts attach

🌍Ingress Routes HTTP(S) by host/path. TLS via cert-manager.
▼

▼

▼

📋ReplicaSet Maintains pod count. Label selector = ownership.
▼

🫛Pod (anihpj-web-abc123) IP: 10.244.1.5. 2 containers: Nginx + Gunicorn/Django.
▼

🔒SecretDB_PASSWORD, KEY
💾PVC → PV/app/media files
