🌐 How a User Request Flows Through the anihpj Stack

Follow a request from the user's browser, through every Kubernetes layer, to the Django application and back.

👤BrowserGET /jobs/
🔀IngressTLS termination
🔌ServiceClusterIP → Pod
🐍Django PodNginx→Gunicorn→DB
📤Response200 OK JSON
🫛PodsSmallest unit. Shared network/IPC. Sidecar/Ambassador/Adapter patterns.
🔄DeploymentsRolling updates, rollbacks, scaling. Owns ReplicaSet → owns Pods.
🔌ServicesStable DNS + IP. ClusterIP/NodePort/LB. Endpoint routing.
🏷️LabelsSelectors connect Services→Pods. Ownership chains. Multi-tenancy.
⚙️ConfigMapsEnv vars / volumes. Non-sensitive. Pods don't auto-reload changes.
🔒SecretsBase64 (not encrypted!). Enable encryption at rest. External Secrets.
🎯 Core Objects Are 60%+ of CNPE Exam Tasks

Almost every exam task involves creating or modifying Pods, Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, or Secrets. Master these patterns:

  • Create + Expose: k create deployment X --image=Y --replicas=N then k expose deployment X --port=P. 30 seconds.
  • Config injection: k create configmap X --from-literal=k=v then k set env deployment/Y --from=configmap/X.
  • Rollback: k set image deployment/X container=image:v2 → pods crash → k rollout undo deployment/X. Reverts in seconds.
  • Debug: k describe pod X (events) → k logs X (logs) → k exec -it X -- /bin/bash (interactive). Always this order.

Generate complex objects with kubectl, then edit. Never write YAML from scratch:

# Pod: k run mypod --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > pod.yaml  → edit probes/volumes
# Deployment: k create deploy myapp --image=nginx --replicas=5 --dry-run=client -o yaml > deploy.yaml
# Service: k expose deploy myapp --port=80 --target-port=8080 --type=ClusterIP --dry-run=client -o yaml
# ConfigMap: k create cm myconfig --from-literal=key1=val1 --from-literal=key2=val2 --dry-run=client -o yaml
# Job: k create job migrate --image=anihpj-web -- python manage.py migrate --dry-run=client -o yaml
⚠️ Top 3 CNPE Object Mistakes
  • Selector mismatch: Service selector doesn't match Pod labels. Fix: kubectl get pods --show-labels, match Service selector exactly. Verify with kubectl get endpoints.
  • ConfigMap/Secret not updating: Pods don't auto-reload mounted ConfigMaps. Fix: kubectl rollout restart deployment/X after updating.
  • Wrong namespace: Created resources in default instead of specified namespace. Fix: kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=target-ns BEFORE creating anything.
Q1: What happens to a Pod's IP when the Pod is deleted and recreated?

▶ Show Answer
The Pod gets a NEW IP. Pod IPs are ephemeral. This is why you NEVER reference pod IPs directly — always use a Service (stable ClusterIP + DNS).
Q2: Your Deployment has replicas:3 but you see 4 pods. Why?

▶ Show Answer
During RollingUpdate with maxSurge:1, total pods can briefly be 4 (3 old + 1 new). Once new pod is healthy, old pod terminates. Total returns to 3. This is normal — zero-downtime updates.
🚀 Beyond CNPE — Advanced K8s Object Patterns for Platform Teams
  • PodDisruptionBudget (PDB): minAvailable: 2 on 3-replica Deployment prevents node drains from evicting more than 1 pod at a time. Essential for production.
  • TopologySpreadConstraints: maxSkew: 1 ensures pods are evenly distributed across zones/hosts. Prevents all replicas landing on same node.
  • External Secrets Operator: Syncs secrets from AWS Secrets Manager / HashiCorp Vault into K8s Secrets every 60 seconds. Automatic rotation + audit logging.
  • Kustomize Overlays: k8s/base/ + k8s/overlays/dev/ + k8s/overlays/production/. Same base, different patches. No copy-paste. No drift.

📖 Chapter 7 Summary: Kubernetes objects form a hierarchy: Namespace contains Deployments → Deployments own ReplicaSets → ReplicaSets own Pods. Services provide stable networking. ConfigMaps and Secrets inject configuration. Labels connect everything. Master these building blocks — they're used in every subsequent chapter.

Chapter 8: Setting Up Your Platform Lab Environment

6-cluster local lab, kubectl, kubeconfig, multi-cluster context switching, deploying anihpj step by step, and verifying everything works.

🟢 Beginner⏱️ ~2 hours🛠️ Hands-On

📖 Chapter Overview: Theory is useless without practice. This chapter guides you through setting up a 6-cluster local lab where you'll run every example in this guide: kubeadm for production-like scenarios, 3 kind clusters for GitOps multi-cluster workflows, minikube for quick testing, and k3d for security experiments. We'll install kubectl, configure kubeconfig for multiple clusters, deploy anihpj, and verify everything.

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • Set up 6 local Kubernetes clusters with different tools
  • Configure kubectl and kubeconfig for multi-cluster management
  • Safely switch between cluster contexts
  • Deploy the full anihpj stack to your lab cluster
  • Verify deployments with describe, logs, exec, and port-forward

8.1 Choosing Local Kubernetes Tools

ToolTypeBest ForStartup TimeMemory Usage
kubeadmProduction-like (VMs)Full control plane experience. etcd backup/restore, static pods, upgrades. Closest to real CNPE exam.5-10 min~4GB
kindDocker-basedFast create/destroy. Multi-node clusters in Docker. Great for CI/CD and GitOps testing.30 sec~500MB/node
minikubeSingle-node VM/containerEasy local dev with built-in addons (ingress, dashboard, metrics-server).2 min~2GB
k3dK3s in DockerUltra-lightweight. K3s is a certified K8s distribution. Good for policy/security experiments.15 sec~300MB/node
💡 Installation Guide — All 4 Tools on Ubuntu
# === kubeadm (requires 2+ VMs or multipass) ===
# On each VM:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl
curl -fsSL https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.29/deb/Release.key | sudo gpg --dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg
echo 'deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg] https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.29/deb/ /' | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y kubelet kubeadm kubectl
sudo apt-mark hold kubelet kubeadm kubectl  # prevent auto-updates

# Install container runtime (containerd)
sudo apt install -y containerd
sudo mkdir -p /etc/containerd
containerd config default | sudo tee /etc/containerd/config.toml
sudo systemctl restart containerd

# On control-plane node:
sudo kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr=10.244.0.0/16
mkdir -p $HOME/.kube && sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/flannel-io/flannel/releases/latest/download/kube-flannel.yml

# On worker nodes (use token from kubeadm init output):
sudo kubeadm join :6443 --token  --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# On Ubuntu/Debian:
[ $(uname -m) = x86_64 ] && curl -Lo ./kind https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/dl/v0.22.0/kind-linux-amd64
chmod +x ./kind && sudo mv ./kind /usr/local/bin/kind

# Create 3 clusters:
kind create cluster --name dev
kind create cluster --name staging
kind create cluster --name prod

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# === minikube ===

😰 "I destroyed my production cluster!" — A Context Horror Story
  • 🔴 What happened: Platform engineer was debugging an issue. Switched to kind-dev to test a fix. Got distracted by a Slack message. Came back, forgot to switch context. Ran kubectl delete namespace anihpj — but current-context was kind-prod, not kind-dev.
  • 🔴 Result: The ENTIRE production namespace — including the Postgres StatefulSet and PVC — was deleted in 2 seconds. No confirmation prompt. No undo.
  • 🔴 Recovery: Velero backup restored the namespace in ~5 minutes. PVC data was recovered from the backup. Downtime: 8 minutes. Root cause: no context verification before destructive commands.
  • 🟡 Prevention: (1) Context in PS1 prompt. (2) kubectl config current-context before DELETE. (3) Production cluster uses a DIFFERENT kubeconfig file entirely — export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/prod-config only when needed. (4) Enable kubectl delete dry-run: alias kdelete='echo "Are you sure? Use: kubectl delete --dry-run=client ... first"'.

8.2 Installing kubectl and Configuring kubeconfig

kubectl is the CLI for Kubernetes. Install via brew install kubectl (macOS), choco install kubernetes-cli (Windows), or apt install kubectl (Linux).

kubeconfig (~/.kube/config) stores cluster connection info, user credentials, and contexts. A context = cluster + user + namespace. Switch between clusters with kubectl config use-context cluster1.

💡 kubectl Plugins and Krew — Extend kubectl with Custom Commands

kubectl has a plugin system: any executable named kubectl-<name> on your PATH becomes a kubectl <name> command. Krew is the plugin manager (like brew for kubectl). Essential plugins for platform engineers:

  • kubectl ctx (kubectx): Interactive context switcher. kubectl ctx → pick from list. Safer than typing context names manually.
  • kubectl ns (kubens): Interactive namespace switcher. kubectl ns → pick namespace. Sets default namespace for current context.
  • kubectl neat: Removes clutter from kubectl get -o yaml output — strips status, managedFields, and default values. Clean YAML for documentation.
  • kubectl tree: Shows ownership hierarchy. kubectl tree deployment anihpj-web → Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods. Visualizes the ownership chain.

Install Krew: follow instructions at krew.sigs.k8s.io. Then: kubectl krew install ctx ns neat tree.

8.3 Managing Multiple Clusters and Contexts

Always verify your current context before destructive commands. kubectl config current-context tells you which cluster you're targeting. Use kubectx (interactive context switcher) for fast switching with visual feedback. The CNPE exam will give you specific contexts per task — using the wrong context = zero points.

⚠️ The CNPE Exam Context Trap — How to Avoid Zero-Point Tasks

Every CNPE exam task specifies a kubectl context. If you stay on the wrong cluster, you execute perfectly but get ZERO points. Before typing ANY command, run kubectl config current-context first. It takes 1 second and has saved thousands of candidates from failing. Add this to your .bashrc:

# Show current k8s context in your prompt
export PS1="[\u@\h \W \$(kubectl config current-context 2>/dev/null)]\$ "
# Prompt: [user@host ~ cluster1-admin@cluster1]$
💡 kubeconfig Deep Dive — clusters, users, contexts

~/.kube/config has 3 sections: clusters (API server URLs + CA certs), users (client certs + keys), and contexts (cluster + user + namespace combinations). A context is a pointer: it references a cluster and a user. current-context is the active one. Merge kubeconfigs with: KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config:~/.kube/config2 kubectl config view --flatten > merged. View with: kubectl config view.

📖 kubeconfig Troubleshooting — "The connection to the server localhost:8080 was refused"

This is the most common kubectl error for beginners. It means kubectl can't find a valid kubeconfig. Here's the debug flowchart:

  1. Does the file exist? ls -la ~/.kube/config. If not, you never ran kubeadm init or copied the admin.conf.
  2. Is KUBECONFIG env var set? echo $KUBECONFIG. If set, it OVERRIDES ~/.kube/config. Unset it or point it to the right file.
  3. Are the paths in the config valid? kubectl config view — check certificate-authority, client-certificate, client-key paths. They must be absolute paths or relative to ~/.kube/.
  4. Is the server reachable? curl -k https://SERVER_IP:6443/healthz. If not, VPN or firewall might be blocking.
  5. Is the certificate still valid? kubectl config view --raw -o jsonpath='{.clusters[0].cluster.certificate-authority-data}' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -dates — check notAfter. K8s CA certs expire after 10 years.

8.5 Step-by-Step Deployment — From Zero to anihpj Running

Follow these steps in order. Each step builds on the previous. If a step fails, fix it before continuing — don't skip ahead.

💡 Step 1: Create the Namespace
kubectl create namespace anihpj
kubectl label ns anihpj app.kubernetes.io/part-of=anihpj environment=staging

Namespaces isolate resources. Label it so tools like Argo CD and Prometheus understand who owns it.

💡 Step 2: Create ConfigMap and Secret
# ConfigMap: Non-sensitive app configuration
kubectl create configmap anihpj-config -n anihpj \
  --from-literal=DEBUG=false \
  --from-literal=DB_HOST=postgres \
  --from-literal=DB_NAME=anihpj \
  --from-literal=REDIS_HOST=redis

# Secret: Sensitive data (base64 encoded, enable encryption at rest!)
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret -n anihpj \
  --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=s3cret-password \
  --from-literal=SECRET_KEY=django-insecure-abc123 \
  --from-literal=REDIS_PASSWORD=redis-secret

These inject configuration WITHOUT hardcoding values in Deployment YAML. The Deployment references them by name via envFrom.

💡 Step 3: Deploy PostgreSQL (StatefulSet + Service)
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/03-postgres-statefulset.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/04-postgres-service.yaml -n anihpj

PostgreSQL runs as a StatefulSet — each replica has a stable identity (postgres-0, postgres-1) and persistent storage via PVC. The Service creates DNS: postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local. Wait for it to be ready: kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pod/postgres-0 -n anihpj --timeout=120s.

Why StatefulSet, not Deployment? Databases need stable network identities, ordered startup/shutdown, and persistent storage per replica. Stateless apps like web servers don't need this — they use Deployments.

💡 Step 4: Deploy Redis (Deployment + Service)
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/05-redis-deployment.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/06-redis-service.yaml -n anihpj

Redis is stateless cache — a Deployment is fine. In production, use Redis Sentinel or Cluster for HA. DNS: redis.anihpj.svc.cluster.local.

💡 Step 5: Deploy anihpj Web Application (Deployment + Service)
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/07-anihpj-web-deployment.yaml -n anihpj
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/08-anihpj-web-service.yaml -n anihpj

The web Deployment runs 3 replicas with 2 containers per pod (Nginx + Gunicorn/Django). The Service makes it reachable at anihpj-web.anihpj.svc.cluster.local:8000.

💡 Step 6: Deploy Ingress — Expose to the Outside World
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/11-ingress.yaml -n anihpj

The Ingress routes external HTTP(S) traffic to the anihpj-web Service based on hostname (Host: anihpj.com) and path (/jobs/, /api/). For local testing without a domain, use port-forward instead.

😰 Common Deployment Failures — What Goes Wrong and Why
  • 🔴 ImagePullBackOff: Wrong image name, private registry without ImagePullSecret, or Docker Hub rate limit. Fix: kubectl describe pod <name> -n anihpj | grep -A5 Events.
  • 🔴 CrashLoopBackOff: Application crashes on startup. Missing ConfigMap/Secret env vars, DB not reachable, or permissions issue. Fix: kubectl logs <pod> -n anihpj --previous to see the crash logs.
  • 🔴 Pending (forever): Scheduler can't find a node. Insufficient CPU/memory, node taints not tolerated, or PVC can't bind. Fix: kubectl describe pod <name> -n anihpj | grep -A10 Events.
  • 🔴 Service has no endpoints: Selector doesn't match any pod labels. Fix: kubectl get endpoints -n anihpj — if column is empty, selector is wrong.

8.6 Verifying Everything — The Platform Engineer's Checklist

Don't just assume everything works. Verify each component methodically. This checklist is what you'd run in a production deployment pipeline.

#CheckCommandExpected Result
1All pods Runningkubectl get pods -n anihpjSTATUS: Running, READY: 1/1 or 2/2
2No crash loopskubectl get pods -n anihpj | grep -v RunningNo output (all pods Running)
3Services have endpointskubectl get endpoints -n anihpjEach Service has IP:port pairs
4Logs show startup successkubectl logs -l app=anihpj-web -n anihpj --tail=10No ERROR/FATAL lines
5Web app respondskubectl port-forward svc/anihpj-web 8080:8000 -n anihpj &
curl http://localhost:8080/healthz		HTTP 200 OK
6DB connectivitykubectl exec -it deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -- python manage.py check --database default"System check identified no issues"
7Redis connectivitykubectl exec -it deploy/redis -n anihpj -- redis-cli PINGPONG
8Resource usagekubectl top pods -n anihpjAll pods show CPU/Memory values
9ConfigMap mountedkubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -- env | grep DB_HOSTDB_HOST=postgres
10Persistent storagekubectl exec postgres-0 -n anihpj -- df -h /var/lib/postgresql/dataPVC shows mounted with size
💡 Verification One-Liner — Check Everything in One Command
# Quick health check for the entire anihpj namespace
echo "=== Pods ===" && kubectl get pods -n anihpj && \
echo "=== Services ===" && kubectl get svc -n anihpj && \
echo "=== Endpoints ===" && kubectl get endpoints -n anihpj && \
echo "=== ConfigMaps ===" && kubectl get configmaps -n anihpj && \
echo "=== Secrets ===" && kubectl get secrets -n anihpj && \
echo "=== PersistentVolumeClaims ===" && kubectl get pvc -n anihpj

Run this after every deployment. If anything looks wrong, use kubectl describe and kubectl logs to investigate. The CNPE exam expects you to debug — not just deploy and hope.

⚠️ If Something Fails — The Platform Engineer's Debugging Protocol

1. Events first: kubectl describe pod <name> -n anihpj | tail -20 — Events tell you EXACTLY what went wrong and when.

2. Logs second: kubectl logs <pod> -n anihpj --tail=50 — Application-level errors. --previous shows logs from the last crashed instance.

3. Exec third: kubectl exec -it <pod> -n anihpj -- /bin/bash — Enter the container and debug live (check files, run commands, test connectivity).

4. Check dependencies: Is the DB pod running? Can the web pod resolve postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local? Run kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -- nslookup postgres.anihpj.svc.cluster.local.

5. Scale to zero and back: Sometimes restarting is the fastest fix: kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=0 -n anihpj && kubectl scale deployment anihpj-web --replicas=3 -n anihpj.

🏋️ Chapter 8 — Hands-On Practice Drills (10 Exercises)

The CNPE is a performance-based exam — you solve tasks in a live Linux terminal. Practice these drills in your lab environment until you can complete each within the target time.

⏱️ Target: 10 minutes
Drill 8.1 — Set Up Your 6-Cluster Lab

Create all 6 clusters and verify they're accessible.

  1. Create cluster1 (kubeadm): follow kubeadm setup guide
  2. Create clusters 2-4 (kind): kind create cluster --name dev, etc.
  3. Create cluster5: minikube start
  4. Create cluster6: k3d cluster create security
  5. Verify all: kubectl config get-contexts
💡 Hint: Use kind create cluster for clusters 2-4. kubectl config get-contexts shows all.
📝 View Solution 
kind create cluster --name dev
kind create cluster --name staging
kind create cluster --name prod
minikube start
k3d cluster create security
kubectl config get-contexts
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 8.2 — Switch Contexts Safely

Practice context switching and always verify before executing.

  1. Switch to cluster1: kubectl config use-context cluster1
  2. Verify: kubectl config current-context
  3. Switch to cluster3 (kind-staging)
  4. List nodes to confirm you're on the right cluster
💡 Hint: kubectl config current-context before EVERY command is the habit that saves you on exam day.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl config use-context kind-dev
kubectl config current-context
kubectl get nodes  # Should show kind-dev nodes only
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 8.3 — Deploy Full anihpj Stack to Your Lab

Deploy the complete anihpj application to cluster1.

  1. Switch to cluster1 context
  2. Create namespace: kubectl create ns anihpj
  3. Apply all base manifests: kubectl apply -f k8s/base/ -n anihpj
  4. Wait for all pods: kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready pods --all -n anihpj --timeout=120s
💡 Hint: Apply base manifests in order (00- to 13-). Or use kubectl apply -f k8s/base/ --recursive.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl config use-context cluster1-admin@cluster1
kubectl create ns anihpj
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/ --recursive -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 8.4 — Debug Using Logs, Describe, and Exec

Use the debugging trifecta on a running pod.

  1. Describe a pod: kubectl describe pod <name> -n anihpj
  2. View logs: kubectl logs <name> -n anihpj --tail=20
  3. Exec into pod: kubectl exec -it <name> -n anihpj -- /bin/bash
  4. Check environment variables inside: env | grep DB_
💡 Hint: Describe = Events + State. Logs = stdout/stderr. Exec = interactive shell.
📝 View Solution 
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
kubectl describe pod $POD -n anihpj | tail -20
kubectl logs $POD -n anihpj --tail=20
kubectl exec -it $POD -n anihpj -- env | grep DB_
⏱️ Target: 3 minutes
Drill 8.5 — Port-Forward and Access the App Locally

Access the anihpj web app from your browser via port-forward.

  1. Port-forward: kubectl port-forward svc/anihpj-web 8080:8000 -n anihpj
  2. Open browser: http://localhost:8080/jobs/
  3. Test API: curl http://localhost:8080/api/jobs/
  4. Test health: curl http://localhost:8080/healthz
💡 Hint: Port-forward runs in the foreground. Use & to background it, or open a second terminal.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl port-forward svc/anihpj-web 8080:8000 -n anihpj &
curl http://localhost:8080/healthz
curl http://localhost:8080/api/jobs/
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 8.6 — Merge Multiple kubeconfig Files

Platform engineers manage dozens of clusters. Merge their kubeconfigs into one file.

  1. Export kubeconfigs: copy each cluster's kubeconfig to /tmp/cluster1.yaml, /tmp/cluster2.yaml, etc.
  2. Merge them: KUBECONFIG=/tmp/cluster1.yaml:/tmp/cluster2.yaml:/tmp/cluster3.yaml kubectl config view --flatten > ~/.kube/merged-config
  3. Backup original: cp ~/.kube/config ~/.kube/config.bak
  4. Replace with merged: cp ~/.kube/merged-config ~/.kube/config
  5. Verify all contexts: kubectl config get-contexts — should show all 6 clusters
💡 Hint: KUBECONFIG env var accepts colon-separated paths. --flatten merges them into one file.
📝 View Solution 
KUBECONFIG=/tmp/cluster1.yaml:/tmp/cluster2.yaml:/tmp/cluster3.yaml \
  kubectl config view --flatten > ~/.kube/merged-config
cp ~/.kube/config ~/.kube/config.bak
cp ~/.kube/merged-config ~/.kube/config
kubectl config get-contexts
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 8.7 — Install and Use kubectl Plugins (krew, ctx, ns)

Install Krew and essential plugins to boost your kubectl productivity.

  1. Install Krew from krew.sigs.k8s.io
  2. Install plugins: kubectl krew install ctx ns neat tree
  3. Switch context: kubectl ctx and pick from interactive list
  4. Switch namespace: kubectl ns and pick from list
  5. Clean YAML: kubectl neat pod anihpj-web-xxx -n anihpj — removes status noise
💡 Hint: kubectl ctx is safer than kubectl config use-context — visual feedback prevents mistakes.
📝 View Solution 
# Install Krew (follow instructions at krew.sigs.k8s.io)
kubectl krew install ctx ns neat tree
kubectl ctx  # Interactive: select cluster
kubectl ns   # Interactive: select namespace
kubectl neat pod $(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -o name | head -1) | head -20
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 8.8 — Deploy anihpj to 3 Clusters (Dev, Staging, Prod)

Apply the full anihpj stack to 3 different kind clusters.

  1. Switch to kind-dev: kubectl ctx kind-dev
  2. Deploy anihpj: kubectl apply -f k8s/overlays/dev/ -n anihpj
  3. Switch to kind-staging, deploy with k8s/overlays/staging/
  4. Switch to kind-prod, deploy with k8s/overlays/production/
  5. Verify each: kubectl get pods -n anihpj on each cluster
💡 Hint: Each overlay has different replica counts, resource limits, and DB configurations.
📝 View Solution 
# Dev
kubectl ctx kind-dev
kubectl apply -f k8s/overlays/dev/ -n anihpj

# Staging
kubectl ctx kind-staging
kubectl apply -f k8s/overlays/staging/ -n anihpj

# Production
kubectl ctx kind-prod
kubectl apply -f k8s/overlays/production/ -n anihpj

# Verify all
for ctx in kind-dev kind-staging kind-prod; do
  kubectl ctx $ctx && kubectl get pods -n anihpj
done
⏱️ Target: 4 minutes
Drill 8.9 — Delete a Cluster Completely and Recreate It

Practice fast cluster creation and deletion — a critical exam skill.

  1. Delete a kind cluster: kind delete cluster --name dev
  2. Verify it's gone: kubectl config get-contexts | grep dev
  3. Recreate: kind create cluster --name dev
  4. Re-deploy anihpj: apply base manifests
  5. Verify everything works: check pods, services, endpoints
💡 Hint: kind delete cluster is instant. Recreate takes ~30 seconds. Perfect for exam practice.
📝 View Solution 
kind delete cluster --name dev
kind create cluster --name dev
kubectl ctx kind-dev
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/ -n anihpj --recursive
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w  # Watch pods start
⏱️ Target: 5 minutes
Drill 8.10 — Troubleshoot a Broken Deployment (Simulated Failure)

Someone deployed anihpj with a wrong DB password. Debug and fix it.

  1. Create a Secret with wrong password: kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=wrongpass -n anihpj
  2. Deploy anihpj — web pods will crash (CrashLoopBackOff) because they can't connect to DB
  3. Debug: kubectl logs <web-pod> -n anihpj --previous — see "password authentication failed"
  4. Fix the Secret: kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=correctpass -n anihpj --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl replace -f -
  5. Restart Deployment: kubectl rollout restart deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
  6. Verify recovery: pods should now be Running
💡 Hint: --previous shows logs from the crashed instance. rollout restart creates new pods with updated Secret.
📝 View Solution 
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=wrongpass -n anihpj
kubectl apply -f k8s/base/ -n anihpj
# Wait for CrashLoopBackOff
kubectl logs $(kubectl get pods -n anihpj -l app=anihpj-web -o name | head -1) -n anihpj --previous
# Fix: replace secret, restart
kubectl create secret generic anihpj-secret --from-literal=DB_PASSWORD=correctpass -n anihpj \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl replace -f -
kubectl rollout restart deployment/anihpj-web -n anihpj
kubectl get pods -n anihpj -w  # Watch recovery

8.7 Day 2 Operations — Maintaining Your Lab Environment

Setting up a lab is easy. Keeping it running, clean, and useful for weeks of study is the real challenge. Here's your maintenance playbook.

💡 Daily Startup Script — Get All 6 Clusters Ready in One Command
#!/bin/bash
# lab-start.sh — Start all 6 clusters and verify
set -e

echo "=== Starting Lab Clusters ==="

# kind clusters (if Docker is running, they auto-start)
for cluster in dev staging prod; do
  if kind get clusters | grep -q "^$cluster$"; then
    echo "kind-$cluster: already exists"
  else
    kind create cluster --name $cluster
  fi
done

# minikube
minikube status &>/dev/null || minikube start

# k3d
k3d cluster list | grep -q security || k3d cluster create security

echo ""
echo "=== Current Contexts ==="
kubectl config get-contexts
echo ""
echo "⚠️  Current: $(kubectl config current-context)"
echo "✅ Lab ready!"
📖 Lab Resource Management — Don't Let Docker Eat Your Laptop

6 clusters = a LOT of containers. Here's how to manage resources:

  • Stop clusters you're not using: kind delete cluster --name dev and recreate later. Takes 30 seconds to restore.
  • Pause Docker: docker pause $(docker ps -q) freezes all containers. docker unpause $(docker ps -aq) to resume. CPU drops to zero while paused.
  • Monitor usage: docker stats --no-stream shows per-container CPU/memory. docker system df shows disk usage.
  • Clean up weekly: docker system prune -a -f --volumes. Removes unused images, containers, volumes. Frees GB of space.
  • Minimum lab: If resources are tight, run just 3 kind clusters + 1 k3d. That's ~2GB RAM vs ~6GB for all 6.
⚠️ Lab Backup Strategy — Protect Your Work

You'll invest dozens of hours in your lab. Don't lose your work:

  • Backup kubeconfig: cp ~/.kube/config ~/.kube/config.backup.$(date +%Y%m%d) — weekly. This is small but irreplaceable.
  • Backup your manifests: All anihpj YAML files should be in Git. git push daily. The lab is disposable; your code is not.
  • Backup etcd (kubeadm cluster): ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd-$(date +%Y%m%d).db — weekly. Test the restore: restore to a NEW data-dir and verify.
  • Disaster recovery test (monthly): Delete all kind clusters. Recreate from scratch. Re-deploy anihpj from Git. Time how long it takes. Target: under 15 minutes.
🎓 The 6-Cluster Lab IS Your Exam Preparation

The CNPE exam gives you MULTIPLE Kubernetes clusters. You must switch between them per task. Before exam day, be able to: (1) Switch context in under 1s. (2) ALWAYS verify before destructive commands. (3) Deploy anihpj to any cluster in under 2 min. (4) Debug failing pods using describe→logs→exec on any cluster. (5) Delete and recreate any cluster in under 30s.

🎯 CNPE Lab Strategy — Which Cluster for Which Practice
ClusterToolPractice FocusCNPE Domain
cluster1kubeadmetcd backup/restore, control plane debugging, static pods, upgradesDomain 1 · Architecture
kind-devkindArgo CD installation + GitOps workflow, Kustomize overlaysDomain 2 · GitOps & CD
kind-stagingkindCanary deployments (Argo Rollouts), smoke tests, pre-prod validationDomains 2+4
kind-prodkindMulti-cluster promotion, RBAC, PDB, HPA, NetworkPolicyDomains 1+5
minikubeminikubeQuick tests, Backstage setup, developer portal experimentationDomain 3
k3d-securityk3dKyverno/OPA policies, Falco runtime detection, Pod Security, TrivyDomain 5 · Security
⚠️ The CNPE Context Trap — How Candidates Lose 30%+ of Points

Every CNPE exam task specifies a kubectl context at the TOP: "Context: cluster3-admin@cluster3. Create a Deployment named 'web' in namespace 'production'..." If you forget to switch, you execute on the WRONG cluster → 0 points. Your ritual: 1. Read context FIRST. 2. kubectl config use-context <given-context>. 3. kubectl config current-context and CONFIRM. 4. Now read the task. 5. Execute. Practice this in your 6-cluster lab until automatic.

Q1: You run kubectl get pods and see error: the server doesn't have a resource type "pods". What are the 3 most likely causes?

▶ Show Answer
1. Wrong context — you're pointing to a misconfigured cluster. 2. kubeconfig issue — server URL or cert paths are wrong. 3. API server unreachable — network issue or API server down. Always check context first: kubectl config current-context.
Q2: What's the fastest way to deploy and expose an application?

▶ Show Answer
kubectl create ns app && kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx --replicas=3 -n app && kubectl expose deployment web --port=80 -n app. Three commands, under 30 seconds. For external access: kubectl port-forward svc/web 8080:80 -n app.
🚀 Beyond CNPE — Production Lab Environments (vCluster, Telepresence)
  • vCluster: Virtual clusters inside a physical cluster. Each developer gets their own vCluster with full admin access. Provisioned in seconds, deleted when PR merged. One physical cluster hosts 50 vClusters.
  • Telepresence: Run a single service locally while connected to remote cluster. Local anihpj-web connects to real postgres/redis in staging. Debug with IDE breakpoints but use real dependencies.
  • Ephemeral Environments: Every PR gets its own full-stack test environment. Auto-created with URL → QA tests → feedback → auto-deleted after inactivity. This is the future of dev environments.

📖 Chapter 8 Summary: Your 6-cluster lab is the foundation for all hands-on practice. Cluster1 (kubeadm) for production-like scenarios, clusters 2-4 (kind) for GitOps multi-cluster workflows, cluster5 (minikube) for quick testing, and cluster6 (k3d) for security experiments. Master kubectl context switching — it's the skill that saves you from catastrophic mistakes on the CNPE exam.

9.1 What Is Platform Architecture? — The Blueprint for Your IDP

Platform architecture is HOW you structure your clusters, networks, storage, and compute to support multiple teams and applications. It's the set of decisions that determine whether your platform scales to 200 developers or collapses at 20.

🧠
The Platform Architect's Mindset

You're not a K8s admin — you're designing the city developers will live in. Think in terms of: blast radius, failure domains, tenant isolation, cost allocation, developer experience. Every decision affects hundreds of developers for years.

📐
Architecture = Trade-Offs

There is no "perfect" architecture — only trade-offs. Simplicity vs isolation. Cost vs control. Speed vs safety. Your job is to understand the trade-offs and choose the best fit for YOUR organization's specific constraints.

🏗️ Platform Architecture = The Foundation of Everything

Think of platform architecture as the city plan for your digital infrastructure. Before you build a single building (deploy an application), you need to decide:

  • Zoning: How do you separate neighborhoods? (multi-tenancy — namespaces, vClusters)
  • Roads: How does traffic flow? (networking — CNI, Service Mesh, Ingress)
  • Utilities: Where does water/electricity come from? (storage — PVs, CSI drivers)
  • Building codes: What are the rules everyone follows? (policies — RBAC, NetworkPolicy, PSS)
  • City limits: One big city or many small towns? (single-cluster vs multi-cluster)

Just like a poorly planned city (traffic jams, power outages, zoning chaos), a poorly architected platform creates constant firefighting. And unlike city planning, you CAN change platform architecture — but it's expensive, disruptive, and risks downtime.

The three fundamental architecture decisions every platform engineer must make:

DecisionOption AOption BKey Trade-Off
1. Cluster Topology Single large cluster Multiple smaller clusters Simplicity vs blast-radius isolation
2. Tenant Isolation Soft (namespaces + RBAC + NetworkPolicy) Hard (vCluster, Kamaji, separate clusters) Operational simplicity vs security isolation
3. Infrastructure Location Cloud (EKS/AKS/GKE) On-Prem / Hybrid / Multi-Cloud Managed convenience vs control/compliance
⚡ Speed Tip — Architecture Decisions Compound

"Architecture is the decisions you wish you could get right early." Changing from single-cluster to multi-cluster after 50 teams are onboarded is a migration project, not a configuration change. Changing tenant isolation from soft to hard means rebuilding every team's namespace. Each decision in this chapter has a reversibility cost — we'll call it out explicitly.

🔀 UTH: "Should We Use One Big Cluster or Many Small Ones?"

🖥️ Uncle: "Just give everyone one big cluster! It's simpler — one API server, one place to manage. K8s can handle thousands of nodes!"

🧑‍💻 Tech Lead: "One cluster means one blast radius. If a developer runs a fork bomb, EVERY team goes down. If you misconfigure an admission webhook, ALL deployments fail. One cluster also means one etcd — if etcd has issues, the entire company is dead in the water."

🧔‍♂️ Hiker: "The answer is 'it depends.' For a 20-person startup, one cluster with good namespace isolation works great. For a 500-engineer enterprise with PCI-DSS workloads, you need separate clusters for compliance boundaries. The real question is: what's your blast radius tolerance?"

The anihpj platform architecture we'll design throughout this part of the guide:

👨‍💻Self-Service Layer: Backstage portal → developers request namespaces, DBs, TLS certs
🚀Delivery Layer: Argo CD (GitOps) → deploys from Git to multiple clusters
☸️Orchestration Layer: 3 clusters (dev/staging/prod) with soft multi-tenancy + network isolation
📊Observability: Prometheus/Grafana/Loki/Tempo — unified across all clusters
🔒Security: Kyverno policies, NetworkPolicy default-deny, mTLS via Cilium
📋 Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) — Documenting WHY

Every architecture decision in this chapter should be documented as an ADR — a lightweight text file in your platform repository explaining:

  1. Title: "ADR-001: Use Multi-Cluster Topology for PCI Compliance"
  2. Context: "3 teams, one requires PCI-DSS. Single cluster would mix PCI/non-PCI workloads."
  3. Decision: "Deploy 2 EKS clusters: one PCI-scoped, one shared for non-PCI teams."
  4. Consequences: "Higher operational cost (2 control planes). But clear compliance boundary."

ADRs live in platform/docs/adr/ in Git — always accessible, always versioned. When someone asks "Why did we choose 3 clusters?", you point them to ADR-001. When a new CTO wants to consolidate to one cluster, you re-read ADR-001 before changing course. CNPE exam tip: Mentioning ADRs in design questions shows architectural maturity.

🔬 Platform Architecture vs System Architecture — What's Different?

A common mistake: applying system architecture thinking to platform architecture. They're fundamentally different disciplines:

DimensionSystem Architecture
(Building ONE system)		Platform Architecture
(Building a system FOR building systems)
UsersEnd users (customers, visitors)Developers — who build FOR end users. Your "customers" are engineers.
OutputA working applicationA self-service capability. The "product" is the ability for others to ship.
Scale measurementRequests per second, concurrent usersNumber of development teams, deployments per day, time-to-first-deploy
Failure impactUsers see errors. Revenue lost.Developers can't ship. ALL teams blocked. Compounding revenue loss.
Success metricUptime, latency, throughputDeveloper satisfaction (NPS), deploy frequency, ticket deflection rate
Change frequencyApplication changes daily/weeklyArchitecture changes are rare — they ripple across ALL teams. Must be right.
⚠️ The Architecture Characteristics You CANNOT Ignore (The "-ilities")

Every platform architecture must satisfy these non-functional requirements. If your design can't answer "yes" to each, you have a gap:

CharacteristicWhat It Means for Your PlatformFailure Mode If Ignored
ScalabilityCan your platform support 10→100→500 developers without redesign?Platform becomes the bottleneck. Developers wait for infra. They bypass the platform.
IsolabilityCan one team's mistake affect another team? (Blast radius)"The payments team took down search AGAIN." Trust erodes. Teams demand separate clusters.
ObservabilityCan you see what's happening across all clusters, namespaces, teams?Debugging takes hours. You don't know WHO deployed WHAT. Incidents drag on.
SecurityIs least privilege enforced? Are secrets rotated? Are images scanned?Data breach. Compliance audit failure. CEO has to explain to the board.
Cost-EfficiencyDo you know what each team costs? Can you optimize without degrading service?$50K/month cloud bill. "We don't know who spent what." CFO demands cuts.
EvolvabilityCan you change architecture decisions without a full rewrite?Architecture becomes legacy after 18 months. Platform team spends all time fighting tech debt.
⚠️ Real Failure Story: The $2M Architecture Mistake

In 2022, a 150-person fintech company built their platform on a SINGLE large EKS cluster with namespace-based isolation. 18 months later, they had 45 teams, 2,000+ namespaces, and a problem: their etcd database was 8GB (the recommended max). API server response times were 3+ seconds. The only fix? A 6-month, $2M migration to split into 8 clusters — rewriting CI/CD pipelines, reconfiguring Argo CD, retraining all 150 developers on new contexts. The root cause: they optimized for day-1 simplicity and ignored the day-500 scaling limit. Lesson: When you choose single-cluster, know your scaling ceiling and plan the transition BEFORE you hit it.

9.2 Cloud Native Design Principles — 12-Factor, Declarative, Immutable

Cloud Native platforms are built on three foundational principles: 12-Factor App methodology, Declarative configuration, and Immutable infrastructure. Every decision in your platform architecture should align with these principles.

📐 The 12-Factor App — Cloud Native Application Design

Originally published by Heroku co-founder Adam Wiggins (12factor.net), the 12-Factor methodology defines how to build applications that thrive in cloud environments. For platform architects, each factor maps to a platform capability you must provide.

#FactorWhat It MeansPlatform Architect Must Provide
ICodebaseOne codebase per app in Git. Many deploys from same codebase.Git repos + CI/CD pipeline. Same commit flows through environments.
IIDependenciesExplicitly declare ALL deps. Never rely on system packages.Container registry + image scanning. Block implicit system deps.
IIIConfigConfig in ENVIRONMENT (env vars), NEVER in code. Config ≠ code.ConfigMaps, Secrets, External Secrets Operator. No config in images.
IVBacking ServicesTreat DBs, caches, queues as ATTACHED resources. Swap via config.DatabaseClaim CRD + Crossplane. Self-service provisioning. Connection string via env var.
VBuild/Release/RunStrict separation: Build → Release (config+build) → Run.CI builds image. Argo CD combines image+config = Release. K8s runs it.
VIProcessesStateless + share-nothing. Persistent data → backing service.StatefulSets + PVs for state. Stateless pods killed/replaced anytime.
VIIPort BindingApp exports via port binding. No external app server needed.Service + Ingress. App listens on $PORT. Platform handles exposure.
VIIIConcurrencyScale OUT (more processes), not UP (bigger processes).HPA + Cluster Autoscaler/Karpenter. Scale pods, not VMs.
IXDisposabilityFast startup + graceful shutdown. Processes disposable anytime.SIGTERM handling. terminationGracePeriodSeconds. PDBs.
XDev/Prod ParityKeep dev, staging, production as SIMILAR as possible.Identical K8s envs. Same CNI, same CSI, same policies. Only scale differs.
XILogsTreat logs as EVENT STREAMS. App writes stdout. Platform routes.Fluent Bit → Loki. NEVER let apps write logs to files. stdout only.
XIIAdmin ProcessesRun admin tasks as ONE-OFF processes. DB migrations, cleanup.Job/CronJob for admin tasks. Never SSH into pods for migrations.
⚡ anihpj/jobpost — 12-Factor Applied
  • Codebase: Single repo at github.com/anihpj/jobpost. One codebase → dev/staging/prod deploys.
  • Dependencies: requirements.txt pinned with exact versions. Docker multi-stage build isolates build deps from runtime.
  • Config: Django settings from env vars. DEBUG=$DEBUG, DB_HOST=$DB_HOST. ConfigMap for non-sensitive, Secret for DB_PASSWORD.
  • Backing Services: PostgreSQL via DatabaseClaim CRD → Crossplane → RDS. Connection string in env var. Swap to local Postgres for dev by changing one env var.
  • Build/Release/Run: GitHub Actions builds image → ECR with git SHA tag → Argo CD combines image+config → K8s runs pods.
  • Logs: Django writes JSON to stdout → Fluent Bit collects → adds K8s metadata → Loki. kubectl logs anihpj-web-xxx shows structured output.
🔀 UTH: Declarative vs Imperative — "Just tell me what to type!"

🖥️ Uncle: "Why do I have to write a 40-line YAML file? Just kubectl run web --image=nginx --replicas=3 — done in 5 seconds!"

🧑‍💻 Tech Lead: "Because when something breaks at 3 AM, you won't remember what commands you ran 6 months ago. The YAML in Git is your DOCUMENTATION, your AUDIT LOG, and your ROLLBACK PLAN."

🧔‍♂️ Hiker: "Use imperative for exploration: kubectl run test --image=busybox --rm -it -- sh. Use declarative for everything that matters: kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml. Save even imperative commands with --dry-run=client -o yaml > file.yaml."

AspectImperative ("How")Declarative ("What")
Examplekubectl run web --image=nginx --replicas=3kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
IdempotencyRe-running may create duplicates or failRe-running = no change (safe to re-apply)
Version ControlCommands in bash history (ephemeral)YAML in Git (versioned, reviewed, auditable)
Drift DetectionNone — can't tell if someone manually changed thingsK8s/GitOps auto-detects and fixes drift
RollbackMust remember previous stategit revert → Argo CD syncs previous state
CNPE ExamUse for quick exploration onlyPREFERRED — leaves YAML artifact examiner can review
⚠️ The Imperative Trap — Why CNPE Marks You Down

The CNPE exam PREFERS declarative approaches. If a task says "Create a Deployment," always: kubectl create deploy web --image=nginx --dry-run=client -o yaml > web.yaml then kubectl apply -f web.yaml. The YAML file is your EVIDENCE — the examiner can review it. Imperative commands leave no artifact.

🧊 Immutable Infrastructure — Never Modify, Destroy and Recreate

Immutable infrastructure means you NEVER modify running infrastructure. If something changes, destroy it and recreate from a known-good, version-controlled template. The mantra: "Cattle, not pets."

⚠️ Mutable vs Immutable — A Tale of Two Servers

❌ Mutable (Snowflake Server): Running for 18 months. 147 packages installed manually. No one remembers what's needed. apt-get update might break everything. Python 3.9 in /usr/local/ but system expects 3.8. The server is a snowflake — unique, irreplaceable, terrifying to reboot.

✅ Immutable (Cattle): Pod running from anihpj-web:abc123. Image built from Dockerfile in Git. Scanned by Trivy (0 CRITICAL). Signed by Cosign. Pod crashes? Replacement starts from SAME image. Update? Build new image → new pods → old pods terminated. No drift. No mystery. Full audit.

🌳 Immutability Decision Tree — How Platform Architects Apply It
Something needs to change?
Config change?
→ Update ConfigMap/Secret
→ kubectl apply
→ Restart pods (new pods pick up config)
App change?
→ Git push new code
→ CI builds new image
→ Argo CD deploys new pods
Infrastructure change?
Cloud infra:
→ Terraform/Crossplane
→ Plan → Apply
→ New infra provisioned, old destroyed
K8s resources:
→ kubectl apply new manifest
→ New pods created
→ Old pods terminated gracefully
How Immutability Protects the anihpj Platform
1Developer pushes code to Git
→
2CI builds immutable image (git SHA tag)
→
3Trivy scans image (block on CRITICAL)
→
4Cosign signs image
→
5Argo CD deploys new pods, terminates old

Every anihpj-web pod is identical. No config drift between staging and production. git log shows every change. docker history shows every layer. Complete traceability.

9.3 Single-Cluster vs Multi-Cluster Topologies

The most consequential platform architecture decision: One big cluster or many small ones? This decision affects blast radius, operational complexity, cost, and team autonomy.

DimensionSingle Large ClusterMultiple Smaller Clusters
Blast Radius🔴 One failure = all teams down. etcd failure = company-wide outage.🟢 One cluster fails = only that team affected. Isolation by default.
Operational Complexity🟢 One API server, one etcd, one set of policies. Simple to manage.🔴 N clusters = N control planes, N etcd, N policy sets. Needs automation.
Cost🟢 One control plane cost shared by all. Higher node utilization (bin-packing).🔴 Each cluster has control plane overhead. More idle capacity across clusters.
Team Autonomy🔴 Shared cluster = shared rules. Teams can't choose their own CNI, CSI, or K8s version.🟢 Teams can choose tools, upgrade independently. "You own your cluster."
Multi-Tenancy🟡 Must implement carefully: namespaces + RBAC + NetworkPolicy + quotas.🟢 Natural isolation — separate clusters for separate teams/concerns.
Compliance🔴 PCI-DSS workloads share infra with non-PCI. Harder to prove isolation.🟢 PCI workloads on dedicated clusters. Clean compliance boundary.
Upgrades🔴 One K8s upgrade = all workloads affected. Must coordinate with all teams.🟢 Canary upgrade: upgrade one cluster, observe, then roll out to others.
Best ForStartups (<50 devs), single application, low compliance requirements.Enterprises (50+ devs), multi-team, PCI-DSS/HIPAA, independent teams.
🔀 UTH: "One Cluster to Rule Them All" — The CTO Debate

🖥️ Uncle (the CTO): "One big cluster! It's simpler, cheaper, and Kubernetes can handle 5,000 nodes. Why would we fragment our infrastructure?"

🧑‍💻 Tech Lead: "Because when the payments team deploys a buggy admission webhook, every team's deployments fail. When analytics runs a Spark job that OOMs the node, the frontend pods get evicted. One cluster = one failure domain."

🧔‍♂️ Hiker: "The middle path: 3-5 clusters organized by ENVIRONMENT (dev/staging/prod) with namespace-based multi-tenancy within each. For highly regulated workloads (PCI-DSS), a dedicated compliance cluster. This gives you 80% of the isolation benefit at 30% of the operational cost of per-team clusters."

💡 The anihpj Multi-Cluster Topology

anihpj uses 3 clusters organized by environment:

  • dev-cluster (kind): Per-developer namespaces. Ephemeral PR environments. Fast iteration. Cheapest.
  • staging-cluster (kind): Mirrors production. Integration tests, smoke tests, UAT. Pre-prod validation gate.
  • prod-cluster (EKS): Production workloads. Strict RBAC. Multi-AZ. Velero backups. PDBs on everything.

GitOps flow: PR merged → Argo CD deploys to dev → tests pass → auto-promote to staging → manual approval → deploy to prod. Each cluster is a promotion gate.

📊 When to Scale OUT (more clusters) vs UP (bigger cluster)
TriggerScale UP (Bigger Cluster)Scale OUT (More Clusters)
New team onboardedAdd namespace + quotas. 5 minutes.Provision new cluster. 30 minutes.
Compliance requirementAdd NetworkPolicy + PSS. May NOT satisfy auditor.Dedicated cluster. Clean compliance boundary. Auditor smiles.
K8s version upgradeOne upgrade = all teams affected. Coordinate carefully.Canary upgrade: upgrade one cluster, observe, roll out.
Noisy neighbor attackResourceQuota + LimitRange mitigate. Not perfect.Separate cluster = COMPLETE isolation. Neighbor can't affect you.
Control plane failureAll teams down. Company-wide outage. CEO calls.One cluster down = one team affected. Others unaffected.
Cost optimizationHigher utilization (bin-packing). One control plane cost.Lower utilization per cluster. N × control plane cost.
🧮 How to Calculate Your Cluster Count — The Math Behind the Decision

There's no magic formula, but here's a systematic way to determine how many clusters you need:

  1. Start with 3 environments: dev, staging, production. That's 3 clusters minimum. (Some merge dev+staging = 2 minimum.)
  2. Add 1 per compliance boundary: PCI-DSS? +1 cluster. HIPAA? +1 cluster. SOX? +1 cluster. Each regulation that requires PROVABLE isolation gets its own cluster.
  3. Add 1 per geographic region: If you have teams in US-East, EU-West, AP-Southeast with data residency requirements, that's +1 per region.
  4. Add 1 per blast-radius concern: If you have a "crown jewel" service (payment processing, auth) that must NEVER go down due to other teams, consider a dedicated cluster.
  5. Subtract if you can merge: If dev+staging can share a cluster (with namespaces), merge them. If non-PCI and PCI teams can use vCluster on the same host, merge them.

Example for a 150-person company: 3 (dev/staging/prod) + 1 (PCI) + 1 (EU data residency) = 5 clusters. This is manageable with Argo CD + Cluster API. Example for a 20-person startup: 2 clusters (dev+staging merged, prod). No compliance boundaries. Simple, cheap, effective.

⚡ Migration Path: From 1 Cluster to N Clusters — The Strangler Fig Pattern

If you already have a single cluster and need to split it, don't attempt a "big bang" migration. Use the Strangler Fig pattern:

  1. Week 1-2: Provision new clusters alongside the old one. Set up Argo CD to deploy to BOTH old and new.
  2. Week 3-4: Migrate ONE low-risk team to the new cluster. Learn from it. Fix the problems.
  3. Week 5-8: Migrate 2-3 more teams. Each migration teaches you something.
  4. Week 9-12: Migrate remaining teams. Old cluster now runs nothing. Keep it as a "canary" for 1 month.
  5. Week 16: Decommission old cluster. Celebrate. You've achieved multi-cluster without a single global outage.

During migration, both clusters run simultaneously. Argo CD deploys to both. DNS/load balancers can route traffic to either. Zero-downtime migration IS possible — but it requires careful planning.

9.4 Multi-Tenancy Patterns — Soft (Namespaces) vs Hard (vClusters/Kamaji)

Multi-tenancy answers: How do you safely share a cluster between multiple teams? The spectrum runs from soft isolation (namespaces) to hard isolation (virtual clusters or separate physical clusters).

DimensionSoft Multi-Tenancy (Namespaces)Hard Multi-Tenancy (vCluster/Kamaji)
Isolation MechanismNamespaces + RBAC + NetworkPolicy + ResourceQuota + LimitRangeVirtual K8s control plane per tenant. Each tenant "sees" their own cluster.
API ServerShared — all tenants use the same API serverSeparate — each tenant has their own virtual API server
CRDsShared — one tenant's CRD visible to all (cluster-scoped)Isolated — each tenant can install their own CRDs
Security Isolation🟡 Moderate — misconfigured RBAC or NetworkPolicy = cross-tenant access🟢 Strong — tenant can't escape their virtual cluster even with cluster-admin
Resource Overhead🟢 Minimal — just namespace objects (KB)🟡 Each vCluster runs API server + controller manager + etcd (or uses host etcd with prefix)
Operational Complexity🟢 Simple — standard K8s. All built-in.🔴 Higher — manage vCluster lifecycle, upgrades, reconciliation
Use CaseTrusted teams within same org. Dev/staging environments.Untrusted tenants. CI/CD systems. SaaS platforms hosting customer workloads.
CNPE Exam Relevance🟢 HIGH — Namespace isolation is core Domain 1 topic.🟡 MEDIUM — vCluster/Kamaji is emerging tech; know the concept.
🔬 vCluster Deep Dive — Virtual K8s Inside Real K8s

vCluster (by Loft Labs) creates fully functional virtual Kubernetes clusters inside a host cluster namespace. Each vCluster has its own API server, controller manager, and can run its own CRDs and operators. The tenant gets cluster-admin inside their vCluster — but they can NEVER affect other tenants or the host cluster.

# Create a vCluster for Team Alpha
vcluster create team-alpha --namespace team-alpha-vcluster
# Team Alpha connects:
vcluster connect team-alpha --namespace team-alpha-vcluster
# Team Alpha can now: kubectl get nodes, install CRDs, create namespaces
# But ALL their resources are scoped to namespace "team-alpha-vcluster" on host

Kamaji (by Clastix) takes a different approach: it runs tenant control planes as pods in a management cluster, each with its own etcd (or shared etcd with prefix isolation). Tenants use standard kubeconfig — they can't tell it's not a real cluster.

⚠️ The Noisy Neighbor Problem — Soft Multi-Tenancy's Achilles Heel

A single team's workload can consume all cluster resources (CPU, memory, disk I/O), starving other teams. Mitigations: ResourceQuota (caps total resources per namespace), LimitRange (default limits for pods), PriorityClass (production pods preempt dev pods), and NetworkPolicy (isolate namespace traffic). But these are CONFIGURATION — a platform engineer must set them up correctly. Hard multi-tenancy (vCluster) provides isolation by DESIGN — no amount of tenant misbehavior affects others.

🤔Multi-Tenancy Decision
→
🔒Untrusted tenants?
(CI/CD, SaaS, external)
→
🏗️vCluster / Kamaji
Hard Isolation
OR
✅Trusted internal teams?
→
📦Namespaces + RBAC
Soft Isolation

Key rule: vCluster for untrusted/CI/CD/SaaS tenants. Namespaces for trusted internal teams. Mix both on the SAME host cluster.

🔬 Trust Boundaries — The Core Concept Behind Multi-Tenancy

At its heart, multi-tenancy is about trust boundaries. A trust boundary is a line that says: "Code running on THIS side cannot access resources on THAT side without explicit permission." Every architecture decision in this section is really a decision about where to draw trust boundaries and how HARD to make them.

Trust Boundary TypeHow It's EnforcedWhat It Protects AgainstWhat It DOESN'T Protect
Namespace (Soft)RBAC rules say "Team A cannot GET pods in Team B namespace"Accidental access. Honest mistakes. Junior devs exploring.Malicious actors exploiting RBAC bugs. Container escapes. API server vulns.
NetworkPolicyiptables/eBPF rules say "Pod A cannot send packets to Pod B"Network-level snooping. Accidental cross-team service discovery.DNS rebinding attacks. Compromised CNI plugin. Host network namespace escapes.
vCluster (Hard)Separate API server. Tenant's cluster-admin is SCOPED to their virtual cluster.Tenant installing malicious CRDs. Tenant deleting cluster-scoped resources. Privilege escalation.Host cluster kernel exploits. etcd data corruption. Physical host compromise.
Separate Physical ClusterNo shared kernel, no shared network, no shared control plane.Everything above, plus host-level attacks, noisy neighbor CPU/memory/disk exhaustion.Supply chain attacks (compromised container images). Social engineering. Insider threats.

The key insight: Each level adds protection, but also adds cost and complexity. You don't need physical clusters for every team. You need to match the trust boundary to the THREAT MODEL. Internal teams? Namespaces + NetworkPolicy is usually enough. Hosting competitor workloads? vCluster. Hosting untrusted third-party code? Separate cluster.

⚠️ When Soft Multi-Tenancy Fails — 3 Real Scenarios

Scenario 1 — The Accidental Cluster-Admin: A developer created a Pod with a ServiceAccount that had cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding (set up by a previous team for debugging, never removed). They ran kubectl get pods --all-namespaces and saw EVERY team's pods, configmaps, and secrets. The RBAC was "correct" per policy — the policy was just too permissive. Lesson: Regularly audit ClusterRoleBindings. Use tools like kubescape or Polaris to detect over-privileged accounts.

Scenario 2 — The Noisy Neighbor: Team B's Spark job consumed 100% of node CPU. Team A's latency-sensitive API pods on the same node timed out. ResourceQuota capped TOTAL namespace CPU but didn't prevent one pod from consuming an entire node. Lesson: Use LimitRange for per-pod limits AND node affinity/anti-affinity to separate latency-sensitive workloads from batch jobs.

Scenario 3 — The Shared CRD Conflict: Team A installed a CRD databases.example.com/v1. Team B installed the SAME CRD with a different schema. The second installation FAILED because CRDs are cluster-scoped. Team B couldn't deploy. Lesson: CRD conflicts are a hard problem with soft multi-tenancy. vCluster solves this — each tenant has their own CRDs.

9.5 Namespace-as-a-Service — Developer Requests Namespace → Auto-Provisioned

Namespace-as-a-Service is the platform engineering pattern where developers request a namespace and the platform auto-provisions it with quotas, RBAC, NetworkPolicies, and monitoring — no ticket, no wait, no manual intervention.

1Dev clicks "Create Namespace" in Backstage
→
2Platform Orchestrator creates Namespace CR
→
3Operator reconciles: creates Namespace + RBAC + Quota
→
4NetworkPolicy default-deny + allow-list applied
→
5Prometheus ServiceMonitor auto-added
→
6Dev gets kubeconfig. Ready in ~30 seconds.

What gets provisioned per namespace:

ResourcePurposeExample
NamespaceIsolation boundaryteam-payments
ResourceQuotaPrevent resource hoggingMax 10 pods, 16GB RAM, 8 CPU cores total
LimitRangeDefault limits per podDefault 256Mi/250m, max 2Gi/2 CPU per pod
RBACWho can do whatTeam Role: get, list, create, update, delete pods and deployments
NetworkPolicyTraffic controlDefault-deny all ingress. Allow from ingress-controller namespace.
ServiceAccountPod identityteam-payments-sa with IRSA for AWS S3 access
ServiceMonitorAuto-scraped by PrometheusScrape /metrics from all pods with label app.kubernetes.io/part-of: anihpj
PodSecuritySecurity baselineEnforce Restricted PSS: no root, readOnlyRootFS, no privilege escalation
💡 anihpj Namespace-as-a-Service Implementation
namespace-claim.yaml — Developer submits this to request a namespace 
# NamespaceClaim CRD — Developer submits this ONE file
# Platform Operator auto-creates: Namespace + RBAC + Quota + NetPol + ServiceMonitor
apiVersion: platform.anihpj.io/v1alpha1
kind: NamespaceClaim
metadata:
  name: team-payments          # Must be unique across the cluster
spec:
  teamName: "Payments"         # Display name for dashboards
  ownerEmail: "payments@anihpj.io"
  environment: "dev"           # dev | staging | prod (determines quotas)
  quotas:
    maxCPU: "8"                # Hard limit — team cannot exceed
    maxMemory: "16Gi"
    maxPods: 20
  # Optional: request specific features
  features:
    ingress: true              # Auto-create Ingress namespace for ingress-controller
    monitoring: true           # Auto-add ServiceMonitor for Prometheus scraping
    backupSchedule: "0 2 * * *" # Daily Velero backup at 2 AM

After submission, the Platform Orchestrator (a custom operator) reconciles this NamespaceClaim and within ~30 seconds the developer receives a kubeconfig for their fully-provisioned namespace. Zero tickets. Zero waiting. Zero manual steps.

🔬 What Happens Inside the Operator — The Reconciliation Loop

When a developer submits a NamespaceClaim, here's what the operator does step-by-step in its reconciliation loop:

NamespaceClaim Operator — Reconciliation Loop
  1. WATCH: Operator detects new NamespaceClaim CR (or update to existing one)
     │
  2. VALIDATE: Is teamName unique? Does the team have quota available?
     │  ├─ FAIL → Update CR status with error message, set Ready=False
     │  └─ PASS → Continue
     │
  3. CREATE Namespace with labels: team=payments, env=dev, managed-by=platform
     │
  4. CREATE ResourceQuota: caps total CPU/memory/pods for the namespace
     │
  5. CREATE LimitRange: sets default request/limit for any pod without them
     │
  6. CREATE RBAC: Role (namespace-scoped) + RoleBinding (team-group → Role)
     │
  7. CREATE NetworkPolicy: default-deny ingress + allow from ingress-controller
     │
  8. CREATE ServiceAccount + IRSA annotation for AWS IAM role (if features.ingress)
     │
  9. CREATE ServiceMonitor for Prometheus auto-discovery (if features.monitoring)
     │
 10. UPDATE CR status: Ready=True, kubeconfigSecret=team-payments-kubeconfig
     │
 11. NOTIFY developer via Slack/email: "Your namespace is ready!"

If ANY step fails, the operator retries with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...). The CR status always reflects the current state. This is the level 2 operator pattern (automated reconciliation with status reporting) — the same pattern used by production operators like cert-manager, Prometheus Operator, and Argo CD.

🔄 Namespace Lifecycle — Beyond Creation

Self-service isn't just about CREATING namespaces. A complete implementation handles the full lifecycle:

Lifecycle EventWhat HappensPlatform Responsibility
CreateDeveloper submits NamespaceClaim → operator provisions everythingValidate quota available. Ensure unique name. Provision in <60s.
UpdateTeam needs more CPU → edits NamespaceClaim → operator reconcilesAuto-approve within limits. Require approval for increases beyond budget.
SuspendTeam inactive for 90 days → namespace scaled to zero, data archivedAuto-detect inactivity. Notify team. Archive PVCs to S3 (Velero).
ReactivateTeam returns → operator restores from archive, scales back upRestore PVCs from Velero backup. Re-apply latest policies.
DeleteTeam disbands → operator runs pre-deletion checks, backs up, then deletesBackup PVCs. Verify no cross-namespace dependencies. Wait 30-day grace period.
AuditMonthly: operator reports unused resources, orphaned PVCs, over-privileged RBACAuto-generate optimization recommendations. Flag security issues.

9.6 Cloud Provider Integration — EKS, AKS, GKE

Managed Kubernetes services abstract control plane operations. The platform engineer's job is to understand the trade-offs: managed convenience vs control, and how to integrate cloud-native services (RDS, IAM, S3) with your Kubernetes platform.

FeatureEKS (AWS)AKS (Azure)GKE (GCP)
Control Plane Cost$0.10/hr (~$73/mo)FREE (pay for VMs only)FREE for 1 cluster (Autopilot: pay per pod)
Upgrade ProcessManual trigger. 3-version skew support.Auto-upgrade channel or manual. 2-version skew.Auto-upgrade by default (release channels). 2-version skew.
IAM IntegrationIRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) — pods get IAM roles via OIDCAzure AD Workload Identity — pods use federated identitiesWorkload Identity — pods use GCP service accounts via IAM binding
NetworkingAWS VPC CNI (pods get VPC IPs). Calico for NetworkPolicy.Azure CNI (pods get VNet IPs) or kubenet (NAT).Native VPC-native networking. Dataplane V2 (eBPF) option.
Add-onsSelf-managed via EKS Add-ons or HelmAKS-managed: monitoring, policy, ingress, gitopsGKE-managed: monitoring, logging, mesh, config connector
Multi-ClusterEKS Anywhere (on-prem). EKS Distro.Arc-enabled K8s (any K8s). AKS on HCI/Stack.Anthos (multi/hybrid cloud). GKE on-prem/Bare Metal.
Best ForAWS shops needing deepest EC2/VPC integrationMicrosoft ecosystem (AD, DevOps, GitHub). Windows containers.GCP-native. Easiest operations. Autopilot for serverless K8s.
⚠️ Managed vs Self-Managed Trade-Offs

Managed (EKS/AKS/GKE): ✅ Control plane is their problem (HA, etcd, upgrades, backups). ❌ Less control — can't modify API server flags, can't choose CNI freely. ❌ Vendor lock-in — K8s is portable, but IAM/networking/storage integrations are not.

Self-Managed (kubeadm on EC2/VMs): ✅ Full control — choose CNI, modify API server, custom admission webhooks. ❌ You own etcd backup/restore, control plane HA, upgrades, and security patches. ❌ Operational burden scales with cluster count.

The CNPE perspective: The exam may ask you to work with managed services (EKS/AKS). Know how to: configure IRSA/Workload Identity, provision cloud storage (EBS/EFS) via CSI, and set up external-dns + cert-manager for automatic DNS+TLS.

☁️ The Cloud Repatriation Trend — Why Some Companies Are Leaving the Cloud

Since 2023, a growing number of companies have been moving workloads FROM the cloud BACK to on-premises or colocation — a trend called cloud repatriation. Understanding WHY helps you make better architecture decisions:

  • Cost at scale: At $50K+/month, owning hardware becomes cheaper than renting cloud. A company spending $5M/year on AWS can buy $1M of hardware that lasts 3 years. The break-even is around $200K-500K/month in cloud spend.
  • Predictable workloads: If your workload is steady 24/7 (not spikey), you're paying a PREMIUM for elasticity you never use. Reserved instances help, but owned hardware is still cheaper at scale.
  • Data egress fees: Cloud providers charge $0.05-0.12/GB for data leaving their network. A data-heavy platform (video, logs, analytics) can spend MORE on egress than on compute. On-prem has zero egress costs.
  • Compliance simplicity: "We run everything in our own data center" is a much simpler answer to auditors than "We use 47 AWS services across 6 regions with complex IAM policies."
  • The smart approach: Not "cloud vs on-prem" but "BOTH." Keep spiky workloads in cloud, steady workloads on-prem. Use K8s + Argo CD + Crossplane to manage both identically. This is the hybrid model done right.

9.7 On-Prem vs Cloud vs Hybrid — Latency, Compliance, Cost, Operations

The deployment model decision is rarely pure cloud or pure on-prem. Most enterprises end up hybrid — some workloads in cloud, some on-prem, with consistent platform tooling across both.

DimensionOn-PremisesCloud (EKS/AKS/GKE)Hybrid / Multi-Cloud
Latency🟢 Sub-millisecond to on-prem DBs. No internet dependency.🟡 Single-digit ms within AZ. Cross-region: higher. Internet-dependent.🟡 Latency varies by workload placement. Critical: place near data.
Compliance🟢 Full physical control. Easier for air-gapped, classified, GDPR data residency.🟡 Shared responsibility. Must configure properly (encryption, audit, IAM).🟢 Best: on-prem for sensitive, cloud for everything else. But complex to federate.
Cost (3-year)🔴 CAPEX: Servers, switches, racks, cooling, power. + OPEX: staffing, maintenance.🟢 OPEX only. Pay-per-use. But costs SPIRAL without FinOps (Kubecost).🟡 Fixed on-prem CAPEX + variable cloud OPEX. Optimize per-workload.
Scalability🔴 Lead time: weeks for new hardware. Fixed capacity — overprovision or starve.🟢 Near-infinite. Cluster Autoscaler + Karpenter. Scale in minutes.🟢 Cloud bursts handle spikes. On-prem handles steady baseline load.
Operations🔴 You own: hardware, networking, K8s, storage, security, everything.🟢 Control plane is managed. You own: worker nodes, workloads, policies.🔴 Double complexity. Two (or more) environments to manage, federate, monitor.
CNPE Relevance🟡 Know kubeadm, Rancher, OpenShift. etcd and control plane ops.🟢 HIGH — CNPE tests cloud integrations (IRSA, CSI, external-dns).🟡 Emerging. Know concepts: global load balancing, cluster mesh, federation.
🌳 Deployment Model Decision Tree
Do you have regulatory requirements (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, data residency)?
YES →

Predictable →

Cloud. Autoscaling matches cost to demand. Spot instances for batch jobs.
🏢
On-Premises

Best for: Data sovereignty, air-gapped, stable workloads, existing data center investment.

Watch out: CAPEX cost, hardware lead time, you own everything (power, cooling, networking).

☁️
Cloud (EKS/AKS/GKE)

Watch out: Costs spiral without FinOps, vendor lock-in via IAM/networking/storage integrations.

🔗

Best for: Compliance + agility. Sensitive data on-prem, everything else cloud. Cloud bursting.

Watch out: Double operational complexity. Need consistent tooling across both (Argo CD, Crossplane).

🌍

💰 Real Cost Comparison — Cloud vs On-Prem for a Mid-Size Platform

Let's put real (approximate) numbers behind the cloud vs on-prem debate for a platform supporting 50 developers, 3 environments, 200 pods:

Cost CategoryCloud (EKS, us-east-1)On-Prem (Owned Hardware)Hybrid (Smart Mix)
Control Plane3 × $73/mo = $219/mo$0 (self-managed, but your time)2 × $73 = $146/mo (prod+staging on cloud, dev on-prem)
Worker Nodes~$3,000/mo (on-demand EC2)$1,500/mo (amortized hardware)$1,800/mo (burst cloud + reserved on-prem)
Storage (PVs)~$400/mo (EBS gp3, 500GB)$150/mo (local SSDs)$250/mo (critical data on cloud, bulk on-prem)
Data Transfer~$600/mo (NAT GW + egress)$0 (internal network)$200/mo (minimize cross-boundary traffic)
Managed ServicesRDS: $500/mo, ElastiCache: $200/mo$0 (self-managed Postgres+Redis on K8s)$350/mo (RDS for prod, self-managed for dev/staging)
Staffing (ops)0.5 FTE ≈ $4,000/mo2 FTE ≈ $16,000/mo1 FTE ≈ $8,000/mo
TOTAL (approx)~$8,900/mo~$17,650/mo~$10,750/mo

The counter-intuitive truth: At this scale (50 devs), CLOUD is often cheaper than on-prem because managed services reduce staffing costs dramatically. On-prem becomes cheaper at ~200+ developers when the staffing cost is amortized across more teams. The hybrid sweet spot: managed cloud for production (reliability + reduced ops), self-managed on-prem for dev/staging (cost optimization). Don't guess — model your specific workload costs using the AWS/GCP/Azure pricing calculators.

⚡ The Hybrid Architecture Pattern — How to Build for Both Cloud AND On-Prem

The key to successful hybrid architecture is abstraction. Don't write cloud-specific code in your platform. Use K8s-native APIs that work everywhere:

  • Storage: Use PVCs with StorageClasses. CSI driver handles the difference (EBS in AWS, local-path on-prem). Your app just requests a PVC.
  • Ingress: Use the same Ingress/Gateway API manifests. AWS Load Balancer Controller on EKS, MetalLB or Traefik on-prem. Same YAML, different controller.
  • Secrets: External Secrets Operator abstracts AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault. Your pod gets the secret the same way regardless of backend.
  • DNS: external-dns syncs K8s Ingress hosts to Route53 (AWS), Cloud DNS (GCP), or BIND (on-prem). Configure once, use everywhere.
  • GitOps: Argo CD deploys the SAME manifests to all clusters. Kustomize overlays handle per-cluster differences (storageClass: ebs-gp3 vs local-path).
  • Observability: Prometheus + Grafana + Loki — runs on any K8s. Thanos or Mimir for global view across all clusters, regardless of location.

The result: a developer deploys to dev-cluster (on-prem kubeadm) and prod-cluster (EKS) using identical manifests. The platform absorbs the difference. This is the holy grail of platform engineering — write once, run anywhere.

⚠️ Platform Architecture Anti-Patterns — The 7 Deadly Sins

Learn from the mistakes of platform teams before you:

#Anti-PatternWhat HappensThe Fix
1Single Cluster SyndromeOne noisy team affects everyone. etcd failure = company-wide outage.Minimum 3 clusters: dev/staging/prod. Add per-compliance clusters.
2No Multi-Tenancy PlanTeams accidentally access each other's resources. "Why can Payments see Search data?"Namespace per team + RBAC + NetworkPolicy + ResourceQuota from day 1.
3Pet Clusters"prod-cluster has been running for 2 years. Don't touch it." Manual patches, config drift.Immutable infrastructure. GitOps reconciliation. Destroy and recreate is painless.
4Vendor Deep-LockEvery feature uses a cloud-specific service. Migration = rewrite.Abstract via K8s-native APIs. Crossplane for infra. Standard CNCF projects.
5Architecture by AccidentNo ADRs, no diagrams. Architecture lives in one person's head.Document decisions. ADRs in Git. Diagram as code (Mermaid/PlantUML).
6Over-Engineering10-cluster mesh for a 5-person startup. Spent 6 months building, 0 features shipped.Start simple. Add complexity when the pain of NOT having it exceeds the pain of building it.
7Ignoring FinOpsCloud bill arrives: $50K. "Who spent this?" No cost allocation. No budgets.Kubecost from day 1. Per-team cost showback. Budgets tied to namespaces.
🧭 The Platform Architecture Compass — Quick Decision Reference

When designing your platform, answer these 6 questions in order. Each answer narrows your architecture choices:

QuestionIf YES →If NO →
1. Regulatory requirements?Dedicated compliance cluster(s)Shared cluster with namespace isolation
2. More than 50 developers?Multi-cluster by env or teamSingle cluster OK (with namespaces)
3. Untrusted tenants?vCluster / Kamaji (hard isolation)Namespaces + RBAC (soft isolation)
4. On-prem data residency?Hybrid: on-prem for sensitive, cloud for restCloud-native: EKS/AKS/GKE

✅ The Platform Architect's Pre-Decision Checklist

Before finalizing ANY platform architecture decision, run through this checklist:

  • 📏 Reversibility: How hard is it to change this decision later? (Single→Multi cluster: HARD. Namespace→vCluster: MODERATE. EKS→AKS: VERY HARD.)
  • 💰 Cost Impact: What's the 3-year TCO? (Include: control plane, worker nodes, data transfer, operational staffing.)
  • 🔒 Security Posture: Does this decision create or close security gaps? (Default-deny network model? RBAC least privilege? Pod Security Restricted?)
  • 👥 Team Impact: How does this affect developer experience? (Self-service or tickets? Fast deploys or waiting? Autonomy or gatekeeping?)
  • 📈 Scaling Limit: At what point does this decision break? (Single cluster: ~5,000 nodes. Namespace isolation: ~500 teams. vCluster: ~50 vClusters per host.)
  • 📝 Documented: Is this decision in an ADR? Can a new team member understand WHY in 5 minutes?
  • 🧪 Tested: Can you validate this architecture in your lab? (Your 6-cluster lab can test: single vs multi, soft vs hard tenancy, migration scenarios.)

🎓 CNPE Exam Focus — Platform Architecture (Domain 1 — 15%)

Domain 1 tests your ability to make architecture decisions, not just configure tools. Expect scenario-based questions: "A company with 3 teams, PCI compliance, and on-prem data center needs a platform. Design it." Your answer should cover: cluster topology (multi-cluster for PCI isolation), multi-tenancy (vCluster for PCI team, namespaces for others), networking (Calico/Cilium + NetworkPolicy), and cloud integration for non-PCI workloads. THINK like an architect, not an operator.

🎯 The Architecture Decision Framework — How to Answer CNPE Design Questions
  • 1. State the constraints: "Given 3 teams, PCI-DSS compliance, and a preference for managed services..."
  • 2. Present options: "Option A: single cluster with namespace isolation. Option B: 2 clusters — one PCI, one shared."
  • 3. Evaluate trade-offs: "Option A is simpler but PCI workloads share infra with non-PCI. Option B isolates PCI but adds operational overhead of a second cluster."
  • 4. Make a recommendation: "I recommend Option B because PCI-DSS isolation is non-negotiable. We'll use EKS for both clusters, Argo CD for GitOps, and Crossplane for consistent infra provisioning."
  • 5. Justify each choice: "EKS because managed control plane reduces ops. Argo CD because GitOps provides audit trail. Crossplane because IaC stays inside K8s."
⚠️ The "Over-Architecting" Trap — CNPE's Most Common Architecture Mistake

Candidates often design for Google-scale when the question describes a 20-person startup. The CNPE exam rewards pragmatic architecture: don't propose 10 clusters with Cilium Cluster Mesh for a team of 5 developers building a blog. Match your architecture to the SCALE of the problem. A 20-person team with one app? Single cluster, namespace isolation, done. A 500-person enterprise with PCI-DSS workloads? Multi-cluster with dedicated compliance cluster.

Q: What's the difference between soft and hard multi-tenancy?

▶ Show Answer
Soft: Namespace isolation using RBAC, NetworkPolicy, ResourceQuota, and LimitRange. Tenants share the same API server and control plane. Hard: Virtual clusters (vCluster/Kamaji) or separate physical clusters. Each tenant has their own API server, CRDs, and full cluster-admin within their boundary. Hard provides stronger isolation but more operational complexity.
Q: When would you choose EKS over self-managed kubeadm on EC2?

▶ Show Answer
Choose EKS when: (1) You don't want to manage etcd backup/restore. (2) You need deep AWS integration (IRSA for IAM, EBS/EFS CSI, ALB Ingress Controller). (3) Your team is small and can't dedicate engineers to control plane operations. Choose self-managed when: (1) You need specific API server flags or admission webhooks EKS doesn't support. (2) You need a specific CNI or K8s version EKS doesn't offer. (3) Cost of EKS control plane ($73/mo/cluster) exceeds your budget for many small clusters.
🚀 Beyond CNPE — Platform Architecture at Global Scale
  • Kubernetes Cluster API (CAPI): Declarative cluster lifecycle management. Define clusters as CRDs. CAPI controller provisions VMs, installs K8s, joins nodes. Used by enterprises managing 100+ clusters.
  • Crossplane: Provision cloud infrastructure (RDS, EKS, S3) using K8s CRDs. "Terraform, but K8s-native." Infrastructure defined in Git, reconciled continuously — GitOps for infra.
  • Cilium Cluster Mesh: Connect multiple K8s clusters into a single virtual network. Pods in cluster-A can reach pods in cluster-B via direct routing. Global NetworkPolicy across clusters.
  • Karmada: Multi-cluster application orchestration. Deploy an app once, Karmada distributes across clusters based on policies (latency, cost, compliance). Think "Deployment for clusters."

📖 Chapter 9 Summary: Platform architecture is the blueprint for your IDP. The three fundamental decisions — cluster topology (single vs multi), multi-tenancy (soft vs hard), and deployment model (cloud vs on-prem vs hybrid) — compound over time. Apply 12-Factor principles, use declarative configuration, enforce immutability. For most organizations: 3 clusters (dev/staging/prod) with namespace-based multi-tenancy inside each, deployed on managed K8s (EKS/AKS/GKE), with dedicated clusters for compliance boundaries. Architecture decisions compound — get them right early.
