🎓 CNPE Relevance
Platform Architecture & Infrastructure Domain 1 — 15%

11.1 Storage Fundamentals — PV, PVC, StorageClass, CSI

Kubernetes storage has four pillars that work together to abstract infrastructure from applications. Understanding how they relate is essential before you can design platform storage:

💾
PersistentVolume (PV)

A cluster-scoped resource representing physical storage. Created by admins (or dynamically by CSI drivers). Exists independently of any pod. Like a "disk" in the cluster.

📝
PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC)

A namespace-scoped request for storage. Developers say "I need 20GB, RWO, fast SSD." Kubernetes binds the PVC to a matching PV. Like a "ticket" for a disk.

🏭
StorageClass

Defines HOW storage is provisioned. "fast-ssd" → AWS EBS gp3. "shared-nfs" → AWS EFS. Enables dynamic provisioning — PVC created → PV auto-created.

🔌
CSI Driver

Container Storage Interface — the plugin that connects K8s to actual storage systems. AWS EBS CSI, Azure Disk CSI, NFS CSI. Pluggable, standardized.

The PV/PVC/StorageClass Relationship — How Storage Flows
  STATIC PROVISIONING (Admin creates PV manually)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Admin: kubectl create -f pv.yaml                                │
  │ ┌──────────────────────┐                                        │
  │ │ PV: anihpj-db-pv     │  "I have a 100GB disk available"       │
  │ │ Capacity: 100Gi      │                                        │
  │ │ AccessMode: RWO      │                                        │
  │ │ StorageClass: fast-ssd│                                       │
  │ │ Status: Available    │                                        │
  │ └──────────┬───────────┘                                        │
  │            │ BINDS TO (capacity ≥ request, modes match)         │
  │            ▼                                                    │
  │ Dev: kubectl create -f pvc.yaml                                 │
  │ ┌──────────────────────┐                                        │
  │ │ PVC: anihpj-db-pvc   │  "I need 20GB, RWO, fast-ssd"         │
  │ │ Request: 20Gi        │                                        │
  │ │ AccessMode: RWO      │                                        │
  │ │ StorageClass: fast-ssd│                                       │
  │ │ Status: Bound         │  ← Automatically bound to PV          │
  │ └──────────┬───────────┘                                        │
  │            │ MOUNTED BY                                         │
  │            ▼                                                    │
  │ Pod: anihpj-db-0                                                │
  │ ┌──────────────────────┐                                        │
  │ │ volumes:              │                                        │
  │ │ - name: pgdata        │                                        │
  │ │   persistentVolumeClaim:                                       │
  │ │     claimName: anihpj-db-pvc                                   │
  │ │ mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data                            │
  │ └──────────────────────┘                                        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  DYNAMIC PROVISIONING (StorageClass + CSI creates PV automatically)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. PVC created: "20GB, RWO, StorageClass=fast-ssd"              │
  │ 2. StorageClass "fast-ssd" has provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com     │
  │ 3. CSI driver creates EBS volume (gp3, 20GB) in AWS             │
  │ 4. CSI driver creates PV object in K8s (references the EBS ID)  │
  │ 5. PVC binds to the new PV                                      │
  │ 6. Pod mounts PVC → CSI driver attaches EBS to node → pod runs  │
  │                                                                 │
  │ ✅ No admin intervention. PVC = self-service storage.           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The key insight: PVs separate the "what" from the "where." A developer writes a PVC requesting "20GB, RWO, fast-ssd." On AWS, that provisioned an EBS volume. On Azure, a Managed Disk. On-prem, a local path on a NAS. The developer's manifest is identical across all environments. This is the storage equivalent of Services abstracting pod IPs.

⚠️ PVs Are NOT Namespaced — A Critical Design Implication

PVs are cluster-scoped resources (like Nodes, ClusterRoles). PVCs are namespace-scoped. This means: (1) A PV can be bound to a PVC in ANY namespace. (2) If you delete a namespace, the PVCs are deleted — but the PV's persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy determines what happens to the actual storage. Retain = PV is released but NOT deleted (data survives, manual cleanup needed). Delete = PV AND the backing storage (EBS volume!) are deleted — DATA IS GONE. For production databases, ALWAYS use Retain and manually clean up after verified backups.

🔬 How Linux Mount Namespaces Make PVs Work

When a pod mounts a PVC, Kubernetes uses Linux mount namespaces to make the host's filesystem appear inside the container:

Volume Mount Sequence — From Cloud Disk to Container Filesystem
  AWS CLOUD                          LINUX NODE                         POD'S MOUNT NAMESPACE
  ┌──────────────┐                   ┌─────────────────────┐           ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ EBS Volume   │──── ATTACH ──────▶│ /dev/nvme1n1        │           │ /var/lib/postgresql/ │
  │ vol-abc123   │   (CSI Node       │ (block device)      │── MOUNT ─▶│     data/            │
  │ 20GB gp3     │    Plugin calls   │                     │   (bind   │     ├── PG_VERSION   │
  │              │    AWS API)       │ /var/lib/kubelet/   │    mount) │     ├── base/        │
  │              │                   │   pods/.../volumes/ │           │     └── pg_wal/     │
  │              │─── SNAPSHOT ─────▶│   csi/pv-xyz/mount │           └──────────────────────┘
  │ EBS Snapshot  │   (CSI creates   │                     │
  │ snap-xyz     │    copy)          │ FORMATTED + MOUNTED │    The pod doesn't know it's
  └──────────────┘                   │ (ext4/xfs) by       │    using a cloud volume — it
                                      │ kubelet              │    just sees a regular directory.
  1. CSI Controller: CreateVolume → EBS volume              │
  2. CSI Node Plugin: AttachVolume → /dev/nvme1n1           │
  3. Kubelet: Formats as ext4, mounts to kubelet path       │
  4. Container Runtime: Bind-mounts into pod namespace      │
  5. Container sees: /var/lib/postgresql/data (a directory) │

The container writes to /var/lib/postgresql/data. The kernel translates that to writes on /dev/nvme1n1 (the EBS volume). This mount namespace abstraction is why you can migrate a PostgreSQL pod from AWS to on-prem without changing a single line of code.

🔬 Reclaim Policies — What Happens When You Delete a PVC

The PV's persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy determines what happens to the actual cloud storage when the PVC is deleted:

PolicyPVC DeletedPV StatusCloud VolumeDataUse When
RetainPV releasedReleasedPreserved✅ SurvivesProduction DBs
DeletePV + volume deletedDeletedDELETED❌ GONEDev/staging only
RecyclePV wiped (rm -rf /)AvailablePreserved❌ WIPEDDEPRECATED
🔬 The PV Controller — How Kubernetes Manages Storage Internally

Every storage operation flows through the persistentvolume-controller inside kube-controller-manager. Understanding its reconciliation loop is essential for debugging:

PV Controller — Reconciliation Loop (Simplified)
  PV CONTROLLER (runs in kube-controller-manager, every ~5 seconds)

  1. FIND unbound PVCs (phase=Pending, no volumeName)
     ├─ PVC has StorageClass with provisioner?
     │   └─ YES → Call external provisioner → CSI creates volume → BIND
     └─ NO → Look for matching STATIC PV

  2. MATCH PVC to PV (static path):
     ├─ StorageClass must match
     ├─ Access mode must be superset
     ├─ Capacity >= request
     ├─ PV must be Available (not Bound/Released)
     ├─ MATCH → Bind PVC to PV (set volumeName)
     └─ NO MATCH → PVC stays Pending forever

  3. HANDLE deletion:
     ├─ PVC deleted, reclaimPolicy=Retain → PV → Released (manual cleanup)
     ├─ PVC deleted, reclaimPolicy=Delete → PV + cloud volume DELETED
     └─ PVC has finalizer → Wait until removed

  ⚠️ If kube-controller-manager is down: PVCs never bind.
  ⚠️ If CSI external-provisioner is down: dynamic provisioning stops.
  Check: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep 'controller-manager\|csi'
🔬 Filesystem Choice — ext4 vs XFS for Platform Storage

When Kubernetes formats a new volume, it uses the filesystem in the StorageClass (default: ext4). This choice affects performance:

Aspectext4 (default)XFS
K8s Default✅ Yes — most CSI drivers❌ No — must set explicitly
PostgreSQL🟢 Well-tested, reliable🟢 Recommended for WAL
Large Files🟡 Good (16 TiB max)🟢 Excellent (8 EiB max)
Online Resize✅ Yes (grow only)✅ Yes (grow only)

Configure in StorageClass: parameters: csi.storage.k8s.io/fstype: xfs. For databases, XFS generally outperforms ext4 — but ext4 is safer (default, more tested in K8s).

11.2 Access Modes — RWO, ROX, RWX, RWOP

Access modes define how many nodes/pods can mount a volume simultaneously. Choosing the wrong access mode is one of the most common causes of "PVC Pending" or "Multi-Attach Error" in production.

ModeFull NameNodesAccessRequiresExample Use Case
RWOReadWriteOnceSingle nodeRead-WriteBlock storage (EBS, Azure Disk, GCE PD)PostgreSQL database — only one pod writes
ROXReadOnlyManyMany nodesRead-OnlyAny shared storageStatic assets, ML models — many pods read, none write
RWXReadWriteManyMany nodesRead-WriteShared filesystem (EFS, NFS, CephFS)Shared file uploads across 5 web replicas
RWOPReadWriteOncePodSingle podRead-WriteCSI driver with SINGLE_NODE_SINGLE_WRITER capabilityPostgreSQL with guaranteed single-writer (K8s 1.22+)
⚠️ The RWO Trap — "ReadWriteOnce" Means ONE NODE, Not ONE POD

RWO allows multiple pods on the SAME node to mount the volume simultaneously. If you have 2 PostgreSQL pods on the same node, both can mount the same RWO volume — corrupting your database. This is why RWOP (ReadWriteOncePod) was introduced in Kubernetes 1.22: it restricts to a SINGLE pod, regardless of node. For databases, always use RWOP if your CSI driver supports it. For older clusters, enforce single-pod access via StatefulSet (replicas: 1) or pod anti-affinity.

🔀 UTH: "Why Can't I Just Use EBS for Everything?"

🖥️ Uncle: "EBS is fast and cheap. Just use RWO for everything. Why complicate things with EFS or NFS?"

🧑‍💻 Tech Lead: "EBS is RWO only — it's attached to a SINGLE node. If you have 5 anihpj-web replicas across 3 nodes, only ONE pod can mount the EBS volume. The other 4 pods get 'Multi-Attach error' and stay Pending. You NEED RWX (EFS/NFS) for shared access across nodes."

🧔‍♂️ Hiker: "Match the storage type to the access pattern. Database (single writer) → RWO/RWOP with EBS. Shared file uploads (many writers) → RWX with EFS. Static content (many readers) → ROX with EFS or use ConfigMap/emptyDir. Don't fight the access mode — choose the right storage backend for each."

11.3 Dynamic Provisioning — StorageClass → PVC → PV Auto-Created

Dynamic provisioning eliminates manual PV creation. When a PVC references a StorageClass, the CSI driver automatically provisions the backing storage (cloud volume, NFS share, etc.) and creates a PV. This is the self-service storage model — developers just create PVCs, and the platform handles the rest.

1Dev creates PVC: "20GB, RWO, StorageClass=fast-ssd"
→
2StorageClass references CSI provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
→
3CSI driver calls AWS API: CreateVolume (gp3, 20GB, us-east-1a)
→
4CSI driver creates PV in K8s with EBS volume ID
→
5PVC immediately binds to the new PV
→
6Pod starts. CSI driver attaches EBS to node. Data flows.
⚡ anihpj StorageClass — Production-Ready Dynamic Provisioning
# StorageClass: fast-ssd (EBS gp3, encrypted)
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-ssd
  annotations:
    storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"  # Default SC
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
  encrypted: "true"
  kmsKeyId: "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456:key/abc-123"  # KMS encryption
allowVolumeExpansion: true  # Allow PVC resize
reclaimPolicy: Retain  # DON'T delete EBS when PVC is deleted
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer  # Wait until pod scheduled (zone-aware)
---
# PVC: anihpj-db needs 20GB, fast SSD
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-pvc
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 20Gi
🔬 WaitForFirstConsumer — Why Zone-Aware Provisioning Matters

volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer tells the CSI driver: "Don't create the EBS volume YET. Wait until a pod actually needs this PVC." Why? Because when the pod is scheduled, K8s knows which Availability Zone the pod will run in. The CSI driver then creates the EBS volume in THAT zone — avoiding cross-AZ attachment errors. Without this, you might create an EBS volume in us-east-1a while the pod gets scheduled to us-east-1b — and EBS volumes can't be attached across AZs. The pod would stay Pending forever. Always use WaitForFirstConsumer for zone-specific storage (EBS, Azure Disk, GCE PD).

🔬 PVC Binding Deep Dive — How Kubernetes Matches PVCs to PVs

When you create a PVC, Kubernetes doesn't just pick any PV — it runs a matching algorithm with specific rules. Understanding this algorithm is essential for debugging "Pending" PVCs:

PVC-to-PV Binding — The Matching Algorithm
  PVC: "I need 20GB, RWO, StorageClass=fast-ssd"
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STEP 1: Filter by StorageClass                              │
  │   • PVC specifies storageClassName: "fast-ssd"              │
  │   • Only PVs with SAME StorageClass are considered          │
  │   • PVC with NO StorageClass only matches PVs with NO SC    │
  │   • PVC with "" StorageClass matches ANY PV (dynamic too)   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STEP 2: Filter by Access Mode                               │
  │   • PVC requests RWO. PV must support RWO.                  │
  │   • If PVC requests RWX, PV must support RWX (RWO-only fails│
  │   • Access modes must be a SUPERSET of what PVC requests    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STEP 3: Filter by Capacity                                  │
  │   • PVC requests 20Gi. PV must have capacity ≥ 20Gi.        │
  │   • 100Gi PV can satisfy 20Gi PVC (wasteful but valid)      │
  │   • 10Gi PV CANNOT satisfy 20Gi PVC                         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STEP 4: Select Best Match                                    │
  │   • From all matching PVs, select the SMALLEST sufficient    │
  │   • 25Gi PV wins over 100Gi PV (less waste)                 │
  │   • If multiple PVs have same capacity: select by name (ABC) │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STEP 5: Bind (One-Way, Immediate)                           │
  │   • PVC → PV binding is IMMEDIATE and PERMANENT             │
  │   • Once bound, PVC ALWAYS uses that PV                     │
  │   • PV status changes: Available → Bound                    │
  │   • OTHER PVCs can no longer claim this PV                   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Common failure modes:
  • No PV matches StorageClass → PVC stays Pending
  • PV exists but access mode doesn't match → PVC stays Pending
  • PV too small → PVC stays Pending
  • PV is "Released" (ReclaimPolicy: Retain) → NOT considered → PVC stays Pending

Pro tip for debugging: kubectl describe pvc <name> tells you exactly WHY binding failed. Look for events like "waiting for a volume to be created" (dynamic provisioning in progress) or "no persistent volumes available for this claim" (static provisioning, no matching PV). The error message is specific — read it carefully.

11.4 StatefulSet Storage — Stable Identity, Persistent Data

StatefulSets are designed for stateful workloads (databases, message queues, distributed caches). Unlike Deployments where pods are interchangeable, StatefulSet pods have stable identities and stable storage — critical for databases where data must survive pod rescheduling.

FeatureDeploymentStatefulSetWhy It Matters
Pod NamesRandom: anihpj-web-7f3a8b-xyzPredictable: anihpj-db-0, anihpj-db-1Database replication uses hostnames
Pod StartupAll pods start simultaneouslyOrdered: db-0 starts, then db-1, then db-2Primary must start before replicas
Pod ShutdownAll pods terminate simultaneouslyReverse order: db-2 stops, then db-1, then db-0Replicas drain before primary
StorageShared PVC (all pods use same volume)volumeClaimTemplate: one PVC per podEach DB pod needs its OWN data
Storage SurvivalPVC deleted with Deployment (if owned)PVCs SURVIVE StatefulSet deletionData persists even if StatefulSet is recreated
Network IdentityRandom pod IP onlyStable DNS: db-0.anihpj-db.anihpj.svcClients can connect to specific replicas
ScalingAny orderSequential: scale up 0→1→2, scale down 2→1→0Safe for stateful applications

volumeClaimTemplates is the magic that makes StatefulSet storage work. Instead of referencing an existing PVC, you define a template. When the StatefulSet creates anihpj-db-0, it automatically creates PVC pgdata-anihpj-db-0. When it creates anihpj-db-1, it creates PVC pgdata-anihpj-db-1. If anihpj-db-0 is deleted and recreated (even on a different node), it reattaches to the SAME PVC — the data is still there.

⚠️ Deleting a StatefulSet Does NOT Delete Its PVCs

This is by design — and it's both a feature and a trap. If you delete a StatefulSet and recreate it with the same name, the new pods reattach to the existing PVCs (data intact). But if you delete a StatefulSet and FORGET about the orphaned PVCs, those EBS volumes keep running up your AWS bill at $0.08/GB/month. A 500GB orphaned volume costs $40/month. Scale that across 50 forgotten PVCs = $2,000/month in waste. Use Kubecost or Cloudability to detect orphaned volumes. Set up alerts for unbound PVCs older than 30 days.

11.5 Cloud Storage Integration — AWS EBS/EFS, Azure Disk/File, GCE PD

Every major cloud provider offers K8s-integrated storage via CSI drivers. Understanding the differences helps you choose the right storage for each workload — and avoid costly mistakes.

Storage ServiceTypeAccess ModeBest ForLimitations
AWS EBSBlockRWODatabases, single-pod workloadsAZ-locked. Can't attach across AZs. Max 16 TiB.
AWS EFSFile (NFS)RWX, ROXShared file uploads, ML datasets, content managementHigher latency than EBS. More expensive ($0.30/GB vs $0.08/GB).
Azure DiskBlockRWODatabases, single-pod workloadsZone-locked (like EBS). Max 32 TiB.
Azure FilesFile (SMB/NFS)RWX, ROXShared storage, Windows containers, lift-and-shiftSMB protocol overhead. Premium tier for low latency.
GCE Persistent DiskBlockRWO (RWX via Regional PD)Databases, single-pod workloadsRegional PD supports RWX (unique among block storage!).
GCE FilestoreFile (NFS)RWXShared storage, high-performance file workloadsHigher cost. Minimum 1 TiB.
🔬 CSI Drivers — How K8s Talks to Cloud Storage

Every cloud storage integration goes through a CSI driver — a set of controllers and node plugins that translate K8s storage operations into cloud API calls. The architecture:

  • CSI Controller: Runs as a Deployment. Handles volume creation/deletion (calls AWS CreateVolume API), snapshotting, and volume expansion. Stateless — can have multiple replicas for HA.
  • CSI Node Plugin: Runs as a DaemonSet (one per node). Handles volume attachment/detachment (calls AWS AttachVolume API), mounting/unmounting, and filesystem formatting. MUST run on every node that might need storage.
  • How they communicate: The controller creates the volume and stores the volume ID in the PV object. The node plugin reads the PV, attaches the volume to the node, formats it (if needed), and mounts it into the pod's filesystem.

Troubleshooting tip: If PVCs are stuck "Pending," check CSI controller pod logs. If pods are stuck "ContainerCreating" with "FailedMount," check CSI node plugin logs on that node. kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep ebs shows both.

🔬 Cross-AZ Storage — The Hidden Complexity of Multi-Zone Clusters

EBS volumes are Availability Zone-locked. An EBS volume created in us-east-1a CANNOT be attached to an EC2 instance in us-east-1b. This creates a fundamental tension with Kubernetes' scheduler, which spreads pods across AZs for high availability:

The AZ Problem — When Pod and Volume Are in Different Zones
  CORRECT (WaitForFirstConsumer)              WRONG (Immediate binding)
  ┌──────────────────────┐                   ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ 1. PVC created       │                   │ 1. PVC created        │
  │    (no PV yet)       │                   │ 2. CSI creates EBS    │
  │                      │                   │    in us-east-1a      │
  │ 2. Pod scheduled     │                   │    (random choice!)   │
  │    → us-east-1b      │                   │                      │
  │                      │                   │ 3. Pod scheduled     │
  │ 3. CSI creates EBS   │                   │    → us-east-1b       │
  │    in us-east-1b     │                   │                      │
  │    (pod's zone!)     │                   │ 4. CSI tries to attach│
  │                      │                   │    EBS (us-east-1a)   │
  │ 4. Attach succeeds ✅│                   │    to EC2 (us-east-1b) │
  │    Same zone!        │                   │    ❌ FAILS!           │
  └──────────────────────┘                   │                      │
                                              │ 5. Pod stuck Pending  │
  Fix: volumeBindingMode:                     │    "Multi-Attach       │
  WaitForFirstConsumer                        │     Error" or         │
                                              │    "volume is in      │
  For non-EBS storage (EFS is                │     us-east-1a but    │
  multi-AZ): Immediate binding               │     node is in        │
  is fine — EFS can attach                   │     us-east-1b"       │
  from any AZ.                               └──────────────────────┘

The multi-AZ strategy for stateful workloads: (1) Use WaitForFirstConsumer so volumes are created in the pod's AZ. (2) Use node affinity to prefer the same AZ for StatefulSet pods (avoids cross-AZ rescheduling). (3) For RWX workloads (shared storage), use EFS/Azure Files/GCE Filestore — these are multi-AZ by design. (4) For true multi-AZ databases, use database replication (primary in AZ-a, replica in AZ-b) rather than trying to make the storage multi-AZ. Each replica gets its OWN EBS volume in its own AZ.

11.6 Backup — Velero for K8s Objects + PV Snapshots

Velero is the standard backup tool for Kubernetes. It backs up BOTH your K8s objects (Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps — everything in etcd) AND your persistent volumes (via CSI snapshots or Restic file-level backup).

Velero Backup Architecture — What Gets Backed Up
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                        VELERO BACKUP FLOW                           │
  │                                                                     │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐                                              │
  │  │ 1. Velero CLI or  │  velero backup create anihpj-daily          │
  │  │    Schedule CR    │                                              │
  │  └────────┬─────────┘                                              │
  │           │                                                        │
  │           ▼                                                        │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐                    │
  │  │ 2. Velero Controller                       │                    │
  │  │    • Lists ALL K8s objects in namespace(s) │                    │
  │  │    • Serializes to JSON                    │                    │
  │  │    • Uploads to S3 (or Azure Blob, GCS)    │                    │
  │  └────────┬───────────────────────────────────┘                    │
  │           │                                                        │
  │           ▼                                                        │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────┐                    │
  │  │ 3. For each PVC:                           │                    │
  │  │    • Calls CSI snapshot API                │                    │
  │  │    • Creates VolumeSnapshot object         │                    │
  │  │    • CSI driver creates cloud snapshot     │                    │
  │  │    (EBS snapshot, Azure Disk snapshot, etc)│                    │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘                    │
  │                                                                     │
  │  Result: S3 bucket contains:                                       │
  │  ├── backups/anihpj-daily-20260121/                                │
  │  │   ├── anihpj-resources.json      (all K8s objects)              │
  │  │   ├── podvolumebackups/           (Restic file-level backups)    │
  │  │   └── volumesnapshots/            (CSI snapshot references)     │
  │  └── ...                                                            │
  │                                                                     │
  │  RESTORE: velero restore create --from-backup anihpj-daily-20260121 │
  │  1. Reads K8s objects from S3 → applies to cluster                 │
  │  2. Creates PVs from snapshots → creates new EBS volumes           │
  │  3. Creates PVCs bound to new PVs → pods mount restored data       │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
AspectVelero Backupetcd Snapshot
What it backs upK8s objects (selected namespaces) + PV data (snapshots)Entire cluster state (ALL namespaces, ALL objects)
What it restoresIndividual apps/namespaces. Selective restore.Entire cluster. All-or-nothing restore.
Data included?✅ Yes — PV snapshots or Restic file backup❌ No — only K8s metadata. PV data NOT in etcd.
Use caseApplication backup/restore, migration, DR of specific servicesCluster disaster recovery. "Lose the cluster, rebuild from etcd."
Commandvelero backup create NAME --include-namespaces anihpjETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db
🔬 How CSI Snapshots Work — Copy-on-Write Magic

When Velero creates a CSI snapshot, it doesn't copy your entire 500GB database. It uses the cloud provider's copy-on-write snapshot mechanism — the snapshot is created in seconds regardless of volume size:

CSI Snapshot — Copy-on-Write in Action
  BEFORE SNAPSHOT                    SNAPSHOT CREATED               AFTER WRITE
  ┌────────────────────┐            ┌────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────┐
  │ EBS Volume         │            │ EBS Volume         │        │ EBS Volume         │
  │ (active)           │            │ (active)           │        │ (active)           │
  │                    │            │                    │        │ Block 5: NEW DATA! │
  │ Block 0: AAAA      │            │ Block 0: AAAA      │        │ Block 0: AAAA      │
  │ Block 1: BBBB      │            │ Block 1: BBBB      │        │ Block 1: BBBB      │
  │ Block 2: CCCC      │            │ Block 2: CCCC      │        │ Block 2: CCCC      │
  │ Block 3: DDDD      │            │ Block 3: DDDD      │        │ Block 3: DDDD      │
  │ Block 4: EEEE      │            │ Block 4: EEEE      │        │ Block 4: EEEE      │
  │ Block 5: FFFF      │            │ Block 5: FFFF      │        │ Block 5: NEW        │
  │ ...                │            │ ...                │        │ ...                │
  └────────────────────┘            └────────────────────┘        └────────────────────┘
                                               │                           │
                                    ┌──────────▼──────────┐      ┌──────────▼──────────┐
                                    │ EBS Snapshot        │      │ EBS Snapshot        │
                                    │ (point-in-time)     │      │ (frozen in time!)   │
                                    │                     │      │                     │
                                    │ Block 0 → volume    │      │ Block 0 → volume    │
                                    │ Block 1 → volume    │      │ Block 1 → volume    │
                                    │ Block 2 → volume    │      │ Block 2 → volume    │
                                    │ Block 3 → volume    │      │ Block 3 → volume    │
                                    │ Block 4 → volume    │      │ Block 4 → volume    │
                                    │ Block 5 → volume    │      │ Block 5 → SNAPSHOT  │
                                    └─────────────────────┘      │   (Copied before    │
                                                                  │    overwrite)       │
  Snapshots use POINTERS, not copies.                            └─────────────────────┘
  A 500GB snapshot takes SECONDS because only metadata is copied.
  The snapshot references the ORIGINAL blocks. Only when you WRITE
  to a block does the original get copied first (copy-on-write).

  RESTORE: Create a NEW EBS volume from the snapshot.
  The new volume has ALL the original data at the snapshot point.

Why this matters for backup strategy: You can take hourly snapshots with near-zero performance impact. Snapshots are incremental at the block level — a 7-day retention with hourly snapshots doesn't use 168× the storage, it uses ~1.2-1.5× for most databases. This makes frequent backups economically feasible.

⚡ anihpj Velero Schedule — RPO: 1 Hour, RTO: 30 Minutes
# Velero Schedule: hourly backup, 30-day retention
apiVersion: velero.io/v1
kind: Schedule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-hourly
  namespace: velero
spec:
  schedule: "0 * * * *"  # Every hour at :00
  template:
    includedNamespaces:
    - anihpj
    snapshotVolumes: true  # CSI snapshots for PVs
    ttl: 720h  # Retain backups for 30 days (720 hours)
---
# Velero BackupStorageLocation: S3 bucket
apiVersion: velero.io/v1
kind: BackupStorageLocation
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: velero
spec:
  provider: aws
  objectStorage:
    bucket: anihpj-velero-backups
    prefix: prod
  config:
    region: us-east-1

11.7 anihpj-db — PostgreSQL StatefulSet Storage Design

Let's put everything together and design the storage architecture for anihpj-db — the PostgreSQL database backing the entire anihpj platform.

🗄️
StatefulSet: anihpj-db

1 replica (single PostgreSQL primary). Stable identity: anihpj-db-0. If pod dies, new pod reattaches to same PVC — data intact.

💾
PVC: 20GB RWO, fast-ssd

EBS gp3 volume, encrypted with KMS. volumeClaimTemplate creates PVC automatically. RWOP access prevents dual-mount corruption.

🔄
Headless Service: anihpj-db

Stable DNS: anihpj-db-0.anihpj-db.anihpj.svc.cluster.local. Applications connect via service name, not pod IP.

🔐
Velero Backup: Daily, S3

Hourly CSI snapshots to S3. 30-day retention. RPO: 1 hour. RTO: 30 minutes (new EBS from snapshot + pod restart).

⚡ anihpj-db — Complete StatefulSet Manifest
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  serviceName: anihpj-db  # Headless Service for stable DNS
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj
      tier: db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj
        tier: db
    spec:
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 999  # PostgreSQL user
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: anihpj-db-creds
              key: password
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5432
        volumeMounts:
        - name: pgdata
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
          subPath: pgdata  # Prevents lost+found issues
        resources:
          requests:
            memory: "512Mi"
            cpu: "500m"
          limits:
            memory: "2Gi"
            cpu: "2000m"
  volumeClaimTemplates:  # ← Creates PVC per pod
  - metadata:
      name: pgdata
    spec:
      storageClassName: fast-ssd
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOncePod]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 20Gi
🔬 PostgreSQL Storage Internals — What Your PVC Actually Stores

When PostgreSQL runs on that 20GB PVC, the data isn't just "the database." Understanding the internal structure helps you optimize storage and debug issues:

PostgreSQL Data Directory — What Lives on Your PVC
  /var/lib/postgresql/data/  (mounted PVC)
  ├── PG_VERSION              ← PostgreSQL version (e.g., "15")
  ├── postgresql.conf         ← Main config (can be overridden via ConfigMap)
  ├── pg_hba.conf             ← Host-Based Authentication
  ├── base/                   ← THE ACTUAL DATA (tables, indexes)
  │   ├── 1/                  ← Template databases
  │   ├── 16384/              ← anihpj database (OID)
  │   │   ├── 16385           ← jobpost_job table data file
  │   │   ├── 16388           ← jobpost_job index file
  │   │   └── ...             ← More tables and indexes
  │   └── ...
  ├── pg_wal/                 ← Write-Ahead Log (CRITICAL for recovery)
  │   └── 000000010000...     ← 16MB WAL segments (sequential writes)
  ├── pg_stat/                ← Statistics (can be rebuilt, not critical)
  ├── pg_tblspc/              ← Tablespace symlinks (rarely used in K8s)
  └── pg_logical/             ← Logical replication slots

  STORAGE PATTERNS:
  • base/ = Random reads/writes (index scans, table access) → IOPS matter
  • pg_wal/ = SEQUENTIAL writes (append-only) → throughput matters
  • This is why EBS gp3 (3000 IOPS baseline) is better than magnetic

  SIZE COMPOSITION (typical web app):
  • 60% base/ (data + indexes)
  • 25% pg_wal/ (depends on write volume)
  • 10% free space (PostgreSQL needs working room)
  • 5% other (logs, stats, temp)

Key operational insight: If pg_wal/ fills up (disk full), PostgreSQL STOPS and refuses all writes. This is a hard crash. Monitor disk usage: kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -- df -h /var/lib/postgresql/data. Set alerts at 80% PVC usage. For resize: kubectl patch pvc pgdata-anihpj-db-0 -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"40Gi"}}}}' (StorageClass must have allowVolumeExpansion: true).

🔬 Restic vs CSI Snapshots — Two Backup Strategies for Velero

Velero supports TWO methods for backing up PV data. Understanding when to use each is critical for your backup strategy:

AspectCSI SnapshotsRestic (File-Level)
How it worksCloud provider creates block-level snapshot (EBS snapshot, etc.)Restic reads files through the pod's filesystem and backs them up to S3
ConsistencyCrash-consistent (like pulling power). NOT app-consistent without quiescing.File-level. Individual files may be inconsistent if app is writing.
Performance🟢 Near-instant (copy-on-write). No impact on pod.🔴 Can be slow — reads entire filesystem. Pod must be running.
Storage backendCloud provider (EBS snapshots). NOT portable across clouds.S3-compatible. PORTABLE across any cloud or on-prem.
CSI driver required?✅ Yes — must support snapshotting❌ No — works with any volume type
Best forProduction databases. Fast, frequent backups with low impact.Cross-cloud migration. Small volumes. Non-CSI storage (NFS, hostPath).

For anihpj-db: Use CSI snapshots for hourly backups (fast, low impact). Consider supplementing with Restic-based weekly backups for cross-cloud portability. For application-consistent PostgreSQL backups, consider Kanister or CloudNativePG which run pg_dump or pg_basebackup BEFORE triggering the snapshot, ensuring the snapshot contains a consistent database state.

⏱️ Target: 10 minutes
Drill 11.1 — Create a PVC and Debug "Pending" Status
  1. Create a PVC requesting 10GB, RWO, StorageClass "fast-ssd"
  2. If "fast-ssd" doesn't exist, observe the PVC staying "Pending"
  3. Create the StorageClass (use ebs.csi.aws.com or kubernetes.io/no-provisioner)
  4. Observe the PVC transition from Pending → Bound (or stay Pending if no CSI driver)
  5. Run kubectl describe pvc and identify the EXACT event message explaining the status
💡 Hint: kubectl describe pvc shows events at the bottom. The last event explains WHY the PVC is in its current state.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create PVC
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: drill-pvc
spec:
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
EOF

# Step 2: Check status (will be Pending if SC doesn't exist)
kubectl get pvc drill-pvc
# NAME        STATUS    VOLUME   CAPACITY   STORAGECLASS
# drill-pvc   Pending                      fast-ssd

# Step 3: Describe to see WHY
kubectl describe pvc drill-pvc
# Events:
#   Type     Reason              Message
#   ----     ------              -------
#   Warning  ProvisioningFailed  storageclass.storage.k8s.io "fast-ssd" not found

# Step 4: Create StorageClass (for local testing, no CSI needed)
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-ssd
provisioner: kubernetes.io/no-provisioner  # No dynamic provisioning
volumeBindingMode: Immediate
EOF

# Step 5: PVC stays Pending because no PV matches
# (no-provisioner doesn't auto-create volumes)
kubectl describe pvc drill-pvc
# Events:
#   Type     Reason              Message
#   ----     ------              -------
#   Normal   FailedBinding       no persistent volumes available for this claim
⏱️ Target: 15 minutes
Drill 11.2 — Deploy PostgreSQL StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates
  1. Create a StorageClass (or use the default one in your cluster)
  2. Create a StatefulSet for PostgreSQL with volumeClaimTemplates requesting 1Gi
  3. Verify the PVC is auto-created: kubectl get pvc — you should see pgdata-anihpj-db-0
  4. Delete the pod: kubectl delete pod anihpj-db-0
  5. Verify: (a) Pod is recreated with same name, (b) PVC still exists, (c) Data survives
💡 Hint: The PVC name pattern is <volumeClaimTemplate-name>-<statefulset-name>-<ordinal>. The PVC outlives the pod.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
spec:
  serviceName: anihpj-db
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-db
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: anihpj-db
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: postgres
        image: postgres:15
        env:
        - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
          value: "temppass"
        volumeMounts:
        - name: pgdata
          mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: pgdata
    spec:
      accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 1Gi
EOF

# Step 2: Verify PVC auto-created
kubectl get pvc
# NAME                   STATUS   VOLUME                  CAPACITY
# pgdata-anihpj-db-0     Bound    pvc-abc123              1Gi

# Step 3: Write some test data
kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -- psql -U postgres -c "CREATE TABLE test (id int);"
kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -- psql -U postgres -c "INSERT INTO test VALUES (1);"

# Step 4: Delete the pod
kubectl delete pod anihpj-db-0
# pod "anihpj-db-0" deleted

# Step 5: Verify pod is recreated with same PVC
kubectl get pods -l app=anihpj-db
# NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
# anihpj-db-0   1/1     Running   0          10s

# Data survives!
kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -- psql -U postgres -c "SELECT * FROM test;"
#  id
# ----
#   1
# (1 row)

🎓 CNPE Exam Focus — Storage Architecture (Domain 1 — 15%)

Storage tasks on the CNPE exam typically involve: (1) Creating PVCs with correct access modes and StorageClass. (2) Troubleshooting "PVC Pending" (wrong StorageClass, no CSI driver, zone mismatch). (3) Configuring StatefulSets with volumeClaimTemplates. (4) Setting up Velero backup schedules. The exam tests your ability to REASON about storage — not just type commands. Know WHY you chose RWOP over RWO, WHY WaitForFirstConsumer matters, and WHY Velero complements etcd snapshots rather than replacing them.

🎯 The PVC Debug Flow — How to Diagnose ANY Storage Issue
  1. Check PVC status: kubectl describe pvc <name>. Look at the Events section — it tells you EXACTLY why it's stuck.
  2. Verify StorageClass exists: kubectl get storageclass. Is the referenced SC present? Is it marked as default?
  3. Check CSI driver health: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep csi. Are both controller and node pods running?
  4. Check for events: kubectl get events -n <namespace> --sort-by='.lastTimestamp'. Provisioning failures appear here.
  5. Verify zone compatibility: If using WaitForFirstConsumer, the PV is created in the pod's zone. Is the pod scheduled? If not, why?
  6. Check pod mount: kubectl describe pod <pod>. "FailedMount" or "Multi-Attach error" → wrong access mode or AZ mismatch.
⚠️ The "Lost PVC" Disaster — When Helm Deletes Your Database

Helm deletes PVCs that are part of a Helm release UNLESS you annotate them with "helm.sh/resource-policy": keep. A platform engineer once ran helm uninstall anihpj — and Helm deleted the PostgreSQL PVC along with the StatefulSet. The 200GB production database vanished in seconds. Velero backup saved them (restored in 8 minutes), but the lesson is permanent: Always annotate StatefulSet PVCs with the Helm keep policy. Always test your backup restore before you need it.

Q: What's the difference between RWO and RWOP?

▶ Show Answer
RWO (ReadWriteOnce): Single NODE can mount read-write. Multiple pods on the same node can mount the same volume — risking data corruption. RWOP (ReadWriteOncePod): Single POD can mount read-write. Guarantees exclusive access regardless of node. Introduced in K8s 1.22. Always use RWOP for databases if your CSI driver supports it.
Q: Velero backup vs etcd snapshot — which one restores my data?

▶ Show Answer
Velero: Backs up K8s objects + PV data (via CSI snapshots or Restic). Can restore individual apps/namespaces WITH their data. etcd snapshot: Backs up ALL K8s metadata only. NO PV data. Restores the entire cluster state. You need BOTH: etcd snapshots for cluster DR (rebuild the cluster), Velero for application DR (restore anihpj with its database).
🚀 Beyond CNPE — Advanced Storage Patterns
  • Database Operators (CloudNativePG, Zalando, CrunchyData): Operators that manage PostgreSQL clusters with automated failover, backups, and scaling. Replace manual StatefulSet management with declarative Postgres cluster CRDs.
  • Rook/Ceph: Run your OWN distributed storage cluster (block, file, object) inside Kubernetes. Provides RWO, RWX, and S3-compatible storage — all managed via K8s CRDs. "AWS EBS, but running in your cluster."
  • VolSync: Asynchronous volume replication across clusters for disaster recovery. Replicate anihpj-db's PV from us-east-1 to eu-west-1 continuously. RPO measured in minutes.
  • Kanister: Application-level backup (not just volume snapshots). Backs up PostgreSQL with pg_dump, MongoDB with mongodump — consistent, application-aware backups.

📖 Chapter 11 Summary: Storage is where state lives. PVs represent physical storage (cluster-scoped). PVCs are developer requests (namespace-scoped). StorageClasses automate provisioning via CSI drivers. Choose RWOP for databases (single writer), RWX for shared storage (many writers). StatefulSets with volumeClaimTemplates give each pod its own persistent identity and storage. Velero backs up both K8s objects AND PV data to S3. etcd snapshots complement Velero for full cluster DR. Always annotate production PVCs with Helm keep policy — one typo can delete your database.

12.1 Resource Requests & Limits — The Foundation of Scheduling

Every container in Kubernetes can specify requests (guaranteed minimum) and limits (maximum allowed). The scheduler uses requests to decide WHERE to place pods. The kubelet uses limits to enforce resource usage. Getting these wrong is the #1 cause of "why is my pod Pending?" and "why is my pod being killed?"

📏
Requests = Guaranteed Minimum

The scheduler ONLY considers requests when deciding if a node has enough capacity. A pod requesting 500m CPU needs a node with at least 500m available. This is what the scheduler uses.

🚦
Limits = Maximum Allowed

CPU: throttled if exceeded (pod slows down, doesn't die). Memory: OOMKilled if exceeded (pod is TERMINATED). Limits are ENFORCED by kubelet, not the scheduler.

QoS ClassConditionPriority (OOM Score)ExampleUse Case
Guaranteedrequest == limit for ALL containers (CPU + Memory)🟢 Highest (least likely to be killed)req: 512Mi/500m, limit: 512Mi/500mProduction databases. Must never be evicted.
Burstablerequest < limit for at least one container🟡 Mediumreq: 256Mi/250m, limit: 512Mi/500mMost web apps. Burst when needed, baseline guaranteed.
BestEffortNo requests or limits set at all🔴 Lowest (FIRST to be killed)(nothing specified)NEVER in production. Dev experiments only.
⚠️ Memory OOMKilled vs CPU Throttling — The Critical Difference

CPU limit exceeded: Kernel throttles the process. Pod SLOWS DOWN but stays alive. Users experience latency but not errors. Memory limit exceeded: Kernel invokes OOM Killer. Pod is TERMINATED immediately. kubectl describe pod shows "OOMKilled" with exit code 137. Users get 5xx errors. This is why memory limits must be set CAREFULLY — too low and your app randomly crashes. Too high and a memory leak takes down the entire node. Golden rule: Set memory requests = limits for production databases.

🔬 How the Linux OOM Killer Decides Which Pod Dies

When a node runs out of memory, the kernel invokes the OOM Killer. It uses a scoring algorithm based on QoS class — this is why BestEffort pods die first:

OOM Killer Scoring — Why QoS Matters
  OOM_SCORE = (memory_used_pct) × 1000 + oom_score_adj

  QoS-based oom_score_adj (set by kubelet):
  • Guaranteed: oom_score_adj = -998  → essentially NEVER killed
  • Burstable:  oom_score_adj = max(0, 1000 - 1000 × request/limit)
  • BestEffort: oom_score_adj = 1000  → FIRST to die

  EXAMPLE: 3 pods when node runs out of memory
  ┌──────────────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
  │ Pod              │ QoS       │ Mem Used │ oom_adj  │ Score    │
  ├──────────────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
  │ anihpj-db        │Guaranteed│   4GB    │   -998   │  ~0      │
  │ anihpj-web       │Burstable │  500MB   │   500    │  ~530    │
  │ dev-experiment   │BestEffort│  200MB   │  1000    │  ~1012   │← KILLED
  └──────────────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┘

  View: cat /proc/<pid>/oom_score on the node
  This is why databases MUST be Guaranteed — they have negative OOM score.
🔬 How CPU Throttling Actually Works — CFS, cgroups, and the Kernel

When you set resources.limits.cpu: 500m, Kubernetes doesn't just "slow down" your pod. It configures the Linux kernel's CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) to limit CPU time:

CPU Throttling — From K8s YAML to Kernel Enforcement
  YOUR YAML: resources.limits.cpu: "500m"
       │
       ▼
  KUBELET translates to cgroup settings:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ cpu.cfs_period_us  = 100000  (100ms — the accounting period)│
  │ cpu.cfs_quota_us   = 50000   (50ms — allowed CPU per period)│
  │                                                             │
  │ Result: Pod gets 50ms of CPU every 100ms = 50% of 1 core   │
  │ This equals 500 millicores (500m)                           │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WHAT HAPPENS WHEN POD EXCEEDS LIMIT:
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Time: 0ms — Pod starts using CPU                            │
  │ Time: 0-50ms — Pod runs normally (within quota)            │
  │ Time: 50ms — Pod has used its 50ms quota                   │
  │ Time: 50-100ms — CPU THROTTLED! Pod is FROZEN by kernel   │
  │ Time: 100ms — New accounting period. Pod runs again.       │
  │ Time: 100-150ms — Pod runs normally                        │
  │ Time: 150-200ms — THROTTLED again                          │
  │                                                             │
  │ The pod sees: "My app is running 50% slower than expected" │
  │ The container doesn't know it's being throttled!           │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  CHECK IF POD IS THROTTLED:
  kubectl top pod anihpj-web  # See current CPU usage
  kubectl describe pod anihpj-web | grep -A2 "State"  # Check for throttling
  # Or check cgroup stats directly on the node:
  # cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu/kubepods/.../cpu.stat
  # nr_throttled: 15234  ← Times this pod was throttled

  KEY INSIGHT: High nr_throttled but low CPU usage = limit too low.
  The pod keeps hitting its limit and being frozen even though
  the NODE has plenty of free CPU. Solution: increase the limit.
⚡ anihpj Resource Configuration — Production-Ready Settings
# anihpj-web: Burstable (can burst above request for traffic spikes)
containers:
- name: django
  resources:
    requests:
      memory: "256Mi"
      cpu: "250m"
    limits:
      memory: "512Mi"
      cpu: "500m"

# anihpj-db: Guaranteed (database must NEVER be OOMKilled)
containers:
- name: postgres
  resources:
    requests:
      memory: "512Mi"
      cpu: "500m"
    limits:
      memory: "512Mi"
      cpu: "500m"

12.2 Scheduling — Node Selectors, Affinity, Taints & Tolerations

The Kubernetes scheduler decides which node runs which pod. By default, it uses a scoring algorithm based on resource availability. But as a platform engineer, you can influence this with four mechanisms:

MechanismHow It WorksStrengthExample
Node SelectorPod specifies required node labels. Simplest mechanism.Hard requirement (MUST match)disktype: ssd → only nodes with this label
Node AffinityPod specifies PREFERRED or REQUIRED node labels with expressions.Soft (preferred) or Hard (required)"prefer nodes in us-east-1a, but OK elsewhere"
Pod AffinityPod wants to be NEAR other pods (same node/zone).Soft or Hard"place web pod near its cache pod for low latency"
Pod Anti-AffinityPod wants to be AWAY from other pods (different node/zone).Soft or Hard"never place two DB replicas on same node"
Taints & TolerationsNode REPELS pods (taint). Pod must ACCEPT (tolerate) to be scheduled there.Hard (NoSchedule) or Soft (PreferNoSchedule)"this node is GPU-only" + pod tolerates "gpu" taint
🔀 UTH: Node Selector vs Node Affinity — "Why Not Just Use Labels?"

🖥️ Uncle: "Just use nodeSelector. It's simple — one line in the pod spec. Why complicate things?"

🧑‍💻 Tech Lead: "Because nodeSelector is all-or-nothing. If no node matches, the pod stays Pending FOREVER. Node affinity gives you preferredDuringScheduling — 'try to put me on an SSD node, but if none exists, HDD is fine.' That flexibility prevents unnecessary Pending pods."

🧔‍♂️ Hiker: "Use nodeSelector for hard requirements (GPU workloads MUST have GPU nodes). Use node affinity with preferred for soft preferences. Use pod anti-affinity for HA (spread replicas across nodes/zones). Use taints for dedicated nodes (monitoring nodes, GPU nodes, compliance nodes)."

🔬 How the Scheduler Scores Nodes — The Algorithm Behind Pod Placement

When a new pod is created, the scheduler runs a two-phase algorithm: Filter (eliminate impossible nodes) then Score (rank remaining nodes). Understanding this helps you predict and debug pod placement:

Kubernetes Scheduler — Filter + Score
  PHASE 1: FILTER (eliminate nodes that CANNOT run the pod)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Starting: 10 nodes                                             │
  │ ├─ Node 1: Tainted (pod doesn't tolerate) → ELIMINATED        │
  │ ├─ Node 2: Insufficient CPU → ELIMINATED                      │
  │ ├─ Node 3: NodeSelector doesn't match → ELIMINATED            │
  │ ├─ Node 4: Pod Anti-Affinity conflict → ELIMINATED            │
  │ ├─ Node 5-10: PASS → Move to SCORE phase                      │
  │ Result: 6 nodes remaining                                      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PHASE 2: SCORE (rank remaining nodes 0-100, pick highest)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Scoring plugins (each contributes 0-100 points):               │
  │                                                                │
  │ • NodeResourcesLeastAllocated: Prefer nodes with MORE free    │
  │   resources. Higher free % = higher score. (Avoids hot spots) │
  │                                                                │
  │ • NodeResourcesBalancedAllocation: Prefer nodes where CPU     │
  │   and memory are BALANCED (not 90% CPU / 10% memory free).    │
  │                                                                │
  │ • ImageLocality: Prefer nodes that already have the container │
  │   image pulled. Saves pull time. +10-20 points.              │
  │                                                                │
  │ • PodTopologySpread: Prefer nodes that minimize skew.         │
  │   If zone-A has 3 pods and zone-B has 1, zone-B scores higher.│
  │                                                                │
  │ • NodeAffinity (preferred): Bonus points for matching         │
  │   preferred affinity rules.                                    │
  │                                                                │
  │ FINAL SCORE = weighted sum of all plugins → PICK HIGHEST      │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  View scheduler decisions:
  kubectl get events --field-selector reason=Scheduled
  kubectl describe pod <pod> | grep -A5 "Events"
🔬 Taint Types Deep Dive — NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute

Taints have three effects, and understanding the difference prevents misconfigurations that silently block pod scheduling:

Taint EffectBehaviorExisting PodsUse Case
NoScheduleNew pods WITHOUT toleration CANNOT be scheduled.Existing pods unaffected.Dedicated GPU nodes: only GPU-tolerating pods can land.
PreferNoScheduleScheduler TRIES to avoid this node, but will use it if no other option.Existing pods unaffected."This node is old/slow — avoid if possible."
NoExecuteNew pods without toleration can't schedule. EXISTING pods without toleration are EVICTED!EXISTING pods EVICTED if they don't tolerate!Node is failing — drain it immediately. Or: node has sensitive data — only specific pods.

NoExecute is the dangerous one. If you taint a running production node with NoExecute and your pods don't have the matching toleration, they'll be EVICTED — including your database pod. Always check existing pod tolerations before applying NoExecute taints to running nodes.

12.3 Topology Spread Constraints — Even Distribution Across Zones

Topology Spread Constraints ensure pods are evenly distributed across failure domains (zones, nodes, regions). Without them, the scheduler might place all 3 replicas in the same AZ — and when that AZ fails, your app is completely down.

Topology Spread — Before vs After
  WITHOUT SPREAD (scheduler optimizes for resource fit only)
  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐
  │ us-east-1a       │  │ us-east-1b       │  │ us-east-1c       │
  │                 │  │                 │  │                 │
  │ [web-1] [web-2] │  │                 │  │ [web-3]         │
  │ [web-4] [web-5] │  │                 │  │                 │
  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘
  ❌ us-east-1a has 4 pods. If 1a fails → 80% capacity lost.

  WITH SPREAD (maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone)
  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────┐
  │ us-east-1a       │  │ us-east-1b       │  │ us-east-1c       │
  │                 │  │                 │  │                 │
  │ [web-1] [web-4] │  │ [web-2] [web-5] │  │ [web-3]         │
  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘  └─────────────────┘
  ✅ Max 2 per zone. If 1a fails → only 40% capacity lost.

maxSkew controls the maximum difference between the most and least populated domains. maxSkew: 1 means "no domain can have more than 1 extra pod compared to any other domain." Combined with PodDisruptionBudget, this ensures your application survives zone failures gracefully.

12.4 Priority & Preemption — Production Pods Evict Dev Pods

PriorityClasses let you assign importance levels to pods. When the cluster is full, high-priority pods can EVICT low-priority pods to make room. This ensures production workloads always get resources, even during contention.

PriorityClassValuePreemption PolicyUse Case
system-cluster-critical2,000,000,000PreemptLowerPriorityCoreDNS, kube-proxy — cluster stops without them
system-node-critical2,000,001,000PreemptLowerPriorityCNI, CSI, kubelet — node stops without them
production-high1,000,000PreemptLowerPriorityCustomer-facing production services
production-medium100,000PreemptLowerPriorityInternal tools, staging environments
development10,000NeverDev environments — first to be evicted
⚠️ Preemption Is Disruptive — The Evicted Pod Is GONE

When a high-priority pod preempts a low-priority pod, the low-priority pod receives SIGTERM and is terminated. There's no graceful migration — the pod is killed. If it's a StatefulSet pod, a new one starts (reattaching to the same PVC). If it's a Deployment pod, a new one starts fresh. Make sure your low-priority workloads are stateless or use StatefulSets so they survive preemption with data intact. Also: PDBs do NOT protect against preemption — PDBs only protect against VOLUNTARY disruptions (drain, node update). Preemption is INVOLUNTARY.

12.5 Node Management — Cordon, Drain, PodDisruptionBudgets

Platform engineers need to manage nodes without disrupting workloads. Three tools make this possible: Cordon (mark unschedulable), Drain (evict pods gracefully), and PodDisruptionBudgets (ensure minimum availability during voluntary disruptions).

🚧
Cordon: Mark Unschedulable

kubectl cordon node-1. Node shows SchedulingDisabled. EXISTING pods keep running. NEW pods cannot be scheduled. Use before maintenance.

🔄
Drain: Evict All Pods

kubectl drain node-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data. Evicts all pods (respects PDBs). Node becomes empty + cordoned.

🛡️
Uncordon: Make Schedulable Again

kubectl uncordon node-1. Removes the taint. New pods CAN be scheduled again. Node returns to normal rotation.

📊
PDB: Protect Minimum Availability

maxUnavailable: 1 on a 3-replica Deployment. Drain will NEVER evict more than 1 pod at a time. Prevents complete outage during maintenance.

⚡ Node Maintenance Workflow — Production-Safe
# 1. Cordon the node (stop new pods)
kubectl cordon node-1

# 2. Drain the node (evict existing pods, respect PDBs)
kubectl drain node-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=60

# 3. Perform maintenance (OS updates, kernel patches, hardware swap)

# 4. Uncordon the node (allow new pods again)
kubectl uncordon node-1

# 5. Verify pods reschedule
kubectl get pods -o wide | grep node-1
🔬 What kubectl drain Actually Does — The API Call Sequence

kubectl drain is not a single API call — it's a sequence of operations that must complete in order. Understanding this helps you debug stuck drains:

kubectl drain — Behind the Scenes
  kubectl drain node-1 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data

  1. CORDON THE NODE
     kubectl cordon node-1
     API: PATCH /api/v1/nodes/node-1
     Body: {"spec":{"unschedulable":true}}
     → Node shows SchedulingDisabled. No new pods.

  2. LIST ALL PODS ON THE NODE
     kubectl get pods --field-selector spec.nodeName=node-1 --all-namespaces
     → Returns list of pods to evict

  3. FOR EACH POD (except DaemonSets and mirror pods):
     a. CHECK PDB:
        GET /apis/policy/v1/namespaces/{ns}/poddisruptionbudgets
        → If eviction would violate PDB (maxUnavailable=1 and already 1 down):
          STUCK! Drain waits until PDB allows it.

     b. CREATE EVICTION (not DELETE!):
        POST /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/pods/{name}/eviction
        Body: {"metadata":{"name":"pod-name"},"deleteOptions":{"gracePeriodSeconds":60}}
        → Respects graceful shutdown (SIGTERM → wait → SIGKILL)
        → Respects PDBs (eviction API checks PDB before proceeding)
        → Creates a DisruptionBudget record

     c. WAIT for pod to terminate:
        Poll GET /api/v1/namespaces/{ns}/pods/{name}
        → Wait until pod is gone or grace period expires

  4. DELETE EMPTYDIR DATA (if --delete-emptydir-data):
     → Removes emptyDir volumes from the node

  5. DONE — node is empty + cordoned

  WHY DRAINS GET STUCK:
  • PDB blocking: maxUnavailable limit reached → manual intervention
  • Pod not terminating: stuck on SIGTERM → check pod logs, increase grace period
  • DaemonSet pods: they restart immediately → use --ignore-daemonsets or --force
  • Pod with no controller: "orphan" pod → --force to delete anyway

12.6 Cluster Autoscaling — Cluster Autoscaler vs Karpenter

When pods can't be scheduled due to insufficient resources, cluster autoscaling adds nodes. When nodes are underutilized, it removes them. Two tools dominate: the traditional Cluster Autoscaler and the next-gen Karpenter.

FeatureCluster Autoscaler (CA)Karpenter
Speed🟡 Minutes (waits for cloud API, node boot)🟢 Seconds (pre-computes capacity, faster instance launch)
Instance Selection🔴 Fixed — uses predefined node groups (ASG)🟢 Dynamic — chooses optimal instance type/size for pending pods
Bin-Packing🔴 Basic — adds nodes, hopes pods fit🟢 Smart — evaluates 50+ instance types, picks best fit
Scale-Down🟡 Periodic (every 10 min), conservative🟢 Continuous — removes idle nodes aggressively
Consolidation❌ No — leaves fragmented nodes✅ Yes — moves pods to consolidate onto fewer nodes
Spot Instance Support🟡 Manual — separate ASG for spot🟢 Native — automatically mixes spot + on-demand
CNPE Relevance🟡 Know the basics🟢 Increasingly tested — cost optimization
🔬 How Karpenter Decides Which Instance to Launch

Karpenter doesn't just "add a node." It evaluates ALL available instance types (hundreds on AWS), scores them against the pending pods' requirements, and picks the optimal one. A pod requesting 2 CPU + 4GB RAM might be scheduled on a c5.large (2 vCPU, 4GB) at $0.085/hr — not a c5.xlarge (4 vCPU, 8GB) at $0.17/hr. Karpenter saves 30-50% on compute costs by eliminating over-provisioning. It also handles: (1) Spot interruption — drains node before AWS terminates it. (2) Drift detection — replaces nodes when AMI or configuration changes. (3) Consolidation — periodically defragments the cluster by moving pods to fewer nodes.

🔬 Karpenter Consolidation — How It Saves 30-50% More

Consolidation is Karpenter's most powerful feature. Without it, you end up with "fragmented" clusters — nodes at 20-30% utilization because pods were scheduled over time without rebalancing. Consolidation fixes this:

Karpenter Consolidation — Defragmenting Your Cluster
  BEFORE CONSOLIDATION (fragmented — 3 nodes, 43% avg utilization)
  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Node 1 (c5.xlarge)│  │ Node 2 (c5.xlarge)│  │ Node 3 (c5.xlarge)│
  │ $0.17/hr         │  │ $0.17/hr         │  │ $0.17/hr         │
  │                  │  │                  │  │                  │
  │ [Pod A: 2CPU/4G] │  │ [Pod C: 1CPU/2G] │  │ [Pod F: 2CPU/4G] │
  │ [Pod B: 1CPU/2G] │  │ [Pod D: 1CPU/1G] │  │ [Pod G: 1CPU/2G] │
  │                  │  │ [Pod E: 1CPU/1G] │  │                  │
  │ Used: 3/4 CPU    │  │ Used: 3/4 CPU    │  │ Used: 3/4 CPU    │
  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘
  Total: $0.51/hr for 3 nodes

  AFTER CONSOLIDATION (compact — 2 nodes, 75% avg utilization)
  ┌────────────────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐
  │ Node 1 (c5.2xlarge — bigger!)      │  │ Node 2 (c5.xlarge) │
  │ $0.34/hr                           │  │ $0.17/hr         │
  │                                    │  │                  │
  │ [Pod A: 2CPU/4G] [Pod C: 1CPU/2G] │  │ [Pod F: 2CPU/4G] │
  │ [Pod B: 1CPU/2G] [Pod D: 1CPU/1G] │  │ [Pod G: 1CPU/2G] │
  │ [Pod E: 1CPU/1G]                  │  │                  │
  │                                    │  │                  │
  │ Used: 6/8 CPU                      │  │ Used: 3/4 CPU    │
  └────────────────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘
  Total: $0.51/hr → $0.34/hr + $0.17/hr = SAME price but 2 nodes vs 3?
  Actually: bigger instances are often cheaper per-CPU!
  c5.xlarge: $0.17/4CPU = $0.0425/CPU-hour
  c5.2xlarge: $0.34/8CPU = $0.0425/CPU-hour (same)
  BUT: m5.xlarge ($0.192) → m5.2xlarge ($0.384) → same per-CPU
  Real savings come from REMOVING unnecessary nodes entirely.

  If Pod E (1CPU/1G) can fit on Node 2 instead:
  → Node 1 REMOVED → $0.17/hr saved → $122/month saved!

12.7 Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) — Right-Size Your Requests

Most teams GUESS resource requests. VPA observes actual usage over time and recommends (or auto-sets) optimal requests. It's the cure for "we set 8GB because we didn't know what to put."

📊
Recommend Mode

VPA observes pod usage for 8+ days, then suggests: "You requested 8GB but only use 500MB. Recommended: 1GB." Human applies the change.

⚡
Auto Mode

VPA automatically updates the Deployment's resource requests. BUT: this RESTARTS the pod. Not suitable for production without careful planning.

⚠️ VPA Restarts Pods — Don't Auto-Apply in Production Without Testing

VPA in Auto mode UPDATES the pod spec AND restarts the pod. If VPA decides your database needs less memory and restarts it mid-day, you have a production outage. Best practice: Use Recommend mode, review recommendations weekly, apply during maintenance windows. For stateless workloads, Auto mode is safer (pods are disposable). For databases, NEVER auto-apply VPA — use Recommend only.

🔬 How VPA Calculates Recommendations — Not Just an Average

VPA doesn't simply average your pod's CPU usage. It uses statistical percentiles to balance safety with efficiency:

VPA Recommendation Algorithm (Simplified)
  INPUT: Pod CPU usage over past 8 days (sample every 1 minute = 11,520 data points)

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STEP 1: Collect usage samples                                   │
  │   Real data: [100m, 150m, 80m, 200m, 120m, 300m (spike!), ...] │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STEP 2: Calculate percentiles                                   │
  │   P50 (median): 150m  — 50% of samples are below this          │
  │   P90: 250m           — 90% of samples are below this          │
  │   P95: 350m           — 95% of samples are below this          │
  │   P99: 500m           — 99% of samples are below (spikes!)     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STEP 3: Set recommendation based on policy                      │
  │                                                                 │
  │   LOWER BOUND (request): P50 × safety_margin (0.9)             │
  │     150m × 0.9 = 135m → "Request at least 135m"               │
  │                                                                 │
  │   TARGET (recommended): P90                                     │
  │     250m → "Recommended request: 250m"                         │
  │     (Covers 90% of observed usage. Ignores extreme spikes.)    │
  │                                                                 │
  │   UPPER BOUND (limit): max(P95 × 2, P99)                       │
  │     max(350m × 2, 500m) = 700m → "Max recommended limit: 700m"│
  │                                                                 │
  │   CONFIDENCE: If < 1 day of data → "Not enough data"          │
  │              If > 8 days → "High confidence"                   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  KEY INSIGHT: VPA uses P90, not average.
  Average would be pulled down by idle periods (nighttime) and
  be too low for daytime traffic. P90 ensures you have enough
  capacity for 90% of observed situations.
  For PRODUCTION databases: consider P95 or P99 for safety.
  For DEV environments: P50 is fine (crashes are acceptable).

12.8 FinOps — Cost Allocation with Kubecost/OpenCost

FinOps is the practice of making cloud costs transparent and accountable. In a multi-tenant platform, the #1 question you'll get is: "Who spent $50,000 on AWS this month?"

ConceptWhat It MeansTool
Cost AllocationTagging resources by team/project/environment for cost attributionAWS Cost Explorer, Azure Cost Management
ShowbackShow teams what they cost — informational only, no billingKubecost, OpenCost dashboards
ChargebackActually BILL teams for their usage — costs deducted from team budgetKubecost Enterprise, CloudHealth
Right-SizingIdentify over-provisioned resources (requested 8GB, used 500MB)VPA + Kubecost recommendations
Commitment DiscountsReserved Instances, Savings Plans — commit to 1-3 years for 30-60% discountAWS Savings Plans, Azure Reserved Instances

Kubecost is the de facto standard for K8s cost visibility. It breaks down costs by namespace, deployment, pod, and even individual labels. A platform engineer can answer "How much does the payments team's namespace cost?" in 5 seconds. OpenCost is the open-source CNCF sandbox project that Kubecost is built on — free, but less polished.

🔬 ResourceQuota & LimitRange — Enforcing Cost Controls Per Namespace

While FinOps tools SHOW costs, ResourceQuota and LimitRange ENFORCE them. These are the platform engineer's primary tools for preventing one team from consuming all cluster resources:

ResourceScopeWhat It DoesExample
ResourceQuotaNamespaceCaps TOTAL resource consumption. Team cannot exceed this.Max 10 pods, 16GB RAM, 8 CPU total
LimitRangeNamespaceSets default request/limit for pods that don't specify them. Also sets min/max per pod.Default 256Mi/250m, max 2Gi/2 CPU per pod

Together they prevent the "noisy neighbor" problem at the resource level: ResourceQuota caps the team's total (they can't deploy 50 pods if the cap is 20). LimitRange ensures every pod has at least some resources specified (no BestEffort pods sneaking in). Combined with NetworkPolicy (Ch 10) for network isolation and RBAC (Ch 27) for access control, you have a complete multi-tenancy enforcement stack.

🔬 How Kubecost Collects Cost Data — The Architecture Behind the Dashboard

Kubecost doesn't magically know your AWS bill. It combines multiple data sources to allocate costs to individual pods and namespaces:

Kubecost Architecture — Data Sources
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ KUBECOST (runs as a Deployment in your cluster)                 │
  │                                                                 │
  │  INPUTS:                                                        │
  │                                                                 │
  │  1. K8s API (free):                                             │
  │     • Pod resource requests (what you ASKED for)               │
  │     • Actual node types (instance type, region, spot/on-demand) │
  │     → Calculates: "What COULD this pod cost based on requests?" │
  │                                                                 │
  │  2. Cloud Provider API (AWS/GCP/Azure — optional but critical): │
  │     • Actual billing data (what you PAID)                       │
  │     • Reserved instance discounts                               │
  │     • Savings Plans                                             │
  │     → Calculates: "What DID this pod actually cost?"           │
  │                                                                 │
  │  3. Prometheus (optional):                                      │
  │     • Actual resource usage metrics (what you USED)             │
  │     → Calculates: "How much is WASTED?" (requested - used)    │
  │                                                                 │
  │  OUTPUTS:                                                       │
  │  • Per-namespace cost: "payments team: $1,234/month"           │
  │  • Per-deployment cost: "anihpj-web: $200/month"               │
  │  • Per-label cost: "env=production: $8,000/month"              │
  │  • Efficiency score: "You're using 35% of requested CPU"       │
  │  • Savings recommendations: "Save $500/month with spot"        │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WITHOUT cloud integration: Kubecost estimates costs based on
  instance types × requests. Reasonably accurate (±10-20%).
  WITH cloud integration: Kubecost uses actual billing data.
  Accurate to the penny. Shows reserved instance savings.

  OpenCost (CNCF Sandbox) provides the core engine for free.
  Kubecost adds: dashboards, alerts, SSO, RBAC, and support.

12.9 Spot Instances — 90% Cheaper, But Can Disappear

Spot instances (AWS) / Spot VMs (GCP) / Spot VMs (Azure) are unused cloud capacity sold at 60-90% discount. The catch: they can be terminated with 2 minutes' notice when the cloud provider needs the capacity back.

Spot Instance Lifecycle — How to Use Them Safely
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ SPOT INSTANCE LIFECYCLE                                         │
  │                                                                 │
  │ 1. Karpenter requests spot instance (bid 60-90% below on-demand)│
  │ 2. AWS allocates instance. Pods scheduled. App runs normally.   │
  │ 3. AWS needs capacity back → sends 2-MINUTE WARNING             │
  │ 4. Karpenter receives warning → IMMEDIATELY:                    │
  │    a. Cordons the node (no new pods)                            │
  │    b. Drains pods (respecting PDBs and graceful shutdown)       │
  │    c. Replaces with on-demand instance (if configured)          │
  │ 5. AWS terminates the spot instance                             │
  │                                                                 │
  │  KEY REQUIREMENTS FOR SPOT SUCCESS:                             │
  │  ✅ Stateless workloads (Deployments over StatefulSets)         │
  │  ✅ Multiple replicas (≥3) spread across spot + on-demand       │
  │  ✅ PDBs to ensure min replicas survive during drain            │
  │  ✅ Graceful shutdown (SIGTERM handling) — drain time ≤ 2 min   │
  │  ✅ Node termination handler (AWS) or Karpenter for auto-drain  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ❌ NEVER run single-replica databases on spot                  │
  │  ❌ NEVER run StatefulSet primaries on spot (no auto-failover)   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

12.10 anihpj Cost Optimization Strategy

Putting it all together — here's the optimized compute strategy for the anihpj platform:

WorkloadInstance TypeSavingsRisk Mitigation
anihpj-web (stateless)Spot (70% discount)$200 → $60/mo3+ replicas, PDB maxUnavailable=1, pod anti-affinity across AZs
anihpj-api (stateless)Spot (70% discount)$200 → $60/moSame as web. If spot reclaimed, on-demand fallback via Karpenter
anihpj-celery (workers)Spot (80% discount)$150 → $30/moIdempotent tasks only. Failed tasks retry. Graceful shutdown drains queue.
anihpj-db (PostgreSQL)Reserved (40% discount)$300 → $180/mo1-year commitment. NEVER spot. Multi-AZ with streaming replica.
anihpj-redis (cache)On-Demand + Spot failover$100 → $70/moRedis Cluster with 3 shards. If spot reclaimed, remaining shards serve.

Total monthly compute: $950 (all on-demand) → $400 (optimized) — 58% savings. Strategy: spot for stateless (web/api/workers), reserved for databases, on-demand as safety net. Karpenter manages the mix automatically. Never sacrifice reliability for cost — the database stays on reserved instances.

⏱️ Target: 10 minutes
Drill 12.1 — Debug a Pending Pod (FailedScheduling)
  1. Create a Deployment requesting 8 CPUs (more than any node has)
  2. Observe the pod stuck in Pending with "0/N nodes are available"
  3. Use kubectl describe pod to identify the exact reason
  4. Create a new node (or reduce the request) to resolve the issue
  5. Verify the pod transitions to Running
💡 Hint: kubectl describe pod shows scheduler events. Look for "Insufficient cpu" or "didn't match Pod's node affinity."
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create oversized pod
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: greedy-app
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: greedy
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: greedy
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "8000m"  # 8 CPUs!
            memory: "16Gi"
EOF

# Step 2: Check status
kubectl get pods -l app=greedy
# NAME                        READY   STATUS    AGE
# greedy-app-xxx              0/1     Pending   30s

# Step 3: Describe to see WHY
kubectl describe pod -l app=greedy | grep -A5 Events
# Events:
#   Type     Reason            Message
#   ----     ------            -------
#   Warning  FailedScheduling  0/2 nodes are available:
#     2 Insufficient cpu. preemption: 0/2 nodes...

# Step 4: Fix — reduce request or add bigger node
⏱️ Target: 12 minutes
Drill 12.2 — Configure Pod Anti-Affinity for HA
  1. Create a 3-replica Deployment of nginx
  2. Verify pods are running — they may all be on the same node
  3. Add podAntiAffinity with requiredDuringScheduling to spread across nodes
  4. Verify each pod is on a different node (if you have ≥3 nodes)
  5. Scale down to 1 node and observe what happens to excess pods
💡 Hint: Use topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname for per-node anti-affinity. Use kubectl get pods -o wide to see which node each pod is on.
📝 View Solution 
# Step 1: Create Deployment with anti-affinity
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: ha-nginx
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ha-nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ha-nginx
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
          - labelSelector:
              matchLabels:
                app: ha-nginx
            topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx
EOF

# Step 2: Check placement
kubectl get pods -l app=ha-nginx -o wide
# NAME                      NODE
# ha-nginx-xxx              node-1
# ha-nginx-yyy              node-2
# ha-nginx-zzz              node-3   ← Each on different node!

# Step 3: If you only have 2 nodes, the 3rd pod stays Pending:
# Warning  FailedScheduling  0/2 nodes available:
#   1 node(s) had untolerated taint, 1 node(s) didn't match
#   pod affinity/anti-affinity rules
