🎓 CNPE Exam Focus — Scheduling & Cost (Domain 1 — 15%)

Scheduling and cost management are increasingly tested on the CNPE exam. Expect tasks like: "Configure resource requests to guarantee QoS class X," "Apply taints and tolerations to dedicate nodes to a workload," "Use pod anti-affinity to ensure HA," or "Calculate cost savings from spot instances." The exam rewards pragmatic finops — not just configuring tools, but making decisions that balance performance and cost.

🎯 The Scheduling Debug Flow — Why Is My Pod Pending?
  1. Check pod events: kubectl describe pod <pod>. The Events section tells you EXACTLY why.
  2. "0/N nodes available": Insufficient resources, node affinity/selector doesn't match, or all nodes tainted.
  3. "1 node had taint": Nodes have taints the pod doesn't tolerate. kubectl describe node | grep Taint.
  4. "pod affinity/anti-affinity": The pod's rules can't be satisfied. Check topology keys and label selectors.
  5. "insufficient memory/cpu": Node has capacity but not enough. Check kubectl describe node for Allocated resources.
  6. PDB blocking drain: kubectl get pdb. Check maxUnavailable. Manually delete pods if safe.
⚠️ The "Set and Forget" Resource Trap — Why Most Clusters Waste 50%+ of CPU

Studies show the average Kubernetes cluster wastes 50-60% of allocated CPU because teams over-request "just to be safe." A team requests 8GB RAM, uses 500MB. Multiply by 50 teams = 375GB wasted. That's $1,500/month in cloud costs for absolutely nothing. The fix: (1) Install VPA in Recommend mode. (2) Review recommendations monthly. (3) Set resource policies (LimitRange) to cap max requests. (4) Use Kubecost to SHOW teams their waste. When developers see they're spending $300/month on unused RAM, behavior changes.

Q: What's the difference between requests and limits?

▶ Show Answer
Requests: Guaranteed minimum. The scheduler uses this to decide if a node has enough capacity. Limits: Maximum allowed. CPU is throttled if exceeded (pod slows down). Memory triggers OOMKill if exceeded (pod is terminated). Set requests based on average usage. Set limits based on worst-case acceptable usage.
Q: When should I use spot instances vs reserved instances?

▶ Show Answer
Spot: Stateless workloads (web, API, workers). 60-90% cheaper but can be terminated with 2-min notice. Must handle graceful shutdown. Reserved: Stateful workloads (databases). Pay upfront for 1-3 year commitment. 30-60% discount. Guaranteed capacity. On-Demand: Safety net. Use when spot is unavailable or for workloads that can't tolerate interruption.
🚀 Beyond CNPE — Advanced Scheduling & Cost Patterns
  • Karpenter Consolidation: Automatically identifies underutilized nodes and moves pods to consolidate onto fewer nodes. Can reduce node count by 30-50% without any manual intervention. This is the next frontier of FinOps automation.
  • Descheduler: The opposite of the scheduler — it EVICTS pods that violate scheduling policies (e.g., "pod was placed before anti-affinity rules existed"). Helps maintain cluster health over time. Use with PDBs.
  • Kube-green: Auto-scales Deployments to zero during off-hours (nights, weekends). Dev environments that nobody uses from 8 PM to 8 AM cost nothing. Simple cron-based scheduling.
  • StormForge: Machine-learning-based resource optimization. Uses real workload patterns to recommend optimal CPU/memory settings. Goes beyond VPA's simple averaging.

📖 Chapter 12 Summary: Scheduling determines WHERE pods run. Resource management determines HOW MUCH they consume. Cost management determines WHAT it all costs. A platform engineer balances all three — performance, efficiency, and economics. Set resource requests based on actual usage (VPA). Spread pods across failure domains (topology constraints). Protect availability during maintenance (PDBs). Use spot instances for stateless workloads (60-90% savings). Use reserved instances for databases (30-60% savings). Monitor costs per team with Kubecost. FinOps is not a project — it's a continuous practice.

13.1 What Is GitOps? — Git as the Single Source of Truth

GitOps is a way to do Continuous Delivery where Git is the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and applications. An agent running inside the cluster (Argo CD or Flux) pulls from Git and syncs the desired state to the cluster. This flips the traditional CI/CD model on its head.

Push-Based CI/CD vs Pull-Based GitOps
  TRADITIONAL PUSH-BASED CI/CD                    GITOPS PULL-BASED
  ┌────────────────────────────┐                  ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ CI System (GitHub Actions) │                  │ CI System (GitHub Actions) │
  │ ✅ Builds image             │                  │ ✅ Builds image             │
  │ ✅ Runs tests               │                  │ ✅ Runs tests               │
  │ 🔴 Pushes to cluster        │                  │ ✅ Pushes image to registry │
  │   (NEEDS cluster creds!)   │                  │ ❌ Does NOT deploy          │
  └────────────────────────────┘                  └────────────────────────────┘
              │                                              │
              │ kubectl apply -f ...                         │ (image is in registry)
              ▼                                              ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────┐                  ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ KUBERNETES CLUSTER         │                  │ ARGO CD / FLUX             │
  │ (passive — receives push)  │                  │ (runs INSIDE the cluster)  │
  └────────────────────────────┘                  │ ✅ Pulls Git repo every 3min│
                                                  │ ✅ Compares desired vs actual│
  ❌ CI needs cluster access                      │ ✅ Fixes drift automatically │
  ❌ What if CI is compromised?                   └────────────────────────────┘
  ❌ No automatic drift detection                              │
  ❌ Manual rollback                                          ▼
                                                  ┌────────────────────────────┐
  ✅ CI never touches cluster                     │ KUBERNETES CLUSTER         │
  ✅ Cluster credentials stay IN cluster          │ (active — pulls desired state)│
  ✅ Git history = audit log                      └────────────────────────────┘
  ✅ Drift auto-detected and auto-fixed
📝
Declarative

Everything is defined as YAML in Git. No manual kubectl edit, no SSH, no clicking in cloud consoles. The desired state IS the Git repo.

📜
Versioned

Every change is a Git commit. git log = complete audit trail. git revert = instant rollback. Who changed what, when, and why.

⬇️
Pull-Based

The agent PULLS from Git. CI never needs cluster credentials. If CI is compromised, the attacker can't reach your production cluster.

🔄
Continuously Reconciled

Every 3 minutes (configurable), Argo CD compares desired state (Git) vs actual state (cluster). Differences = auto-fixed. Drift = impossible.

13.2 GitOps Principles — The Four Pillars

The OpenGitOps project defines four principles. Understanding WHY each exists helps you make better platform decisions:

PrincipleWhat It MeansAnti-Pattern (What NOT to Do)
1. DeclarativeEverything described declaratively (YAML). System is defined as code.❌ "Just SSH in and run these 5 commands." No artifact. No audit.
2. VersionedDesired state stored in Git. Immutable history. Every change traceable.❌ "I edited the Deployment YAML directly on the server. Trust me."
3. Pull-BasedSoftware agent PULLS desired state. Cluster credentials stay in cluster.❌ CI pushes to cluster with admin credentials baked into environment variables.
4. Continuously ReconciledAgent monitors actual state and AUTO-CORRECTS drift. Desired = Actual.❌ "Deploy once and forget." Drift accumulates silently for months.
⚠️ "I Already Use Git and kubectl apply — Isn't That GitOps?"

No. Running kubectl apply -f from a CI pipeline is NOT GitOps. Why? (1) It's PUSH-based, not pull-based. CI holds cluster credentials — a security risk. (2) There's no continuous reconciliation — if someone manually edits a Deployment, the CI pipeline won't know or fix it. (3) The CI pipeline is the source of truth, not Git — if CI is down, you can't deploy. True GitOps means Argo CD or Flux running INSIDE the cluster, pulling from Git, reconciling continuously.

13.3 Repo Structure — Monorepo vs Polyrepo vs App of Apps

How you organize your Git repositories directly affects team autonomy, deployment speed, and operational complexity. There are three main patterns:

PatternStructureProsConsBest For
MonorepoOne repo for ALL teams and ALL appsSingle source of truth, easy cross-team changesLarge repo, merge conflicts, slow clones, permission issuesSmall orgs (<10 teams), tightly coupled apps
PolyrepoOne repo per app/teamTeam autonomy, fast clones, clear ownershipHard to enforce standards across repos, cross-team coordination harderLarge orgs (10+ teams), independent microservices
App of AppsRoot Argo CD App deploys child AppsSingle entry point, hierarchical, scales to 100+ appsAdds indirection, needs careful organizationANY org using Argo CD — this IS the standard pattern
⚡ App of Apps Pattern — The Standard Argo CD Architecture
# ROOT APP: points to a directory of child Application definitions
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: root-app
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/platform-gitops
    path: apps/           # ← This directory contains child Application YAMLs
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: argocd

# CHILD APPS: each team/app gets its own Application
# apps/anihpj-web.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/anihpj-k8s
    path: overlays/production
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: anihpj
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true      # Delete resources not in Git
      selfHeal: true   # Auto-fix drift

13.4 Argo CD — The De Facto GitOps Operator

Argo CD is a Kubernetes-native GitOps tool. It runs inside your cluster, watches Git repositories, and ensures the cluster state matches the desired state. It's the most widely adopted GitOps tool in the CNCF ecosystem (graduated project).

📦
Application

The core CRD. Defines: WHERE is the source (Git repo + path), WHERE to deploy (cluster + namespace), and HOW to sync (auto/manual, prune, self-heal). One Application = one deployable unit.

🔒
AppProject

RBAC for Applications. Limits: WHICH source repos, WHICH destination clusters/namespaces, WHAT resource types. "Team A can only deploy to dev namespace."

🔄
Sync

Auto (3-min interval) or Manual. Prune: delete resources removed from Git. Self-Heal: revert manual changes. Sync Waves: order deployments (DB first, then web).

🖥️
Web UI + CLI

Visual dashboard shows every app's health. Drift visualization. Manual sync/rollback. argocd CLI for scripting and CI integration.

Argo CD Architecture — How It Works
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                          ARGO CD ARCHITECTURE                        │
  │                                                                     │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐                                              │
  │  │  Git Repository   │  github.com/anihpj/platform-gitops          │
  │  │  (desired state)  │                                              │
  │  └────────┬─────────┘                                              │
  │           │ Every 3 minutes: git pull                              │
  │           ▼                                                        │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐                      │
  │  │  ARGO CD (running in argocd namespace)    │                      │
  │  │                                          │                      │
  │  │  ┌────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  │                      │
  │  │  │ repo-server    │  │ application-   │  │                      │
  │  │  │ (clones repos) │  │ controller     │  │                      │
  │  │  └───────┬────────┘  └───────┬────────┘  │                      │
  │  │          │                   │           │                      │
  │  │          ▼                   ▼           │                      │
  │  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────┐  │                      │
  │  │  │ COMPARE: desired (Git) vs actual   │  │                      │
  │  │  │ (cluster). Diff found → SYNC       │  │                      │
  │  │  └────────────────┬───────────────────┘  │                      │
  │  └───────────────────┼──────────────────────┘                      │
  │                      │                                            │
  │                      ▼                                            │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐                      │
  │  │  KUBERNETES CLUSTER (target)             │                      │
  │  │  Namespace: anihpj                       │                      │
  │  │  ├── Deployment: anihpj-web (3 replicas) │                      │
  │  │  ├── Service: anihpj-web (ClusterIP)     │                      │
  │  │  └── Ingress: anihpj-web (TLS)           │                      │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────┘                      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 The Argo CD Three-Way Diff Engine — How Sync Detects Drift

Argo CD doesn't blindly kubectl apply. It runs a three-way merge comparing: (1) Desired state from Git (cloned every 3 min), (2) Live state from the cluster (queried via K8s API), (3) Last-applied configuration (stored in kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation). This allows Argo CD to detect whether a change was made by Argo CD itself or by someone running kubectl edit manually. If selfHeal is enabled and someone manually changes replicas from 2 to 5, Argo CD sees: desired=2, live=5, last-applied=2 → manual change detected → revert to 2. The diff is visible in the Web UI and via argocd app diff anihpj-web.

Sync phases: PreSync hooks run BEFORE deployment (e.g., run database migrations). Sync applies manifests. PostSync hooks run AFTER (e.g., smoke tests). If PreSync fails, the entire sync is aborted. Sync waves (annotation: argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "2") control deployment order — lower numbers deploy first. All resources in Wave N must be healthy before Wave N+1 begins.

🔬 How Argo CD Stores State — Redis, Git, and the Internal Architecture

Argo CD doesn't just "read from Git." It maintains its own internal state using Redis for caching and performance, with Git as the source of truth for recovery:

Argo CD Internal State Management
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ ARGO CD COMPONENTS (running in argocd namespace)                │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐   │
  │  │ redis        │   │ repo-server  │   │ application-     │   │
  │  │ (cache)      │   │ (git clone)  │   │ controller       │   │
  │  │              │   │              │   │ (reconciliation) │   │
  │  │ Stores:      │   │ Stores:      │   │                  │   │
  │  │ • App cache  │   │ • Git clones │   │ • Compares       │   │
  │  │ • Manifest   │   │   (/tmp)     │   │   desired vs     │   │
  │  │   cache      │   │ • Helm charts│   │   actual         │   │
  │  │ • Cluster    │   │ • Kustomize  │   │ • Triggers sync  │   │
  │  │   info       │   │   output     │   │ • Updates status │   │
  │  └──────────────┘   └──────────────┘   └──────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  DATA FLOW:                                                     │
  │  1. User creates Application CR → controller detects it         │
  │  2. Controller tells repo-server: "clone this repo"            │
  │  3. Repo-server clones Git, generates manifests, caches in Redis│
  │  4. Controller reads cached manifests, queries cluster (Live)   │
  │  5. Controller diffs Desired vs Live → updates App status       │
  │  6. If OutOfSync + auto-sync enabled → applies changes          │
  │                                                                 │
  │  WHAT IF REDIS FAILS?                                           │
  │  • App status shows "Unknown" temporarily                       │
  │  • Repo-server re-clones Git repos (slower but functional)      │
  │  • Argo CD is DESIGNED to survive Redis loss                    │
  │  • Git is the ULTIMATE source of truth — Redis is just a cache  │
  │                                                                 │
  │  PRODUCTION TIP: Run Redis with persistence (AOF) in Argo CD.   │
  │  Without Redis persistence, cache rebuild takes 10-30x longer.  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

13.5 App of Apps Pattern — Scaling GitOps to 100+ Applications

The App of Apps pattern solves the bootstrap problem: how do you deploy Argo CD itself AND all your applications from Git? Answer: a root Application that points to a directory of child Application definitions.

App of Apps — Hierarchical Deployment Tree
  Root App (bootstrap)
  ├── Infrastructure Apps
  │   ├── cert-manager
  │   ├── ingress-nginx
  │   ├── external-dns
  │   └── prometheus-stack
  ├── Platform Apps
  │   ├── crossplane (infra provisioning)
  │   ├── kyverno (policy engine)
  │   └── velero (backup)
  └── Team Apps
      ├── anihpj-web
      ├── anihpj-api
      ├── anihpj-db
      └── anihpj-redis

  Deployment order via Sync Waves:
  Wave 0: cert-manager (required by everything with TLS)
  Wave 1: ingress-nginx, external-dns (networking foundation)
  Wave 2: Infrastructure apps (monitoring, backup)
  Wave 3: Platform apps (policies, crossplane)
  Wave 4: Team apps (anihpj-web, anihpj-api, anihpj-db)

13.6 ApplicationSets — Templated Apps for Multi-Cluster and Multi-Env

ApplicationSets automate the creation of multiple Argo CD Applications from a template. Instead of writing 12 separate Application YAMLs (4 apps × 3 environments), you write ONE template and a generator produces all 12.

Generator TypeHow It WorksExample
ListFixed list of values. Simplest.Cluster list: [dev, staging, prod]
GitScans directories in a Git repo. Each subdirectory = one app.apps/*/kustomization.yaml → one app per dir
ClusterAuto-discovers clusters registered with Argo CD.Every new cluster added → app auto-deployed
MatrixCombines two generators (e.g., apps × environments).[web,api,db] × [dev,staging,prod] = 9 apps
⚡ anihpj ApplicationSet — Deploy to 3 Environments with One YAML
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  generators:
  - list:
      elements:
      - env: dev
        cluster: dev-cluster
        namespace: anihpj-dev
      - env: staging
        cluster: staging-cluster
        namespace: anihpj-staging
      - env: production
        cluster: prod-cluster
        namespace: anihpj
  template:
    metadata:
      name: 'anihpj-{{env}}'
    spec:
      project: default
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/anihpj/anihpj-k8s
        path: 'overlays/{{env}}'
        targetRevision: main
      destination:
        server: '{{cluster}}'
        namespace: '{{namespace}}'
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true

13.7 Flux CD — The Alternative GitOps Operator

Flux CD is Argo CD's primary competitor in the GitOps space. Both are CNCF graduated projects. Flux takes a more modular, composable approach — you compose small CRDs together rather than one monolithic Application CRD.

ConceptArgo CDFlux CD
Core CRDApplication (one CRD does everything)GitRepository + Kustomization / HelmRelease (composable)
SourcerepoURL + path in Application specGitRepository CRD (separate resource)
Sync EngineBuilt into Application controllerKustomization or HelmRelease controllers
Multi-TenancyAppProjects (limit source repos, destinations)Namespace-based (each namespace can have its own Flux)
Web UI🟢 Rich dashboard with drift visualization🔴 Basic UI (Weave GitOps). CLI-focused.
Image Automation🟡 Argo CD Image Updater (separate tool)🟢 Built-in: ImageRepository + ImagePolicy + ImageUpdateAutomation
Best ForTeams wanting full-featured GitOps with UITeams wanting modular, programmable GitOps with GitOps Toolkit
⚡ Flux Example — Deploy anihpj with Kustomize
# Source: where to pull from
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: GitRepository
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 3m
  url: https://github.com/anihpj/anihpj-k8s
  ref:
    branch: main
---
# Kustomization: what to apply
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: anihpj
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 5m
  path: ./overlays/production
  prune: true
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: anihpj
🔬 Flux Image Automation — Auto-Update Images Without Manual Tag Bumps

One of Flux's standout features is built-in image automation. Instead of manually updating image tags in Git (which defeats the purpose of automation), Flux watches your container registry and auto-commits new tags:

Flux Image Automation Pipeline
  FULLY AUTOMATED FLOW (zero manual steps after CI):
  CI builds + pushes image → Flux detects new tag → Flux updates Git
  → Flux reconciles Kustomization → new pod with new image

  THREE CRDs WORKING TOGETHER:
  1. ImageRepository: "Watch ECR for new anihpj-web images every 5 min"
  2. ImagePolicy: "Only promote tags matching semver ~1.0.x, pick newest"
  3. ImageUpdateAutomation: "When new tag found, commit to Git and push"

  Flux YAML example:
  apiVersion: image.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1beta2
  kind: ImageRepository
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-web
  spec:
    image: 12345.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj-web
    interval: 5m
  ---
  apiVersion: image.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1beta2
  kind: ImagePolicy
  metadata:
    name: anihpj-web
  spec:
    imageRepositoryRef:
      name: anihpj-web
    policy:
      semver:
        range: ">=1.0.0"
  ---
  apiVersion: image.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1beta2
  kind: ImageUpdateAutomation
  metadata:
    name: anihpj
  spec:
    interval: 5m
    sourceRef:
      kind: GitRepository
      name: anihpj
    git:
      push:
        branch: main
    update:
      strategy: Setters

  This is what \"GitOps at scale\" looks like:
  CI builds → registry → Flux detects → Git updated → cluster synced.
  The ONLY manual step is merging the PR that changes application code.

13.8 Secrets in GitOps — Encrypt, Don't Expose

The #1 question about GitOps: "How do I store secrets in Git safely?" You don't store plaintext secrets. You encrypt them. Three main approaches:

ToolHow It WorksProsCons
Sealed SecretsEncrypts Secret → SealedSecret CRD. Only the controller in YOUR cluster can decrypt.K8s-native. No external dependency. Great for small/medium teams.Tied to a specific cluster. Rotating the encryption key is complex.
SOPSEncrypts YAML/JSON files with cloud KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault).Cloud-agnostic. File-level encryption. Integrates with Argo CD and Flux.Requires cloud KMS access. Key management is your responsibility.
External SecretsSyncs secrets FROM external stores (AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) INTO K8s Secrets.Single source of truth in cloud. Auto-rotation. Audit trail.Depends on cloud provider. Adds latency. More complex setup.
🔀 UTH: "Can't I Just Base64 Encode My Secrets?"

🖥️ Uncle: "Kubernetes Secrets are already base64-encoded. That's encryption, right? Just commit them to Git."

🧑‍💻 Tech Lead: "Base64 is ENCODING, not encryption. echo 'cGFzc3dvcmQ=' | base64 -d → password. Anyone with access to your Git repo can decode every secret in 1 second. NEVER commit plain Secrets to Git."

🧔‍♂️ Hiker: "Use External Secrets Operator for production. Secrets live in AWS Secrets Manager / Azure Key Vault. ESO syncs them into K8s. No secrets in Git. For simpler setups, Sealed Secrets work great — encrypt with the cluster's public key, only that cluster can decrypt."

13.9 Infrastructure GitOps — Crossplane and Terraform

GitOps isn't just for applications. You can apply the same principles to infrastructure — databases, message queues, object storage, load balancers. Two main approaches:

☁️
Crossplane

K8s-native. Define cloud resources as CRDs. An RDS database is just a YAML file. Git → Argo CD/Flux → Crossplane → AWS API. "Terraform, but running inside K8s, reconciled continuously."

🏗️
Terraform (via Flux TF-Controller)

Flux's TF-controller runs Terraform from Git. Commit a Terraform module → Flux detects it → runs terraform plan + apply. Existing Terraform investments preserved.

⚡ Crossplane Example — DatabaseClaim for anihpj
# Developer submits THIS. Platform handles the rest via GitOps.
apiVersion: platform.anihpj.io/v1alpha1
kind: DatabaseClaim
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
spec:
  engine: postgres
  version: "15"
  size: 20GB
  storageClass: fast-ssd
# Crossplane composition translates this → RDS instance via AWS API
# All managed through GitOps: commit → Argo CD → Crossplane → AWS

13.10 Multi-Cluster GitOps — Hub-and-Spoke Architecture

One Argo CD instance can manage multiple Kubernetes clusters. The pattern: a "hub" cluster runs Argo CD, and "spoke" clusters are registered as deployment targets. This is how enterprises manage 50+ clusters from a single Git repo.

Hub-and-Spoke GitOps Architecture
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  GIT REPOSITORY (single source of truth)                            │
  │  github.com/anihpj/platform-gitops                                  │
  │  ├── apps/                                                          │
  │  │   ├── anihpj-web.yaml    (targets: dev, staging, prod)          │
  │  │   └── anihpj-db.yaml     (targets: prod only)                   │
  │  └── infra/                                                         │
  │      ├── cert-manager.yaml  (targets: ALL clusters)                │
  │      └── monitoring.yaml    (targets: ALL clusters)                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                    │
                    │ Pulled by Argo CD (every 3 min)
                    ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  HUB CLUSTER (management cluster)                                   │
  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Argo CD (with cluster secrets for each spoke)                 │ │
  │  │  • dev-cluster     (kind, local)                               │ │
  │  │  • staging-cluster (kind, local)                               │ │
  │  │  • prod-cluster    (EKS, us-east-1)                            │ │
  │  │  • eu-cluster      (EKS, eu-west-1)                            │ │
  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
         │              │              │
         ▼              ▼              ▼
  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
  │ DEV      │  │ STAGING  │  │ PRODUCTION    │
  │ CLUSTER  │  │ CLUSTER  │  │ CLUSTER       │
  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────────┘

  Benefits:
  ✅ Single control plane for all clusters
  ✅ Same Git repo deploys to all environments
  ✅ Cluster credentials stay in hub cluster (not in CI)
  ✅ Add a new cluster = register it in Argo CD + add destinations
🔬 How Argo CD Sync Actually Works — The Three-Way Diff Engine

When Argo CD "syncs," it runs a three-way diff: (1) DESIRED state from Git, (2) LIVE state from the cluster, (3) LAST APPLIED configuration from annotations. This lets it distinguish manual changes from Argo CD's own changes. If selfHeal is enabled and a kubectl edit manually changes replicas from 2 to 5, Argo CD detects the drift (DESIRED ≠ LIVE) and reverts to 2. The diff is displayed visually in the Web UI and via argocd app diff anihpj-web.

Sync phases: PreSync (run hooks before deploy) → Sync (apply manifests) → PostSync (run hooks after deploy). If PreSync fails, Sync is skipped — preventing broken deploys. Sync waves (annotations: argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave: "2") control deployment order: lower numbers deploy first. All resources in Wave N must be healthy before Wave N+1 begins. Use negative waves for infrastructure (cert-manager: -1), positive for applications.

🔬 GitOps Disaster Recovery — Rebuilding Everything from Git

Scenario: Your production EKS cluster is completely gone. All nodes, all data, all configs. Here's the recovery using only your Git repos:

  1. Provision new cluster: eksctl create cluster or Terraform apply. 15-20 minutes.
  2. Install Argo CD: kubectl apply -k argocd/ from your bootstrap repo. 2 minutes.
  3. Apply the root Application: Points to your platform-gitops repo. Argo CD discovers all child apps.
  4. Argo CD syncs all apps: cert-manager → ingress → monitoring → anihpj (DB, API, Web). ~5 minutes.
  5. Restore data from Velero: velero restore create --from-backup latest. PVCs recreated from snapshots.
  6. DNS update: Point DNS to new LoadBalancer. Traffic flows.

Total RTO: ~30 minutes. The key insight: Git holds your ENTIRE platform definition. The cluster is disposable — Git is the only thing you can't lose. This is why GitOps is not just a deployment strategy — it's a DR strategy.

🔬 Helm vs Kustomize in GitOps — Which Should You Use?

Both Argo CD and Flux support Helm and Kustomize. The choice depends on your use case:

AspectHelmKustomize
What it doesTemplates YAML with Go templates. Package and distribute charts.Patches base YAML. Overlays for per-environment variation.
GitOps modelvalues.yaml in Git, chart from repo or OCI registryBase + overlays in Git. kubectl built-in (no binary needed).
Best forPackaging and distributing apps. Third-party software (Prometheus, cert-manager).Your OWN applications. Environment-specific customization. Simple YAML patching.
Argo CD support✅ Native. Renders chart + values → plain YAML → applies.✅ Native. Runs kustomize build → applies.
Secret management❌ Helm values have secrets. Use External Secrets or SOPS alongside.❌ Same issue. Use Sealed Secrets or External Secrets.

Pattern: Use Helm for infrastructure (cert-manager, ingress-nginx, prometheus) — these are packaged as charts. Use Kustomize for your own applications (anihpj-web, anihpj-api) — simple patching across dev/staging/prod. Both work flawlessly with Argo CD and Flux.

🔬 Why Pull-Based GitOps Is More Secure — Attack Surface Comparison

The fundamental security advantage of GitOps: cluster credentials never leave the cluster.

Security Comparison — Push vs Pull Attack Surface
  PUSH-BASED (Traditional CI/CD)                 PULL-BASED (GitOps)
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ CI SYSTEM                     │              │ CI SYSTEM                     │
  │                               │              │                               │
  │ Attack surface:               │              │ Attack surface:               │
  │ ✅ Source code (GitHub)       │              │ ✅ Source code (GitHub)       │
  │ ✅ CI config (pipeline YAML)  │              │ ✅ CI config (pipeline YAML)  │
  │ 🔴 K8s CLUSTER CREDENTIALS   │              │ ❌ NO cluster credentials!     │
  │ 🔴 Container registry push   │              │ ✅ Container registry push     │
  │ 🔴 Could kubectl delete all   │              │ ❌ CANNOT touch cluster        │
  └──────────────────────────────┘              └──────────────────────────────┘
              │                                              │
              │ kubectl apply (push)                         │ Only pushes images
              ▼                                              ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ KUBERNETES CLUSTER            │              │ KUBERNETES CLUSTER            │
  │ (passive receiver)            │              │ (active puller)               │
  │                               │              │                               │
  │ Attack surface:               │              │ Attack surface:               │
  │ 🔴 API server exposed to CI   │              │ ✅ API server (normal)        │
  │ 🔴 CI compromise = cluster    │              │ ✅ Argo CD (only tool with    │
  │    compromise                  │              │    cluster access)            │
  └──────────────────────────────┘              │ ✅ Git credentials (read-only) │
                                                 └──────────────────────────────┘
  GITOPS ADVANTAGE:                              GITOPS RISK:
  • CI never has cluster access                  • Argo CD itself must be secured
  • Cluster pulls — no inbound firewall holes    • Git repo becomes critical infra
  • Git history = complete audit trail           • Compromised Git = compromised cluster
  • Revoke Git access = stop deployments         • Protect Git with: branch protection,
  • No credentials in CI environment variables     required reviews, signed commits
🧭 GitOps Maturity Model — From Manual to Fully Automated

Where does your platform fall on the GitOps maturity spectrum?

LevelDescriptionToolsCNPE Expectation
L0: ManualSSH into servers, run scripts. No version control for infra.bash, SSH❌ Not acceptable
L1: Scriptedkubectl apply from CI. Git has YAML, but CI pushes.GitHub Actions, Jenkins❌ Not GitOps
L2: GitOps (Basic)Argo CD/Flux pulls from Git. Auto-sync enabled. Drift detection.Argo CD, Flux✅ CNPE minimum
L3: GitOps (Advanced)App of Apps, ApplicationSets, sync waves, secrets via External Secrets, multi-cluster hub-and-spoke.Argo CD + ESO + Crossplane✅ CNPE target
L4: GitOps (Elite)Progressive delivery (Argo Rollouts), image auto-update, rendered-branch pattern, signed commits, fully automated rollbacks.Argo CD + Rollouts + Cosign🚀 Beyond CNPE
🏷️ Argo CD Application Health — Understanding the Statuses
🟢
Synced + Healthy

Desired = Actual. All pods running. No drift. This is the target state for every Application.

🟡
Synced + Degraded

Manifests match Git, but pods are crashing. App is deployed correctly but broken. Fix the code, not the config.

🟠
OutOfSync

Cluster state differs from Git. Someone manually changed something, or a new commit wasn't synced yet. Argo CD will fix it (if auto-sync).

🔴
Unknown

Argo CD can't determine status. Cluster unreachable? API server down? Network issue? Check connectivity.

⏱️ Target: 15 minutes
Drill 13.1 — Install Argo CD and Deploy an Application
  1. Install Argo CD on a kind cluster: kubectl create namespace argocd && kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml
  2. Port-forward to the UI: kubectl port-forward -n argocd svc/argocd-server 8080:443
  3. Create a test Application pointing to a public Git repo (e.g., nginx demo)
  4. Observe the Application progress through: OutOfSync → Synced → Healthy
  5. Edit the Deployment manually and watch Argo CD revert it back
💡 Hint: Use argocd admin initial-password -n argocd to get the admin password. The default Application YAML for a public nginx demo is available in the Argo CD docs.
⏱️ Target: 12 minutes
Drill 13.2 — Set Up an ApplicationSet for Multi-Environment Deployment
  1. Create a Git repo with directories: overlays/dev/, overlays/staging/, overlays/production/
  2. Each directory contains a kustomization.yaml referencing base resources and env-specific patches
  3. Create an ApplicationSet with a List generator for the 3 environments
  4. Verify Argo CD creates 3 Applications (one per environment)
  5. Verify each Application deploys to the correct namespace
💡 Hint: Use argocd appset list to see all ApplicationSets. Each ApplicationSet generates Applications named app-name-env based on your template.
📝 View Solution 
# Directory structure in Git:

# overlays/staging/kustomization.yaml (namespace: anihpj-staging, replicas: 2)
# overlays/production/kustomization.yaml (namespace: anihpj, replicas: 3)

🎓 CNPE Exam Focus — GitOps (Domain 2 — 25%)

This is the HIGHEST weighted domain on the CNPE exam. Expect tasks like: "Create an Argo CD Application that deploys from Git," "Configure an ApplicationSet for multi-environment deployment," "Debug why an Application is OutOfSync," or "Set up a GitOps workflow for infrastructure." The exam tests your ability to think in GitOps terms: everything is declarative, versioned, pull-based, and continuously reconciled. Never push from CI. Always pull from Git.

🎯 GitOps Decision Framework — Choosing Your Toolchain
  1. Argo CD if you want: rich web UI, visual drift detection, App of Apps pattern, large community.
  2. Flux CD if you want: modular components, built-in image automation, GitOps Toolkit flexibility.
  3. External Secrets Operator for production secrets — sync from AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault. Never in Git.
  4. Crossplane for infrastructure GitOps — manage cloud resources as K8s CRDs. Declarative infra.
  5. Hub-and-Spoke for multi-cluster — one Argo CD instance manages many clusters from one Git repo.
⚠️ The "CI Pushes to Cluster" Anti-Pattern — Why It Costs Points on CNPE

The CNPE exam explicitly tests whether you understand the difference between push-based CI/CD and pull-based GitOps. If a task says "set up deployment from Git," do NOT write a CI pipeline that runs kubectl apply. Create an Argo CD Application or Flux GitRepository+Kustomization. CI builds and pushes images to a registry. Argo CD/Flux pulls the desired state from Git and syncs to the cluster. CI never touches the cluster.

Q: What are the 4 GitOps principles?

▶ Show Answer
1. Declarative: Everything described as code (YAML). 2. Versioned: Desired state in Git, immutable history. 3. Pull-Based: Agent pulls from Git (not CI pushes to cluster). 4. Continuously Reconciled: Agent monitors and auto-corrects drift. These ensure deployments are auditable, reproducible, and self-healing.
Q: What's the difference between an Argo CD Application and ApplicationSet?

▶ Show Answer
Application: Defines ONE deployment (source repo + path + destination cluster/namespace). ApplicationSet: A TEMPLATE that generates multiple Applications from a generator (list, git, cluster, matrix). Use ApplicationSet when you need the same app deployed to multiple environments or clusters. One ApplicationSet can replace dozens of individual Application YAMLs.
🚀 Beyond CNPE — Advanced GitOps Patterns
  • Progressive Delivery with Argo Rollouts: Extend Argo CD with canary and blue/green deployments. AnalysisRuns query Prometheus during rollout — auto-promote or auto-rollback based on real metrics.
  • GitOps for Edge Computing: Deploy to hundreds of edge clusters using the same GitOps principles. Flux is particularly well-suited for edge due to its lightweight footprint.
  • Rendered-Branch Pattern: A CI pipeline renders Helm charts/Kustomize into plain YAML and commits to a separate "deploy" branch. Argo CD watches the deploy branch. Separates "source of config" from "source of rendered manifests."
  • Notary/Co-Signing for GitOps: Sign Git commits and container images with Cosign/Sigstore. Argo CD verifies signatures before deploying. Ensures only trusted changes reach production.

📖 Chapter 13 Summary: GitOps makes deployments auditable, reproducible, and self-healing. Git is the single source of truth. Argo CD is the de facto standard — it pulls from Git, compares desired vs actual, and auto-fixes drift. The App of Apps pattern scales to hundreds of applications. ApplicationSets template apps across environments. Secrets are encrypted (Sealed Secrets, SOPS, External Secrets) — never in plaintext. Infrastructure GitOps with Crossplane brings the same principles to cloud resources. Hub-and-spoke architecture manages multiple clusters from a single control plane. CNPE Domain 2 (25%) tests GitOps extensively — master this chapter.

14.1 CI vs CD vs Continuous Deployment — Know the Difference

These three terms are often confused. The CNPE exam expects you to use them precisely:

🔨
CI (Continuous Integration)

Automatically build and test code on every push. Goal: catch integration issues early, merge frequently. CI is about FEEDBACK. Every commit triggers: lint → test → build. Failures block the PR.

🚀
CD (Continuous Delivery)

Every change that passes CI is automatically deployed to a staging environment. Production deployment is a manual decision. The code is ALWAYS ready to deploy — someone just needs to press the button.

⚡
Continuous Deployment

Every change that passes CI/CD goes straight to production. No human intervention. Requires extreme confidence in testing and rollback. Netflix, Amazon do this — most companies don't.

📋
CNPE Exam Tip

The exam uses "CD" to mean Continuous Delivery (manual prod deploy). If a question says "automate deployment to production," that's Continuous Deployment. Know the difference.

CIBuild + Test
→
CDAuto-deploy to Staging
→
🔘Manual Approval
→
🚀Deploy to Production

14.2 Pipeline Stages — Lint → Test → Build → Scan → Push → Deploy

A well-designed CI/CD pipeline has distinct stages, each with a specific purpose. Skipping stages creates risk. Here's the standard cloud-native pipeline:

Standard CI/CD Pipeline — 6 Stages
  GIT PUSH
     │
     ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STAGE 1: LINT          ⏱️ ~30s                                      │
  │ Tools: flake8 (Python), ESLint (JS), hadolint (Dockerfile)          │
  │ Purpose: Catch style issues, obvious bugs, anti-patterns.           │
  │ Failure: BLOCK the pipeline. Fix is usually trivial.                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │
     ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STAGE 2: TEST          ⏱️ ~2-5 min                                  │
  │ Tools: pytest, Jest, JUnit. Unit tests + integration tests.         │
  │ Purpose: Verify code BEHAVES correctly. Catch regressions.          │
  │ Strategy: Run fast tests first. Parallelize by test suite.          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │
     ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STAGE 3: BUILD         ⏱️ ~2 min                                    │
  │ Tools: docker build, Kaniko, Buildpacks                             │
  │ Purpose: Create immutable container image. Multi-stage for size.    │
  │ Output: Docker image tagged with git SHA.                           │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │
     ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STAGE 4: SCAN          ⏱️ ~1 min                                    │
  │ Tools: Trivy, Grype, Snyk. Check OS packages + app dependencies.   │
  │ Purpose: Find known CVEs. BLOCK on CRITICAL. Warn on HIGH.         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │
     ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STAGE 5: PUSH          ⏱️ ~30s                                      │
  │ Tools: docker push, skopeo, crane                                   │
  │ Purpose: Upload scanned image to registry (ECR, Harbor, GHCR).     │
  │ After push: Cosign sign the image. Attach SBOM.                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
     │
     ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ STAGE 6: DEPLOY        ⏱️ ~1-5 min (Argo CD sync)                  │
  │ Tools: Argo CD (GitOps), Flux                                       │
  │ Purpose: Update desired state in Git. Argo CD syncs to cluster.    │
  │ Strategy: Auto-deploy to dev/staging. Manual approval for prod.    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

14.3 GitHub Actions — The Most Popular CI Platform

GitHub Actions is the dominant CI platform for cloud-native projects. It's deeply integrated with GitHub, has a massive marketplace of actions, and supports matrix builds for testing across multiple environments.

⚡ anihpj GitHub Actions Workflow — Complete CI Pipeline
# .github/workflows/ci.yaml
name: CI Pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
      with: {python-version: '3.12'}
    - run: pip install flake8
    - run: flake8 . --count --max-complexity=10 --statistics

  test:
    needs: lint
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        python-version: ['3.11', '3.12']  # Test on multiple versions
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
      with: {python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}}
    - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
    - run: pytest --cov=jobpost --cov-report=xml

  build-and-push:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
      with:
        role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456:role/github-actions
        aws-region: us-east-1
    - uses: aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2
    - run: |
        docker build -t $ECR_REGISTRY/anihpj:${{ github.sha }} .
        docker push $ECR_REGISTRY/anihpj:${{ github.sha }}
📊
Matrix Builds

Test against multiple Python versions (3.11, 3.12), OS versions, or dependency versions simultaneously. Catch compatibility issues before they hit production.

🔄
Reusable Workflows

Define CI once, reuse across 50 repos. Update the shared workflow and all repos get the fix. No copy-paste drift across teams.

14.4 GitLab CI — Integrated DevOps Platform

GitLab CI is GitHub Actions' primary competitor, especially in enterprise environments. It uses .gitlab-ci.yml with stages, jobs, and artifacts.

FeatureGitHub ActionsGitLab CI
Config File.github/workflows/*.yml.gitlab-ci.yml (single file, multi-stage)
Runner ModelGitHub-hosted or self-hosted runnersGitLab-hosted or self-hosted runners (more flexible)
ArtifactsUpload/download between jobsBuilt-in artifact system (pass files between stages)
EnvironmentsDeployment environments with protection rulesBuilt-in environment tracking with rollback
Container RegistryGHCR (GitHub Container Registry)Built-in per-project container registry
Best ForOpen source, GitHub-native teamsEnterprise, self-hosted, compliance-heavy orgs

14.5 Tekton — Kubernetes-Native CI/CD

Tekton is a K8s-native CI/CD framework. Unlike GitHub Actions (SaaS) or GitLab CI (runs on VMs), Tekton runs inside your Kubernetes cluster as pods. Every pipeline step is a container.

📦
Task

A single step: "run pytest," "build Docker image." Defined as a CRD. Reusable across pipelines. Each step runs in its OWN container.

🔗
Pipeline

A sequence of Tasks: lint → test → build → deploy. Defined as a CRD. Can pass data between tasks via workspaces (PVCs).

🔔
Trigger

Event listener that kicks off a Pipeline when code is pushed. Webhook from GitHub/GitLab → Trigger → PipelineRun.

☸️
K8s-Native Advantage

Pipelines run as pods. Scaling = K8s scaling. Logs = kubectl logs. Secrets = K8s Secrets. No external CI server to manage.

🔬 Tekton Pipeline YAML — A Complete Example

Tekton pipelines pass data between tasks using workspaces (shared volumes) and results (small string outputs). Here's a complete anihpj CI pipeline in Tekton:

⚡ anihpj Tekton Pipeline — Clone → Test → Build → Push
# Task: Clone Git repo
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
kind: Task
metadata:
  name: git-clone
spec:
  workspaces:
  - name: source
  params:
  - name: url
  steps:
  - name: clone
    image: alpine/git
    script: |
      git clone $(params.url) $(workspaces.source.path)/src
---
# Task: Run tests
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
kind: Task
metadata:
  name: pytest
spec:
  workspaces:
  - name: source
  steps:
  - name: test
    image: python:3.12
    script: |
      cd $(workspaces.source.path)/src
      pip install -r requirements.txt
      pytest --junitxml=/results/test-results.xml
---
# Pipeline: Assembles tasks
apiVersion: tekton.dev/v1
kind: Pipeline
metadata:
  name: anihpj-ci
spec:
  workspaces:
  - name: shared-workspace
  tasks:
  - name: clone
    taskRef:
      name: git-clone
    workspaces:
    - name: source
      workspace: shared-workspace
  - name: test
    taskRef:
      name: pytest
    runAfter: [clone]
    workspaces:
    - name: source
      workspace: shared-workspace
  - name: build-and-push
    taskRef:
      name: kaniko
    runAfter: [test]
    workspaces:
    - name: source
      workspace: shared-workspace

# Key insight: All tasks share the SAME PVC (shared-workspace).
# Clone writes code → Test reads and runs → Build reads and builds.
# Results stored at: /tekton/results/ (automatic volume mount).

14.6 Argo Workflows — DAG-Based Workflow Engine

Argo Workflows is a K8s-native workflow engine for complex, multi-step pipelines. Unlike linear CI pipelines, Argo Workflows supports DAGs (Directed Acyclic Graphs) — steps can run in parallel, branch, and merge.

Argo Workflows — DAG vs Step-Based
  LINEAR PIPELINE (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI)    DAG PIPELINE (Argo Workflows)
  ┌──────┐                                       ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Lint │                                       │        Lint          │
  └──┬───┘                                       └──────────┬───────────┘
     │                                                       │
     ▼                                          ┌────────────┼────────────┐
  ┌──────┐                                      │            │            │
  │ Test │                                      ▼            ▼            ▼
  └──┬───┘                                 ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐ ┌─────────┐
     │                                      │Test Py3 │ │Test Py3 │ │  Lint   │
     ▼                                      │   .11   │ │   .12   │ │ Docker  │
  ┌──────┐                                  └────┬────┘ └────┬────┘ └────┬────┘
  │Build │                                       │           │           │
  └──┬───┘                                       └───────────┼───────────┘
     │                                                       │
     ▼                                                       ▼
  ┌──────┐                                             ┌──────────┐
  │ Push │                                             │  Build    │
  └──────┘                                             └────┬─────┘
                                                            │
  Argo Workflows excels at:                                ▼
  • ML pipelines (data prep → train → evaluate)       ┌──────────┐
  • ETL jobs (extract → transform → load)             │  Deploy  │
  • Multi-cloud deployments (deploy to 3 clouds)      └──────────┘

14.7 Image Building — Kaniko, Buildah, Buildpacks, DinD

Building container images inside CI pipelines requires careful tool choice. The wrong choice creates security vulnerabilities or slow builds:

ToolHow It WorksSecuritySpeedBest For
KanikoBuilds images without Docker daemon. Works in unprivileged containers.🟢 Excellent — no privileged mode needed🟡 GoodStandard CI pipelines. Default choice.
BuildahDaemonless. Builds OCI images without Docker. Rootless mode available.🟢 Excellent — rootless builds possible🟡 GoodSecurity-conscious orgs. OpenShift environments.
BuildpacksAuto-detects language/framework. No Dockerfile needed. Heroku-compatible.🟢 Good🟢 Fast (cached layers)Standard apps (Python, Node, Java). No Dockerfile expertise needed.
DinDDocker-in-Docker. Runs Docker daemon inside CI container.🔴 Poor — requires privileged mode🟡 GoodLegacy. NOT recommended. Use Kaniko instead.
⚠️ Why DinD Is Dangerous — And Why CNPE Tests This

Docker-in-Docker requires --privileged mode, which gives the container access to ALL host devices. A compromised CI pipeline with DinD can escape the container and compromise the CI server. The CNPE exam expects you to know: use Kaniko or Buildpacks for CI image building — never DinD in production pipelines.

🔬 Buildpacks Deep Dive — Auto-Detect Language, No Dockerfile

Cloud Native Buildpacks (CNB) automatically detect your app's language and build an OCI image — no Dockerfile needed. This is how Heroku and Google Cloud Run build apps:

Buildpacks — Auto-Detection and Layered Builds
  pack build anihpj-web --builder heroku/builder:22

  1. DETECT: Scans code → finds requirements.txt → Python. Finds manage.py → Django.
  2. BUILD:  Layer 1 (Python runtime, cached) → Layer 2 (pip deps, cached) → Layer 3 (app source)
  3. EXPORT: OCI image pushed to registry. SBOM auto-attached (CycloneDX/SPDX).

  KEY ADVANTAGE: Auto-rebasing. When Python gets a security patch:
  pack rebase anihpj-web  →  Updates base layer ONLY. App code unchanged.
  No rebuild. No Dockerfile edit. 30 seconds instead of 5 minutes.

14.8 Image Tagging — Git SHA, SemVer, and NEVER :latest

How you tag container images determines traceability, reproducibility, and security. Here's the definitive guide:

StrategyExampleImmutabilityTraceabilityUse Case
Git SHAanihpj:a1b2c3d🟢 Immutable (unique per commit)🟢 Traces to exact commitCI builds. Every build gets a unique tag.
SemVeranihpj:1.2.3🟡 Mutable (can be retagged)🟡 Traces to release (not commit)Human-readable releases. Tag AFTER testing.
:latestanihpj:latest🔴 Highly mutable❌ No traceabilityNEVER in production. Dev only.
⚡ anihpj Tagging Strategy — Git SHA + SemVer
# CI builds: tag with git SHA (immutable, traceable)
docker build -t 123456.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:${GITHUB_SHA} .

# After staging tests pass: add SemVer tag (human-readable)
docker tag 123456.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:${GITHUB_SHA} \
           123456.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.2.3
docker push 123456.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj:v1.2.3

# NEVER tag with :latest in CI
# :latest breaks rollback — you can't know which commit it points to

14.9 Artifact Promotion — Dev → Staging → Production

Artifact promotion ensures the EXACT image that passed tests is the image deployed to production. You don't rebuild — you promote the existing image through a trust chain:

Artifact Promotion Pipeline — The Trust Chain
  DEV                    STAGING                   PRODUCTION
  ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────┐         ┌──────────────┐
  │ ECR: dev      │      │ ECR: staging  │         │ ECR: prod     │
  │              │      │              │         │              │
  │ anihpj:abc123│─────▶│ anihpj:abc123│────────▶│ anihpj:abc123│
  │              │ copy │              │  copy   │              │
  │ [scan pass]  │      │ [smoke tests]│         │ [prod deploy]│
  └──────────────┘      └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘

  EACH PROMOTION ADDS ATTESTATION:
  • Dev:       Image built + scanned (Trivy). 0 CRITICAL CVEs.
  • Staging:   Smoke tests passed. Integration tests green.
  • Production: Manual approval granted. Compliance check passed.

  THE GOLDEN RULE:
  The image digest (sha256:abc...) is the SAME across all registries.
  You're not rebuilding — you're COPYING + ADDING METADATA.
  This guarantees: "What ran in staging is EXACTLY what runs in production."

14.10 Pipeline Security — SAST, DAST, Secret Scanning, Dependency Checks

Your CI/CD pipeline is a prime attack target. If an attacker compromises your pipeline, they can inject malicious code into production. Defense in depth:

Security CheckWhat It DoesToolWhen to Run
SASTStatic analysis of source code. Finds bugs, security flaws BEFORE runtime.Bandit (Python), SonarQube, SemgrepLint stage (early)
DASTDynamic testing of RUNNING application. Finds runtime vulnerabilities.OWASP ZAP, Burp SuiteStaging (before prod)
Secret ScanningDetects accidentally committed credentials, API keys, tokens.GitHub Secret Scanning, GitGuardian, truffleHogPre-commit + CI
Dependency ScanChecks known CVEs in pip/npm/maven dependencies.Dependabot, Snyk, pip-auditEvery CI run
Container ScanScans OS packages + app deps in the built image.Trivy, Grype, ClairAfter build
🎯 Pipeline Security Strategy — What to Block vs Warn
  • BLOCK on: CRITICAL CVEs, leaked secrets (revoke immediately), SAST high-confidence findings
  • WARN on: HIGH CVEs (review, may have mitigating controls), deprecated dependencies
  • IGNORE (with justification): CVEs in dev dependencies, CVEs with no known exploit, false positives

Putting it all together — the complete anihpj CI/CD pipeline from code commit to production deployment:

anihpj Complete CI/CD Pipeline
  DEVELOPER
  git push
     │

  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

🔬 Monorepo CI Strategy — How to Build Only Changed Services

In a monorepo with 10+ microservices, rebuilding everything on every push wastes time and money. The solution: path-based filtering.

Monorepo CI — Path-Based Triggering
  GitHub Actions path filtering:
  on:
    push:
      paths:
      - 'services/web/**'       → Only trigger web CI
      - 'services/api/**'       → Only trigger api CI
      - 'shared/lib/**'         → Trigger ALL (shared code changed)

  OR use tools like Nx/Turborepo:
  nx affected:test --base=main~1   → Only test changed services
  nx affected:build --base=main~1  → Only build changed services
  nx affected:docker --base=main~1 → Only build Docker images for changed

  RESULT: PR changes services/web/ only → 1 build instead of 10.
  Pipeline time: 22 min → 3 min. Cost: $0.50 → $0.05 per commit.
🔬 How Kaniko Works Without Docker — User-Space Image Building

Kaniko doesn't need a Docker daemon because it reimplements Dockerfile commands in userspace. It parses the Dockerfile, downloads base images, extracts filesystems, and creates new layers — all without talking to /var/run/docker.sock. This means: (1) No privileged mode needed. (2) Runs in any Kubernetes pod. (3) Each layer is cached in the container registry itself (not on the CI runner). Kaniko pushes each layer as it's built, so if a build fails at step 8/10, steps 1-7 are already cached in the registry. Next build reuses them — significantly faster than Docker builds in ephemeral CI environments.

⏱️ Target: 12 minutes
Drill 14.1 — Build a Complete CI Pipeline with GitHub Actions
  1. Create a .github/workflows/ci.yaml with stages: lint → test → build → push
  2. Add matrix testing for 2 Python versions
  3. Add Trivy vulnerability scanning after build
  4. Configure the pipeline to only run on PRs to main
  5. Test: push a PR and verify all stages run successfully
💡 Hint: Use aws-actions/amazon-ecr-login@v2 for ECR authentication. Use aquasecurity/trivy-action@master for scanning.
⏱️ Target: 10 minutes
Drill 14.2 — Set Up Multi-Stage Artifact Promotion
  1. Create two ECR repositories: anihpj-staging and anihpj-prod
  2. Write a promotion script that copies an image by digest from staging to prod
  3. Verify the image digest is identical in both registries
  4. Add a manual approval step before production promotion
💡 Hint: Use docker pull + docker tag + docker push, or crane copy for direct registry-to-registry copy. Verify with docker inspect --format='{{.RepoDigests}}'.
🔬 Database Migrations in CI/CD — The Hardest Part of Deployment

Running python manage.py migrate in CI/CD is dangerous. Here's why and how to do it safely:

ApproachRiskWhen to Use
PreSync Hook (Argo CD)Migration runs BEFORE new pods. If migration fails, old pods keep running (safe).Additive migrations (new tables/columns). Safest default.
Job (K8s Job)Migration runs as a separate Job. Must complete before Deployment updates.Complex migrations. Can be monitored and retried independently.
CI Pipeline (direct)🔴 Migration runs during CI. If it fails mid-way, you have a half-migrated DB.NEVER for production. Dev environments only.

Golden rules: (1) Migrations must be BACKWARD-COMPATIBLE — old code must work with new schema. (2) Add columns before removing old ones (expand-contract pattern). (3) Never run migrations automatically in production CI — use Argo CD PreSync hooks or K8s Jobs. (4) Always test migrations on a staging database (identical to production) before production.

📊 CI/CD Metrics — How to Measure Pipeline Performance

You can't improve what you don't measure. Track these 4 metrics for your CI/CD pipeline:

⏱️
Pipeline Duration

Time from git push to deployable artifact. Target: <10 min. Track P50 (median) and P95 (worst-case). Optimize the slowest stage.

✅
Success Rate

% of pipeline runs that succeed. Target: >95%. Flaky tests destroy trust. Fix or quarantine flaky tests immediately.

🔄
Mean Time to Recovery (MTTR)

Time from pipeline failure to fix deployed. Target: <30 min. Fast rollback + good monitoring = fast MTTR.

📈
Deployment Frequency

Deploys per day. Elite: multiple per day. High: 1/day. Medium: 1/week. Low: 1/month. Track trend, not absolute.

🎯 Pipeline Optimization — How to Cut CI Time by 60%

The most common CI complaint: "Our pipeline takes 20+ minutes." Here's how to fix it:

⚡
Parallelize Independent Stages

Lint, unit tests, integration tests run SIMULTANEOUSLY. Matrix builds test multiple Python versions in parallel. Time: 12→3 min.

💾
Cache Dependencies

Cache ~/.cache/pip. Docker layer caching via registry. Time: 5→0.5 min for dep install.

📦
Skip Unnecessary Work

Path filtering: only build changed services. Docs-only PR? Skip entire build. Time: 15→0 min.

🔗
Merge Sequential Steps

Combine build+push in one job. Multi-stage Docker builds minimize final image. Time: 8→2 min.

🎓 CNPE Exam Focus — CI/CD Pipeline Design (Domain 2 — 25%)

CI/CD is a core component of Domain 2 (GitOps & CD). Expect tasks like: "Write a CI pipeline that builds, scans, and pushes an image," or "Configure artifact promotion between registries." The exam tests your ability to DESIGN pipelines, not just copy-paste YAML. Know: (1) The standard stages and their order. (2) Why Kaniko over DinD. (3) Git SHA vs SemVer tagging. (4) How to prevent secret leaks. (5) The relationship between CI (builds images) and GitOps (deploys them).

⚠️ The "CI Deploys to Production" Anti-Pattern

Many candidates confuse CI with CD. CI builds and tests. It does NOT deploy. Deployment is handled by GitOps (Argo CD/Flux). The CI pipeline pushes images to a registry. The GitOps operator pulls the desired state from Git and syncs to the cluster. If your CI pipeline has kubectl apply or helm upgrade in it, you're doing it wrong for the CNPE exam. CI builds. GitOps deploys. Never the other way around.

Q: What's the difference between CI, CD, and Continuous Deployment?

▶ Show Answer
CI: Automatically build + test on every push. CD (Continuous Delivery): Auto-deploy to staging. Manual approval for production. Continuous Deployment: Auto-deploy to production with NO manual step. Most orgs use CI + CD. Elite orgs (Netflix, Amazon) use Continuous Deployment.
Q: Why is Kaniko preferred over Docker-in-Docker for CI pipelines?

▶ Show Answer
Security: Kaniko runs without privileged mode — no access to host Docker daemon. Architecture: Kaniko builds images in userspace by emulating Dockerfile commands, no daemon needed. DinD requires --privileged, giving the CI container root access to the host. A compromised DinD pipeline = compromised CI server. Kaniko eliminates this attack vector entirely.

📖 Chapter 14 Summary: A well-designed CI/CD pipeline is fast, secure, and reliable. Lint → Test → Build → Scan → Push → Deploy. Use GitHub Actions or GitLab CI for standard pipelines. Use Tekton or Argo Workflows for K8s-native, complex DAG workflows. Build images with Kaniko (never DinD). Tag with Git SHA for immutability. Promote artifacts — never rebuild between environments. Scan everything: SAST for code, Trivy for images, secret scanning for leaks. The pipeline is the GATE between code and production. A weak gate means weak production.
