15.1 Helm Charts — The Package Manager for Kubernetes

🧠 What Is Helm? Helm is to Kubernetes what apt is to Debian or brew is to macOS — a package manager. A Chart is a Helm package: a collection of templated YAML files that describe a related set of Kubernetes resources. Instead of writing 10 separate YAML files by hand, you write ONE chart and parameterize it with values.yaml.

❌ Before Helm — The "kubectl apply -f *.yaml" Hell

Imagine deploying anihpj to 3 environments (dev, staging, prod) with raw kubectl:

  • 🔴 12 YAML files per environment (deployment, service, ingress, configmap, secret, pdb, hpa, serviceaccount, networkpolicy, certificate, servicemonitor, namespace). 3 envs × 12 = 36 files.
  • 🔴 Copy-paste drift: Dev changes replicas from 2 to 3. Did staging get the same change? Prod? Nobody knows.
  • 🔴 No versioning: Which version of anihpj is running in staging? Check the image tag in 3 different YAML files.
  • 🔴 No rollback: Deployment broke? Hope you saved the old YAML files somewhere.
  • 🔴 No reuse: Your anihpj deployment pattern can't be shared with another team's project.

Helm solves ALL of these: One chart → parameterize with values → version with SemVer → rollback with helm rollback → share via OCI registry.

🔬 Helm 3 Architecture — No More Tiller

Helm 2 (deprecated) used a server-side component called Tiller that ran inside the cluster with cluster-admin privileges — a massive security risk. Helm 3 (current) removed Tiller entirely. The helm CLI now talks directly to the Kubernetes API using your kubeconfig, just like kubectl. Release state is stored as Kubernetes Secrets (or ConfigMaps) in the release namespace. No server-side component = no extra attack surface. This is why Helm 3 is considered production-safe.

Helm Chart Anatomy — What's Inside a Chart
  mychart/
  ├── Chart.yaml          ← Metadata: name, version, appVersion, description
  ├── values.yaml         ← DEFAULT configuration values (overridable)
  ├── charts/             ← Sub-charts (dependencies)
  │   └── postgresql-12.1.6.tgz
  ├── templates/          ← K8s YAML templates (Go template syntax)
  │   ├── deployment.yaml
  │   ├── service.yaml
  │   ├── ingress.yaml
  │   ├── configmap.yaml
  │   ├── secret.yaml
  │   ├── pdb.yaml
  │   ├── hpa.yaml
  │   ├── serviceaccount.yaml
  │   ├── _helpers.tpl    ← Reusable template helpers (naming, labels)
  │   └── NOTES.txt       ← Post-install message shown to user
  ├── .helmignore         ← Files to exclude from the package
  └── README.md           ← Documentation for chart users

  KEY FILES:
  Chart.yaml   → Who am I? (name, version, type: application/library)
  values.yaml  → What are my defaults? (replicas, image, resources)
  templates/   → How do I render into K8s YAML? (Go templates)
  charts/      → What else do I depend on? (sub-charts)
Helm ConceptAnalogyExample
Chart.deb package / gemhelm create anihpj → scaffolds chart skeleton
ReleaseInstalled instance of a packagehelm install anihpj-prod ./anihpj -f prod-values.yaml
RepositoryAPT repo / RubyGemshelm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
values.yamlDefault config filereplicaCount: 3, image.tag: "v1.2.3"
TemplateERB (Ruby) / Jinja2 (Python)image: {{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}
⚡
Speed Tip: helm create mychart scaffolds a complete chart with best-practice defaults (Deployment, Service, HPA, Ingress, ServiceAccount). Always start with helm create — never write chart scaffolding from scratch. Then customize the generated templates for your needs.
🔬 How Helm Stores Release State — The Secret Inside Secrets

When you helm install, Helm creates Kubernetes Secrets (by default, or ConfigMaps) in the release namespace to track everything about that release. Each revision gets its own Secret. Understanding this internal storage is critical for debugging and disaster recovery.

Release Secret Structure (what Helm stores internally)
# kubectl get secret -n anihpj -l owner=helm,status=deployed
sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v1   ← Type: helm.sh/release.v1
sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v2   ← Revision 2 (after first upgrade)
sh.helm.release.v1.anihpj.v3   ← Revision 3 (latest)

# Each Secret contains (base64-encoded + gzipped):
{
  "name": "anihpj",           ← Release name
  "version": 3,               ← Revision number
  "namespace": "anihpj",       ← Target namespace
  "chart": { ... },            ← Full Chart.yaml metadata
  "config": { ... },           ← Merged values used for this release
  "manifest": "---\napiVersion...",  ← FULL rendered K8s YAML
  "info": {
    "status": "deployed",      ← deployed | failed | pending-install | ...
    "first_deployed": "2025-01-15T10:30:00Z",
    "last_deployed": "2025-01-16T14:20:00Z"
  }
}

Why this matters: (1) helm history reads these Secrets. (2) helm rollback copies the manifest from an old revision's Secret and creates a new one. (3) If you delete a release's Secrets, Helm loses track — the resources still exist but can't be managed. (4) Default max: 10 revisions. Configure with helm install --history-max 20. Never manually delete sh.helm.release.v1.* Secrets — use helm uninstall instead.

🔬 Chart.yaml — Every Field Explained
FieldRequired?What It Means + Example
apiVersion: v2✅ YesHelm API version. Always v2 for Helm 3. v1 was Helm 2 (deprecated).
name:✅ YesChart name. Must match the directory name. Used in resource naming: {{ .Chart.Name }}.
version:✅ YesChart version (SemVer). MUST be incremented on every change. Helm uses this to detect upgrades.
appVersion:NoThe version of the APPLICATION inside (e.g., "2.1.0"). Informational — not used by Helm engine. Displayed in helm list.
description:NoSingle-line description. Shown in helm search output. Keep it under 80 chars.
type:Noapplication (default) — deploys resources. library — provides reusable templates only, never installed directly. Library charts have no templates that produce K8s resources — only _*.tpl helpers.
dependencies:NoList of sub-charts. Each needs name, version, repository. Optional condition, alias, tags, import-values.
keywords:NoSearch keywords. helm search hub django uses these. Example: ["django", "job-board", "web"].
maintainers:NoPeople responsible. Each has name + email + optional url. Informational only — no access control.
icon:NoURL to an SVG/PNG icon. Displayed in chart repositories (Artifact Hub, Harbor).
kubeVersion:NoSemVer constraint for required K8s version. ">=1.25.0 <1.29.0". Helm refuses to install if cluster version doesn't match.
annotations:NoArbitrary metadata map. Used by tools: artifacthub.io/changes, category, license.

15.2 values.yaml — The Configuration Layer

values.yaml is the single source of truth for your chart's configuration. It defines sensible defaults that users can override at install time. This is what makes Helm charts reusable — one chart, many deployments, different values.

📦
values.yaml (Default)

The chart author sets safe defaults. Users should NOT edit this file directly — it's the baseline. Example: replicaCount: 1, image.tag: "latest".

🔄
Override at Install

Users provide their own values file: helm install anihpj ./chart -f my-values.yaml. Only override what you need — the rest falls back to defaults.

🔗
Multiple Values Files

Merge multiple files with left-to-right precedence: helm install anihpj . -f base.yaml -f prod.yaml. prod.yaml wins over base.yaml on conflicts.

💻
Inline Override

Set individual values on CLI: --set replicaCount=5, --set image.tag=v2.1.0. Useful for CI/CD or quick testing. Prefer files for production.

values.yaml — Complete anihpj Example
# Default values for anihpj Helm chart
replicaCount: 2

image:
  repository: ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web
  pullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  tag: "v1.2.0"

imagePullSecrets: []
nameOverride: ""
fullnameOverride: ""

serviceAccount:
  create: true
  annotations: {}
  name: ""

podAnnotations: {}
podSecurityContext: {}
securityContext: {}

service:
  type: ClusterIP
  port: 8080

ingress:
  enabled: true
  className: nginx
  hosts:
    - host: anihpj.example.com
      paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix
  tls:
    - secretName: anihpj-tls
      hosts:
        - anihpj.example.com

resources:
  limits:
    cpu: 500m
    memory: 512Mi
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 256Mi

autoscaling:
  enabled: false
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 10
  targetCPUUtilizationPercentage: 80

# Application-specific configuration
config:
  database:
    host: anihpj-db
    port: 5432
    name: anihpj
  redis:
    host: anihpj-redis
    port: 6379
  django:
    debug: false
    allowedHosts: "anihpj.example.com"
⚡
Speed Tip: helm show values bitnami/nginx dumps the full values.yaml for any chart. Use this to understand what you CAN configure before installing. Combine with grep: helm show values bitnami/postgresql | grep -A5 auth.
🔬 values.schema.json — Catch Invalid Values BEFORE Install

Helm supports JSON Schema validation of values.yaml. Place values.schema.json alongside values.yaml, and Helm validates user-supplied values against it before rendering. This catches replicas: "three" (string instead of integer) at install time, NOT at apply time.

values.schema.json — Enforce Types & Required Values
// This goes in your chart root, next to values.yaml
{
  "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft-07/schema#",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["replicaCount", "image"],  // These MUST be present
  "properties": {
    "replicaCount": {
      "type": "integer",
      "minimum": 1,
      "maximum": 100,
      "description": "Number of pod replicas (1-100)"
    },
    "image": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["repository", "tag"],
      "properties": {
        "repository": { "type": "string", "pattern": "^[a-zA-Z0-9._/-]+$" },
        "tag": { "type": "string", "minLength": 1 },
        "pullPolicy": { "type": "string", "enum": ["Always", "IfNotPresent", "Never"] }
      }
    },
    "service": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "type": { "enum": ["ClusterIP", "NodePort", "LoadBalancer"] }
      }
    }
  }
}

Validation happens automatically at helm install/upgrade/template/lint. If validation fails, Helm prints which field violated which constraint. This is a CNPE best practice: add a schema to every chart you build. It prevents the #1 cause of failed deployments — invalid values.

🔬 Values Precedence — Who Wins When Values Conflict?

When you provide values from multiple sources, Helm merges them in a strict order. Understanding this precedence chain is critical for debugging "why is my value not taking effect?"

Values Merge Precedence (Highest → Lowest)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ 1. --set (CLI flags)                          HIGHEST PRIORITY  │
  │    helm install anihpj . --set replicaCount=5                  │
  │    ▸ Overrides EVERYTHING below. Use sparingly in production.   │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 2. -f last-file.yaml (last file wins)                          │
  │    helm install anihpj . -f base.yaml -f prod-overrides.yaml   │
  │    ▸ prod-overrides.yaml wins over base.yaml on conflicts.     │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 3. -f first-file.yaml                                          │
  │    ▸ Earlier files lose to later files on same keys.           │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 4. Sub-chart values (parent values.yaml → child values)         │
  │    postgresql:                    ← Parent umbrella overrides   │
  │      auth:                            child's own values.yaml   │
  │        username: anihpj                                        │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 5. Child chart's own values.yaml                               │
  │    ▸ The sub-chart's built-in defaults.                        │
  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 6. Chart's values.yaml (the chart you're installing)           │
  │    ▸ The DEFAULT values set by the chart author.               │
  │    ▸ LOWEST PRIORITY — everything else overrides this.         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  KEY RULE: Helm does a DEEP MERGE of values, not a full replacement.
  If you set image.tag, other image.* keys (repository, pullPolicy)
  are NOT lost — only the specific key you overrode changes.
ScenarioCommandWhich replicaCount wins?
values.yaml has replicaCount: 1. CLI sets --set replicaCount=3helm install anihpj . --set replicaCount=33 (CLI wins)
base.yaml has replicaCount: 2. prod.yaml has replicaCount: 5helm install anihpj . -f base.yaml -f prod.yaml5 (last file wins)
--set and -f both set same keyhelm install anihpj . -f values.yaml --set replicaCount=1010 (--set beats -f always)

15.3 Go Templating — The Rendering Engine

Helm templates use Go's text/template library with Sprig function extensions. Understanding the template syntax is essential for writing and debugging Helm charts.

How Helm Renders a Template
  values.yaml          templates/deployment.yaml          RENDERED K8s YAML
  ───────────          ────────────────────────          ─────────────────
  replicaCount: 3  ──→  replicas: {{ .Values.        ──→  replicas: 3
                          replicaCount }}
                     ──→  image: {{ .Values.image.   ──→  image: ghcr.io/anihs/
                          repository }}:{{ .Values.        anihpj-web:v1.2.0
                          image.tag }}
Template ConstructSyntaxUse Case
Value access{{ .Values.image.tag }}Insert a value from values.yaml
Conditional{{ if .Values.ingress.enabled }}...{{ end }}Include section only if condition is true
Loop{{ range .Values.env }}...{{ end }}Iterate over a list or map
With block{{ with .Values.resources }}...{{ end }}Change scope (dot) to a sub-object
Default{{ .Values.port | default 8080 }}Use default if value is empty
Quote{{ .Values.name | quote }}Wrap output in double-quotes
Indent{{ .Values.data | indent 4 }}Indent multi-line block by N spaces
nindent{{ toYaml .Values.podLabels | nindent 6 }}Newline + indent (most common for YAML blocks)
toYaml{{ toYaml .Values.resources }}Convert object to YAML string
include{{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}Call a named template from _helpers.tpl
tpl{{ tpl .Values.configTemplate . }}Evaluate a string as a template
templates/deployment.yaml — Go Templates in Action
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  {{- if not .Values.autoscaling.enabled }}
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  {{- end }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "anihpj.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}
  template:
    metadata:
      {{- with .Values.podAnnotations }}
      annotations:
        {{- toYaml . | nindent 8 }}
      {{- end }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: {{ .Chart.Name }}
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: {{ .Values.service.port }}
          {{- with .Values.resources }}
          resources:
            {{- toYaml . | nindent 12 }}
          {{- end }}
⚠️
Gotcha — Whitespace Control: {{- ... }} (with dash) strips whitespace BEFORE the tag. {{ ... -}} strips whitespace AFTER. {{- ... -}} strips both. Without the dash, Go templates leave empty lines in the output. Always test with helm template . --debug to see exactly what gets rendered.
🔬 _helpers.tpl — Named Templates (DRY for Helm)
{{/*
  _helpers.tpl — Reusable template fragments.
  Define ONCE, use EVERYWHERE via {{ include "name" . }}
  The trailing dot (.) passes the current scope/context.
*/}}

{{/* Expand the chart name (used in resource names) */}}
{{- define "anihpj.name" -}}
{{- default .Chart.Name .Values.nameOverride | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }}
{{- end }}

{{/* Fully qualified app name: release-name + chart-name */}}
{{- define "anihpj.fullname" -}}
{{- if .Values.fullnameOverride }}
{{- .Values.fullnameOverride | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }}
{{- else }}
{{- $name := default .Chart.Name .Values.nameOverride }}
{{- if contains $name .Release.Name }}
{{- .Release.Name | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }}
{{- else }}
{{- printf "%s-%s" .Release.Name $name | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }}
{{- end }}
{{- end }}
{{- end }}

{{/* Common labels applied to EVERY resource */}}
{{- define "anihpj.labels" -}}
helm.sh/chart: {{ include "anihpj.chart" . }}
{{ include "anihpj.selectorLabels" . }}
{{- if .Chart.AppVersion }}
app.kubernetes.io/version: {{ .Chart.AppVersion | quote }}
{{- end }}
app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: {{ .Release.Service }}
{{- end }}

{{/* Selector labels (must match Pod template labels) */}}
{{- define "anihpj.selectorLabels" -}}
app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ include "anihpj.name" . }}
app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .Release.Name }}
{{- end }}

{{/* ServiceAccount name — reusable logic */}}
{{- define "anihpj.serviceAccountName" -}}
{{- if .Values.serviceAccount.create }}
{{- default (include "anihpj.fullname" .) .Values.serviceAccount.name }}
{{- else }}
{{- default "default" .Values.serviceAccount.name }}
{{- end }}
{{- end }}
🔬 Essential Sprig Template Functions (Beyond Basic Go Templates)

Helm bundles the Sprig function library — 70+ template functions. Here are the ones you'll actually use:

CategoryFunctionsExample Output
Stringquote, upper, lower, trim, nospace, trunc N{{ "hello" | upper | quote }} → "HELLO"
Defaultdefault, empty, required{{ .Values.port | default 8080 }} → 8080
Encodingb64enc, b64dec, sha256sum{{ "pass" | b64enc }} → cGFzcw==
Date/Timenow, date, dateModify{{ now | date "2006-01-02" }}
Listsfirst, last, append, join, sortAlpha{{ list "b" "a" | sortAlpha | join "," }} → a,b
Dictsdict, set, keys, values, hasKey{{ dict "key" "val" | keys }} → [key]
Mathadd, sub, mul, div, max, min{{ mul 2 .Values.replicaCount }}
Flow Controlternary (inline if/else){{ ternary "prod" "dev" .Values.isProd }}
TypekindOf, kindIs, typeOf{{ kindOf .Values.replicas }} → int
Requiredrequired (fails if empty){{ required "DB host required" .Values.db.host }}
🔬 Template Debugging — 5 Techniques When Things Go Wrong
  1. helm template . --debug --dry-run — Renders templates to stdout WITHOUT installing. The debug flag shows computed values at each step. Always start here.
  2. {{ fail "message" }} — Deliberately crash template rendering with a message. Use inside {{ if not .Values.requiredField }}{{ fail ".Values.requiredField is required" }}{{ end }}. Better than required for custom logic.
  3. {{ . | toYaml }} / {{ . | toJson }} — Dump the CURRENT scope (dot) to see what values are available. Place temporarily in any template: {{ .Values | toYaml }} prints ALL values.
  4. helm get manifest anihpj — For an ALREADY INSTALLED release, dump the exact YAML that was applied. Compare with helm template output to find discrepancies.
  5. helm get values anihpj --all — Show ALL computed values (merged from defaults + user overrides + sub-charts). If your value isn't there, check precedence.
⚠️
🔬 Named Templates — The Dot (.) Scope Trap: When you call a named template via {{ include "mytemplate" . }}, the trailing dot (.) passes the current scope. Inside the named template, . refers to whatever was passed — NOT the global root. This is why {{ include "anihpj.labels" . }} passes the root scope . so the template can access .Values, .Chart, .Release.

Common mistake: Calling {{ include "mytemplate" .Values.someDict }} changes . to someDict inside the template — .Chart.Name will FAIL because . is now a dict, not the root. Solution: Either always pass $ (the root) as {{ include "mytemplate" $ }}, or use template (not include) which always gets the same scope. include = pass scope explicitly. template = inherits caller's scope (but can't be piped).

15.4 Helm Hooks & Rollback — Lifecycle Management

Helm hooks let you run Kubernetes resources at specific points in the release lifecycle. Rollback lets you undo a failed upgrade.

Helm Release Lifecycle + Hooks
  helm install          helm upgrade           helm uninstall
       │                     │                      │
       ▼                     ▼                      ▼
  ┌─────────┐          ┌─────────┐            ┌─────────┐
  │PRE-INSTALL│         │PRE-UPGRADE│           │PRE-DELETE│
  │ (Job)     │         │ (Job)     │           │ (Job)    │
  │ DB migration│       │ Schema    │           │ Cleanup  │
  └────┬────┘          └────┬────┘            └────┬────┘
       │                     │                      │
       ▼                     ▼                      ▼
  ┌─────────┐          ┌─────────┐            ┌─────────┐
  │ K8s Resources│       │ K8s Resources│        │ DELETE  │
  │ (Deployment, │       │ (updated)   │        │Resources│
  │  Service...) │       │             │        └────┬────┘
  └────┬────┘          └────┬────┘               │
       │                     │                      ▼
       ▼                     ▼               ┌──────────┐
  ┌──────────┐         ┌──────────┐          │POST-DELETE│
  │POST-INSTALL│        │POST-UPGRADE│         │(cleanup)  │
  │(smoke test)│        │(health chk)│         └──────────┘
  └──────────┘         └──────────┘
🪝
Helm Hooks

Annotations on any K8s resource: "helm.sh/hook": pre-install. Hooks run as Jobs by default. Hook weights ("helm.sh/hook-weight": "5") control execution order. Lower numbers run first.

⏪
Helm Rollback

helm rollback anihpj 3 — reverts to revision 3. Blueprint: Helm stores release history as Secrets (default) or ConfigMaps. helm history anihpj shows all revisions.

📜
History & Revisions

Each helm install/upgrade/rollback creates a new revision. Default: max 10 revisions stored. helm history anihpj --max 20. Old revisions auto-purged (configurable via --history-max).

🔍
Debugging Failed Releases

helm status anihpj — current state. helm get values anihpj --revision 3 — values used in revision 3. helm get manifest anihpj — rendered YAML. helm template . --debug — dry-run render.

Hook Example — DB Migration Job (pre-upgrade)
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: {{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}-db-migrate
  annotations:
    # This Job runs BEFORE the upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0"
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          command: ["python", "manage.py", "migrate"]
          env:
            - name: DATABASE_URL
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: anihpj-db-creds
                  key: url
🎯
Exam Tip: The CNPE exam may ask you to make a Deployment wait for a migration Job. Answer: Use a Helm pre-upgrade hook with hook-weight ordering. The hook Job runs to completion BEFORE the Deployment pods are updated. The hook-delete-policy: hook-succeeded annotation auto-cleans the Job pod after success.
🔬 Complete Helm Hook Types — When Each One Fires
HookFires WhenTypical Use Case
pre-installAfter templates rendered, BEFORE any resources createdDB schema creation, secret generation, pre-flight checks
post-installAfter ALL resources are created and readySmoke tests, data seeding, notification/webhook
pre-deleteBefore ANY resources are deletedData backup, drain connections, unregister from LB
post-deleteAfter ALL resources are deletedCleanup external resources (DNS, cloud volumes)
pre-upgradeAfter templates rendered, BEFORE upgrading resourcesDatabase migrations, schema changes
post-upgradeAfter ALL resources upgraded and readyHealth checks, cache warming, notification
pre-rollbackBefore rolling back to previous revisionSnapshot current state, reverse migration prep
post-rollbackAfter rollback completesVerify old version is healthy, notify on-call
testWhen helm test <release> is runIntegration/acceptance tests (separate from post-install)
💡 Hook Deletion Policies — Control Cleanup

The "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy" annotation controls when hook resources are deleted:

  • before-hook-creation — Delete previous hook resource BEFORE creating a new one (default). Good for idempotent hooks.
  • hook-succeeded — Delete AFTER the hook succeeds. Use for cleanup-heavy hooks like migration Jobs.
  • hook-failed — Delete ONLY if the hook FAILS. Use for debugging — keep the pod for kubectl logs inspection.

You can combine policies: "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": "before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded". The CNPE exam likes this combination — it ensures idempotency AND cleanup on success.

15.5 Kustomize — Native Kubernetes Configuration Management

🧠 What Is Kustomize? Kustomize is Kubernetes' native configuration customization tool, built into kubectl apply -k. Unlike Helm (which uses templates), Kustomize works with pure YAML — it takes a base set of Kubernetes manifests and applies patches to customize them per environment. No templating, just strategic merging.

Kustomize Structure — Bases + Overlays
  kustomize/
  ├── base/                          ← COMMON configuration (all envs)
  │   ├── kustomization.yaml         ← Lists all resources
  │   ├── deployment.yaml            ← Base Deployment (replicas: 1, image: anihpj)
  │   ├── service.yaml               ← Base Service (ClusterIP, port 8080)
  │   ├── configmap.yaml             ← Base ConfigMap
  │   └── ingress.yaml               ← Base Ingress
  │
  ├── overlays/
  │   ├── dev/                       ← DEV environment overlay
  │   │   ├── kustomization.yaml     ← patches base, adds dev config
  │   │   ├── replica-patch.yaml     ← replicas: 1 (dev doesn't need scale)
  │   │   └── ingress-patch.yaml     ← host: dev.anihpj.example.com
  │   │
  │   ├── staging/                   ← STAGING overlay
  │   │   ├── kustomization.yaml
  │   │   ├── replica-patch.yaml     ← replicas: 2
  │   │   └── ingress-patch.yaml     ← host: staging.anihpj.example.com
  │   │
  │   └── production/                ← PRODUCTION overlay
  │       ├── kustomization.yaml
  │       ├── replica-patch.yaml     ← replicas: 5
  │       ├── resource-patch.yaml    ← CPU/memory increased
  │       └── ingress-patch.yaml     ← host: anihpj.example.com, TLS enabled
overlays/production/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

# Reference the base
resources:
  - ../../base

# Strategic merge patches
patches:
  - path: replica-patch.yaml
  - path: ingress-patch.yaml
  - path: resource-patch.yaml

# Set image tag for production
images:
  - name: ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web
    newTag: v2.1.0

# Add production labels
commonLabels:
  environment: production
  tier: frontend

# Add namespace prefix to all resources
namespace: anihpj-prod

# Generate ConfigMap from file
configMapGenerator:
  - name: anihpj-config
    files:
      - application.properties
    literals:
      - DJANGO_DEBUG=false
Kustomize FeatureWhat It DoesExample
patchesStrategicMergeOverride specific fields in base YAMLChange replicas: 1 → 5
patchesJson6902JSON Patch (RFC 6902) for precise edits- op: replace, path: /spec/replicas, value: 5
imagesChange image name/tag across all resourcesnewTag: v2.1.0
commonLabels / commonAnnotationsAdd labels/annotations to ALL resourcesenvironment: production
namePrefix / nameSuffixAdd prefix/suffix to all resource namesPrefix: prod- → prod-anihpj-deploy
configMapGeneratorGenerate ConfigMaps with content hashHash changes → rolling restart
secretGeneratorGenerate Secrets (not for Git!)Use with external secret stores
replacementsCross-resource field replacement (Kustomize v5+)Copy Service name into Deployment env var
⚡
Speed Tip: kubectl kustomize overlays/production renders the final YAML without applying it. Pipe to a file: kubectl kustomize overlays/prod > rendered.yaml. For Argo CD, point it at the overlay directory — Argo CD runs kustomize build automatically.
🚀
🔬 Kustomize Components — Reusable Configuration Modules (Kustomize v5+)

Components are Kustomize's answer to Helm's sub-charts — reusable, composable configuration modules that can be included in multiple overlays. Unlike bases (which can only be used once per kustomization), components can be used multiple times and accept arguments.

Component Example — TLS Cert Injector
# components/tls/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component

# This component adds TLS to ANY Ingress that matches
patches:
  - target:
      kind: Ingress
      name: .*  # match ALL Ingresses
    patch: |-
      - op: add
        path: /spec/tls
        value:
          - hosts:
            - anihpj.example.com
            secretName: anihpj-tls

# Usage in overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml:
components:
  - ../../components/tls        # Add TLS to all Ingresses
  - ../../components/monitoring  # Add ServiceMonitor to all Services
  - ../../components/networkpolicy # Add default-deny policies

Use Components when: (1) You have cross-cutting concerns across multiple services (TLS, monitoring, network policies). (2) You want to compose features additively. (3) One overlay needs cert-manager TLS, another needs certbot TLS — components let you swap implementations.

🔬 Kustomize Replacements — Cross-Resource Field Copying (v5+)

Replacements are Kustomize v5's answer to the age-old problem: "How do I copy a Service's clusterIP into a ConfigMap?" Before replacements, you'd use vars (deprecated). Now replacements provide a declarative, type-safe way to copy fields between resources.

Replacements Example — Copy Service Name into Deployment Env
# Problem: Deployment needs DB_HOST=anihpj-db. But the Service name might
# change with namePrefix (e.g., prod-anihpj-db). How to keep them in sync?

# Solution: Use replacements to copy Service.metadata.name → Deployment env
replacements:
  - source:           # WHERE to get the value FROM
      kind: Service
      name: anihpj-db
      fieldPath: metadata.name  # Copy THIS field...
    targets:            # WHERE to put the value
      - select:
          kind: Deployment
          name: anihpj-web
        fieldPaths:
          - spec.template.spec.containers.[name=anihpj].env.[name=DB_HOST].value
          # ...INTO this specific env var

# result: spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[0].value = "prod-anihpj-db"
# If namePrefix changes, the replacement updates automatically!

Replacements vs vars: vars (deprecated) mixed template-like syntax into Kustomize's pure-YAML philosophy. replacements are fully declarative — just YAML. They support any field path, can transform values with options.delimiter and options.index, and work across any resource kind.

15.6 Helm vs Kustomize — The Decision Matrix

This is the most debated topic in Kubernetes configuration. The CNPE exam expects you to know when to use which — not just what they do.

DimensionHelm 🎩Kustomize ✂️
Mental modelPackage manager (apt/brew)Patch overlay (diff/patch)
Config languageGo templates in YAMLPure YAML (no templating)
Best forPackaging & DISTRIBUTING chartsCUSTOMIZING existing configs per env
SharingChart repositories (OCI, ChartMuseum)Git repos (just YAML files)
VersioningSemVer (chart version + appVersion)Git version (no built-in versioning)
DependenciesSub-charts, umbrella chartsRemote bases (URLs to other repos)
Release mgmtInstall/Upgrade/Rollback/UninstallJust kubectl apply -k
HooksYes (pre/post install/upgrade/delete)No (use init containers or Jobs)
Built into kubectlNo (requires helm CLI)Yes (kubectl apply -k)
Learning curveMedium (Go templates can be tricky)Low (it's just YAML)
🎩
Use Helm When...
  • You need to distribute your chart to others
  • You want release management (install/upgrade/rollback)
  • Your app has complex conditional logic (if TLS enabled → include cert resources)
  • You need lifecycle hooks (DB migrations before deploy)
  • Third-party charts exist (Bitnami, Grafana, Prometheus)
✂️
Use Kustomize When...
  • You're customizing existing YAML per environment
  • You want pure YAML (no template syntax to learn)
  • You use Argo CD (native Kustomize support)
  • You need simple overlays (dev/staging/prod)
  • You want to avoid Helm's complexity for simple configs
🤝
The Combined Pattern (Most Real-World Platforms)

Helm for packaging and distributing the chart (defines WHAT to deploy). Kustomize for environment-specific customization of that chart (defines HOW it varies). helm template ./chart | kubectl kustomize — render with Helm, patch with Kustomize.

🎯
CNPE Exam Decision Rule

"Deploy with Helm, customize with Kustomize." If the question asks about packaging/sharing/releasing → Helm. If it asks about environment-specific overrides → Kustomize. If it asks about both → Combined pattern.

🔬 Real-World Scenarios — What Would You Use?
ScenarioAnswer & Why
You're a SaaS vendor. You need customers to install your app on their K8s clusters.Helm. Package as a chart, push to OCI/Hub. Customers helm install with their values.
You have 30 microservices. Each needs minor tweaks per env (replica count, resource limits, log level).Kustomize. One base per service, 3 overlays (dev/staging/prod). No template complexity needed.
You're deploying a complex stateful app (PostgreSQL, Kafka, Redis) from a vendor.Helm. You can't write base YAML for external apps. Use the vendor's chart, override values.
Your platform team provides a "golden path" that dev teams customize for their service.Helm (package) + Kustomize (customize per team). Chart defines the standard. Kustomize overlays add team-specific labels, ingress hosts, resource sizes.
You need to deploy the same app to 10 regions with different storage classes, cert issuers, and node selectors.Kustomize. One base, 10 overlays. Each overlay patches region-specific fields. Far simpler than 10 values files.
You're building an Internal Developer Platform. Developers click a button to deploy a new service.Helm. Backstage/Portal generates a values.yaml from the form, calls helm install. Kustomize is too manual for self-service.

15.7 Programmatic Config — When YAML Templating Breaks Down

Helm's Go templates work well for simple parameterization, but when your config has complex logic, type validation, or deeply nested conditions, pure YAML templating becomes painful. Enter programmatic configuration languages:

ToolParadigmBest ForAdoption
JsonnetData templating language (JS-like)Complex JSON/YAML generation with functions, loops, conditionals. Used by Tanka (Grafana Labs) and kubecfg.Mature, production-proven (Grafana, Bitnami)
CUEConstraint-based configuration languageType-safe configuration with built-in validation. Unifies config + schema + validation in one language. Think "JSON with types."Growing (Istio uses CUE for operator APIs)
PklConfiguration language (Apple, 2024)Strongly-typed config with IDE support. Designed to replace YAML/JSON for complex config. Outputs JSON/YAML/properties.New but promising (Apple-backed)
CDK8sProgramming language (TS/Python/Go/Java)Define K8s resources using real programming languages. Full power of OOP — classes, inheritance, unit tests.AWS-backed, growing
When YAML Templating Breaks — The Complexity Threshold
  Configuration Complexity
       ▲
       │                                          ┌──────────────┐
       │                                          │   CDK8s/Pulumi│  ← "I need real
       │                                    ┌─────┤  (full PL)    │     programming"
       │                                    │     └──────────────┘
       │                              ┌─────┤
       │                              │     │     ┌──────────────┐
       │                        ┌─────┤     └─────┤ CUE / Jsonnet│  ← "I need types,
       │                        │     │           │ (typed DSL)  │     logic, validation"
       │                  ┌─────┤     │           └──────────────┘
       │                  │     │     │
       │            ┌─────┤     └─────┤           ┌──────────────┐
       │            │     │           └───────────┤    Helm      │  ← "I need conditionals,
       │      ┌─────┤     │                      │ (Go templates)│     loops, values"
       │      │     │     │                      └──────────────┘
       │      │     │     │
       │      │     └─────┤                      ┌──────────────┐
       │      │           └──────────────────────┤  Kustomize   │  ← "Just env-specific
       │      │                                 │ (pure YAML)   │     overrides"
       │      │                                 └──────────────┘
       │      │
       │      └─────────────────────────────────┌──────────────┐
       │                                        │  Raw YAML    │  ← "Simple, static"
       │                                        │  (kubectl)   │
       └────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┴──────────►
                                              Use Case Complexity
🚀
Beyond CNPE: Jsonnet powers Tanka (Grafana Labs' K8s deployment tool) and the entire Grafana monitoring stack configuration. CUE is used by Istio for its operator APIs. Pkl is Apple's answer to "configuration as code." For the CNPE exam, know these exist and their use cases. For your platform career, invest in learning Jsonnet or CUE — they solve the pain of complex YAML at scale.
🔧
Jsonnet — Data Templating Approach

// Define a function that generates a Deployment
local deployment(name, replicas) = {
  apiVersion: "apps/v1",
  kind: "Deployment",
  metadata: { name: name },
  spec: { replicas: replicas }
};
local base = deployment("web", 3);
local prod = base { spec+: { replicas: 5 } }; // Override

Best for: Generating many similar K8s objects with shared logic. Functions, conditionals, list comprehensions. Used by Grafana for dashboards and Tanka for deployments.

✅
CUE — Constraint + Validation Approach

// Define TYPES and CONSTRAINTS — then CONCRETE values
#Deployment: {
  apiVersion: "apps/v1"
  kind: "Deployment"
  spec: replicas: >=1 & <=100 // TYPE CHECK!
}
web: #Deployment & { spec: replicas: 3 } // Validated!
// replicas: "three" → ERROR at eval time, not apply time

Best for: Configuration that MUST be validated. Unifies schema + data + policy in one language. Built-in type checking prevents entire classes of bugs.

15.8 Umbrella Charts — Deploy Your Entire Stack in One Command

An umbrella chart is a parent Helm chart that includes multiple sub-charts as dependencies. Think of it as a meta-package that deploys your entire application stack with one helm install.

Umbrella Chart — anihpj Full Stack
  anihpj-umbrella/
  ├── Chart.yaml              ← name: anihpj-umbrella, version: 1.0.0
  ├── values.yaml             ← Global + per-sub-chart values
  └── charts/                 ← Sub-charts (dependencies)
      ├── anihpj-web/         ← Django web application
      │   ├── Chart.yaml
      │   ├── values.yaml
      │   └── templates/
      ├── anihpj-db/          ← PostgreSQL (or depends on Bitnami chart)
      │   ├── Chart.yaml
      │   ├── values.yaml
      │   └── templates/
      ├── anihpj-redis/       ← Redis (for Celery task queue)
      │   ├── Chart.yaml
      │   ├── values.yaml
      │   └── templates/
      └── anihpj-worker/      ← Celery worker
          ├── Chart.yaml
          ├── values.yaml
          └── templates/

  INSTALLATION:
  helm install anihpj-stack ./anihpj-umbrella

  ONE COMMAND → Web + DB + Redis + Worker are ALL deployed.
  Values cascade: umbrella values.yaml → sub-chart values.yaml
  Order: DB first → Redis → Web + Worker
Chart.yaml — Umbrella with Dependencies
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj-umbrella
description: Full anihpj stack — Web, DB, Redis, Worker
type: application
version: 1.0.0
appVersion: "2.0.0"

# Method 1: Dependencies in Chart.yaml (preferred)
dependencies:
  - name: anihpj-web
    version: 1.2.0
    repository: oci://ghcr.io/anihs/charts
    condition: web.enabled
  - name: postgresql
    version: 12.1.6
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: postgresql.enabled
  - name: redis
    version: 17.11.3
    repository: https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami
    condition: redis.enabled
  - name: anihpj-worker
    version: 1.0.5
    repository: oci://ghcr.io/anihs/charts
    condition: worker.enabled
⚠️
Gotcha — Dependency Update: After editing dependencies in Chart.yaml, you MUST run helm dependency update to download the sub-charts into charts/. Without this, helm install fails with "chart not found." The Chart.lock file pins exact versions (like package-lock.json).
🔬 Sub-Chart Value Override — How Parent Values Flow to Children

The umbrella chart's values.yaml can override ANY value in a sub-chart by using the dependency name as a key. This is how you customize Bitnami PostgreSQL without touching its chart.

umbrella values.yaml — Overriding Sub-Chart Values
# Global values (accessible in ALL sub-charts via .Values.global)
global:
  imageRegistry: ghcr.io/anihs
  storageClass: standard
  postgresql:
    auth:
      username: anihpj
      database: anihpj_db
      existingSecret: anihpj-db-creds  # Reference external secret

# Sub-chart overrides (key = dependency name from Chart.yaml)
postgresql:            ← Matches dependency name "postgresql"
  enabled: true           ← Ties to condition: postgresql.enabled
  architecture: standalone
  primary:
    persistence:
      size: 20Gi            ← Override Bitnami's default 8Gi
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: 512Mi
        cpu: 500m

redis:
  enabled: true
  architecture: standalone
  auth:
    enabled: false          ← Disable Redis auth for dev
  master:
    persistence:
      enabled: false        ← No persistence for cache

anihpj-web:
  replicaCount: 3
  ingress:
    enabled: true

anihpj-worker:
  enabled: true
  replicaCount: 2
⚠️
Gotcha — Dependency Alias: If you need the same sub-chart TWICE (e.g., two PostgreSQL instances), use alias in dependencies: - name: postgresql, alias: app-db and - name: postgresql, alias: analytics-db. Override values via app-db: and analytics-db: keys respectively. Without alias, you can only include a dependency once.
🔬 Dependency Control — Tags, Conditions & Import-Values

Beyond basic dependency inclusion, Helm gives you three powerful mechanisms for controlling sub-charts:

MechanismHow It WorksExample
condition:Enable/disable a dependency based on a boolean value path. Evaluated as YAML boolean.condition: postgresql.enabled → set postgresql.enabled: false in values to skip this dependency.
tags:Enable/disable MULTIPLE dependencies at once. Each dependency lists tags; the values file sets which tags are active.tags: ["db", "storage"] → set tags.db: false to disable ALL dependencies with the "db" tag.
import-values:Copy values FROM a child chart UP to the parent. Used when the child generates data the parent needs (e.g., child creates a Secret name the parent references).import-values: [{child: service.port, parent: dbPort}] → copies PostgreSQL's port to the parent's .Values.dbPort.

Tag vs Condition: condition is a direct boolean check on a single path. tags let you group dependencies and toggle entire groups with one flag. Use tags when you have optional feature groups: tags: ["monitoring"] on Prometheus, Grafana, and AlertManager dependencies — one tags.monitoring: false disables all three.

15.9 anihpj Helm Chart — Complete Working Example

Here is the complete Helm chart for the anihpj Django job posting application. This is the chart you would use to deploy anihpj on your CNPE exam cluster.

Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: anihpj
description: Django job posting application — anihpj
type: application
version: 1.0.0
appVersion: "2.0.0"
keywords:
  - django
  - job-board
  - anihpj
maintainers:
  - name: platform-team
    email: platform@anihs.com
1
Scaffold

helm create anihpj

Generates best-practice chart skeleton with Deployment, Service, HPA, Ingress, ServiceAccount

2
Configure

Edit values.yaml

Set image, replicas, resources, ingress host, app config — all in one file

3
Template

Customize templates/

Add ConfigMap, Secret, PDB, NetworkPolicy. Use Go templates for dynamic values

4
Validate

helm lint ./anihpj

Catch syntax errors, missing required values, template bugs BEFORE install

5
Preview

helm template --debug

Render YAML to stdout — inspect every line. Pipe to kubectl diff

6
Deploy

helm install anihpj ./anihpj

Create a named release. Tracked as revision 1. Rollback-able forever

📦
Templates Included

deployment.yaml — Django web + Celery worker. service.yaml — ClusterIP. ingress.yaml — NGINX Ingress with TLS. configmap.yaml — Django settings. secret.yaml — DB credentials (sealed). pdb.yaml — PodDisruptionBudget (min 1). hpa.yaml — HorizontalPodAutoscaler. serviceaccount.yaml — Dedicated SA.

🎛️
Key values.yaml Overrides

replicaCount: 2 (dev) / 5 (prod). image.tag: git SHA. config.database.host: DB service name. config.redis.host: Redis service name. ingress.tls.enabled: true for prod. resources.limits.memory: 512Mi (dev) / 2Gi (prod).

📦 Packaging & Distribution: Package the chart: helm package ./anihpj → creates anihpj-1.0.0.tgz. Push to OCI registry: helm push anihpj-1.0.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/anihs/charts. Users install: helm install anihpj oci://ghcr.io/anihs/charts/anihpj --version 1.0.0. OCI registries are the modern standard for Helm chart distribution (replacing ChartMuseum).

templates/configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: {{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}-config
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
data:
  DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE: "anihpj.settings"
  DATABASE_HOST: {{ .Values.config.database.host | quote }}
  DATABASE_PORT: {{ .Values.config.database.port | quote }}
  DATABASE_NAME: {{ .Values.config.database.name | quote }}
  REDIS_HOST: {{ .Values.config.redis.host | quote }}
  REDIS_PORT: {{ .Values.config.redis.port | quote }}
  DJANGO_DEBUG: {{ .Values.config.django.debug | quote }}
  DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS: {{ .Values.config.django.allowedHosts | quote }}
templates/pdb.yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: {{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  {{- if .Values.pdb.minAvailable }}
  minAvailable: {{ .Values.pdb.minAvailable }}
  {{- else }}
  maxUnavailable: {{ default 1 .Values.pdb.maxUnavailable }}
  {{- end }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "anihpj.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}
templates/hpa.yaml
{{- if .Values.autoscaling.enabled }}
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: {{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: {{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}
  minReplicas: {{ .Values.autoscaling.minReplicas }}
  maxReplicas: {{ .Values.autoscaling.maxReplicas }}
  metrics:
    {{- if .Values.autoscaling.targetCPUUtilizationPercentage }}
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: {{ .Values.autoscaling.targetCPUUtilizationPercentage }}
    {{- end }}
{{- end }}
templates/secret.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: {{ include "anihpj.fullname" . }}-secret
  labels:
    {{- include "anihpj.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
type: Opaque
stringData:
  {{/* Values from .Values.secrets; inject at deploy via External Secrets */}}
  DATABASE_URL: {{ .Values.secrets.databaseUrl | quote }}
  SECRET_KEY: {{ .Values.secrets.djangoSecretKey | quote }}
  REDIS_URL: {{ .Values.secrets.redisUrl | quote }}
Drill 15.1 Create a Helm Chart for anihpj

Scenario: You're deploying anihpj to a new cluster. Create a Helm chart from scratch.

  1. helm create anihpj — scaffold the chart
  2. Edit values.yaml — set image.repository to ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web, image.tag to v2.0.0, replicaCount to 3
  3. Add a ConfigMap template in templates/configmap.yaml with DB host, Redis host, and Django debug flag from values
  4. Add a Secret template for DB credentials (reference from values, not hardcoded)
  5. helm lint ./anihpj — verify no syntax errors
  6. helm template anihpj ./anihpj --debug — inspect rendered YAML
  7. helm install anihpj ./anihpj --namespace anihpj --create-namespace
💡 Hint: Use {{ .Values.config.database.host }} in templates. For Secrets, use {{ .Values.secrets.dbPassword | b64enc | quote }} — but NEVER put real secrets in values.yaml. Use external secret stores (Vault, Sealed Secrets).
Drill 15.2 Helm Upgrade & Rollback

Scenario: Your helm upgrade anihpj ./anihpj --set image.tag=v2.1.0 broke production. Roll back.

  1. Check release history: helm history anihpj
  2. Identify the last working revision (e.g., revision 4)
  3. Rollback: helm rollback anihpj 4
  4. Verify: helm status anihpj — should show revision 6 (rollback counts as a new revision!)
  5. Check what values revision 4 used: helm get values anihpj --revision 4
  6. For extra safety, run helm rollback anihpj 4 --dry-run first to preview changes
💡 Hint: A rollback creates a NEW revision — it doesn't delete the bad one. This is intentional: you can roll-forward to the "bad" revision if the rollback itself was a mistake. helm history preserves the full audit trail.
Drill 15.3 Kustomize Overlay for Dev vs Prod

Scenario: You have a base anihpj deployment. Dev needs 1 replica + NodePort. Prod needs 5 replicas + LoadBalancer + TLS.

  1. Create base/ with deployment.yaml (replicas: 1), service.yaml (ClusterIP), ingress.yaml
  2. Create overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml → resources: ../../base, patches (service → NodePort)
  3. Create overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml → resources: ../../base, patches (replica→5, service→LB, ingress TLS), namespace: anihpj-prod
  4. Render: kubectl kustomize overlays/prod | grep replicas — should show 5
  5. Apply: kubectl apply -k overlays/prod
💡 Hint: Use patchesStrategicMerge for simple field overrides. For precise control, use patches with target and patch. Always render first with kubectl kustomize before applying.
Q1: Create a Helm chart for anihpj with values for replicas, image tag, and DB host.

▶ Show Answer
helm create anihpj, then edit values.yaml to add replicaCount: 3, image.tag: "v2.0.0", config.database.host: anihpj-db. In templates/deployment.yaml: replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}, image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}". In templates/configmap.yaml: DATABASE_HOST: {{ .Values.config.database.host }}.
Q2: helm upgrade anihpj . fails. How do you rollback?

▶ Show Answer
helm history anihpj to find the last working revision. helm rollback anihpj <revision>. Verify with helm status anihpj. The rollback creates a new revision number (it's tracked as a new deployment).
Q3: You need anihpj-web to wait for anihpj-db before starting. Use Helm hooks.

▶ Show Answer
Add a pre-install/pre-upgrade Job that runs pg_isready -h anihpj-db (or a migration). Annotate with "helm.sh/hook": pre-install,pre-upgrade and "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0". The Deployment waits because Helm runs hooks BEFORE installing/upgrading resources. Add "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": hook-succeeded to clean up the Job pod. Use initContainers as a lightweight alternative for simple wait-for-DB checks.
Q4: Kustomize overlay — dev uses 1 replica + NodePort, prod uses 3 replicas + LoadBalancer. Write the overlay structure.

▶ Show Answer
Base: base/deployment.yaml (replicas: 1), base/service.yaml (ClusterIP). Dev overlay: overlays/dev/ with patch setting service type to NodePort. Prod overlay: overlays/prod/ with patches increasing replicas to 3 and changing service type to LoadBalancer. Each overlay's kustomization.yaml references ../../base in resources and lists patch files.
Q5: Helm vs Kustomize — your platform has 20 services deployed to 4 environments each. Which tool for which purpose?

▶ Show Answer
Helm: Package each of the 20 services as a chart. Kustomize: Create 4 overlays (dev/staging/qa/prod) that patch each chart's rendered YAML with env-specific values. Use the combined pattern: helm template ./chart | kubectl kustomize overlays/prod. Or better: use Argo CD with Helm + Kustomize combined in the Application manifest.
Q6: Umbrella chart for anihpj — web, db, redis as dependencies.

▶ Show Answer
Create anihpj-umbrella/Chart.yaml with dependencies: listing anihpj-web, postgresql (Bitnami), redis (Bitnami), anihpj-worker. Run helm dependency update to download sub-charts. Set sub-chart values via umbrella's values.yaml: postgresql.auth.database: anihpj, redis.auth.enabled: false. Install with helm install anihpj-stack ./anihpj-umbrella — deploys everything in dependency order.
Q7: Helm values have secrets. How do you NOT commit them to Git?

▶ Show Answer
Options: (1) Sealed Secrets: Encrypt with kubeseal, commit the SealedSecret CR. Only the cluster controller can decrypt. (2) External Secrets Operator: Store secrets in Vault/AWS Secrets Manager, reference in ExternalSecret CR. (3) SOPS: Encrypt values file with sops, commit encrypted file. (4) Never put real secrets in plain values.yaml — even in private repos.
Q8: Jsonnet/CUE/Pkl — when does YAML templating break down?

▶ Show Answer
YAML templating breaks when you need: (1) Type safety — catching replicas: "three" before apply. (2) Complex logic — nested conditionals, list comprehensions, math. (3) Reusable functions — Helm's named templates are limited. (4) Validation — CUE validates schemas as part of the language. (5) Large-scale config — managing 100+ services with shared config requires programmatic abstraction.
Q9: kubectl apply -k overlays/production — walk through what Kustomize does.

▶ Show Answer
1. Reads overlays/production/kustomization.yaml. 2. Loads resources (../../base). 3. Applies patches (replica-patch, ingress-patch). 4. Sets images (newTag). 5. Adds commonLabels. 6. Generates ConfigMaps with content hashes. 7. Sets namespace. 8. Renders final YAML. 9. Sends to kubectl apply. Each generated ConfigMap name includes a hash — if config changes, the Deployment gets a rolling restart.
Q10: Chart Museum vs OCI registry for Helm charts — compare.

▶ Show Answer
ChartMuseum: Legacy Helm chart repository. Simple HTTP server. No auth built-in. OCI Registry: Modern standard (Helm 3.8+). Uses the same registry as container images (ghcr.io, ECR, Harbor). Built-in auth, RBAC, scanning. CNPE Exam: Know that OCI is the current standard. helm push ./chart.tgz oci://ghcr.io/org/charts. OCI registries support both container images AND Helm charts — one registry for everything.

📖 Chapter 15 Summary: Helm for packaging, Kustomize for customization. Helm charts define WHAT to deploy — use helm create to scaffold, values.yaml for defaults, Go templates for parameterization, hooks for lifecycle management, and helm rollback for safety. Kustomize defines HOW configuration varies per environment — use bases for common config, overlays for env-specific patches. The combined pattern (Helm + Kustomize) is the real-world gold standard. Umbrella charts deploy entire stacks in one command. When YAML templating breaks, programmatic config (Jsonnet, CUE, Pkl) provides type safety and logic. Together they form a complete configuration management strategy for any cloud native platform.

🎩
Helm

Package manager. Chart = templated K8s resources + default values. Release lifecycle with hooks, rollback, history. Share via OCI.

✂️
Kustomize

Configuration customizer. Base + overlays + patches. Pure YAML. Built into kubectl. Strategic merge FTW.

🤝
Combined

Helm packages the app. Kustomize customizes per env. helm template | kubectl kustomize or Argo CD helm+kustomize.

☂️
Umbrella

One chart → entire stack. Web + DB + Redis + Worker in one helm install. Values cascade to sub-charts.

How do I configure my K8s app?
Packaging / Sharing
Use Helm
Env Customization
Use Kustomize
Complex Logic / Types
Use Jsonnet / CUE
Best Platform Strategy?
Helm (package) + Kustomize (customize) + OCI (distribute)

Chapter 16: Progressive Delivery Strategies

Rolling Updates, Blue/Green, Canary, A/B Testing, Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Feature Flags, and Dark Launching — how to deploy safely and reduce risk with every release.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~3 hours🚀 Domain 2 · 25%

📖 Chapter Overview: Deploying software is the most dangerous thing you do in production. Every deploy is an opportunity to break something. Progressive delivery strategies reduce that risk — from simple Rolling Updates (the default) to sophisticated Canary deployments with automated analysis. This chapter covers: Rolling Update mechanics (maxSurge/maxUnavailable), Blue/Green with instant rollback, Canary with gradual traffic shifting, A/B Testing for feature experimentation, Argo Rollouts (K8s-native progressive delivery), Flagger (service mesh integration), Deployment safety fundamentals (probes, PDBs), Feature Flags (LaunchDarkly, OpenFeature), and Dark Launching (testing with zero user impact). CNPE Domain 2 (GitOps & CD — 25%).

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand the four core deployment strategies: Rolling, Blue/Green, Canary, A/B Testing
  • ✅ Configure Rolling Update parameters: maxSurge, maxUnavailable, minReadySeconds
  • ✅ Implement Blue/Green with Service selector switching and instant rollback
  • ✅ Design Canary deployments with gradual traffic percentages and automated analysis
  • ✅ Use Argo Rollouts for K8s-native BlueGreen, Canary, and AnalysisRuns
  • ✅ Integrate Flagger with service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) for progressive delivery
  • ✅ Apply Deployment safety: Readiness probes, Liveness probes, PodDisruptionBudgets
  • ✅ Decouple deployment from release with Feature Flags and Dark Launching
