16.1 Rolling Updates — The Default Strategy

🧠 What Is a Rolling Update? A Rolling Update gradually replaces old Pods with new ones, one (or a few) at a time. This is the default strategy for Kubernetes Deployments. The goal: zero downtime — traffic is always served by some healthy Pods while others are being replaced. But there's a brief window where old and new versions coexist.

Rolling Update — Step by Step (replicas: 4, maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0)
  TIME ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────►

  STEP 1: All old Pods running              STEP 2: 1 new Pod created (maxSurge)
  ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐             ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐
  │ v1.0 │ v1.0 │ v1.0 │ v1.0 │             │ v1.0 │ v1.0 │ v1.0 │ v1.0 │ v2.0 │
  └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘             └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘
  Service → all 4 old Pods                  Service → all 4 old + 1 new Pod

  STEP 3: 1 old Pod terminated              STEP 4: Repeat until all are new
  ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐             ┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┐
  │ v1.0 │ v1.0 │ v1.0 │ v2.0 │             │ v2.0 │ v2.0 │ v2.0 │ v2.0 │
  └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘             └──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┘
  Service → 3 old + 1 new                   Service → all new Pods ✓

  KEY: maxSurge=1 means at most 1 EXTRA pod above desired count.
        maxUnavailable=0 means no pods go down before a new one is ready.
        RESULT: Zero downtime, but ~25% of traffic briefly hits v2.0 during transition.
ParameterWhat It ControlsExampleEffect
maxSurgeHow many EXTRA Pods can be created ABOVE desired countmaxSurge: 14 replicas → up to 5 pods during rollout
maxUnavailableHow many Pods can be UNAVAILABLE during rolloutmaxUnavailable: 0No pod removed before new one is ready (safest)
minReadySecondsHow long a NEW Pod must be healthy before considering it "available"minReadySeconds: 30Pod must pass readiness probe for 30s before rollout continues
revisionHistoryLimitHow many old ReplicaSets to keep (for rollback)revisionHistoryLimit: 10Keep last 10 revisions — kubectl rollout undo uses these
✅
When Rolling Updates Shine
  • Stateless web apps (anihpj-web)
  • You have limited cluster resources
  • Gradual rollout is acceptable
  • New version is BACKWARD-COMPATIBLE with old
  • You use standard K8s Deployments (no extra tools)
⚠️
Rolling Update Limitations
  • Brief mixed-version window (old + new coexist)
  • No automated health-based rollback (manual kubectl rollout undo)
  • Can't control traffic % to new version
  • One bad pod can cause partial failures before detection
  • Not suitable for database schema changes
⚠️
Gotcha — Mixed Version Window: During a rolling update, old and new Pods coexist. If v2.0 writes data in a new format that v1.0 can't read, you have a problem. Always ensure backward compatibility of data formats, API contracts, and database schemas across at least ONE version. This is called the "N-1 compatibility rule."
🔬 The "Changing Tires on a Moving Car" Analogy

maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0 is like changing one tire at a time while the car keeps moving. You lift one corner (add a new pod), swap the tire (new pod becomes ready), lower that corner (remove old pod), then move to the next. At no point is the car on fewer than 4 wheels. But for a brief moment, one wheel is the new model while the others are old — the car handles slightly differently.

maxUnavailable=1, maxSurge=0 is like removing one tire FIRST, driving on 3 wheels briefly, then putting the new one on. Faster? Yes (no extra pods needed). Riskier? Absolutely — you're running degraded during the swap.

📊 Rolling Update Progress — 5 Replicas, maxSurge=1, maxUnavailable=0
Start (0%)
0%
5 old, 0 new
Step 1
16%
5 old + 1 new (surge)
Step 2
20%
4 old, 1 new (old removed)
Step 3
40%
3 old, 2 new
Step 5
80%
1 old, 4 new
Done (100%)
100%
0 old, 5 new ✓
🔬 kubectl rollout — Essential Commands for Rolling Update Control
CommandWhat It Does
kubectl rollout status deploy/anihpj-webWatch rollout progress — blocks until complete or failed. Shows "Waiting for rollout to finish: 2 of 5 updated replicas are available..."
kubectl rollout pause deploy/anihpj-webPause a rolling update mid-rollout. Existing pods continue serving. Use when you suspect an issue and want to investigate before continuing.
kubectl rollout resume deploy/anihpj-webResume a paused rollout. New pods continue replacing old ones.
kubectl rollout undo deploy/anihpj-webRollback to the PREVIOUS revision. Uses the old ReplicaSet. Add --to-revision=3 to rollback to a specific revision.
kubectl rollout history deploy/anihpj-webList all revisions with CHANGE-CAUSE (if you set kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation). Add --revision=3 to see details of revision 3.
kubectl rollout restart deploy/anihpj-webRestart all pods via a rolling restart. Adds an annotation to the Pod template, triggering a new ReplicaSet. Useful for config changes that don't change the image.

CNPE Exam: You'll almost certainly use kubectl rollout status and kubectl rollout undo. Memorize: status blocks and shows progress. undo goes back one revision by default. history shows what happened. restart creates a new ReplicaSet without changing anything.

🔬 Inside the Deployment Controller — How Rolling Updates Actually Work

The Deployment controller doesn't directly manage pods. It creates and scales ReplicaSets. Each time you change the Pod template (new image tag, new env var), the controller creates a NEW ReplicaSet and scales it up while scaling the OLD one down. Here's the exact algorithm:

1
Detect Change

Deployment spec changed (new image tag). Controller detects difference between desired and observed state.

2
New ReplicaSet

Controller creates new ReplicaSet with updated Pod template. Initially scaled to 0 replicas.

3
Scale Up New

New ReplicaSet scaled up by 1 (maxSurge). Old still at full count. Total pods = desired + surge.

4
Wait Ready

New pod must pass readiness probe + minReadySeconds. If it fails, rollout stalls — not proceeds.

5
Scale Down Old

Old ReplicaSet scaled down by 1 (maxUnavailable). Pod receives SIGTERM. Graceful shutdown begins.

6
Repeat

Loop steps 3-5 until new ReplicaSet = desired replicas, old ReplicaSet = 0. Old ReplicaSet kept for rollback.

Key insight: The controller never deletes the old ReplicaSet — it scales it to 0. This preserves the exact Pod template for kubectl rollout undo. Rolling back simply reverses the process: scale old ReplicaSet up, scale new one down. revisionHistoryLimit controls how many old ReplicaSets are kept. When the limit is exceeded, the OLDEST ReplicaSet (not the one scaled to 0 but the one from revision N-revisionHistoryLimit) is deleted.

16.2 Blue/Green Deployments — Instant Rollback, Double Resources

Blue/Green maintains two complete, independent environments. Blue = current production (live). Green = new version (idle, tested). To deploy, you switch traffic from Blue to Green by changing a Service selector. To rollback, switch it back. Rollback is instant — just change the label.

Blue/Green Deployment — The Label Switch Pattern
  BEFORE SWITCH (Blue is LIVE)              AFTER SWITCH (Green is LIVE)
  ┌──────────────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │     LOAD BALANCER        │              │     LOAD BALANCER        │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐  │              │  ┌────────────────────┐  │
  │  │   Service: anihpj  │  │              │  │   Service: anihpj  │  │
  │  │   selector:        │  │              │  │   selector:        │  │
  │  │     version: blue ─│──┼───► BLUE ✓   │  │     version: green─│──┼───► GREEN ✓
  │  └────────────────────┘  │              │  └────────────────────┘  │
  └──────────────────────────┘              └──────────────────────────┘
           │                                        │
           ▼                                        ▼
  ┌──────────────────┐                 ┌──────────────────┐
  │  BLUE ENVIRONMENT │                 │  BLUE ENVIRONMENT │
  │  ┌──────┬──────┐  │                 │  ┌──────┬──────┐  │
  │  │ v1.0 │ v1.0 │  │ ← LIVE         │  │ v1.0 │ v1.0 │  │ ← IDLE (standby)
  │  └──────┴──────┘  │                 │  └──────┴──────┘  │
  └──────────────────┘                 └──────────────────┘
  ┌──────────────────┐                 ┌──────────────────┐
  │  GREEN ENVIRONMENT│                 │  GREEN ENVIRONMENT│
  │  ┌──────┬──────┐  │                 │  ┌──────┬──────┐  │
  │  │ v2.0 │ v2.0 │  │ ← IDLE         │  │ v2.0 │ v2.0 │  │ ← LIVE
  │  └──────┴──────┘  │                 │  └──────┴──────┘  │
  └──────────────────┘                 └──────────────────┘

  THE SWITCH: kubectl patch service anihpj -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}'
  ROLLBACK:   kubectl patch service anihpj -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"blue"}}}'
⚡
Blue/Green Advantages
  • Instant rollback: One label change → all traffic back to Blue
  • Pre-deployment testing: Test Green fully before switching
  • No mixed versions: All users see either v1.0 OR v2.0, never both
  • Simple mental model: Just two environments, one label switch
💸
Blue/Green Disadvantages
  • 2x resource cost: Both environments run simultaneously during switch
  • Database is shared: Schema changes must be backward-compatible (both versions share the DB)
  • Session loss: In-flight user sessions may break (sticky sessions tied to Blue pods)
  • Cold start: Green's cache is empty — first requests are slow (warm cache before switch)
🎯
Exam Tip: The CNPE exam might ask: "Why is Blue/Green harder for databases than stateless apps?" Answer: Databases share persistent storage. You can't have two database instances writing to the same volume. For databases, use Rolling Updates or schema migration tools — Blue/Green works for stateless apps, not stateful ones (unless you use a separate DB per environment, which doubles storage cost).
🔬 Session Stickiness & Cache Warming — Blue/Green Pitfalls Solved

Two problems bite Blue/Green adopters:

🔗
Session Loss Problem

User has an active session on a Blue pod. Traffic switches to Green — session data is gone (stored in-memory on Blue). Solutions: (1) Externalize sessions to Redis — both Blue and Green read/write the same Redis. (2) Use stateless JWT tokens — session encoded in the token, no server-side storage. (3) Set sessionAffinity: ClientIP on the Service — same user IP always goes to same pod type, but doesn't survive pod restarts.

🔥
Cold Cache Problem

Green pods start with empty caches. First requests after the switch are SLOW (cache misses, DB hits spike). Solutions: (1) Cache warming script: Before switching, replay recent production requests against Green to populate caches. (2) Gradual warm-up: Route 5% traffic to Green for 10 min before the full switch. (3) Shared cache: Use an external cache (Redis/Memcached) shared between Blue and Green — no cold start.

📊 Resource Cost Comparison — Deployment Strategies (4 replicas, 2 CPU / 4Gi each)
Rolling
10 CPU / 20Gi
maxSurge=1 → 5 pods peak
Blue/Green
16 CPU / 32Gi
2× environments → 8 pods
Canary
10.5 CPU / 21Gi
4 stable + 1 canary → 5 pods

Blue/Green is 60% more expensive than Canary for the same deployment. This is why Canary is preferred for routine deployments — you get automated analysis AND lower cost. Blue/Green is reserved for critical releases where instant rollback justifies the cost.

🔬 Ingress-Level Blue/Green — Production-Grade Traffic Switching

The basic Service selector switch works, but production platforms need more control. Ingress-level Blue/Green uses the Ingress controller to route traffic based on annotations or host headers, providing:

🔀
NGINX Ingress Canary Annotations

NGINX Ingress supports canary/blue-green natively via annotations on a SECOND Ingress resource:

nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary: "true"
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-weight: "100"
# 100 = full switch to Green. 0 = all Blue.

Create TWO Ingresses: one for Blue (stable, no annotations), one for Green (canary annotations). Adjust canary-weight from 0→100 to switch.

🌐
Istio VirtualService Weight

Istio routes traffic by weight at the mesh level — no Ingress changes needed:

spec:
http:
- route:
- destination:
host: anihpj-web
subset: blue
weight: 0
- destination:
host: anihpj-web
subset: green
weight: 100

Production recommendation: Use Ingress-level Blue/Green (not Service selector) when you need: (1) Sticky sessions that survive the switch, (2) Header-based routing for internal testers during the Blue phase, (3) Gradual weight shifting (not all-or-nothing), (4) Integration with cert-manager for automatic TLS on both environments.

16.3 Canary Deployments — The Gold Standard

A Canary deployment routes a small percentage of real production traffic to the new version, monitors it, and gradually increases the percentage. If the new version shows errors, traffic is automatically shifted back. This is the safest and most sophisticated deployment strategy.

Canary Deployment — Gradual Traffic Shifting with Automated Analysis
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                           CANARY LIFECYCLE                                  │
  │                                                                             │
  │  STEP 1              STEP 2              STEP 3              STEP 4         │
  │  5% → v2.0          25% → v2.0          50% → v2.0         100% → v2.0     │
  │  ┌───┬───┐          ┌───┬───┐          ┌───┬───┐          ┌───┬───┐        │
  │  │v1 │v2 │          │v1 │v2 │          │v1 │v2 │          │v2 │v2 │        │
  │  │95%│ 5%│          │75%│25%│          │50%│50%│          │0% │100%│       │
  │  └───┴───┘          └───┴───┘          └───┴───┘          └───┴───┘        │
  │    │                  │                  │                  │               │
  │    ▼                  ▼                  ▼                  ▼               │
  │  ┌─────────┐       ┌─────────┐       ┌─────────┐       ┌─────────┐        │
  │  │ANALYZE  │       │ANALYZE  │       │ANALYZE  │       │ PROMOTE │        │
  │  │5 min    │──────►│5 min    │──────►│5 min    │──────►│ ✓ FULL  │        │
  │  │✓ healthy│       │✓ healthy│       │✓ healthy│       │   v2.0  │        │
  │  └─────────┘       └─────────┘       └─────────┘       └─────────┘        │
  │                                                                             │
  │  IF ANY STEP FAILS (error rate > threshold):                                │
  │  ┌─────────┐                                                                │
  │  │ ABORT!  │  ← Immediately shift 100% back to v1.0                        │
  │  │ Rollback│                                                                │
  │  └─────────┘                                                                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ANALYSIS CHECKS (run at every step):
  • Error rate < 1% (Prometheus: rate(http_errors[5m]) / rate(http_requests[5m]))
  • P99 latency < 500ms (Prometheus: histogram_quantile(0.99, http_latency))
  • No crash loops (kubectl get pods — any restarts > 0?)
Canary vs Rolling vs Blue/Green — At a Glance
DimensionRolling UpdateBlue/GreenCanary
Traffic controlNone — mixed by pod countAll-or-nothing switchPrecise % per step (5%, 25%, 50%, 100%)
Rollback speedSlow (kubectl rollout undo re-rolls)Instant (label switch)Instant (shift traffic back)
Resource costNormal + maxSurge overhead2x during deploymentNormal + canary pods
Automated analysisNone (manual)None (manual)Built-in (AnalysisRuns)
Mixed versionsBrief windowNoneControlled coexistence
Best forStateless apps, simple setupsCritical releases, instant rollbackHigh-traffic, risk-averse, automated
RequiresStandard K8s DeploymentService + selector managementService mesh OR Argo Rollouts
⚡
Speed Tip: The canary step duration is critical. Too short (30s) — you miss slow-burn errors. Too long (30 min) — deployments take hours. A good rule: each step should be 5-10 minutes, long enough to see a statistically significant sample of traffic. For low-traffic services, use longer intervals.
🔬 How to Set Canary Analysis Thresholds (Not Guesswork!)

Setting thresholds too tight (error rate > 0.1% → abort) causes false positives — every minor traffic fluctuation triggers an abort. Setting them too loose (error rate > 10% → abort) defeats the purpose. Here's the systematic approach:

MetricHow to Set the ThresholdExample
Error rateTake your P95 error rate over the last 30 days. Multiply by 2. That's your threshold.P95 = 0.4% → threshold = 0.8%. If canary > 0.8%, abort.
P99 latencyTake P99 latency baseline. Threshold = baseline × 1.5.Baseline P99 = 800ms → threshold = 1200ms. If canary > 1200ms, abort.
CPU/MemoryCanary usage should be within 20% of stable version's usage.Stable uses 200m CPU → canary threshold = 240m. Beyond that, investigate.
Crash loopsAny restarts in the canary pods during the analysis window = abort.count: 1, failureLimit: 0 — abort on first restart.

Golden rule: Your threshold should be wider than normal variance but narrower than "definitely broken." A 2× multiplier on P95 values works well for most services. Also: use count (consecutive successes required) to avoid flapping — a single spike above threshold doesn't abort. Require 2-3 consecutive failures before aborting.

🔬 Istio Canary — VirtualService + DestinationRule
# DestinationRule: Define subsets (stable vs canary)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
spec:
  host: anihpj-web
  subsets:
    - name: stable      # v1.0 pods
      labels:
        version: stable
    - name: canary      # v2.0 pods
      labels:
        version: canary

# VirtualService: Split traffic by weight
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: VirtualService
spec:
  hosts:
    - anihpj-web
  http:
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: anihpj-web
            subset: stable
          weight: 80     # 80% → stable v1.0
        - destination:
            host: anihpj-web
            subset: canary
          weight: 20     # 20% → canary v2.0
🔬 Handling Stateful Canary — The DB Write Problem

When canary pods write to the SAME database as stable pods, schema changes or new data formats can corrupt data. Three solutions:

  • Backward-compatible schema: New columns must be NULLABLE or have defaults. Old code ignores new columns. New code handles missing columns gracefully. This is the "expand-contract" pattern.
  • Separate DB per version: Canary pods write to anihpj-db-v2, stable to anihpj-db-v1. At full promotion, switch the app to v2 DB and decommission v1. Doubles DB cost during canary.
  • Read-only canary: Canary pods handle reads only. Writes go to stable pods. Works for read-heavy services (search, catalog). Requires app-level routing logic.

Golden rule for databases: Never run schema migrations that break backward compatibility during a canary. Migrate in two phases: Phase 1 = add new columns (safe, old code ignores them). Phase 2 = remove old columns AFTER full promotion and verification.

16.4 A/B Testing — Feature Experimentation, Not Safety

⚠️ Important Distinction: A/B Testing is NOT a deployment safety strategy. It's a product experimentation technique. Canary = "Is v2.0 stable?" A/B = "Do users prefer the blue button or the green button?" Both versions are considered stable — you're testing user behavior, not code quality.

A/B Testing — Route Users Based on Headers/Cookies
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                       LOAD BALANCER                              │
  │                                                                  │
  │  Request: GET /                                                  │
  │  Header: X-User-Group: A              Header: X-User-Group: B    │
  │  Cookie: feature=new-search           Cookie: feature=old-search │
  │         │                                     │                  │
  │         ▼                                     ▼                  │
  │  ┌──────────────┐                      ┌──────────────┐         │
  │  │  VARIANT A   │                      │  VARIANT B   │         │
  │  │  New search  │ ← 10% of users       │  Old search  │ ← 90%   │
  │  │  UI (v2.0)   │                      │  UI (v1.0)   │         │
  │  └──────────────┘                      └──────────────┘         │
  │         │                                     │                  │
  │         ▼                                     ▼                  │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐       │
  │  │              ANALYTICS PLATFORM                      │       │
  │  │  • Variant A: 12% conversion rate, 3.2s avg session │       │
  │  │  • Variant B: 8% conversion rate,  2.1s avg session │       │
  │  │  → Variant A wins on conversion! Roll out to 100%.  │       │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧪
A/B Testing Tools
  • Istio VirtualService: Route by HTTP header/cookie weight
  • NGINX Ingress: Canary by header (nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/canary-by-header)
  • LaunchDarkly: Feature flag with user targeting
  • Optimizely / Google Optimize: Client-side A/B
📊
Metrics to Compare
  • Conversion rate (signups, purchases)
  • Session duration / engagement
  • Error rate (does new UI cause more bugs?)
  • Page load time (performance impact)
  • User satisfaction (NPS, survey)
🎯
Exam Tip: The CNPE exam expects you to distinguish between Canary and A/B Testing. Canary = safety check (is the new version stable?). A/B = product experiment (which version do users prefer?). In a canary, you WANT all users to eventually get v2.0. In A/B, you're comparing metrics between variants to decide IF v2.0 should win.

16.5 Argo Rollouts — K8s-Native Progressive Delivery

🧠 What Is Argo Rollouts? Argo Rollouts is a Kubernetes controller that replaces the standard Deployment with a Rollout resource. Rollouts support BlueGreen and Canary strategies with built-in AnalysisRuns — automated checks that query Prometheus, Datadog, or custom metrics to decide whether to promote or abort. This is the CNPE exam's preferred progressive delivery tool.

Argo Rollout — Canary for anihpj-web
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
spec:
  replicas: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 20           # Step 1: 20% traffic → v2.0
        - pause: {duration: 5m}      # Wait 5 minutes, monitor
        - setWeight: 40           # Step 2: 40% traffic
        - pause: {duration: 5m}
        - setWeight: 100          # Step 3: 100% traffic → FULL PROMOTION
  template:
    # ... standard Pod template (same as Deployment) ...
AnalysisTemplate — Automated Health Check via Prometheus
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: anihpj-health-check
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: error-rate
      interval: 1m            # Query every 1 minute
      count: 5                 # Must pass 5 consecutive times
      failureLimit: 2         # 2 failures → ABORT rollout
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
          query: |
            rate(http_requests_total{
              app="anihpj-web",
              status=~"5.."
            }[5m]) / rate(http_requests_total{
              app="anihpj-web"
            }[5m])
      successCondition: result < 0.01  # Error rate < 1%
    - name: p99-latency
      interval: 1m
      count: 3
      provider:
        prometheus:
          query: |
            histogram_quantile(0.99,
              rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{
                app="anihpj-web"
              }[5m]))
      successCondition: result < 1.0  # P99 < 1 second
🎯
Exam Tip: The AnalysisRun is where most candidates lose points. Remember: count = number of consecutive successes needed. failureLimit = number of failures before abort (default 0 = abort on first failure). successCondition must be a valid expression that evaluates to true/false. The query result is available as result in the expression. Common mistake: forgetting that failureLimit: 1 still requires one failure to trigger — set failureLimit: 0 for immediate abort on first failure.
🔬 Argo Rollout — BlueGreen Strategy
strategy:
  blueGreen:
    activeService: anihpj-web-active  # Points to LIVE
    previewService: anihpj-web-preview # Points to STAGING
    autoPromotionEnabled: false  # Manual promotion
    prePromotionAnalysis:          # Run analysis BEFORE switch
      templates:
        - templateName: anihpj-health-check
    postPromotionAnalysis:         # Run analysis AFTER switch
      templates:
        - templateName: anihpj-smoke-test

# Manual promotion: kubectl argo rollouts promote anihpj-web
# Auto-rollback: kubectl argo rollouts abort anihpj-web
🔬 kubectl argo rollouts CLI Quick Reference
  • kubectl argo rollouts get rollout anihpj-web — Current status, step, weight
  • kubectl argo rollouts get rollout anihpj-web --watch — Live stream the rollout progress
  • kubectl argo rollouts promote anihpj-web — Skip remaining steps, jump to 100%
  • kubectl argo rollouts abort anihpj-web — Immediately abort, traffic back to stable
  • kubectl argo rollouts retry rollout anihpj-web — Retry a failed/aborted rollout
  • kubectl argo rollouts dashboard — Open local web UI at localhost:3100
  • kubectl argo rollouts set image anihpj-web *=ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.1.0 — Update image (triggers rollout)

BlueGreen specific: activeService always points at the LIVE environment. previewService points at the STAGING environment (not live). After promotion, the "preview" ReplicaSet becomes the new "active" and vice versa. This is more sophisticated than the basic label-switch Blue/Green.

🔬 AnalysisRun Providers — Beyond Prometheus

Argo Rollouts AnalysisRuns support multiple metric providers. You're not limited to Prometheus. Here's when to use each:

ProviderWhat It QueriesBest ForExample
PrometheusAny PromQL metricError rate, latency, throughput, saturationrate(http_errors[5m]) / rate(http_requests[5m]) < 0.01
DatadogDatadog metrics APITeams already on Datadog. APM traces, logs correlationError rate from Datadog APM, custom metrics from app
NewRelicNRQL queriesNewRelic APM usersSELECT rate(count(*), 5 minutes) FROM TransactionError WHERE appName='anihpj'
JobRuns a K8s Job. Success = Job completes (exit 0). Fail = any other exit codeCustom validation: integration tests, DB query, external API checkRun pytest against canary endpoint, verify all tests pass
WebHTTP POST to an external endpoint. Success = 2xx responseCustom webhooks: pipeline status, security scan results, approval gatesPOST to Jenkins/GitHub Actions for CI check status
WavefrontWavefront Query LanguageVMware Tanzu usersError rate from Wavefront metrics
CloudWatchAWS CloudWatch metricsAWS-native monitoringALB 5xx count, ECS task health
KayentaCanary analysis from Netflix/SpinnakerStatistical canary analysis (Mann-Whitney U test)Compare canary vs baseline metrics with statistical significance

CNPE relevance: The exam doesn't expect you to know every provider. But you MUST know: (1) The Job provider runs arbitrary K8s Jobs — this is the escape hatch for ANY custom check. (2) The Web provider integrates with external systems via HTTP. (3) successCondition always evaluates result — the query output is always named result.

16.6 Flagger — Progressive Delivery WITH Your Existing Deployments

🧠 Flagger vs Argo Rollouts: Argo Rollouts replaces the Deployment resource entirely (you use kind: Rollout instead of kind: Deployment). Flagger works alongside your existing Deployments — it creates and manages canary resources automatically. If you can't change your Deployment to a Rollout, use Flagger.

Flagger Architecture — How It Works WITH Your Deployment
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                         FLAGGER CONTROLLER                         │
  │                                                                    │
  │  1. Watch for changes in Deployment (new image tag)               │
  │  2. Create canary Deployment + canary Service                      │
  │  3. Configure mesh/ingress to split traffic                        │
  │  4. Run analysis (query Prometheus/Datadog/CloudWatch)            │
  │  5. PROMOTE: Update primary Deployment to new image               │
  │     OR ABORT: Delete canary, traffic stays on old version         │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
           │                    │                    │
           ▼                    ▼                    ▼
  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐
  │ YOUR          │    │ CANARY        │    │ SERVICE MESH  │
  │ Deployment    │    │ Deployment    │    │ (Istio/Linkerd│
  │ (unchanged!)  │    │ (auto-managed)│    │  NGINX/Contour│
  │              │    │              │    │  App Mesh)    │
  └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘
FeatureArgo RolloutsFlagger
Resource typeReplaces Deployment (kind: Rollout)Works WITH existing Deployment
Service mesh required?No (can use basic traffic routing)Yes (needs Istio, Linkerd, NGINX, etc.)
AnalysisAnalysisRun + AnalysisTemplate (Prometheus, Datadog, Job, Web)Canary analysis (Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch, Graphite)
StrategiesBlueGreen, CanaryCanary, A/B Testing, Blue/Green (via Canary)
Webhook notificationsNative (Slack, Teams, generic)Native (Slack, Teams, Discord, generic)
Best forGitOps-native teams already using Argo CDTeams with existing mesh, want minimal changes
⚡
Speed Tip: If your CNPE exam question mentions "existing Deployments that can't be modified" — the answer is Flagger, not Argo Rollouts. If the question mentions "GitOps with Argo CD already in place" — the answer is Argo Rollouts. Context matters.
🔬 Flagger Canary CRD — Declarative Progressive Delivery for anihpj
apiVersion: flagger.app/v1beta1
kind: Canary
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  # Reference YOUR existing Deployment (unchanged!)
  targetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: anihpj-web
  # How traffic reaches the app (mesh/ingress)
  service:
    port: 8080
    gateways:              # Istio-specific
      - istio-system/public-gateway
  # Canary strategy definition
  analysis:
    interval: 1m             # Check every 1 minute
    threshold: 5             # Max failures before rollback
    maxWeight: 50            # Max canary traffic %
    stepWeight: 10           # Increase by 10% each step
    stepWeightPromotion: 10  # Steps after passing checks
    metrics:
      - name: request-success-rate
        thresholdRange:
          min: 99          # Must be > 99% success
        interval: 1m
      - name: request-duration
        thresholdRange:
          max: 500        # P99 must be < 500ms
        interval: 1m
    webhooks:                 # Optional: external checks
      - name: smoke-test
        type: pre-rollout       # Run BEFORE traffic shift
        url: http://flagger-loadtester.anihpj/
        timeout: 30s
⚠️
Gotcha — Flagger Creates Resources Automatically: When you apply this Canary CR, Flagger creates: a canary Deployment, a canary Service, and modifies your Istio VirtualService. Do NOT manually create these — Flagger manages them. If you delete the Flagger-created canary Deployment, Flagger re-creates it. The primary Deployment stays untouched.

16.7 Deployment Safety — Probes, PDBs, and Graceful Shutdown

Progressive delivery strategies are only as good as the safety mechanisms underneath. Three Kubernetes primitives form the foundation of safe deployments:

🏥
Readiness Probe

Question: "Is this Pod ready to receive traffic?" If the probe FAILS, the Pod is removed from the Service's endpoints — no traffic is sent to it. Use for: warm-up time, dependency checks (DB reachable?), cache loading.

readinessProbe:
httpGet:
path: /healthz
port: 8080
initialDelaySeconds: 10
periodSeconds: 5

💀
Liveness Probe

Question: "Is this Pod still alive, or should we restart it?" If the probe FAILS, the Pod is KILLED and restarted. NEVER check external dependencies — if your DB is down, restarting the Pod won't fix it. Check internal health only.

livenessProbe:
httpGet:
path: /live
port: 8080
initialDelaySeconds: 30
periodSeconds: 10

🛡️
PodDisruptionBudget (PDB)

Question: "How many Pods can be down simultaneously during VOLUNTARY disruptions (node drain, cluster upgrade)?" Prevents ALL Pods from being evicted at once. PDB does NOT protect against involuntary disruptions (node crash).

spec:
minAvailable: 2
# OR maxUnavailable: 1
selector:
matchLabels:
app: anihpj-web

⏱️
Graceful Shutdown

When a Pod is terminated: (1) SIGTERM sent to container. (2) terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30s) countdown begins. (3) If still running, SIGKILL. Your app must handle SIGTERM gracefully: stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, close DB connections.

spec:
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60
# Give app 60s to clean up

⚠️
Gotcha — Readiness vs Liveness: A readiness probe failure says "don't send traffic to this Pod." A liveness probe failure says "kill this Pod and restart it." Never put external dependency checks in your liveness probe. If your DB goes down, ALL pods fail liveness → ALL pods restart → cascading failure. Use readiness for dependency checks, liveness for internal deadlocks (thread exhaustion, infinite loops).
🚀
🔬 Startup Probe — For Slow-Starting Apps

If your app takes 60s to start (legacy monolith, ML model loading), a liveness probe with initialDelaySeconds: 60 is fragile. Instead, use a startup probe: it runs FIRST, and until it succeeds, liveness and readiness are DISABLED. This prevents premature restarts of slow-starting apps.

startupProbe:
httpGet:
path: /startup
port: 8080
failureThreshold: 30
periodSeconds: 10
# Gives app up to 300s (30×10s) to start

🪝
🔬 preStop Hook — Graceful Connection Draining

Problem: Pod receives SIGTERM. kube-proxy removes it from endpoints. But there's a RACE: new connections may still arrive before iptables rules update. Solution: Add a preStop hook that sleeps 5-10 seconds BEFORE the container receives SIGTERM. This gives kube-proxy time to update.

lifecycle:
preStop:
exec:
command: ["/bin/sh","-c",
"sleep 10"]
# Sleep 10s → iptables updated →
# THEN SIGTERM sent to app

🔬 Pod Termination Lifecycle — The Full Sequence of Events

When a Pod is deleted (rolling update, node drain, scale-down), a precise sequence of events unfolds. Understanding this sequence is critical for zero-downtime deployments:

1
DELETE

API Server marks Pod for deletion. deletionTimestamp set. terminating state.

2
preStop

If preStop hook defined, it runs FIRST. Sleep 5-10s here gives kube-proxy time to update iptables.

3
SIGTERM

Container receives SIGTERM. App should: stop accepting connections, finish in-flight work, close DB pools.

4
GRACE PERIOD

terminationGracePeriodSeconds countdown (default 30s). App has this long to shut down.

5
SIGKILL

If still running after grace period, SIGKILL (force stop). No chance to clean up. Data loss possible.

6
REMOVED

Pod removed from API Server. Endpoints updated. Replacement Pod scheduled if needed.

Key timing insight: The race condition between steps 2-3 and kube-proxy is real. Even with preStop, some requests MAY still reach the dying Pod. That's why your app must handle SIGTERM gracefully — stop accepting but finish processing. Don't just crash.

🔬 PodDisruptionBudget — The Math Behind Safe Disruptions

A PDB doesn't PREVENT disruptions — it LIMITS them. During voluntary disruptions (node drains, cluster upgrades), the eviction API checks the PDB: "If I evict this Pod, will the PDB still be satisfied?" If not, the eviction is REJECTED (HTTP 429).

PDB SettingWith 5 ReplicasMax Pods Evictable at OnceBest For
minAvailable: 4At least 4 must be running1 (5 − 4 = 1)Critical services that need most pods running
minAvailable: 3At least 3 must be running2 (5 − 3 = 2)Balanced safety vs drain speed
minAvailable: 1At least 1 must be running4 (5 − 1 = 4)Fast drains, but risk of single point of failure
maxUnavailable: 1At most 1 can be down1Same as minAvailable:4 — expressed differently
maxUnavailable: 25%At most 25% can be down1 (25% of 5 = 1.25, rounded down to 1)Dynamic scaling — works with HPA

minAvailable vs maxUnavailable: Use minAvailable when you think in terms of "I need X pods running." Use maxUnavailable when you think in terms of "I can tolerate X pods down." They're mathematically equivalent: minAvailable = replicas − maxUnavailable. The difference is mental model. maxUnavailable with percentages works better with HPA because it scales automatically.

CNPE Exam Gotcha: PDBs only protect against voluntary disruptions (evictions). A node crash (involuntary) ignores the PDB entirely. Also: if you set minAvailable: 5 with 5 replicas, no Pod can ever be evicted — not even one at a time. This blocks cluster upgrades. Always leave at least 1 pod of "headroom" in your PDB.

16.8 Feature Flags — Decouple Deploy from Release

🧠 The Big Idea: Deployment ≠ Release. Deployment = code is running in production. Release = users can see/use the feature. Feature flags let you deploy code that's toggled OFF — you can test it in production with internal users, then gradually release to real users, all without a new deployment.

Feature Flag Lifecycle — Deploy Dark, Release Gradually
  CODE MERGED                    FEATURE FLAGGED ON                 FEATURE FLAG REMOVED
       │                              │                                   │
       ▼                              ▼                                   ▼
  ┌──────────┐                 ┌──────────────┐                  ┌──────────────┐
  │ DEPLOY   │                 │ RELEASE TO   │                  │ CLEAN UP     │
  │ Code is  │                 │ 10% internal │                  │ Remove flag  │
  │ in prod  │  ───────────►   │ users first  │  ───────────►   │ from code    │
  │ but OFF  │                 │              │                  │ Feature is   │
  │          │                 │ Then 5% real │                  │ permanent    │
  └──────────┘                 └──────────────┘                  └──────────────┘

  THE FLAG CHECK (in application code):
  if (featureFlag.isEnabled("new-payment-flow", user.id)) {
      return newPaymentFlow.process(payment);   // NEW code path
  } else {
      return legacyPaymentFlow.process(payment); // OLD code path (safe default)
  }
🏗️
Feature Flag Tools
  • OpenFeature: CNCF incubating — open standard for feature flags. Vendor-neutral API. Switch providers without code changes.
  • LaunchDarkly: SaaS feature management. Real-time flag updates, user targeting, experiments.
  • Flagsmith: Open-source alternative. Self-hosted or cloud.
  • ConfigMap-based: Simple flags via K8s ConfigMap (no dynamic updates without restart).
🎯
Feature Flag Use Cases
  • Kill switch: Turn off a misbehaving feature instantly
  • Beta testing: Release to internal users before public
  • Percentage rollout: 5% → 25% → 100% of users
  • Targeted release: Only users in EU region, or on enterprise plan
  • Trunk-based development: Merge incomplete features to main, toggle off
⚡
Speed Tip: Test feature flags in staging by toggling them via environment variables: FEATURE_NEW_PAYMENT=true. In production, use a feature flag service for dynamic control. Never use environment variables for flags in production — they require a pod restart to change, defeating the purpose of instant toggling.
🔬 OpenFeature — Vendor-Neutral Flag API (Python/Django)
# pip install openfeature-sdk
from openfeature import api
from openfeature.provider import no_op_provider

# Set provider (LaunchDarkly, Flagsmith, or no-op for testing)
api.set_provider(no_op_provider.NoOpProvider())
client = api.get_client()

# Boolean flag — is feature enabled for this user?
if client.get_boolean_value(
    "new-payment-flow",  # Flag key
    False,                 # Default value (safe!)
    evaluation_context={
        "userId": user.id,
        "region": user.region
    }
):
    return new_payment_flow.process(payment)
else:
    return legacy_payment_flow.process(payment)
🔬 Feature Flag Technical Debt — The Cleanup Problem

Flags multiply. After 6 months, you have 200 flags, nobody knows which are still needed, and the code is littered with if flag.isEnabled() branches. Solution: Flag lifecycle management.

  • Every flag gets an expiration date. Flag service auto-notifies the owner after 30 days.
  • Flag removal is part of "definition of done." After full rollout, create a ticket to remove the flag from code.
  • Use kill switches sparingly. Permanent kill switches are OK (payment gateway failover). Feature toggles should be temporary.
  • Audit quarterly. List all flags. Delete any not toggled in 90 days.
  • Test BOTH paths. CI must test with flag ON and OFF. If the OFF path rots (nobody tests it), toggling OFF breaks production.

16.9 Dark Launching — Test With Real Traffic, Zero User Impact

Dark Launching (also called "traffic shadowing" or "mirroring") sends a COPY of real production traffic to the new version, but discards the response. Users never see the new version's output — but you can monitor its behavior under real load.

Dark Launching — Production Traffic Mirrored to v2.0
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     LOAD BALANCER                            │
  │                                                              │
  │  User Request ──► v1.0 (PRIMARY) ──► Response to User ✓     │
  │       │                                                      │
  │       └────► v2.0 (SHADOW)   ──► Response DISCARDED ✗       │
  │                    │                                         │
  │                    ▼                                         │
  │              ┌──────────┐                                    │
  │              │ MONITOR  │                                    │
  │              │ • Errors │  ← Compare v2.0 errors vs v1.0    │
  │              │ • Latency│  ← v2.0 P99 vs v1.0 P99           │
  │              │ • Memory │  ← v2.0 memory leak under load?   │
  │              │ • CPU    │  ← v2.0 CPU spike at scale?       │
  │              └──────────┘                                    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE (Istio VirtualService traffic mirroring):
  apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1beta1
  kind: VirtualService
  spec:
    http:
    - route:
      - destination:
          host: anihpj-web
          subset: v1
        weight: 100
      mirror:
        host: anihpj-web     ← Mirror 100% of v1 traffic to v2
        subset: v2
      mirrorPercentage:
        value: 100.0          ← Mirror ALL traffic (can reduce to 10%)
✅
Dark Launching Benefits
  • Zero user impact: v2.0 responses are discarded
  • Real traffic patterns: Not synthetic — actual user behavior
  • Performance testing: Find memory leaks, CPU spikes under real load
  • Safe for stateful: v2.0 can write to a test DB while v1.0 writes to real DB
⚠️
Dark Launching Risks
  • Double writes: If v2.0 writes to the SAME DB as v1.0, you get duplicate data
  • External API calls: v2.0 calls payment APIs — those calls are REAL, not mirrored
  • Resource cost: v2.0 pods consume real CPU/memory
  • Not for A/B comparison: Can't compare user-facing metrics (responses discarded)
🔬 Dark Launching vs Canary — Don't Confuse These!
Dark LaunchingCanary
Traffic is MIRRORED (copied) to v2.0Traffic is ROUTED (redirected) to v2.0
v2.0 response is DISCARDED — user never sees itv2.0 response is RETURNED — user sees it
v1.0 receives 100% of trafficv1.0 receives decreasing % as canary grows
Goal: Performance testing under real loadGoal: Safety validation before full rollout
Runs before/during development — test new codeRuns during deployment — validate new version
Side effects (DB writes) must be isolated or discardedSide effects are REAL — v2.0 is the live version for its users
No traffic % control needed — it's a copyPrecise traffic % control required (5% → 25% → 100%)
Use when: you want to see if v2.0 SURVIVES real trafficUse when: you want to safely ROLL OUT v2.0 to users
Drill 16.1 Configure an Argo Rollout for anihpj-web

Scenario: Deploy anihpj-web with a canary rollout: 20% → 40% → 100%, 5 minutes between steps, with automated Prometheus analysis.

  1. Create a Rollout resource (not Deployment) with strategy.canary.steps
  2. Set steps: setWeight: 20 → pause: {duration: 5m} → setWeight: 40 → pause: {duration: 5m} → setWeight: 100
  3. Create an AnalysisTemplate with Prometheus query for error rate < 1%
  4. Reference the AnalysisTemplate in the Rollout under strategy.canary.analysis.templates
  5. Apply: kubectl apply -f rollout.yaml and watch: kubectl argo rollouts get rollout anihpj-web --watch
💡 Hint: The AnalysisTemplate must use successCondition: result < 0.01. The Rollout references it via analysis.templates[0].templateName, not a direct inline definition.
Drill 16.2 Blue/Green Service Switch

Scenario: Deploy v2.0 to Green, test it, then switch the Service from Blue to Green. Verify rollback.

  1. Label Blue pods: version: blue. Label Green pods: version: green
  2. Create Service with selector: {version: blue} — initially pointing at Blue
  3. Deploy Green pods. Test directly via port-forward: kubectl port-forward pod/anihpj-green-xxx 8080:8080
  4. Switch: kubectl patch svc anihpj -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}'
  5. Verify: kubectl describe svc anihpj — endpoints should show only Green pod IPs
  6. Rollback: Switch selector back to version: blue
💡 Hint: The switch is INSTANT — as soon as the Service selector changes, kube-proxy updates iptables/IPVS rules. Existing connections may linger (depending on sessionAffinity).
Drill 16.3 Deployment Safety Check

Scenario: Your anihpj Deployment has no probes and keeps failing during rollout. Add readiness, liveness, and a PDB.

  1. Add readinessProbe with httpGet /healthz, initialDelaySeconds: 10, periodSeconds: 5
  2. Add livenessProbe with httpGet /live, initialDelaySeconds: 30, periodSeconds: 10
  3. Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45 to allow in-flight requests to complete
  4. Create a PDB with minAvailable: 2 for your 3-replica Deployment
  5. Test: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets — should respect PDB
💡 Hint: minAvailable: 2 with 3 replicas means only 1 pod can be disrupted at a time. If you try to drain 2 nodes simultaneously, the second drain will hang until the first pod is rescheduled and ready.
Q1: Configure an Argo Rollout for anihpj-web with canary: 20% → 40% → 100%, 5 min between steps.

▶ Show Answer
Create a Rollout resource with strategy.canary.steps: [{setWeight: 20}, {pause: {duration: 5m}}, {setWeight: 40}, {pause: {duration: 5m}}, {setWeight: 100}]. The Rollout replaces the Deployment resource entirely — you reference the same Pod template.
Q2: Blue/Green for anihpj-db — why is this harder than for web pods?

▶ Show Answer
Databases share persistent storage. Blue/Green for a database means TWO instances writing to the same volume — data corruption. For stateless web pods, Blue and Green are independent. For databases, use Rolling Updates with backward-compatible schema migrations, or use a separate volume per environment (doubling storage cost).
Q3: During canary, Prometheus shows error rate 2.5% (threshold 1%). What should happen?

▶ Show Answer
The AnalysisRun should ABORT the rollout. Traffic immediately shifts back to the stable version (v1.0). The canary pods are terminated. The platform sends an alert to the on-call channel. The deployment team investigates the error spike before re-attempting.
Q4: Flagger vs Argo Rollouts — compare.

▶ Show Answer
Argo Rollouts: Replaces Deployment with Rollout CRD. Native GitOps (Argo CD integration). No service mesh required. Flagger: Works alongside existing Deployment. Requires service mesh (Istio/Linkerd). Auto-creates canary resources. Choose Argo Rollouts for GitOps-native teams; Flagger for teams with existing mesh and Deployments they can't change.
Q5: A/B testing for anihpj — show new job search UI to 10% of users. How do you implement?

▶ Show Answer
(1) Deploy both UI versions as separate Deployments (or use a feature flag). (2) Configure Istio VirtualService to route by X-User-Group header or cookie. (3) Route 10% to "variant-new-search", 90% to "variant-current". (4) Track conversion rates, session duration, error rates per variant. (5) If variant-new-search wins, roll out to 100%.
Q6: Readiness probe returns 503 for 30 seconds but the pod is healthy. What happens?

▶ Show Answer
The Pod is removed from the Service's endpoints — no traffic is sent to it for those 30 seconds. If this is during a rolling update, the rollout stalls because maxUnavailable pods are "unavailable." The pod continues running (it's not killed — that's liveness). After the probe succeeds again, the pod is re-added to endpoints.
Q7: Feature flag for "new payment flow" in anihpj — deploy code but toggle off. How to test in staging before production?

▶ Show Answer
(1) Deploy code to staging with flag OFF. (2) Use environment variable or flag service to enable for test users only. (3) Run integration tests against the new flow. (4) Verify old flow still works when flag is OFF. (5) In production, enable for 5% internal users → 10% beta users → 50% → 100%. If issues arise, toggle OFF instantly — no rollback needed.
Q8: Dark launch anihpj-api v2 — send 100% of traffic to v1 AND v2, discard v2 responses. Why do this?

▶ Show Answer
To test v2 under real production load without affecting users. v2 receives the exact same requests as v1, processes them, but its responses are discarded. You monitor v2's error rate, latency, memory, and CPU against v1's baseline. If v2 has a memory leak that only appears under real traffic patterns, you catch it before releasing to users.
Q9: Argo Rollouts AnalysisRun queries Prometheus. Write the AnalysisTemplate.

Show Answer
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1; kind: AnalysisTemplate; spec.metrics: [{name: error-rate, interval: 1m, count: 5, failureLimit: 2, provider: {prometheus: {address: http://prometheus:9090, query: "rate(http_errors[5m])/rate(http_requests[5m])"}}, successCondition: "result < 0.01"}]. Key: count = consecutive successes needed; failureLimit = failures before abort.
Q10: Your Blue/Green switch caused all user sessions to be lost. Why? How to fix?

▶ Show Answer
Why: User sessions were stored in-memory on Blue pods. When traffic switched to Green, the session data was gone. Fix: (1) Externalize sessions to Redis or a shared database — both Blue and Green read/write the same session store. (2) Use sticky sessions with sessionAffinity: ClientIP on the Service — but this doesn't survive a pod restart. (3) Use JWT tokens or cookie-based sessions (stateless). Best practice: externalize session state.

📖 Chapter 16 Summary: Progressive delivery is the art of reducing deployment risk. Rolling Updates are the default — simple, zero-downtime, but no health-based abort. Blue/Green gives instant rollback at 2x resource cost. Canary is the gold standard — gradual traffic shifting with automated Prometheus analysis. Argo Rollouts brings Canary + BlueGreen + AnalysisRuns natively to Kubernetes. Flagger works alongside existing Deployments with service mesh integration. Underneath it all, Readiness probes, Liveness probes, and PDBs form the safety foundation. Feature flags decouple deployment from release — deploy dark, release gradually. Dark launching tests with real traffic and zero user impact. The best strategy depends on your risk tolerance, resource budget, and observability maturity.

🔄
Rolling

Default K8s strategy. Gradual pod replacement. maxSurge + maxUnavailable. Zero downtime, mixed version window.

🔵🟢
Blue/Green

Two environments. Service selector switch. Instant rollback. 2x resources. Best for critical releases.

🐤
Canary

Gradual traffic %. Automated analysis. Auto-abort on errors. Gold standard for high-traffic services.

🏴‍☠️
Dark Launch

Mirror traffic to new version. Discard responses. Test under real load. Zero user impact.

Which deployment strategy should I use?
Simple App, Low Risk
Rolling Update
Critical, Instant Rollback
Blue/Green
High Traffic, Automated

Chapter 17: Container Registries & Image Management

Docker Hub, ECR, Harbor, GHCR, Quay — the "app store" for your platform. How images are stored, pulled, scanned, promoted, and kept secure across environments.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2.5 hours🚀 Domain 2 · 25%

📖 Chapter Overview: Container registries are where your images live. Every kubectl apply that creates a Pod triggers a registry pull. Understanding registries is understanding the supply chain of your platform. This chapter covers: the five major registry types (Docker Hub, ECR, Harbor, GHCR, Quay), pull policies and when to use each, ImagePullSecrets for private registry auth, digest pinning for immutability, the dangers of the :latest tag, lifecycle policies to manage storage, cross-region replication for speed and DR, pull-through caching to reduce latency and egress costs, vulnerability scanning with Trivy/Clair/ECR Scan, and image promotion pipelines from dev to production. CNPE Domain 2 (GitOps & CD — 25%).

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Choose the right registry for your platform: Docker Hub, ECR, Harbor, GHCR, or Quay
  • ✅ Configure pull policies correctly: Always, IfNotPresent, Never
  • ✅ Authenticate to private registries using ImagePullSecrets
  • ✅ Pin images by digest (sha256:...) for immutability and security
  • ✅ Understand why :latest is dangerous and what to use instead
  • ✅ Manage registry storage with lifecycle policies and replication
  • ✅ Set up pull-through caching to reduce latency and egress costs
  • ✅ Scan images for vulnerabilities with Trivy, Clair, and ECR Scan
  • ✅ Build image promotion pipelines from dev → staging → production
🎓 CNPE Relevance
GitOps & Continuous Delivery Domain 2 — 25% Security & Policy Domain 5 — 15%

17.1 Registry Types — The "App Store" for Your Platform

🧠 What Is a Container Registry? A container registry stores and distributes container images. When you docker push, images go to a registry. When Kubernetes creates a Pod, the kubelet docker pulls from a registry. Think of it as the "app store" for your platform — developers publish images, clusters download them.

RegistryTypeAuthScanningBest For
Docker HubPublic SaaSUsername/Password, Access TokenDocker Scout (basic)Open-source, public images, small teams
ECR (Elastic Container Registry)AWS-nativeIAM roles (no password needed!)ECR Scan (Basic + Enhanced)AWS workloads, EKS clusters
HarborSelf-hostedLDAP, OIDC, DB, local usersClair (built-in), Trivy plug-inAir-gapped, compliance, enterprise
GHCR (GitHub Container Registry)GitHub-integratedGITHUB_TOKEN, OIDC, PATDependabot, CodeQL integrationGitHub Actions CI/CD, OCI artifacts
QuayRed Hat SaaS / self-hostedOAuth, Robot AccountsClair (built-in)OpenShift, Red Hat ecosystem
ACR (Azure Container Registry)Azure-nativeAzure AD, Managed IdentityMicrosoft DefenderAzure workloads, AKS clusters
GCR/Artifact RegistryGCP-nativeService Accounts, Workload IdentityContainer Analysis (Grype)GCP workloads, GKE clusters
🏢
Self-Hosted (Harbor)
  • Full control: You own the data, the network, the auth
  • Air-gapped ready: Works without internet
  • RBAC + Projects: Per-team registries within one Harbor instance
  • Built-in scanning: Clair + Trivy without external tools
  • Replication: Pull from Docker Hub, push to your Harbor
☁️
Cloud-Native (ECR/GHCR/ACR)
  • Zero infrastructure: No servers to manage
  • IAM integration: No passwords — use cloud IAM roles
  • Cross-region replication: Built-in, one checkbox
  • Lifecycle policies: Auto-delete old images
  • Lower latency: Same region as your cluster = faster pulls
⚡
Speed Tip: For the CNPE exam, know these: Harbor = self-hosted with scanning. ECR = AWS-native, IAM auth (no passwords). GHCR = GitHub-integrated, supports OCI artifacts (Helm charts too). The exam may ask you to choose the right registry for a scenario — air-gapped → Harbor, AWS EKS → ECR, GitHub Actions → GHCR.
🔬 How Each Registry Handles Authentication — Deep Dive

Each registry authenticates differently. Understanding this prevents ImagePullBackOff errors:

RegistryAuth MechanismHow K8s AuthenticatesToken Expiry
Docker HubUsername + Password OR Personal Access Token (PAT)kubectl create secret docker-registry with username/tokenPAT: never expires. Password: until changed.
ECRIAM role → STS → temporary credentials (valid 12 hours)IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) — NO static secret. Or docker-registry secret refreshed by cron.12 hours. Must refresh or use IRSA which auto-refreshes.
GHCRGITHUB_TOKEN (Actions, expires per job) OR Personal Access Token (PAT, long-lived)docker-registry secret with PAT. In Actions: auto-injected via ghcr.io credentials.GITHUB_TOKEN: 1 hour (job lifetime). PAT: configurable (7d to never).
HarborLocal users, LDAP, OIDC, Robot Accounts (per-project tokens)docker-registry secret with Robot Account credentialsRobot Account: never expires (unless rotated).
ACRAzure AD → Managed Identity OR Admin credentialsaz acr login on nodes, or docker-registry secretManaged Identity tokens: auto-refreshed by Azure.

The ECR/IRSA pattern is the most elegant: K8s ServiceAccount annotated with an AWS IAM role ARN. The EKS pod identity webhook injects AWS credentials automatically. No static secret. No token rotation. No cron job. The pod authenticates to ECR the same way an EC2 instance does — via IAM.

Which registry should I use for anihpj?
Air-gapped / Compliance
Harbor (self-hosted)
On AWS EKS
ECR (IAM, no passwords)
GitHub Actions CI/CD
GHCR (auto-auth)
OpenShift / Red Hat
Quay (built-in Clair)
Multi-cloud platform?
Harbor (one registry everywhere) OR cloud-native per cloud (ECR+AWS, ACR+Azure, GCR+GCP)
🔬 OCI (Open Container Initiative) — The Universal Standard Behind Every Registry

All modern registries — Docker Hub, ECR, Harbor, GHCR — implement the same OCI Distribution Specification. This is why docker pull works with ANY registry, not just Docker Hub. OCI standardizes three things:

📦
OCI Image Spec

Defines the image format: manifests, configs, layer tarballs. Standardizes how images are constructed so ANY tool (Docker, Podman, Kaniko, Buildpacks) produces compatible images.

cnpe.html uses this! When you docker build -t anihpj-web . the output is OCI-compliant. Any OCI-compliant registry can store it.

📡
OCI Distribution Spec

Defines the REST API for pushing/pulling images. Every registry implements the same endpoints: GET /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>, PUT /v2/<name>/blobs/uploads/, etc.

This is why crane, skopeo, and regctl can interact with ANY registry — they speak OCI Distribution API.

🏃
OCI Runtime Spec

Defines how to run a container from an OCI image. Standardizes config.json (mounts, namespaces, cgroups). Implemented by runc, crun, youki.

🎯
Why OCI Matters for CNPE

You're not locked into Docker. Podman, Kaniko, Buildpacks all produce OCI images. Harbor, ECR, GHCR all accept OCI images. OCI = vendor neutrality. The CNPE exam expects you to know that OCI is the standard, not Docker.

17.2 Pull Policies — When Does Kubernetes Pull Your Image?

The imagePullPolicy on a container tells the kubelet when to check the registry for a new image. Getting this wrong causes stale images (running old code) or rate-limiting (Docker Hub blocks you).

PolicyBehaviorWhen to UseRisk
AlwaysPull from registry EVERY time a Pod starts. Even if image exists locally. Checks for updated tag.Development, CI/CD, when using mutable tags like :dev or :stagingRate-limiting from Docker Hub (100 pulls/6h free). Slower pod starts.
IfNotPresentPull ONLY if image is NOT cached on the node. If cached, use cached version.Production with immutable tags (v1.2.3 or digest). Saves bandwidth, avoids rate limits.If tag IS reused (bad practice), node may run old image.
NeverNEVER pull from registry. Image MUST exist on the node already (pre-loaded).Air-gapped environments, offline clusters, pre-seeded images via ctr image importPod won't start if image isn't pre-loaded. Hard to manage at scale.
Pull Policy Decision Flow — What Happens on Pod Start
  Pod Created
       │
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ imagePullPolicy?                                             │
  │                                                              │
  │  Always ─────────────────────────────────────────────────►  │
  │  │  Pull from registry EVERY time. Use digest to verify.    │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐           │
  │  │  │ Registry │───►│  kubelet │───►│   Pod    │           │
  │  │  └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘           │
  │  │                                                          │
  │  IfNotPresent ────────────────────────────────────────────► │
  │  │  Is image on node?                                       │
  │  │  ├── YES → Use cached image (FAST — no network)         │
  │  │  └── NO  → Pull from registry                           │
  │  │                                                          │
  │  Never ───────────────────────────────────────────────────► │
  │     Is image on node?                                       │
  │     ├── YES → Use local image                               │
  │     └── NO  → ErrImageNeverPull → Pod FAILS                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
1
Pod Created

Scheduler assigns Pod to a Node. kubelet on that Node receives the Pod spec including the image reference.

2
Check Cache

kubelet checks local image cache. If imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent and image exists → SKIP to step 6.

3
Authenticate

If private registry: read ImagePullSecrets from Pod spec OR ServiceAccount. Decode credentials.

4
Pull Layers

Fetch image manifest → pull each layer (parallel for uncached, skip cached layers). Check digest if specified.

5
Verify Digest

If @sha256:... specified: compute hash of pulled image. MUST match exactly. Mismatch → ErrImagePull.

6
Start Container

Image unpacked → container runtime (containerd/CRI-O) creates container from the image layers. Container starts.

⚠️
Gotcha — The :latest Default: If you omit the tag (or use :latest), Kubernetes defaults imagePullPolicy to Always. This means EVERY pod restart pulls from the registry — even if nothing changed. For production, always specify a tag AND set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent. This one setting can save you from Docker Hub rate limits and 3-second pod start delays.
🔬 Docker Hub Rate Limits — Why Your CI/CD Is Suddenly Failing

Docker Hub imposed strict rate limits that catch many platform teams off guard. Understanding the exact limits is critical for platform reliability:

Account TypePull LimitReset PeriodConsequence if Exceeded
Anonymous (no login)100 pulls6 hoursHTTP 429 Too Many Requests. Pod stays in ErrImagePull.
Free (logged in)200 pulls6 hoursHTTP 429. Same as anonymous but doubled.
Pro5,000 pulls24 hoursRarely reached by small-medium teams.
Team/BusinessUnlimited—No limits. Recommended for production workloads.

The math that kills you: 10 microservices × 2 replicas × 3 rolling updates/day = 60 pulls/day from a single node. Add CI/CD builds (10 builds × 5 pulls = 50). That's 110 pulls in 6 hours — you just exceeded the anonymous limit. Solutions: (1) Authenticate all pulls (100 → 200 limit). (2) Use a pull-through cache (Harbor/ECR pull-through). (3) Set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent to avoid unnecessary pulls. (4) Mirror critical images to your own registry.

17.3 ImagePullSecrets — Authenticating to Private Registries

Public images (Docker Hub official images) require no authentication. Private registries (ECR, Harbor, GHCR private repos) need credentials. ImagePullSecrets are Kubernetes Secrets of type kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson that store registry credentials and are attached to Pods or ServiceAccounts.

Creating an ImagePullSecret for GHCR
# Step 1: Create the Secret from Docker config
kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-secret \
  --docker-server=ghcr.io \
  --docker-username=anihs \
  --docker-password=$GITHUB_TOKEN \
  --docker-email=platform@anihs.com \
  --namespace=anihpj-prod

# Step 2: Reference in Pod spec
spec:
  imagePullSecrets:
    - name: ghcr-secret
  containers:
    - name: anihpj-web
      image: ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0

# Step 3: OR attach to ServiceAccount (recommended for all Pods)
kubectl patch serviceaccount default \
  -p '{"imagePullSecrets": [{"name": "ghcr-secret"}]}' \
  -n anihpj-prod
🔑
Per-Pod ImagePullSecret

Specify in spec.imagePullSecrets. Works but requires EVERY Pod manifest to include it. Easy to forget. Good for one-off Pods.

👤
ServiceAccount ImagePullSecret (Recommended)

Attach the secret to a ServiceAccount. ALL Pods using that SA automatically get the pull secret. No per-Pod config needed. This is the production pattern.

🎯
Exam Tip: ECR has NO password — it uses IAM. You can't kubectl create secret docker-registry with a password for ECR. Instead, use aws ecr get-login-password | kubectl create secret docker-registry ... or better, use eksctl create iamserviceaccount with an IAM role that has ECR pull permissions. The CNPE exam may test this distinction.
🔬 ECR IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) — No Static Secrets
# Step 1: Create IAM policy for ECR pull access
# (Attach AWS-managed: arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly)

# Step 2: Create IAM role with trust relationship for K8s SA
# Trust policy allows sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from EKS OIDC provider

# Step 3: Create K8s ServiceAccount with IAM role annotation
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: anihpj-sa
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789:role/anihpj-ecr-read

# Step 4: Use the SA in your Pod
spec:
  serviceAccountName: anihpj-sa
  containers:
    - image: 123456789.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/anihpj-web:v2.0.0
# NO imagePullSecrets needed! EKS webhook injects AWS creds automatically.

# What happens under the hood:
# 1. Pod starts with anihpj-sa ServiceAccount
# 2. EKS pod identity webhook sees the eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn annotation
# 3. Webhook injects AWS_WEB_IDENTITY_TOKEN_FILE + AWS_ROLE_ARN env vars
# 4. AWS SDK in kubelet calls sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity
# 5. Gets temporary ECR credentials → authenticates → pulls image

17.4 Digest Pinning — Immutability by Hash

⚠️ The Problem: Tags are MUTABLE. anihpj:v1.0.0 can point to image A today and image B tomorrow. If an attacker pushes a malicious image with the same tag, your cluster pulls it automatically. Between your scan and your deploy, the image could change — this is the TOCTOU (Time-Of-Check-Time-Of-Use) vulnerability.

Digest Pinning — The Solution to TOCTOU
  ❌ TAGS (Mutable — Dangerous)              ✅ DIGESTS (Immutable — Safe)
  ┌─────────────────────────┐               ┌─────────────────────────────┐
  │ anihpj:v1.0.0           │               │ anihpj@sha256:              │
  │                         │               │   a1b2c3d4e5f6...           │
  │ Monday:  → Image A      │               │                             │
  │ Tuesday: → Image B (!)  │               │ FOREVER: → Image A          │
  │                         │               │ (the exact same bytes)      │
  │ Same tag, DIFFERENT img │               │                             │
  └─────────────────────────┘               └─────────────────────────────┘

  HOW TO GET THE DIGEST:
  docker pull ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0
  docker inspect ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0 --format='{{.RepoDigests}}'
  # Output: [ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web@sha256:a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8e9f0a1b2]

  USE THE DIGEST:
  image: ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web@sha256:a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8e9f0a1b2
⚡
Speed Tip: In CI/CD, after docker push, capture the digest from the push output and use it in your Kubernetes manifests. GitOps tools like Argo CD and Flux support digest references natively. Never deploy by tag in production — always deploy by digest. Tags are for humans. Digests are for machines.
🔬 How Image Digests Work — The Merkle Tree Inside Every Image

A container image digest isn't just a hash of the image file — it's a content-addressable Merkle tree of all the image layers. Understanding this explains why digests are cryptographically immutable:

Image Digest = Hash of the Manifest (which hashes all layers)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    IMAGE DIGEST (sha256:a1b2c3...)          │
  │                    = hash(Manifest JSON)                    │
  │                         │                                   │
  │         ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐                  │
  │         ▼               ▼               ▼                  │
  │  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐           │
  │  │  Layer 1   │  │  Layer 2   │  │  Layer 3   │           │
  │  │ sha256:A1  │  │ sha256:B2  │  │ sha256:C3  │           │
  │  │ (OS base)  │  │ (apt deps) │  │ (app code) │           │
  │  └────────────┘  └────────────┘  └────────────┘           │
  │                                                             │
  │  Manifest JSON = {                                          │
  │    "config":    { "digest": "sha256:cfg..." },              │
  │    "layers": [                                              │
  │      { "digest": "sha256:A1...", "size": 75123456 },       │
  │      { "digest": "sha256:B2...", "size": 23456789 },       │
  │      { "digest": "sha256:C3...", "size": 1234567 }         │
  │    ]                                                        │
  │  }                                                          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WHY THIS MATTERS:
  • If ANY byte in ANY layer changes → layer hash changes
  • If ANY layer hash changes → manifest changes
  • If manifest changes → IMAGE DIGEST CHANGES
  • Two images with the SAME digest are guaranteed byte-for-byte IDENTICAL
  • This is why digest pinning prevents TOCTOU attacks — the hash chain is unbreakable

Practical implication: Even a 1-byte change in your application code produces a completely different digest. This means you can't "update" a digest — you can only reference a new digest. This is exactly what you want for supply chain security: every image is uniquely and immutably identified.

🔬 Multi-Architecture Images — How One Tag Serves arm64 AND amd64

A single tag like anihpj:v2.0.0 can serve different image binaries for different CPU architectures. This is done using an image index (also called a "fat manifest") that points to platform-specific manifests:

Image Index — Platform-Specific Routing
  docker pull anihpj-web:v2.0.0
       │
       ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              IMAGE INDEX (sha256:idx...)            │
  │                                                     │
  │  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐  │
  │  │ linux/amd64         │  │ linux/arm64         │  │
  │  │ manifest sha256:A1  │  │ manifest sha256:B2  │  │
  │  └────────┬────────────┘  └────────┬────────────┘  │
  └───────────┼────────────────────────┼────────────────┘
              │                        │
    ┌─────────▼──────────┐   ┌────────▼───────────┐
    │ AMD64 Image        │   │ ARM64 Image        │
    │ ├─ Layer: amd64 OS │   │ ├─ Layer: arm64 OS │
    │ ├─ Layer: amd64 pkg│   │ ├─ Layer: arm64 pkg│
    │ └─ Layer: app code │   │ └─ Layer: app code │
    └────────────────────┘   └────────────────────┘

  HOW TO BUILD MULTI-ARCH IMAGES:
  docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
    -t ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0 --push .

  This creates ONE tag that serves AMD64 on Intel/AMD nodes
  and ARM64 on Graviton/Apple Silicon nodes — automatically.

Why this matters for CNPE: If your platform runs on mixed-architecture clusters (EKS with Graviton + x86, or on-prem with ARM servers), you need multi-arch images. Without them, an ARM64 node CANNOT run an AMD64 image (and vice versa). docker buildx handles this transparently — it builds both architectures in parallel and creates the index automatically.

17.5 :latest Dangers — The Most Dangerous 7 Characters in Kubernetes

The :latest tag is the default when no tag is specified. It's convenient for development but catastrophic for production. Here's why, with concrete scenarios:

🔴 Scenario 1: The "It Works for Me" Mystery
  • Monday 9am: Developer pushes anihpj:latest. Cluster pulls and runs it. App works.
  • Monday 6pm: CI pipeline pushes a new anihpj:latest (v2.1.0) with a bug.
  • Monday 7pm: A crashed node restarts. Pod rescheduled. kubelet pulls anihpj:latest — gets the NEW, BROKEN image.
  • No code was deployed. No GitOps change. No CI trigger. Just a Pod restart. And production is down.
❓
Unpredictable

What EXACT version is :latest right now? Only the registry knows. Two Pods starting 5 minutes apart may run different code with the same manifest.

🔄
Non-Reproducible

Last week's deployment used :latest = Image A. This week's deployment uses :latest = Image B. If B has a regression, you can't "rollback to last week's :latest" — it's been overwritten.

🔍
Untraceable

Production is broken. Which git commit is running? With :latest, you don't know. With :git-sha-abc123, you know exactly. With a digest, you know the exact bytes.

⏱️
Always Pulled

:latest forces imagePullPolicy: Always. Every Pod restart = registry pull = latency + Docker Hub rate limit risk.

📊 Probability of :latest Causing an Incident (increases with time & activity)
Week 1
5%
Only 1 push, low risk
Month 1
30%
Multiple pushes, devs overwriting
Month 3
60%
Pod restart = surprise new version
Month 6
85%
Node failure → reschedule → crash
Year 1
99%
Only a matter of time before incident

:latest in production is not "if" it breaks — it's "when." The longer you use it, the more pushes accumulate, and the more likely a Pod restart pulls a broken version. Switch to explicit tags or digests TODAY.

🎯
Exam Tip: The CNPE exam WILL test your understanding of why :latest is dangerous. The answer must include: (1) mutability — same tag, different images over time, (2) non-reproducibility — can't rollback to "yesterday's latest", (3) untraceability — can't map running code to a git commit. Always use explicit version tags or digests in production manifests.

17.6 Lifecycle Policies — Don't Let Your Registry Become a Landfill

Every CI pipeline push creates a new image. With 20 microservices × 10 commits/day × 30 days = 6,000 images/month. Without cleanup, your registry fills up and costs skyrocket. Lifecycle policies automatically delete old images based on rules.

📦
ECR Lifecycle Policy (JSON)

{
"rules": [{
"rulePriority": 1,
"selection": {
"tagStatus": "any",
"countType": "imageCountMoreThan",
"countNumber": 10
},
"action": { "type": "expire" }
}]
}

Keeps the 10 most recent images. Deletes the 11th oldest. Runs automatically every 24 hours.

🗑️
Common Policy Patterns
  • Keep last N: Keep most recent 10 images per repo
  • Age-based: Delete images older than 30 days
  • Tag-based: Delete all :dev-* tags after 7 days
  • Untagged only: Delete images with no tags (dangling)
  • Harbor: Per-project retention policies in UI
⚠️
Gotcha — Lifecycle Policies Don't Recover Space Immediately: ECR lifecycle policies only "expire" images — they become un-pullable but the storage isn't freed until ECR's garbage collection runs (typically within 24 hours). Harbor's garbage collection must be triggered manually or scheduled. Also: if an image is referenced by digest in a running Deployment, deleting it from the registry won't affect the running Pods — they already pulled it. But if those Pods restart, they WON'T be able to pull the deleted image.
🔬 Harbor Retention Policies vs ECR Lifecycle Policies
FeatureECR LifecycleHarbor Retention
ConfigurationJSON policy document (CLI/Console/Terraform)UI-based per-project retention rules
Rule typesKeep N most recent, delete by age, tag pattern matchingKeep N most recent, keep by days, exclude pinned/tagged
ScheduleAutomatic (runs every 24h, you can't trigger manually)Manual trigger OR scheduled (cron-like). You control when.
Garbage collectionAutomatic within 24h of expirationMust trigger manually via Harbor UI or API. Not automatic.
Preview/SimulateYes — lifecycle policy preview shows what WOULD be deletedYes — retention rule shows matching artifacts before execution
ScopePer-registry (applies to ALL repos matching filter)Per-project (more granular, one project = one team's images)
Best forAWS-native, set-and-forget, Terraform-managedTeams who need control over WHEN cleanup happens

17.7 Replication — Images Where You Need Them

If your cluster is in Singapore but your registry is in us-east-1, every image pull crosses the Pacific — adding 2-3 seconds of latency per pull, per Pod. Replication copies images to registries in multiple regions for faster pulls and disaster recovery.

Multi-Region Replication — Faster Pulls, DR Ready
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     CI/CD (us-east-1)                                │
  │                     ┌──────────┐                                     │
  │                     │ Push     │                                     │
  │                     │ anihpj   │                                     │
  │                     └────┬─────┘                                     │
  └──────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
                             ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ECR us-east-1 (SOURCE)                                              │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │ anihpj-web@sha256:a1b2c3...  ← Pushed by CI                  │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │
                    ┌────────┴────────┐
                    ▼                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ ECR eu-west-1        │  │ ECR ap-southeast-1   │
  │ (Ireland)            │  │ (Singapore)          │
  │ ┌──────────────────┐ │  │ ┌──────────────────┐ │
  │ │ anihpj-web@      │ │  │ │ anihpj-web@      │ │
  │ │ sha256:a1b2c3... │ │  │ │ sha256:a1b2c3... │ │
  │ └──────────────────┘ │  │ └──────────────────┘ │
  └──────────┬───────────┘  └──────────┬───────────┘
             │                         │
             ▼                         ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ EKS eu-west-1        │  │ EKS ap-southeast-1   │
  │ Pull latency: 50ms   │  │ Pull latency: 50ms   │
  │ (vs 2s from us-east) │  │ (vs 3s from us-east) │
  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘
⚡
Speed Tip: ECR cross-region replication is a single checkbox in the AWS Console. Harbor replication is configured per-project with filters (by tag, by repository, by label). Registry replication is NOT the same as image promotion. Replication copies everything. Promotion moves only approved images through quality gates.
