17.8 Registry Caching — Pull-Through Cache for Speed and Savings

A pull-through cache is a local registry that proxies requests to an upstream registry. The first pull fetches from upstream and caches locally. Subsequent pulls serve from cache — reducing latency and egress costs.

Pull-Through Cache Architecture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Without Cache                     With Cache                    │
  │                                                                    │
  │  Pod ──► Registry (us-east)       Pod ──► Cache (local)          │
  │  │          │                      │         │                    │
  │  │   3s latency                    │   50ms  │ (first pull only)  │
  │  │          │                      │         ▼                    │
  │  ▼          ▼                      │    Registry (us-east)        │
  │  Image                           ▼                              │
  │  Egress: $0.09/GB                 Image (from cache)             │
  │                                    Egress: $0 (local)            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  HARBOR PROXY CACHE CONFIGURATION:
   Registries → New Endpoint → Provider: Docker Hub / ECR / GHCR
   Enable "Proxy Cache" — Harbor acts as a transparent proxy
   Configure cache retention: keep images for 7 days, max 500GB
   Point your cluster's image references to Harbor instead of upstream:
      image: harbor.anihs.com/proxy-docker.io/library/nginx:1.25
⚡
Cache Benefits
  • Faster pulls: 50ms (local) vs 3000ms (cross-region)
  • Zero egress cost: Images served from local cache
  • Docker Hub rate limit bypass: Cache absorbs repeated pulls
  • Offline resilience: Cached images available during upstream outage
⚠️
Cache Limitations
  • First pull is slow: Cache miss = full upstream pull
  • Stale cache: If upstream image updates, cache may serve old version
  • Storage cost: Cache is another registry — needs its own lifecycle policies
  • Digests break proxying: Some proxies can't resolve digest references
🇸🇬
Singapore → us-east-1 (No Cache)
❌ 3,200ms avg pull

EKS in ap-southeast-1 pulling from ECR in us-east-1. Cross-Pacific latency. $0.09/GB egress × 500 pulls/day = $1,350/month.

🇸🇬
Singapore → ap-southeast-1 (Replication)
✅ 50ms avg pull

ECR cross-region replication to ap-southeast-1. Same-region pull. $0.02/GB replication cost. Total: ~$300/month.

🇸🇬
Singapore + Harbor Cache
✅ 45ms avg pull (cached)

Harbor pull-through cache in the cluster. First pull: 3s (cache miss). Subsequent: 45ms. Egress: $0. Storage: local only.

🌍
Multi-Region + Cache
✅ 40ms avg pull worldwide

ECR replication to 3 regions + Harbor cache per cluster. Sub-50ms pulls globally. Best of both worlds: replication + caching.

17.9 Image Scanning — Find CVEs Before Attackers Do

Container images bundle OS packages and application dependencies — both can have known vulnerabilities (CVEs). Image scanning checks every layer of your image against vulnerability databases and blocks deployment if critical issues are found.

ScannerHow It WorksIntegrationBest For
Trivy (Aqua)Scans OS packages + language deps (pip, npm, gem). Fast, single binary. Outputs SARIF, JSON, table.CLI, CI (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI), Harbor plug-in, K8s operatorCI/CD pipelines. trivy image ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0
Clair (Quay/Harbor)Indexes image layers → matches against vulnerability DBs (NVD, Alpine SecDB, Red Hat OVAL). API-driven.Built into Harbor and Quay. No CLI needed — auto-scans on push.Self-hosted registries (Harbor, Quay). Set-and-forget.
ECR Scan (AWS)Basic: scans on push, uses Clair DB. Enhanced: continuous scanning, uses Inspector + Snyk.AWS-native. Results in ECR console + EventBridge.ECR users. Enhanced = continuous monitoring.
Grype (Anchore)Fast, local scanner. Same vulnerability DBs as Trivy. Outputs JSON, table, CycloneDX.CLI, CI, K8s admission controllerLocal dev + CI. grype ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0
SnykCommercial. Scans images + infrastructure-as-code + open-source deps.SaaS + CLI + CI + registry webhooksEnterprise with compliance requirements
🔬 Vulnerability Severity Levels — When to Block Deployment
SeverityActionExample
CRITICALBLOCK deployment immediately. Fix NOW.RCE in log4j (CVE-2021-44228). CVSS 9.0+
HIGHBLOCK deployment. Fix within 24 hours.SQL injection in Django (CVSS 7.0-8.9)
MEDIUMWARN but allow deployment. Fix in next sprint.Information disclosure. CVSS 4.0-6.9
LOWLog. No action required.Theoretical exploit. CVSS 0.1-3.9

Pipeline integration: Add Trivy/Grype as a CI stage AFTER build, BEFORE push. If CRITICAL or HIGH CVEs are found, the pipeline FAILS and the image is never pushed. Use trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 to fail the build on critical/high findings.

🔬 Trivy in GitHub Actions — Scan Before Push, Block on Failure
name: Scan anihpj Image
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build image
        run: docker build -t anihpj-web:${{ github.sha }} .
      - name: Scan with Trivy
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: anihpj-web:${{ github.sha }}
          format: sarif
          output: trivy-results.sarif
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          exit-code: '1'          # FAIL pipeline on findings
          vuln-type: os,library  # Scan OS + language deps
      - name: Push if clean
        if: success()              # Only push if scan passed
        run: |
          docker tag anihpj-web:${{ github.sha }} \
            ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:${{ github.sha }}
      - name: Upload SARIF results
        if: always()
        uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v3
        with:
          sarif_file: trivy-results.sarif

Key pattern: severity: CRITICAL,HIGH + exit-code: '1' = pipeline fails on critical/high CVEs. if: success() on push step ensures compromised images never reach the registry. The SARIF upload (always runs for visibility) creates a security dashboard in GitHub's Security tab.

📋
🔬 SBOM — Software Bill of Materials

An SBOM is a machine-readable inventory of EVERY component in your image — OS packages, language libraries, transitive dependencies. Formats: SPDX (Linux Foundation) and CycloneDX (OWASP). Generate with Syft:

syft ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0 -o spdx-json > anihpj-sbom.spdx.json

Why SBOM matters: When Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) hit, teams with SBOMs knew in MINUTES whether they were affected. Teams without had to manually audit every image. SBOMs are now required by US Executive Order 14028 for federal software.

Attach to image: cosign attach sbom --sbom anihpj-sbom.spdx.json ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0

✍️
🔬 Cosign — Cryptographic Image Signing

Cosign (Sigstore project) signs container images with cryptographic keys OR keyless (OIDC-based). Signed images can be verified before deployment — preventing supply chain attacks where an attacker pushes a malicious image to your registry.

# Keyless signing (uses GitHub OIDC)
cosign sign ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0

# Verify before deployment
cosign verify ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0 --certificate-identity platform@anihs.com --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

CNPE integration: Add cosign verify as an admission controller (Kyverno/OPA) or as an Argo CD pre-sync check. If the signature is invalid or missing, the deployment is BLOCKED. This is the last line of defense in your supply chain.

17.10 Image Promotion — From Dev to Production, Safely

Image promotion moves an image through a pipeline of registries, each with increasing quality gates. You build ONCE, scan, and promote the SAME image (by digest) — never rebuild between environments.

Image Promotion Pipeline — Build Once, Promote Many
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                       IMAGE PROMOTION PIPELINE                           │
  │                                                                          │
  │  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐          │
  │  │  BUILD   │    │   SCAN   │    │  STAGE   │    │  PROD    │          │
  │  │          │    │          │    │          │    │          │          │
  │  │ CI builds│───►│ Trivy    │───►│ Deploy   │───►│ Deploy   │          │
  │  │ image    │    │ scan     │    │ to       │    │ to       │          │
  │  │          │    │          │    │ staging  │    │ prod     │          │
  │  └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘    └────┬─────┘          │
  │       │               │               │               │                │
  │       ▼               ▼               ▼               ▼                │
  │  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  DEV REGISTRY          STAGING REGISTRY       PROD REGISTRY     │   │
  │  │  (dev-anihpj)          (staging-anihpj)       (prod-anihpj)     │   │
  │  │                       │                                          │   │
  │  │  anihpj@sha256:abc    │  anihpj@sha256:abc    │  anihpj@sha256:abc│  │
  │  │  ↑ SAME IMAGE ────────┼─── SAME IMAGE ───────┼─── SAME IMAGE    │  │
  │  │                       │                      │                  │   │
  │  │  Access: devs write   │  Access: CI only     │  Access: CI only │   │
  │  │  Scan: optional       │  Scan: required      │  Scan: required  │   │
  │  │  Lifecycle: 7 days    │  Lifecycle: 30 days  │  Lifecycle: 90 days│  │
  │  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  PROMOTION COMMAND (copy image between registries without re-pulling):
  crane copy dev-registry/anihpj@sha256:abc staging-registry/anihpj@sha256:abc

  WHY crane? It copies directly between registries WITHOUT docker pull/push.
  This preserves the digest and avoids local disk usage.
✅
Promotion Best Practices
  • Build ONCE: Never rebuild between environments
  • Promote by digest: crane copy ...@sha256:abc
  • Separate registries: Different access controls per stage
  • Gate at each stage: Scan → Test → Approve → Promote
  • Audit trail: Every promotion logged with who, when, what
🔧
Promotion Tools
  • crane: Google's Go tool for registry operations. crane copy, crane digest
  • skopeo: Red Hat's image manipulation tool. skopeo copy docker://src docker://dst
  • regctl: regclient's CLI. Registry API operations
  • Harbor replication: Built-in push/pull replication rules
🔬 Complete Image Promotion Script — 4 Quality Gates
#!/bin/bash — IMAGE PROMOTION WITH QUALITY GATES
# Usage: ./promote.sh <src-registry> <dst-registry> <image:tag>

set -e  # Exit on any error — any gate failure stops the pipeline

SRC="$1"        # e.g., dev-registry.anihs.com
DST="$2"        # e.g., staging-registry.anihs.com
IMG="$3"        # e.g., anihpj-web:v2.0.0

# GATE 1: Get immutable digest (fail if image doesn't exist)
DIGEST=$(crane digest ${SRC}/${IMG}) || {
  echo "FAILED GATE 1: Image not found in source registry"
  exit 1
}
echo "GATE 1 PASSED: Digest = ${DIGEST}"

# GATE 2: Scan for vulnerabilities (fail on CRITICAL or HIGH)
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 \n  ${SRC}/${IMG} || {
  echo "FAILED GATE 2: CRITICAL or HIGH vulnerabilities found"
  exit 2
}
echo "GATE 2 PASSED: No critical/high vulnerabilities"

# GATE 3: Verify image signature (Cosign — supply chain integrity)
cosign verify --key cosign.pub ${SRC}/${IMG} || {
  echo "FAILED GATE 3: Image signature invalid or missing"
  exit 3
}
echo "GATE 3 PASSED: Signature verified"

# GATE 4: Verify SBOM attestation exists
cosign verify-attestation --key cosign.pub \
  --type spdx ${SRC}/${IMG} || {
  echo "FAILED GATE 4: No SBOM attestation found"
  exit 4
}
echo "GATE 4 PASSED: SBOM verified"

# ALL GATES PASSED — Promote by immutable digest
crane copy ${SRC}/${IMG}@${DIGEST} ${DST}/${IMG}@${DIGEST}
echo "✅ PROMOTED: ${IMG}@${DIGEST} → ${DST}"
# Log: who=$(git config user.email) when=$(date -Iseconds) what=${DIGEST}

Each gate is an exit point. If any gate fails, the image never reaches the destination registry. This pattern — scan → verify → attest → promote — is the industry standard for secure image promotion. The same image (by digest) is moved; it's never rebuilt between environments.

Drill 17.1 Create ImagePullSecret & Deploy from Private Registry

Scenario: anihpj-web image is in GHCR (private). Create the secret and deploy.

  1. kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-secret --docker-server=ghcr.io --docker-username=YOUR_USER --docker-password=$GITHUB_TOKEN --docker-email=platform@anihs.com -n anihpj-prod
  2. Attach to ServiceAccount: kubectl patch sa default -p '{"imagePullSecrets":[{"name":"ghcr-secret"}]}' -n anihpj-prod
  3. Deploy with image: ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0
  4. Verify: kubectl describe pod -n anihpj-prod | grep -A5 "Pulled"
💡 Hint: If the pod stays in ImagePullBackOff, run kubectl describe pod and check the Events section for the exact error (401 Unauthorized, 404 Not Found, etc.).
Drill 17.2 Scan an Image with Trivy & Block on Critical CVEs

Scenario: Add Trivy scanning to your CI pipeline. Block on CRITICAL or HIGH CVEs.

  1. Install: curl -sfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/trivy/main/contrib/install.sh | sh
  2. Scan: trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0
  3. If exit code 1 → pipeline FAILS → image never pushed to staging
  4. Check output format: trivy image --format sarif --output trivy-results.sarif ghcr.io/anihs/anihpj-web:v2.0.0
💡 Hint: --exit-code 1 makes Trivy return non-zero on findings — this is what CI platforms use to fail the job. Without this flag, Trivy always exits 0 (success) even when CVEs are found.
Drill 17.3 Promote an Image Between Registries

Scenario: Image passed CI + scan. Promote from dev registry to staging registry.

  1. Get digest: crane digest dev-registry.anihs.com/anihpj-web:v2.0.0 → sha256:abc123...
  2. Promote: crane copy dev-registry.anihs.com/anihpj-web@sha256:abc123 staging-registry.anihs.com/anihpj-web@sha256:abc123
  3. Verify: crane digest staging-registry.anihs.com/anihpj-web@sha256:abc123 → same digest
  4. Update Argo CD: point staging at staging-registry.anihs.com/anihpj-web@sha256:abc123
💡 Hint: crane copy copies directly between registries WITHOUT pulling to your local machine. This is MUCH faster than docker pull → docker tag → docker push and preserves the digest exactly.
Q1: Configure ECR as private registry for anihpj. Create ImagePullSecret. Attach to Deployment.

▶ Show Answer
ECR auth is IAM-based, not password-based. Use aws ecr get-login-password --region us-east-1 | kubectl create secret docker-registry ecr-secret --docker-server=ACCOUNT.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com --docker-username=AWS --docker-password-stdin -n anihpj-prod. Attach via spec.imagePullSecrets: [{name: ecr-secret}]. For EKS, use IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) instead — no secret needed.
Q2: Image tag is anihpj:v1.0.0. Attacker pushes malicious image with same tag. How does digest pinning prevent?

▶ Show Answer
Tags are pointers — they can change. anihpj:v1.0.0 can point to Image A (your scan) and later to Image B (attacker's). Digest pinning uses anihpj@sha256:abc123... — a cryptographic hash of the image content. The hash changes if ANY byte changes. Your Deployment specifies the exact hash → kubelet verifies the pulled image matches that hash → attacker's image with a different hash is REJECTED. This prevents TOCTOU attacks.
Q3: Harbor vs ECR for an air-gapped environment.

▶ Show Answer
Harbor wins for air-gapped. Harbor is self-hosted — you install it inside the air-gapped network. Images are pushed directly via internal network. ECR is AWS SaaS — requires internet access. For air-gapped ECR, you'd need AWS Outposts or ECR on EKS Anywhere (limited). Also: Harbor's built-in Clair scanner works offline — it pre-downloads vulnerability databases.
Q4: :latest tag in production — a developer says "it works for me." Explain 3 dangers.

▶ Show Answer
(1) Mutability: :latest today ≠ :latest yesterday. A Pod restart pulls a different image with no deployment change. (2) Non-reproducibility: Can't rollback to "last week's latest" — it's been overwritten. Use :v2.0.0 or @sha256:.... (3) Untraceability: Production is broken — which git commit is running? With :latest you don't know. With :git-abc123 you know immediately.
Q5: ECR lifecycle policy — keep last 10 images, delete older than 30 days.

▶ Show Answer
Create two rules: Rule 1 (priority 1): "selection": {"tagStatus": "any", "countType": "imageCountMoreThan", "countNumber": 10}, "action": {"type": "expire"}. Rule 2 (priority 2): "selection": {"tagStatus": "any", "countType": "sinceImagePushed", "countUnit": "days", "countNumber": 30}, "action": {"type": "expire"}. Rules are evaluated in priority order; the first matching rule wins. Images matching Rule 1 (top 10) are never evaluated against Rule 2.
Q6: Multi-region ECR replication — us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Configure.

▶ Show Answer
In ECR console → Private registry → Replication → Create rule. Source: us-east-1 registry. Destination: eu-west-1 registry. Filters: all repositories, or specific repos like anihpj-*. ECR replicates within minutes. For cross-account replication, add a registry policy in the destination account allowing the source account to replicate. Note: replication is push-based (source pushes to destination), not pull-based.
Q7: Trivy scan in CI finds CRITICAL CVE. What's your pipeline's response?

▶ Show Answer
Pipeline FAILS immediately. The image is never pushed to the registry. Alert sent to #platform-security Slack channel with CVE ID, severity, affected package, and fix version. Developer must: (1) update the vulnerable package, (2) rebuild, (3) re-scan. If the CVE is in a base image (python:3.11-slim), update FROM to a newer digest. Never suppress or ignore CRITICAL CVEs — even if "not exploitable" — let the security team decide.
Q8: Registry cache — Singapore cluster pulls from ECR us-east-1. 3s latency per pull. Fix it.

▶ Show Answer
Option 1 (best): ECR cross-region replication to ap-southeast-1. Cluster pulls from local region → 50ms latency. Option 2: Deploy Harbor in Singapore as a pull-through cache. Configure proxy cache for ECR us-east-1. Point cluster's image references to Harbor. First pull: 3s. Subsequent pulls: 50ms. Option 3: ECR pull-through cache (new feature). Create a pull-through cache rule in ap-southeast-1 pointing to us-east-1.
Q9: Image promotion — dev:abc123 → staging → production. What gates must the image pass?

▶ Show Answer
Dev → Staging gates: (1) CI pipeline passes (lint, test, build). (2) Trivy scan — 0 CRITICAL, 0 HIGH CVEs. (3) Image pushed to dev registry. Staging → Production gates: (1) Staging deployment succeeds. (2) Smoke tests pass (health check, critical flows). (3) Performance test within 20% of baseline. (4) Manual approval (optional, for Continuous Delivery). (5) crane copy to production registry. (6) Argo CD syncs production to new digest.
Q10: GHCR vs ECR for GitHub Actions CI/CD. Compare auth, cost, integration.

▶ Show Answer
GHCR: Auth via GITHUB_TOKEN (automatic in Actions — no setup). Free for public repos. Private: included in GitHub Teams/Enterprise. Native OCI support (Helm charts too). ECR: Auth via aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials → IAM role. Free tier: 500MB/month. After: $0.10/GB/month. Cross-region replication costs extra. For GitHub Actions: GHCR wins on simplicity — zero config auth. For EKS on AWS: ECR wins on latency (same region) and IAM integration (IRSA).

📖 Chapter 17 Summary: Registries hold your images. Digest pinning keeps them immutable. Scanning keeps them secure. Promotion pipelines move them safely from dev to production. Choose the right registry for your platform: Harbor for air-gapped/self-hosted, ECR for AWS, GHCR for GitHub Actions. Set imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent in production with explicit tags. Always deploy by digest (@sha256:...) — tags are mutable pointers. Never use :latest in production. Use lifecycle policies to auto-clean old images. Replicate to regions near your clusters. Cache locally to reduce latency and egress. Scan EVERY image with Trivy/Clair — block on CRITICAL and HIGH. Promote images (never rebuild) through dev → staging → production registries with quality gates at each stage.

🏪
Registry Types

Docker Hub, ECR, Harbor, GHCR, Quay. Cloud-native or self-hosted. Choose by auth, scanning, latency.

🔒
Digest Pinning

@sha256:abc... = immutable. Prevents TOCTOU. Always deploy by digest. Tags are for humans.

🔍
Scanning

Trivy, Clair, Grype. Block CRITICAL + HIGH. Scan in CI, not just in registry. Never skip.

📦
Promotion

Build once, promote many. crane copy between registries. Gates at each stage: scan → test → approve.

Chapter 18: Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) — Extending Kubernetes

Create your OWN Kubernetes API types — CRDs are what separate a platform engineer from a K8s administrator. Define the schema, K8s handles storage and API.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~3 hours🚀 Domain 3 · 25%

📖 Chapter Overview: CRDs are THE foundational concept of platform engineering on Kubernetes. They let you create your own API types — DatabaseClaim, NamespaceRequest, TLSCertificate — that Kubernetes treats as first-class citizens alongside built-in resources like Pods and Deployments. This chapter covers: what CRDs are and why they matter, schema definition with OpenAPI v3 validation, versioning (v1alpha1→v1) with conversion webhooks, printer columns for custom kubectl get output, categories for grouping, subresources (/status, /scale), server-side apply support, and a complete DatabaseClaim CRD for anihpj. CNPE Domain 3 (Platform APIs & Self-Service — 25%).

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Understand CRDs and why they're the foundation of platform engineering
  • ✅ Define custom resource schemas with OpenAPI v3 validation
  • ✅ Manage CRD versioning from v1alpha1 through v1 with conversion webhooks
  • ✅ Customize kubectl get output with printer columns
  • ✅ Group CRDs with categories and subresources (/status, /scale)
  • ✅ Build a complete DatabaseClaim CRD for the anihpj platform
  • ✅ Apply CRD best practices for production-grade platforms
🎓 CNPE Relevance
Platform APIs & Self-Service Domain 3 — 25%

18.1 What Are CRDs? — Create Your Own K8s API

🧠 What Is a CRD? A Custom Resource Definition (CRD) extends the Kubernetes API with your OWN resource type. Just as kind: Pod and kind: Deployment are built-in, kind: DatabaseClaim can become YOUR custom resource type. Kubernetes handles the API server, storage (etcd), RBAC, and versioning — you just define the schema and behavior.

CRD Architecture — How Your Custom Type Integrates with K8s
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     KUBERNETES API SERVER                            │
  │                                                                      │
  │  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐   │
  │  │ Pod      │  │ Deploy   │  │ Service  │  │ DatabaseClaim    │   │
  │  │ (built-in)│  │(built-in)│  │(built-in)│  │ (YOUR CRD!)     │   │
  │  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────────────┘   │
  │                                                    │                │
  │  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼────────────── │
  │  │ ALL share the same infrastructure:               │               │
  │  │ • etcd for storage                               │               │
  │  │ • RBAC for access control                        │               │
  │  │ • API versioning (v1alpha1 → v1)                 │               │
  │  │ • kubectl apply/get/delete                       │               │
  │  │ • Admission webhooks                             │               │
  │  │ • Server-side apply                              │               │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  WITH CRDs, YOU GET:
  kubectl get databaseclaims          ← Same UX as kubectl get pods
  kubectl describe databaseclaim mydb ← Same UX as kubectl describe pod
  kubectl apply -f dbclaim.yaml       ← Same UX as kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
🏗️
Without CRDs (TicketOps)
  • Developer files a JIRA ticket: "Need a PostgreSQL DB"
  • Ops team manually provisions RDS/Cloud SQL
  • Ops emails connection string to developer
  • Developer manually updates their ConfigMap
  • Time: 3-7 days. Touchpoints: 5+
🚀
With CRDs (Self-Service)
  • Developer writes: kind: DatabaseClaim
  • kubectl apply -f mydb.yaml
  • Operator/Crossovere provisions the database
  • Connection string automatically injected as Secret
  • Time: 5 minutes. Touchpoints: 1
⚡
Speed Tip: CRDs are the foundation of EVERY platform engineering pattern. Operators = CRDs + controllers. Self-service = CRDs + web UI. Crossplane = CRDs + cloud provisioning. The CNPE exam will test your ability to CREATE and VALIDATE CRDs — this is Domain 3 (25% of the exam).
🔬 CRD vs ConfigMap — Don't Use a ConfigMap When You Need a CRD
Use a ConfigMap When...Use a CRD When...
You need simple key-value configurationYou need typed, validated data with a schema
Data is consumed by a Pod as env vars or filesData is consumed by a controller/operator that takes action
No versioning needed — one format foreverYou need API versioning (v1alpha1 → v1)
No business logic — just data storageYou want RBAC per resource type (who can create DB claims?)
No status tracking neededYou need /status subresource ("is my DB ready?")
No custom kubectl output neededYou want printer columns for operational visibility
Example: Django settings, feature flagsExample: DatabaseClaim, TLSCertificate, NamespaceRequest
Do I need a CRD for this?
Just key-value data for Pods?
ConfigMap / Secret
Need controller to act on changes?
YES — Use a CRD
Need typed validation + RBAC?
YES — Use a CRD
Need status tracking?
YES — Use a CRD
If you answered YES to any of the right 3 → Use a CRD. Otherwise → ConfigMap/Secret.

18.2 CRD Schema Definition — The Anatomy of a CRD

A CRD minimally needs a group (API group, like anihs.com), a kind (resource type name), and a schema (what fields the resource has). Everything else — validation, versioning, columns — builds on this foundation.

Minimal CRD — DatabaseClaim for anihpj
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: databaseclaims.anihs.com  # <plural>.<group>
spec:
  # API group — your organization's namespace in the K8s API
  group: anihs.com
  # Versions this CRD supports
  versions:
    - name: v1alpha1
      served: true          # This version is served by the API
      storage: true         # This version is stored in etcd
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                engine:
                  type: string
                  enum: [postgresql, mysql, redis]
                version:
                  type: string
                  pattern: '^\d+\.\d+$'  # e.g., "15.4"
                size:
                  type: string
                  enum: [small, medium, large]
                storageGB:
                  type: integer
                  minimum: 10
                  maximum: 1000
  # Names: plural, singular, short names, kind
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: databaseclaims
    singular: databaseclaim
    shortNames:
      - dbc
    kind: DatabaseClaim
    listKind: DatabaseClaimList
🎯
Exam Tip: The CRD metadata.name MUST be <plural>.<group>. For group: anihs.com and plural: databaseclaims, the name is databaseclaims.anihs.com. If these don't match, the CRD is rejected. Also: only ONE version can have storage: true — this is the version etcd stores.
⚠️
🔬 Structural Schemas Required (Kubernetes 1.22+): Since K8s 1.22, all CRDs MUST have a structural schema. A structural schema means: (1) Every properties value has a type specified. (2) No ambiguous additionalProperties: true without a defined type. (3) type: object fields must specify either properties or additionalProperties. This requirement exists because CRDs without structural schemas can't use features like Server-Side Apply, pruning, or `kubectl explain`. If your CRD is missing types, K8s rejects it with: spec.versions[0].schema.openAPIV3Schema: does not contain a structural schema. Fix: Add type: string (or appropriate type) to EVERY property. Never leave a property without a type.
🔬 CRD Pruning — How Kubernetes Auto-Removes Unknown Fields

By default, Kubernetes prunes (removes) any field submitted in a CR that is NOT defined in the schema. This is a safety mechanism — if a developer typos engnie: postgresql (instead of engine), K8s silently removes it rather than storing garbage.

SettingBehaviorWhen to Use
preserveUnknownFields: false (default)Unknown fields are silently REMOVED. The resource is stored WITHOUT them.Almost always. Prevents typos from persisting. Required for structural schemas.
preserveUnknownFields: trueUnknown fields are PRESERVED. Stored as-is in etcd.Migration from pre-1.16 CRDs. NOT recommended for new CRDs.
x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields: true (per-field)Only THIS field preserves unknown sub-fields. Rest of the resource is pruned.When a field contains arbitrary JSON (like config: {arbitrary: json}).

Gotcha: Pruning is SILENT. kubectl apply succeeds, but the typos'd field is gone. Always kubectl get -o yaml after apply to verify your fields were stored. For critical fields, use required in the schema — if a required field is misspelled, the apply is REJECTED (not silently pruned).

18.3 OpenAPI v3 Validation — Catch Errors Before They Hit etcd

The openAPIV3Schema in your CRD defines the schema for your custom resource. Kubernetes validates EVERY create/update against this schema and rejects invalid resources with clear error messages — no admission webhook needed for basic validation.

Validation TypeOpenAPI KeywordExampleRejects
Required fieldsrequired: [engine, size]spec MUST contain engine and size{spec: {}} — missing required fields
Type checkingtype: integerstorageGB must be an integerstorageGB: "fifty" — string, not int
Enum valuesenum: [small, medium, large]size must be one of thesesize: xlarge — not in enum
Numeric boundsminimum: 10, maximum: 1000storageGB between 10-1000storageGB: 5 — below minimum
Pattern matchingpattern: '^\d+\.\d+$'Version must be N.N formatversion: "latest" — doesn't match
String lengthminLength: 1, maxLength: 63Name field length constraintsname: "" — below minLength
Array constraintsminItems: 1, maxItems: 10replicas array sizeEmpty array with minItems: 1
Default valuesdefault: "medium"Default size if not specifiedN/A — provides default, doesn't reject
⚠️
Gotcha — Schema Validation is Structural ONLY: OpenAPI validation checks field TYPES and VALUES, not business logic. It can ensure storageGB is an integer between 10-1000, but it CAN'T check "does this team have budget for 1000GB?" For business logic validation, use admission webhooks (ValidatingWebhookConfiguration). Schema validation is the first line of defense — webhooks are the second.

18.4 Versioning — v1alpha1 → v1beta1 → v1

CRDs evolve. Your first version (v1alpha1) may have a rough API. After feedback, you stabilize it (v1beta1) and eventually graduate it (v1). Kubernetes supports serving MULTIPLE versions simultaneously while storing only ONE.

CRD Version Lifecycle
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     CRD VERSION LIFE CYCLE                          │
  │                                                                     │
  │  v1alpha1                  v1beta1                     v1          │
  │  (Experimental)            (Pre-release)              (Stable)     │
  │  ┌──────────┐             ┌──────────┐             ┌──────────┐   │
  │  │ Breaking │             │ API is   │             │ API is   │   │
  │  │ changes  │  ────────►  │ stable   │  ────────►  │ locked   │   │
  │  │ allowed  │  feedback   │ but may  │  graduation │ forever  │   │
  │  │ anytime  │             │ change   │             │          │   │
  │  └──────────┘             └──────────┘             └──────────┘   │
  │       │                        │                        │          │
  │       ▼                        ▼                        ▼          │
  │  served: true              served: true              served: true  │
  │  storage: true             storage: true             storage: true │
  │  deprecated: false         deprecated: false         deprecated: false │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  TYPICAL MIGRATION:
  Step 1: v1alpha1 is the ONLY version (served + storage)
  Step 2: Add v1beta1 (served: true, storage: true). Deprecate v1alpha1.
  Step 3: Add v1 (served: true, storage: true). Deprecate v1beta1.
  Step 4: Remove v1alpha1 completely.

  CRITICAL RULE: Resources stored in etcd are ALWAYS in the STORAGE version.
  When a client requests v1alpha1, K8s converts from storage (v1) to v1alpha1
  using a CONVERSION WEBHOOK (if the schema changed).
⚡
Speed Tip: CNPE exam versioning rules: (1) Only ONE version has storage: true. (2) Multiple versions can have served: true. (3) Deprecated versions still work but show a warning. (4) Removing a served version while resources of that version exist in etcd requires migration — use conversion webhooks.
🔬 Version Deprecation Policy — How to Retire Old CRD Versions Safely

Kubernetes follows a strict deprecation policy. Applied to CRDs, here's the safe retirement path:

1
Announce

Add deprecated: true + deprecationWarning: "v1alpha1 is deprecated, use v1beta1" to the version

2
Wait

Keep served: true for at least 1 release cycle (3 months). Users see warnings when using old version.

3
Stop Serving

Set served: false. Old version no longer accessible via API. Storage must have been migrated already.

4
Remove

Delete the version from the CRD spec. No resources of this version remain in etcd. Version history preserved.

Never skip steps. Removing a version that has storage: true causes data loss. Removing a version that has served: true breaks clients. The deprecationWarning is shown in kubectl get output and API responses — it's your communication channel to API consumers.

18.5 Conversion Webhooks — Bridging CRD Versions

When your CRD serves multiple versions, Kubernetes needs to convert between them. If the schema is identical (just renamed), K8s does it automatically. If the schema CHANGED (new fields, renamed fields, different structure), you need a conversion webhook — an HTTPS endpoint that translates between versions.

CRD with Conversion Webhook Configuration
spec:
  conversion:
    strategy: Webhook
    webhook:
      # The webhook that handles conversion requests
      clientConfig:
        service:
          namespace: anihpj-platform
          name: crd-conversion-webhook
          path: /convert
          port: 443
        # OR use a URL (for external webhooks)
        # url: https://conversion.anihs.com/convert
      # TLS certificate for the webhook (must be trusted)
      conversionReviewVersions:
        - v1
        - v1beta1

# The webhook receives:
# POST /convert with ConversionReview request
# {
#   "request": {
#     "desiredAPIVersion": "anihs.com/v1",
#     "objects": [
#       { "apiVersion": "anihs.com/v1alpha1", ... }
#     ]
#   }
# }
#
# Webhook responds with converted objects in desiredAPIVersion
⚠️
Gotcha — Webhook Availability is CRITICAL: If your conversion webhook is DOWN, ALL operations on your CRD FAIL — create, update, read, delete. The API server calls the webhook synchronously for every request. Always deploy conversion webhooks with high availability (at least 2 replicas, PDB). If the webhook is unreachable, kubectl get databaseclaims returns an error.
🔬 Admission Webhooks for CRDs — Beyond Schema Validation

OpenAPI and CEL validate structure and cross-field logic. Admission webhooks validate against external state — things the API server can't know. They come in two flavors:

🔍
ValidatingWebhookConfiguration

Question: "Is this resource allowed?" Webhook returns allowed: true/false. Cannot modify the resource. Use for: quota checks ("has this team exceeded their DB limit?"), policy enforcement ("is encryption enabled?"), external validation.

For anihpj: Validate that a team can only have 3 DatabaseClaims. Check against an external quota service. Reject if exceeded.

🔧
MutatingWebhookConfiguration

Question: "Can I modify this resource before it's stored?" Webhook returns a JSON patch to apply. Use for: defaulting values, injecting sidecars, adding labels.

For anihpj: If a DatabaseClaim doesn't specify version, mutate it to default: "15.4". Add team label automatically based on namespace.

⚠️
CRITICAL: If your ValidatingWebhook has failurePolicy: Fail and the webhook is DOWN, ALL operations on matched resources are REJECTED — same as conversion webhooks. Always configure failurePolicy: Ignore for non-critical validation or ensure webhook HA. The API server calls admission webhooks AFTER schema validation passes — so structural errors are caught first.

18.6 Printer Columns — Customize kubectl get Output

By default, kubectl get databaseclaims only shows NAME and AGE. Printer columns let you display custom fields — engine, version, size, status — directly in the table output.

CRD with Printer Columns — Rich kubectl Output
spec:
  versions:
    - name: v1alpha1
      served: true
      storage: true
      additionalPrinterColumns:
        - name: Engine
          type: string
          jsonPath: .spec.engine        # Pulls from resource JSON
          description: Database engine
        - name: Version
          type: string
          jsonPath: .spec.version
        - name: Size
          type: string
          jsonPath: .spec.size
        - name: Storage
          type: integer
          jsonPath: .spec.storageGB
          format: int64
        - name: Status
          type: string
          jsonPath: .status.phase        # From status subresource

# RESULT: kubectl get databaseclaims
# NAME        ENGINE       VERSION   SIZE    STORAGE   STATUS    AGE
# anihpj-db   postgresql   15.4      medium  100       Ready     5m
# analytics   mysql        8.0       large   500       Pending   30s
🔬 Priority Column — Integer-Based Sorting in kubectl get

By default, kubectl get sorts alphabetically. Adding a priority field to a printer column enables integer-based sorting, which is essential for resources like QueueDepth or Priority:

Without PriorityWith Priority
{name: Size, type: string, jsonPath: .spec.size}{name: Size, type: integer, jsonPath: .spec.size, priority: 1, format: int64}
Sorts alphabetically: "large" → "medium" → "small"Sorts by priority: small(1) → medium(2) → large(3) or any custom order

Add priority to your most important columns. Lower priority numbers appear FIRST. The column with the lowest priority becomes the primary sort column. Without priority, kubectl sorts by NAME.

18.7 Categories — Group CRDs for Discovery

Categories let you group multiple CRDs under a common label. kubectl get <category> returns ALL resources in that category — including built-in ones. This is how kubectl get all works (it's a category that includes Pods, Services, Deployments, ReplicaSets).

Adding Categories to CRDs
spec:
  names:
    categories:
      - anihpj          # Project-specific category
      - platform        # All platform-provisioned resources
      - all             # Include in kubectl get all

# USAGE:
# kubectl get anihpj — returns all anihpj CRDs (DatabaseClaim, NamespaceRequest, etc.)
# kubectl get platform — returns all platform-provisioned resources
# kubectl get all — includes your CRDs alongside Pods, Services, etc.
⚠️
Gotcha — Category Overlap: Adding all to your CRD's categories means kubectl get all returns your custom resources alongside Pods and Services. This can be overwhelming in large clusters. Only add all if your CRD is truly an "infrastructure-wide" resource. For project-specific CRDs, use your own category name.

18.8 Subresources — /status and /scale

Subresources are additional REST endpoints on your CRD. The two most important are /status (separates spec from status — users write spec, controllers write status) and /scale (enables kubectl scale and HPA support).

Enabling Subresources on a CRD
spec:
  versions:
    - name: v1alpha1
      subresources:
        # /status subresource — SEPARATE spec from status
        status: {}
        # /scale subresource — enable kubectl scale + HPA
        scale:
          specReplicasPath: .spec.replicas     # Path to desired count
          statusReplicasPath: .status.replicas  # Path to current count
          labelSelectorPath: .status.selector   # Optional: pod selector

# WHY /status MATTERS:
# Without /status: kubectl apply updates BOTH spec and status.
# With /status: User writes spec. Controller writes status. No conflict.
# RBAC: User → update spec. Controller → update status. Separate roles.
🎯
Exam Tip: The CNPE exam expects you to know: (1) Enable status: {} on EVERY CRD that has a controller — it's a platform best practice. (2) /scale requires specReplicasPath AND statusReplicasPath — both are required. (3) Without /status, kubectl apply overwrites the controller's status updates — this is a common bug in CNPE exam scenarios.
🔬 Finalizers — The Safety Net for Resource Deletion

When you kubectl delete a resource with a finalizer, the resource is NOT immediately removed. Instead, it enters a terminating state. The controller responsible for the finalizer must perform cleanup (delete the cloud database, release the IP, remove from LB) and then REMOVE its finalizer. Only when ALL finalizers are gone does K8s actually delete the resource.

1
Delete Request

User runs kubectl delete dbc anihpj-db. API server sets deletionTimestamp.

2
Finalizer Blocks

Resource has finalizers: [anihs.com/dbCleanup]. K8s WON'T delete until this is removed.

3
Controller Cleans Up

DatabaseClaim controller sees deletionTimestamp. Deletes the RDS instance. Takes final backup.

4
Remove Finalizer

Controller patches the resource to remove its finalizer. Now no finalizers remain.

5
Actually Deleted

K8s removes the resource from etcd. Without finalizer → external resources would be orphaned.

Platform pattern: Your DatabaseClaim CRD should have a finalizer anihs.com/dbCleanup. When a claim is deleted, the controller: (1) deletes the RDS instance, (2) deletes the credentials Secret, (3) removes the finalizer. Without a finalizer, deleting the DatabaseClaim orphaned the RDS instance — you'd keep paying for it forever.

18.9 Server-Side Apply — Field-Level Ownership for CRDs

Server-Side Apply (SSA) tracks which "manager" (user, controller, tool) owns each field in a resource. This prevents conflicts when multiple actors modify the same resource — the controller owns .status, the user owns .spec, and neither can overwrite the other's fields.

Server-Side Apply — Field Ownership Model
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  DatabaseClaim Resource                          │
  │                                                                  │
  │  spec:                          status:                          │
  │  ┌────────────────────┐        ┌────────────────────┐           │
  │  │ engine: postgresql │        │ phase: Ready       │           │
  │  │ version: "15.4"    │        │ endpoint: db...rds │           │
  │  │ size: medium       │        │ created: 2025-01.. │           │
  │  │ storageGB: 100     │        │ replicas: 1        │           │
  │  └────────────────────┘        └────────────────────┘           │
  │         ▲                              ▲                        │
  │         │                              │                        │
  │    OWNED BY:                      OWNED BY:                     │
  │    User (kubectl apply)           DatabaseClaim Controller      │
  │                                                                  │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
  │  With SSA: User can't accidentally overwrite status.            │
  │  Controller can't overwrite user's spec.                        │
  │  Conflicts are detected at the FIELD level, not resource level. │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📜
cert-manager
CRDs: Certificate, Issuer, ClusterIssuer

Extends K8s with kind: Certificate. Developer requests a TLS cert → cert-manager controller provisions it via Let's Encrypt. 30M+ downloads. The gold standard for CRD design.

☁️
Crossplane
CRDs: RDSInstance, GKE, IAMRole...

Every cloud resource is a CRD. kind: RDSInstance provisioned via AWS API. Composition CRDs let you build your own cloud abstractions.

🚀
Argo CD
CRDs: Application, AppProject

kind: Application defines what to deploy and from where. The Application CR is the single source of truth for GitOps deployments.

🔧
Your Platform (anihpj)
CRDs: DatabaseClaim, NamespaceRequest

Your platform CRDs follow the same patterns as these industry leaders. DatabaseClaim → Crossplane → RDS. Self-service in 5 minutes.

18.10 DatabaseClaim CRD for anihpj — Complete Example

Here is the complete DatabaseClaim CRD as it would be used in the anihpj platform. Developers create a DatabaseClaim resource, and the platform controller (or Crossplane) provisions the actual database.

Complete DatabaseClaim CRD with All Features
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: databaseclaims.anihs.com
spec:
  group: anihs.com
  names:
    plural: databaseclaims
    singular: databaseclaim
    shortNames: [dbc]
    kind: DatabaseClaim
    categories: [anihpj, platform]
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
    - name: v1alpha1
      served: true
      storage: true
      subresources:
        status: {}
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          required: [spec]
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              required: [engine]
              properties:
                engine:
                  type: string
                  enum: [postgresql, mysql]
                version:
                  type: string
                  default: "15.4"
                size:
                  type: string
                  enum: [small, medium, large]
                  default: medium
            status:
              type: object
              properties:
                phase:
                  type: string
                  enum: [Pending, Provisioning, Ready, Failed, Deleting]
                endpoint:
                  type: string
                message:
                  type: string
      additionalPrinterColumns:
        - name: Engine
          type: string
          jsonPath: .spec.engine
        - name: Size
          type: string
          jsonPath: .spec.size
        - name: Status
          type: string
          jsonPath: .status.phase
        - name: Endpoint
          type: string
          jsonPath: .status.endpoint
Using the DatabaseClaim — Developer Workflow
# 1. Developer creates a claim
apiVersion: anihs.com/v1alpha1
kind: DatabaseClaim
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db
  namespace: team-priya
spec:
  engine: postgresql
  size: medium

# 2. Controller picks it up, provisions RDS, updates status
# kubectl get dbc — shows Engine, Size, Status, Endpoint

# 3. Connection string auto-injected as Secret
# kubectl get secret anihpj-db-credentials
1
Claim Created

Developer kubectl applys a DatabaseClaim. Phase = Pending. CRD validation passes.

2
Controller Picks Up

DatabaseClaim controller (or Crossplane) detects new claim. Phase → Provisioning.

3
Infra Provisioned

Controller calls cloud API (RDS, Cloud SQL). Creates DB instance, security group, subnet.

4
Credentials Injected

Controller creates Secret with endpoint, username, password. Updates status.endpoint.

5
Ready

DB is ready. Phase → Ready. Application reads credentials from Secret. Self-service complete!

🔬 controller-gen — Auto-Generate CRDs from Go Structs (Kubebuilder)
// Instead of hand-writing 200 lines of CRD YAML, write Go structs with markers.
// controller-gen reads the markers and generates the CRD YAML automatically.

// +kubebuilder:object:root=true
// +kubebuilder:subresource:status
// +kubebuilder:resource:shortName=dbc,categories=anihpj,platform
// +kubebuilder:printcolumn:name="Engine",type=string,JSONPath=".spec.engine"
// +kubebuilder:printcolumn:name="Size",type=string,JSONPath=".spec.size"
// +kubebuilder:printcolumn:name="Status",type=string,JSONPath=".status.phase"
type DatabaseClaim struct {
    metav1.TypeMeta   `json:",inline"`
    metav1.ObjectMeta `json:"metadata,omitempty"`

    // +kubebuilder:validation:Required
    Spec   DatabaseClaimSpec   `json:"spec,omitempty"`
    Status DatabaseClaimStatus `json:"status,omitempty"`
}

type DatabaseClaimSpec struct {
    // +kubebuilder:validation:Enum=postgresql;mysql;redis
    // +kubebuilder:validation:Required
    Engine string `json:"engine"`

    // +kubebuilder:validation:Enum=small;medium;large
    // +kubebuilder:default:=medium
    Size string `json:"size,omitempty"`

    // +kubebuilder:validation:Minimum=10
    // +kubebuilder:validation:Maximum=1000
    StorageGB int `json:"storageGB,omitempty"`
}

// Generate CRD YAML: controller-gen crd paths=./api/... output:crd:artifacts:config=crds/
// This ONE command generates the complete CRD YAML with all validation from markers!

CNPE relevance: You don't need to write Go for the exam. But knowing the +kubebuilder markers helps you READ CRDs generated by tools like Kubebuilder and Operator SDK. These markers are the industry standard for CRD generation. The markers map directly to CRD YAML fields: +kubebuilder:validation:Enum → enum: [...], +kubebuilder:printcolumn → additionalPrinterColumns.

18.11 CRD Best Practices — Production-Grade Platform Design

✅
DO
  • Always start with v1alpha1 — it signals instability
  • Always enable /status subresource
  • Use OpenAPI validation for structural checks
  • Add printer columns for operational visibility
  • Add shortNames for developer convenience
  • Use categories for logical grouping
  • Set default values for optional fields
  • Document deprecation warnings in version descriptions
❌
DON'T
  • Don't start at v1 — you'll regret locking the API
  • Don't skip /status — spec and status must be separate
  • Don't use webhooks for simple validation — OpenAPI is faster
  • Don't forget to plan for version evolution
  • Don't add CRDs without RBAC rules for them
  • Don't remove a stored version without migration
  • Don't run conversion webhooks with single replica
  • Don't use required: [] for deeply nested objects
📊 CRD Maturity — From Prototype to Production-Grade
Level 1: Works
Schema + Validation
CRD exists. Basic schema. No status. No versioning plan.
Level 2: Usable
+ Status + Columns
/status subresource. Printer columns. ShortNames. Categories.
Level 3: Stable
+ Versioning + RBAC
v1alpha1 → v1beta1. Conversion webhooks. Dedicated RBAC.
Level 4: Production
+ Webhooks + SSA
Admission webhooks. SSA. kubectl explain. Deprecation policy.

Target Level 3+ before offering as self-service. Level 1-2 is fine for internal platform team use. Level 3-4 is required when other teams depend on your CRD as a stable API contract.

Drill 18.1 Create a DatabaseClaim CRD from Scratch

Scenario: Your anihpj platform needs a DatabaseClaim CRD. Create it with full validation.

  1. Write a CRD YAML: group=anihs.com, kind=DatabaseClaim, plural=databaseclaims
  2. Add OpenAPI schema: engine (enum: postgresql, mysql), size (enum: small, medium, large), storageGB (int, 10-1000)
  3. Enable /status subresource with phase, endpoint, message fields
  4. Add printer columns: Engine, Size, Status
  5. kubectl apply -f databaseclaim-crd.yaml
  6. Create a test claim: kubectl apply -f test-dbc.yaml
  7. Verify: kubectl get dbc — should show custom columns
💡 Hint: The CRD metadata.name MUST be databaseclaims.anihs.com. If you use a different name, the CRD is rejected.
Drill 18.2 CRD Version Migration

Scenario: DatabaseClaim v1alpha1 has been stable for 6 months. Add v1beta1 without breaking existing resources.

  1. Add v1beta1 to the CRD's versions list with served: true, storage: false (initially)
  2. Verify v1beta1 is served: kubectl get databaseclaims.v1beta1.anihs.com
  3. After testing, switch storage to v1beta1: set v1alpha1.storage=false, v1beta1.storage=true
  4. Verify existing resources are accessible via both versions
  5. Deprecate v1alpha1: set deprecated: true, deprecationWarning: "use v1beta1"
💡 Hint: When you switch storage versions, K8s automatically converts all stored resources to the new version. If your schema changed, you need a conversion webhook BEFORE switching storage.
Drill 18.3 Add Validation & Printer Columns

Scenario: A developer created a DatabaseClaim with engine: "mongodb" (not supported). Fix the validation and improve kubectl output.

  1. Add enum: [postgresql, mysql, redis] to the engine field in OpenAPI schema
  2. Test: kubectl apply -f bad-claim.yaml — should be REJECTED with clear error
  3. Add additionalPrinterColumns for Engine, Version, Size, Status
  4. Add categories: [anihpj, platform]
  5. Verify: kubectl get platform — should list all platform CRDs
💡 Hint: OpenAPI validation errors include the exact field and constraint violated. Users see: spec.engine: Unsupported value: "mongodb": supported values: "postgresql", "mysql", "redis".
Q1: Create a DatabaseClaim CRD for anihpj with engine, version, size fields and enum validation.

▶ Show Answer
Write a CRD with group: anihs.com, names.kind: DatabaseClaim, names.plural: databaseclaims. In openAPIV3Schema.properties.spec.properties: engine: {type: string, enum: [postgresql, mysql]}, version: {type: string}, size: {type: string, enum: [small, medium, large]}. The CRD name must be databaseclaims.anihs.com.
Q2: A developer submits a DatabaseClaim with storageGB: 5. The minimum is 10. What happens?

▶ Show Answer
The API server REJECTS the request with: The DatabaseClaim "mydb" is invalid: spec.storageGB: Invalid value: 5: spec.storageGB in body should be greater than or equal to 10. This happens at APPLY time, before the resource is stored in etcd. No webhook needed — OpenAPI validation handles it natively.
Q3: You need to add a new field to DatabaseClaim v1alpha1 without breaking existing resources. How?

▶ Show Answer
Add the new field to the OpenAPI schema with a default value. Existing resources (created before the field existed) don't have this field — K8s treats missing fields as valid unless they're in required. New resources get the default if they don't specify it. Never add a field to required — that would break all existing resources.
Q4: Why is /status subresource important for CRDs with controllers?

▶ Show Answer
Without /status, kubectl apply overwrites both spec AND status. The user's apply could wipe out the controller's status updates (phase, endpoint, conditions). With /status: user writes spec via the main resource endpoint, controller writes status via the /status subresource. RBAC can restrict: user → update spec, controller → update status. No conflicts.
Q5: You have v1alpha1 (stored) and v1beta1 (served). How do you switch storage to v1beta1?

▶ Show Answer
Update the CRD: set v1alpha1.storage: false and v1beta1.storage: true. K8s automatically converts all stored resources from v1alpha1 to v1beta1 format. If the schema is identical between versions, no conversion webhook is needed — K8s handles it natively. If the schema changed, you MUST have a conversion webhook deployed BEFORE switching storage.
Q6: How do you make kubectl get databaseclaims show the engine and status?

▶ Show Answer
Add additionalPrinterColumns to the CRD version: - {name: Engine, type: string, jsonPath: .spec.engine} and - {name: Status, type: string, jsonPath: .status.phase}. The jsonPath pulls from the resource's JSON representation. You need to update the CRD and re-apply it — existing resources immediately show the new columns.
Q7: What happens if your conversion webhook is down?

▶ Show Answer
ALL CRUD operations on the CRD FAIL. The API server calls the conversion webhook synchronously for every request involving a non-storage version. kubectl get databaseclaims returns an error. kubectl apply fails. This is why conversion webhooks must be highly available (min 2 replicas, PDB). If the webhook is permanently removed, remove non-storage versions from the CRD first.
Q8: How do you group DatabaseClaim and NamespaceRequest CRDs so kubectl get anihpj shows both?

▶ Show Answer
Add categories: [anihpj] to BOTH CRDs' spec.names. Categories are additive — a resource can belong to multiple categories. kubectl get anihpj returns ALL resources with anihpj in their categories, regardless of API group or kind. This is how kubectl get all works — it's a built-in category.
Q9: Server-Side Apply — user patches .spec.engine, controller patches .status.phase. What happens?

▶ Show Answer
Both patches succeed because they modify DIFFERENT fields managed by DIFFERENT managers. SSA tracks field ownership: user is the manager of .spec.engine, controller is the manager of .status.phase. If the user accidentally tried to set .status.phase, SSA would REJECT it because the controller owns that field. This prevents field-level conflicts.
Q10: You want to delete v1alpha1 from your CRD. What must you check first?

▶ Show Answer
(1) Ensure v1alpha1 is NOT the storage version — if it is, switch storage to another version first. (2) Ensure all existing resources have been converted to the new storage version. (3) Ensure v1alpha1 has served: false for at least one release cycle before removal. (4) Check if any clients or operators still reference v1alpha1. Removing a stored version without migration causes data loss.

📖 Chapter 18 Summary: CRDs are the foundation of platform engineering. They extend Kubernetes with your own API types — DatabaseClaim, NamespaceRequest, TLSCertificate — that look and feel exactly like built-in resources. Define schemas with OpenAPI v3 validation to catch errors at apply time. Manage versioning from v1alpha1 (experimental) through v1 (stable) with conversion webhooks for schema changes. Use printer columns for rich kubectl get output, categories for logical grouping, and /status subresources to separate user intent from controller state. Server-Side Apply provides field-level ownership to prevent spec/status conflicts. A well-designed CRD is the API contract between your platform and its users — design it carefully.

📝
Schema

OpenAPI v3 validation. Types, enums, patterns, defaults. Catch errors at apply time. No webhook needed.

🔄
Versioning

v1alpha1 → v1beta1 → v1. Only one storage version. Conversion webhooks bridge schema changes.

📊
Presentation

Printer columns for kubectl get. Categories for grouping. ShortNames for convenience.

🔒
Safety

/status subresource. Server-Side Apply. RBAC separation. Conversion webhook HA.

CRDs + custom controllers = Operators. They encode human operator knowledge into software — "If X happens, do Y." The reconciliation loop is the heart of every operator.

19.1 The Operator Pattern — CRD + Controller = Operator

🧠 What Is an Operator? An operator is a Kubernetes controller that manages a custom resource (CRD). It watches for changes to CRs and takes action to make reality match the desired state. Think of it as an "automated SRE" — it knows how to provision, configure, heal, and upgrade your application.

Operator Architecture — The Big Picture
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                           OPERATOR PATTERN                                │
  │                                                                           │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────────────────┐          │
  │  │      USER         │          │       OPERATOR (Controller)  │          │
  │  │                   │          │                              │          │
  │  │ kubectl apply -f  │          │  ┌────────────────────────┐  │          │
  │  │ databaseclaim.yaml│          │  │  RECONCILIATION LOOP   │  │          │
  │  │                   │          │  │                        │  │          │
  │  │  kind: Database   │  watch   │  │  1. OBSERVE            │  │          │
  │  │  Claim            │─────────►│  │     Get DatabaseClaim  │  │          │
  │  │  spec:            │          │  │     from API server    │  │          │
  │  │    engine: pg     │          │  │                        │  │          │
  │  └──────────────────┘          │  │  2. ANALYZE            │  │          │
  │                                │  │     Does RDS exist?    │  │          │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐          │  │     Is it correct size?│  │          │
  │  │   CLOUD / INFRA   │          │  │                        │  │          │
  │  │                   │◄─────────│  │  3. ACT                │  │          │
  │  │  RDS PostgreSQL   │  create  │  │     Create/Update/     │  │          │
  │  │  instance         │          │  │     Delete RDS         │  │          │
  │  └──────────────────┘          │  └────────────────────────┘  │          │
  │                                │                              │          │
  │  ┌──────────────────┐          │  Updates status:             │          │
  │  │   K8s SECRET      │◄─────────│  • phase: Ready             │          │
  │  │   credentials     │  inject  │  • endpoint: db.xxx.rds...  │          │
  │  └──────────────────┘          └──────────────────────────────┘          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📝
CRD = WHAT

The CRD defines the API — the schema, validation, versioning. It's the contract: "I want a PostgreSQL database, medium size." Created once, consumed by developers via kubectl.

⚙️
Controller = HOW

The controller implements the logic — provisioning, configuration, healing. It's the automation: "Call RDS API, wait for creation, inject credentials." Runs continuously, reconciles all instances.

📊 Operator Capability Levels — From Basic Install to Fully Autonomous
Level I: Basic Install
Install + Config
Helm-like: installs the app. No day-2 ops.
Level II: Seamless Upgrades
+ Upgrade + Rollback
Handles version upgrades with pre/post checks.
Level III: Full Lifecycle
+ Backup + Restore + Scale
Automated backup/restore. Storage scaling. Reconfiguration.
Level IV: Deep Insights
+ Metrics + Alerts + Health
Prometheus metrics. Status conditions. Auto-healing common issues.
Level V: Auto-Pilot
+ Auto-Tuning + Prediction
Predicts failures. Auto-scales. Tunes config. Human only for exceptions.

Most CNPE-relevant operators target Level III-IV. Helm charts are Level I. A production DatabaseClaim operator should be at least Level III — handles provisioning, backup, scaling, and health monitoring.

19.2 The Reconciliation Loop — Observe, Analyze, Act

The reconciliation loop is the HEART of every operator. It runs continuously (triggered by resource changes or on a timer) and ensures the ACTUAL state matches the DESIRED state.

Reconciliation Loop — Level-Triggered, Not Edge-Triggered
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                    RECONCILIATION LOOP                               │
  │                                                                      │
  │                        ┌──────────┐                                  │
  │              ┌────────►│ OBSERVE  │◄──────── event (CR changed)     │
  │              │         │ Get CR   │         or timer (every N sec)  │
  │              │         └────┬─────┘                                  │
  │              │              │                                        │
  │              │              ▼                                        │
  │              │         ┌──────────┐                                  │
  │   Requeue    │         │ ANALYZE  │                                  │
  │   (retry)    │         │ Compare  │                                  │
  │              │         │ Desired  │                                  │
  │              │         │ vs Actual│                                  │
  │              │         └────┬─────┘                                  │
  │              │              │                                        │
  │              │    ┌─────────┴─────────┐                             │
  │              │    ▼                   ▼                             │
  │              │  Match?             Mismatch?                        │
  │              │    │                   │                             │
  │              │    ▼                   ▼                             │
  │              │  Done               ┌──────────┐                     │
  │              │  (no-op)            │   ACT    │                     │
  │              │                     │ Create/  │                     │
  │              │                     │ Update/  │                     │
  │              │                     │ Delete   │                     │
  │              │                     └────┬─────┘                     │
  │              │                          │                            │
  │              │              ┌───────────┴────────────┐              │
  │              │              ▼                        ▼              │
  │              │          Success                  Error              │
  │              │              │                        │              │
  │              └──────────────┘               Requeue with backoff    │
  │                                                                    │
  │  KEY PRINCIPLE: Level-triggered (reconcile current state)          │
  │  NOT edge-triggered (don't just react to events).                  │
  │  Every reconciliation is a FULL check of the world state.          │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🎯
Exam Tip: The CNPE exam expects you to understand: (1) Reconciliation is level-triggered, not edge-triggered — every reconcile is a full state check, not a reaction to a single event. (2) If reconciliation fails, return an error — the controller will requeue with exponential backoff. (3) Never assume you saw all intermediate states — a Pod can go from "Pending" to "Running" in one event; you might miss "ContainerCreating."
🔬 The Golden Rule of Reconciliation: Idempotency

Every reconcile MUST be idempotent. Calling reconcile 1 time, 5 times, or 100 times must produce the SAME result — no duplicate resources, no double charges, no race conditions. This is harder than it sounds:

✅
Idempotent Patterns
  • Check before create: "Does RDS exist?" If yes, skip creation
  • Use deterministic names: RDS instance named dbc-{namespace}-{name}
  • Compare specs: "Is existing RDS correct size?" Only update if different
  • Owner references: Secret owned by CR → auto-deleted when CR is deleted
❌
Non-Idempotent Anti-Patterns
  • Create without check: "Always create RDS" → duplicate instances on retry
  • Random names: db-{randomID} → new instance every reconcile
  • Overwrite always: "Always update RDS config" → unnecessary API calls, possible downtime
  • No error handling: Create fails → reconcile retries → create again (but first one might have worked!)

Test idempotency: Run your operator, then trigger reconciliation manually 10 times. Count how many RDS instances exist. Should be exactly 1. If it's more, your reconcile isn't idempotent.

🔬 Watches & Informers — Not Polling, But Watching

Operators DON'T poll the API server every second (that would be inefficient). Instead, they use watches and informers — a sophisticated caching + event notification system:

1
List

On startup, the informer does a LIST to get all existing resources of the watched type.

2
Watch

Then opens a WATCH connection (long-lived HTTP). API server pushes ADDED/MODIFIED/DELETED events.

3
Cache

Informer maintains an in-memory cache of all resources. No API call needed for Get/List — uses cache.

4
Enqueue

On any event (or periodic sync), the resource key is added to a workqueue. Deduplication built-in.

5
Reconcile

Worker goroutines pull keys from the workqueue and call your Reconcile function.

Why not polling? Polling every 1 second with 1000 resources = 1000 API calls/second. Watches: 1 persistent connection, events pushed only when something changes. For 99.9% of a resource's lifetime, NOTHING changes — polling would waste API calls. Watches are near-zero overhead when idle.

19.3 Operator SDK & Kubebuilder — Scaffolding Operators

🧠 Don't Write Operators from Scratch. Operator SDK and Kubebuilder generate the boilerplate code (CRD schema, controller skeleton, RBAC manifests, webhooks) so you can focus on the reconciliation logic. Operator SDK is built ON TOP of Kubebuilder — they share the same codebase.

Scaffolding a DatabaseClaim Operator with Operator SDK
# Step 1: Initialize a new operator project
operator-sdk init --domain anihs.com --repo github.com/anihs/databaseclaim-operator

# Step 2: Create the DatabaseClaim API (generates CRD Go types)
operator-sdk create api --group platform --version v1alpha1 --kind DatabaseClaim \
  --resource --controller

# Step 3: Generated file structure
# ├── api/v1alpha1/
# │   ├── databaseclaim_types.go    ← Go structs (spec, status)
# │   └── groupversion_info.go      ← API group/version registration
# ├── internal/controller/
# │   └── databaseclaim_controller.go ← YOUR reconciliation logic
# ├── config/
# │   ├── crd/                      ← Generated CRD manifests
# │   └── rbac/                     ← Generated RBAC manifests
# └── Makefile                      ← Build, test, deploy targets

# Step 4: Write reconciliation logic in the controller
# (see section 19.12 for the full anihpj DatabaseClaim controller)

19.4 Controller RBAC — Least Privilege for Operators

Operators need access to Kubernetes resources. They need to READ their CRDs, UPDATE status, CREATE Secrets, and DELETE finalizers. Every operator must follow least privilege — only the permissions it absolutely needs.

RBAC Manifests for DatabaseClaim Operator (generated by +kubebuilder markers)
# Generated from Go markers like:
# +kubebuilder:rbac:groups=platform.anihs.com,resources=databaseclaims,verbs=get;list;watch;create;update;patch;delete
# +kubebuilder:rbac:groups=platform.anihs.com,resources=databaseclaims/status,verbs=get;update;patch
# +kubebuilder:rbac:groups=platform.anihs.com,resources=databaseclaims/finalizers,verbs=update
# +kubebuilder:rbac:groups=core,resources=secrets,verbs=get;list;watch;create;update;delete

# Resulting ClusterRole:
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: databaseclaim-operator
rules:
  - apiGroups: [platform.anihs.com]
    resources: [databaseclaims]
    verbs: [get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete]
  - apiGroups: [platform.anihs.com]
    resources: [databaseclaims/status]
    verbs: [get, update, patch]  # Status-only access
  - apiGroups: [""]  # Core API group
    resources: [secrets]
    verbs: [get, list, watch, create, update, delete]

19.5 Leader Election — Only ONE Controller Running at a Time

Running multiple replicas of your operator for HA creates a problem: if BOTH try to provision the same database, you get two RDS instances. Leader election ensures only ONE replica is the active controller at any time.

Leader Election — Active/Standby Pattern
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                  LEADER ELECTION (via Lease Lock)                 │
  │                                                                   │
  │  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐       │
  │  │  OPERATOR    │    │  OPERATOR    │    │  OPERATOR    │       │
  │  │  REPLICA 1   │    │  REPLICA 2   │    │  REPLICA 3   │       │
  │  │  ★ LEADER    │    │  (standby)   │    │  (standby)   │       │
  │  │  reconciling │    │  waiting     │    │  waiting     │       │
  │  └──────┬───────┘    └──────┬───────┘    └──────┬───────┘       │
  │         │                   │                   │                │
  │         ▼                   ▼                   ▼                │
  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │              LEASE LOCK (ConfigMap/Lease in kube-system) │   │
  │  │                                                          │   │
  │  │  holderIdentity: operator-replica-1                      │   │
  │  │  leaseDurationSeconds: 15                                │   │
  │  │  renewTime: 2025-01-15T10:30:05Z                         │   │
  │  │                                                          │   │
  │  │  Replica 1 renews every 10s. If it stops renewing for    │   │
  │  │  15s → Replica 2 takes leadership. Only ONE reconciler.  │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 Controller-Runtime — The Engine Under Every Kubebuilder Operator

sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime is the library that powers both Kubebuilder AND Operator SDK. Understanding its internals helps you debug operator behavior:

ComponentWhat It DoesWhy It Matters
ManagerBootstraps everything: clients, caches, webhooks, leader election. Single entry point.Controls the operator lifecycle. ctrl.NewManager() creates the world.
CacheIn-memory read cache of watched resources. Populated by informers.r.Get(ctx, key, &obj) reads from CACHE, not API server. Super fast but eventually consistent.
ClientRead/write interface to the API server. Used for both cache reads and direct API writes.Split client: reads from cache, writes direct. r.Create/Update/Delete go to API server.
WorkqueueRate-limiting queue. Deduplicates keys. Handles exponential backoff on errors.If reconcile returns error: requeue with backoff. If returns success: item consumed.
PredicatesFilters events BEFORE they reach the reconciler. Skip irrelevant changes.Filter by generation change, label selector, annotation. Reduces unnecessary reconciles.

Critical insight: r.Get() reads from the cache, which may be stale by a few milliseconds. This is fine for reconciliation (it's already async). For strong consistency, use r.APIReader.Get() which goes directly to the API server — slower but always current.

19.6 Finalizers — Safe Resource Cleanup

When a user deletes a DatabaseClaim, the operator must delete the external RDS instance FIRST, then remove the finalizer to let K8s delete the CR. Without finalizers, deleting the CR orphans the cloud resource.

Finalizer Logic in Go (Operator SDK controller)
// MyFinalizerName is the finalizer this controller uses
const databaseClaimFinalizer = "platform.anihs.com/dbCleanup"

func (r *DatabaseClaimReconciler) Reconcile(ctx context.Context, req ctrl.Request) (ctrl.Result, error) {
    // 1. Get the DatabaseClaim
    var dbClaim platformv1alpha1.DatabaseClaim
    if err := r.Get(ctx, req.NamespacedName, &dbClaim); err != nil {
        return ctrl.Result{}, client.IgnoreNotFound(err)
    }

    // 2. Check if being deleted (deletionTimestamp is set)
    if dbClaim.DeletionTimestamp.IsZero() {
        // NOT being deleted → add finalizer if missing
        if !controllerutil.ContainsFinalizer(&dbClaim, databaseClaimFinalizer) {
            controllerutil.AddFinalizer(&dbClaim, databaseClaimFinalizer)
            return ctrl.Result{}, r.Update(ctx, &dbClaim)
        }
        // ... normal reconciliation logic ...
    } else {
        // IS being deleted → run cleanup logic
        if controllerutil.ContainsFinalizer(&dbClaim, databaseClaimFinalizer) {
            // Delete the RDS instance
            if err := r.deleteRDSInstance(ctx, &dbClaim); err != nil {
                return ctrl.Result{}, err  // Requeue — try again
            }
            // Remove finalizer — NOW K8s can delete the CR
            controllerutil.RemoveFinalizer(&dbClaim, databaseClaimFinalizer)
            return ctrl.Result{}, r.Update(ctx, &dbClaim)
        }
    }
    return ctrl.Result{}, nil
}

19.7 Status Conditions — Making Operator State Observable

Operators should report their state via status conditions. This is how users and monitoring systems answer: "Is my database ready? Did provisioning fail? Why is it taking so long?"

Status Conditions — Standard Format (K8s API Conventions)
status:
  conditions:
    - type: Ready
      status: "True"        # True, False, or Unknown
      reason: ProvisioningComplete
      message: "RDS instance db-anihpj-prod is ready"
      lastTransitionTime: "2025-01-15T10:35:00Z"
    - type: DatabaseProvisioned
      status: "True"
      reason: RDSAvailable
      message: "RDS endpoint: db-anihpj.xxxx.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com"
      lastTransitionTime: "2025-01-15T10:34:00Z"

# KEY RULES for Status Conditions (from K8s API conventions):
# • type: PascalCase, describes the condition (Ready, Available, Progressing)
# • status: MUST be "True", "False", or "Unknown" — NOT a boolean
# • reason: Machine-readable CamelCase (ProvisioningFailed, RDSUnreachable)
# • message: Human-readable explanation for operators
# • lastTransitionTime: MUST change when status changes — used for alerting
✅ How Status Conditions Enable Self-Service
  • Developer: kubectl apply -f dbclaim.yaml → "I need a database"
  • Operator: Sets status.conditions[0]={type:Ready, status:"False", reason:"Provisioning"}
  • Developer: kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready dbc/anihpj-db --timeout=10m — blocks until ready!
  • 5 minutes later: RDS created → status.conditions[0].status="True" → kubectl wait exits
  • CI/CD script: kubectl apply -f dbclaim.yaml && kubectl wait --for=condition=Ready dbc/anihpj-db --timeout=15m && ./run-migrations.sh

This is self-service. No ticket. No email. No "is my DB ready?" Slack message. The developer's script blocks until the operator reports Ready. Status conditions turn asynchronous provisioning into synchronous workflows.

🔬 Operator Metrics — What Every Operator Should Expose

Operator SDK automatically exposes a /metrics endpoint. But you should define CUSTOM metrics that reflect YOUR operator's domain:

Custom Metrics for DatabaseClaim Operator
// Define metrics in your controller (Go)
var (
    // Counter: total reconciles
    reconcileTotal = prometheus.NewCounterVec(
        prometheus.CounterOpts{Name: "dbc_reconcile_total"},
        []string{"namespace", "result"},  // success/error/requeue
    )
    // Gauge: current number of DatabaseClaims
    dbClaimsActive = prometheus.NewGaugeVec(
        prometheus.GaugeOpts{Name: "dbc_active"},
        []string{"phase"},  // Pending/Provisioning/Ready/Failed
    )
    // Histogram: how long provisioning takes
    provisionDuration = prometheus.NewHistogram(
        prometheus.HistogramOpts{
            Name: "dbc_provision_duration_seconds",
            Buckets: []float64{30, 60, 120, 300, 600, 1800},
        },
    )
)

// CNPE-relevant alerts:
// • rate(dbc_reconcile_total{result="error"}[5m]) > 0 → Operator is failing
// • dbc_active{phase="Failed"} > 0 → A database claim failed to provision
// • dbc_provision_duration_seconds > 600 → Provisioning taking too long
