22.1 The Three Pillars of Observability

Observability is the ability to understand what's happening inside a system from its external outputs. In cloud native platforms, observability has three pillars:

📊
1. Metrics

Numeric measurements over time. CPU usage, request rate, error count, latency. Answer: "How much? How fast?" Stored in time-series databases (Prometheus TSDB). Lightweight. Aggregatable.

📝
2. Logs

Immutable timestamped events. "User Priya logged in at 14:32:15." Answer: "What happened?" Stored in Loki / Elasticsearch. High volume. Need parsing.

🔍
3. Traces

End-to-end request journeys across services. Answer: "Where is the bottleneck?" Stored in Jaeger / Tempo. Shows latency contribution per service.

🔬 The Observability Maturity Model — How Monitoring Evolves

Organizations don't jump from "no monitoring" to "full observability" overnight. Understanding where you are helps you know what to build next:

🚫
LEVEL 1
None

No metrics. Users report outages. "The site is slow" is the only alert.

❌ Flying Blind
📊
LEVEL 2
Basic Metrics

CPU/memory graphs. Prometheus + Grafana deployed. RED dashboards for key services.

⚠️ Reactive
🚨
LEVEL 3
Proactive Alerting

AlertManager routes alerts. SLO-based alerting (not threshold-based). On-call rotations.

✅ Proactive
🔗
LEVEL 4
Correlated

Metrics + Logs + Traces linked. trace_id in logs. Exemplars link metrics to traces. Thanos for long-term.

✅ Full Observability
🧠
LEVEL 5
Predictive

ML-powered anomaly detection. Predicts outages before they happen. Auto-remediation.

🌟 AIOps
🔺 The Observability Pyramid — Start With Metrics
                          ┌─────────────┐
                          │   TRACES     │  ← Debug specific slow requests
                          │  5% of data  │     Jaeger / Tempo / OpenTelemetry
                         ┌┴─────────────┴┐
                         │     LOGS       │  ← Deep-dive into specific events
                         │   15% of data  │     Loki / Elasticsearch / Fluent Bit
                        ┌┴───────────────┴┐
                        │     METRICS      │  ← Always-on, lightweight, aggregatable
                        │    80% of data   │     Prometheus + Grafana
                        └──────────────────┘

    🔑 START WITH METRICS. They're the cheapest to collect and store. They answer
       "Is there a problem?" Then use logs to answer "What happened?" Then use
       traces to answer "Where exactly is the bottleneck?"
🔴
RED Method For Services
RateRequests per second
ErrorsFailed requests per second
DurationLatency (P50, P95, P99)

Every service should expose RED metrics. This is the minimum useful monitoring.

🔵
USE Method For Infrastructure
Utilization% of resource used (CPU, memory, disk)
SaturationAmount of queued work (load average, queue depth)
ErrorsHardware/OS errors, packet drops

USE monitors the infrastructure UNDER the services. Nodes, disks, networks.

22.2 Prometheus Architecture — The Pull Model

Prometheus is fundamentally different from most monitoring systems: it pulls metrics from targets instead of waiting for them to push. This is the single most important architectural decision in Prometheus — and it's why Prometheus works so well with Kubernetes.

📤
Push Model (Nagios, Graphite)

Agents push metrics to a central server. The server is passive — it just receives. If the server is down, metrics are lost. Need to configure each agent with the server address.

❌ Problem: Who monitors the monitor? Server overload = lost metrics.

📥
Pull Model (Prometheus) 🏆

Prometheus scrapes targets on a schedule. Targets expose /metrics endpoints. Prometheus discovers targets via service discovery. If a target is down, Prometheus knows.

✅ "If I can't scrape you, you're not healthy." Prometheus IS the health check.

🏗️ Prometheus Architecture — How It All Fits Together
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                          PROMETHEUS ARCHITECTURE                                │
│                                                                                │
│   ┌──────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐      │
│   │ Kubernetes Pods   │     │ Node Exporter     │     │ External Targets │      │
│   │ :9090/metrics     │     │ :9100/metrics     │     │ (RDS, API, etc.) │      │
│   └────────┬─────────┘     └────────┬─────────┘     └────────┬─────────┘      │
│            │                        │                        │                 │
│            └────────────────────────┼────────────────────────┘                 │
│                                     │ SCRAPE (pull every 15s)                  │
│                                     ▼                                          │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│   │                         PROMETHEUS SERVER                              │    │
│   │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐                 │    │
│   │  │ Service      │  │ TSDB         │  │ PromQL        │                 │    │
│   │  │ Discovery    │─►│ (Time-Series │─►│ Query Engine  │                 │    │
│   │  │ (K8s API)    │  │  Database)   │  │               │                 │    │
│   │  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────┬────────┘                 │    │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                  │                              │
│                    ┌─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────┐           │
│                    ▼                             ▼                  ▼           │
│   ┌────────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────┐      │
│   │ Grafana            │  │ AlertManager        │  │ Prometheus API     │      │
│   │ (Dashboards)       │  │ (Alert Routing)     │  │ (External Queries) │      │
│   └────────────────────┘  └────────────────────┘  └────────────────────┘      │
│                                                                                │
│   TSDB: 2-hour blocks. 15-day default retention. ~1.5 bytes/sample.            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧠 Key Prometheus Components You MUST Know
  • TSDB (Time-Series Database): Custom storage engine. Data stored in 2-hour blocks. ~1.5 bytes per sample. Default retention: 15 days.
  • Scrape Config: Defines what to scrape, how often (default 15s), and what labels to add.
  • Service Discovery: Prometheus queries the Kubernetes API to find pods, services, and endpoints automatically.
  • Relabeling: Transforms labels before ingestion. Drop unwanted metrics. Add cluster/env labels.
  • Pushgateway: For short-lived jobs that can't be scraped (CronJobs, batch). Use sparingly — it's an anti-pattern for long-running services.
🔬 TSDB Under the Hood — How Prometheus Actually Stores Your Metrics

Understanding TSDB internals helps you debug performance issues and avoid data loss. Here's what happens inside:

📦 Prometheus TSDB Storage Lifecycle
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         PROMETHEUS TSDB STORAGE                                 │
│                                                                                │
│   INGESTION                         STORAGE                        RETENTION   │
│   ─────────                         ───────                        ─────────   │
│                                                                                │
│   ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐               │
│   │ SCRAPE   │───►│  WAL     │───►│  HEAD    │───►│  BLOCKS  │───► S3 (Thanos)│
│   │ (every   │    │ (Write-  │    │ (In-Mem  │    │ (Disk    │               │
│   │  15-30s) │    │  Ahead   │    │  Chunks) │    │  immut-  │               │
│   │          │    │  Log)    │    │          │    │  able)   │               │
│   └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘    └──────────┘               │
│                        │               │               │                      │
│                        ▼               ▼               ▼                      │
│                   Crash recovery  2-hour window   Compaction:                  │
│                   Replays WAL on   of samples in    2h → 6h → 18h blocks      │
│                   restart to      memory (fast      (reduces disk usage,       │
│                   recover data    query)           improves query speed)      │
│                                                                                │
│   KEY PARAMETERS:                                                              │
│   • --storage.tsdb.retention.time=15d   (delete blocks older than 15 days)    │
│   • --storage.tsdb.retention.size=50GB  (delete oldest blocks when > 50GB)    │
│   • --storage.tsdb.max-block-duration=2h (max time range per block)            │
│   • --storage.tsdb.min-block-duration=2h (min time before block is written)    │
│                                                                                │
│   ⚠️ WAL checkpoint: Every 2 hours, in-memory data is flushed to a block       │
│      on disk. If Prometheus crashes BEFORE the flush, data since last          │
│      checkpoint is in WAL and will be replayed on restart.                     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🧠 MEMORY TRICK: "WAL protects against crashes. Head Block serves fast queries. Compaction saves disk space." If Prometheus is slow, check if compaction is falling behind. If Prometheus OOMs, reduce retention or increase memory. The TSDB stores ~3 bytes of index per sample in memory.

🔬 The Prometheus Data Model — Understanding Time Series at the Core

To master PromQL, you must first understand what a time series actually IS:

🧬 Anatomy of a Prometheus Time Series
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    A TIME SERIES = METRIC NAME + LABEL SET                     │
│                                                                                │
│   http_requests_total{service="anihpj-web", method="GET", status="200"}       │
│   ──────────────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────     │
│        METRIC NAME                      LABEL SET (key=value pairs)           │
│                                                                                │
│   Each unique combination of name + labels = ONE time series.                 │
│   If you add status="404", that's a DIFFERENT time series.                    │
│   If you add a new pod, that pod's metrics form NEW time series.              │
│                                                                                │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│   │  TIME SERIES DATA (timestamp, value)                                 │    │
│   │  ─────────────────────────────────                                   │    │
│   │  t=14:00:00  value=1500   (timestamp in milliseconds since epoch)    │    │
│   │  t=14:00:15  value=1503                                              │    │
│   │  t=14:00:30  value=1508   ← Each scrape adds one (t,v) sample        │    │
│   │  t=14:00:45  value=1512                                              │    │
│   └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                                                                │
│   VECTOR TYPES:                                                                │
│   • Instant Vector: ONE sample per time series at a SINGLE timestamp          │
│     (e.g., http_requests_total — the latest scraped value)                     │
│   • Range Vector: MULTIPLE samples per time series over a TIME RANGE          │
│     (e.g., http_requests_total[5m] — all samples in the last 5 minutes)       │
│                                                                                │
│   THE __name__ LABEL: Internally, the metric name IS a label.                 │
│   {__name__="http_requests_total", service="anihpj-web"} ≡ the metric above    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🧠 KEY INSIGHT: Labels are what make Prometheus powerful. They turn "how many requests?" into "how many requests per service, per endpoint, per status code?" But labels are also the #1 performance killer — every unique label combination is a separate time series with its own memory and disk footprint.

22.3 PromQL — The Query Language You MUST Master

PromQL (Prometheus Query Language) is a functional query language that lets you select, aggregate, and transform time-series data. The CNPE exam WILL test your PromQL skills. Here are the queries that matter most:

FunctionWhat It DoesMust-Know ExampleWhy It Matters
rate()Per-second rate of increase over a rangerate(http_requests_total[5m])Converts counters to per-second rates. Most used function in PromQL.
sum()Aggregate across dimensionssum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) by (service)Combine multiple series. Group by labels.
histogram_quantile()Calculate percentile from histogramhistogram_quantile(0.99, rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]))P99 latency. CRITICAL for SLOs.
avg()Average across seriesavg(node_cpu_seconds_total)Use with caution — averages hide outliers.
increase()Total increase over a rangeincrease(http_requests_total[1h])"How many requests in the last hour?"
irate()Instant rate (last 2 samples)irate(http_requests_total[5m])More sensitive to spikes. Good for graphs.
📊 PromQL — The 10 Queries Every Platform Engineer Must Know
# ── REQUEST RATE ──
# "How many requests per second is anihpj handling?"
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="anihpj-web"}[5m]))

# ── ERROR RATE ──
# "What percentage of requests are failing?"
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="anihpj-web",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  /
sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="anihpj-web"}[5m])) * 100

# ── P99 LATENCY ──
# "What's the 99th percentile latency?"
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="anihpj-web"}[5m])) by (le))

# ── CPU USAGE % ──
# "How much CPU is anihpj using vs its request?"
sum(rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{container="anihpj-web"}[5m]))
  /
sum(kube_pod_container_resource_requests{container="anihpj-web",resource="cpu"}) * 100

# ── POD RESTARTS ──
# "Are anihpj pods crashing?"
rate(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{container="anihpj-web"}[1h])

# ── MEMORY USAGE % ──
# "Is anihpj close to its memory limit?"
sum(container_memory_working_set_bytes{container="anihpj-web"})
  /
sum(kube_pod_container_resource_limits{container="anihpj-web",resource="memory"}) * 100

# ── REQUEST DURATION BY STATUS CODE ──
# "Are errors slower than successes?"
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_sum{service="anihpj-web"}[5m])) by (status)
  /
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{service="anihpj-web"}[5m])) by (status)

# ── TOP 5 ENDPOINTS BY LATENCY ──
# "Which endpoint is the slowest?"
topk(5,
  histogram_quantile(0.99,
    sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (le, endpoint)))

# ── AVAILABILITY % (Uptime) ──
# "What percentage of time was the service up?"
avg(up{service="anihpj-web"}[30d]) * 100

# ── PREDICT DISK FULL (Linear Regression) ──
# "When will the disk be full?"
predict_linear(node_filesystem_free_bytes{mountpoint="/"}[1h], 24*3600) < 0
⚡ PromQL Exam Tips — Avoid These Common Mistakes
  • ALWAYS use rate() on counters: Counters only go up. rate() converts to per-second. Never graph raw counter values.
  • histogram_quantile() needs the le dimension: Always aggregate by (le) before calling histogram_quantile().
  • sum() without by aggregates everything: Add by (service, namespace) to keep dimensions.
  • rate() needs a range vector: [5m] is NOT optional. PromQL will error without it.
  • Labels are case-sensitive: service="anihpj-web" ≠ service="Anihpj-Web".
🔬 rate() vs irate() — When to Use Each

This is one of the most common PromQL interview questions — and a CNPE exam trap. Both compute per-second rates, but they behave VERY differently with counter resets and spikes.

Aspectrate()irate()
CalculationAverage rate over the entire range windowInstant rate using the last TWO samples only
Counter Reset Handling✅ Handles resets gracefully (detects decrease, adjusts)⚠️ Can produce spikes on reset (only sees last 2 samples)
Graph AppearanceSmooth, averaged line. Good for dashboards.Spiky, responsive line. Shows every micro-spike.
Best ForAlerts, SLO calculations, long-term trendsDebugging, investigating sudden traffic changes
Examplerate(http_requests_total[5m])irate(http_requests_total[5m])

🎯 RULE OF THUMB: Use rate() for alerts and dashboards — it's stable and handles counter resets. Use irate() when you're actively debugging and need to see every spike. Never use raw counter values in graphs — counters only increase, so your graph will always trend up and to the right, telling you nothing.

🔬 Advanced PromQL — The Operators That Separate Beginners from Experts

Beyond rate() and sum(), these operators unlock advanced querying patterns:

OperatorWhat It DoesReal-World ExampleWhen to Use
offsetShift query back in time by a durationrate(http_requests_total[5m] offset 1h)Compare current traffic vs 1 hour ago. "Is this spike normal for this time of day?"
boolReturn 0/1 instead of filteringrate(http_errors[5m]) > bool 10Count how many series exceed a threshold. Useful for "how many services have error rate > 10/s?"
unlessSet subtraction — keep A where no matching Bup == 1 unless on(instance) ALERTS{alertname="Silenced"}Exclude targets that are silenced. "Show me unhealthy targets that are NOT silenced."
andSet intersection — keep A where matching B existsrate(http_requests[5m]) > 100 and on(service) up == 1Only show high-traffic services that are up. "Don't alert on high traffic if the service is already down."
orSet union — fill gaps with fallback valuenode_memory_MemAvailable or node_memory_MemFreeFallback metric. "Use MemAvailable if it exists, otherwise use MemFree."
@ modifierEvaluate at a specific timestamphttp_requests_total @ 1609459200Query what a value WAS at a specific time. Debugging: "What was the error rate at 3 AM?"

🎯 CNPE TIP: The offset modifier is commonly tested — comparing current vs historical values. The bool modifier is the secret to "how many things are failing?" queries. The unless operator is for excluding maintenance windows.

22.4 Grafana Dashboards — Making Metrics Visible

Prometheus stores the data. Grafana visualizes it. A well-designed Grafana dashboard tells a story — you can look at it for 5 seconds and know if everything is healthy or if something is wrong.

📊
1. RED Panels First

Rate (requests/sec), Errors (error %), Duration (P50/P95/P99 latency). These are the three most important panels. Put them at the TOP of the dashboard.

🔴🟡🟢
2. Color With Meaning

Green = healthy. Yellow = warning. Red = critical. Use thresholds on stat panels. A red panel should mean "someone needs to look at this NOW."

📐
3. Use Variables

Dashboard variables ($service, $namespace, $pod) let one dashboard serve ALL services. Don't create one dashboard per service — that doesn't scale.

📊 anihpj Grafana Dashboard — Layout Design
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ANIHPJ-WEB — SERVICE DASHBOARD                          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  ROW 1: OVERVIEW (Big Numbers)                                            │
│  ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐        │

⚡ Dashboard-as-Code — Never Build Dashboards by Hand

Grafana dashboards should be provisioned as code, not built by clicking in the UI. Use ConfigMaps or the Grafana Dashboard Provisioning system. This means dashboards are version-controlled, reviewed in PRs, and deployed via GitOps.

# grafana-dashboard-configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: anihpj-dashboard
  labels:
    grafana_dashboard: "1"  # Auto-discovered by Grafana sidecar
data:
  anihpj.json: |
    { ... dashboard JSON ... }
🔬 Grafana Provisioning — Dashboards, Datasources & Variables as Code

Grafana should NEVER be configured by clicking in the UI. Everything must be code. Here's the complete provisioning pattern:

📊 Dashboard Provisioning
# grafana-dashboards ConfigMap
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  labels:
    grafana_dashboard: "1"
data:
  anihpj-red.json: |-
    { "title": "anihpj RED", ... }
  anihpj-infra.json: |-
    { "title": "anihpj Infra", ... }

# Grafana sidecar auto-discovers
# ConfigMaps with this label and
# loads them as dashboards.
🔧 Dashboard Variables
# Grafanavariables make ONE dashboard
# serve ALL services. Define in JSON:

# $service — pick a service
"query": "label_values(up, service)"

# $namespace — auto-filtered
"query": "label_values(kube_pod_info{service=\"$service\"}, namespace)"

# $pod — depends on $namespace
"query": "label_values(kube_pod_info{namespace=\"$namespace\"}, pod)"

# PromQL uses variables:
rate(http_requests_total{service="$service",namespace="$namespace"}[5m])
🔬 Grafana Alerting — When to Alert from Grafana vs Prometheus

Grafana has its own alerting system. But should you use it instead of Prometheus AlertManager? The answer depends on the type of alert:

Alert TypeUse Prometheus AlertManagerUse Grafana Alerting
Infrastructure alerts (node down, disk full)✅ Native. Built-in rules.⚠️ Possible but adds latency
Application SLO alerts (error budget burn)✅ Recording rules pre-compute. AlertManager evaluates.⚠️ Grafana re-queries data source on each eval
Multi-source alerts (Prometheus + Loki + PostgreSQL)❌ Prometheus-only data✅ Grafana can query MULTIPLE data sources in one alert
Dashboard-linked alerts (alert on what you see)⚠️ Need separate rule file✅ Right-click panel → "Create Alert"
Complex correlation (metric X AND log pattern Y)❌ Single data source✅ Multi-source expressions

🎯 RECOMMENDATION: Use Prometheus AlertManager for infrastructure and SLO alerts (fast, reliable, purpose-built). Use Grafana Alerting only when you need multi-source queries or UI-driven alert creation. Never duplicate — one alert, one system.

22.5 ServiceMonitor & Auto-Discovery

The Prometheus Operator introduces the ServiceMonitor CRD — a Kubernetes-native way to tell Prometheus WHAT to scrape. Instead of editing prometheus.yml config files, you create a ServiceMonitor resource. The operator watches for these and updates the Prometheus configuration automatically.

🔄 ServiceMonitor — Auto-Discovery Flow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    SERVICEMONITOR AUTO-DISCOVERY FLOW                           │
│                                                                                │
│   1. CREATE                  2. WATCH                   3. GENERATE             │
│   ┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐    │
│   │ ServiceMonitor   │      │ Prometheus       │      │ prometheus.yml   │    │
│   │ ──────────────── │      │ Operator         │      │ ──────────────── │    │
│   │ selector:        │─────►│ ──────────────── │─────►│ scrape_configs:  │    │
│   │   app: anihpj    │      │ Watches for new  │      │   - job: anihpj  │    │
│   │ endpoints:       │      │ ServiceMonitors  │      │     targets:     │    │
│   │   - port: metrics│      │ in the cluster   │      │     - 10.1.2.3   │    │
│   │ interval: 30s    │      │                  │      │     - 10.1.2.4   │    │
│   └──────────────────┘      └──────────────────┘      └──────────────────┘    │
│                                                                                │
│   4. DISCOVER                   5. SCRAPE                   6. QUERY            │
│   ┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐    │
│   │ Prometheus       │      │ GET /metrics      │      │ PromQL:          │    │
│   │ finds Pods with  │─────►│ on each target    │─────►│ http_requests_   │    │
│   │ label app:anihpj │      │ every 30 seconds  │      │ total{app=anihpj}│    │
│   │ via K8s API      │      │                   │      │                  │    │
│   └──────────────────┘      └──────────────────┘      └──────────────────┘    │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 ServiceMonitor for anihpj-web
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: monitoring        # ServiceMonitor lives in monitoring NS
  labels:
    release: prometheus        # Matches Prometheus' serviceMonitorSelector
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web           # Find Services with this label
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames:
      - anihpj                  # Only look in this namespace
  endpoints:
    - port: metrics             # Scrape the port named "metrics"
      interval: 30s             # Scrape every 30 seconds
      path: /metrics             # Default metrics path
      relabelings:               # Add labels to scraped metrics
        - sourceLabels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_node_name]
          targetLabel: node
🔬 kube-prometheus-stack — The Complete Monitoring Ecosystem

The kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart (formerly "prometheus-operator") deploys more than just Prometheus. It's an entire monitoring ecosystem that you need to understand for CNPE:

ComponentWhat It DoesKey MetricsCNPE Relevance
Prometheus OperatorManages Prometheus, AlertManager, ServiceMonitor CRDsN/A (controller)⭐ Core — deploys and manages Prometheus
PrometheusScrapes and stores metricsAll application + infra metrics⭐ Core — the metrics engine
AlertManagerRoutes, groups, deduplicates alertsN/A (alert router)⭐ Core — alert delivery
GrafanaDashboards and visualizationN/A (UI)⭐ Core — visualization
kube-state-metricsGenerates metrics about K8s objects (Deployments, Pods, Nodes)kube_deployment_status_replicas, kube_pod_status_phase⭐ Know these metric names
Node ExporterExposes node-level metrics (CPU, memory, disk, network)node_cpu_seconds_total, node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes⭐ Know these metric names
prometheus-adapterExposes Prometheus metrics via K8s Metrics API (for HPA)Custom metrics for autoscaling⚠️ Know it exists for HPA

🎯 CNPE EXAM TIP: You may be asked to query kube-state-metrics to check deployment status or node_exporter for node health. Memorize these prefixes: kube_* (K8s objects), node_* (node hardware), container_* (cAdvisor/container metrics).

🔬 The Prometheus Operator Reconciliation Loop — How CRDs Become Config

The Prometheus Operator is a Kubernetes controller that watches CRDs and reconciles the desired state with the actual state. Understanding this loop helps you debug when monitoring breaks:

1
WATCH: Operator watches for Prometheus, ServiceMonitor, PodMonitor, Alertmanager, and PrometheusRule CRDs via the K8s API. Any create/update/delete triggers reconciliation.
2
FILTER: Operator checks serviceMonitorSelector on the Prometheus CR. Only ServiceMonitors with matching labels are selected. This prevents one Prometheus from accidentally scraping another team's targets.
3
GENERATE: Operator generates prometheus.yml from ServiceMonitor definitions. Each ServiceMonitor → one scrape_config job. The operator fills in K8s SD configs, relabelings, and TLS settings automatically.
4
APPLY: Operator writes the generated config as a Kubernetes Secret (prometheus-<name>). Prometheus watches this Secret and hot-reloads its configuration — no restart needed.
5
MANAGE: Operator also manages the StatefulSet (replicas, resources, storage), the Service (for dashboard access), and RBAC (ServiceAccount for K8s API access).
⚠️ Why Your ServiceMonitor Isn't Working — Debug Checklist
  1. Does the ServiceMonitor have the label that matches serviceMonitorSelector on the Prometheus CR?
  2. Is the ServiceMonitor in a namespace that Prometheus is allowed to watch? (Check serviceMonitorNamespaceSelector)
  3. Does the target Service have the labels matching selector.matchLabels in the ServiceMonitor?
  4. Does the target Pod expose a port named exactly as specified in endpoints[].port?
  5. Check Prometheus Operator logs: kubectl logs -n monitoring deploy/prometheus-operator

22.6 Recording Rules & Alerting Rules

Prometheus has two types of rules: Recording Rules pre-compute expensive queries and save the results as new time series. Alerting Rules evaluate conditions and fire alerts when thresholds are breached.

💾
Recording Rules

Pre-compute expensive queries. Results stored as new metrics with record: name. Useful for dashboards — query the pre-computed result instead of re-running the expensive query every time.

# Pre-compute per-second request rate
groups:
  - name: anihpj_rules
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      - record: job:http_requests_total:rate5m
        expr: rate(http_requests_total[5m])
🚨
Alerting Rules

Evaluate conditions. When true → fire alert. Alerts go to AlertManager for routing, deduplication, grouping, and notification.

# Alert if error rate > 5% for 5 minutes
groups:
  - name: anihpj_alerts
    rules:
      - alert: HighErrorRate
        expr: |
          rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])
          /
          rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05
        for: 5m  # Must be true for 5 min
        labels:
          severity: critical
        annotations:
          summary: "High error rate on {{ $labels.service }}"
SeverityWhen to UseNotification ChannelResponse Time
🔴 CriticalService is down. Users affected. Revenue impact.PagerDuty (wakes someone up)5 minutes
🟡 WarningSomething is trending wrong. P99 > 500ms. Disk 80% full.Slack channel1 hour
🔵 InfoInformational. Deployment completed. Scaling event.Slack thread / no notificationNo action needed
🔬 Recording Rules — Naming Conventions That Scale

Recording rule names follow a specific convention that makes them self-documenting and queryable. The standard pattern is: level:metric:operation

PatternMeaningExampleWhen to Use
level:metric:operationStandard naming conventionjob:http_requests_total:rate5mAlways. Makes rules discoverable and prevents name collisions.
levelAggregation leveljob, instance, clusterThe dimension you aggregated BY. Tells you what labels remain.
metricOriginal metric namehttp_requests_totalKeep the source metric name so you know where it came from.
operationWhat transformation was appliedrate5m, sum, quantile99Documents the operation so you don't double-apply rate().
📋 The Golden Signals Recording Rules (RED + USE)
# These 6 recording rules pre-compute the MOST common dashboard queries.
# Your dashboards should query these, not the raw metrics.

groups:
  - name: golden_signals
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      # ── RED: Rate ──
      - record: job:http_requests_total:rate5m
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m])) by (job)
      # ── RED: Errors ──
      - record: job:http_errors_total:rate5m
        expr: sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])) by (job)
      # ── RED: Duration (P99) ──
      - record: job:http_request_duration:p99_5m
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])) by (job, le))
      # ── USE: CPU Utilization ──
      - record: instance:node_cpu_utilization:rate5m
        expr: 1 - avg(rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}[5m])) by (instance)
      # ── USE: Memory Saturation ──
      - record: instance:node_memory_utilization:avg5m
        expr: 1 - (avg(node_memory_MemAvailable_bytes) by (instance) / avg(node_memory_MemTotal_bytes) by (instance))
      # ── USE: Disk Saturation ──
      - record: instance:node_disk_utilization:avg5m
        expr: 1 - (avg(node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"}) by (instance) / avg(node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/"}) by (instance))

22.7 AlertManager — Routing, Grouping & Silencing

AlertManager handles alerts fired by Prometheus. It deduplicates, groups, and routes them to the right notification channel (PagerDuty, Slack, email, webhook). Without AlertManager, you get alert fatigue — 50 emails for the same problem.

🔔 AlertManager Pipeline
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         ALERTMANAGER PIPELINE                                   │
│                                                                                │
│   Prometheus fires alerts ──► AlertManager receives ──► Pipeline processing   │
│                                                                                │
│   ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐                  │
│   │ INHIBITION   │────►│ SILENCING    │────►│ ROUTING       │                  │
│   │ If cluster   │     │ If silenced  │     │ Route to      │                  │
│   │ is down,     │     │ (maintenance │     │ correct       │                  │
│   │ suppress     │     │  window),    │     │ receiver      │                  │
│   │ per-node     │     │ drop alert   │     │ (Slack/PD/etc)│                  │
│   │ alerts       │     │              │     │               │                  │
│   └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────┬────────┘                  │
│                                                     │                          │
│                       ┌─────────────────────────────┼──────────────┐          │
│                       ▼                             ▼              ▼          │
│                 ┌──────────┐                 ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────┐     │
│                 │ GROUPING │                 │ TIMING   │    │ RECEIVER │     │
│                 │ Group by │                 │ group_   │    │ PagerDuty│     │
│                 │ alertname│                 │ wait: 30s│    │ Slack    │     │
│                 │ + cluster│                 │ repeat:  │    │ Email    │     │
│                 │          │                 │  4h      │    │ Webhook  │     │
│                 └──────────┘                 └──────────┘    └──────────┘     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 AlertManager Config — Routing Critical vs Warning Alerts
route:
  group_by: [alertname, cluster]
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h
  receiver: slack-warning
  routes:
    - match:
        severity: critical
      receiver: pagerduty-critical
      repeat_interval: 1h
    - match:
        severity: warning
      receiver: slack-warning

receivers:
  - name: pagerduty-critical
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key: "<PD_KEY>"
        severity: critical
  - name: slack-warning
    slack_configs:
      - channel: "#platform-alerts"
🔬 Alert Inhibition — Suppress the Noise, Amplify the Signal

Inhibition rules prevent alert storms. When a cluster-wide problem occurs (e.g., network partition), you don't need 50 per-pod alerts — you need ONE alert saying "cluster is down."

📋 AlertManager Inhibition Rules
# If a Critical alert fires, suppress Warning alerts from same cluster
inhibit_rules:
  - source_match:              # WHEN this alert fires...
      severity: critical
      alertname: KubeNodeNotReady
    target_match:              # SUPPRESS these alerts...
      severity: warning
    equal: [cluster, namespace]  # ...only if they share these labels

  # If the entire cluster is unreachable, suppress ALL per-pod alerts
  - source_match:
      alertname: TargetDown
      severity: critical
    target_match_re:
      alertname: KubePod.*        # Suppress all pod-level alerts
    equal: [cluster]

# AlertManager HA: Run 3 replicas. They form a gossip cluster.
# Each AlertManager receives ALL alerts (Prometheus sends to all).
# The gossip protocol deduplicates — only ONE notification is sent.
# Flags: --cluster.peer=am2:9094 --cluster.peer=am3:9094
🔬 AlertManager Routing Tree — How Alerts Find Their Receiver

The AlertManager route is a tree, not a flat list. Each route can have child routes. Alerts traverse the tree top-down, matching the FIRST route whose match/match_re conditions are satisfied.

📋 Nested Route Tree — Teams Get Their Own Slack Channels
route:
  receiver: fallback-email       # Default — if nothing matches
  routes:                       # Top-level routes
    - match:
        severity: critical        # ALL critical → PagerDuty
      receiver: pagerduty
      continue: true             # IMPORTANT: Continue to child routes!
      routes:                   # Child routes ALSO fire for critical alerts
        - match:
            team: priya
          receiver: slack-priya-team
        - match:
            team: platform
          receiver: slack-platform-team
    - match:
        severity: warning        # Warning → team Slack only
      routes:
        - match:
            team: priya
          receiver: slack-priya-team
        - match:
            team: platform
          receiver: slack-platform-team

# KEY: continue: true means "match this route AND continue to children."
# Without continue: true, only the FIRST matching route fires.
# With continue: true, the alert goes to PagerDuty AND the team Slack.

22.8 Thanos — Long-Term Storage & Global Query View

Prometheus is great for short-term metrics (15-day retention). Thanos extends Prometheus with: long-term storage (years in object storage like S3), global query view across multiple Prometheus instances, and high availability with deduplication.

🏗️ Thanos Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                              THANOS ARCHITECTURE                               │
│                                                                                │
│   CLUSTER A                      CLUSTER B                      CLUSTER C      │
│   ┌──────────────────┐          ┌──────────────────┐          ┌──────────┐   │
│   │ Prometheus        │          │ Prometheus        │          │Prometheus│   │
│   │ + Sidecar         │          │ + Sidecar         │          │+ Sidecar │   │
│   │   │ (uploads TSDB)│          │   │ (uploads TSDB)│          │   │      │   │
│   └───┼──────────────┘          └───┼──────────────┘          └───┼──────┘   │
│       └────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────┘          │
│                                    ▼                                           │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│   │                    OBJECT STORAGE (S3 / GCS / Azure)                  │    │
│   │                    Years of metrics. Cheap. Durable.                  │    │
│   └────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                    │                                           │
│                                    ▼                                           │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│   │                    THANOS QUERIER (Global PromQL Endpoint)            │    │
│   │                    De-duplicates HA pairs. Merges recent + historical.│    │
│   └────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│                                    │                                           │
│                                    ▼                                           │
│                              ┌──────────┐                                      │
│                              │ Grafana  │  ← One dashboard, all clusters      │
│                              └──────────┘                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🧠 Thanos Components
  • Sidecar: Runs alongside Prometheus. Uploads TSDB blocks to object storage.
  • Querier: Global query endpoint. De-duplicates HA data. Merges recent + historical.
  • Store Gateway: Serves historical data from object storage.
  • Compactor: Downsamples and compacts blocks. Reduces storage cost.
  • Ruler: Evaluates recording/alerting rules against Thanos Querier.
🔬 Long-Term Storage Showdown — Thanos vs Cortex vs VictoriaMetrics

Prometheus alone can't store years of metrics. Three major projects solve this. You need to know the differences for CNPE architecture decisions.

FeatureThanosCortexVictoriaMetrics
ArchitectureSidecar per Prometheus. Uploads blocks to S3.Push-based. Prometheus remote_write to Cortex.Push OR pull. Drop-in Prometheus replacement.
Global Query✅ Thanos Querier merges results✅ Built-in. Single query endpoint✅ VictoriaMetrics Cluster
HA De-duplication✅ Querier de-dupes HA pairs✅ Built-in. Distributor handles it✅ Built-in dedup
StorageObject storage (S3/GCS/Azure) — cheapObject storage OR local disksCustom storage format — compressed
ComplexityMedium. Sidecar + Querier + Store + CompactorHigh. 7+ microservices (distributor, ingester, querier, etc.)Low. Single binary. Simple to deploy.
Best ForMultiple Prometheus instances, HA pairs, multi-clusterLarge scale (100M+ active series), multi-tenantSimple setup, low resource usage, single cluster
Downsampling✅ Compactor downsamples (raw → 5m → 1h)❌ No built-in downsampling❌ No built-in downsampling

🎯 CNPE RECOMMENDATION: Thanos is the most common choice for CNPE exam scenarios. It's CNCF-graduated, integrates directly with Prometheus (no remote_write needed), and the downsampling feature is unique. For the exam, know Thanos thoroughly.

📦
Adobe — Thanos at Scale
📈 900M+ active series

Adobe runs 100+ Kubernetes clusters. Thanos provides a single global query view. Sidecars upload to S3. Querier de-duplicates HA pairs. Compactor reduces storage costs 10x via downsampling.

🎮
ByteDance — VictoriaMetrics
📈 1B+ active series

ByteDance (TikTok) chose VictoriaMetrics over Thanos for its lower resource usage. Single binary deployment. 7x less RAM than Prometheus for equivalent workloads. Handles 50M samples/sec ingestion.

🏦
Grafana Labs — Cortex
📈 Multi-tenant SaaS

Grafana Cloud runs Cortex as the backend. Multi-tenant by design — each customer's data is isolated. Horizontally scalable: add more ingesters/distributors as tenant count grows.

☸️
anihpj — Thanos (Recommended)
📈 3 clusters, 1 dashboard

For the CNPE exam scenario, Thanos is the right choice: 3 Kubernetes clusters, Sidecar per Prometheus, S3 bucket for long-term storage, Querier for global view, Compactor for downsampling.

22.9 RED & USE Methodologies — What to Monitor

Now that you know HOW to collect and visualize metrics, the question becomes: WHAT should you monitor? Two methodologies answer this:

🔴
RED — For Every Service
R
Rate: Requests/sec. rate(http_requests_total[5m])
E
Errors: Failed requests. rate(http_requests_total{status=~\"5..\"}[5m])
D
Duration: Latency. histogram_quantile(0.99, ...)

From Google's SRE book. Every service MUST expose RED metrics.

🔵
USE — For Every Resource
U
Utilization: % used. CPU %, memory %, disk %.
S
Saturation: Queued work. Load average, queue depth.
E
Errors: Hardware/OS. Disk errors, network drops, OOM kills.

From Brendan Gregg. Apply to every resource: CPUs, memory, disks, network.

🎯 The Golden Rule: RED for Services + USE for Infrastructure
🔴 RED = "Is my service healthy?"

Apply to: anihpj-web, anihpj-worker. Every microservice gets a RED dashboard.

🔵 USE = "Is my infrastructure healthy?"

Apply to: K8s nodes, disks, network. Every resource gets USE checks.

🔬 Beyond RED/USE — The 4 Golden Signals (Google SRE)

Google's Site Reliability Engineering book defines 4 Golden Signals that go beyond RED. These are the MINIMUM metrics for any user-facing system:

⚡
1. Latency

Time to serve a request. Measure BOTH successful and failed requests separately. Failed requests can be fast (immediate 500) — they'll drag down your average if mixed. Always separate by status code.

📈
2. Traffic

Demand on your system. For HTTP: requests per second. For streaming: I/O rate. For queues: messages per second. Traffic spikes often precede problems — correlate with latency.

❌
3. Errors

Rate of failed requests. Explicit errors (HTTP 5xx). Implicit errors (HTTP 200 but wrong content). Policy errors (you said SLO is 100ms, but P99 is 150ms — that's an error against the SLO).

🔄
4. Saturation

How "full" your service is. CPU %, memory %, queue depth, connection pool utilization. Services degrade BEFORE they hit 100% — measure the knee in the curve, not the ceiling.

🎯 HOW THEY MAP: Latency + Traffic + Errors ≈ RED. Saturation ≈ USE. The 4 Golden Signals are the superset. If you monitor these 4 for every service, you have 80% of the observability you need.

22.10 Prometheus Operator — Kubernetes-Native Prometheus

The Prometheus Operator (kube-prometheus-stack) makes running Prometheus on Kubernetes feel native. Instead of ConfigMaps and StatefulSets, you create Prometheus, ServiceMonitor, and AlertManager CRDs.

Without OperatorWith Prometheus Operator
Edit prometheus.yml config file manuallyCreate ServiceMonitor CRD ✅
Restart Prometheus to pick up new targetsOperator auto-reloads config ✅
Manage StatefulSet, PVC, Service yourselfCreate Prometheus CRD ✅
Manual AlertManager configCreate AlertmanagerConfig CRD ✅
No built-in HAPrometheus CRD spec.replicas for HA ✅
📋 Prometheus CRD Example
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: Prometheus
metadata:
  name: platform
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  replicas: 2                       # HA pair
  retention: 15d
  serviceMonitorSelector:
    matchLabels:
      release: prometheus
  resources:
    requests:
      memory: 2Gi
      cpu: 500m
  storage:
    volumeClaimTemplate:
      spec:
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 100Gi
🔬 PrometheusRule CRD — Declarative Alerting & Recording Rules

With the Prometheus Operator, you don't edit prometheus.yml to add rules. You create a PrometheusRule CRD. The operator picks it up via label matching and injects the rules into the Prometheus configuration.

📋 PrometheusRule — anihpj Alerts as Kubernetes Resource
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: anihpj-alerts
  namespace: anihpj
  labels:
    release: prometheus        # Must match Prometheus' ruleSelector
    team: priya
spec:
  groups:
    - name: anihpj-alerts
      rules:
        - alert: HighErrorRate
          expr: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="anihpj-web",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="anihpj-web"}[5m])) > 0.05
          for: 5m
          labels:
            severity: critical
            team: priya
          annotations:
            summary: "anihpj-web error rate > 5%"
            description: "Error rate is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }}. Check /api/v1/health."
            runbook_url: "https://wiki.anihpj.example.com/runbooks/high-error-rate"
        - alert: HighLatency
          expr: |
            histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="anihpj-web"}[10m])) by (le)) > 0.5
          for: 10m
          labels:
            severity: warning
            team: priya
          annotations:
            summary: "anihpj-web P99 latency > 500ms"
            runbook_url: "https://wiki.anihpj.example.com/runbooks/high-latency"

🎯 BEST PRACTICE: Always include a runbook_url annotation in your alerts. When someone gets paged at 3 AM, they need to know EXACTLY what to do. A link to the runbook can mean the difference between a 5-minute fix and a 2-hour debugging session.

22.11 anihpj Metrics & Dashboards — Complete Setup

Let's instrument the anihpj Django application with Prometheus metrics and build a complete monitoring setup — exactly the kind of task on the CNPE exam.

🐍 Instrumenting Django (anihpj) for Prometheus
# pip install django-prometheus

# In settings.py:
INSTALLED_APPS += ['django_prometheus']
MIDDLEWARE = [
    'django_prometheus.middleware.PrometheusBeforeMiddleware',
    ...
    'django_prometheus.middleware.PrometheusAfterMiddleware',
]

# In urls.py:
urlpatterns += [path('', include('django_prometheus.urls'))]

# Now anihpj exposes /metrics with:
# django_http_requests_total_by_view_transport_method_total
# django_http_responses_total_by_status_total
# django_http_requests_latency_seconds (histogram)
📊
Step 1: Instrument

Add django-prometheus. Expose /metrics. Add port named "metrics" to Service.

🔍
Step 2: Discover

Create ServiceMonitor selecting app: anihpj-web. Prometheus auto-discovers.

📈
Step 3: Visualize

Grafana dashboard with RED panels. Provision as ConfigMap via GitOps.

✅ anihpj Complete Monitoring Setup — The Full Picture
  • Instrumentation: django-prometheus in anihpj-web. celery-prometheus-exporter for anihpj-worker. postgres_exporter sidecar for anihpj-db.
  • Kubernetes Layer: Prometheus Operator deployed via Helm. ServiceMonitors for anihpj-web, anihpj-worker, anihpj-db. kube-state-metrics for Deployment/ReplicaSet status. Node Exporter DaemonSet for node-level metrics.
  • Visualization: 3 Grafana dashboards: (1) anihpj RED Dashboard — Rate, Errors, Duration. (2) anihpj Infrastructure — CPU, Memory, Disk, Network. (3) anihpj Business — Job posts created/min, active users, DB query latency.
  • Alerting: 5 alerts: HighErrorRate (5xx > 5% for 5min → PagerDuty), HighLatency (P99 > 500ms for 10min → Slack), PodRestarting (restarts > 0 for 5min → Slack), DiskFull (predicted < 10% in 24h → PagerDuty), DeadMansSwitch (Prometheus self-monitoring → PagerDuty).
  • Long-Term: Thanos Sidecar in each cluster. S3 bucket for TSDB blocks. Thanos Querier for global dashboard. 2-year retention for capacity planning.

22.12 Prometheus Best Practices

After running Prometheus in production, certain patterns emerge. Here are the rules that will save you pain:

🏷️
1. Label Everything, Don't Over-Label

Labels enable PromQL. Add service, namespace, cluster. But NEVER put user IDs, emails, or request IDs in labels — cardinality explosion kills TSDB.

📏
2. Histograms > Summaries

Summaries calculate quantiles client-side (not aggregatable). Histograms let you calculate ANY quantile server-side. Always use histograms for latency.

💾
3. Set Resource Limits

Set --storage.tsdb.retention.time=15d AND --storage.tsdb.retention.size=50GB. Whichever hits first wins. Without limits, Prometheus WILL OOM.

🔄
4. Run HA Pairs

Run 2 identical Prometheus instances. Query redundancy. Add Thanos for de-duplication across the pair.

⚠️ Cardinality Explosion — The #1 Prometheus Outage Cause

Cardinality = number of unique label combinations. If you add a user_id label with 100,000 unique values, you create 100,000 NEW time series — each consuming ~1.5 bytes/sample + index overhead. At 15-second scrape intervals, this adds GBs of memory per day.

🛡️ Defense: Never put unbounded values in labels. Use structured logs for those. Monitor prometheus_tsdb_head_series (should stay under 10M). Set --storage.tsdb.max-block-duration.

🔬 Scaling Prometheus — Federation vs Remote Write

A single Prometheus can handle ~10 million active series. Beyond that, you need to scale. Two strategies exist:

🏢
Hierarchical Federation

Global Prometheus scrapes local Prometheus instances (not the apps directly). Local Prometheus stores detailed data (15s scrape). Global scrapes aggregated data (1m scrape) from locals via /federate endpoint.

# Global Prometheus scrape config:
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: federate
    honor_labels: true
    params:
      match[]:
        - '{__name__=~"job:.*"}'  # Only aggregated
    static_configs:
      - targets: [prometheus-cluster-a:9090]

✅ Simple. ❌ Global is SPOF. Limited aggregation.

📤
Remote Write (Recommended)

Prometheus pushes metrics to a remote storage backend (Thanos, Cortex, VictoriaMetrics). Local Prometheus handles short-term. Remote handles long-term + global queries.

# prometheus.yml:
remote_write:
  - url: http://cortex-distributor:9009/api/v1/push
    queue_config:
      max_samples_per_send: 5000
      batch_send_deadline: 5s
      max_shards: 200

✅ Scales to 100M+ series. ✅ Global query. ⚠️ Complex backend needed.

🎯 CNPE GUIDANCE: For the exam, know that Federation uses /federate endpoint and match[] params. Remote Write uses remote_write config with a URL. Federation is simpler for small setups (< 3 clusters). Remote Write is the enterprise pattern for scale.

⚠️ When to Shard Prometheus — The Scaling Decision Tree

Not every scaling problem needs Thanos or Cortex. Sometimes you just need to split Prometheus workloads:

ProblemSymptomSolution
Single Prometheus OOMprometheus_tsdb_head_series > 10MFunctional Sharding: One Prometheus per domain (infra metrics, app metrics, business metrics). Each has its own targets + retention.
Scrape interval too slowScrape duration > scrape intervalHorizontal Sharding: Multiple Prometheus instances scraping different subsets of targets (hashmod on pod name).
Need global view across clustersCan't see all clusters in one dashboardThanos/Cortex: Remote storage + global query. Use Thanos Querier or Cortex Query Frontend.
Long-term retention neededNeed > 15 days of dataThanos Sidecar: Upload blocks to S3. Local Prometheus keeps 15 days. S3 keeps 2 years.

🛡️ GOLDEN RULE: Start with ONE Prometheus. When it reaches 50% memory usage of its limit, plan your scaling strategy. Don't wait until it OOMs at 3 AM. Monitor prometheus_tsdb_head_series and prometheus_engine_query_duration_seconds — they tell you when it's time to scale.

Ch 23: Logging & Log Aggregation

Logs answer "what happened." Loki is the Prometheus of logging — same label-based approach, same architecture philosophy. Fluent Bit collects from nodes and enriches with Kubernetes metadata. Together they form the modern logging stack.

23.1 Logs vs Metrics vs Traces — Where Logs Fit

In the observability triad, logs answer "what happened." While metrics tell you "is there a problem?" and traces tell you "where is the bottleneck?", logs give you the detailed narrative of a specific event.

📊
Metrics

Question: "Is there a problem?"
Data: Numbers over time
Cost: Cheap. ~1.5 bytes/sample
Tool: Prometheus
Example: P99 latency = 450ms

📝
Logs

Question: "What happened?"
Data: Timestamped text events
Cost: Medium. ~200 bytes/line
Tool: Loki / Elasticsearch
Example: "User Priya: payment failed — CC declined at 14:32:15"

🔍
Traces

Question: "Where is the bottleneck?"
Data: Request spans across services
Cost: Expensive. ~1KB/span
Tool: Tempo / Jaeger
Example: "auth-service took 320ms, DB query took 180ms"

🎯 When to Use Logs (and When NOT To)
✅ Use Logs For
  • Debugging specific failures: "Why did this payment fail?"
  • Audit trails: "Who deleted this deployment?"
  • Error stack traces: "What line of code panicked?"
  • Business events: "User X upgraded to premium plan"
  • Security forensics: "What IPs accessed the API at 3 AM?"
❌ Don't Use Logs For
  • Real-time alerting — use metrics (faster, cheaper)
  • Performance trending — use metrics (aggregatable)
  • Request tracing across services — use traces (structured)
  • Counting things — use metrics counters (1.5 bytes vs 200 bytes)
📊
MetricsPrometheus
+
📝
LogsLoki
+
🔍
TracesTempo
→
📈
GrafanaUnified Dashboard
→
🎯
Answer"What's wrong?"

Metrics tell you there's a problem. Logs tell you what happened. Traces tell you where. Together in Grafana, you have the full picture.

23.2 The Kubernetes Logging Pipeline — stdout → kubelet → Fluent Bit

In Kubernetes, the logging pipeline follows a simple but powerful path. Understanding this path is essential for debugging when logs go missing.

🔄 The Kubernetes Logging Pipeline — End to End
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     KUBERNETES LOGGING PIPELINE                                │
│                                                                                │
│   1. APPLICATION          2. CONTAINER RUNTIME      3. KUBELET                 │
│   ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────┐        │
│   │ anihpj-web       │    │ containerd /      │    │ kubelet          │        │
│   │ ──────────────── │    │ CRI-O             │    │ ──────────────── │        │
│   │ print() or       │───►│ ────────────────  │───►│ Reads log files  │        │
│   │ logging.info()   │    │ Captures stdout   │    │ from /var/log/   │        │
│   │ → stdout/stderr  │    │ and stderr streams│    │ containers/      │        │
│   └──────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘    └──────────────────┘        │
│                                                                                │
│   4. LOG AGENT (Fluent Bit)         5. LOG STORAGE (Loki)                      │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────────────┐          │
│   │ Fluent Bit (DaemonSet)        │  │ Loki (StatefulSet)            │          │
│   │ ────────────────────────────  │  │ ────────────────────────────  │          │
│   │ • Tails log files on node     │  │ • Receives pushed logs        │          │
│   │ • Parses log lines            │  │ • Indexes by labels           │          │
│   │ • Adds K8s metadata           │  │ • Stores compressed chunks    │          │
│   │   (pod, namespace, container) │  │ • Exposes LogQL API           │          │
│   │ • Pushes to Loki              │  │                               │          │
│   └──────────────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────────────┘          │
│                                                                                │
│   FILE PATH ON NODE:                                                           │
│   /var/log/containers/anihpj-web_default_anihpj-web-abc123.log                 │
│   ──────────────────────── ─────── ───────────────────                         │
│          pod name          namespace    container name + pod UID               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 Fluent Bit — DaemonSet Configuration
# Fluent Bit runs as a DaemonSet — one pod per node.
# It reads ALL container logs from the node's filesystem.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: fluent-bit
  namespace: logging
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: fluent-bit
          image: fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
          volumeMounts:
            - name: varlog
              mountPath: /var/log          # Node's log directory
            - name: varlibdockercontainers
              mountPath: /var/lib/docker/containers
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: varlog
          hostPath:
            path: /var/log
        - name: varlibdockercontainers
          hostPath:
            path: /var/lib/docker/containers
🔬 Fluent Bit Pipeline — Input → Parser → Filter → Output

Fluent Bit processes logs through a 4-stage pipeline. Understanding each stage helps you debug when logs go missing or contain wrong data:

1
INPUT: Tails log files. Kubernetes filter auto-discovers new containers. tail plugin reads /var/log/containers/*.log. systemd plugin reads journald for node-level logs.
2
PARSER: Extracts fields from log lines. json parser for JSON logs. regex parser for custom formats. docker parser strips Docker's JSON wrapper to get the actual log message.
3
FILTER: Modifies/enriches records. kubernetes filter adds pod name, namespace, container name, labels, annotations. modify filter adds/removes fields. nest filter restructures JSON.
4
OUTPUT: Sends processed logs to destination. loki output pushes to Loki with labels. es output for Elasticsearch. s3 output for archival.
📋 Fluent Bit Pipeline Config
# INPUT: Tail container logs + systemd journal
[INPUT]
    Name              tail
    Path              /var/log/containers/*.log
    Parser            docker          # Strip Docker JSON wrapper
    Tag               kube.*
    Refresh_Interval  10

# FILTER: Enrich with Kubernetes metadata
[FILTER]
    Name              kubernetes
    Match             kube.*
    Kube_URL          https://kubernetes.default.svc:443
    Merge_Log         On              # Merge parsed JSON into root
    K8S-Logging.Parser On
    K8S-Logging.Exclude On

# OUTPUT: Push to Loki with K8s labels
[OUTPUT]
    Name              loki
    Match             kube.*
    Host              loki-gateway.logging.svc
    Port              80
    Labels            {job="fluent-bit"}
    Label_keys        $namespace, $pod_name, $container_name
🔬 The 12-Factor App — Why stdout Is the Only Way

The 12-Factor App methodology (Heroku, 2011) has one rule for logging: "A twelve-factor app never concerns itself with routing or storage of its output stream. Each running process writes its event stream, unbuffered, to stdout." This is exactly how Kubernetes logging works:

✅ The Right Way
  • Application writes to stdout/stderr only
  • No log files. No log rotation. No syslog.
  • Container runtime captures stdout
  • kubelet makes logs available at /var/log/containers/
  • Fluent Bit / Promtail picks them up from there
  • Application doesn't know or care WHERE logs go
❌ The Wrong Way
  • Writing to /var/log/app.log inside container
  • Using a logging sidecar to tail a file
  • Sending logs directly to Elasticsearch from the app
  • Configuring syslog in the container
  • Rotating log files within the container
FeatureFluent BitPromtail
LanguageC (very lightweight, ~450KB binary)Go (heavier, ~15MB binary)
Resource Usage✅ ~20MB RAM, minimal CPU⚠️ ~100MB RAM, moderate CPU
K8s Integration✅ Native Kubernetes filter✅ Native (built by Grafana for Loki)
Best ForResource-constrained environments, edge nodesDeep Loki integration, automatic label extraction
🔬 kubectl logs — The Magic Behind the Command

When you run kubectl logs anihpj-web-abc123, here's what actually happens behind the scenes:

1
kubectl → API Server: kubectl sends a GET request to /api/v1/namespaces/anihpj/pods/anihpj-web-abc123/log. The API server authenticates and authorizes the request.
2
API Server → kubelet: The API server proxies the request to the kubelet on the node where the pod is running (node3:10250).
3
kubelet reads file: kubelet reads the log file at /var/log/containers/anihpj-web_default_anihpj-web-abc123.log. This is a symlink to the CRI's actual log location.
4
CRI log format: containerd/CRI-O wraps each line in JSON: {"log":"...","stream":"stdout","time":"..."}. kubelet strips this wrapper and returns the raw log content.
5
Response flows back: kubelet → API Server → kubectl → your terminal. Fluent Bit/Promtail reads the SAME files directly from disk (bypassing the API server).

🧠 WHY THIS MATTERS: kubectl logs reads from the CURRENT container. If the pod restarts, kubectl logs shows the NEW container's logs. Use kubectl logs --previous to see the CRASHED container's logs. But Loki has BOTH — because Fluent Bit reads from disk, it captures ALL logs, including from crashed containers.

⚠️ Log Rotation — Why Logs Disappear and How to Control It

Kubernetes doesn't store container logs forever. The kubelet rotates log files when they reach a configured size limit. If you don't configure this properly, you lose logs — and Fluent Bit loses them too:

kubelet FlagDefaultWhat It ControlsRecommendation
--container-log-max-size10MiMax size of a single log file before rotation50Mi for production (fewer files, easier for Fluent Bit)
--container-log-max-files5Max number of rotated log files to keep10 (more history for debugging)
--maximum-dead-containers-1 (unlimited)Max dead containers to keep logs for50 (prevents disk fill from crash loops)

🧠 THE MATH: With defaults: 5 files × 10Mi = 50Mi per container. With 50 containers/node: 2.5GB for logs. With recommendation: 10 files × 50Mi = 500Mi per container. 50 containers = 25GB. Plan your node disk size accordingly!

23.3 Loki Architecture — The Prometheus of Logging

Loki is Grafana's log aggregation system. Its key innovation: it doesn't index the full text of logs. Instead, it indexes only labels (metadata) — exactly like Prometheus indexes labels on metrics. The actual log content is stored in compressed chunks. This makes Loki dramatically cheaper to run than Elasticsearch.

FeatureLoki (Grafana)Elasticsearch (ELK/EFK)
IndexingIndexes LABELS only. Content stored as chunks.Indexes EVERY WORD (full-text index).
Storage Cost✅ Low. ~1/10th of Elasticsearch.⚠️ High. Full-text index is expensive.
Query ModelLogQL (PromQL-like). Label filter + text search.Lucene/KQL. Full-text search engine.
K8s Integration✅ Native. Labels map to K8s metadata (pod, namespace).⚠️ Works but requires more config.
Best ForKubernetes logs. "Show me all ERROR logs from anihpj-web in the last hour."Full-text search. "Show me all logs containing 'credit card 4532...'"
Grafana Integration✅ Native. Same UI as Prometheus. Correlate metrics + logs.✅ Supported via data source plugin.
🔀 Should I Use Loki or Elasticsearch?
🤔 Are you running on Kubernetes?
✅ YESLoki — native K8s labels. Fluent Bit + Loki is the standard K8s logging stack.
❌ NOConsider Elasticsearch — more flexible for non-K8s environments.
🤔 Do you need full-text search (e.g., find "credit card 4532...")?
✅ YESElasticsearch — full-text inverted index is purpose-built for this.
❌ NOLoki — label + grep-style search is sufficient and 10x cheaper.
🤔 Is budget a major concern?
✅ YESLoki — ~1/10th the storage cost of Elasticsearch. S3 backend is cheap.
❌ NOEither works. Loki is simpler. Elasticsearch is more powerful for search.
🔬 Loki Write Path — How Logs Flow from Fluent Bit to Object Storage

Understanding the write path helps you tune Loki for reliability and performance:

1
Distributor receives: Fluent Bit sends compressed protobuf over HTTP. Distributor validates (timestamps, labels, tenant ID). Hashes by tenant ID + labels to determine target ingester(s).
2
Replication factor (default 3): Each log stream is replicated to N ingesters using a consistent hash ring. If replication_factor=3, 3 ingesters receive the same data. You need at least 2 of 3 to acknowledge for a successful write (quorum).
3
Ingester buffers: Logs accumulate in memory. When chunk reaches target size (~1.5MB) or age (1h), it's compressed (gzip) and flushed to object storage. Ingester acknowledges back to the distributor.
4
Durability guarantee: Logs are in memory until flushed. If an ingester crashes before flushing, logs are LOST unless you've configured a Write-Ahead Log (WAL). Enable WAL with ingester.wal.enabled=true for production.
⚠️ ALWAYS Enable WAL in Production!

Without WAL: ingester crash = up to 1 hour of logs lost. With WAL: ingester replays WAL on restart, recovers unflushed data. WAL uses local disk (needs fast storage). Configure: ingester.wal.dir=/var/loki/wal with at least 50GB.

🏗️ Loki Architecture — Components & Data Flow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                              LOKI ARCHITECTURE                                  │
│                                                                                │
│   WRITE PATH                                                                    │
│   ──────────                                                                    │
│   ┌──────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐      │
│   │ Fluent Bit /      │────►│ Distributor       │────►│ Ingester         │      │
│   │ Promtail          │     │ (Validates,       │     │ (Builds chunks,  │      │
│   │ (Collectors)      │     │  hashes by tenant,│     │  flushes to      │      │
