🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS: Without this pipeline, alerts become noise. Engineers get paged at 2 AM for CPU spikes that users never noticed. With symptom-based alerting + runbooks + escalation paths, every alert = real user impact with a clear action path.

🔬 How Alertmanager Routes, Groups, and Inhibits Alerts — The Full Pipeline

Prometheus fires alerts → Alertmanager decides WHO gets paged, WHEN, and HOW. Understanding this pipeline prevents both alert fatigue AND missed incidents:

📡 Alertmanager Pipeline: Route → Group → Inhibit → Silence → Notify
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     ALERTMANAGER PROCESSING PIPELINE                         │
│                                                                             │
│  Prometheus ──→ [ROUTE] ──→ [GROUP] ──→ [INHIBIT] ──→ [SILENCE] ──→ NOTIFY│
│                                                                             │
│  🔀 ROUTE: Which team gets this alert?                                      │
│     route:                                                                  │
│       receiver: 'platform-team'        # Default receiver                   │
│       routes:                                                                │
│         - match:                                                             │
│             severity: critical          # Critical → Page on-call            │
│           receiver: 'pagerduty-critical'                                     │
│         - match:                                                             │
│             severity: warning           # Warning → Slack only               │
│           receiver: 'slack-platform'                                         │
│                                                                             │
│  📦 GROUP: Multiple alerts → ONE notification                               │
│     group_by: ['alertname', 'cluster']  # Group by alert + cluster          │
│     group_wait: 30s                     # Wait 30s for more alerts          │
│     group_interval: 5m                  # Send updates every 5 min          │
│     repeat_interval: 4h                # Re-notify every 4h if unresolved  │
│                                                                             │
│  🚫 INHIBIT: Suppress child alerts when parent is firing                    │
│     inhibit_rules:                                                           │
│       - source_match:                                                        │
│           alertname: 'NodeDown'         # If node is DOWN...                │
│         target_match:                                                       │
│           alertname: 'PodNotReady'      # ...don't also page for pod alerts  │
│         equal: ['node']                # ...on the same node                │
│                                                                             │
│  🔇 SILENCE: Manual mute for maintenance windows                             │
│     silences last 2h during scheduled upgrades. Alerts still fire in        │
│     Prometheus — they're just not routed to humans during the window.       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔑 WHY INHIBITION MATTERS: Without inhibition, a single node failure triggers 50 alerts: NodeDown, 10× PodNotReady, 10× DeploymentUnavailable, 10× ServiceDown, etc. The on-call engineer gets paged 50 times for ONE problem. Inhibition rules collapse the alert storm into ONE actionable notification.

25.5 Blameless Postmortems — Learning Without Fear

A blameless postmortem analyzes an incident to find root causes and prevent recurrence — without blame. Fix the SYSTEM, not the person.

✅ Blameless Culture

"What in our SYSTEM allowed this?" → fixes. Engineers report incidents immediately.

❌ Blame Culture

"WHO caused this?" → hiding. Engineers conceal incidents. Same ones repeat.

📋 Postmortem Template — anihpj-web Outage
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TIMELINE: 14:32 Deploy v2.1.0 → 14:35 Alert P99>500ms                  │
│            14:38 DB pool exhausted → 14:40 Rollback → 14:42 Restored     │
│                                                                          │
│  ROOT CAUSE: v2.1.0 opened 5 DB connections/request (was 1).             │
│             At 100 req/s, saturated the 20-connection pool in seconds.   │
│                                                                          │
│  ACTION ITEMS:                                                            │
│  1. [P0] Alert: "DB pool > 80% utilized"                                 │
│  2. [P1] Enforce canary deployments for ALL releases                     │
│  3. [P1] Add load testing to CI (simulate prod traffic)                  │
│                                                                          │
│  WHAT WENT WELL: Alert fired in 3 min. Rollback automated.               │
│                  7 min total downtime (within 43-min error budget).       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 How to Build a Blameless Postmortem Culture — 5 Practical Steps
1
Leadership models it: When the CTO causes an outage, they write the postmortem first. If leadership blames, the culture dies. If leadership is vulnerable, the culture thrives.
2
Focus on "How" not "Who": Every sentence starts with "How did the system allow..." not "Who did..." Replace "Priya pushed bad code" with "The canary deployment policy was not enforced."
3
Action items are tracked: Every postmortem produces JIRA tickets. Track them to completion. An open action item from a past incident = a future incident waiting to happen.
4
Celebrate postmortems: Thank the author. Share learnings widely. A good postmortem prevents dozens of future incidents. It's one of the highest-leverage activities an engineer can do.
5
Review old postmortems: Quarterly, review past incidents. Did the action items work? Did the same class of incident happen again? If so, your postmortems aren't effective — fix the process.
🔬 The "5 Whys" Technique — From Symptom to System-Level Root Cause

In a postmortem, you must go beyond "what happened" to "WHY the system allowed it." The 5 Whys technique (from Toyota Production System) is the simplest and most powerful tool:

🔍 5 Whys: anihpj DB Pool Exhaustion Incident
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        THE 5 WHYS — LAYER BY LAYER                          │
│                                                                             │
│  SYMPTOM: anihpj-web returns 500 errors at 14:35                           │
│      │                                                                      │
│      ▼                                                                      │
│  WHY #1: Why did it return 500s?                                           │
│  → The DB connection pool was exhausted. All 20 connections were in use.    │
│      │                                                                      │
│      ▼                                                                      │
│  WHY #2: Why was the pool exhausted?                                       │
│  → v2.1.0 opened 5 connections per request instead of 1. At 100 req/s,     │
│    that's 500 connections — saturating the 20-connection pool instantly.    │
│      │                                                                      │
│      ▼                                                                      │
│  WHY #3: Why did v2.1.0 open 5 connections per request?                   │
│  → A developer added connection retry logic but didn't reuse connections.   │
│    The code created a new connection for each retry attempt.                │
│      │                                                                      │
│      ▼                                                                      │
│  WHY #4: Why wasn't this caught before production?                          │
│  → The canary deployment was configured but the canary analysis only        │
│    checked HTTP 200 status — not P99 latency or DB connection count.        │
│      │                                                                      │
│      ▼                                                                      │
│  WHY #5: Why did canary analysis only check HTTP 200?                      │
│  → The canary configuration was copied from another service without         │
│    customizing the analysis metrics. No template or validation exists.      │
│      │                                                                      │
│      ▼                                                                      │
│  ROOT CAUSE (System-Level): The platform lacks a standardized canary        │
│  deployment template with required metrics (P99 latency, error rate,        │
│  DB connections, resource usage). Every team configures canary manually.    │
│                                                                             │
│  ACTION ITEM: Create a platform-enforced canary template that ALWAYS        │
│  checks P99 latency AND error rate AND resource metrics before promotion.   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔑 THE RULE OF 5 WHYS: Stop when you reach a SYSTEM-LEVEL cause, not a person-level cause. "Priya made a mistake" is not a root cause. "The system allowed Priya's mistake to reach production without detection" IS a root cause. Every "Why" should point at a system, a process, a tool, or a policy — never a person.

⚠️ ANTI-PATTERN: "Why did Priya push bad code? Because she was tired. Why was she tired? Because she worked late. Why did she work late? Because the deadline was unrealistic." — This is PERSON-focused, not SYSTEM-focused. It leads to "hire more people" or "be nicer to Priya" — not system improvements. The CORRECT path: "Why did the system allow bad code to deploy? Because the canary didn't check DB connections."

25.6 M.O.R.E. Methodology — Structured Incident Response

M.O.R.E. ensures you don't skip critical steps during an incident:

🔍
M — Mitigate

STOP the bleeding FIRST. Rollback, failover, scale. Don't debug — restore service. Debug in postmortem.

🔬
O — Observe

Gather data AFTER mitigation. Dashboards, logs, traces. Build complete picture before forming theories.

🧠
R — Resolve

Fix ROOT CAUSE. Not the symptom. If DB pool exhausted, fix code — not just increase pool size.

📋
E — Educate

Write postmortem. Update runbooks. Add alerts. Train team. This class of incident NEVER happens again.

⚡ At 2 AM: Mitigate (5 min) → Observe (10 min) → Resolve (next day) → Educate (48 hours)
🔬 M.O.R.E. Incident Response Pipeline — Structured, Repeatable, Measurable
🔍
MITIGATE STOP the bleeding.
Rollback / Failover / Scale.
Don't debug now.
Goal: Restore service.
→
🔬
OBSERVE Gather data.
Dashboards + Logs + Traces.
Build full picture.
No theories yet.
→
🧠
RESOLVE Fix ROOT CAUSE.
Not the symptom.
Code fix, not config hack.
Verify with monitoring.
→
📋
EDUCATE Postmortem + Runbooks.
New alerts + Training.
This class of incident
NEVER happens again.

⚠️ COMMON MISTAKE: Engineers skip MITIGATE and jump straight to RESOLVE. At 2 AM, the goal is service restoration — not root cause analysis. You can debug tomorrow. Users can't wait until tomorrow.

25.7 Health Checks & Probes — The First Line of Defense

Kubernetes probes automatically detect and recover from failures:

ProbeChecksOn FailureWhen to Use
Liveness"Is the app alive or deadlocked?"KILLS and restartsWhen app can deadlock. Use sparingly.
Readiness"Is the app ready for traffic?"Removes from Service⭐ ALWAYS. DB, cache, dependencies.
Startup"Has the app finished starting?"KILLS if never succeedsSlow-starting apps (legacy, JVM).
📋 anihpj-web Probes
livenessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /healthz            # 200 = process alive
    port: 8000
  initialDelaySeconds: 15
  periodSeconds: 20
  failureThreshold: 3       # Restart after 3 failures (60s)

readinessProbe:
  httpGet:
    path: /ready              # Checks: DB, cache, dependencies
    port: 8000
  initialDelaySeconds: 5
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 2       # Fast removal from service
⚠️ The 3 Deadly Probe Mistakes
1. Liveness Probe Too Aggressive

initialDelaySeconds: 5 with failureThreshold: 1. App takes 10s to start → killed before it's ready → restart loop FOREVER.

Fix: Use startupProbe for slow-starting apps.

2. Readiness Depends on External Services

Readiness checks the DB. DB is slow → readiness fails → pod removed from Service → ALL pods fail → cascade failure.

Fix: Readiness should check LOCAL state. Use circuit breakers for external deps.

3. No Probes At All

App hangs but process is alive → Kubernetes thinks it's healthy → traffic keeps flowing → users get timeouts.

Fix: ALWAYS add readiness probe. Add liveness only if your app can deadlock.

🔬 How Probes Actually Work — kubelet → Container Runtime → Your App

Understanding the mechanics helps you debug probe failures and avoid the deadly mistakes:

⚙️ Probe Execution Chain
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    HOW A READINESS PROBE EXECUTES                           │
│                                                                             │
│  Step 1: KUBELET reads Pod spec. Sees readinessProbe configured.           │
│          Waits initialDelaySeconds (5s) before first check.                │
│                                                                             │
│  Step 2: Every periodSeconds (10s), kubelet executes the probe:            │
│          • httpGet: kubelet makes HTTP GET to container's IP:port/path      │
│          • tcpSocket: kubelet attempts TCP connection to port               │
│          • exec: kubelet runs command INSIDE the container                  │
│                                                                             │
│  Step 3: kubelet evaluates the result:                                      │
│          • HTTP 2xx/3xx → SUCCESS                                           │
│          • HTTP 4xx/5xx → FAILURE                                           │
│          • TCP connected → SUCCESS                                          │
│          • Exec exit code 0 → SUCCESS                                       │
│                                                                             │
│  Step 4: On FAILURE:                                                        │
│          • Readiness: kubelet removes Pod IP from Endpoints.                │
│            Service stops sending traffic. Pod keeps running.                │
│          • Liveness: kubelet KILLS the container (SIGTERM → SIGKILL).       │
│            Pod restarts (if restartPolicy: Always).                         │
│          • Startup: Same as liveness, but ONLY during initial startup.      │
│                                                                             │
│  Step 5: After failureThreshold consecutive failures:                       │
│          Readiness: Pod marked NotReady. No traffic.                        │
│          Liveness/Startup: Container restarted.                             │
│                                                                             │
│  CRITICAL: Readiness failures DON'T restart the pod. They only stop traffic.│
│            Liveness failures DO restart the pod. Use liveness sparingly.    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 Probe Endpoints in Python/Django (anihpj), Go, and Node.js
# ── PYTHON / DJANGO (anihpj-web) ──
# urls.py — Two separate endpoints for liveness vs readiness
from django.http import HttpResponse
from django.db import connection

def healthz(request):
    # Liveness: Is the PROCESS alive? Minimal check.
    # Do NOT check DB, cache, or external deps here.
    return HttpResponse("OK", status=200)

def ready(request):
    # Readiness: Is the app ready to SERVE TRAFFIC?
    # Check: DB connectivity, migrations applied, cache reachable.
    try:
        with connection.cursor() as cursor:
            cursor.execute("SELECT 1")  # DB check
    except Exception:
        return HttpResponse("DB not ready", status=503)
    # Add: cache check, migration check, disk space check
    return HttpResponse("Ready", status=200)

# ── GO ──
// Simple HTTP handlers for health/readiness
func healthzHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    w.Write([]byte("OK"))
}

func readyHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    // Check DB connectivity
    if err := db.Ping(); err != nil {
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
        w.Write([]byte("DB not ready"))
        return
    }
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    w.Write([]byte("Ready"))
}

# ── NODE.JS / EXPRESS ──
// Separate endpoints for liveness and readiness
app.get('/healthz', (req, res) => {
    // Liveness: just confirm the process is running
    res.status(200).send('OK');
});

app.get('/ready', async (req, res) => {
    // Readiness: check DB, Redis, external deps
    try {
        await db.raw('SELECT 1');          // PostgreSQL
        await redis.ping();                  // Redis cache
        res.status(200).send('Ready');
    } catch (err) {
        res.status(503).send('Not Ready: ' + err.message);
    }
});

# ⚠️ CRITICAL: /healthz should NEVER check external dependencies.
# If /healthz depends on DB and DB is slow → liveness fails →
# kubelet kills the pod → restart → DB still slow → kill →
# INFINITE RESTART LOOP. The pod never stabilizes.

25.8 Runbooks & Playbooks — Turning Panic Into Process

A runbook is a step-by-step guide for a specific alert. A playbook handles a class of incidents. At 2 AM, the runbook remembers what you forgot.

📖
Runbook Must Include
  1. Alert name + severity
  2. Symptoms ("P99 > 500ms")
  3. Step 1: Check Grafana dashboard
  4. Step 2: Check DB connection pool
  5. Step 3: Check recent deployments
  6. Escalation path + time limits
📋
Playbook Must Include
  1. Incident type ("DB Outage")
  2. Roles: IC, Ops Lead, Comms Lead
  3. Communication: #incidents, status page
  4. Mitigation: Failover, scale, restore
  5. Post-incident: Postmortem within 48h
🔬 Runbook Engineering — Store, Test, Automate, and Prevent Rot

A runbook that nobody can find at 2 AM is worse than no runbook — it wastes time searching. Runbooks are CODE that humans execute. Treat them like code:

📁 Where to STORE Runbooks
  • Git repo alongside code: anihpj/runbooks/db-pool-exhausted.md. Version-controlled. Reviewed in PR. Deployable.
  • Linked from the alert: Every Alertmanager alert has runbook_url annotation. One click from PagerDuty → runbook.
  • NOT a wiki: Wikis rot. They're not versioned with code. Nobody updates them. 2 years later, they reference deprecated commands.
  • NOT Slack history: "Check the #incidents channel from March" is NOT a runbook. That's institutional amnesia waiting to happen.
🧪 How to TEST Runbooks
  • Game days: Monthly. Inject a real failure (kill a DB replica). Have an on-call engineer follow the runbook. Time them. Improve.
  • Dry-run automation: Script the runbook steps. Run in CI against staging. "Does kubectl logs actually return logs?" "Is the dashboard URL still valid?"
  • Peer review: Every runbook gets reviewed by someone who DIDN'T write it. If the reviewer can't follow it, rewrite it.
  • Version in alert: runbook_url: ".../v2.3/db-pool-exhausted.md". When the runbook changes, bump the version. Old alerts link to old versions.
🔬 Automating Runbook Steps — From "Human Types Commands" to "Human Approves Script"
# TRADITIONAL RUNBOOK (Human executes each step — error-prone at 2 AM):
# 1. Check Grafana dashboard: https://grafana.anihpj.dev/d/db-pool
# 2. Run: kubectl get pods -n anihpj | grep web
# 3. Run: kubectl logs -n anihpj deployment/anihpj-web --tail=100
# 4. Run: kubectl describe hpa -n anihpj anihpj-web

# AUTOMATED RUNBOOK (Script does the work — human reviews output):
#!/bin/bash
# runbook-db-pool-exhausted.sh — Auto-diagnose DB pool exhaustion
# Triggered by: Alert "DBConnectionPoolExhausted"
# Run: ./runbook-db-pool-exhausted.sh anihpj

NAMESPACE=${1:-anihpj}
echo "=== DB Pool Diagnostic for namespace: $NAMESPACE ==="

# Step 1: Check active DB connections
echo "\n📊 Active DB Connections (last 5 min):"
kubectl exec -n $NAMESPACE deploy/anihpj-web -- \
  python -c "from django.db import connection; print(connection.execute('SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity'))"

# Step 2: Check pod status
echo "\n📋 Pod Status:"
kubectl get pods -n $NAMESPACE -l app=anihpj-web

# Step 3: Recent deployments (possible trigger)
echo "\n🔄 Recent Deployments (last 1h):"
kubectl get events -n $NAMESPACE --field-selector reason=ScalingReplicaSet \
  --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -5

# Step 4: Check HPA status
echo "\n📈 HPA Status:"
kubectl describe hpa -n $NAMESPACE

# Step 5: Quick mitigation (if safe)
echo "\n💡 SUGGESTED ACTIONS:"
echo "1. If recent deploy caused this → kubectl rollout undo deploy/anihpj-web -n $NAMESPACE"
echo "2. If traffic spike → kubectl scale deploy/anihpj-web --replicas=5 -n $NAMESPACE"
echo "3. If DB is the bottleneck → Check RDS console for DB metrics"

🎯 THE GOAL: Phase 1: Runbook is a Markdown file. Phase 2: Runbook is a script that DIAGNOSES (shows data). Phase 3: Runbook is a script that DIAGNOSES + SUGGESTS (shows data + recommended actions). Phase 4: Runbook is AUTO-REMEDIATION (script fixes the problem, human is notified for review). The CNPE exam tests Phase 1-2 — know what belongs in a runbook and how to structure it for 2 AM clarity.

25.9 Incident Lifecycle — From Alert to Resolution

Every incident follows a predictable 5-stage lifecycle:

1
DETECT: Alert fires (Prometheus → PagerDuty). Automated before users report.
2
ACKNOWLEDGE: On-call acknowledges within 5 min. Declares in #incidents. Assigns severity.
3
MITIGATE: Stop bleeding. Rollback, failover, scale. Restore service — NOT find root cause.
4
RESOLVE: Service restored. Verify with monitoring. Communicate RESOLVED.
5
LEARN: Blameless postmortem within 48h. Action items tracked. Runbooks updated.

🔬 Incident Communication — What to Say, When, and to Whom

During an incident, communication is as critical as technical response. Poor communication causes: executives escalating (making it worse), customers tweeting (PR nightmare), and teams duplicating effort (nobody knows who's doing what).

📢 Status Page Updates (External — Customers)

🚨 Initial (SEV1, < 5 min):
"We are investigating reports of elevated error rates on anihpj-web. Affected users may experience slow page loads or 500 errors. Our engineering team is actively investigating. Next update in 30 minutes."

🔧 Investigating (SEV1, every 30 min):
"We have identified the root cause as a database connection pool exhaustion following a configuration deploy. We are rolling back the change. ETA to resolution: 15 minutes."

✅ Resolved (any SEV):
"The issue has been resolved. anihpj-web is fully operational. The root cause was a database connection configuration change that has been reverted. A postmortem will be published within 48 hours."

💬 Internal Communication (Slack/Teams — Engineers)

🔔 Incident Declared (#incidents):
"🚨 SEV1: anihpj-web 500 errors. IC: @priya. Comms: @james. Ops: @alex. War room: https://meet.google.com/abc. Start: 14:35 UTC. Dashboard: grafana.anihpj.dev/d/web-errors"

📊 Status Update (every 15 min):
"[14:50] Status: Rollback in progress. 80% of pods on v2.0.9 (previous). Error rate dropping. ETA 5 min to full rollback."

✅ Resolved:
"[15:02] RESOLVED. All pods on v2.0.9. Error rate 0%. 500 errors: 0 for last 5 min. Postmortem scheduled for tomorrow 10 AM. Postmortem doc: link. Great work team!"

🔑 THE GOLDEN RULE OF INCIDENT COMMS: Communicate what you KNOW, what you DON'T KNOW, and when you'll update next. Never say "we think it might be..." — speculation creates confusion. Say "we are investigating X, Y, and Z. Next update in 15 minutes." Silence is the worst communication — even "still investigating" is better than radio silence.

25.10 Capacity Planning — Don't Run Out of Resources

Provision resources BEFORE you need them:

📈
1. Measure

Track CPU, memory, disk trends via Prometheus/Grafana. 30-day rolling average. Watch for inflection points (growth accelerating).

🔮
2. Predict

predict_linear() — "Will disk be full in 7 days?" Extrapolate current trend into future. Buffer: provision at 70% — don't wait for 95%.

📦
3. Provision

HPA (CPU/memory) + Cluster Autoscaler (nodes). Resource requests/limits on ALL pods. Vertical Pod Autoscaler for right-sizing.

🎯 THE GOAL: Move from Reactive → Predictive. Every minute spent on capacity planning prevents 10 minutes of emergency firefighting. The CNPE exam expects you to know predict_linear() and HPA configuration.

🔬 HPA Configuration Deep Dive — Metrics, Behavior, and Cost Optimization

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler isn't just "scale up when CPU is high." Modern HPA supports multiple metrics, custom scaling behavior, and cost-aware policies:

📋 Production-Grade HPA for anihpj-web
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-hpa
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: anihpj-web
  minReplicas: 2                     # NEVER less than 2 (HA minimum)
  maxReplicas: 10                    # Cap at 10 (cost control + DB pool limit)
  metrics:
  - type: Resource                     # CPU-based scaling
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 70          # Scale at 70% CPU (headroom for spikes)
  - type: Resource                     # Memory-based scaling (secondary)
    resource:
      name: memory
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 80          # Scale at 80% memory
  - type: Pods                        # Custom metric: requests per pod
    pods:
      metric:
        name: http_requests_per_second
      target:
        type: AverageValue
        averageValue: "100"             # Scale when > 100 req/s per pod
  behavior:                           # Fine-tuned scaling behavior
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300  # Wait 5 min before scaling DOWN
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 50
        periodSeconds: 60              # Max scale down: 50% of pods/min
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0    # Scale UP immediately (no delay)
      policies:
      - type: Percent
        value: 100
        periodSeconds: 15              # Max scale up: 100% of pods/15s
      - type: Pods
        value: 4
        periodSeconds: 15              # Or: max 4 pods/15s
      selectPolicy: Max                 # Use whichever allows MORE scaling

🔑 KEY INSIGHTS: (1) stabilizationWindowSeconds on scaleDown prevents flapping — without it, every CPU dip causes a scale-down, followed by immediate scale-up. (2) Use minReplicas: 2 minimum — single replica = no HA. (3) maxReplicas is your COST control — set it based on budget, not theoretical max. (4) Multiple metrics: HPA picks the metric that would produce the HIGHEST replica count — it scales to satisfy ALL constraints.

25.11 Platform SLAs — Promises to Your Developers

Your platform has customers: developers. A Platform SLA defines what you promise:

CapabilitySLO (Internal)SLA (Developer Promise)
Deployment Pipeline< 15 min (P95)< 30 min or escalation
DB Provisioning< 10 min (P95)< 30 min or escalation
Platform API99.9% uptime99.5% uptime or credits
🎓 Platform SLAs vs Service SLAs — A CNPE Exam Distinction

The CNPE exam tests your understanding that a platform SLA is different from an application SLA:

  • Platform SLA: What the PLATFORM promises to DEVELOPERS. E.g., "Deployments will complete in < 30 min." The customer is the developer.
  • Application SLA: What the APPLICATION promises to END-USERS. E.g., "anihpj-web will be 99.9% available." The customer is the user.
  • Platform → App relationship: If the platform SLA is 99.5% and the app SLA is 99.9%, the app WILL breach its SLA. The platform SLA MUST be tighter than the apps running on it.

🔑 EXAM TIP: If asked to define platform SLAs, always identify WHO the customer is first. Platform SLAs serve developers. Application SLAs serve end-users. The platform enables the application — platform reliability is the FOUNDATION.

⚠️ What Happens When You BREACH an SLA? — The Notification and Credits Flow

SLA breaches are not just "oops, we missed the target." They trigger a BUSINESS process — credits, customer notifications, and trust repair. You need a defined flow:

1
DETECT: Automated SLA monitoring detects breach. E.g., "Platform API uptime = 99.3% this month, SLA = 99.5%. BREACH." Detection must be AUTOMATIC — never rely on customers to report.
2
VERIFY: Platform team verifies the measurement is accurate. Was there a monitoring gap? A false positive? If verified, acknowledge the breach internally within 24 hours.
3
NOTIFY: Notify affected customers (developers). "Platform API availability was 99.3% in June, below our 99.5% SLA. As per our SLA terms, you are eligible for a 10% service credit. Postmortem: [link]." Be PROACTIVE — don't make them ask.
4
CREDIT: Issue credits automatically if possible. Manual credit processes create friction and resentment. "We've applied a 10% credit to your July invoice." If credits are manual, customers feel like they need to FIGHT for what they're owed.
5
LEARN & PREVENT: Postmortem published. Action items tracked. The SAME type of breach should not happen twice. If it does, your action items aren't effective — escalate to platform leadership.

🔑 THE TRUST EQUATION: Customers forgive ONE SLA breach if you're transparent, proactive, and fix the root cause. They DON'T forgive repeated breaches, hidden breaches, or making them beg for credits. Your SLA breach response is a test of your platform's integrity — pass it.

🎓 CNPE Exam Strategy — Domain 4 Reliability Tasks

Domain 4 (Observability & Operations, 20%) includes reliability design. Expect these task patterns:

  • Define SLOs for a given service: Given a scenario ("an e-commerce app"), write 3 SLIs with PromQL queries and set SLO targets. Include error budget calculation.
  • Configure alerts: Write Prometheus alert rules. Must be symptom-based (P99 latency, error rate) — NOT cause-based (CPU, memory). Bonus: multi-window burn rate alert.
  • Write a postmortem template: Include timeline, root cause (system-level), action items (P0/P1/P2), what went well, what went wrong. Demonstrate blameless language.
  • Configure probes: Liveness, readiness, startup probes in a Deployment manifest. Know the difference between each and when to use them.
  • Design incident response: M.O.R.E. methodology. Severity levels (SEV1-SEV4). Escalation paths. Communication plan.

🔑 KEY INSIGHT: The CNPE exam values PRACTICAL reliability design over theoretical knowledge. You're not just defining SLOs — you're building the entire reliability stack: measurement → target → alert → response → learning. Every piece connects.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2h CNPE Domain 5: 15%

📋 CNPE Exam Relevance — Domain 5 (15%)

Domain 5 tests your ability to configure secure service-to-service communication. You will be asked to write NetworkPolicies, configure mTLS, and set up cert-manager for automated TLS. Expect 2-3 security-focused tasks. NetworkPolicy YAML is a guaranteed exam topic.

26.1 Zero-Trust Networking — "Never Trust, Always Verify"

The traditional security model assumes the internal network is safe — if you're inside the firewall, you're trusted. This is called the "hard shell, soft center" approach. It fails catastrophically when an attacker breaches the perimeter — they have free rein inside.

Zero-trust flips this: no traffic is trusted by default, even inside the cluster. Every connection must be explicitly allowed and authenticated.

🏢 The Apartment Building Analogy — Why Zero-Trust Makes Intuitive Sense

Think of your Kubernetes cluster as an apartment building:

🔓 Perimeter Security (Traditional)

The building has ONE lock on the front door. Once you're inside the lobby, every apartment door is UNLOCKED. Anyone in the building can walk into any apartment, open any fridge, read any mail. If a criminal gets past the front door (picks the lock, follows a resident in), they have access to EVERYTHING.

This is how Kubernetes works WITHOUT NetworkPolicies: all pods can talk to all pods.

🔐 Zero-Trust (NetworkPolicy + mTLS)

Every apartment has its OWN lock. Apartment 3A's key ONLY opens 3A. Apartment 5B's key ONLY opens 5B. Plus, every resident carries a verified ID badge (mTLS certificate) that proves "I actually live in 3A." Even if a criminal gets into the building, they can't enter ANY apartment without the right key AND the right ID.

NetworkPolicy = apartment locks. mTLS = verified ID badge. Together: defense-in-depth.

🔑 THE INSIGHT: In the physical world, we instinctively understand that shared spaces need individual locks. We don't leave our apartments unlocked because "the front door is locked." Zero-trust applies the SAME logic to networks — every pod-to-pod connection is a "door" that needs its own lock and identity verification.

🏰 Traditional Perimeter vs Zero-Trust Networking
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              TRADITIONAL (Perimeter-Based)          │    ZERO-TRUST           │
│                                                     │                         │
│   ┌─────────────────────────────┐                   │  ┌───┐     ┌───┐       │
│   │  🛡️ FIREWALL (Perimeter)    │                   │  │Pod│◄───►│Pod│       │
│   │  ┌───┐  ┌───┐  ┌───┐       │                   │  │ A │ mTLS│ B │       │
│   │  │Pod│  │Pod│  │Pod│       │                   │  └───┘     └───┘       │
│   │  │ A │◄─►│ B │◄─►│ C │       │                   │   🔒 Every connection   │
│   │  └───┘  └───┘  └───┘       │                   │      authenticated     │
│   │  ✅ All traffic inside       │                   │                         │
│   │     perimeter is TRUSTED     │                   │  ┌───┐     ┌───┐       │
│   └─────────────────────────────┘                   │  │Pod│  ✗  │Pod│       │
│                                                     │  │ A │────►│ D │       │
│   ❌ If attacker breaches                             │  └───┘     └───┘       │
│      perimeter → FULL ACCESS                         │   🚫 BLOCKED: No       │
│      to everything inside                            │      NetworkPolicy      │
│                                                     │      allows this        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🔑 ZERO-TRUST PRINCIPLES:
   1. No implicit trust based on network location (inside ≠ safe)
   2. Every connection is authenticated (mTLS) AND authorized (NetworkPolicy)
   3. Least privilege: pods can ONLY talk to what they NEED to talk to
   4. Assume breach: design as if the attacker is already inside
✅ Zero-Trust in Kubernetes
  • NetworkPolicy: "Pod A can talk to Pod B on port 5432. Nothing else." — AUTHORIZATION
  • mTLS (Service Mesh): "Pod A must present a valid certificate to talk to Pod B." — AUTHENTICATION + ENCRYPTION
  • RBAC: "ServiceAccount X can GET pods in namespace Y." — API AUTHORIZATION
  • Pod Security: "This pod cannot run as root." — RUNTIME SECURITY
❌ Without Zero-Trust
  • All pods can talk to all pods: A compromised frontend pod can scan the entire cluster, find the DB, and exfiltrate data.
  • No encryption in transit: Traffic between pods is plaintext. Anyone with network access can sniff credentials.
  • No identity verification: Pod B can't verify that the request really came from Pod A — anyone can impersonate Pod A.
🎓 CNPE Exam: Zero-Trust Philosophy

The CNPE exam expects you to APPLY zero-trust, not just define it. Every NetworkPolicy you write should follow the principle of least privilege: the policy should allow ONLY the specific traffic required for the application to function — nothing more. If a question asks "secure this application," start with a default-deny NetworkPolicy and then add specific allow rules.

PERIMETER
"Firewall protects us."

→
🚫
NETWORK POLICY
Default-deny. Allow lists.
podSelector defines rules.
Least privilege enforced.
Kubernetes-native.
→
🔐

No plaintext anywhere.
Google BeyondCorp model.
🔬 Why Zero-Trust NOW? — The Breaches That Killed Perimeter Security

Zero-trust isn't a trendy buzzword — it's a response to catastrophic breaches that proved perimeter security is dead:

💥 Capital One (2019) — 106M Records

Attacker exploited a misconfigured WAF to get AWS credentials via SSRF. From ONE compromised host, they accessed S3 buckets containing 106 million credit applications. Perimeter didn't help — the attacker was already "inside" the trusted network.

Lesson: If the Capital One breach happened in Kubernetes with NetworkPolicy + mTLS, the compromised pod couldn't have reached S3 (egress blocked) or any other pod (default-deny).

💥 SolarWinds (2020) — 18,000 Orgs

Attackers injected malware into SolarWinds Orion updates. Once inside customer networks, they moved LATERALLY to find high-value targets. Internal traffic was trusted — no microsegmentation, no service-to-service auth.

Lesson: With mTLS, the malware couldn't have impersonated legitimate services. With NetworkPolicy, lateral movement would have been blocked. Each hop requires explicit authorization.

🔑 THE SHIFT: These breaches (and dozens more) proved that the "trusted internal network" is a myth. Every major security framework now mandates zero-trust: NIST SP 800-207, CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model, Executive Order 14028. The CNPE exam aligns with these standards.

26.2 NetworkPolicy Selectors — The Building Blocks of Kubernetes Firewall Rules

A NetworkPolicy is a Kubernetes resource that controls traffic flow between pods. It's a firewall rule expressed as YAML. NetworkPolicies use THREE selector types to identify traffic sources and destinations:

🎯 The 3 NetworkPolicy Selectors
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     NETWORKPOLICY SELECTOR TYPES                               │
│                                                                               │
│  1. podSelector         2. namespaceSelector        3. ipBlock                │
│  ┌─────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────┐           │
│  │ Match pods by    │   │ Match namespaces  │   │ Match IP ranges   │           │
│  │ LABELS           │   │ by LABELS         │   │ (CIDR blocks)     │           │
│  │                  │   │                   │   │                   │           │
│  │ app: web         │   │ team: priya       │   │ 10.0.0.0/8        │           │
│  │ tier: frontend   │   │ env: staging      │   │ 172.16.0.0/12     │           │
│  │                  │   │                   │   │                   │           │
│  │ ✅ "Pods WITH     │   │ ✅ "Pods IN        │   │ ✅ "Traffic FROM   │           │
│  │    these labels"  │   │    namespaces     │   │    this IP range" │           │
│  │                  │   │    with these      │   │                   │           │
│  │                  │   │    labels"         │   │ ⚠️ Only for       │           │
│  │                  │   │                   │   │    ingress from   │           │
│  │                  │   │                   │   │    OUTSIDE the    │           │
│  │                  │   │                   │   │    cluster        │           │
│  └─────────────────┘   └──────────────────┘   └──────────────────┘           │
│                                                                               │
│  COMBINING SELECTORS: Inside a single "from" entry, selectors are ANDed.       │
│  Multiple "from" entries are ORed.                                             │
│                                                                               │
│  Example: "Allow traffic from pods labeled app=web IN namespaces labeled      │
│            env=prod, OR from the load balancer at 203.0.113.0/24"             │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Selector TypeMatchesScopeTypical Use Case
podSelectorPods by labelAny namespace (if combined with namespaceSelector) or same namespace"Allow traffic from app: anihpj-web pods"
namespaceSelectorNamespaces by labelCluster-wide"Allow traffic from any pod in namespaces labeled team: priya"
ipBlockCIDR IP rangesExternal to cluster"Allow ingress from the corporate VPN at 10.0.0.0/8"
podSelector + namespaceSelectorSpecific pods in specific namespacesCross-namespace"Allow app: web pods in ns: frontend to talk to app: db in ns: backend"
📋 NetworkPolicy Selector Examples — From Simple to Complex
# ── EXAMPLE 1: Simple podSelector (same namespace) ──
ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:                    # Allow pods with label app=web
        matchLabels:
          app: anihpj-web
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8000

# ── EXAMPLE 2: namespaceSelector (all pods in labeled namespaces) ──
ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:              # Allow ALL pods in namespaces with
        matchLabels:                    # label team=priya
          team: priya

# ── EXAMPLE 3: podSelector + namespaceSelector (AND logic) ──
ingress:
  - from:
    - namespaceSelector:              # Pods MUST be in namespaces
        matchLabels:                    # labeled env=prod
          env: prod
      podSelector:                    # AND pods MUST have label
        matchLabels:                    # app=anihpj-web
          app: anihpj-web

# ── EXAMPLE 4: ipBlock (external traffic) ──
ingress:
  - from:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.0.0.0/8              # Allow corporate network
        except:
        - 10.0.99.0/24                # EXCEPT this subnet (blocked)

# ── EXAMPLE 5: Multiple from entries (OR logic) ──
ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:                    # ALLOW from app=web
        matchLabels:
          app: anihpj-web
    - namespaceSelector:              # OR from monitoring namespace
        matchLabels:
          purpose: monitoring
⚡ Selector Rules of Thumb
  • podSelector alone matches pods in the SAME namespace as the NetworkPolicy.
  • namespaceSelector + podSelector matches specific pods in specific namespaces (cross-namespace).
  • ipBlock is for traffic from OUTSIDE the cluster (load balancers, VPNs, external services).
  • Empty selector {} matches ALL pods or ALL namespaces. Use with caution.
  • Multiple "from" entries are ORed — traffic matching ANY entry is allowed.
📋 EGRESS NetworkPolicy Examples — Controlling OUTBOUND Traffic
# ⚠️ Egress policies are just as important as ingress!
# A compromised pod can exfiltrate data if egress is unrestricted.

# ── EXAMPLE 1: Allow egress to DNS ONLY ──
egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:           # Allow egress to CoreDNS
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53

# ── EXAMPLE 2: Allow egress to a database in another namespace ──
egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:           # Only db namespace
        matchLabels:
          purpose: database
      podSelector:                 # Only postgres pods
        matchLabels:
          app: postgres
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432

# ── EXAMPLE 3: Allow egress to external API (github.com) ──
egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 140.82.0.0/16        # GitHub's IP range
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443                    # HTTPS only

# ── EXAMPLE 4: Allow egress to ALL external HTTPS (0.0.0.0/0) ──
# Use with caution — this allows pods to reach ANY server on port 443.
egress:
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 0.0.0.0/0
        except:
        - 169.254.0.0/16           # Block link-local (metadata service)
        - 10.0.0.0/8               # Block internal cluster CIDR
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443

# ── FULL anihpj-web Egress Policy (Least Privilege) ──
# Web pod needs: DNS, DB, Redis, external GitHub API, and nothing else.
egress:
  - to:                                 # 1. DNS resolution
    - namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}}
      podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}}
    ports: [{protocol: UDP, port: 53}]
  - to:                                 # 2. Database
    - podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj-db}}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 5432}]
  - to:                                 # 3. Redis cache
    - podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj-redis}}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 6379}]
  - to:                                 # 4. GitHub API (webhooks)
    - ipBlock: {cidr: 140.82.0.0/16}
    ports: [{protocol: TCP, port: 443}]
⚠️ Egress Security — The Most Commonly Overlooked Attack Vector

Most teams focus on INGRESS (blocking incoming traffic) and forget about EGRESS (blocking outgoing traffic). But egress is where DATA EXFILTRATION happens. If an attacker compromises a pod, their first action is almost always to connect OUT to a command-and-control server. A NetworkPolicy that only restricts ingress is like locking your front door but leaving the back door wide open.

Key egress flows to explicitly allow: DNS (CoreDNS on UDP 53), database (TCP 5432/3306), cache (TCP 6379), specific external APIs (by IP range on 443). Everything else should be blocked by default-deny egress.

🔬 How Multiple NetworkPolicies COMBINE — The Union of Allows

When multiple NetworkPolicies apply to the same pod, Kubernetes takes the UNION of all allow rules. If ANY policy allows a connection, it's allowed. This is critical to understand — you CAN'T make a "deny" policy that overrides an "allow" policy.

ScenarioPolicy A AllowsPolicy B AllowsResult
Two policies, same podIngress from app=web on :5432Ingress from app=monitor on :9090✅ BOTH allowed. Union of rules.
Policy A allows, B has no rulesIngress from app=web on :5432(empty — no ingress/egress section)✅ app=web on :5432 allowed. Policy B doesn't change anything.
Policy A allows all, B is default-denyIngress from {} (all)No ingress section (deny all)✅ ALL traffic allowed! Union wins — Policy A's "allow all" takes effect.
Neither policy allows the trafficIngress from app=web on :5432Ingress from app=monitor on :9090❌ Traffic from app=other on :8080 is DENIED by both.

⚠️ CRITICAL: NetworkPolicies are additive-only — you CANNOT write a "deny" policy. If ANY policy covering a pod allows a connection, that connection is allowed. The only way to block traffic is to ensure NO policy allows it. This is why default-deny is so important — it sets the baseline to "nothing allowed," then allow policies add specific permissions.

⚡ How to TEST If Your NetworkPolicy Is Working — Practical Commands
  • Test ALLOWED traffic: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-web -- curl -s --max-time 3 http://anihpj-db:5432 → Should succeed. If it times out, the policy is wrong.
  • Test BLOCKED traffic: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-web -- curl -s --max-time 3 http://anihpj-redis:6379 → Should timeout/fail. If it succeeds, the policy isn't restrictive enough.
  • Test from a DIFFERENT namespace: kubectl run test-pod --rm -it --image=busybox -n default -- wget -O- --timeout=3 http://anihpj-web.anihpj:8000 → Should fail with default-deny.
  • Verify DNS works: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-web -- nslookup kubernetes.default → Should resolve. If not, DNS egress is blocked.
  • Describe the policy: kubectl describe netpol -n anihpj → Shows which pods are selected and what rules apply.
🌳 Which NetworkPolicy Selector Should I Use?
🤔 Where is the traffic coming FROM?
🔷 INSIDE the cluster
🔶 OUTSIDE the cluster
🤔 Same namespace?
✅ Use podSelector only.
podSelector: {app: web}
Matches pods in THIS namespace.
🤔 Different namespace?
✅ Use namespaceSelector + podSelector
namespaceSelector: {env: prod}
podSelector: {app: web}
Both must match (AND logic).
🔶 Use ipBlock
ipBlock: {cidr: 203.0.113.0/24}
For: Load balancers, VPNs, external APIs, corporate networks.
🤔 Need to block a specific subnet?
✅ Use ipBlock with except
cidr: 10.0.0.0/8
except: [10.0.99.0/24]
Allows 10.0.0.0/8 EXCEPT 10.0.99.0/24.

26.3 Default-Deny Stance — Block Everything, Then Allow What's Needed

Kubernetes has a dangerous default: all pods can communicate with all other pods across all namespaces. This is an open bar. The default-deny stance closes the bar — you must explicitly allow every connection.

🚫 Default-Deny: Before and After
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  ❌ KUBERNETES DEFAULT (No NetworkPolicy):                                   │
│  ┌─────┐      ┌─────┐      ┌─────┐      ┌─────┐                            │
│  │ Pod │◄────►│ Pod │◄────►│ Pod │◄────►│ Pod │   ALL pods can talk to      │
│  │  A  │      │  B  │      │  C  │      │  D  │   ALL other pods on ALL     │
│  └─────┘      └─────┘      └─────┘      └─────┘   ports. No restrictions.   │
│                                                                             │
│  ✅ DEFAULT-DENY (NetworkPolicy Applied):                                    │
│  ┌─────┐      ┌─────┐      ┌─────┐      ┌─────┐                            │
│  │ Pod │  ✗   │ Pod │  ✗   │ Pod │  ✗   │ Pod │   ALL traffic BLOCKED      │
│  │  A  │──────│  B  │──────│  C  │──────│  D  │   unless explicitly         │
│  └──┬──┘      └─────┘      └──┬──┘      └─────┘   allowed by a policy.      │
│     │                         │                                              │
│     │    ┌─────────────────┐  │                                              │
│     └───►│  ALLOW: A → C   │◄─┘   After adding specific allow rules,        │
│          │  (port 5432)    │       only A→C traffic flows. Everything       │
│          └─────────────────┘       else is blocked by default.              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 Default-Deny NetworkPolicy — The First Policy You Apply
# ── DEFAULT-DENY ALL INGRESS ──
# Apply this to EVERY namespace. Blocks ALL incoming traffic.
# Then add specific NetworkPolicies to allow required traffic.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector: {}           # {} = ALL pods in this namespace
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress                  # Block all INCOMING traffic
  # No "ingress:" section = nothing is allowed

# ── DEFAULT-DENY ALL EGRESS ──
# Blocks ALL outgoing traffic from pods in the namespace.
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-egress
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector: {}           # {} = ALL pods
  policyTypes:
  - Egress                   # Block all OUTGOING traffic

# ⚠️ WARNING: Default-deny egress breaks DNS (pods can't reach CoreDNS).
# You MUST also allow egress to DNS:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns-egress
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:                         # Allow DNS queries to CoreDNS
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
      podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          k8s-app: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
⚠️ Default-Deny Gotchas — What WILL Break
🧩 DNS Resolution

Default-deny egress blocks DNS. Pods can't resolve service names. You MUST explicitly allow egress to CoreDNS (UDP/TCP 53) in kube-system.

📊 Monitoring & Metrics

Prometheus can't scrape metrics. Liveness/readiness probes from kubelet are NOT affected (they use the pod IP directly, not the network), BUT Prometheus scraping IS blocked. Allow ingress from monitoring namespace.

🌐 Internet Egress

Pods can't reach external APIs, container registries, or cloud services. Allow egress to 0.0.0.0/0 on specific ports, or use an egress gateway.

🎯 The Default-Deny Rollout Strategy

Don't apply default-deny to production on Day 1. The safe approach:

1
OBSERVE: Deploy a NetworkPolicy in "audit" mode (use Cilium or a CNI that supports logging). Log all traffic flows for 1 week. Build a traffic map.
2
ALLOW: Create allow-list NetworkPolicies based on OBSERVED traffic. Web needs port 5432 → DB. Web needs port 53 → DNS. Web needs port 6379 → Redis.
3
DENY: Apply default-deny. All observed traffic is already allowed. New unexpected traffic is blocked.
4
MONITOR: Watch for blocked traffic. If a legitimate connection is blocked, add an allow rule. If it's unexpected, investigate — it might be an attacker.
😱 BEFORE Default-Deny — The Compromised Frontend

A WordPress plugin vulnerability in a marketing blog pod gives an attacker a shell. From the blog pod, they:

  • 🔍 Scan the entire cluster: nmap 10.0.0.0/8 — finds the DB at 10.0.1.5:5432
  • 💉 Connect to DB: psql -h 10.0.1.5 -U postgres — no auth required, it's "internal"
  • 📤 Exfiltrate: SELECT * FROM users; — dumps all user data to an external server
  • 💸 Impact: 500,000 user records stolen. GDPR fine: €10M. All because there was no NetworkPolicy.
✅ AFTER Default-Deny — The Attack Blocked

Same WordPress vulnerability. Attacker gets a shell in the blog pod. But NOW:

  • 🚫 nmap shows NO other pods — NetworkPolicy blocks all egress except DNS
  • 🚫 Cannot reach DB — podSelector requires app: web, blog has app: blog
  • 🚫 Cannot exfiltrate — egress to internet is blocked by default-deny
  • 📊 OBSERVABILITY: Cilium logs show DROP: blog → db:5432 (policy: default-deny)
  • 🔔 ALERT: Security team paged on unexpected egress attempts
  • ✅ Impact: Attack contained to one pod. Zero data loss. Incident response investigates and patches.
🔬 How NetworkPolicy Is ACTUALLY Enforced — iptables vs eBPF

NetworkPolicy is just a Kubernetes resource. It doesn't DO anything by itself — it needs a CNI plugin that implements it. Different CNIs enforce policies very differently:

CNI PluginEnforcement MechanismPerformanceObservabilityBest For
Calicoiptables (legacy) or eBPF (modern). Converts NetworkPolicy → iptables rules or eBPF programs.iptables: ⚠️ degrades at 1000+ rules. eBPF: ✅ scales linearly.Calico Cloud / Calico Enterprise provide flow logs and policy visualization.Most popular. Enterprise-ready. Both iptables and eBPF modes.
CiliumeBPF exclusively. Compiles NetworkPolicy into eBPF programs that run in the kernel. NO iptables at all.✅✅ Best performance. Kernel-level enforcement. Near-zero overhead.✅ Hubble — real-time flow observability with service-level visibility.Performance-critical. eBPF-native. Built-in observability via Hubble.
Weave NetCustom userspace firewall. Less efficient than kernel-level enforcement.⚠️ Userspace = context switches. Slower than iptables/eBPF.Basic. Weave Scope provides some visibility.Simple setups. Not recommended for production at scale.
AntreaOpen vSwitch (OVS). Flow-based enforcement using OVS rules.✅ Good. OVS is mature and performant.Antrea Traceflow for packet tracing.VMware/vSphere environments. OVS-based networking.

🔑 CNPE EXAM NOTE: You don't need to know every CNI, but you MUST understand that NetworkPolicy requires a CNI that supports it. If a question says "NetworkPolicy is not working," your first check should be: kubectl get pods -n kube-system | grep -E 'calico|cilium|weave|antrea' — is a NetworkPolicy-aware CNI installed? Vanilla Flannel does NOT support NetworkPolicy.

😰
LEVEL 1
Open Bar

No NetworkPolicies. All pods talk to all pods. Kubernetes default.

❌ Zero Protection
🚫
LEVEL 2
Default-Deny

Block all ingress. Allow specific flows. DNS egress permitted. Monitoring namespace allowed.

⚠️ Basic Segmentation
🔐
LEVEL 3
mTLS + Identity

All traffic encrypted AND authenticated. Mesh enforces identity. STRICT mode. No plaintext.

✅ Encrypted + Authenticated
🛡️
LEVEL 4
Zero-Trust Complete

NetworkPolicy + mTLS + RBAC + Admission Control + Runtime Security. Defense-in-depth at all layers.

🌟 Full Zero-Trust

26.4 mTLS via Service Mesh — Encrypt AND Authenticate Pod-to-Pod Traffic

Mutual TLS (mTLS) is regular TLS with one critical difference: BOTH sides present certificates. The client proves its identity to the server, AND the server proves its identity to the client. This prevents impersonation and man-in-the-middle attacks.

🔐 TLS vs mTLS — What's the Difference?
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  TLS (One-Way):                          │  mTLS (Mutual):                    │
│                                          │                                    │
│  ┌──────┐                    ┌──────┐    │  ┌──────┐                ┌──────┐  │
│  │Client│                    │Server│    │  │Client│                │Server│  │
│  │      │──── Hello! ───────►│      │    │  │      │── Hello+Cert ─►│      │  │
│  │      │                    │      │    │  │      │                │      │  │
│  │      │◄─── Cert ──────────│      │    │  │      │◄── Cert ──────│      │  │
│  │      │  "Am I the real   │      │    │  │      │  "Am I real?"  │      │  │
│  │      │   server?"         │      │    │  │      │                │      │  │
│  │      │                    │      │    │  │      │── My Cert ───►│      │  │
│  │  ✅  │ Server verified.   │      │    │  │      │  "I am real"   │      │  │
│  │      │ Client unverified. │      │    │  │      │                │      │  │
│  └──────┘                    └──────┘    │  │  ✅  │ BOTH verified. │  ✅  │  │
│                                          │  └──────┘                └──────┘  │
│  ⚠️ Server identity proven.              │                                    │
│     Client identity NOT proven.          │  ✅ BOTH identities proven.        │
│     Anyone can connect.                  │     Only authorized pods connect.  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔐 What mTLS Gives You
  • Encryption: All pod-to-pod traffic is encrypted. No plaintext on the wire. Sniffing the network reveals nothing.
  • Authentication: Pod A proves "I AM anihpj-web" with a certificate. Pod B proves "I AM anihpj-db." No impersonation possible.
  • Identity-based authorization: NetworkPolicy says "allow app=web → app=db:5432." mTLS ENFORCES that the connecting pod IS actually app=web.
  • Zero configuration for apps: The service mesh sidecar proxy handles all TLS. Your application code doesn't change — it still talks HTTP to localhost.
⚠️ Without mTLS — The Risks
  • Traffic sniffing: Any pod on the same node can tcpdump the network interface and read plaintext traffic — including DB passwords in connection strings.
  • Pod impersonation: A compromised pod can spoof labels and bypass NetworkPolicy. Without mTLS, NetworkPolicy only checks IPs/labels — not cryptographic identity.
  • Man-in-the-middle: An attacker can intercept and modify traffic between pods. mTLS detects tampering via certificate validation.
🔄 How a Service Mesh Implements mTLS — Sidecar Proxy Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    SERVICE MESH mTLS — SIDECAR ARCHITECTURE                    │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────┐       ┌─────────────────────────────┐       │
│  │          Pod: anihpj-web    │       │          Pod: anihpj-db     │       │
│  │                             │       │                             │       │
│  │  ┌───────────────────────┐  │       │  ┌───────────────────────┐  │       │
│  │  │   App Container        │  │       │  │   App Container        │  │       │
│  │  │   (Django, port 8000)  │  │       │  │   (PostgreSQL, 5432)  │  │       │
│  │  │                        │  │       │  │                        │  │       │
│  │  │   App thinks it talks  │  │       │  │   DB listens on        │  │       │
│  │  │   plain HTTP to DB     │  │       │  │   localhost:5432       │  │       │
│  │  └───────────┬───────────┘  │       │  └───────────┬───────────┘  │       │
│  │              │ localhost     │       │              │ localhost     │       │
│  │              ▼               │       │              ▼               │       │
│  │  ┌───────────────────────┐  │ mTLS  │  ┌───────────────────────┐  │       │
│  │  │   Envoy Sidecar       │◄─┼───────┼─►│   Envoy Sidecar       │  │       │
│  │  │   (istio-proxy)       │  │       │  │   (istio-proxy)       │  │       │
│  │  │                        │  │       │  │                        │  │       │
│  │  │   1. Receives HTTP     │  │       │  │   3. Receives mTLS     │  │       │
│  │  │   2. Wraps in mTLS     │  │       │  │   4. Unwraps to HTTP   │  │       │
│  │  │   5. Presents cert     │  │       │  │   6. Validates cert    │  │       │
│  │  │      "I am anihpj-web" │  │       │  │      "You are web ✓"   │  │       │
│  │  └───────────────────────┘  │       │  └───────────────────────┘  │       │
│  └─────────────────────────────┘       └─────────────────────────────┘       │
│                                                                               │
│  🔑 THE APP CODE NEVER TOUCHES TLS. The sidecar proxy transparently           │
│     upgrades all HTTP→mTLS (egress) and downgrades mTLS→HTTP (ingress).      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 Istio mTLS Configuration for anihpj
# ── ENABLE STRICT mTLS FOR THE ENTIRE MESH ──
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT            # ALL pods MUST use mTLS. No plaintext allowed.

# ── ALTERNATIVE: PERMISSIVE (use during migration) ──
# mode: PERMISSIVE allows both mTLS and plaintext. Use this while
# migrating apps to mTLS. Switch to STRICT after migration is complete.

# ── NAMESPACE-SPECIFIC mTLS ──
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: anihpj-mtls
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: anihpj-web       # Only apply to anihpj-web pods
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
⚡ mTLS Implementation Path
  • Step 1: Install service mesh (Istio/Linkerd/Consul). Sidecars auto-injected.
  • Step 2: Start with PERMISSIVE mode. Both mTLS and plaintext work. Monitor for issues.
  • Step 3: Verify ALL traffic is using mTLS (Istio: Kiali graph shows lock icons).
  • Step 4: Switch to STRICT mode. Plaintext connections are now rejected.
  • Step 5: Combine with NetworkPolicy for defense-in-depth: mTLS authenticates, NetworkPolicy authorizes.
🔬 Service Mesh Showdown — Istio vs Linkerd vs Cilium

Not all service meshes are equal. Choosing the right one impacts complexity, performance, and operational burden:

FeatureIstioLinkerdCilium (eBPF)
ArchitectureEnvoy sidecar proxylinkerd-proxy (Rust, lightweight)eBPF in kernel (NO sidecar!)
mTLS✅ Automatic. SPIFFE identities.✅ Automatic. Simpler config.✅ Via WireGuard or IPSec. No sidecar.
Performance overhead⚠️ Moderate (Envoy is heavy)✅ Low (Rust proxy, ~1ms P99)✅✅ Near-zero (kernel-level, no proxy)
Complexity🔴 High. 10+ CRDs. Steep learning curve.🟡 Low. 4 CRDs. "Just works."🟡 Medium. eBPF is powerful but new paradigm.
NetworkPolicy integrationSeparate from CNISeparate from CNI✅ Built-in (Cilium IS the CNI)
ObservabilityKiali, Jaeger, Grafanaviz + GrafanaHubble (eBPF-based, extremely detailed)
Best forLarge enterprises. Multi-cluster. Complex routing.Simplicity-first. Smaller teams. "It just works."Performance-critical. Already using Cilium CNI. eBPF-native.
CNPE relevance✅ HIGH — most commonly tested🟡 Know the concept🟡 Growing. eBPF is the future.

🎯 FOR CNPE: Focus on Istio — it's the most commonly tested service mesh. Know PeerAuthentication (STRICT vs PERMISSIVE), sidecar injection, and how mTLS integrates with NetworkPolicy. Understand that Linkerd and Cilium exist as alternatives with different tradeoffs.

🔬 SPIFFE — How mTLS Knows "WHO" a Pod Really Is

mTLS requires certificates. But how does a pod GET a certificate, and how does that certificate prove "I am anihpj-web" — not just "I have some random cert"? The answer is SPIFFE (Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone).

🆔 SPIFFE Identity Flow — From ServiceAccount to mTLS Certificate
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         SPIFFE IDENTITY FLOW                                   │
│                                                                               │
│  1. Kubernetes assigns a ServiceAccount to the pod                            │
│     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                       │
│     │ Pod: anihpj-web-7d8f9-abcde     │                                       │
│     │ ServiceAccount: anihpj-web      │                                       │
│     │ JWT token mounted at:           │                                       │
│     │ /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/ │                                       │
│     │   serviceaccount/token          │                                       │
│     └──────────────┬──────────────────┘                                       │
│                    │                                                          │
│                    ▼                                                          │
│  2. SPIFFE Agent (in sidecar or node) reads the ServiceAccount JWT             │
│     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                       │
│     │ SPIFFE Agent validates JWT      │                                       │
│     │ with Kubernetes API Server      │                                       │
│     │ ("Is this token valid?")        │                                       │
│     │                                 │                                       │
│     │ Generates SPIFFE ID:            │                                       │
│     │ spiffe://cluster.local/ns/      │                                       │
│     │   anihpj/sa/anihpj-web          │                                       │
│     └──────────────┬──────────────────┘                                       │
│                    │                                                          │
│                    ▼                                                          │
│  3. SPIFFE Agent requests X.509 certificate from SPIRE Server                 │
│     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                       │
│     │ Certificate includes:           │                                       │
│     │ • SPIFFE ID as SAN (Subject      │                                       │
│     │   Alternative Name)             │                                       │
│     │ • Short-lived (1 hour TTL)      │                                       │
│     │ • Auto-rotated before expiry    │                                       │
│     └──────────────┬──────────────────┘                                       │
│                    │                                                          │
│                    ▼                                                          │
│  4. Sidecar proxy uses this certificate for mTLS                              │
│     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                       │
│     │ Envoy presents cert to DB pod:   │                                       │
│     │ "I am spiffe://cluster.local/    │                                       │
│     │  ns/anihpj/sa/anihpj-web"        │                                       │
│     │                                 │                                       │
│     │ DB pod validates:               │                                       │
│     │ • Is the SPIFFE ID trusted?      │                                       │
│     │ • Is it in the allow-list?       │                                       │
│     │ • Is the cert NOT expired?       │                                       │
│     │ ✅ All checks pass → mTLS established                            │
│     └─────────────────────────────────┘                                       │
│                                                                               │
│  🔑 KEY INSIGHT: SPIFFE ID is bound to the Kubernetes ServiceAccount —       │
│     NOT the pod IP, NOT the pod name, NOT a manually configured cert.         │
│     If a pod is deleted and recreated, it gets the SAME identity              │
│     (because it has the same ServiceAccount). This is cryptographic           │
│     identity tied to the K8s RBAC identity — identity at scale.               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

🎯 WHY THIS MATTERS: Without SPIFFE, mTLS certificates would need to be manually distributed to every pod — impossible at scale. SPIFFE automates identity provisioning so that every pod gets a unique, verifiable, auto-rotating identity with zero human involvement. This is what makes zero-trust practical, not just theoretical.

⚡ How to VERIFY mTLS Is Actually Working — Command-Line Checks

Don't just trust Kiali's lock icon. Verify with real commands:

  • Check TLS mode per namespace: istioctl authn tls-check anihpj-web-7d8f9-abcde.anihpj — shows whether mTLS is active for a specific pod, the certificate SPIFFE ID, and the peer's certificate details.
  • Dump certificates from sidecar: istioctl proxy-config secret deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj — shows the actual X.509 certificate the sidecar is using, including SAN (SPIFFE ID), issuer, and expiry time.
  • Capture traffic to verify encryption: kubectl exec -n anihpj deploy/anihpj-web -c istio-proxy -- tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 5432 — if mTLS is working, you'll see encrypted gibberish, not readable SQL queries.
  • Test with a plaintext pod (no sidecar): Deploy a test pod WITHOUT the Istio sidecar injection label. That pod CANNOT communicate with any pod protected by STRICT mTLS. The connection will fail with "connection reset" — this PROVES mTLS is enforcing authentication.
  • Check PeerAuthentication status: kubectl get peerauthentication -A — verify STRICT mode is applied to the intended namespaces. A common mistake: STRICT is set in istio-system but the app namespace is still using PERMISSIVE (or no policy at all).

26.5 cert-manager — Automate TLS Certificate Lifecycle

cert-manager is a Kubernetes operator that automates the issuance, renewal, and management of TLS certificates. No more manual cert generation with OpenSSL, no more expired certificates at 3 AM, no more "copy the .crt file to 12 servers."

📜 cert-manager Architecture — Automatic Certificate Lifecycle
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        cert-manager WORKFLOW                                   │
│                                                                               │
│  1. YOU CREATE a Certificate resource (YAML)                                  │
│     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                       │
│     │ kind: Certificate               │                                       │
│     │ spec:                           │                                       │
│     │   secretName: anihpj-tls        │                                       │
│     │   dnsNames:                     │                                       │
│     │   - anihpj.example.com          │                                       │
│     │   issuerRef:                    │                                       │
│     │     name: letsencrypt-prod      │                                       │
│     └──────────────┬──────────────────┘                                       │
│                    │                                                          │
│                    ▼                                                          │
│  2. CERT-MANAGER detects the Certificate resource                             │
│     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                       │
│     │ cert-manager controller         │                                       │
│     │ • Watches for Certificate CRs   │                                       │
│     │ • Creates CertificateRequest    │                                       │
│     │ • Calls Issuer (ACME/CA/Vault)  │                                       │
│     └──────────────┬──────────────────┘                                       │
│                    │                                                          │
│                    ▼                                                          │
│  3. ISSUER obtains certificate from CA                                        │
│     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                       │
│     │ Issuer Types:                   │                                       │
│     │ • ACME (Let's Encrypt): HTTP-01  │                                       │
│     │   or DNS-01 challenge           │                                       │
│     │ • CA: Internal corporate CA     │                                       │
│     │ • Vault: HashiCorp Vault PKI    │                                       │
│     │ • SelfSigned: For testing only   │                                       │
│     └──────────────┬──────────────────┘                                       │
│                    │                                                          │
│                    ▼                                                          │
│  4. CERT-MANAGER stores cert+key in a Kubernetes Secret                        │
│     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                       │
│     │ Secret: anihpj-tls              │                                       │
│     │   tls.crt:         │                                       │
│     │   tls.key:         │                                       │
│     └──────────────┬──────────────────┘                                       │
│                    │                                                          │
│                    ▼                                                          │
│  5. INGRESS references the Secret for TLS termination                         │
│     ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                       │
│     │ Ingress TLS section:            │                                       │
│     │   - hosts:                       │                                       │
│     │     - anihpj.example.com        │                                       │
│     │     secretName: anihpj-tls      │                                       │
│     └─────────────────────────────────┘                                       │
│                                                                               │
│  6. AUTO-RENEWAL: cert-manager renews 30 days before expiry.                  │
│     Zero human intervention. Certificate NEVER expires.                       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 cert-manager Resources — Issuer + Certificate for anihpj
# ── STEP 1: Create a ClusterIssuer (Let's Encrypt) ──
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer              # ClusterIssuer = available cluster-wide
metadata:                          # Issuer = namespace-scoped
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory  # Production CA
    email: platform@anihpj.example.com      # Expiry notifications sent here
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account-key
    solvers:
    - http01:                               # HTTP-01 challenge (needs Ingress)
        ingress:
          class: nginx

# ── STEP 2: Request a Certificate ──
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: anihpj-tls
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  secretName: anihpj-tls-cert         # Secret where cert will be stored
  duration: 2160h                      # 90 days (Let's Encrypt maximum)
  renewBefore: 360h                    # Renew 15 days before expiry
  dnsNames:
  - anihpj.example.com
  - api.anihpj.example.com              # SAN: multiple domains supported
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-prod
    kind: ClusterIssuer

# ── VERIFY ──
# kubectl get certificate -n anihpj
# NAME         READY   SECRET            AGE
# anihpj-tls   True    anihpj-tls-cert   5m
#
# kubectl describe certificate anihpj-tls -n anihpj
# Events:
#   Normal  Issuing    5m    cert-manager  Issuing certificate as Secret exists
#   Normal  Reused     5m    cert-manager  Reusing private key in existing Secret
#   Normal  Requested  4m    cert-manager  Created new CertificateRequest
#   Normal  Issued     3m    cert-manager  Certificate issued successfully
🎓 CNPE Exam: cert-manager Patterns

The CNPE exam may ask you to configure cert-manager for a domain. Key facts to remember:

  • ClusterIssuer vs Issuer: ClusterIssuer is cluster-wide (any namespace can use it). Issuer is namespace-scoped. Use ClusterIssuer for shared CAs like Let's Encrypt.
  • ACME challenges: HTTP-01 (needs Ingress, port 80 accessible) for public domains. DNS-01 (needs DNS provider credentials) for wildcard certs and internal services.
  • Certificate stores result in a Secret: spec.secretName — then reference that Secret in your Ingress TLS section.
  • Auto-renewal is automatic: cert-manager renews certificates based on spec.renewBefore. No cron job needed. No manual intervention.
⚠️ cert-manager Troubleshooting — 4 Common Problems and Their Fixes
🔴 Certificate Stuck in "Pending"

Symptom: kubectl get certificate shows READY=False forever.

Causes:
1. HTTP-01 challenge: port 80 not reachable from internet. Check Ingress and firewall.
2. DNS-01 challenge: DNS provider credentials wrong/missing. Check Secret.
3. Rate limiting: Let's Encrypt staging has high limits. Production has strict limits (5 certs/domain/week).
4. Issuer not found: issuerRef.name doesn't match any existing Issuer/ClusterIssuer.

Debug: kubectl describe certificaterequest -n anihpj and kubectl describe order -n anihpj to see ACME challenge status.

🔴 Certificate Expired Despite cert-manager

Symptom: Browsers show "Certificate Expired" warning.

Causes:
1. renewBefore not set — defaults to 1/3 of duration, but if duration is short, renewal window may be too narrow.
2. cert-manager pod is down — controller not running.
3. Issuer is misconfigured — renewal attempt fails silently.
4. Secret was manually deleted — cert-manager doesn't know to recreate it.

Fix: Delete the Certificate resource AND the Secret. Re-apply Certificate YAML. This forces a fresh issuance.

🟡 Let's Encrypt Rate Limit Hit

Symptom: "too many certificates already issued for this exact set of domains"

Cause: Let's Encrypt production limits: 5 duplicate certificates per week for the same domain. During testing, you can exhaust this quickly.

Fix: Use Let's Encrypt STAGING environment (https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory) during development. Only switch to production after everything works.

🟡 Secret Not Created

Symptom: Certificate shows READY=True but kubectl get secret doesn't show the expected secret.

Cause: spec.secretName in Certificate doesn't match tls.secretName in Ingress. The Secret IS created — just with a different name than you're looking for.

Fix: kubectl get secrets -n anihpj | grep tls to see all TLS secrets. Match the exact name in Ingress TLS section.
