26.6 Ingress TLS Termination — Decrypt at the Edge

TLS termination means the Ingress Controller decrypts HTTPS traffic at the cluster edge and forwards plain HTTP to backend pods. The certificate lives on the Ingress, not in every pod.

🔓 TLS Termination at Ingress — Decrypt at Edge, HTTP Inside
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     INGRESS TLS TERMINATION PATTERN                            │
│                                                                               │
│  Internet                    Cluster Edge                  Cluster Internal   │
│  ┌──────┐    HTTPS     ┌──────────────┐     HTTP      ┌──────────────────┐  │
│  │Client│─────────────►│NGINX Ingress │──────────────►│ anihpj-web Pod   │  │
│  │      │   🔒 TLS     │ Controller   │  🔓 Plaintext │ (Django :8000)   │  │
│  │      │              │              │               │                  │  │
│  │      │              │ TLS Cert:    │               │ ✅ Pod code stays │  │
│  │      │              │ anihpj-tls   │               │    simple. No TLS │  │
│  │      │              │ (from cert-  │               │    handling needed│  │
│  │      │              │  manager)    │               │                  │  │
│  └──────┘              └──────────────┘               └──────────────────┘  │
│                                                                               │
│  PROS:                           CONS:                                        │
│  ✅ Single place to manage TLS   ❌ Traffic inside cluster is plaintext       │
│  ✅ Simple pod code              ❌ If an attacker is inside the cluster,     │
│  ✅ cert-manager auto-renewal       they can sniff pod-to-pod traffic         │
│  ✅ Lower CPU on pods (no TLS)   ❌ Not zero-trust compliant                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 Ingress with TLS Termination — anihpj
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod  # Auto-provision TLS
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"   # Force HTTPS
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:                                    # TLS SECTION
  - hosts:
    - anihpj.example.com
    - api.anihpj.example.com
    secretName: anihpj-tls-cert          # Created by cert-manager Certificate
  rules:
  - host: anihpj.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj-web
            port:
              number: 8000              # Backend receives HTTP (TLS stripped)
⚠️ Ingress TLS Termination + mTLS: Defense in Depth

Ingress TLS termination protects traffic from the INTERNET → your cluster. But inside the cluster, traffic is plaintext. For full zero-trust, combine:

1
Ingress TLS Termination: Encrypts internet → cluster edge. Uses cert-manager for auto-renewal.
2
mTLS (Service Mesh): Encrypts pod → pod traffic inside the cluster. Sidecar proxies handle TLS transparently.
3
NetworkPolicy: Restricts which pods can communicate. Defense in depth — even if mTLS fails, NetworkPolicy blocks unexpected connections.
🔬 Forcing HTTPS — Redirect + HSTS for Maximum Security

TLS termination only works if clients actually USE HTTPS. You must enforce it:

🔄 HTTP→HTTPS Redirect

What it does: Any HTTP (port 80) request gets a 301/308 redirect to HTTPS (port 443).

Nginx Ingress annotation:

nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"

Alternative — Separate Ingress: Create a second Ingress on port 80 that only does redirect. Cleaner separation of concerns.

🛡️ HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)

What it does: Tells browsers "ALWAYS use HTTPS for this domain for the next 6 months." Prevents SSL stripping attacks.

Nginx annotation:

nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/hsts: "true"
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/hsts-max-age: "31536000"
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/hsts-include-subdomains: "true"

⚠️ Warning: Once HSTS is set, browsers will REFUSE HTTP connections for the duration of max-age. Make sure HTTPS works perfectly before enabling.

26.7 Gateway API TLS Passthrough — End-to-End Encryption

The Gateway API is the next-generation Ingress. Unlike Ingress TLS termination (decrypt at edge), TLS passthrough forwards encrypted traffic directly to backend pods. The pod handles TLS — the gateway just routes TCP.

FeatureIngress TLS TerminationGateway API TLS Passthrough
Where TLS is terminatedAt the Ingress Controller (edge)At the backend Pod (end-to-end)
Traffic inside clusterPlain HTTP — sniffableEncrypted TLS — not sniffable
Certificate managementSingle cert on Ingress (easy)Cert on every pod or via mTLS mesh
L7 routing✅ Path-based, header-based routing❌ Gateway can't read headers (encrypted)
Use caseStandard web apps. Simple setup.Zero-trust compliance. Regulated industries.
CNPE exam relevance✅ HIGH — know TLS section in Ingress🟡 Know the concept and tradeoffs
📋 Gateway API with TLS Passthrough
# ── GATEWAY (cluster operator creates this) ──
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: tls-passthrough-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: nginx
  listeners:
  - name: anihpj-https
    port: 443
    protocol: TLS                  # TLS passthrough mode
    tls:
      mode: Passthrough            # 🔑 KEY: Don't terminate. Pass through.
    hostname: "*.anihpj.example.com"

# ── HTTPRoute with TLS passthrough reference ──
# The Gateway routes based on SNI (Server Name Indication) — the
# hostname in the TLS handshake. It CANNOT inspect HTTP paths/headers.
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: TLSRoute
metadata:
  name: anihpj-tls-route
namespace: anihpj
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: tls-passthrough-gateway
  hostnames:
  - anihpj.example.com
  rules:
  - backendRefs:
    - name: anihpj-web
      port: 8443                  # Pod listens on TLS port
🎯 When to Use TLS Passthrough vs Termination
✅ Use TLS TERMINATION when:
  • You need L7 routing (path-based: /api → backend-A, /web → backend-B)
  • You want simple certificate management (one cert on Ingress, not per pod)
  • You don't have strict compliance requirements for end-to-end encryption
  • Your pods don't have TLS configured (most legacy apps)
🔐 Use TLS PASSTHROUGH when:
  • You need end-to-end encryption for compliance (PCI-DSS, HIPAA, FedRAMP)
  • Your app already handles TLS (mTLS with service mesh)
  • You have a zero-trust requirement — no plaintext anywhere
  • Traffic must be encrypted even from the load balancer to the pod
🔬 SNI — How TLS Passthrough Routes Without Decrypting

TLS passthrough seems magical — how does the Gateway know WHERE to send traffic if it can't decrypt it? The answer is SNI (Server Name Indication).

🔍 SNI — The Unencrypted Hostname in the TLS Handshake
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         TLS HANDSHAKE WITH SNI                                │
│                                                                               │
│  Client                                  Gateway                              │
│  ┌──────┐                               ┌────────┐                           │
│  │      │── 1. ClientHello ────────────►│        │                           │
│  │      │   "I want to talk to          │        │                           │
│  │      │    anihpj.example.com"  ←──── │        │  🔑 SNI is INSIDE the     │
│  │      │   (SNI field — UNENCRYPTED!)   │        │     ClientHello message.  │
│  │      │                               │        │     It's sent BEFORE the  │
│  │      │                               │        │     TLS session is        │
│  │      │◄── 2. ServerHello ────────────│        │     established, so it's  │
│  │      │   + Server Certificate        │        │     VISIBLE to the Gateway│
│  │      │                               │        │     even in passthrough   │
│  │      │                               │        │     mode.                  │
│  │      │── 3. [Encrypted from here] ──►│        │                           │
│  │      │                               │        │                           │
│  └──────┘                               └────────┘                           │
│                                                                               │
│  🔑 GATEWAY READS SNI → "anihpj.example.com" → Routes to anihpj-web:8443     │
│     WITHOUT decrypting the traffic. SNI is like the ADDRESS on an envelope —  │
│     the post office doesn't need to open the letter to know where to send it.│
│                                                                               │
│  LIMITATIONS OF SNI-BASED ROUTING:                                            │
│  ❌ Can't route by URL path (/api vs /web) — the path is inside the encrypted │
│     HTTP request, invisible to the gateway.                                    │
│  ❌ Can't inspect HTTP headers for canary routing, A/B testing, etc.          │
│  ❌ Can't terminate TLS at the edge for WAF inspection or caching.            │
│  ✅ CAN route different hostnames to different backends (SNI is visible).     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 Why Gateway API Was Created — The Problems With Ingress

The standard Kubernetes Ingress resource has been around since v1.0, but it has fundamental limitations that Gateway API addresses:

Problem with IngressHow Gateway API Solves It
One-size-fits-all: Ingress is a single resource that tries to do everything. Annotations are vendor-specific and not portable.Separation of concerns: Gateway (infra admin), HTTPRoute (app developer), TLSRoute (security team). Each role manages their own resource.
No TLS passthrough: Ingress only supports TLS termination. No built-in passthrough or mTLS support.TLSRoute + Gateway with Passthrough mode: Native support for end-to-end encryption and SNI-based routing.
Limited routing: Only host + path routing. No header-based, weight-based, or method-based routing.Rich routing: HTTPRoute supports header matching, query param matching, traffic splitting (canary), and method-based routing.
No cross-namespace: Ingress rules can only reference Services in the same namespace.Cross-namespace references: Routes can reference backends in any namespace (with ReferenceGrant for security).
No standardized roles: Who creates Ingress? App dev? Platform team? Unclear ownership.Clear RBAC model: Gateway = platform team. HTTPRoute = app team. Each has their own RBAC scope.

🎯 FOR CNPE: Gateway API is the FUTURE of Kubernetes ingress. While the exam may still test Ingress (it's the current standard), understanding Gateway API demonstrates platform engineering maturity. Know that Ingress = "old way," Gateway API = "new way," and TLSRoute with Passthrough mode is the zero-trust-compliant option.

🛠️ Drill 1: Write NetworkPolicy for anihpj

Scenario: anihpj-web (app: web) needs to talk to anihpj-db (app: db) on port 5432. Nothing else should be allowed.

Task:

  1. Write a NetworkPolicy allowing ingress to anihpj-db ONLY from anihpj-web on port 5432
  2. Write the default-deny-ingress policy for the anihpj namespace
  3. Write the allow-DNS-egress policy so pods can resolve service names
  4. Verify with: kubectl describe netpol -n anihpj

Time: 15 min

💡 Hints
  • Policy #1 targets anihpj-db: podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj-db}}, ingress from podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: anihpj-web}} on TCP 5432.
  • Policy #2 (default-deny): podSelector: {} with policyTypes: [Ingress] and NO ingress section.
  • Policy #3 (DNS): egress to namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system}} + podSelector: {matchLabels: {k8s-app: kube-dns}} on UDP 53.
  • Test: kubectl exec deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj -- nc -zv anihpj-db 5432 should succeed. Same command targeting Redis on 6379 should fail.
🛠️ Drill 2: Configure mTLS for anihpj

Scenario: Enable strict mTLS between anihpj-web and anihpj-db using Istio.

Task:

  1. Create a PeerAuthentication resource with STRICT mode for the anihpj namespace
  2. Verify mTLS is active: check Kiali dashboard for lock icons
  3. Test: deploy a test pod WITHOUT Istio sidecar. Verify it CANNOT reach anihpj-db

Time: 15 min

💡 Hints
  • PeerAuthentication: apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1beta1, kind: PeerAuthentication, spec.mtls.mode: STRICT. Apply in the anihpj namespace.
  • Verify via CLI: istioctl authn tls-check deploy/anihpj-web -n anihpj should show "STATUS: OK" with mTLS mode "STRICT".
  • Test pod without sidecar: kubectl run test-no-mesh --rm -it --image=busybox -n anihpj --labels=sidecar.istio.io/inject=false -- wget -O- --timeout=5 http://anihpj-db:5432 — should fail with "Connection refused" or timeout.
🛠️ Drill 3: cert-manager + Ingress TLS

Scenario: Set up automatic TLS for anihpj.example.com.

Task:

  1. Create a ClusterIssuer using Let's Encrypt (staging first, then prod)
  2. Create a Certificate resource for anihpj.example.com
  3. Configure Ingress with TLS section referencing the cert-manager Secret
  4. Verify: curl -vI https://anihpj.example.com shows valid certificate

Time: 15 min

💡 Hints
  • Use Let's Encrypt STAGING first: server: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory. Staging has much higher rate limits for testing.
  • Certificate spec.secretName must match Ingress tls.secretName. Common mistake: Certificate stores in anihpj-tls-cert but Ingress references anihpj-tls.
  • Ingress annotation: cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod triggers auto-provisioning. Without this annotation, cert-manager won't act on the Ingress.
  • Verify chain: kubectl get certificate -n anihpj → READY=True, then kubectl get secret anihpj-tls-cert -n anihpj → should have tls.crt and tls.key.
  • Debug stuck certs: kubectl describe certificaterequest -n anihpj and kubectl describe order -n anihpj show the ACME challenge progress.
🧠 Knowledge Check — 10 Questions

Q1: What is zero-trust networking and how does it differ from perimeter-based security?

Q2: What are the 3 NetworkPolicy selector types and when do you use each?

Q3: What does a default-deny NetworkPolicy look like? What breaks when you apply it?

Q4: What is mTLS and how does it differ from regular TLS?

Q5: How does a service mesh sidecar implement mTLS without changing application code?

Q6: What is cert-manager and what problem does it solve?

Q7: Difference between ClusterIssuer and Issuer in cert-manager?

Q8: What is TLS termination? Where does it happen in Kubernetes?

Q9: What is TLS passthrough and when would you use it instead of termination?

Q10: How do NetworkPolicy + mTLS + Ingress TLS work together for defense-in-depth?

🎓 CNPE Exam Strategy — Domain 5 Security Tasks

Domain 5 (Security & Policy, 15%) tests your ability to configure secure communication. Key task patterns to expect:

  • Write a NetworkPolicy from scratch: Given a diagram showing web→api→db, write policies allowing ONLY those flows. Default-deny everything else. Remember DNS egress!
  • Identify why a NetworkPolicy isn't working: Common traps: (a) Forgot to allow DNS egress, (b) CNI doesn't support NetworkPolicy (Flannel), (c) namespaceSelector needs namespace labels, (d) podSelector in wrong namespace.
  • Configure mTLS: Know PeerAuthentication YAML. STRICT vs PERMISSIVE modes. How to verify mTLS is working (Kiali lock icons, istioctl authn tls-check).
  • cert-manager + Ingress TLS: Create ClusterIssuer → Certificate → reference Secret in Ingress TLS section. The full 3-resource chain. Verify with kubectl get certificate showing READY=True.

🔑 EXAM MINDSET: The CNPE security tasks are about LAYERS. No single tool solves everything. NetworkPolicy = Authorization. mTLS = Authentication + Encryption. cert-manager = Certificate Lifecycle. Together they form defense-in-depth. Every security answer should address at least 2 layers.

📋 Chapter 26 Summary — Secure Service-to-Service Communication
🚫
NetworkPolicy

Default-deny blocks all traffic. Allow rules use podSelector, namespaceSelector, and ipBlock. Least privilege: only allow what's needed.

🔐
mTLS

Mutual TLS encrypts AND authenticates pod-to-pod traffic. Service mesh sidecar proxies handle it transparently. STRICT mode blocks plaintext.

📜
cert-manager

Automates TLS certificate lifecycle. ACME (Let's Encrypt) for public domains. Auto-renews 30 days before expiry. Zero manual intervention.

🎨 Visual Summary — The Secure Communication Stack

    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                 THE SECURE COMMUNICATION STACK                 │
    │                                                               │
    │   Internet → Ingress TLS Termination → mTLS (Mesh) → Pod     │
    │                                                               │
    │   NetworkPolicy: WHO can talk to WHOM (Authorization)         │
    │   mTLS:         WHO are you REALLY? (Authentication)          │
    │   cert-manager: TLS certs automatically issued & renewed      │
    │                                                               │
    │   🔑 ZERO-TRUST = NetworkPolicy + mTLS + Least Privilege      │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🛡️ Defense-in-Depth: How Each Layer Blocks Different Attacks
🌐
LAYER 1 Ingress TLS
Encrypts external traffic
Stops: Sniffing, MITM
cert-manager auto-renews
→
🚫
LAYER 2 NetworkPolicy
Default-deny all traffic
Stops: Lateral movement
Least privilege enforced
→
🔐
LAYER 3 mTLS (Mesh)
Authenticates every connection
Stops: Impersonation
Encrypts pod-to-pod
→
📊
LAYER 4 Observability
Logs all denied traffic
Detects: Reconnaissance
Alerts security team

🛡️ NO SINGLE LAYER is enough. An attacker who bypasses Ingress TLS still hits NetworkPolicy. If they spoof labels, mTLS blocks them. If all else fails, observability detects the attempt. Defense-in-depth = layers that compensate for each other's weaknesses.

Ch 27: RBAC & Access Control

Who can do what in your cluster — and who CANNOT. ServiceAccounts give pods an identity. Roles and ClusterRoles define permissions. RoleBindings connect identities to permissions. Least privilege is the principle. Every permission is explicitly granted — nothing is default.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~1.5h CNPE Domain 5: 15%
🎯 What You'll Learn
  • ServiceAccounts — how pods get an identity in Kubernetes (not users — pods)
  • Roles and ClusterRoles — namespace-scoped vs cluster-wide permissions
  • RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings — connecting identities to permissions
  • kubectl auth can-i — the essential RBAC testing tool
  • RBAC Aggregation — composing ClusterRoles from multiple sources
  • How to design RBAC for anihpj — least privilege for every component
📋 CNPE Exam Relevance — Domain 5 (15%)

Domain 5 tests your ability to apply RBAC and security controls across platform resources. You will be asked to create Roles, ClusterRoles, and Bindings for specific scenarios. RBAC is a guaranteed exam topic — expect 1-2 tasks requiring you to create or troubleshoot RBAC configurations.

27.1 Service Accounts — Pod Identity in Kubernetes

A ServiceAccount (SA) is an identity for a pod — not a human user. When a pod calls the Kubernetes API ("list my pods," "update my deployment"), it authenticates as its ServiceAccount. Every pod ALWAYS has exactly one ServiceAccount.

🍽️ The Restaurant Analogy — Authentication vs Authorization

Think of the Kubernetes API Server as a restaurant kitchen:

🪪 1. AUTHENTICATION (Who are you?)

The ServiceAccount token is your employee ID badge. When you swipe it at the kitchen door, the system verifies: "This badge is valid. You are Priya from the anihpj team." You're now inside.

SA Token = Employee Badge.
API Server validates the token = Security guard checks your badge at the door.

📋 2. AUTHORIZATION (What can you do?)

Now that you're inside, RBAC determines which stations you can access. Priya can use the prep station (GET pods) and the plating station (LIST services). She CANNOT enter the manager's office (delete deployments) or the vault (read secrets).

Role = Station access card.
RoleBinding = "Priya gets prep + plating access."

🔑 3. THE SPLIT

Authentication says WHO you are. It happens FIRST. If the badge is fake, you never get in. Authorization says WHAT you can do. It happens SECOND. Even with a valid badge, you can only access your assigned stations.

AuthN ≠ AuthZ.
Both must pass for ANY API request to succeed.

🆔 ServiceAccount — The Bridge Between Pod and API Server
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    SERVICE ACCOUNT IDENTITY FLOW                               │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │                              POD: anihpj-web                              │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────────────┐   │ │
│  │  │   App Container       │        │  Mounted ServiceAccount Token    │   │ │
│  │  │   (Django)            │        │  /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/ │   │ │
│  │  │                       │        │    serviceaccount/               │   │ │
│  │  │   When Django calls   │        │    ├── token      ← JWT token    │   │ │
│  │  │   the K8s API:        │        │    ├── ca.crt     ← API Server CA│   │ │
│  │  │   "GET /api/v1/pods"  │        │    └── namespace ← namespace name│   │ │
│  │  │                       │        │                                   │   │ │
│  │  │   It uses the mounted │        │  🔑 This token PROVES:            │   │ │
│  │  │   token to            │        │  "I am ServiceAccount 'anihpj-web'│   │ │
│  │  │   authenticate        │        │   in namespace 'anihpj'"         │   │ │
│  │  └──────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────────────────┘   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │                         API SERVER AUTHENTICATION                         │ │
│  │                                                                          │ │
│  │  1. Pod sends request with JWT token in Authorization header             │ │
│  │  2. API Server validates token signature (signed by K8s control plane)  │ │
│  │  3. API Server extracts identity:                                        │ │
│  │     User: system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web                        │ │
│  │     Groups: system:serviceaccounts, system:authenticated                 │ │
│  │  4. API Server checks RBAC: "Does 'system:serviceaccount:anihpj:        │ │
│  │     anihpj-web' have permission to GET pods in namespace anihpj?"        │ │
│  │  5. If YES → returns pod list. If NO → 403 Forbidden.                   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                               │
│  🔑 SA USERNAME FORMAT: system:serviceaccount::           │
│     Example: system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 ServiceAccount YAML — Creating Pod Identities
# ── CREATE A SERVICE ACCOUNT ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj

# ── USE SA IN A DEPLOYMENT ──
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: anihpj-web  # 🔑 This pod uses this SA
      automountServiceAccountToken: true  # Default: true. Set false if pod
      # doesn't need K8s API access.
      containers:
      - name: django
        image: anihpj-web:latest

# ── THE DEFAULT SERVICE ACCOUNT ──
# If you don't specify serviceAccountName, Kubernetes uses the
# "default" ServiceAccount in the pod's namespace.
# ⚠️ SECURITY: NEVER use the "default" SA for production workloads.
# Create dedicated SAs per component (web, db, worker, etc.).

# ── DISABLE AUTO-MOUNT (Best Practice) ──
# If your pod doesn't need K8s API access, disable token mounting:
automountServiceAccountToken: false
# This prevents the token from being mounted at all, reducing
# the attack surface. If an attacker compromises the pod, they
# can't steal the SA token to access the K8s API.
⚡ ServiceAccount Best Practices
  • One SA per component: anihpj-web gets its own SA. anihpj-db gets its own. Don't share.
  • Disable automount when not needed: If the pod doesn't call the K8s API, set automountServiceAccountToken: false. Defense in depth.
  • NEVER use the "default" SA: It often accumulates permissions over time. Create dedicated SAs with explicit RBAC.
  • SA username format for RBAC: system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<sa-name>. Memorize this — you'll need it for RoleBindings.
🔬 SA Token Types — Legacy Tokens vs Bound Tokens (Kubernetes 1.24+)

Kubernetes 1.24 fundamentally changed how SA tokens work. Understanding this difference is critical for security:

FeatureLegacy Token (Pre-1.24)Bound Token (1.24+)
StorageStored in a Secret (created automatically with SA)NOT stored in a Secret. Projected into pod as a file. Exists only while pod runs.
Expiry⚠️ NEVER expires. Token lives forever.✅ Expires after 1 hour (default). Auto-refreshed by kubelet.
ScopeNot bound to any specific pod.🔑 Bound to a SPECIFIC pod. Token includes pod UID. If pod is deleted, token is invalid.
Revocation❌ Delete the Secret (manual). Token could be copied before deletion.✅ Delete the pod → token invalid. Auto-expiring → no manual cleanup.
AudienceGeneric — valid for any K8s API server.🔑 Audience-bound — token only works for the K8s API (or a specified audience).
CNPE ImpactYou no longer see auto-created "sa-token-*" Secrets. If exam asks "where is the SA token?" — it's in the pod, not a Secret.New way: kubectl create token <sa-name> -n <ns> creates a time-limited token for testing.

🔑 CNPE GOTCHA: If the exam asks you to "create a ServiceAccount token," use kubectl create token anihpj-web -n anihpj — NOT kubectl get secret. The auto-Secret-creation behavior was removed in 1.24. This is a common exam trap for those familiar with older Kubernetes versions.

27.2 Role — Namespace-Scoped Permissions

A Role defines WHAT you can do and TO WHAT — but only within a SINGLE namespace. A Role says: "In namespace anihpj, you can GET, LIST, and WATCH pods." Outside that namespace, the Role has no effect.

RBAC ConceptWhat It DefinesScopeAnalogy
ServiceAccountWHO you are (identity)NamespaceYour employee ID badge
RoleWHAT you can do (permissions)Namespace"Can access the 3rd floor break room"
ClusterRoleWHAT you can do (permissions)Cluster-wide"Can access ALL floors in ALL buildings"
RoleBindingWHO gets WHICH RoleNamespace"Priya gets 3rd-floor-break-room access"
ClusterRoleBindingWHO gets WHICH ClusterRoleCluster-wide"Priya gets ALL-floors access"
📋 Role YAML — Defining Namespace-Scoped Permissions
# ── ROLE: anihpj-developer (namespace: anihpj) ──
# Permissions for developers working on the anihpj application
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: anihpj-developer
  namespace: anihpj              # 🔑 Role is ALWAYS in a namespace
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]                # "" = core API group (pods, services, etc.)
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log", "services", "configmaps", "secrets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]  # Read-only. Can't create/delete.

- apiGroups: ["apps"]             # apps/v1 API group (deployments)
  resources: ["deployments"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "update", "patch"]
  # Can update deployments (e.g., change image tag) but not create/delete

- apiGroups: ["batch"]            # batch/v1 API group (jobs, cronjobs)
  resources: ["jobs", "cronjobs"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "create", "delete"]
  # Full control over jobs — devs can run database migrations as jobs

# ── KEY RBAC VERB MEANINGS ──
# get     = Read a single resource by name
# list    = List all resources of a type
# watch   = Stream changes (used by controllers)
# create  = Create a new resource
# update  = Replace an existing resource
# patch   = Partially update a resource
# delete  = Delete a resource
# deletecollection = Delete multiple resources at once
# *       = ALL verbs (use with extreme caution)
⚠️ Role Traps — What the CNPE Exam Tests
🔑 apiGroups: [""]

The CORE API group is represented by an EMPTY string "" — NOT "core", NOT "v1". Writing apiGroups: ["v1"] is WRONG and the Role will grant zero permissions. This is the #1 RBAC mistake.

🔑 resources vs resourceNames

resources: ["pods"] grants access to ALL pods. resourceNames: ["anihpj-web-abcde"] restricts to a SPECIFIC pod. Use resourceNames for fine-grained control (e.g., "can only update THIS specific ConfigMap").

🔑 Sub-resources need explicit permission

pods/log and pods/exec are SUB-RESOURCES. Permission to "get pods" does NOT grant access to "pods/log." You must explicitly list sub-resources in the Role.

⚡ How to DISCOVER API Groups & Resources — Never Guess Again

The most common RBAC error is using the wrong apiGroups or resources value. These commands tell you EXACTLY what to write:

  • List ALL API resources: kubectl api-resources — Shows every resource, its API group, and whether it's namespaced. Use this to find the CORRECT apiGroup for any resource.
  • Filter by API group: kubectl api-resources --api-group=apps — Shows only resources in the apps API group (deployments, statefulsets, daemonsets).
  • List all API groups: kubectl api-versions — Shows all available API groups. Core group shows as v1 — remember, in RBAC YAML, core is "", not "v1".
  • Check a specific resource: kubectl api-resources | grep deploy — Find deployments: deployments deploy apps/v1 true Deployment. The API group is apps, resource name is deployments.
  • Check if namespaced: If true in the NAMESPACED column → can use Role. If false → MUST use ClusterRole (e.g., nodes, namespaces, PVs, storageclasses).
🧠 How the API Server Decides: ALLOW or DENY?
📨
REQUEST Pod sends:
GET /api/v1/namespaces/
anihpj/pods
→
🪪
AUTHENTICATE Validate SA token.
Extract identity:
system:serviceaccount:
anihpj:anihpj-web
→
📋
AUTHORIZE Check ALL Roles
bound to this SA.
ANY match = ALLOW.
NO match = DENY.
→
🔓
ADMISSION Mutating + Validating
webhooks run.
(Only for writes —
reads skip this.)
→
✅
RESPONSE 200 OK + pod list
OR
403 Forbidden

🔑 THE RBAC RULE: In the AUTHORIZE step, the API Server checks ALL RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings for the requesting identity. If ANY binding grants the requested verb+resource, access is ALLOWED. If NO binding grants it, access is DENIED with 403. There is no "deny" rule — RBAC is allow-only. You can only add allows, never add denials.

🌳 Which RBAC Verb Should I Grant?
🤔 What does the identity NEED to do?
🔍 READ-ONLY
✏️ MODIFY
📖 get, list, watch — Read existing resources. Can't change anything. Safe for monitoring, debugging, dashboards.
🤔 Need to read pod logs?
📋 Add pods/log as a resource. "get pods" does NOT include "get pods/log." Sub-resources are separate.
🤔 Creating NEW resources?
✏️ create — Make something new. Deployments, pods, jobs, configmaps.
🤔 Updating EXISTING resources?
🔧 update (full replace) or patch (partial update). patch is safer — less risk of overwriting unintended fields.
🤔 Deleting resources?
🗑️ delete, deletecollection — DANGEROUS. Grant only when absolutely necessary. Use resourceNames to limit scope.

27.3 ClusterRole — Cluster-Wide Permissions

A ClusterRole is like a Role, but with CLUSTER-WIDE scope. It can grant access to cluster-scoped resources (nodes, namespaces, PersistentVolumes) AND namespace-scoped resources across ALL namespaces.

When to UseRoleClusterRole
Manage pods in ONE namespace✅ Use Role❌ Overkill
Manage pods in ALL namespaces❌ Would need a Role in every ns✅ Use ClusterRole
Access cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs)❌ Not possible✅ MUST use ClusterRole
Access non-resource endpoints (/healthz, /metrics)❌ Not possible✅ MUST use ClusterRole
Platform admin (manage all namespaces)❌✅ Use ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding
App developer (manage own namespace)✅ Use Role⚠️ Use ClusterRole only if needed cross-ns
📋 ClusterRole YAML — Cluster-Wide Permissions
# ── CLUSTERROLE: platform-admin ──
# Full read access across the entire cluster. Cannot modify.
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: platform-readonly         # No namespace — ClusterRole is cluster-scoped
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "services", "configmaps", "namespaces", "nodes"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]   # Read-only across ALL namespaces

- apiGroups: ["apps"]
  resources: ["deployments", "statefulsets", "daemonsets"]
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]

- nonResourceURLs: ["/healthz", "/metrics", "/api/*"]
  verbs: ["get"]                     # Access API server health/metrics

# ── CLUSTERROLE: node-reader ──
# Nodes are CLUSTER-SCOPED — MUST use ClusterRole
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: node-reader
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["nodes"]             # Nodes don't belong to any namespace
  verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
🎓 CNPE Exam: Role vs ClusterRole Decision

The exam will test your ability to choose the RIGHT resource type:

  • Given: "Developer needs to manage pods in namespace 'anihpj'." → Use Role + RoleBinding. ClusterRole would be incorrect (overly permissive).
  • Given: "Monitoring system needs to read pods in ALL namespaces." → Use ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding. A Role only works in one namespace.
  • Given: "Admin needs to view nodes." → MUST use ClusterRole. Nodes are cluster-scoped — Role can't grant node access.
  • CRITICAL: A ClusterRole used with a RoleBinding grants permissions ONLY in that namespace — the ClusterRole becomes namespace-scoped by the binding. This is a common CNPE trick.
⚡ Built-in ClusterRoles — Use These Instead of Writing Your Own

Kubernetes ships with powerful built-in ClusterRoles. For the CNPE exam, knowing these saves you from writing YAML from scratch:

ClusterRolePermissionsUse CaseCNPE Note
cluster-admin⭐ EVERYTHING. All resources, all verbs, all namespaces. Bound to system:masters group by default.Cluster administrator. USE WITH EXTREME CAUTION.⚠️ The "nuclear button." Never bind to app SAs.
adminFull control within a namespace (when used with RoleBinding). Can manage Roles and RoleBindings within that ns.Namespace admin. Developer team lead.✅ Aggregated — includes edit + view + RBAC management.
editCreate, update, delete most namespace resources. Cannot manage RBAC.Developer who deploys and manages apps.✅ Most common for CI/CD SAs. Aggregated from view.
viewRead-only across all namespace resources. No secrets by default.Monitoring, dashboards, read-only access.✅ Perfect for Prometheus. Bind with ClusterRoleBinding for cluster-wide.

🔑 EXAM SHORTCUT: If the task says "grant read-only access to all namespaces" → ClusterRoleBinding with roleRef: {kind: ClusterRole, name: view}. Done in one YAML. No need to write custom rules.

🔬 Operator RBAC Pattern — What Every Operator Needs

The cnpe.txt mentions "Operator RBAC" as a key topic. Kubernetes Operators (like cert-manager, Argo CD, Prometheus Operator) follow a consistent RBAC pattern:

🤖 Operator RBAC — The 3-Layer Pattern
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      OPERATOR RBAC PATTERN                                     │
│                                                                               │
│  Layer 1: ServiceAccount                                                      │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                         │
│  │ kind: ServiceAccount            │  ← Identity the operator runs as        │
│  │ name: <operator>-controller     │                                         │
│  └───────────────┬─────────────────┘                                         │
│                  │                                                            │
│                  ▼                                                            │
│  Layer 2: ClusterRole (or Role)                                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                         │
│  │ kind: ClusterRole               │  ← Permissions to watch/manage CRDs     │
│  │ rules:                          │     AND the resources they control      │
│  │ - apiGroups: [""]               │     (pods, services, deployments)       │
│  │   resources: [pods, services]   │                                         │
│  │   verbs: [get,list,watch,       │                                         │
│  │           create,update,patch,  │                                         │
│  │           delete]               │                                         │
│  │ - apiGroups: [cert-manager.io]  │  ← Permissions for its OWN CRDs         │
│  │   resources: [certificates,     │                                         │
│  │               issuers, orders]  │                                         │
│  │   verbs: ["*"]                 │  ← Full control over own resources      │
│  └───────────────┬─────────────────┘                                         │
│                  │                                                            │
│                  ▼                                                            │
│  Layer 3: ClusterRoleBinding (or RoleBinding)                                │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                         │
│  │ kind: ClusterRoleBinding        │  ← Connect SA to ClusterRole            │
│  │ subjects:                       │                                         │
│  │ - kind: ServiceAccount          │                                         │
│  │   name: <operator>-controller   │                                         │
│  │ roleRef:                        │                                         │
│  │   kind: ClusterRole             │                                         │
│  │   name: <operator>-role         │                                         │
│  └─────────────────────────────────┘                                         │
│                                                                               │
│  🔑 THE PATTERN: Every operator needs:                                        │
│     1. A ServiceAccount to run as                                            │
│     2. A ClusterRole with permissions for:                                   │
│        a. The resources it MANAGES (pods, services, etc.) — CRUD             │
│        b. Its OWN Custom Resources (CRDs) — full control                     │
│        c. Core resources for leader election (configmaps, leases)            │
│     3. A Binding connecting the SA to the ClusterRole                        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ The system:masters Group — RBAC's "God Mode" Backdoor

There's a group in Kubernetes that completely bypasses RBAC: system:masters. Any user or certificate belonging to this group has unrestricted cluster-admin access — forever. No RoleBinding needed. No ClusterRole needed. It's hardcoded into the API Server.

🔑 How system:masters Works
  • The API Server has a built-in check: if the authenticated user's GROUP includes system:masters, skip ALL RBAC checks. Grant everything.
  • The default cluster-admin ClusterRoleBinding binds to system:masters — but even WITHOUT that binding, system:masters would still work because it's HARDCODED.
  • How do you get into system:masters? The /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf kubeconfig uses a client certificate with O=system:masters in the Subject. The "O" (Organization) field maps to the group.
🛡️ Security Implications
  • NEVER share admin.conf: Anyone with that file is cluster-admin. No RBAC can stop them.
  • Audit certificate creation: kubectl get csr — check for suspicious certificate signing requests that include O=system:masters.
  • Use OIDC instead of certs: With OIDC, you control group membership through your identity provider — not through certificate attributes.
  • CNPE exam: Know that system:masters exists and bypasses RBAC. The exam may ask: "How do you prevent someone from using system:masters?" Answer: Don't give them the certificate/key pair.

27.4 RoleBinding & ClusterRoleBinding — Connecting Identity to Permission

A Role or ClusterRole is useless on its own — it just DEFINES permissions. A Binding GRANTS those permissions to a specific identity (ServiceAccount, user, or group). Think of it as: Role = "what you can do." Binding = "YOU get to do it."

🔗 How RoleBindings Connect Identity to Permissions
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    RBAC BINDING RELATIONSHIPS                                  │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌──────────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────┐  │
│  │   WHO (Subject)   │────►│   BINDING     │────►│   WHAT (Role/ClusterRole) │  │
│  │                   │     │               │     │                          │  │
│  │ ServiceAccount    │     │ RoleBinding   │     │ Role                     │  │
│  │ User              │     │ (namespace)   │     │ (namespace permissions)  │  │
│  │ Group             │     │               │     │                          │  │
│  └──────────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌──────────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────────────────┐  │
│  │   WHO (Subject)   │────►│   BINDING     │────►│   WHAT (ClusterRole)      │  │
│  │                   │     │               │     │                          │  │
│  │ ServiceAccount    │     │ ClusterRole   │     │ ClusterRole              │  │
│  │ User              │     │ Binding       │     │ (cluster-wide)           │  │
│  │ Group             │     │ (cluster)     │     │                          │  │
│  └──────────────────┘     └──────────────┘     └──────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                               │
│  🔑 SPECIAL CASE: ClusterRole + RoleBinding                                   │
│     A ClusterRole bound with a RoleBinding grants the ClusterRole's           │
│     permissions ONLY within the RoleBinding's namespace. This lets you        │
│     reuse a ClusterRole definition across namespaces without granting         │
│     cluster-wide access.                                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 RoleBinding & ClusterRoleBinding YAML
# ── ROLEBINDING: Grant anihpj-developer Role to anihpj-web SA ──
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web-developer
  namespace: anihpj              # Binding is namespace-scoped
subjects:                         # WHO gets the permissions
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: anihpj-web               # The SA we created earlier
  namespace: anihpj
roleRef:                           # WHAT permissions they get
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role                     # References a Role (or ClusterRole!)
  name: anihpj-developer         # The Role we created in 27.2

# ── CLUSTERROLEBINDING: Grant platform-readonly to monitoring SA ──
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: monitoring-readonly      # No namespace — cluster-scoped
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: prometheus
  namespace: monitoring
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: view                     # Built-in ClusterRole: read-only access

# ── SUBJECT TYPES ──
# subjects can be:
# - kind: ServiceAccount  (for pods/automation)
# - kind: User            (for human users via auth plugin)
# - kind: Group           (for groups of users)
🎯 The Binding Decision Matrix — Which Binding When?
🔷 Use RoleBinding when:
  • Permissions should be limited to ONE namespace
  • Binding a Role → namespace-scoped permissions
  • Binding a ClusterRole → ClusterRole's permissions but ONLY in this namespace (the ClusterRole is "scoped down")
  • Example: "anihpj-web SA can manage pods in anihpj namespace only"
🔶 Use ClusterRoleBinding when:
  • Permissions should span ALL namespaces
  • Access to cluster-scoped resources (nodes, PVs, namespaces)
  • Access to non-resource endpoints (/healthz, /metrics)
  • Example: "Prometheus SA can read pods in ALL namespaces"
🔬 Impersonation — Testing RBAC as Another Identity

When debugging RBAC, you often need to "become" another identity to test permissions. Kubernetes supports impersonation — acting as another user or ServiceAccount:

📋 Impersonation Commands
# ── IMPERSONATE A SERVICE ACCOUNT ──
kubectl get pods -n anihpj --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web

# ── IMPERSONATE WITH SPECIFIC GROUPS ──
kubectl get pods --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web \
  --as-group system:serviceaccounts

# ── FULL IMPERSONATION (user + groups + extra scopes) ──
kubectl get pods -n anihpj \
  --as=system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web \
  --as-group=system:serviceaccounts \
  --as-group=system:authenticated

# ⚠️ IMPERSONATION REQUIRES PERMISSION:
# To impersonate, YOUR identity needs the "impersonate" verb on
# the target identity type (users, groups, serviceaccounts).
# ClusterRole rule for impersonation:
# - apiGroups: [""]
#   resources: ["users", "groups", "serviceaccounts"]
#   verbs: ["impersonate"]

# ── REVOKE ACCESS (remove binding) ──
kubectl delete rolebinding anihpj-web-developer -n anihpj
# Access is IMMEDIATELY revoked. No restart needed. No cache to clear.

🔑 RBAC IS INSTANT: Creating a RoleBinding grants access IMMEDIATELY. Deleting it revokes access IMMEDIATELY. There's no cache, no propagation delay, no restart required. The API Server evaluates RBAC on EVERY request. This is both powerful (instant fix) and dangerous (instant break if you delete the wrong binding).

🔬 RBAC for Human Users — How OIDC Connects Developers to Roles

ServiceAccounts are for pods. But what about human developers using kubectl? They authenticate via OIDC (OpenID Connect) — and their identity flows into RBAC just like a ServiceAccount:

👤 Human User RBAC Flow — OIDC → Identity → Role
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    HUMAN USER RBAC WITH OIDC                                   │
│                                                                               │
│  1. Developer Priya runs: kubectl get pods -n anihpj                         │
│                                                                               │
│  2. kubeconfig has OIDC configuration:                                        │
│     users:                                                                    │
│     - name: priya                                                             │
│       user:                                                                   │
│         exec:                                                                 │
│           command: kubectl oidc-login                                         │
│           args:                                                               │
│           - --oidc-issuer-url=https://auth.anihpj.example.com                │
│           - --oidc-client-id=kubectl                                          │
│                                                                               │
│  3. OIDC flow: browser opens → Priya logs in → receives ID token              │
│     ID Token contains:                                                        │
│       sub: "priya@anihpj.example.com"          ← User identifier              │
│       groups: ["anihpj-developers", "platform"]  ← Group membership           │
│                                                                               │
│  4. API Server extracts identity:                                             │
│     User: https://auth.anihpj.example.com#priya@anihpj.example.com           │
│     Groups: [anihpj-developers, platform, system:authenticated]               │
│                                                                               │
│  5. RBAC checks: Does "anihpj-developers" group have a RoleBinding?           │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│  │ RoleBinding: anihpj-developers-binding                               │     │
│  │ subjects:                                                             │     │
│  │ - kind: Group                     ← 🔑 Bind to GROUP, not User!      │     │
│  │   name: anihpj-developers         ← Matches OIDC "groups" claim      │     │
│  │   apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io                                 │     │
│  │ roleRef:                                                              │     │
│  │   kind: Role                                                          │     │
│  │   name: anihpj-developer                                              │     │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                                                               │
│  🔑 BEST PRACTICE: Bind to GROUPS, not individual users. When Priya joins     │
│     the anihpj team, add her to the "anihpj-developers" OIDC group —          │
│     she instantly gets all the right permissions. When she leaves, remove     │
│     her from the group — access revoked instantly. No RBAC YAML changes.      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

27.5 kubectl auth can-i — The RBAC Testing Tool

kubectl auth can-i is the single most important RBAC command. It answers: "Can THIS identity perform THIS action on THIS resource?" Without it, you're guessing whether your RBAC works.

📋 kubectl auth can-i — Essential Commands
# ── TEST AS YOURSELF (current kubeconfig user) ──
kubectl auth can-i get pods -n anihpj           # Can I get pods?
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n anihpj  # Can I create deployments?
kubectl auth can-i delete secrets -n anihpj      # Can I delete secrets?
kubectl auth can-i '*' '*' -n anihpj             # Can I do EVERYTHING?

# ── TEST AS A SERVICE ACCOUNT ──
kubectl auth can-i get pods -n anihpj \
  --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web   # Test as anihpj-web SA

kubectl auth can-i list deployments -n anihpj \
  --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web

# ── TEST WITH SPECIFIC SUB-RESOURCE ──
kubectl auth can-i get pods/log -n anihpj \
  --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web   # Can SA read pod logs?

kubectl auth can-i create pods/exec -n anihpj \
  --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web   # Can SA exec into pods?

# ── LIST ALL PERMISSIONS ──
kubectl auth can-i --list -n anihpj \
  --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-web   # List ALL permissions

# ── TROUBLESHOOTING: Why is my RBAC not working? ──
# Step 1: Test the exact permission that's failing
kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> -n <ns> --as <sa>
# Step 2: If "no" → check the Role and RoleBinding
kubectl describe role <role-name> -n <ns>
kubectl describe rolebinding <binding-name> -n <ns>
# Step 3: Common issues: wrong apiGroup, missing sub-resource, wrong namespace
⚡ CNPE Exam: kubectl auth can-i Is Your Debugging Tool

If the exam gives you an RBAC task and your configuration isn't working, use kubectl auth can-i to diagnose. It tells you EXACTLY whether the permission is granted. The CNPE exam expects you to use this command to verify your RBAC configurations.

🔬 kubectl auth reconcile — Declarative RBAC Management

While kubectl apply works for most resources, RBAC has a special command: kubectl auth reconcile. It's designed for managing Roles and ClusterRoles that use aggregation:

📋 kubectl auth reconcile — Declarative RBAC
# ── RECONCILE A ROLE FROM A FILE ──
# Unlike apply, reconcile handles RBAC-specific logic:
# 1. Preserves aggregated rules (doesn't overwrite auto-collected rules)
# 2. Merges rules from multiple sources correctly
# 3. Removes rules that are no longer in the source file
kubectl auth reconcile -f role.yaml

# ── RECONCILE ALL RBAC IN A DIRECTORY ──
kubectl auth reconcile -f rbac/

# ⚠️ apply vs reconcile for RBAC:
# kubectl apply: Overwrites the ENTIRE rules list. If you have aggregated
#   rules (from aggregationRule), apply may DELETE them!
# kubectl auth reconcile: MERGES rules. Preserves aggregated rules.
#   Removes only rules that are in the file AND no longer needed.
#
# 🔑 RULE: Use kubectl auth reconcile for Roles/ClusterRoles.
#   Use kubectl apply for RoleBindings/ClusterRoleBindings.
🔬 Automating RBAC Verification — Testing Permissions in CI/CD Pipelines

RBAC that works today can break tomorrow. Automate permission testing in your CI pipeline to catch regressions BEFORE they hit production:

📋 RBAC Test Script for CI/CD (GitHub Actions / GitLab CI)
#!/bin/bash
# rbac-test.sh — Run in CI to verify RBAC is correct
# Fails the pipeline if ANY permission is wrong.
set -e  # Exit on first failure

SA="system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd"
NS="anihpj"

# ── TEST 1: CICD SA CAN update deployments (SHOULD PASS) ──
if kubectl auth can-i update deployments -n $NS --as $SA; then
  echo "✅ PASS: CI/CD can update deployments"
else
  echo "❌ FAIL: CI/CD CANNOT update deployments — RBAC is broken!"
  exit 1
fi

# ── TEST 2: CICD SA CANNOT delete deployments (SHOULD FAIL) ──
if kubectl auth can-i delete deployments -n $NS --as $SA; then
  echo "❌ FAIL: CI/CD CAN delete deployments — RBAC is too permissive!"
  exit 1
else
  echo "✅ PASS: CI/CD cannot delete deployments (least privilege enforced)"
fi

# ── TEST 3: CICD SA CANNOT read secrets (SHOULD FAIL) ──
if kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n $NS --as $SA; then
  echo "❌ FAIL: CI/CD CAN read secrets — security violation!"
  exit 1
else
  echo "✅ PASS: CI/CD cannot read secrets"
fi

# ── TEST 4: Full permission dump (audit trail) ──
kubectl auth can-i --list -n $NS --as $SA > rbac-audit-$SA.txt
echo "📋 Permission audit saved to rbac-audit-$SA.txt"

echo "\n🎉 All RBAC tests passed!"

🔑 CI/CD RBAC TESTING PATTERN: For each ServiceAccount, test BOTH: (1) permissions that SHOULD exist (positive tests) and (2) permissions that SHOULD NOT exist (negative tests). The negative tests are MORE important — they catch privilege escalation. Run this script on every PR that changes RBAC YAML files.

27.6 RBAC Aggregation — Composing ClusterRoles from Multiple Sources

Aggregation lets you build a ClusterRole by combining rules from multiple ClusterRoles using label selectors. Instead of copy-pasting the same rules, you label ClusterRoles and aggregate them.

🧩 RBAC Aggregation — Composing Permissions
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     RBAC AGGREGATION PATTERN                                   │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐                                                      │
│  │ ClusterRole:         │  ← "Aggregate" ClusterRole                          │
│  │ platform-admin       │    Uses aggregationRule to collect rules            │
│  │                      │    from all ClusterRoles with matching labels       │
│  │ aggregationRule:     │                                                      │
│  │   clusterRoleSelectors:                                                    │
│  │   - matchLabels:     │                                                      │
│  │       rbac.anihpj.dev/                                                      │
│  │       aggregate-to-   │                                                      │
│  │       admin: "true"   │                                                      │
│  └─────────┬───────────┘                                                      │
│            │                                                                   │
│            │  Collects rules from:                                             │
│            ▼                                                                   │
│  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌─────────────────────┐   │
│  │ ClusterRole:         │  │ ClusterRole:         │  │ ClusterRole:         │   │
│  │ pod-reader           │  │ deploy-manager       │  │ secret-reader        │   │
│  │ labels:              │  │ labels:              │  │ labels:              │   │
│  │  aggregate-to-admin: │  │  aggregate-to-admin: │  │  aggregate-to-admin: │   │
│  │    "true"            │  │    "true"            │  │    "true"            │   │
│  │ rules: [get pods]    │  │ rules: [manage depl] │  │ rules: [get secrets] │   │
│  └─────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────┘  └─────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                               │
│  🔑 RESULT: platform-admin ClusterRole now contains ALL rules from            │
│     pod-reader + deploy-manager + secret-reader — automatically!              │
│     Adding a new labeled ClusterRole instantly grants its rules to            │
│     platform-admin. No manual editing needed.                                 │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 RBAC Aggregation YAML
# ── AGGREGATE CLUSTERROLE (collects rules) ──
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: anihpj-platform-admin
aggregationRule:
  clusterRoleSelectors:
  - matchLabels:
      rbac.anihpj.dev/aggregate-to-platform-admin: "true"
# rules: []  ← Rules are collected from labeled ClusterRoles

# ── CONTRIBUTOR CLUSTERROLE (provides rules to aggregates) ──
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: anihpj-pod-admin
  labels:
    rbac.anihpj.dev/aggregate-to-platform-admin: "true"  # 🔑 This label triggers aggregation
rules:
- apiGroups: [""]
  resources: ["pods", "pods/log", "pods/exec"]
  verbs: ["*"]                     # Full pod management

# ── VERIFY AGGREGATION ──
# kubectl describe clusterrole anihpj-platform-admin
# Look for "Labels: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-..."
# in the Rules section — these are auto-collected.
🎓 CNPE Exam: Aggregation Patterns

Kubernetes itself uses aggregation for built-in ClusterRoles! The admin, edit, and view ClusterRoles are all aggregates. Check: kubectl describe clusterrole admin — you'll see aggregation labels. The CNPE exam may ask you to create a custom aggregate ClusterRole or to explain how the built-in roles work.

😰
NO RBAC
Everyone is cluster-admin.
Default SA used everywhere.
One mistake = cluster destroyed.
Startup phase. Fix immediately.
→
🆔
DEDICATED SAs
One SA per component.
Dedicated namespaces.
Automount disabled where safe.
Basic hygiene.
→
📋
LEAST PRIVILEGE
Roles with minimal verbs.
resourceNames for fine-grained.
kubectl auth can-i verified.
CNPE-ready.
→
🧩
AGGREGATED + AUDITED
