Monthly permission audits.
Automated RBAC testing in CI.
Enterprise-grade.

27.7 anihpj RBAC Design — Least Privilege for Every Component

Let's design the complete RBAC model for the anihpj platform — ServiceAccounts, Roles, ClusterRoles, and Bindings for every component. The principle: every component gets EXACTLY the permissions it needs and NOTHING more.

ComponentServiceAccountRole/ClusterRolePermissionsReason
anihpj-webanihpj-webanihpj-web-roleGET/LIST pods, services, configmaps in anihpj nsWeb app reads its own config. Doesn't need to create/delete.
anihpj-workeranihpj-workeranihpj-worker-roleGET/LIST pods, CREATE jobs in anihpj nsWorker launches migration jobs. Needs job creation.
CI/CD Pipelineanihpj-cicdanihpj-cicd-roleGET/LIST/UPDATE deployments, CREATE jobs in anihpj nsCI/CD updates deployments (new image). Runs DB migrations.
Argo CDargocd-app-controllerClusterRole: argocdFull management of apps in assigned namespacesArgo CD needs broad permissions — managed by its own RBAC.
PrometheusprometheusClusterRole: viewGET/LIST/WATCH pods, services, nodes in ALL namespacesMonitoring needs cluster-wide read access.
cert-managercert-managerClusterRole: cert-managerManage Certificate CRDs, Secrets, IngressesInstalled with cert-manager — cluster-wide by design.
Human DeveloperN/A (OIDC user)Role: anihpj-developerGET/LIST/WATCH pods, deployments, services, configmaps; CREATE jobs in anihpj nsDevelopers debug their app. Can run migration jobs. Can't delete anything critical.
✅ anihpj RBAC Strategy — Production-Ready Least Privilege
  • Dedicated SA per component: web, worker, cicd, monitoring — each has its own identity.
  • Namespace isolation: Each app gets its own namespace. Web in ns "anihpj" can't touch pods in ns "payments."
  • Read-only by default: Most SAs get only GET/LIST/WATCH. Write permissions (CREATE/UPDATE/DELETE) are explicitly justified.
  • Secrets are locked down: Only CI/CD and cert-manager can read Secrets. Web reads config from ConfigMaps, not Secrets directly.
  • Aggregation for platform admins: Platform admin ClusterRole aggregates from component-specific ClusterRoles via labels.
  • Regular audit: Monthly kubectl auth can-i --list for each SA. Remove unused permissions.
💥 RBAC FAILURE — The Compromised CI/CD Pipeline

A developer accidentally commits a GitHub Actions workflow file with overly broad permissions. The CI/CD SA has verbs: ["*"] on resources: ["*"] in ALL namespaces — effectively cluster-admin.

An attacker compromises a GitHub token and:

  • 🔍 Scans all namespaces: kubectl get pods -A — finds the payments database namespace
  • 📤 Exfiltrates secrets: kubectl get secret db-credentials -n payments -o yaml — dumps DB password
  • 💣 Deletes production: kubectl delete namespace production — destroys everything
  • 💸 Impact: Production outage (4 hours), data breach (exposed credentials), financial loss

Root cause: The CI/CD SA was granted "*" verbs on "*" resources instead of specific UPDATE/PATCH on deployments and CREATE on jobs. One wildcard destroyed the principle of least privilege.

✅ RBAC DONE RIGHT — The Attack Contained

Same scenario, but with proper RBAC from this chapter. The CI/CD SA only has UPDATE/PATCH on deployments and CREATE on jobs — in ONE namespace.

  • 🚫 Cannot scan namespaces: kubectl get pods -A → 403 Forbidden. SA can only see anihpj namespace.
  • 🚫 Cannot read secrets: kubectl get secret db-credentials -n payments → 403 Forbidden. SA has no secret access.
  • 🚫 Cannot delete namespaces: kubectl delete namespace production → 403 Forbidden. Not even in the Role.
  • 📊 DETECTED: API audit logs show 403s from CI/CD SA trying to access secrets — security alert triggered.
  • ✅ Impact: Attack contained. Zero data loss. Zero downtime. The attacker's token is useless beyond updating a deployment image.

Lesson: Least privilege RBAC doesn't just limit what legitimate users can do — it limits what an ATTACKER can do when they steal credentials. Every wildcard verb is an attacker's superpower.

🔬 RBAC Audit Logging — Detecting Permission Violations

Even with perfect RBAC, you need to KNOW when someone tries to do something they shouldn't. Kubernetes audit logging records every API request — including DENIED ones:

📋 Audit Log Entry — Detecting RBAC Violations
# Audit log entry for a DENIED request (403 Forbidden)
{
  "kind": "Event",
  "level": "RequestResponse",
  "stage": "ResponseComplete",
  "user": {
    "username": "system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd",
    "groups": ["system:serviceaccounts", "system:authenticated"]
  },
  "verb": "delete",                              ← What they tried to do
  "requestURI": "/api/v1/namespaces/production",   ← What they targeted
  "responseStatus": {
    "code": 403,                               ← FORBIDDEN!
    "reason": "Forbidden"
  },
  "annotations": {
    "authorization.k8s.io/decision": "forbid",
    "authorization.k8s.io/reason": "RBAC: denied"
  }
}

# 🔑 WHAT TO ALERT ON:
# 1. Repeated 403s from the same SA → possible attack or misconfiguration
# 2. 403s on sensitive resources (secrets, namespaces) → high-priority alert
# 3. 403s from SAs that normally don't access those resources → anomaly
# 4. Successful access to secrets by unexpected SAs → possible breach
🛠️ Drill 1: Create RBAC for anihpj Developer

Scenario: Developer Priya needs read access to pods, services, deployments, and logs in the anihpj namespace. She also needs to create jobs for DB migrations.

Task:

  1. Create a ServiceAccount named "priya" in namespace anihpj
  2. Create a Role with GET/LIST/WATCH for pods, pods/log, services, deployments
  3. Add CREATE permission for jobs (apiGroups: ["batch"])
  4. Create a RoleBinding connecting the SA to the Role
  5. Verify with: kubectl auth can-i --list -n anihpj --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:priya

Time: 15 min

💡 Hints
  • SA: kubectl create sa priya -n anihpj — simplest way. Or YAML: kind: ServiceAccount, name: priya.
  • Role apiGroups: pods/services = [""] (core), deployments = ["apps"], jobs = ["batch"].
  • RoleBinding: subjects: [{kind: ServiceAccount, name: priya, namespace: anihpj}], roleRef: {kind: Role, name: priya-developer}.
  • Verify positive: kubectl auth can-i get pods -n anihpj --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:priya → yes.
  • Verify negative: kubectl auth can-i delete secrets -n anihpj --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:priya → no.
🛠️ Drill 2: ClusterRole for Platform Admin

Scenario: Create a cluster-wide read-only role for the platform monitoring system (Prometheus).

Task:

  1. Create a ServiceAccount "prometheus" in namespace "monitoring"
  2. Create a ClusterRole allowing GET/LIST/WATCH on pods, services, nodes, namespaces in ALL namespaces
  3. Create a ClusterRoleBinding connecting the SA to the ClusterRole
  4. Verify Prometheus can read nodes (cluster-scoped resource)
  5. Verify Prometheus CANNOT create or delete anything

Time: 15 min

💡 Hints
  • Shortcut: Use built-in view ClusterRole! kubectl create clusterrolebinding prometheus-view --clusterrole=view --serviceaccount=monitoring:prometheus — done in ONE command. No YAML needed.
  • If writing custom: nodes go in resources list with apiGroups: [""]. Namespaces too.
  • ClusterRoleBinding has NO namespace field. It's cluster-scoped.
  • Verify nodes: kubectl auth can-i get nodes --as system:serviceaccount:monitoring:prometheus → yes.
  • Verify no delete: kubectl auth can-i delete pods --as system:serviceaccount:monitoring:prometheus → no.
🛠️ Drill 3: RBAC for CI/CD Service Account

Scenario: The CI/CD pipeline (GitHub Actions) needs to update deployments and create jobs in the anihpj namespace.

Task:

  1. Create a ServiceAccount "anihpj-cicd" in namespace anihpj
  2. Create a Role granting UPDATE/PATCH on deployments and CREATE on jobs
  3. Create a RoleBinding. Verify with kubectl auth can-i
  4. Test: Can the CI/CD SA delete a deployment? (It should NOT be able to.)
  5. Test: Can it create a secret? (It should NOT be able to.)

Time: 15 min

💡 Hints
  • Role verbs: update + patch for deployments (apps group), create for jobs (batch group). Don't grant delete or deletecollection.
  • CRITICAL: The CI/CD SA also needs GET on deployments to READ the current deployment before updating. Without GET, kubectl can't fetch the resource to patch it.
  • Verify positive: kubectl auth can-i update deployments -n anihpj --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd → yes.
  • Verify negative: kubectl auth can-i delete deployments -n anihpj --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd → no.
  • Verify negative: kubectl auth can-i create secrets -n anihpj --as system:serviceaccount:anihpj:anihpj-cicd → no.
🧠 Knowledge Check — 10 Questions

Q1: What is a ServiceAccount and how does it differ from a user account?

Q2: What is the difference between a Role and a ClusterRole?

Q3: What is the format of a ServiceAccount username in RBAC?

Q4: What does a RoleBinding do? How is it different from a ClusterRoleBinding?

Q5: What happens when you bind a ClusterRole with a RoleBinding?

Q6: How do you test if a ServiceAccount has a specific permission?

Q7: What is the correct apiGroup for core resources like pods and services?

Q8: What is RBAC aggregation and when would you use it?

Q9: Why should you set automountServiceAccountToken to false?

Q10: Design the RBAC for anihpj: what SAs, Roles, and Bindings are needed?

📋 Chapter 27 Summary — RBAC & Access Control
🆔
ServiceAccounts

Pod identity. Every pod has one SA. Format: system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>. Disable automount when not needed.

📋
Roles & ClusterRoles

Role = namespace-scoped permissions. ClusterRole = cluster-wide. Roles define WHAT you can do — not WHO gets to do it.

🔗
Bindings

RoleBinding connects SA/User to Role. ClusterRoleBinding connects to ClusterRole. ClusterRole + RoleBinding = namespace-scoped ClusterRole.

🎨 Visual Summary — The RBAC Chain

    ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    │                     THE RBAC CHAIN                             │
    │                                                               │
    │   ServiceAccount → RoleBinding → Role → Permission           │
    │   (WHO)            (GRANTS)      (WHAT)  (CAN DO)             │
    │                                                               │
    │   🔑 LEAST PRIVILEGE: Every SA gets EXACTLY what it needs     │
    │   🔍 VERIFY: kubectl auth can-i --as <SA>                    │
    │   🧩 AGGREGATE: Build complex roles from simple ones          │
    └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🎓 CNPE Exam Strategy — Domain 5 RBAC Tasks

Domain 5 (Security & Policy, 15%) includes RBAC configuration. Expect 1-2 RBAC tasks:

  • Create RBAC from scratch: Given a scenario ("CI/CD needs to update deployments"), create SA → Role → RoleBinding. Know the exact YAML structure for all three resources. The apiVersion is rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1.
  • Troubleshoot broken RBAC: Given a non-working configuration, identify the error. Use kubectl auth can-i --as to test. Common issues: wrong apiGroup ("" vs "v1"), missing sub-resource (pods/log), wrong namespace in subject.
  • Built-in ClusterRoles: Know when to use view, edit, admin, cluster-admin. Using built-in roles is faster and less error-prone than writing custom rules — a common exam time-saver.
  • ClusterRole + RoleBinding trick: The exam WILL test this: "Grant ClusterRole X to User Y, but only in namespace Z." Answer: ClusterRole + RoleBinding (not ClusterRoleBinding). The RoleBinding scopes the ClusterRole down to one namespace.

🔑 EXAM MINDSET: Every RBAC task follows the same pattern: Identity → Role → Binding → Verify. Create the SA first (WHO), then the Role (WHAT), then the Binding (GRANT), then kubectl auth can-i (VERIFY). Missing any step = no permissions. The exam tests the FULL chain — not just one piece.

Ch 28: Pod Security & Admission Control

What pods are ALLOWED to do — enforced BEFORE they run. Pod Security Standards define three hardening levels. Pod Security Admission enforces them per-namespace. Security contexts lock down individual pods. Admission webhooks validate and mutate resources. Runtime security protects the node after the pod starts.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~1.5h CNPE Domain 5: 15%
🎯 What You'll Learn
  • The 3 Pod Security Standard levels: Privileged, Baseline, and Restricted
  • How Pod Security Admission enforces PSS policies per namespace via labels
  • Security contexts — the pod-level and container-level fields that lock down behavior
  • Admission webhooks — how they validate and mutate resources before persistence
  • Runtime security with seccomp profiles and AppArmor — defense after the pod starts
  • How to design a complete pod security posture for anihpj
📋 CNPE Exam Relevance — Domain 5 (15%)

Domain 5 tests your ability to apply security controls across platform resources. You will be asked to configure Pod Security Admission labels, write security contexts, and configure admission webhooks. PSS/PSA is a guaranteed exam topic — know the 3 levels and how to enforce them.

28.1 PSS Levels — Privileged, Baseline, and Restricted

Pod Security Standards (PSS) define three tiers of pod security. They specify what pods are ALLOWED to do — from completely unrestricted (Privileged) to tightly locked down (Restricted). PSS replaces the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy (PSP), which was removed in Kubernetes 1.25.

🔬 Why PSP Was REMOVED — The Migration to PSS

PodSecurityPolicy existed since Kubernetes 1.3 but was ALWAYS problematic. Understanding WHY it failed helps you appreciate PSS's design:

Problem with PSPHow PSS Solves It
Complex RBAC: PSP required creating a Policy, a Role to USE the policy, and a RoleBinding to grant access — AND the Pod's SA needed permission. 4 resources to enable 1 pod.Namespace labels: One label on the namespace. Done. No extra RBAC, no extra resources. Simpler = more likely to be used correctly.
Silent failures: If RBAC was misconfigured, the pod would be created with ZERO policy applied. No warning. No error. The pod just ran unrestricted.Fail-closed: If enforce=restricted is set, ALL pods are checked. No silent bypass. If the label is missing, you know immediately.
Ordering madness: PSPs were ordered by name. The FIRST matching PSP (alphabetically!) was applied. Changing a PSP name could change security posture. Naming became a security concern.Single level: Each namespace has ONE enforce level. No ordering. No ambiguity. The label IS the policy.
No dry-run: You couldn't test what a PSP would block without actually deploying. Trial-and-error in production.warn + audit modes: Test enforcement without blocking. See exactly what would fail before you turn on enforce.

🔑 THE LESSON: PSP was "powerful but dangerous" — too complex for most teams to use correctly. PSS is "simple and safe" — hard to misconfigure. For the CNPE exam: know that PSP is GONE (removed in 1.25) and PSS is the ONLY built-in option. If a question mentions PSP, the answer is "migrate to PSS."

🛡️ The 3 Pod Security Standard Levels — Pyramid of Hardening
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    POD SECURITY STANDARDS — 3 LEVELS                           │
│                                                                               │
│                         ┌─────────────────┐                                   │
│                         │   RESTRICTED     │  ← MOST SECURE                    │
│                         │  (Hardened)      │     • MUST run as non-root       │
│                        ┌┴─────────────────┴┐    • MUST use readOnlyRootFS     │
│                        │    BASELINE        │  ← RECOMMENDED MINIMUM           │
│                        │  (Minimal)         │    • No hostPath, hostPort      │
│                       ┌┴───────────────────┴┐   • No privileged containers    │
│                       │    PRIVILEGED        │  ← UNRESTRICTED                 │
│                       │  (Everything allowed)│    • No restrictions at all    │
│                       └─────────────────────┘    • Only for system workloads  │
│                                                                               │
│  📜 PSP → PSS MIGRATION: PodSecurityPolicy was DEPRECATED and REMOVED in      │
│     Kubernetes 1.25. PSS is the REPLACEMENT — simpler, label-based, built-in. │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
PSS LevelWhat It MeansKey RestrictionsUse For
🔴 PrivilegedNo restrictions. Everything is allowed.None. Privileged containers, hostPath, hostNetwork, hostPID — all allowed.System pods (kube-proxy, CNI, CSI drivers). NEVER for application pods.
🟡 BaselineMinimal hardening. Blocks known-dangerous settings.❌ No hostPath volumes. ❌ No hostPort. ❌ No hostNetwork/PID/IPC. ❌ No privileged containers. ❌ No CAP_SYS_ADMIN. Allows running as root.Minimum bar for ALL application workloads. Start here, then tighten to Restricted.
🟢 RestrictedHardened. Follows pod hardening best practices.All Baseline restrictions PLUS: ❌ MUST run as non-root. ❌ MUST use readOnlyRootFS. ❌ No privilege escalation. ❌ Seccomp profile must be set. ❌ Capabilities dropped to NET_BIND_SERVICE only.Production workloads. Security-sensitive apps (payments, auth, customer data).
🎓 CNPE Exam: PSS Level Selection

The exam will test your ability to choose the RIGHT PSS level:

  • "A CI/CD tool needs hostPath to access the Docker socket." → Privileged (only way to allow hostPath). But question WHY — can it use a different approach?
  • "A web application that doesn't need root." → Restricted. Always choose the highest level the workload can support.
  • "A monitoring agent that needs hostNetwork for accurate metrics." → Privileged (hostNetwork is blocked by Baseline and above).
  • DEFAULT: Start at Baseline for all namespaces. Exception: production namespaces should be Restricted. System namespaces may need Privileged.
🌳 Which PSS Level Should I Enforce?
🤔 Does the workload need host access (hostPath, hostNetwork, hostPID)?
🔴 YES — Needs host access
🟢 NO — Pure container workload
🔴 Privileged — Only for system workloads (CNI, CSI, kube-proxy, monitoring agents). Lock down with RBAC: only cluster-admin can deploy here.
🤔 Can the app run as non-root with read-only filesystem?
🟢 Restricted — Production-ready. Highest security. runAsNonRoot + readOnlyRootFS + drop ALL capabilities.
🤔 Does the app need to run as root OR write to root FS?
🟡 Baseline — Minimum hardening. Blocks host access and privileged containers but allows root. Plan migration to Restricted.

28.2 Pod Security Admission — Enforcing PSS Per Namespace

Pod Security Admission (PSA) is a built-in admission controller that ENFORCES PSS levels. You set namespace labels to define the security level — and PSA rejects pods that violate it. No external tools needed.

🏷️ PSA Namespace Labels — The 3 Enforcement Modes
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    POD SECURITY ADMISSION — NAMESPACE LABELS                   │
│                                                                               │
│  Namespace: anihpj                                                             │
│  Labels:                                                                      │
│    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted    ← ENFORCE mode           │
│    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: baseline        ← AUDIT mode             │
│    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: baseline         ← WARN mode              │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  MODE           │  BEHAVIOR                                             │   │
│  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │  enforce        │  🔴 REJECTS pods that violate the policy.             │   │
│  │                 │  Pod is NOT created. User gets 403 Forbidden.         │   │
│  │                 │  This is what BLOCKS insecure pods.                   │   │
│  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │  audit          │  🟡 LOGS policy violations to the audit log.          │   │
│  │                 │  Pod IS created (no block). Useful for testing.       │   │
│  │                 │  "What would break if we enforced this?"              │   │
│  ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤   │
│  │  warn           │  🟠 SHOWS a WARNING to the user (kubectl output).     │   │
│  │                 │  Pod IS created. Educates without blocking.           │   │
│  │                 │  "This pod will be rejected in a future version."     │   │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│                                                                               │
│  🔑 ROLLOUT STRATEGY:                                                         │
│     Step 1: Set warn=restricted → users see warnings, nothing blocked.       │
│     Step 2: Set audit=restricted → violations logged, nothing blocked.       │
│     Step 3: Set enforce=restricted → violations REJECTED. Production-ready.  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 PSA Namespace Label Configuration
# ── ENFORCE RESTRICTED ON PRODUCTION (blocks insecure pods) ──
kubectl label ns anihpj \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest

# ── WARN + AUDIT FIRST (safe rollout) ──
kubectl label ns anihpj \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=baseline \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit=restricted \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version=latest

# ── CHECK CURRENT PSA LABELS ──
kubectl get ns anihpj --show-labels | grep pod-security

# ── DRY-RUN: Check if a pod WOULD be rejected ──
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml --dry-run=server -n anihpj
# If rejected, you'll see: "pods 'my-pod' is forbidden: violates PodSecurity"

# ── REMOVE PSA (no enforcement) ──
kubectl label ns anihpj \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce- \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn- \
  pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit-
🔬 Real PSA Error Messages — What You'll Actually See

When PSA rejects a pod, the error message tells you EXACTLY what to fix. Learning to read these messages saves hours of debugging:

📋 PSA Rejection Messages — Decoded
# ── ERROR 1: Pod running as root (most common) ──
Error: pods "nginx" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest":
  runAsNonRoot != true (container "nginx" must not set securityContext.runAsNonRoot=false)
# FIX: Add runAsNonRoot: true AND runAsUser: 1000 to securityContext

# ── ERROR 2: Writable root filesystem ──
Error: pods "my-app" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest":
  readOnlyRootFilesystem != true (container "my-app" must set securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem=true)
# FIX: Add readOnlyRootFilesystem: true + mount emptyDir for writable paths

# ── ERROR 3: Privilege escalation allowed ──
Error: pods "my-app" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest":
  allowPrivilegeEscalation != false (container "my-app" must set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false)
# FIX: Add allowPrivilegeEscalation: false

# ── ERROR 4: Capabilities not fully dropped ──
Error: pods "my-app" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest":
  unrestricted capabilities (container "my-app" must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"])
# FIX: Add capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]

# ── ERROR 5: Seccomp not set ──
Error: pods "my-app" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest":
  seccompProfile (container "my-app" must set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost")
# FIX: Add seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}

🔑 PATTERN: Every PSA error follows the format: violates PodSecurity "<level>:<version>": <field> <expected_value>. Read the field name and expected value — that's EXACTLY what you need to add to your securityContext. The error IS the fix.

⚠️ PSA Gotchas — What Breaks When You Enforce Restricted
🔑 Containers running as root

Restricted requires runAsNonRoot: true. Most default container images run as root (UID 0). You MUST either: (a) set runAsNonRoot: true + runAsUser: 1000, or (b) rebuild the image to use a non-root user.

🔑 Writable root filesystem

Restricted requires readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. Apps that write to /tmp will FAIL. Fix: mount an emptyDir volume at /tmp, or configure the app to write elsewhere.

🔑 Capabilities NOT dropped

Restricted requires dropping ALL capabilities except NET_BIND_SERVICE. Most containers start with a default set. Fix: securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"] + add back only what's needed.

🔬 PSA Exemptions — When You Must Run a Privileged Pod in a Restricted Namespace

Sometimes you need ONE pod to bypass PSA enforcement — a migration job that needs to run as root, or an init container that modifies system settings. PSA supports per-pod exemptions via a specific username pattern:

📋 PSA Exemption — Allow a Specific Pod to Bypass Enforcement
# ── METHOD 1: Exempt by ServiceAccount username ──
# Pods running as this SA are exempt from PSA enforcement.
# The SA username format is: system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa-name>
# In the PSA admission configuration (API Server flags or config file):
exemptions:
  usernames:
  - "system:serviceaccount:anihpj:db-migration"
  # Pods running as SA "db-migration" bypass PSA. Everything else is enforced.

# ── METHOD 2: Exempt entire namespaces ──
# Namespaces matching these labels are EXCLUDED from PSA.
exemptions:
  namespaces:
  - "kube-system"
  - "monitoring"
  # Use sparingly — only for truly necessary system namespaces.

# ⚠️ Exemptions are configured at the CLUSTER level
# (API Server flags or admission configuration file),
# NOT at the namespace level. This requires cluster-admin access.

🔑 THE RULE: Exemptions are a PRESSURE RELEASE VALVE, not a design pattern. Use them temporarily while you fix the pod to comply with PSA. Track exemptions and set a deadline for removal. Every exemption is a potential security gap.

😰
LEVEL 1
No Controls

All pods run as root. No PSS. No security contexts. Containers have full host access.

❌ Vulnerable
🟡
LEVEL 2
Baseline PSS

No hostPath/hostNetwork. No privileged containers. PSA warn+audit mode. Planning Restricted migration.

⚠️ Minimal Hardening
🟢
LEVEL 3
Restricted PSS

Non-root. Read-only root FS. Capabilities dropped. Seccomp enforced. Webhooks block :latest.

✅ Production Hardened
🛡️
LEVEL 4
Zero-Trust Pod Security

Custom seccomp per app. AppArmor profiles. Falco runtime detection. Image signing enforced.

🌟 Defense-in-Depth

28.3 Security Contexts — Locking Down Individual Pods

A securityContext defines privilege and access control settings for a pod or container. It's applied at TWO levels: Pod-level (applies to all containers) and Container-level (overrides pod-level for specific containers).

📋 Complete Security Context — Pod-Level + Container-Level
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  namespace: anihpj
spec:
  # ── POD-LEVEL Security Context (applies to ALL containers) ──
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true            # 🔑 MUST run as non-root (UID != 0)
    runAsUser: 1000               # Run as UID 1000 (not root)
    runAsGroup: 3000              # Run as GID 3000
    fsGroup: 2000                 # Filesystem group for volume mounts
    seccompProfile:                # Seccomp profile (syscall filtering)
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
  - name: django
    image: anihpj-web:v2
    # ── CONTAINER-LEVEL Security Context (overrides pod-level) ──
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false  # 🔑 Cannot gain MORE privileges
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true     # 🔑 Root filesystem is READ-ONLY
      privileged: false                # NOT a privileged container
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]                # 🔑 Drop ALL Linux capabilities
        add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]     # Only add back what's needed
      volumeMounts:
      - name: tmp
        mountPath: /tmp              # Mount writable volume for /tmp
  volumes:
  - name: tmp
    emptyDir: {}                   # Writable temp storage
FieldWhat It DoesRequired BySecurity Impact
runAsNonRootForces container to run as UID != 0Restricted PSS🔑 Prevents root-level container breakout to host.
runAsUserSpecifies the UID to run asRecommended🔑 Runs as least-privileged user. Combine with non-root image.
readOnlyRootFilesystemMakes root filesystem read-onlyRestricted PSS🔑 Attackers can't modify binaries or write backdoors.
allowPrivilegeEscalationPrevents setuid binaries from escalatingRestricted PSS🔑 Stops sudo-like privilege escalation inside container.
privilegedGrants FULL host access (all devices, all capabilities)MUST be false⚠️ Never set true for app containers. Equivalent to root on the node.
capabilitiesLinux capabilities (fine-grained root powers)Restricted: drop ALL🔑 Instead of full root, grant only specific powers (NET_BIND_SERVICE, SYS_TIME).
seccompProfileSyscall filter — limits what syscalls the container can makeRestricted PSS🔑 If app is compromised, attacker can only use allowed syscalls.
⚡ Security Context Quick Reference
  • Pod-level fields: runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, runAsGroup, fsGroup, seccompProfile — apply to ALL containers.
  • Container-level fields: allowPrivilegeEscalation, readOnlyRootFilesystem, privileged, capabilities — per-container overrides.
  • Container-level OVERRIDES pod-level: If both are set, container-level wins. Useful when one container needs different settings.
  • Minimum for Restricted PSS: runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, capabilities.drop: ["ALL"], seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault.
🔬 Linux Capabilities — What Root ACTUALLY Means (and Why You Must Drop Them)

On Linux, "root" isn't one permission — it's ~40 fine-grained capabilities. Dropping capabilities eliminates specific root powers without losing root UID. Here are the most dangerous ones:

CapabilityWhat It AllowsAttack Vector If KeptShould You Keep It?
CAP_SYS_ADMINMount filesystems, load kernel modules, change namespaces⚠️ Mount host filesystem → escape container. Load malicious kernel module → root the node.❌ NEVER. This is the "new root" — the most powerful capability.
CAP_NET_RAWRaw sockets, packet sniffing⚠️ tcpdump other pods' traffic. ARP spoofing. Network-level attacks.❌ DROP unless app legitimately needs raw sockets.
CAP_SYS_PTRACEDebug OTHER processes⚠️ Attach debugger to other containers. Read their memory. Inject code.❌ NEVER for app containers.
CAP_SYS_BOOTReboot the node⚠️ Reboot the host node. Denial of service.❌ NEVER.
CAP_DAC_OVERRIDEBypass file permission checks⚠️ Read/write ANY file regardless of ownership. Read /etc/shadow.❌ DROP unless absolutely needed.
NET_BIND_SERVICEBind to ports < 1024Minimal. Port binding only.✅ KEEP — most web servers need this for port 80/443.

🔑 THE RULE: Start with drop: ["ALL"]. Then add back ONLY what the app actually needs — discovered by testing. If you don't know which capabilities your app needs, drop ALL and add back based on crash logs. The default capability set is a security liability, not a feature.

⚠️ What BREAKS with readOnlyRootFilesystem — And How to Fix Each App

The single most common failure when hardening pods: the app crashes because it can't write to the filesystem. Here's exactly what breaks and how to fix it for common frameworks:

App / FrameworkWhat Tries to WriteWhere It WritesFix
Django (Python).pyc bytecode cacheSame directory as .py filesSet PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 env var. Mount emptyDir at Django project root.
Node.js / Expressnpm cache, tmp files/tmp, /home/node/.npmMount emptyDir at /tmp. Set npm config set cache /tmp/npm.
GoGenerally nothing! Go binaries are self-contained.—✅ Go apps usually work with readOnlyRootFS out of the box. Easiest to harden.
Java / Spring BootJVM temp files, class data sharing/tmpMount emptyDir at /tmp. Set -Djava.io.tmpdir=/tmp.
NginxClient body temp, proxy temp, FastCGI temp/var/cache/nginx, /var/runMount emptyDirs at /var/cache/nginx and /var/run. Or configure nginx to use /tmp for all buffers.
PostgreSQLData directory (MUST be writable)/var/lib/postgresql/data⚠️ Databases CANNOT use readOnlyRootFS. Mount a PersistentVolume at the data directory. The root FS can still be read-only.

🔑 THE PATTERN: Apps need THREE things to be writable: (1) /tmp — universal temp directory. (2) App-specific cache/log directories. (3) Data directories (for databases). Mount emptyDirs or PVs at these paths. Everything else can be read-only.

28.4 Admission Webhooks — Custom Validation and Mutation

PSS/PSA handles basic pod security. But what about CUSTOM rules? "Block images with the :latest tag." "Require the team label on every pod." "Automatically add resource limits." These require admission webhooks — HTTP callbacks that the API Server calls before persisting a resource.

🔗 Admission Webhook Flow — Validate and Mutate Before Persistence
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ADMISSION WEBHOOK REQUEST FLOW                              │
│                                                                               │
│  User: kubectl apply -f pod.yaml                                             │
│         │                                                                     │
│         ▼                                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐         │
│  │                    API SERVER ADMISSION CHAIN                     │         │
│  │                                                                  │         │
│  │  1. AUTHENTICATION: Who are you? (SA token, OIDC, cert)          │         │
│  │  2. AUTHORIZATION:  Are you allowed to create pods? (RBAC)       │         │
│  │                                                                  │         │
│  │  3. MUTATING ADMISSION WEBHOOKS:  ← Can MODIFY the resource     │         │
│  │     ┌────────────────────┐                                       │         │
│  │     │ MutatingWebhook    │  Example: Add sidecar container,      │         │
│  │     │ POST /mutate       │  inject labels, set default limits     │         │
│  │     └────────┬───────────┘                                       │         │
│  │              │ JSONPatch response                                │         │
│  │              ▼                                                    │         │
│  │  4. OBJECT SCHEMA VALIDATION: Does it match the CRD schema?      │         │
│  │                                                                  │         │
│  │  5. VALIDATING ADMISSION WEBHOOKS:  ← Can REJECT (not modify)   │         │
│  │     ┌────────────────────┐                                       │         │
│  │     │ ValidatingWebhook  │  Example: Block :latest images,       │         │
│  │     │ POST /validate     │  require labels, enforce policies     │         │
│  │     └────────┬───────────┘                                       │         │
│  │              │ Allowed: true/false                               │         │
│  │              ▼                                                    │         │
│  │  6. PERSIST to etcd                                             │         │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘         │
│                                                                               │
│  🔑 KEY DISTINCTION:                                                          │
│     Mutating webhooks run FIRST. They can ADD things (defaults, sidecars).    │
│     Validating webhooks run SECOND. They can only say YES or NO.              │
│     Mutating webhooks see the ORIGINAL resource.                              │
│     Validating webhooks see the MUTATED resource (after all mutations).       │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 ValidatingWebhookConfiguration — Block :latest Images
# ── VALIDATING WEBHOOK: Reject pods using :latest tag ──
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingWebhookConfiguration
metadata:
  name: block-latest-tag
webhooks:
- name: block-latest.anihpj.dev        # Must be a fully qualified domain name
  clientConfig:
    service:                            # Webhook service in the cluster
      name: admission-webhook
      namespace: anihpj
      path: /validate-image-tag
    caBundle: <base64-encoded-CA-cert>  # TLS certificate for HTTPS
  rules:
  - apiGroups: [""]
    apiVersions: ["v1"]
    operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]     # When to trigger
    resources: ["pods"]                  # What resources to intercept
  failurePolicy: Fail                   # 🔑 Fail = REJECT if webhook is down!
  # Use Ignore for non-critical webhooks to avoid blocking all deploys.
  sideEffects: None
  admissionReviewVersions: ["v1"]

# ⚠️ CRITICAL: failurePolicy: Fail means if YOUR webhook service is down,
# ALL matching operations are REJECTED. Use Ignore for non-critical webhooks
# or ensure the webhook service is highly available (multiple replicas).
🎓 CNPE Exam: Admission Webhooks

The exam may ask you to configure or troubleshoot admission webhooks:

  • Mutating vs Validating: Mutating can MODIFY resources (add labels, inject sidecars). Validating can only ACCEPT or REJECT. Mutating runs FIRST.
  • failurePolicy: Fail = if webhook is unreachable, REJECT the request. Ignore = if webhook is unreachable, ALLOW the request. Use Fail for security policies, Ignore for non-critical policies.
  • TLS is mandatory: All webhooks MUST use HTTPS. The caBundle is the CA certificate that signed the webhook server's TLS cert.
  • Timeout: Default 10 seconds. If your webhook takes longer, the request is rejected (if failurePolicy=Fail).
🔬 Building a Simple Admission Webhook Server — Python/Flask Example

You don't need a complex framework for admission webhooks. A simple HTTP server that parses AdmissionReview JSON and returns an AdmissionResponse is all you need:

📋 Python Webhook Server — Block :latest Images
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
import json

app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route('/validate-image-tag', methods=['POST'])
def validate():
    # Parse the AdmissionReview request
    admission_review = request.get_json()
    pod_spec = admission_review['request']['object']['spec']

    # Check EVERY container's image for :latest tag
    for container in pod_spec.get('containers', []):
        image = container['image']
        if ':latest' in image or ':' not in image:
            # Reject: :latest tag or no tag at all
            return jsonify({
                'apiVersion': 'admission.k8s.io/v1',
                'kind': 'AdmissionReview',
                'response': {
                    'uid': admission_review['request']['uid'],
                    'allowed': False,
                    'status': {
                        'code': 403,
                        'message': f"Image '{image}' uses :latest tag or no tag. Pinned versions only."
                    }
                }
            })

    # All containers pass — allow
    return jsonify({
        'apiVersion': 'admission.k8s.io/v1',
        'kind': 'AdmissionReview',
        'response': {
            'uid': admission_review['request']['uid'],
            'allowed': True
        }
    })

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Run with TLS (REQUIRED for admission webhooks)
    app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=8443,
            ssl_context=('/certs/tls.crt', '/certs/tls.key'))

🔑 CRITICAL DETAILS: (1) The response MUST include the uid from the request — Kubernetes uses it to correlate requests. (2) The webhook MUST use HTTPS — plain HTTP is rejected. (3) The AdmissionReview wraps both request and response — your server receives AdmissionReview and returns AdmissionReview.

🔬 Mutating Webhooks — Automatically Injecting Defaults

While validating webhooks say YES/NO, mutating webhooks MODIFY resources. The most common use case: automatically adding resource limits to pods that don't specify them:

📋 Mutating Webhook — Inject Default Resource Limits
# If a pod has NO resource limits, add default limits:
#   limits.cpu: 500m, limits.memory: 512Mi
# The mutation is a JSONPatch operation — adding fields to the pod spec.

# ── JSONPatch Response from Mutating Webhook ──
{
  "apiVersion": "admission.k8s.io/v1",
  "kind": "AdmissionReview",
  "response": {
    "uid": "<request-uid>",
    "allowed": true,
    "patchType": "JSONPatch",     # 🔑 Mutating webhooks return a PATCH
    "patch": "W3sib3AiOiJhZGQiLC...",  # Base64-encoded JSONPatch
    # Decoded patch (for understanding):
    # [
    #   {"op": "add", "path": "/spec/containers/0/resources", "value": {
    #     "limits": {"cpu": "500m", "memory": "512Mi"},
    #     "requests": {"cpu": "100m", "memory": "128Mi"}
    #   }},
    #   {"op": "add", "path": "/metadata/labels/platform", "value": "anihpj"}
    # ]
  }
}

# 🔑 MUTATING WEBHOOK ORDER MATTERS:
# Multiple mutating webhooks run in ALPHABETICAL ORDER by name.
# Webhook A "add-resource-limits.anihpj.dev" runs BEFORE
# Webhook B "inject-sidecar.anihpj.dev".
# Use naming to control execution order when it matters.

🎯 COMMON MUTATIONS: (1) Add default resource limits. (2) Inject Istio/Linkerd sidecar containers. (3) Add required labels (team, environment, cost-center). (4) Set default securityContext values. (5) Rewrite image registries (docker.io → internal registry). Mutating webhooks are the "platform defaults" layer — they ensure every pod meets minimum standards without the developer needing to know.

28.5 Runtime Security — seccomp and AppArmor

PSS and PSA protect pods at ADMISSION time (before they start). But what protects the NODE after a container is running? seccomp and AppArmor provide runtime protection — limiting what a running container can do at the kernel level.

Featureseccomp (Secure Computing Mode)AppArmor (Application Armor)
What it doesFilters SYSTEM CALLS. A container can only use allowed syscalls.Restricts FILE and CAPABILITY access. A container can only access allowed paths.
ScopePer container (via securityContext)Per container (via annotation: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/)
Example blockBlock ptrace (prevent debugging other processes). Block mount (prevent mounting filesystems).Block writes to /etc/passwd. Block access to /proc/sys/ (kernel tuning).
Default profileRuntimeDefault — blocks ~300 of 435+ syscalls. Safe default for most apps.runtime/default — distribution-specific profile. Blocks common dangerous operations.
Custom profilesJSON file defining allowed syscalls. Path: /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/Loaded into kernel. Defined in /etc/apparmor.d/. Per-profile enforcement.
Kubernetes support✅ Native since 1.19 (GA). securityContext.seccompProfile✅ Supported via annotations. Not yet a first-class field.
Required byRestricted PSSNot required by PSS (yet). Recommended for defense-in-depth.
📋 seccomp Profile — Restrict Django to Essential Syscalls
# ── SECCOMP PROFILE: anihpj-web.json ──
# Stored at: /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/anihpj-web.json
{
  "defaultAction": "SCMP_ACT_ERRNO",   ← DEFAULT: BLOCK all syscalls
  "architectures": ["SCMP_ARCH_X86_64"],
  "syscalls": [
    {
      "names": [
        "read", "write", "open", "close",     ← ALLOW: Essential I/O
        "fstat", "lseek", "mmap",           ← ALLOW: Memory & file ops
        "accept", "bind", "listen",         ← ALLOW: Network (Django needs this)
        "connect", "sendto", "recvfrom",  ← ALLOW: Network I/O
        "futex", "nanosleep", "clock_gettime" ← ALLOW: Thread & timing
      ],
      "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW"
    }
  ]
}

# In Pod spec:
securityContext:
  seccompProfile:
    type: Localhost
    localhostProfile: anihpj-web.json  # References file on the NODE

# ⚠️ seccomp profiles are node-local files. They must exist on EVERY node
# that could run the pod. Use a DaemonSet or node config management
# to distribute profiles. Or use RuntimeDefault (built-in, works everywhere).
⚡ seccomp & AppArmor for CNPE
  • RuntimeDefault is your starting point: seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault — safe, built-in, no custom files needed. Works on all nodes.
  • Custom seccomp for high-security apps: Start with RuntimeDefault, monitor which syscalls are actually used (strace), then build a minimal allowlist.
  • AppArmor for defense-in-depth: Even with seccomp, AppArmor adds FILE-level restrictions. Use together.
  • CNPE exam: Know that seccomp is in the securityContext, AppArmor is via annotation. Both restrict what a running container can do at the kernel level.
📋 AppArmor Profile — Restrict anihpj-web File Access
# ── APPARMOR PROFILE: /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-web ──
# Loaded on the node: sudo apparmor_parser -r /etc/apparmor.d/anihpj-web

#include <tunables/global>

profile anihpj-web flags=(attach_disconnected,mediate_deleted) {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  #include <abstractions/nameservice>    # DNS resolution

  # ── ALLOW ──
  /app/**                          r,              # Read application code
  /app/static/**                   rw,             # Write static files (collectstatic)
  /tmp/**                          rw,             # Write temp files
  /usr/local/lib/python**          r,              # Read Python libraries
  /usr/local/bin/python*           rix,            # Execute Python

  # ── DENY (explicit blocks — defense in depth) ──
  deny /etc/passwd                 w,              # CANNOT modify password file
  deny /etc/shadow                 rw,             # CANNOT access shadow passwords
  deny /proc/sys/**                w,              # CANNOT modify kernel settings
  deny /boot/**                    rw,             # CANNOT access boot files
  deny /root/**                    rw,             # CANNOT access root home

  # ── NETWORK ──
  network inet  tcp,                              # Allow TCP (HTTP, DB)
  network inet  udp,                              # Allow UDP (DNS)

  # ── CAPABILITIES ──
  capability net_bind_service,                    # Bind to ports < 1024
}

# ── APPLY TO POD (via annotation) ──
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: anihpj-web
  annotations:
    container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/django: localhost/anihpj-web
    # Format: container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<container-name>
    # Value: localhost/<profile-name> or runtime/default or unconfined
spec:
  containers:
  - name: django
    image: anihpj-web:v2

# ⚠️ AppArmor profiles must exist on the NODE before the pod starts.
# Use a DaemonSet or node bootstrap script to distribute profiles.
🔬 How to BUILD a Custom seccomp Profile — The strace Workflow

You don't guess which syscalls your app needs — you MEASURE them:

1
RUN with RuntimeDefault: Deploy with seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault. Verify the app works. RuntimeDefault blocks ~300 dangerous syscalls out of 435+.
2
RECORD syscalls: In a TEST env: strace -c -p $(pgrep python) -o /tmp/syscalls.log. Exercise ALL app features under load for 15 minutes. The app must call every code path.
3
EXTRACT allowlist: cat /tmp/syscalls.log | awk '{print $NF}' | sort -u > allowed-syscalls.txt. Typical Django app: 30-50 syscalls needed. Typical Go app: 15-25. Typical Node: 40-60.
4
BUILD profile: Create JSON file with defaultAction: SCMP_ACT_ERRNO and extracted syscalls. Distribute to /var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/ on all nodes via DaemonSet.
5
TEST and ITERATE: Deploy with custom profile. If app crashes → check logs for blocked syscall names → add to allowlist → redeploy. Repeat until stable.

🔑 CNPE NOTE: For the exam, RuntimeDefault is sufficient — custom profiles are advanced. But understanding the workflow demonstrates platform engineering maturity. The exam may ask: "How would you create a custom seccomp profile?"

🔬 How Containers Escape — And How PSS + seccomp + AppArmor Stop Them

Every security control in this chapter exists because attackers have exploited its absence. Here are the 3 most common container escape techniques and how our controls block each one:

💥 Escape #1: Privileged Container Breakout

Attack: Attacker gets shell in a privileged container. Runs nsenter --mount=/proc/1/ns/mnt -- /bin/bash to enter the HOST namespace. Now has root on the node.

Blocked by:
• PSS Baseline: privileged: false blocks privileged containers entirely.
• allowPrivilegeEscalation: false prevents gaining additional privileges.
• seccomp: RuntimeDefault blocks nsenter syscall.

💥 Escape #2: HostPath Volume Mount

Attack: Attacker mounts /var/run/docker.sock via hostPath. Uses Docker socket to launch a privileged container on the host — effectively root on the node.

Blocked by:
• PSS Baseline: hostPath volumes are FORBIDDEN.
• PSS Restricted: Also forbids hostPath.
• AppArmor: Can deny access to Docker socket path.

💥 Escape #3: Kernel Module Loading

Attack: Attacker loads a malicious kernel module via insmod. The module runs in kernel space with full system access — bypassing ALL container isolation.

Blocked by:
• capabilities.drop: [ALL] removes CAP_SYS_MODULE.
• seccomp: RuntimeDefault blocks init_module and finit_module syscalls.
• AppArmor: Denies writes to /lib/modules/.

🔑 WHY LAYERS MATTER: Each control blocks DIFFERENT attack paths. Privileged container → PSS stops it. hostPath → PSS stops it. Kernel module → capabilities stop it. syscall attack → seccomp stops it. File access → AppArmor stops it. No single control is sufficient — defense-in-depth is the only reliable strategy.

28.6 anihpj Pod Security Design — Complete Defense Strategy

Let's design the complete pod security posture for anihpj — combining PSS enforcement, security contexts, admission webhooks, and runtime security into one coherent strategy.

NamespacePSS EnforcePSS AuditKey SecurityContext FieldsAdditional Controls
anihpj-prodRestrictedRestrictedrunAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFS, allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, capabilities.drop=[ALL], seccomp=RuntimeDefaultValidating webhook: block :latest. AppArmor: deny /proc/sys writes.
anihpj-stagingBaselineRestrictedSame as prodWarning label: "This namespace will be enforced Restricted next month."
anihpj-devBaselineRestrictedrunAsNonRoot, allowPrivilegeEscalation=falseDevelopers can test Restricted compliance before moving to staging.
monitoringPrivilegedBaselineMinimal (Prometheus node-exporter needs hostNetwork)RBAC: tightest possible. Only monitoring team can deploy here.
kube-systemPrivileged—System workloads (CNI, kube-proxy) need privileged accessNever deploy application pods here.
✅ anihpj Pod Security Strategy — Production-Ready
  • Production: Restricted PSS enforced. No root containers. Read-only root FS. All capabilities dropped. Seccomp required. This blocks 99% of container escape techniques.
  • Validating webhook: block :latest tags. Any pod using :latest is REJECTED immediately. No exceptions. This prevents version drift and rollback failures.
  • Mutating webhook: inject defaults. If a pod doesn't specify resource limits, the webhook adds limits.cpu: 500m, limits.memory: 512Mi. Never allow unbounded resources.
  • seccomp: RuntimeDefault minimum. Every pod must have seccomp enabled. Custom profiles for high-security components (payments, auth).
  • Regular audit: Monthly review of PSA audit logs. What pods would fail Restricted? Plan to fix them before enforcement tightens.
  • Images built non-root: All anihpj images use USER 1000 in Dockerfile. No container starts as root — even without securityContext.
🔬 Pod Security Checklist — Every PR Should Verify These 8 Items

Copy this checklist into your team's PR template. Every pod deployment should pass ALL 8 checks before merging:

☑️ Admission-Time Checks
  1. PSS level correct? Production namespaces MUST have enforce=restricted. Check: kubectl get ns -l pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce!=restricted
  2. No :latest tags? Every container image must have an explicit version tag or digest. Validated by admission webhook.
  3. Resource limits set? Every container must specify resources.limits and resources.requests. Injected by mutating webhook if missing.
  4. Required labels present? app, team, environment labels on every pod. Validated by admission webhook.
☑️ Runtime-Time Checks
  1. runAsNonRoot: true? Every container MUST run as non-root UID. Check: kubectl get pods -o json | jq '.items[].spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsNonRoot'
  2. readOnlyRootFilesystem: true? Root FS read-only with emptyDir mounts for writable paths. Verified in securityContext.
  3. seccomp enabled? RuntimeDefault minimum. Check: kubectl get pods -o json | jq '.items[].spec.securityContext.seccompProfile.type'
  4. capabilities dropped? drop: ["ALL"] with only necessary capabilities added back. Verified in securityContext.

🔑 AUTOMATE THIS: Don't manually check these 8 items — encode them in CI. A script that runs kubectl auth can-i + parses pod YAML for securityContext fields. Fail the PR if any check fails. Security that relies on human memory is not security.

🛠️ Drill 1: Enforce Restricted PSS on anihpj

Scenario: The anihpj production namespace currently has no PSS enforcement.

Task:

  1. Add warn=restricted and audit=restricted labels to the anihpj namespace
  2. Deploy a test pod running as root. Verify you get a WARNING but the pod is created
  3. Add enforce=restricted label to the namespace
  4. Deploy the same pod again. Verify it is REJECTED
  5. Fix the pod by adding a proper securityContext and verify it deploys successfully

Time: 15 min

💡 Hints
  • Warn label: kubectl label ns anihpj pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn=restricted.
  • Test pod (will trigger warning but deploy): kubectl run test-root --image=nginx -n anihpj — nginx runs as root by default.
  • Enforce label: kubectl label ns anihpj pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce=restricted --overwrite.
  • After enforce, same nginx pod will be REJECTED. Fix: add securityContext: {runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 101} (nginx user is 101).
🛠️ Drill 2: Security Context for anihpj-web

Scenario: The anihpj-web deployment currently runs as root with no security restrictions.

Task:

  1. Add pod-level securityContext: runAsNonRoot=true, runAsUser=1000, seccompProfile=RuntimeDefault
  2. Add container-level: readOnlyRootFilesystem=true, allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, capabilities.drop=[ALL]
  3. Mount an emptyDir at /tmp (Django needs writable temp)
  4. Verify the pod starts successfully and serves traffic

Time: 15 min

💡 Hints
  • Pod-level: spec.securityContext: {runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 1000, runAsGroup: 3000, fsGroup: 2000, seccompProfile: {type: RuntimeDefault}}.
  • Container-level: securityContext: {allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities: {drop: [ALL]}}.
  • CRITICAL: If the pod crashes with "permission denied" on /tmp, add: volumes: [{name: tmp, emptyDir: {}}] and mount at /tmp.
  • Django also writes to its project directory for .pyc files — you may need emptyDir at the app directory too, or set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 env var.
🛠️ Drill 3: Admission Webhook to Block :latest

Scenario: Create an admission webhook that rejects any pod using the :latest image tag.

Task:

  1. Deploy a simple webhook server (can use a pre-built image or write a small HTTP server)
  2. Configure a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration for pods on CREATE/UPDATE
  3. Test: deploy a pod with image: nginx:latest — should be REJECTED
  4. Test: deploy a pod with image: nginx:1.25 — should be ALLOWED

Time: 15 min

💡 Hints
  • Webhook server: Write a simple Python/Go HTTP server that parses the AdmissionReview JSON, checks spec.containers[].image for :latest suffix, and returns {"allowed": false, "message": ":latest tag is not allowed"}.
  • Critical: failurePolicy: Fail means ALL pod creates are blocked if your webhook is down. During testing, use failurePolicy: Ignore instead.
  • Test: kubectl run test-latest --image=nginx:latest -n anihpj → REJECTED. kubectl run test-pinned --image=nginx:1.25 -n anihpj → ALLOWED.
  • The webhook server needs a TLS certificate. For testing, use cert-manager to create a self-signed cert, or use openssl to generate one.

🎓 CNPE Exam Strategy — Domain 5 Pod Security Tasks

Domain 5 (Security & Policy, 15%) includes pod security. Expect 1-2 pod security tasks:

  • Apply PSA labels: Given a scenario ("production namespace needs Restricted enforcement"), set the correct labels. Know the exact label format: pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce, pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn, pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit.
  • Fix a pod rejected by PSA: Given an error message like "runAsNonRoot != true," add the correct securityContext fields. Know the 5 Restricted requirements: runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFS, allowPrivilegeEscalation=false, capabilities.drop=[ALL], seccompProfile=RuntimeDefault.
  • Write a securityContext: Given a pod spec, add pod-level AND container-level security contexts. Know which fields go where: pod-level (runAsUser, fsGroup, seccompProfile) vs container-level (readOnlyRootFS, allowPrivilegeEscalation, capabilities).
  • Configure an admission webhook: Know ValidatingWebhookConfiguration YAML structure. Key fields: clientConfig (service + caBundle), rules (apiGroups, resources, operations), failurePolicy (Fail vs Ignore).

🔑 EXAM MINDSET: Pod security is about LAYERS. PSA = namespace-level gate. SecurityContext = pod-level hardening. Webhooks = custom policies. Runtime = kernel-level protection. A secure pod has ALL layers configured. The exam tests the full stack — not just one piece.

Ch 29: Policy Engines & Governance

Policies as code — enforce rules automatically at admission time. OPA/Gatekeeper uses Rego to define constraint-based policies. Kyverno uses YAML for generate/mutate/validate patterns. CEL-based ValidatingAdmissionPolicy is built into Kubernetes — no webhook needed. Together they form a complete governance layer.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2h CNPE Domain 5: 15%
🎯 What You'll Learn
  • OPA/Gatekeeper — constraint-based policy engine using Rego language
  • Kyverno — YAML-based policy engine with generate, mutate, and validate capabilities
  • Common policies every platform should enforce (block :latest, require labels, enforce limits)
  • Policy-as-code in CI/CD pipelines — testing policies before deployment
  • ValidatingAdmissionPolicy — native CEL-based validation built into Kubernetes 1.26+
  • How to combine all policy engines into a complete anihpj governance stack
📋 CNPE Exam Relevance — Domain 5 (15%)

Domain 5 tests your ability to use policy engines and admission controllers for governance. You will be asked to create Kyverno policies, write OPA constraints, and configure CEL-based validation. Policy engines are a key differentiator for CNPE vs CKA — CKA focuses on RBAC, CNPE adds policy-as-code.

29.1 OPA/Gatekeeper — Constraint-Based Policy Engine

OPA (Open Policy Agent) is a general-purpose policy engine. Gatekeeper integrates OPA with Kubernetes as an admission controller. You define ConstraintTemplates (written in Rego) that describe WHAT to check, and Constraints that specify the PARAMETERS for those checks.

🔍 Why Policy Engines? — The Problem They Solve

Kubernetes RBAC controls WHO can do WHAT. But RBAC doesn't control WHAT they create. A developer with Deployment creation rights can deploy a container running as root, with no resource limits, using an untagged :latest image from Docker Hub. RBAC is authorization. Policy engines are VALIDATION.

❌ Without Policy Engines
  • • Dev creates pod with image: nginx:latest → allowed
  • • Dev creates pod as runAsUser: 0 (root) → allowed
  • • Dev creates pod with no CPU/memory limits → allowed
  • • Dev creates pod with privileged: true → allowed
  • Result: Cluster is a ticking time bomb. Every pod is a potential security incident.
✅ With Policy Engines
  • • Dev creates pod with image: nginx:latest → BLOCKED
  • • Dev creates pod as root → BLOCKED
  • • Dev creates pod without limits → Kyverno MUTATES to add defaults
  • • Dev creates pod with privileged → BLOCKED
  • Result: Every deployment is safe by default. Policy is code — versioned, tested, enforced automatically.

🔑 THE SHIFT: From "trust developers to do the right thing" → "the platform guarantees the right thing happens." This is the essence of platform engineering. You don't ask developers to be security experts. You build security into the platform so it's automatic, invisible, and non-negotiable.

🧠 OPA/Gatekeeper Architecture — ConstraintTemplate + Constraint
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    OPA/GATEKEEPER POLICY MODEL                                 │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                         │
│  │     ConstraintTemplate           │  ← Written ONCE by platform team        │
│  │     (Rego code)                  │     "WHAT to check"                     │
│  │                                  │     Rego language logic                 │
│  │  Example: "Check if any          │                                         │
│  │  container image has the         │                                         │
│  │  :latest tag. If yes, deny."     │                                         │
│  └───────────────┬─────────────────┘                                         │
│                  │                                                            │
│                  │  Instantiated by:                                          │
│                  ▼                                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                         │
│  │     Constraint                   │  ← Created per-use by anyone            │
│  │     (YAML parameters)            │     "HOW to check"                      │
│  │                                  │     Specific parameters                 │
│  │  Example: "Apply the BlockLatest │                                         │
│  │  template to ALL pods in         │                                         │
│  │  namespace anihpj-prod."         │                                         │
│  └───────────────┬─────────────────┘                                         │
│                  │                                                            │
│                  ▼                                                            │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐                                         │
│  │  Gatekeeper Admission Webhook    │  ← Enforces at admission time          │
│  │  • Intercepts CREATE/UPDATE      │                                         │
│  │  • Runs Rego on the resource     │                                         │
│  │  • Returns allow/deny             │                                         │
│  └─────────────────────────────────┘                                         │
│                                                                               │
│  🔑 KEY CONCEPT: ConstraintTemplate = Rego logic (WHAT). Constraint = params  │
│     (HOW). Platform team writes templates. App teams create constraints.      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔬 Admission Webhook Internals — How the API Server Actually Calls Your Policy Engine

Understanding the HTTP-level mechanics of admission webhooks is critical. When a policy blocks a deployment and developers are screaming "why can't I deploy?!", you need to know exactly what happened under the hood:

🌐 Admission Webhook — The Full HTTP Request/Response Lifecycle
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              ADMISSION WEBHOOK — STEP-BY-STEP HTTP FLOW                            │
│                                                                                   │
│  ┌──────────┐      ┌──────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐                    │
