│        │                    │             │────────────────────────────────────────▶│
│        │                    │             │                                         │
│        │                    │             │ ⑧ AdmissionResponse JSON                 │
│        │                    │             │    { "allowed": true/false,              │
│        │                    │             │      "status": { "message": "..." } }   │
│        │                    │             │◀────────────────────────────────────────│
│        │                    │             │                                         │
│        │                    │ ⑨ If all pass →                                     │
│        │                    │    Store in etcd                                    │
│        │                    │    Return 201 Created                                │
│        │◀───────────────────│                                                      │
│        │                    │                                                      │
│  🔑 CRITICAL DETAILS:                                                              │
│  • AdmissionReview wraps the object in JSON: {"kind":"AdmissionReview",           │
│    "request":{"uid":"...","object":{...pod spec...},"oldObject":null,...}}         │
│  • Policy engine receives input.review.object = the pod spec                      │
│  • Mutating webhooks return JSON Patches (RFC 6902) to modify the object          │
│  • Validating webhooks return allowed: true/false with an optional message        │
│  • If ANY webhook returns allowed: false → ENTIRE request is rejected             │
│  • Timeout: default 10s. If webhook doesn't respond in time → failurePolicy kicks in│
│  • failurePolicy: Fail = reject request. Ignore = allow request (DANGEROUS!)      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
⚠️ The Webhook Availability Problem — Why Policy Engines Can Break Your Cluster

If your policy engine pods are DOWN (crash, OOM, network partition) and failurePolicy: Fail is set, ALL resource creation/update requests will be REJECTED. This includes critical system operations — new nodes joining, system pods restarting, even the policy engine itself trying to restart. This is called the "webhook deadlock": your cluster is down because the policy engine is down, but the policy engine can't restart because the cluster rejects pod creation.

🔑 THE FIX: Always run policy engines with high availability (2+ replicas, pod anti-affinity). Set failurePolicy: Ignore on webhook configurations during maintenance windows. Monitor webhook latency and availability with Prometheus alerts. Kyverno's Helm chart defaults to 3 replicas for this exact reason.

📋 OPA/Gatekeeper — Block :latest Images
# ── STEP 1: ConstraintTemplate (Rego logic — written once) ──
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8sblocklatesttag
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sBlockLatestTag       # This becomes the Constraint kind
  targets:
  - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
    rego: |
      package k8sblocklatesttag

      # Check every container in every pod
      violation[{"msg": msg}] {
        # Find all containers across all pods
        container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
        # Check if image ends with :latest
        endswith(container.image, ":latest")
        # Build error message
        msg := sprintf("container <%v> uses :latest tag — pinned version required", [container.name])
      }

# ── STEP 2: Constraint (parameters — applied per namespace) ──
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sBlockLatestTag           # Matches ConstraintTemplate name
metadata:
  name: block-latest-in-production
spec:
  match:
    kinds:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      kinds: ["Pod"]
    namespaces: ["anihpj-prod"]      # Only enforce in production

# ── VERIFY ──
# kubectl get constrainttemplates
# kubectl get k8sblocklatesttag
# kubectl describe k8sblocklatesttag block-latest-in-production
⚡ OPA/Gatekeeper Quick Reference
  • ConstraintTemplate = the Rego logic (written by platform team). Defines the policy CHECK.
  • Constraint = the parameters (created per-namespace/team). Defines WHERE and HOW STRICT.
  • Rego = OPA's policy language. Declarative: you describe WHAT violates policy, not HOW to check.
  • violation[{...}] = The Rego rule that defines what constitutes a policy violation. Empty = compliant.
  • input.review.object = The Kubernetes resource being validated (pod, deployment, etc.).
🔬 Rego Patterns — The 3 Most Common Policy Idioms

Rego is a declarative logic language. You describe WHAT a violation looks like, not HOW to find it. Here are the 3 patterns you'll use in 90% of OPA policies:

PatternRego CodeWhat It DoesWhen to Use
Field Checkviolation[{"msg": msg}] {
input.review.object.spec.containers[_].securityContext.runAsNonRoot != true
msg := "must run as non-root"
}		Check if a specific field has the right value. Most common pattern.Require labels, enforce limits, block :latest, check securityContext.
Deny Listviolation[{"msg": msg}] {
forbidden := {"latest", "stable", "dev"}
image := input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image
tag := split(image, ":")[1]
forbidden[tag]
msg := sprintf("tag %v is forbidden", [tag])
}		Block specific values from an allowed set. Check if value IS in forbidden list.Block specific image registries, block dangerous capabilities, block specific hostPaths.
Must Existviolation[{"msg": msg}] {
container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]
not container.resources.limits.cpu
msg := sprintf("container %v has no CPU limit", [container.name])
}		Verify a field EXISTS. Use not to check absence. A violation occurs when the field is MISSING.Require resource limits, require probes, require specific annotations.

🔑 REGO MENTAL MODEL: Think of Rego as a QUERY language, not a programming language. You write rules that FIND violations. If the query returns results → policy is violated. If the query returns empty → policy is satisfied. violation[{...}] is the query that finds violations. No results = compliant.

🔬 Rego Step-by-Step — How OPA Actually Evaluates a Policy

Let's trace through a real Rego policy evaluation to understand EXACTLY how OPA thinks. We'll use a policy that blocks containers without both CPU and memory limits:

📋 Rego Policy — Require CPU + Memory Limits (Annotated)
# ── THE POLICY ──
package k8srequirelimits

# violation is a PARTIAL RULE — it generates MULTIPLE results
# Each iteration of the rule body that succeeds = one violation
violation[{"msg": msg}] {
    # STEP 1: Iterate over ALL containers in the pod
    # containers[_] means "for each container in the array"
    # _ is an anonymous variable — "I don't care about the index"
    container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]

    # STEP 2: Check if CPU limit is MISSING
    # not = negation. If the field doesn't exist OR is undefined, this is true
    # container.resources.limits.cpu accesses nested fields
    not container.resources.limits.cpu

    # STEP 3: Check if Memory limit is MISSING
    # Combined with STEP 2 via logical AND (all statements must be true)
    not container.resources.limits.memory

    # STEP 4: Build the error message
    # sprintf formats a string with variables
    msg := sprintf("container <%v> is missing CPU and memory limits", [container.name])
}

# ── HOW OPA EVALUATES THIS ──
# Given this input pod:
# containers:
#   - name: anihpj-web
#     resources:
#       limits:
#         cpu: "500m"
#         (memory is MISSING)
#   - name: redis
#     (resources is MISSING entirely)

# OPA evaluation trace:
# ITERATION 1: container = anihpj-web
#   not container.resources.limits.cpu → cpu="500m" EXISTS → this is FALSE
#   → Rule body FAILS (logical AND requires all statements true)
#   → No violation generated for anihpj-web

# ITERATION 2: container = redis
#   not container.resources.limits.cpu → resources is MISSING → this is TRUE
#   (Rego treats missing fields as undefined, and not undefined = true)
#   not container.resources.limits.memory → resources is MISSING → TRUE
#   → ALL statements true → Rule body SUCCEEDS
#   → Generates: violation[{"msg": "container  is missing CPU and memory limits"}]

# RESULT: 1 violation. Pod is REJECTED.

# ── KEY REGO CONCEPTS DEMONSTRATED ──
# 1. [_] = iteration over arrays — processes ALL containers
# 2. not = negation — true when something is absent/undefined
# 3. := = assignment — binds a variable locally
# 4. Logical AND — all statements in body must be true
# 5. Partial rules — generate MULTIPLE results (one per matching container)
# 6. Undefined handling — accessing missing fields returns undefined, not error

🧠 WHY THIS MATTERS: Rego's "undefined is not an error" behavior is both powerful and dangerous. not container.resources.limits.cpu catches BOTH "cpu limit is not set" AND "resources block doesn't exist" AND "container spec is malformed" — all in one statement. But it also means a TYPO like container.resources.limitts.cpu (double 't') silently evaluates to undefined and not(undefined)=true — your policy always passes but for the WRONG reason. Always use precise field names and test your policies with deliberate error cases.

29.2 Kyverno — YAML-Based Policy Engine

Kyverno (Greek for "govern") is a policy engine designed specifically for Kubernetes. Unlike OPA's Rego, Kyverno policies are written in YAML — the same language as Kubernetes manifests. No new language to learn.

FeatureOPA/GatekeeperKyverno
Policy languageRego (custom DSL)YAML (Kubernetes-native)
Learning curve🔴 Steep. Rego is a logic programming language.🟢 Gentle. If you know YAML, you know Kyverno.
Policy typesValidate only (deny/allow)✅ Validate + Mutate + Generate
Mutation❌ Separate mutating webhook needed✅ Built-in. Can add labels, defaults, sidecars.
Generation❌ Not supported✅ Auto-create resources (ConfigMaps, Secrets, NetworkPolicies)
EcosystemLarger. Used beyond Kubernetes (Terraform, Envoy, API gateways)Kubernetes-only. Tighter K8s integration.
CNPE exam🟡 Know the concept and Rego structure✅ HIGH — most commonly tested policy engine
📋 Kyverno Policies — Validate, Mutate, Generate
# ── VALIDATE: Require team label on all pods ──
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-team-label
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce   # Enforce = REJECT. Audit = LOG only.
  rules:
  - name: check-team-label
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Pod"]
    validate:
      message: "Every pod must have a 'team' label"
      pattern:
        metadata:
          labels:
            team: "?*"                    # Must exist and can be any value

# ── MUTATE: Add default resource limits ──
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: add-default-resources
spec:
  rules:
  - name: add-resource-limits
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Pod"]
    mutate:
      patchStrategicMerge:
        spec:
          containers:
          - (name): "*"                # All containers
            resources:
              requests:
                cpu: "100m"
                memory: "128Mi"
              limits:
                cpu: "500m"
                memory: "512Mi"

# ── GENERATE: Auto-create a NetworkPolicy per namespace ──
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: auto-generate-netpol
spec:
  rules:
  - name: generate-default-deny
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Namespace"]
    generate:
      kind: NetworkPolicy
      name: default-deny-ingress
      data:
        spec:
          podSelector: {}
          policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
🎓 CNPE Exam: Kyverno = Most Likely Policy Engine

Kyverno is the most commonly tested policy engine on the CNPE exam because: (1) It's YAML-based — no new language to learn in an exam setting. (2) It supports validate, mutate, AND generate — the exam can test all three. (3) Its validationFailureAction: Audit mode is perfect for "test the policy first" scenarios. Expect at least 1 Kyverno task on the exam.

🔬 Kyverno Background Scan — Policing EXISTING Resources, Not Just New Ones

Admission controllers only check NEW or UPDATED resources. What about hundreds of pods ALREADY running that violate policy? Kyverno's background scan periodically checks ALL existing resources against policies and generates reports:

📋 Kyverno Background Scan & Policy Reports
# ── POLICY REPORT (auto-generated by Kyverno) ──
# Shows which EXISTING resources violate which policies
kubectl get policyreport -n anihpj -o wide
# NAME                  KIND   PASS   FAIL   WARN   ERROR
# cpol-require-labels   Pod    12     3      0      0
# → 3 pods in namespace anihpj are violating "require-team-label" policy
# → These pods were created BEFORE the policy existed. They won't be blocked.
# → But they're REPORTED so you can fix them.

# ── CLUSTER POLICY REPORT (cluster-wide) ──
kubectl get clusterpolicyreport
# Shows violations across ALL namespaces for cluster-wide policies

# ── DETAIL VIEW ──
kubectl describe policyreport cpol-require-labels -n anihpj
# Results:
#   - policy: require-team-label
#     result: fail
#     resources:
#     - name: old-pod-1
#       message: "Every pod must have a 'team' label"
#     - name: old-pod-2
#       message: "Every pod must have a 'team' label"

# 🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Background scan tells you the "blast radius" of a new
# policy BEFORE you switch from Audit to Enforce. If a policy would
# block 50 production pods, you fix them first — then enforce.

29.3 Common Policies — The Policies Every Platform Should Enforce

There are 5 policies that EVERY production Kubernetes cluster should enforce. These are not optional — they're the minimum viable governance for a platform:

#PolicyWhat It BlocksKyvernoOPA/GatekeeperPriority
1Block :latest tagPods using image:latest (version drift, rollback impossible)✅ Validate✅ ConstraintTemplate🔴 P0 — Immediate
2Require labelsPods without team, app, environment labels (no ownership, no cost tracking)✅ Validate✅ ConstraintTemplate🔴 P0 — Immediate
3Enforce resource limitsPods without CPU/memory limits (noisy neighbor, node OOM)✅ Validate or Mutate (add defaults)✅ ConstraintTemplate🔴 P0 — Immediate
4Block privileged containersPods with privileged: true (container-to-node escape)✅ Validate✅ ConstraintTemplate🟡 P1 — Within month
5Require non-root userPods running as UID 0 (container-to-node escape via root)✅ Validate✅ ConstraintTemplate🟡 P1 — Within month
⚠️ Policy Enforcement Order — Which Takes Priority?

When multiple admission controllers and policies are configured, they execute in a specific order. Understanding this prevents "my policy should have blocked that!" moments:

1
PSA (Built-in): Pod Security Admission runs FIRST. If the pod violates Restricted PSS, it's rejected before any policy engine sees it.
2
Mutating Webhooks / Kyverno Mutate: Run SECOND. Add defaults, inject sidecars, set labels. The resource is modified before validation.
3
Validating Webhooks / Kyverno Validate / OPA: Run THIRD. Check the MUTATED resource against policies. If any policy rejects, the request is denied.

🔑 WHY THIS MATTERS: Kyverno's Mutate rules run BEFORE its Validate rules. So a Mutation that adds team: anihpj label will satisfy a Validation that requires the team label. The developer doesn't need to add it — Kyverno adds it, then Kyverno validates it exists. This is the "platform defaults" pattern.

🌳 Should This Policy Be Kyverno or OPA/Gatekeeper?
🤔 Does the policy need to MUTATE or GENERATE resources?
✅ YES — Need mutation/generation
❌ NO — Validate only
📋 Use Kyverno — Only Kyverno supports Mutate (add defaults, inject sidecars) and Generate (auto-create resources). OPA/Gatekeeper cannot do either.
🤔 Does the validation query other cluster resources?
🧠 Use OPA/Gatekeeper — Rego's k8s_introspection can query pods, services, namespaces. "Does this Service have a matching NetworkPolicy?"
🤔 Is it a simple field check (label, image tag, resource limit)?
⚡ Use VAP (CEL) — Fastest. Built-in. No webhook. If VAP can express it, use VAP. Fall back to Kyverno if you need YAML simplicity.

🎯 THE HEURISTIC: Need mutation? → Kyverno. Cross-resource validation? → OPA. Simple field check? → VAP (CEL). YAML-based validate-only? → Kyverno or VAP. Rego required? → OPA.

🔬 The Policy Engine Ecosystem — Where Each Tool Fits in Your Platform

Policy engines aren't competitors — they're complementary tools in a layered governance strategy. Think of them like security layers: you don't pick ONE — you use the right tool for each layer:

🏗️
PSA (Built-in)

Pod Security Admission. Fastest path. privileged/baseline/restricted profiles. No installation. Blocks hostPath, hostNetwork, privilege escalation at the API server level.

⚡
VAP (CEL)

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy. Built-in K8s 1.26+. CEL expressions. No webhook latency. Type-safe compile checks. Best for simple field validations (labels, tags, limits).

📋
Kyverno

YAML-based. Validate + Mutate + Generate. Kubernetes-native. Image verification. Background scanning. Cleanup policies. Best for platform teams that want simplicity.

🧠
OPA/Gatekeeper

Rego language. Cross-resource lookups. Multi-domain (K8s + Terraform + Envoy). Large community library. Best for complex logic and multi-cluster governance.

🔬
Conftest

OPA-based testing CLI. Test policies against structured data (YAML, JSON, Terraform plans, Dockerfiles). Runs in CI. Catches policy violations BEFORE deployment.

📊
Policy Reporter

Aggregates PolicyReports from Kyverno + OPA. Dashboards. Metrics. Slack/Teams notifications. Shows policy compliance across ALL clusters in one view.

🧩 THE COMPLETE PICTURE: PSA blocks the worst offenses (kernel-level). VAP handles simple checks (fast, built-in). Kyverno adds mutation + generation (platform defaults). OPA handles complex cross-resource logic ("does this Service have a NetworkPolicy?"). Conftest tests everything in CI. Policy Reporter shows compliance status. Together, they form a complete governance fabric — not a single tool, but a layered defense.

29.4 Policy-as-Code in CI/CD — Testing Policies Before Deployment

Policy engines are powerful, but testing policies before they hit the cluster is critical. A misconfigured policy can block ALL deployments. The solution: test policies in CI/CD pipelines using the same tools the engines themselves provide.

🔄 Policy-as-Code CI/CD Pipeline
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              POLICY-AS-CODE CI/CD PIPELINE                                │
│                                                                           │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌────────────┐  │
│  │ DEVELOPER │───▶│  PR OPENED    │───▶│  CI CHECKS    │───▶│  MERGE TO  │  │
│  │ writes     │    │  Policy YAML  │    │  Run Tests    │    │  policy/   │  │
│  │ policy.yaml│   │  in policy/    │    │               │    │  main      │  │
│  └──────────┘    └──────────────┘    └──────┬────────┘    └─────┬──────┘  │
│                                             │                     │        │
│                    ┌────────────────────────┘                     │        │
│                    ▼                                               ▼        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                     CI TEST SUITE (policy-test.yaml)                 │  │
│  │                                                                      │  │
│  │  ┌─────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌────────────────┐  │  │
│  │  │ 1. kyverno test     │  │ 2. OPA conftest   │  │ 3. gator verify │  │  │
│  │  │ kyverno test        │  │ conftest test     │  │ gator verify    │  │  │
│  │  │ policy.yaml         │  │ policy/           │  │ constraint.yaml │  │  │
│  │  │ -f test-resources/  │  │                   │  │ -f fixtures/    │  │  │
│  │  │ ✅ PASS / ❌ FAIL    │  │ ✅ PASS / ❌ FAIL  │  │ ✅ PASS / ❌ FAIL│  │  │
│  │  └─────────────────────┘  └──────────────────┘  └────────────────┘  │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                    │                                       │
│                                    ▼                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                    GITOPS DEPLOYMENT (ArgoCD / Flux)                  │  │
│  │  • Policies synced to cluster                                        │  │
│  │  • Kyverno/OPA picks up new CRDs automatically                       │  │
│  │  • Audit mode first → Enforce mode after validation                  │  │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 Policy Testing — Kyverno, OPA, and Gatekeeper
# ── KYVERNO: Test policy against sample resources ──
# kyverno test <policy-dir>
kyverno test ./policies/
# Directory structure:
# policies/
# ├── require-team-label.yaml          (the ClusterPolicy)
# └── tests/
#     ├── good-pod.yaml                (should PASS)
#     ├── bad-pod.yaml                 (should FAIL)
#     └── kyverno-test.yaml            (test expectations)

# ── OPA: Test Rego policies with conftest ──
# conftest test <resource.yaml> -p <policy-dir>
conftest test deployment.yaml -p policies/rego/
# Output:
# FAIL - deployment.yaml - main container uses :latest tag
# 1 test, 0 passed, 1 warning, 1 failure

# ── GATEKEEPER: gator verify for ConstraintTemplates ──
# gator verify constraint.yaml -f fixtures/
gator verify ./block-latest-constraint.yaml -f ./test-fixtures/
# Output:
# ok    block-latest-in-production    must-block-latest-tag     0.042s
# ok    block-latest-in-production    must-allow-pinned-tag     0.038s

# ── GITHUB ACTIONS EXAMPLE: Policy CI Pipeline ──
name: Policy Validation
on: [pull_request]
jobs:
  policy-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Kyverno Test
        run: |
          kyverno test ./kyverno-policies/
      - name: OPA Conftest
        run: |
          conftest test ./kyverno-policies/tests/*.yaml -p ./rego-policies/
      - name: Gatekeeper gator verify
        run: |
          gator verify ./gatekeeper-constraints/ -f ./test-fixtures/
🔬 The Policy Adoption Journey — From Zero to Full Governance

You don't go from zero policies to blocking everything overnight. Policy adoption is a JOURNEY — each stage builds on the previous one. Here's the path every platform team follows:

🏴
Stage 0: Nothing
No policies. Developers deploy anything. "We trust our team." Every pod is a potential incident.
📋
Stage 1: Audit
Policies deployed in Audit mode. Violations logged but NOT blocked. "What would we break?" Learn the blast radius.
⚡
Stage 2: Enforce P0
Block :latest, require labels, enforce limits. The 3 non-negotiables. "The minimum viable security."
🔒
Stage 3: Full Governance
PSA + VAP + Kyverno + OPA. All policies in CI. Policy Reports dashboards. "Every deployment is verified."

🔑 KEY INSIGHT: Stage 1 (Audit) is the most important stage people skip. Deploying a policy in Audit mode for 2 weeks tells you: (a) how many resources violate this policy, (b) whether the policy has false positives, (c) whether the error messages make sense. Never skip Audit. Never go straight to Enforce. The platform team that skips Audit is the platform team that accidentally blocks all production deployments on a Friday afternoon.

🎯 Policy Testing Strategy — The Audit-Enforce Ladder
1
Write & Test Locally: Use kyverno test / conftest test / gator verify on your machine.
2
CI Validation: Tests run automatically on every PR. Block merge if tests fail.
3
Deploy as Audit: Deploy policy with validationFailureAction: Audit (Kyverno) or enforcementAction: dryrun (Gatekeeper).
4
Monitor Violations: Watch audit logs for 1-2 weeks. Identify false positives. Tune policy.
5
Promote to Enforce: Switch to Enforce mode. Policy now blocks violations at admission.

29.5 ValidatingAdmissionPolicy — Built-In CEL Validation (No Webhook)

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP), introduced in Kubernetes 1.26 (GA in 1.30), is the native validation mechanism using Common Expression Language (CEL). Unlike OPA and Kyverno, VAP runs inside the API server — no external webhooks, no extra pods, no additional latency.

FeatureValidatingAdmissionPolicy (VAP)Kyverno / OPA
Runs inAPI server (built-in)External webhook pods
LanguageCEL (Common Expression Language)YAML (Kyverno) / Rego (OPA)
Latency✅ Minimal (no network hop)⚠️ Webhook overhead (~10-50ms)
Installation✅ Built-in. Enable ValidatingAdmissionPolicy feature gate (K8s <1.30)❌ Must install Kyverno/OPA separately
Mutate/Generate❌ Validate only✅ Kyverno supports all three
Type checking✅ Compile-time type checking (catches errors before apply)❌ Runtime errors only
Parameterization✅ Via ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding✅ Constraint parameters (OPA) / Policy rules (Kyverno)
When to useSimple validations (field checks, min/max, required labels)Complex logic (cross-resource, external data lookups)
📋 ValidatingAdmissionPolicy — CEL-Based Validation
# ── ValidatingAdmissionPolicy: Block :latest images ──
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: block-latest-tag
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail                 # Fail = reject if policy errors
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
    - apiGroups: [""]
      apiVersions: ["v1"]
      operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
      resources: ["pods"]
  validations:
  - expression: >
      object.spec.containers.all(c,
        !c.image.endsWith(':latest')
      )
    message: "Container images must not use :latest tag"
    reason: Invalid

# ── ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding: Bind to namespace ──
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: block-latest-binding
spec:
  policyName: block-latest-tag
  matchResources:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        environment: production     # Only in production namespaces

# ── VAP with parameters (like Gatekeeper Constraint params) ──
# First, define what params look like:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-resource-limits
spec:
  paramKind:
    apiVersion: v1
    kind: ConfigMap                    # Params come from a ConfigMap
  validations:
  - expression: >
      object.spec.containers.all(c,
        has(c.resources) &&
        has(c.resources.limits) &&
        has(c.resources.limits.cpu) &&
        has(c.resources.limits.memory)
      )
    message: "All containers must have CPU and memory limits"
⚡ CEL Quick Reference for VAP
  • object.spec = the submitted resource (pod, deployment, etc.). Access ANY field.
  • oldObject.spec = the previous version (available on UPDATE operations).
  • .all(c, condition) = check if ALL containers satisfy the condition. Use .exists(c, condition) for "at least one".
  • has(field) = check if an optional field exists. Prevents null-pointer errors.
  • params = the parameter resource bound via ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding.
  • Type checking: VAP validates CEL expressions against the CRD schema at apply time — catches field name typos BEFORE deployment.
⚠️ VAP Limitation — Validate ONLY

ValidatingAdmissionPolicy can ONLY validate (allow/deny). It cannot mutate resources. If you need to add default labels, inject sidecars, or modify resources at admission time, you still need Kyverno or a custom mutating webhook. VAP replaces simple Kyverno/OPA validation use cases — not mutation or generation.

🔬 Real-World Policy Engine Adoption — Who Uses What and Why

Policy engines aren't theoretical. Here's how major organizations use them in production. These patterns inform YOUR platform decisions:

🏦
Capital One
OPA/Gatekeeper — 200+ Constraints

Uses OPA across Kubernetes AND Terraform AND Envoy. One policy language (Rego) governs all infrastructure — not just K8s. The "OPA everywhere" pattern.

🛒
Shopify
Kyverno — 500+ ClusterPolicies

Chose Kyverno because YAML-based policies meant platform team and app teams spoke the same language. Mutation rules automatically add labels, annotations, and resource defaults.

🎬
Netflix
Custom Admission + OPA

Uses OPA for cross-resource validation ("does every Service have a corresponding NetworkPolicy?"). Custom controllers for Spinnaker integration. Policy is a first-class product.

☁️
Google (GKE)
PSA + VAP + Gatekeeper

GKE Autopilot uses PSA (Restricted) by default. Recommends VAP for simple validations (no webhook latency matters at Google scale). Gatekeeper for complex multi-tenant policies.

🔑 PATTERN: Organizations don't pick ONE policy engine — they pick the RIGHT engine for each layer. PSA for baseline security. VAP for simple field checks (fastest path). Kyverno for mutation and generation (platform defaults). OPA for cross-resource and multi-domain governance. Your platform should follow the same layered approach.

29.6 Combining All Policy Engines — The Complete Governance Stack

No single policy engine does everything. The CNPE-grade platform combines built-in PSA + VAP + Kyverno + OPA for complete governance:

29.7 anihpj Policy Stack — Governance for the Platform

Here's how the anihpj Django job board platform implements its governance stack. This is a real-world example of combining all the policy engines from this chapter:

🏢 anihpj Production Governance Stack
🔒
PSA: Restricted (Baseline)
All anihpj namespaces labelled pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted. Blocks privileged containers, hostPath, hostNetwork at the built-in level.
📋
VAP: Block :latest + Require Labels
Two CEL-based ValidatingAdmissionPolicies. Fast, no webhook cost. All pods in anihpj-prod MUST have pinned versions and team/app labels.
🔄
Kyverno: Mutate Defaults
Auto-adds team: anihpj label, app: jobboard label, default resource limits (100m CPU/128Mi RAM requests, 500m/512Mi limits) if not specified.
📜
Kyverno: Generate NetworkPolicy
Every new anihpj namespace auto-gets a default-deny-ingress NetworkPolicy. Dev teams opt-in to allowed sources.
🧠
OPA: Complex Cross-Resource Check
OPA validates that every Service in anihpj-prod has a corresponding NetworkPolicy that explicitly allows traffic. Prevents "orphan services" with no access control.
🔬
CI/CD: Policy Testing
All policies live in anihpj-infra/policies/. GitHub Actions runs kyverno test + conftest test + gator verify on every PR. Policies are GitOps-deployed via ArgoCD.
🛠️ Drill 1: Kyverno Require Team Label

Scenario: All pods in anihpj-prod must have the team label.

Task: Create a Kyverno ClusterPolicy that validates the team label exists on all Pods in namespaces labeled environment: production. Test with a valid pod and an invalid pod.

Time: 15 min

🛠️ Drill 2: OPA/Gatekeeper Block :latest

Scenario: No pod in any namespace should use :latest image tag.

Task: Write a ConstraintTemplate (Rego) and a Constraint that blocks pods with :latest tag across the entire cluster. Test with gator verify.

Time: 15 min

🛠️ Drill 3: Kyverno Mutate Resource Limits

Scenario: Pods without resource limits should automatically get defaults: CPU 100m/500m, Memory 128Mi/512Mi.

Task: Create a Kyverno ClusterPolicy with a Mutate rule that adds default resource requests/limits to containers that don't specify them. Test that a pod without limits gets defaults injected.

Time: 15 min

🛠️ Drill 4: CEL-Based Validation — Block Non-Root Containers

Scenario: All containers in anihpj-prod must run as non-root. No container should use runAsUser: 0.

Task: Create a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy that blocks any Pod where securityContext.runAsNonRoot != true. Bind it to namespaces with label environment: production. Test your policy by submitting a pod that runs as root and verifying it's rejected.

Time: 15 min

💡 Hint: Use object.spec.containers.all(c, has(c.securityContext) && c.securityContext.runAsNonRoot == true) in your CEL expression. Remember you need BOTH a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy AND a ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding.

🛠️ Drill 5: Policy Testing Pipeline — kyverno test + conftest

Scenario: Your platform team maintains 5 Kyverno policies and 2 OPA policies in anihpj-infra/policies/. Every PR must pass automated policy tests.

Task: Set up a policy test directory structure with kyverno-test.yaml expectations. Write good-pod.yaml and bad-pod.yaml test fixtures. Run kyverno test and conftest test locally. Create a GitHub Actions workflow that runs both. Verify that a bad policy change fails CI.

Time: 20 min

💡 Hint: Directory structure: policies/require-team-label/ → policy.yaml + tests/good.yaml + tests/bad.yaml + kyverno-test.yaml with expected pass/fail results.

🎓 CNPE Exam Strategy — Domain 5 Policy Engines

Domain 5 (Security & Policy, 15%) includes policy engines. Expect 1-2 policy engine tasks:

  • Write a Kyverno policy: Most likely task. Know Validate (deny), Mutate (add defaults), and Generate (auto-create). YAML syntax is straightforward — match + action.
  • Write an OPA ConstraintTemplate: Know the Rego violation[{...}] pattern. Understand ConstraintTemplate (Rego logic) vs Constraint (parameters + scope).
  • Choose the right engine: Given a scenario, pick Kyverno (mutation/generation), OPA (cross-resource), or VAP (simple field check). Justify your choice.
  • Policy testing: Know kyverno test and conftest test. The exam may ask you to validate a policy against test resources.

🔑 EXAM MINDSET: CNPE is a PLATFORM exam — you're building governance for ALL developers. Your policies should balance security (block dangerous things) with developer experience (add helpful defaults, give clear error messages). A policy that blocks everything is easy. A policy that enables safe velocity is engineering.

🧠 Knowledge Check — Ch 29: Policy Engines & Governance

Q1. What determines WHAT a Gatekeeper policy checks — the ConstraintTemplate or the Constraint?

A: The ConstraintTemplate contains the Rego logic (WHAT to check). The Constraint specifies WHERE and with WHAT PARAMETERS. Platform team writes the template once. App teams create constraints from it.

Q2. What are the three policy actions Kyverno supports that OPA/Gatekeeper does NOT?

A: Mutate (add defaults, inject sidecars), Generate (auto-create resources like NetworkPolicies on namespace creation), and Cleanup (TTL-based resource cleanup). OPA/Gatekeeper only validates (allow/deny).

Q3. Why does ValidatingAdmissionPolicy have lower latency than Kyverno or OPA?

A: VAP runs inside the API server (built-in). There's no webhook call, no network hop, no external pod to contact. CEL expressions are compiled and cached. Kyverno and OPA require an HTTP call to an external webhook pod.

Q4. In the admission chain, when do Mutating webhooks (Kyverno Mutate) run relative to Validating webhooks?

A: Mutating webhooks run BEFORE validating webhooks. This means a Kyverno Mutate policy that adds a team label will satisfy a Kyverno Validate policy that requires the team label — the mutation happens first, then validation checks the mutated resource.

Q5. What's the CNPE-recommended strategy for deploying a new policy to production?

A: The Audit-Enforce Ladder: (1) Write & test locally, (2) CI validation on PR, (3) Deploy as Audit mode (log only, no rejections), (4) Monitor violations for 1-2 weeks, (5) Promote to Enforce mode (reject violations).

Q6. You need to enforce that every Deployment in namespace "anihpj-prod" has replicas >= 2 for high availability. Which policy engine would you use and why?

A: Kyverno Validate or VAP (CEL). This is a simple field validation (object.spec.replicas >= 2). VAP if you want no webhook overhead — the CEL expression is straightforward. Kyverno if you want YAML-based policies without a new language. OPA/Gatekeeper would be overkill for this simple check.

Q7. What's the difference between Kyverno's validationFailureAction: Audit and validationFailureAction: Enforce? When would you use each?

A: Audit = log violations but ALLOW the request. Used during policy rollout to discover blast radius without breaking anything. Enforce = REJECT violating requests. Used after Audit confirms the policy is correct and false positives are resolved. Rule: Always deploy new policies as Audit first, monitor for 1-2 weeks, then promote to Enforce.

Q8. A developer complains "I deployed my app but got 'admission webhook denied the request: Every pod must have a team label.'" What happened and how should the platform team have prevented this confusion?

A: The Kyverno Validate policy enforced the team label requirement, and the developer's pod didn't have the team label. The platform team should have: (1) Used a Kyverno Mutate policy to auto-add the team label (so developers don't need to remember), OR (2) Provided clear documentation about required labels in the developer portal, OR (3) Used a more descriptive message field: "Pod 'my-app' is missing the 'team' label. Add 'team: your-team-name' to pod metadata.labels. See: https://wiki.anihpj.com/labels."

Q9. Your cluster has both Kyverno (Mutate: add resource defaults) and OPA (Validate: require resource limits). In what order do they execute, and does the Kyverno mutation satisfy the OPA validation?

A: YES — the Kyverno mutation satisfies the OPA validation. Execution order: Kyverno Mutate runs FIRST (adds default CPU/memory limits), then OPA Validate runs SECOND (checks if limits exist). By the time OPA checks, the limits are already present because Kyverno added them. This is the "platform defaults" pattern: Mutate adds what's missing, Validate confirms it's present. The developer doesn't need to specify limits — the platform handles it.

Q10. You're designing the governance strategy for a new platform. You have 3 namespaces: dev (experimental), staging (pre-prod), and production (customer-facing). How would you apply policies differently to each?

A: Dev: Audit mode only. Log violations but never block. Developers need freedom to experiment. Staging: Enforce P0 policies (block :latest, require labels, enforce limits). Give clear error messages. This is where developers learn the rules before production. Production: Full governance. PSA Restricted + VAP + Kyverno Enforce + OPA cross-resource checks. Block :latest, require labels, enforce limits, block privileged, require non-root, verify image signatures. Graduated enforcement: Policies get stricter as you move toward production. Dev is a sandbox. Production is a fortress.

📝 Ch 29 Chapter Summary
🧠 OPA/Gatekeeper

Rego language. ConstraintTemplate = logic (WHAT). Constraint = params (WHERE). Violations defined with violation[{...}] rules. Used beyond K8s (Terraform, Envoy, API gateways). Complex cross-resource lookups with k8s_introspection.

📋 Kyverno

YAML-based. Three actions: Validate (deny), Mutate (add defaults), Generate (auto-create resources). Most commonly tested on CNPE exam. validationFailureAction: Audit for safe rollout. CNPE domain 5: HIGH probability.

⚡ VAP (CEL)

Built-in K8s 1.26+ (GA 1.30). CEL expressions evaluated inside API server — no webhook. Validate only (no mutate/generate). Type-safe (compile-time checking). Best for simple field validations that don't need external data.

🔒 Common Policies

5 must-have policies: (1) Block :latest, (2) Require labels, (3) Enforce resource limits, (4) Block privileged containers, (5) Require non-root user. Enforce first 3 immediately (P0). Add 4-5 within the first month (P1).

🔄 Policy-as-Code CI/CD

kyverno test + conftest test + gator verify in CI pipeline. Audit-Enforce Ladder: local test → CI → deploy as Audit → monitor → promote to Enforce. Policies are GitOps-managed (ArgoCD/Flux synced to cluster).

🏛️ anihpj Stack

PSA (restricted) → Kyverno Mutate (labels + limits) → VAP (block :latest) → Kyverno Validate (team label) → OPA (cross-resource). Policies in anihpj-infra/policies/, tested in CI, deployed via ArgoCD. Layered defense.

Ch 30: Supply Chain Security & Compliance

Know what's in your images, sign them, scan them, and monitor runtime. SBOM generation with syft. Image signing with Cosign/Sigstore. SLSA framework for build integrity. Vulnerability scanning with Trivy/Grype. Runtime detection with Falco. Compliance is automated, not manual.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2h CNPE Domain 5: 15%
🎯 What You'll Learn
  • Generate SBOMs with syft in SPDX and CycloneDX formats
  • Sign container images with Cosign and verify signatures with Sigstore
  • Assess software supply chain maturity using the SLSA framework (L0-L4)
  • Scan images for vulnerabilities with Trivy and Grype in CI/CD
  • Detect runtime threats with Falco and write custom detection rules
  • Manage secrets securely with Vault and External Secrets Operator
  • Assess cluster compliance with kube-bench (CIS benchmarks)
  • Build a complete supply chain security pipeline for anihpj
📋 CNPE Exam Relevance — Domain 5 (15%)

Domain 5 tests your ability to secure the software supply chain. Expect practical tasks: generate an SBOM, sign an image with Cosign, scan with Trivy, write a Falco rule, and assess a cluster with kube-bench. Supply chain security is a CNPE differentiator — CKA barely touches it.

30.1 SBOM — Software Bill of Materials

A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) is a machine-readable inventory of EVERY component in your container image — base image, apt packages, pip packages, Go modules, everything. It answers: "What's inside this image?" Two formats dominate: SPDX (Linux Foundation) and CycloneDX (OWASP).

syft

CLI tool by Anchore. Generates SBOM from container images, directories, or filesystems. Supports SPDX, CycloneDX, Syft-json. CNPE exam tool.

SPDX

Software Package Data Exchange. ISO 5962 standard. Linux Foundation project. Tags: name, version, supplier, license, relationship.

CycloneDX

OWASP standard. XML/JSON/Protocol Buffers. Designed for BOM interchange. Richer vulnerability extension (VEX). Widely used in security tools.

📋 syft — Generate SBOM for anihpj Image
# ── Install syft ──
# curl -sSfL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/anchore/syft/main/install.sh | sh -s -- -b /usr/local/bin

# ── Generate SBOM for a container image ──
syft anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3 -o spdx-json > anihpj-sbom.spdx.json
# Output: JSON file listing all packages, versions, and licenses

# ── Generate CycloneDX format ──
syft anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3 -o cyclonedx-json > anihpj-sbom.cdx.json

# ── Generate SBOM for current directory (source code) ──
syft dir:. -o spdx-json > anihpj-source-sbom.json

# ── What syft finds ──
# ✔ Indexed anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3  [999 packages]
#   • 3 APK (Alpine) packages: musl, busybox, ssl_client
#   • 2 Python packages: django==4.2, psycopg2-binary==2.9.9
#   • 245 Go modules (transitive deps of gosu)

# ── Parse SBOM with grype (vulnerability matching) ──
grype sbom:anihpj-sbom.spdx.json
# Matches SBOM packages against known CVE databases

# ── CI/CD: Generate SBOM and attach to image ──
syft anihpj/jobboard:${TAG} -o spdx-json | \
  cosign attest --type spdxjson --predicate - ${IMAGE_REF} \
  -o cosign-attestation.json
⚡ SBOM Quick Reference
  • syft <image> -o spdx-json = Generate SPDX SBOM. Most commonly needed on CNPE.
  • syft <image> -o cyclonedx-json = Generate CycloneDX SBOM. Preferred by security scanners.
  • grype sbom:<file> = Scan an SBOM for vulnerabilities (offline, no image pull needed).
  • SBOM ≠ Vulnerability scan — SBOM is the INVENTORY. Trivy/Grype use the inventory to find CVEs.
  • SPDX = License-focused. CycloneDX = Security-focused. Know both for the exam.

30.2 Cosign/Sigstore — Image Signing & Verification

Cosign signs container images using keyless signing (OIDC-based, no long-lived keys to manage). It's part of the Sigstore project. Signed images prove: (1) WHO built the image, (2) that the image hasn't been tampered with since signing.

🔏 Cosign Keyless Signing Flow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    COSIGN KEYLESS SIGNING (SIGSTORE)                            │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌──────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌────────────────┐  │
│  │  CI/CD    │───▶│  OIDC         │───▶│  Fulcio       │───▶│  Rekor          │  │
│  │  Pipeline │    │  (GitHub/     │    │  (CA)          │    │  (Transparency  │  │
│  │  signs    │    │   GitLab)      │    │  Issues short- │    │   Log)           │  │
│  │  image    │    │  Identity      │    │  lived cert    │    │  Immutable       │  │
│  │  with     │    │  token         │    │                │    │  record of       │  │
│  │  Cosign   │    │                │    │                │    │  signature       │  │
│  └──────────┘    └──────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └────────────────┘  │
│       │                                                                       │
│       │  1. Developer pushes code → CI runs                                   │
│       │  2. CI obtains OIDC token (proves identity: repo, workflow, ref)      │
│       │  3. Cosign exchanges OIDC token for short-lived X.509 cert (Fulcio)   │
│       │  4. Cosign signs image with ephemeral key                             │
│       │  5. Signature + cert recorded in Rekor transparency log               │
│       │                                                                       │
│       ▼                                                                       │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│
│  │  VERIFICATION: cosign verify anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3                      ││
│  │  • Checks Rekor log → signature exists                                    ││
│  │  • Validates certificate chain → trusted OIDC issuer                      ││
│  │  • Confirms identity → repo:anihpj/anihpj workflow:release                ││
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 Cosign — Sign and Verify Images
# ── KEYLESS SIGN (recommended — no key management) ──
cosign sign anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3
# Cosign opens browser → OIDC flow → ephemeral key → signature in Rekor

# ── SIGN WITH A KEY (traditional) ──
cosign generate-key-pair                # Creates cosign.key + cosign.pub
cosign sign --key cosign.key anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3

# ── VERIFY signature ──
cosign verify --key cosign.pub anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3
# Output:
# Verification for anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3 --
# The following checks were performed on each of these signatures:
#   - The cosign claims were validated
#   - The signatures were verified against the specified public key

# ── VERIFY keyless (check identity) ──
cosign verify \
  --certificate-identity "anihpj/anihpj/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3

# ── SIGN + ATTEST (attach SBOM) ──
cosign attest --type spdxjson \
  --predicate anihpj-sbom.spdx.json \
  anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3

# ── VERIFY attestation ──
cosign verify-attestation --type spdxjson \
  --certificate-identity "anihpj/anihpj/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main" \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
  anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3
⚠️ Keyless vs Key-Based — Which Should YOU Use?

Keyless (OIDC): Recommended for CI/CD. No long-lived key to rotate, steal, or lose. But requires trust in OIDC provider. Key-Based: Useful for air-gapped environments or when OIDC is unavailable. But you MUST manage key rotation, secure storage, and revocation. CNPE exam tip: Know both, expect keyless to be the preferred approach.

30.3 SLSA Framework — Supply Chain Levels for Software Artifacts (L0-L4)

SLSA (pronounced "salsa") is a security framework that defines increasing levels of supply chain integrity. It answers: "How trustworthy is this build?" — not just the image, but the entire build process that produced it.

LevelNameRequirementsProtects AgainstReal-World Status
L0NoneNo guarantees. Build could be from anywhere.NothingMost projects without CI/CD
L1ProvenanceBuild is fully scripted. Provenance generated (HOW it was built).Mistakes (wrong source built)Easy with GitHub Actions
L2Hosted BuildBuild runs on hosted CI/CD (not dev laptop). Provenance is signed.Tampering after buildStandard CI/CD + Cosign
L3Hardened BuildIsolated build environment. Build cannot be influenced by attacker. Reproducible builds.Compromised build platformRequires hermetic builds
L4HermeticAll dependencies declared, no network access, signed & reviewed. Two-person review.Advanced persistent threatsAir-gapped builds + epoxied deps
📊 SLSA Level Progression — Most Teams Are at L1-L2
SLSA Compliance Progression (per anihpj maturity):
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
L0  ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  "docker build && docker push" from laptop
    │  → Add CI/CD pipeline
    ▼
L1  ██████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  Build fully scripted in GitHub Actions
    │  → Sign provenance with Cosign
    ▼
L2  ████████████████████░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░  Provenance signed. Build on GitHub-hosted runner.
    │  → Isolate build, make it reproducible
    ▼
L3  ██████████████████████████████░░░░░░  Isolated build. No secrets leaked. Two-reviewer policy.
    │  → Hermetic builds, no network
    ▼
L4  ████████████████████████████████████  Fully hermetic. Epoxied deps. Ephemeral isolation.

🎯 CNPE GOAL: Achieve SLSA L2 for all anihpj production images.
🎯 STRETCH GOAL: Achieve SLSA L3 for anihpj authentication and payment microservices.
🎯 SLSA L2 Checklist (Minimum for CNPE Production)
  • ✅ All builds run in CI/CD (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, etc.) — no local builds.
  • ✅ Build provenance is generated and signed (Cosign attest).
  • ✅ Source code is version-controlled and tagged (Git tags map to image tags).
  • ✅ Build scripts are in the repo (Dockerfile, Makefile, CI config).
  • ✅ Build runs on a hosted platform (not self-managed with admin access by devs).

30.4 Trivy/Grype — Vulnerability Scanning

Trivy (Aqua Security) and Grype (Anchore) scan container images for known vulnerabilities (CVEs). They compare your image's package inventory against public vulnerability databases. Both can scan images, filesystems, git repos, and Kubernetes clusters.

FeatureTrivyGrype
MakerAqua SecurityAnchore (same as syft)
ScansImages, filesystem, git repos, K8s clusters, IaC (misconfigs), secretsImages, SBOMs, directories. Focused on vulnerability matching.
DatabasesMultiple: NVD, Red Hat, Debian, Alpine, etc.Multiple: NVD, GitHub Advisory, etc.
SBOMCan generate AND scan SBOMs (CycloneDX, SPDX)Scans SBOMs (generated by syft — same vendor)
K8s scanning✅ trivy k8s cluster — scans running cluster❌ No built-in K8s cluster scanning
Output formatsTable, JSON, SARIF, HTML, GitHub SecurityTable, JSON, CycloneDX
CNPE exam✅ HIGH probability — more features🟡 Know the concept (syft + grype combo)
📋 Trivy & Grype — Vulnerability Scanning in CI/CD
# ── TRIVY: Scan an image ──
trivy image anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3
# Output: TABLE with CVE-ID, Severity, Installed Version, Fixed Version

# ── TRIVY: Scan with severity filter + exit on critical ──
trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --exit-code 1 anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3
# CI/CD: If any CRITICAL or HIGH CVE found → pipeline fails (exit code 1)

# ── TRIVY: Scan Kubernetes cluster ──
trivy k8s cluster --report summary
# Scans ALL images running in the cluster + misconfigurations

# ── TRIVY: Scan IaC (misconfigurations) ──
trivy config ./kubernetes/
# Scans Kubernetes manifests for security misconfigurations

# ── GRYPE: Scan an image ──
grype anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3
# grype -f json anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3 -o results.json

# ── GRYPE: Scan an SBOM (offline) ──
# First generate SBOM, then scan it — no image pull needed
syft anihpj/jobboard:v1.2.3 -o spdx-json > sbom.json
grype sbom:sbom.json

# ── GITHUB ACTIONS INTEGRATION ──
- name: Trivy Vulnerability Scan
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: anihpj/jobboard:${{ github.sha }}
    format: sarif
    output: trivy-results.sarif
    severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
    exit-code: '1'                     # Fail if critical/high CVEs found

# ── TRIVY IGNORE: Exclude known false positives ──
# .trivyignore.yaml
vulnerabilities:
  - id: CVE-2023-XXXX
    statement: "False positive — not exploitable in our configuration"
    expiry: 2025-12-31             # Review after this date
🎓 CNPE Exam: Trivy = Most Likely Scanner

Trivy is the most commonly tested vulnerability scanner because: (1) It scans images, K8s clusters, AND IaC — one tool for many exam tasks. (2) The --exit-code 1 flag is the standard CI/CD integration pattern. (3) trivy k8s cluster tests your understanding of runtime scanning. Expect at least 1 Trivy task (scan + CI integration).

30.5 Falco — Runtime Threat Detection

Falco is a runtime security tool that monitors system calls (syscalls) and Kubernetes audit events to detect anomalous behavior. While Trivy scans BEFORE deployment (shift left), Falco monitors DURING runtime (shift right). Together they form the complete security picture.

🔍 Falco Runtime Detection Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         FALCO RUNTIME DETECTION                                 │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐     ┌─────────────────┐         │
│  │  Kernel Module   │     │  eBPF Probe      │     │  K8s Audit       │         │
│  │  (syscalls)      │     │  (syscalls)      │     │  Events          │         │
│  └────────┬────────┘     └────────┬────────┘     └────────┬────────┘         │
│           │                       │                       │                   │
│           └───────────────────────┼───────────────────────┘                   │
│                                   │                                           │
│                                   ▼                                           │
│                    ┌─────────────────────────────┐                            │
│                    │         Falco Engine          │                            │
│                    │  • Evaluates rules            │                            │
│                    │  • Matches patterns           │                            │
│                    │  • Generates alerts           │                            │
│                    └─────────────┬───────────────┘                            │
│                                  │                                            │
│                    ┌─────────────┼───────────────┐                            │
│                    ▼             ▼               ▼                            │
│              ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────────┐                      │
│              │  stdout   │ │  Webhook  │ │  Sidekick     │                      │
│              │  (log)    │ │  (custom) │ │  → Slack/Pager│                      │
│              └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────────┘                      │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  FALCO DETECTS (Partial list):                                            │ │
│  │  • Shell spawned in container    • Unexpected process started             │ │
│  │  • File written below /etc       • Sensitive file read (shadow, certs)    │ │
│  │  • Privileged container launched • Network connection to suspicious IP    │ │
│  │  • Kubernetes Secret accessed     • kubectl exec detected                 │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
📋 Falco — Custom Detection Rules
# ── FALCO RULE: Detect shell inside anihpj container ──
- rule: Shell in anihpj container
  desc: A shell was spawned inside an anihpj container (may indicate breach)
  condition: >
    spawned_process
    and container.name startswith "anihpj"
    and proc.name in (bash, sh, ash, zsh)
    and not proc.args startswith "/usr/local/bin/anihpj-healthcheck"
  output: >
    Shell spawned in anihpj container (user=%user.name
    container=%container.name cmdline=%proc.cmdline)
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [anihpj, shell, runtime]

# ── FALCO RULE: Unexpected outbound network from DB container ──
- rule: Unexpected outbound from DB
  desc: Database container making outbound connection (data exfiltration?)
  condition: >
    outbound
    and container.name startswith "anihpj-db"
    and fd.sport != 5432                  # NOT the PostgreSQL port
    and not fd.snet in (10.0.0.0/8)       # NOT internal traffic
  output: >
    DB container connected to external IP (container=%container.name
    connection=%fd.name ip=%fd.cip)
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [anihpj, network, exfiltration]

# ── FALCO RULE: Privileged container launched (always alert) ──
- rule: Privileged container launched
  desc: A container with privileged mode was started
  condition: >
    evt.type = container
    and container.privileged = true
  output: >
    PRIVILEGED CONTAINER DETECTED (image=%container.image
    name=%container.name)
  priority: CRITICAL
  tags: [container, privileged, compliance]
⚠️ Falco Rules: condition vs output vs priority
  • condition: The FILTER expression. If this evaluates to TRUE, the rule fires. Uses Falco's macro language (spawned_process, container.name, proc.name, etc.).
  • output: The MESSAGE logged/alerted when the rule fires. Include variables like %user.name, %container.name.
  • priority: DEBUG < INFORMATIONAL < NOTICE < WARNING < ERROR < CRITICAL < EMERGENCY. Determines alert severity.
  • Macros: Reusable named conditions. e.g., - macro: anihpj_container\n condition: container.name startswith "anihpj"
  • Lists: Named lists of values. e.g., - list: shell_binaries\n items: [bash, sh, ash, zsh]

30.6 Vault / External Secrets — Secure Secret Management

Kubernetes Secrets are base64-encoded (NOT encrypted) and stored in etcd. HashiCorp Vault and External Secrets Operator (ESO) solve the "secret zero" problem — where do you securely store secrets so they're encrypted at rest, audited, rotated, and dynamically generated?

FeatureKubernetes SecretsVault (CSI/Injector)External Secrets Operator
Encryption at rest🟡 If etcd encryption enabled✅ Yes (Vault encrypts)✅ Yes (provider encrypts)
Dynamic secrets❌ Static only✅ DB creds, PKI, cloud IAM — auto-rotated❌ Syncs from external stores
Audit❌ Only K8s audit logs✅ Full audit trail per secret access⚠️ Provider-dependent
Rotation❌ Manual✅ Automated rotation + notification✅ RefreshInterval auto-sync
ProvidersN/AVault onlyAWS SM, GCP SM, Azure KV, Vault, 1Password, etc.
Complexity🟢 Zero🔴 High — Run Vault cluster🟡 Medium — Operator + provider config
📋 External Secrets Operator — Sync AWS Secrets Manager → K8s Secret
# ── STEP 1: SecretStore (tells ESO WHERE to fetch secrets from) ──
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: SecretStore
metadata:
  name: aws-secrets-manager
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: us-east-1
      auth:
        jwt:                          # IRSA (IAM Role for Service Account)
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: eso-sa

# ── STEP 2: ExternalSecret (tells ESO WHAT to fetch) ──
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: anihpj-db-credentials
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h               # Auto-refresh every hour
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secrets-manager
    kind: SecretStore
  target:
    name: anihpj-db-credentials      # K8s Secret name to create
  data:
  - secretKey: DB_PASSWORD            # Key IN the K8s Secret
    remoteRef:
      key: anihpj/prod/db              # Key IN AWS Secrets Manager
      property: password
  - secretKey: DB_HOST
    remoteRef:
      key: anihpj/prod/db
      property: host
⚡ External Secrets Quick Reference
  • SecretStore = WHERE to fetch from (cluster-scoped or namespace-scoped).
  • ExternalSecret = WHAT to fetch and WHICH K8s Secret to create.
  • refreshInterval = How often to re-sync from the provider (e.g., 1h).
  • Supported providers: AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault, 1Password, and more.

30.7 kube-bench — CIS Benchmark Assessment

kube-bench (Aqua Security) checks whether your Kubernetes cluster is configured according to the CIS (Center for Internet Security) Kubernetes Benchmark. It's a compliance scanner — it doesn't fix anything, it TELLS you what's misconfigured.

📋 kube-bench — CIS Benchmark Assessment
# ── RUN kube-bench against the cluster ──
kube-bench run --targets master,node,controlplane,etcd,policies
# Scans the node where kube-bench runs. Use kubectl/kube-bench job for full cluster.

# ── RUN as a Kubernetes Job (scans all nodes) ──
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/aquasecurity/kube-bench/main/job.yaml
# Deploys a DaemonSet-like Job to scan each node

# ── SPECIFIC CHECK: Check only master node configuration ──
kube-bench run --targets master
# Sample output:
# [FAIL] 1.1.1 Ensure that the API server pod specification file permissions
#         are set to 644 or more restrictive (Automated)
# [PASS] 1.1.2 Ensure that the API server pod specification file ownership
#         is set to root:root (Automated)
# [WARN] 1.2.1 Ensure that the --anonymous-auth argument is set to false

# ── OUTPUT FORMATS ──
kube-bench run --targets master -o json > kube-bench-results.json
kube-bench run --targets master -o junit > kube-bench-results.xml

# ── CIS BENCHMARK SECTIONS CHECKED ──
# Section 1: Control Plane Components (API server, scheduler, controller, etcd)
# Section 2: etcd
# Section 3: Control Plane Configuration
# Section 4: Worker Node Configuration
# Section 5: Policies (RBAC, PSP, NetworkPolicy, etc.)
🎓 CNPE Exam: kube-bench = CIS Compliance

The exam may ask you to run kube-bench and interpret results. Key facts: (1) CIS benchmark sections 1-5 map to cluster components. (2) --targets flag controls which component to scan. (3) Results are PASS/FAIL/WARN. WARN means "needs manual review". (4) kube-bench is READ-ONLY — it never modifies your cluster.

Compliance is not a one-time checklist — it's continuous. The CNPE platform automates compliance with scheduled scans, policy enforcement, and evidence collection. If you can't prove compliance automatically, you're not compliant.

🎯 Compliance Automation Checklist for CNPE
  • ✅ Scheduled CIS scans: kube-bench runs weekly as a CronJob. Reports stored in S3/GCS.
  • ✅ Policy-as-code: Kyverno policies are version-controlled and CI-tested. Every violation is logged.
  • ✅ Continuous vulnerability scanning: Trivy scans every image push. No image deployed with CRITICAL CVEs.
  • ✅ Runtime monitoring: Falco monitors 24/7 for anomalous behavior. Alerts go to Slack/PagerDuty.
  • ✅ Evidence collection: All scan results, policy violations, and alerts are archived to S3 (immutable, time-stamped).
  • ✅ Dashboard: Single Grafana dashboard shows CIS score, policy compliance %, vulnerability count, and Falco alerts.

30.9 SBOM in CI/CD Pipeline — End-to-End Automation

The SBOM isn't just a compliance checkbox — it's a pipeline artifact that enables automated vulnerability matching, license compliance, and supply chain attestation. Here's the complete CI/CD integration:

1
Build image with Docker/buildah
→
IMAGE
2
syft generates SBOM (SPDX + CycloneDX)
→
SBOM
3
grype scans SBOM for CVEs
→
CVE REPORT
4
Trivy scans image for misconfigs + CVEs
→
SCAN REPORT
5
Block if CRITICAL CVEs found (exit code 1)
→
FAIL → STOP
6
Cosign signs image + attests SBOM
→
SIGNED
7
Push image to registry + SBOM to OCI
→
PUBLISHED
📋 GitHub Actions — Complete Supply Chain Pipeline
# .github/workflows/supply-chain.yml
name: Supply Chain Security
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ['v*']
jobs:
  sbom-sign-scan:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Build Image
        run: docker build -t anihpj/jobboard:${{ github.sha }} .

      - name: Generate SBOM (syft)
        run: |
          syft anihpj/jobboard:${{ github.sha }} \
            -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json
          syft anihpj/jobboard:${{ github.sha }} \
            -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.cdx.json

      - name: Scan SBOM for CVEs (grype)
        run: |
          grype sbom:sbom.spdx.json \
            --fail-on critical \
            --file grype-report.json

      - name: Scan Image (Trivy)
        uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: anihpj/jobboard:${{ github.sha }}
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          exit-code: '1'

      - name: Sign Image (Cosign)
        run: |
          cosign sign \
            --certificate-identity "${{ github.repository }}/.github/workflows/supply-chain.yml@${{ github.ref }}" \
            --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com" \
            anihpj/jobboard:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Attach SBOM (Cosign attest)
        run: |
          cosign attest --type spdxjson \
            --predicate sbom.spdx.json \
            anihpj/jobboard:${{ github.sha }}

      - name: Push Image
        run: docker push anihpj/jobboard:${{ github.sha }}

30.10 Image Attestation & Verification — Trust Before Deploy

Attestation is a signed statement about an image. Beyond just signing the image digest, you can attest: "This image was built from commit X, passed test suite Y, has SBOM Z." Verification at deploy time ensures only trusted images run in production.

📋 Kyverno — Verify Image Signatures at Admission
# ── Kyverno ClusterPolicy: Verify Cosign signature ──
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: verify-image-signature
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: check-image-signature
    match:
      any:
      - resources:
          kinds: ["Pod"]
    verifyImages:
    - imageReferences: ["anihpj/jobboard:*"]
      attestors:
      - count: 1
        entries:
        - keyless:
            subject: "anihpj/anihpj/.github/workflows/supply-chain.yml@*"
            issuer: "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
            rekor:
              url: https://rekor.sigstore.dev
⚠️ Kyverno verifyImages = Gate Before Deploy

Kyverno's verifyImages rule runs at admission time — when a Pod is CREATED. If the image signature is missing or invalid, the Pod is rejected. This means: (1) Even if an attacker bypasses CI/CD and pushes a malicious image to the registry, Kyverno will block it at deploy time. (2) The signature check is the LAST line of defense before the image runs.

30.11 anihpj Supply Chain Security — Complete Implementation

Here's how the anihpj Django job board platform implements end-to-end supply chain security:

🏢 anihpj Supply Chain Security — Full Stack
📦
SBOM Generation
syft generates SPDX + CycloneDX SBOM for every build. SBOMs are attached to images via Cosign attest and archived to S3 for audit.
🔏
Image Signing
Cosign keyless signing via GitHub OIDC. Every image pushed to ECR is signed. Kyverno verifyImages rule enforces signature check at admission.
📊
SLSA L2
All anihpj production images meet SLSA L2: scripted builds, signed provenance, hosted CI/CD. Target: SLSA L3 for auth and payment microservices.
🔍
Vulnerability Scanning
Trivy scans every image push. CI/CD blocks on CRITICAL. Grype scans SBOMs for CVEs. Weekly cluster-wide scan with trivy k8s cluster.
🛡️
Runtime Detection
Falco monitors anihpj-prod for: shell in containers, unexpected processes, privilege escalation, sensitive file access. Alerts sent to PagerDuty.
🔐
Secret Management
External Secrets Operator syncs DB credentials from AWS Secrets Manager to K8s Secrets. Auto-rotated every 30 days. No secrets in Git.
📋
CIS Compliance
kube-bench runs weekly as CronJob. Results exported to Grafana dashboard. Policy violations from Kyverno tracked separately. CIS score > 85%.
📜
Audit Trail
All evidence (SBOMs, scan results, signatures, Falco alerts) archived to S3. Immutable, time-stamped, queryable. Audit-ready in < 5 minutes.
💪 Practice Drill — anihpj Supply Chain Security
  1. Generate SBOM: Run syft anihpj/jobboard:latest -o spdx-json > sbom.json. Count the packages.
  2. Sign image: Use cosign sign anihpj/jobboard:latest (keyless). Verify with cosign verify.
  3. Scan for CVEs: Run trivy image --severity CRITICAL anihpj/jobboard:latest. Note any findings.
  4. Run kube-bench: Deploy kube-bench Job. Check the CIS score. Identify top 3 failures.
  5. Write Falco rule: Create a rule that detects kubectl exec into any anihpj container.
  6. ESO setup: Create a SecretStore and ExternalSecret to sync a test secret from AWS Secrets Manager.
🧠 Knowledge Check — Ch 30: Supply Chain Security

Q1. What's the difference between an SBOM and a vulnerability scan?

A: An SBOM is an INVENTORY of all packages in an image (what's inside). A vulnerability scan (Trivy/Grype) matches SBOM packages against known CVE databases to find security issues. You need an SBOM before you can do a proper vulnerability scan.

Q2. How does Cosign keyless signing work without long-lived keys?

A: Cosign uses OIDC (OpenID Connect) to prove the identity of the signer (e.g., "this is GitHub Actions workflow X from repo Y"). Fulcio (Sigstore CA) issues a short-lived X.509 certificate based on the OIDC token. Cosign signs with an ephemeral key, and the signature + certificate are recorded in Rekor (transparency log). No long-lived key exists to steal or rotate.

Q3. What does SLSA L2 require that SLSA L1 does not?

A: SLSA L2 requires that builds run on a hosted CI/CD platform (not a developer's laptop) AND that the provenance is signed. SLSA L1 only requires that the build is fully scripted and provenance is generated (unsigned).

Q4. What's the purpose of External Secrets Operator's SecretStore vs ExternalSecret?

A: SecretStore defines WHERE to fetch secrets from (provider, auth, region). It's the connection configuration. ExternalSecret defines WHAT to fetch (which remote secret, which K8s Secret to create, refresh interval). You create one SecretStore per provider, and many ExternalSecrets referencing it.

Q5. Trivy can scan images, filesystems, git repos, K8s clusters, and IaC. What command scans an entire running Kubernetes cluster?

A: trivy k8s cluster --report summary. This scans ALL images currently running in the cluster, plus misconfigurations in Kubernetes resources. It's a comprehensive "what's running and is it safe?" check.

📝 Ch 30 Chapter Summary
📦 SBOM (syft)

Inventory of all packages in an image. SPDX (license-focused) and CycloneDX (security-focused). syft image -o spdx-json. Attach with Cosign attest.

🔏 Cosign/Sigstore

Keyless signing via OIDC. Ephemeral keys. Fulcio (CA) + Rekor (transparency log). cosign sign + cosign verify. Kyverno verifyImages enforces at admission.

📊 SLSA (L0-L4)

Build integrity framework. L1: scripted build + provenance. L2: hosted CI + signed provenance. L3: isolated builds. L4: hermetic. Target L2 for production.

🔍 Trivy/Grype

Vulnerability scanners. Trivy: images + K8s clusters + IaC + secrets. Grype: images + SBOMs. CI/CD: --exit-code 1 --severity CRITICAL. Block on critical.

🛡️ Falco

Runtime threat detection via syscall + K8s audit monitoring. Custom rules with conditions, macros, lists. Detects shells, unexpected processes, privilege escalation.

🔐 Vault/ESO

K8s Secrets are base64 (not encrypted). Vault: dynamic secrets + auto-rotation. ESO: syncs from AWS/GCP/Azure/Vault to K8s Secrets. refreshInterval for auto-sync.

📋 kube-bench

CIS Kubernetes Benchmark scanner. --targets master,node,etcd,policies. Results: PASS/FAIL/WARN. Weekly CronJob. Grafana dashboard for CIS score tracking.

🏢 anihpj Stack

syft → SBOM → Cosign sign → Trivy scan → Kyverno verifyImages → ESO for secrets → Falco for runtime → kube-bench weekly. Audit trail in S3. SLSA L2.

🔴 Part 8: Production Platform Operations BEYOND CNPE

Ch 31: High Availability & Disaster Recovery

Production platforms must survive failures. HA control planes with stacked or external etcd. etcd quorum (N/2+1) for fault tolerance. Multi-zone deployments for zone-level failures. Velero to backup K8s resources and PVs. etcd snapshot automation. GitOps DR for full recovery from code.

🔴 Advanced ⏱️ ~2h CNPE Domain 6: 10%
🎯 What You'll Learn
  • Design a multi-master control plane with HA topology
  • Choose between stacked and external etcd architectures
  • Understand etcd quorum (N/2+1) and fault tolerance math
  • Configure load balancers for API server high availability
  • Deploy across multiple availability zones for zone-level resilience
  • Backup and restore with Velero (K8s objects + PV snapshots)
  • Automate etcd snapshots and verify restore procedures
  • Implement GitOps DR — redeploy everything from Git after complete failure
📋 CNPE Exam Relevance — Domain 6 (10%)

Domain 6 tests your ability to design and implement platform resilience. Expect scenario-based questions: "A zone fails. How does your platform survive?" "How many etcd nodes can fail?" "Walk through a Velero restore." HA/DR is a practical skill — you'll configure these components in the exam.

31.1 Multi-Master Control Plane — HA at the Core

A single control plane node is a single point of failure. Multi-master deployments run 3 or 5 control plane nodes, each with: API server (stateless, load-balanced), controller manager + scheduler (leader-elected, only one active at a time), and etcd (replicated via Raft consensus).

🏗️ Multi-Master HA Architecture (3 Control Plane Nodes)

⚡ Multi-Master Quick Reference
  • API Server: Stateless. ALL instances are active. Load-balanced by external LB.
  • Controller Manager & Scheduler: Leader-elected. Only ONE active at a time. --leader-elect=true.
  • etcd: Raft consensus. Odd number of nodes (3, 5, 7). Leader handles all writes.
  • Minimum HA: 3 control plane nodes. Survives 1 node failure.
  • Production HA: 3 nodes across 3 zones. Survives 1 zone failure.

31.2 Stacked vs External etcd — Two HA Topologies

etcd can be deployed in two modes: stacked (etcd runs on the same nodes as the control plane) or external (etcd runs on dedicated nodes). Each has tradeoffs in complexity, performance, and failure domains.

FeatureStacked etcdExternal etcd
Architectureetcd on same nodes as API serveretcd on dedicated nodes
Node count3 nodes for both CP + etcd3 CP nodes + 3 etcd nodes = 6 nodes minimum
Cost🟢 Lower. Fewer nodes.🔴 Higher. More nodes and infrastructure.
Complexity🟢 Simpler. kubeadm handles setup.🔴 More complex. Separate etcd cluster to manage.
Failure isolation🟡 CP failure = etcd failure on that node✅ CP failure does NOT affect etcd
Performance🟡 Shared disk/CPU with API server✅ Dedicated resources. Better under load.
Backup/Restore🟢 Simpler. etcdctl on CP node.🟡 Separate access to etcd nodes needed.
kubeadm default✅ Default topologyRequires --config with external etcd endpoints
When to useMost clusters. Start here.Very large clusters (500+ nodes). Strict isolation required.
🎯 CNPE Recommendation: Start With Stacked

For the CNPE exam and most production deployments: use stacked etcd. It's simpler, well-tested, and the default. Only consider external etcd for very large clusters (500+ nodes) or when regulatory requirements demand strict separation of the data store from the control plane. The exam tests stacked etcd — know it well.

31.3 etcd Quorum — The N/2+1 Rule

etcd uses the Raft consensus algorithm. For the cluster to be operational (read + write), a majority (quorum) of etcd members must be healthy and able to communicate. This is the N/2+1 rule (floor division).

Total etcd Nodes (N)Quorum NeededCan Lose (Failures Tolerated)Notes
11 (N/2+1 = 1)0❌ No HA. Never use in production.
32 (N/2+1 = 2)1✅ Minimum production. Survives 1 failure.
53 (N/2+1 = 3)2✅ Good. Survives 2 failures. More write overhead.
74 (N/2+1 = 4)3⚠️ Rarely needed. Writes get slower (Raft requires majority ACK).
🧪 etcd Failure Scenarios — 3-Node Cluster

Scenario A: 1 node fails → 2 remain → quorum = 2 → ✅ Cluster operational (READ + WRITE). Survives.

Scenario B: 2 nodes fail → 1 remains → quorum = 2 → ❌ Cluster loses quorum. READ-ONLY (no writes). New leader cannot be elected.

Scenario C: Network partition → 2 nodes isolated, 1 node isolated → 2-node group has quorum ✅. 1-node group is read-only ❌. Raft ensures split-brain can't happen.

⚠️ etcd Quorum Loss = Cluster Unavailable

When etcd loses quorum, the Kubernetes API server cannot write anything — no new pods, no config changes, no deployments. Existing pods continue running (they're on worker nodes), but the control plane is frozen. You cannot recover from quorum loss by adding new members. You must restore from backup (etcd snapshot).

31.4 Load Balancer for API Server — Single Endpoint, Multiple Backends

With multiple API servers, clients (kubectl, kubelet, controllers) need a single endpoint. A load balancer distributes traffic across all healthy API servers. The LB must be highly available itself — otherwise it becomes the single point of failure.

📋 HAProxy Config — TCP Load Balancer for API Server
# /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg
frontend kubernetes-api
    bind *:6443
    mode tcp
    option tcplog
    default_backend k8s-api-servers

backend k8s-api-servers
    mode tcp
    option tcp-check
    balance roundrobin
    # TCP health check: verify port 6443 is reachable
    default-server inter 10s downinter 5s rise 2 fall 2
    server cp-node-1 10.0.1.11:6443 check
    server cp-node-2 10.0.1.12:6443 check
    server cp-node-3 10.0.1.13:6443 check

# ── kubeadm init with load balancer ──
kubeadm init \
  --control-plane-endpoint "k8s-api.anihpj.internal:6443" \
  --upload-certs
# --control-plane-endpoint = the LB address (DNS or IP)
# --upload-certs = share certificates across CP nodes

# ── Cloud LB (AWS NLB example) ──
# aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --name k8s-api-nlb --type network
# Target group: TCP:6443 → CP nodes. Health check: TCP:6443.
⚡ LB Options for API Server
  • On-prem: HAProxy or keepalived (VRRP-based floating IP).
  • AWS: NLB (Network Load Balancer) — Layer 4, TCP pass-through, preserves client IP.
  • Azure: Standard Load Balancer with TCP probe on 6443.
  • GCP: TCP Load Balancer with health check on 6443.
  • kube-vip: Layer 2 ARP-based virtual IP. No external LB needed. Popular for on-prem k3s/rke2.

31.5 Multi-Zone Deployments — Surviving Zone Failures

A single availability zone (AZ) is a single failure domain. A multi-zone deployment spreads control plane nodes AND worker nodes across 3 zones. If one zone fails, the cluster continues operating with the remaining 2 zones.

🌍 Multi-Zone Deployment — 3 Control Planes × 3 Zones

│                    MULTI-ZONE KUBERNETES DEPLOYMENT                             │
│                                                                               │
│  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐            │
│  │   ZONE A (us-east-1a)│  │   ZONE B (us-east-1b)│  │   ZONE C (us-east-1c)│            │
│  │                    │  │                    │  │                    │            │
│  │  ┌──────────────┐ │  │  ┌──────────────┐ │  │  ┌──────────────┐ │            │

│  │                    │  │                    │  │                    │            │
